title: Wasted Potential
text:
Some things about this book just don't work for me, I'll try to set them out, but even my complaints seem muddled, so be patient with me.

1. Unreliable narrator- Esther's 'voice' vascillates between a hyper, naive ten year old to a world weary, old before her time tween. Which made it hard to form a vision of her. My expectations for her character development were continuously smashed as she made strange decisions and acted foolishly on and off throughout the story.

2. Variants\Mutants - These just did not work either, not as hermaphroditic hobbits, nor as peace loving, earth motherlike, farmers. Whenever the variants entered the story I found my attention wandering; 'should I have another cup of coffee? Is the itchy spot on my foot a wart? I wonder what I did with my chinese jumprope?' There's no credible reason for their inclusion in the story, they might as well have intruduced mutated hedgehogs or giant squid.

3. The worldbuilding - Some of the worldbuilding reminded me, in a distant way, of Enclave by Anne Aquirre, but the similarities ended as I tried to work out how people could survive for several generations in such bizarre circumstances. Without food, 'cept for what they find, without even trying to grow anything.

4. The other characters, Skar, especially seem to exist just to add interesting background for Esther.

All in all, I'd give this book a miss.

title: Such an annoying and idiotic heroine
text:
You end up drugged, taken to a remote villa, your clothing removed, your jewelry and watch taken and wake up to a strange man who tells you that your freedom depends on the actions of your fiance's father, what would you think?

I think there is only one thing to think, that is that your kidnapper bears a grudge for your future father-in-law and that you are the unlucky pawn. Also, and I can't even believe this has to be stated, but here it is, you have been kidnapped.

For some strange reason, Maddie, the heroine of Count Valieri's Prisoner, doesn't get that. She repeatedly asks her captor if she's free to go, when she can leave (after the already stated action on the side of the future in-law) and if he is going to hold her against her will!

I know! Total mind bender! Get it through your silly head, Maddie, you have been KIDNAPPED. Abducted, shanghaied, snatched, held for ransom, etc., etc. But for Maddie, the concept seems to be beyond her ability to comprehend and this is where the story hits its first major snag.

The second most annoying thing about this book is Jeremy, Maddie's fiance. He is the worst kind of wimpy, whipped love interest. He won't even stay the night at her place after they have sex because he's worried what his daddy will think about him. Also, he's a bad lover and has allowed his stepmother to hijack the wedding. He never speaks up for Maddie, thinks her career as a journalist is a lame hobby and in pretty much every way possible is unlikable. I have a hard time understanding or respecting Maddie because she still wants to marry him and then after just a few hours around Andrea (aka Tall, Dark and Kidnapp-y) she's getting hot and bothered over another man, ugh, so flighty.

There's the requisite escape attempt, where Maddie has to be rescued from sexily torn clothing, wolves and trees, then they have to share a bed, he sleeps and she spends the whole night thinking about him. Oddly enough, taking her out of the castle and to the deserted cottage moved the story to a more believable place, but then Maddie started in with her maddeningly inane conversation and my interest faded away again.

All in all, I'd give this one a miss. There are better Craven novels to spend your time and money on.

title: A girl, a guy and a bird.
text:
This review will take the form of prose, in the style of Elizabeth Barrett Browning, but with examples taken from the story itself.

How do I hate thee? Let me count the ways.

I hate thee for thine bizarro, unpunctuated, over-the-top prose that peppers this story from page one on.

'I hate the lackadaisical ennui of a sun too preoccupied with itself to notice the infinite hours we spend in its presence.' P. 26

I hate thee for talking about a bird, every couple of pages, thereby adding a mysterious, crazy-girl ambiance when the reader already knows Juliette is a tinfoil hat away from crazytown.

'There will be a bird today.' P. 9

'There will be a bird.' P. 11

'Maybe a bird will fly today.' P. 28

'Birds used to fly.' P. 36

I've dreamt about the same bird flying through the same sky for exactly 10 years.' P. 36

'I don't know how to find the white bird.' P. 113

'I glance at the window and wonder if I'll ever see a bird fly by.' P. 115

'A white bird with streaks of gold like a crown atop its head. It's flying.' P. 120

'I'm the bird and I'm flying away.' P. 121

'I need to see the bird.' P. 176

I hate thee to the level of shoving this book into a composter, after finishing a particularly silly part about Adam's manly chest and Juliette's need to snuggle.

'My face is pressed against his chest and the world is suddenly bigger, beautiful - -the entire universe stops in place and spins the other direction and I'm the bird.' (Gah, that darned bird again!).

I hate thee with a passion put to use with my trusty highligher pen as the story veered from events and people into waiting and Juliette's 'pulse pounding romance' (back cover of the book) which wasn't very romantic or pulse pounding.

'the sun and the moon have merged and the earth is upside down. I feel like I can be exactly who I want to be in his arms. '

I hate thee with a bitterness that seemed to grow as I had to read almost 51 pages of purple prose before something really happens.

'Warner Stops walking. "I want you on my team."
'We're in the middle of a war,' he says a little impatiently.'

With my lost time, the hours I spent on this book can never be regained, and so, I think, even unto death, I shall hate thee more.

title: Still waiting for the Infinite Bliss
text:
I love vampire stories. I also love angel stories (well, okay, I've loved two of the three angel stories I've read so far) so from the title alone, I thought this book was appealing.

Sadly not.

The book starts out on a seemingly ordinary day for the heroine, Barbey Bardot. Barbey is the most beautiful girl ever. She's also super duper talented; she acts, dances, sings and has a cure for cancer (no, not really). Everyone around her is struck by her beauty and in awe of the aforementioned talents. So when the cutest guy starts to go out with her it isn't a surprise. This was problem one, ethereally lovely popular girl dates dashingly handsome boy, so what?

Now onto the meat of the story; vampires and angels.

This is where the author shows the readers how NOT perfect the life of even the most perfect person can get. Sadly, the story never really takes off. The writing is a big part of the non-starter'ness, plus the lack of a cohesive and believable storyline which goes something like this:

Barbey becomes a snackaroo for a naughty vampire and then meets up with angels. During this all I could think about was the pile of dishes in and around my kitchen sink. When Barbey starts to act a bit bloodthirsty, I noticed that the uncomfortable lump in the couch I was sitting on was Han Solo's head (a lego head that is, don't be weird).

There were odd bits of dialogue that were meant to be humorous (or adorable, I honestly can't tell, I'm so confused by this book) injected into the story at random moments, He ogled her chest, "but you chichis es muy grande, ha!' or this truly eye popping part, "I can't eat a thing,' she said, now suddenly speaking in her sultry Marilyn Monroe voice. She then escalated her act with a childlike giggle that always made every man wild with passion. Really?

There are lots of instances where Barbey talks to herself, giggles or twirls around so that her dress flips up a little. I'm not sure why she does this so often, but the self awareness of this character quickly grated on my nerves.

Sadly, I gave up on this book before the ending. I kinda wanted to see Barbey's transformation from a childlike doll to a real young woman, but I pooped out and decided to clean my kitchen instead.

title: Reads like a student documentary on Oil Scarcity
text:
I hate to be so harsh, really, I do, I don't give one star reviews without a lot of soul searching (and whining to my pals about what a lovely story this could have been), but Empty is a great big disappointment to me.

Following are my three reasons for giving this such a low rating;

One, the characters are vehicles for exposing the problem of oil scarcity (a noble goal) but it is so stolidly done that it is hard to like or care for them. Over and over the reader is subjected to the characters laments over the rising price of lipstick, gasoline, everything under the sun, instead of giving names to the main characters they could have been labeled, 'average jock teen, angry young man, and shy girl with greasy hair.' Dullsville and it makes it hard to differentiate them whenever something happened. The characters spend most of their time wandering around hot, sweaty and worried, but the story never really does much to motivate them to do something.

Two, frequent interruptions by news reports. At first sight, the news reports were a clever choice. The news articles speak of rising unrest, oil scarcity and the game of thrones that is happening as the world fights over the last oil rich reserves. But instead of using the news articles as a nice info dump so that your characters don't have to ghost around saying stuff like, 'I hear there could be a war with______ which could lead to terrible _______' So clumsy and a complete waste of valuable dialogue time. Teens at school, crushing on their schoolmates, hanging out with friends, mostly oblivious to the rising storm would have been more believable than teens discussing politics and world events with each other while walking to class.

Three, Unsatisfying ending. Naturally, I can't tell you what happens at the end, that would be a major spoiler, but by the time I got to the end of the book, I was hoping for a good ending, or at least a fun cliffhanger that would lead into the next book but instead its just the end.

If you are looking for a dystopian or a 'everything goes to hell in a fashionably rustic basket' novel check out Gone, How I live Now, The Carbon Diaries, Matched, The Giver, The Handsmaids Tale or Life as We Knew It. If you absolutely must read this, get it from the library.

title: Not a high recommendation.
text: Don't buy this book. I have no clue who these other people are who are rating it. Anyone with a blank piece of paper who can draw a square will find it insulting to have been suckered into this thing. I'll enclose some photos for you. It has a FEW pages that suggest supplies needed to tangling, one page donated to "introduction to tangling". Most of the book are blank pages with just frames to draw in (like you can't just use your own paper). It's not a child's book either. There are two pages of something called "Fibonacci spiral" a mathematics thing even I, a college grad, don't understand and another page called "the golden ratio" from the authors perspective as a photographer (it's a math thing, I'll take a pic). Nothing is explained well and of 149 pages only 21 have any writing. The adorable little animals are all on the back cover, only one is inside .  I've learned nothing (except I must not remember the math I took because it's really not something I was taught).  I didn't feel this was made to help normal people or published to help, serve or teach . It's my fourth zentangle book . On the upside, the back cover is adorable. I think these authors are artists more than teachers .

title: Apparently I Hate Wolves Because of My Christian European Ancestry
text: I received this book as a gift from my dear daughter and I appreciated it and enjoyed it -- up until page 119.  There, authors Dutcher's release their version of CWT  -- Critical Wolf Theory.  No, they don't use that term but their anti Christian message is crystal clear.  They write, "With the rise of Christianity... it reached a population [Europe] that increasingly envisioned itself as separate from nature.  It couldn't have helped that Christians adopted the motif of God the Shepherd."  No, Mr. and Mrs. Dutcher, Christians didn't "adopt" the motif of God the Shepherd.  The 23rd Psalm, one of the most beloved and moving scriptures, was GIVEN to us by God.  Christ himself said, "I am the good shepherd." (John 10:11)  Shepherding was a common occupation during Biblical times and it was something everyone could understand; and yes, wolves did attack flocks of sheep; and yes, the job of the shepherd was to protect their flock.  It is a symbolism that I, and billions of people, cherish.  Never in my life have I imaged this symbolism as a basis for hatred of wolves.  In fact, I support wolf reintroduction, I have "adopted" a wolf at NWF, and I give regularly to NWF.  Your indiscriminate bashing of Christians is unwarranted, unwelcome, and diminishes your otherwise praiseworthy message.

Across the top of page 4 and 5 a magnificent 28 inch wide photo of gases, stars, and nebulae.  The caption:  "panorama of intricately rippled sand" from a crater in Mars.  then on page 6-7 a gorgeous photo with stars so dense the page is almost white.  Where in the universe is this?  No clue.  There is no caption.  If the rest of the book is like the first seven pages and I if you don't read and you just like to look at the pictures, then this is a nice book. text: As an intermediate watercolor painter, I bought this book for those days that I don’t feel inspired yet want to work on technique and have easy, no-sketch designs to paint. Its like painting on heavier printer paper. Makes for a very frustrating experience I would never recommend a beginner paint in this book. . Buy a watercolor sketch book to do the ‘experiments’ in and trace the finished pieces onto a sheet of watercolor paper but don’t paint in the book.

I came to the reviews to see why this issue was occurring. I do like however as you can be creative and continue painting other things around the animal as if it really was in the jungle. title: OMG, want to confirm your own jealous opinion?
text:
I love my local library, which buys a lot of modern biographies for the gossip-mongers in my town, bless their hearts. So I waited patiently - and then my neighbor, who gobbled it down in 2 days, loaned it to me b4 it was due back. What a load of dung. Seriously, with all the author's supposed 'research' it's just a rehashing of the hateful branch of the British press. No racism, huh? Can't imagine Harry as a man with his own mind, huh? The golden William/Kate couple? The evil manipulative American trope. The evil woman who leads a weak man astray was Wallis Simpson, dears. And thank God for that - King Edward was a Nazi sympathizer and is credited with passing on Allied plans to the Germans that allowed them to wipe France off the map in weeks. This American is referred to as a no-talent b#$%^ thanks to no research deeper than every unhappy-about-her-crummy-life woman's jealousy. SOMEONE - likely His Present Majesty, although William is the next best candidate, did express concerns about Archie's color. And maligning a man who's actually been in combat? Lower than low.
I'm SO glad that my library bought this tripe so all of us in my town can read it for free and not be tempted by the 'solidly researched.' What it is, is cleverly created to trigger the same visceral jealous tear-her-down that has plagued women from the dawn of mass media. Packs of hounds howling for a chance to tear down the person who has what you wish you had. The reason you don't have it is the structural misogyny of American and British culture, creating an economy that doesn't work for anyone who's not white male, rich by birth or marriage and just plain lucky. The current season of The Crown is veering right-wing as well, trashing Diana and presenting a conniving woman who is poised to be crowned queen next year as the True Love, not the woman who betrayed her own marriage and busted up Charles'. That in-your-face, unrepentant for 20 years actual long-term strategist is the Madonna in this man's hands.

Read really-researched biographies by actual professional historians who have to have their work peer-reviewed, whose any veer to sensational, racist, sexist tropes gets red-penciled as it deserves. Do yourself a favor and improve the quality of the 'food' you feed yourself. There's so much good brain-food out there, you don't have to fill up on junk.

title: My God, what a mess!
text:
I got this one from my public library - try b4 I buy. Where did this guy get a PhD - a Cracker Jack box? Now, I'm a BIG fan of Johnnie Glover and his doughty mariners - who ran off to sea to get rich as privateers as soon as Congress started providing Letters of Marque, so hold the OMG, WHAT A CONSUMMATE PATRIOT cheers for a sec.... But he did his part before that self-serving swerve. In several key battles, like in the various fights to try to save New York.

This guy goes on and on about what an uneducated moron Washington was, based on his insistence on trying to save New York. A city with deep water on three sides, when you have no navy and your invaders has a big one - is hopeless. Which Washington told Congress - repeatedly. A 'professional historian' could have access to those resources. Heck, I did, just cuz I'm interested, I read his dispatches! Congress refused, implied he was lacking in manly virtues for 'not wanting to confront the enemy' - and you know what that means! His enemies were going to use that to get him removed from command in favor of Horatio Gates! The true moron, who did not win the battle of Saratoga/Freeman's Farm (that was his brigadiers), and then not only bungled Camden but ran away while his army was slaughtered and a better man than him stood and fought a powerful rearguard so that part of the American army could escape and be the core of Nathanael Greene's new army.

THAT is why Washington had to try to defend New York! The Brooklyn redoubt would have been a repeat of Breed;s Hill at least, if Sullivan (another idiot) hadn't left a gully undefended.

Even Hannibal couldn't have kept the Brits out of New York, that cornerstone of the country. Neither he nor Alexander would have tried, true. But they didn't have a bunch of politicians able to sack them, and who would have done so because a silver-tongued coward had mesmerized them. Or perhaps Lee? The guy who nearly lost Monmouth!? That was another top contender if Washington had tried to be truly in charge.

Rule of ethics: if people don't have power, you don't get to blame them! And if you (for whatever career-enhancing reason) don't want to do an ethical job, here you are. Yeah, you get publishing buzz for being startling and contrarian. You also get sales - ooh, the inside story, ooh, let's tear down a sacred cow. But this is a pile of well-written trash. There are some good, accurate biographies of Johnnie and his merry men. Read/buy one of them.

text: There's quite a bit of hyperbole in the book's description.  There aren't pictures of fronts and backs of finished garments.  Drawings of the dresses and fabric descriptions don't seem very attractive.  A new sewer could do just as well with a pattern from the big three, some basic tools and muslin yardage for a mock up.  That's how I learned to sew dresses.  One style, the shift, is quite similar to a dress I made in the ' 70's.  A vintage pattern from that time would be easy for a beginner or trace out a t shirt, making it wider at the hem.  Make it up in a knit fabric, and there is a dress that will fit better and be cheaper.  If needing a fun book, try, Little Green Dress.  Get a basic sewing book, like a Singer one from the library.  Pattern instruction sheets provide a wealth of information as does the Internet.  Check this book and her others from the library first for utility.  The patterns are merely basic.  If you don't think a shift or dirndl would be right for you, that wipes out 40% of the book. There are complete courses in fitting shoulders, bust, armholes, sleeves, waist, hips, back, and if one has a small or large deviation from the norm, money would be better spent on making trial garments and having someone help with fitting issues.  This means, when it comes to sewing, it isn't flowery words that get the job done.  Therefore, I don't recommend this book; neither for the newcomer to sewing or the experienced sewist.

title: Decide if this shape is both flattering and comfortable. The open sweaters provide no middle
text:
Place a pillow case up to your torso. Pin it to your t shirt, and move your arms forward and back. Notice if it pooches out at the bust line. The patterns in this book are essentially pillowcases or tabards, just rectangles. There is no neckline shaping. Fashion has advanced since the Middle Ages. Women need armhole and neckline shaping. Most women need darts for accommodating shape features beyond size A bra cup and flat bellies. Before making a featured garment, cut out your desired sweater in a muslin. Use the measurements provided in the diagrams. Pin it on one side with pins facing the outside. Once it is on, pin the other side and shoulder. Allow an extra few inches to make up for the small ease allowed for the sweaters and wearability. Then, once it is on, maintaining the rectangular shape, bring the pins in slightly. Now, swing your arms, and move your neck from side to side and up and down. Decide if this shape is both flattering and comfortable.

The open sweaters provide no middle, midriff coverage. Their sleeves are bulky and shapeless with fussy features such as wrist ruffles. Even a beginner can learn the following swiftly: increasing, decreasing, placing stitches on a holder and picking up stitches for neckline and armhole ribbing. There's no need to feel the need to wear unflattering sweaters due to perceived lack of expertise. Before actually making a sweater, become proficient in the basics such as yarn choice, gauge and fixing errors. Many books will help with those skills. This is not one of those. Therefore, it is of no use to the beginner. Whereas, a little course at the local fabric store or an hour with a friend would help. Check this book out from the library first to avoid disappointment. A garment that is made with wool or a blend that rubs against the neck or impedes arm movements is useless and will be a wadder. But that is an expense in time and money that can be avoided.

Many books easily exceed the promises of this one. There are no tricks worthy of the purchase price within the covers. Rather, spend money or check the following which constitute a mere sampling of the many useful books on the market:
Edmonds, M. & Moore, A., When Bad Things Happen to Good Knitters: Herzog, A., Knit to Flatter: Barnden, B., 200 Knitting Tips, Techniques & Trade Secrets.

I will be donating my book to charity.

title: Despite the author's best efforts, the samples look like crochet afghans
text: The sweaters are clearly created by an artist and might have been trendy in the '80's.  Now, they are outdated and oversized.  There is too much ornamentation.  However, one might take this information and apply to, for example, a pillow slip.  I couldn't see altering the pattern to meet today's fashion trends and my size demands, plus calculating the yarn amount and end up paying lots of money for the suggested type of yarn, mohair for one, only to be doing an experiment.  This book puts me off of creating crochet sweaters.  Despite the author's best efforts, the samples look like crochet afghans.  Various color changes and decorative stitches, like bobbles, do not help.  Maybe, one can benefit by matching the charts to the gauge to the finished product, then, learning how to master the art of sweater creation in like manner.  In that way, the book could be useful as a teaching device.  As far as going directly from the pattern to a wearable creation, I don't advise that.  Crocheted ponchos, capes and shawls, if done in a lacy look, might be useful for out of the home.  A large sweater would only be good for use in a very cold home, one without heat in the winter. The following book provides examples of what to wear for various occasions without appearing to be swimming within a garment:  "Knit and Crochet Poinchos, Wraps, Capes and Shrugs" Edie Eckman, ed.

title: Protesting Tooooooo Much
text:
I was hoping THIS would be the book that offered plausible, objective theories as to who may have committed this crime and why they may have done so. Instead I got 462+ pages of "The Ramsey's are innocent because their legal dream team says they're innocent." No investigation of disgruntled employees, no details about family friends or acquaintances who may have kept hidden shady or criminal pasts. We're told over and over and over again WHY the Ramsey's DIDN'T do it, and why it's unfair, inept, bumbling, corrupt, and evil for law enforcement to continue to keep them on a list of suspects.

I should've realized what a pro-Ramsey piece this was going to be when the Prologue consists of a leisurely conversation the author had with the victim's father at the Ramsey's vacation home. But I went ahead and read it anyway, coming away with no solid opinion about WHO the child's killer was. Who killed JonBenet Ramsey? You'll get no ideas or information here. But be advised: the Ramsey's legal defense team says it wasn't the Ramsey's.

text:
Ummm. Am I delirious? What in the name of god happened so that this book was published? We've got a wacked-out doormat of a woman who falls in love with a truly frightening man who has obsessed over her for twenty five years. He proposes a "marriage of convenience" when they run into each other again in their forties after knowing each other briefly in high school. And when I say briefly I mean they spoke possibly four sentences to each other when she turned him down for the prom and he cried like a baby whose toy had been taken away. He basically rapes her when they get married, and not in a lusty Scarlett and Rhett sort of way, but a cold and humiliating type of way. All of a sudden she's in love with him (no explanation as to why, except that she's possibly completely insane) and brooding throughout the whole book about their weird, abusive relationship. Which is so disgusting in any normal human's frame of reference that I had to repeatedly put down the book to wonder at what mental illnesses the author must suffer from to think that this was in any way okay.

title: Eons of boredom
text:
I am not sure what the point of this book is, but it was exhausting. It starts with an interesting mystery of a strange asteroid which suddenly appears in orbit around the earth and the story unfolds with people trying to avert a nuclear war because of the information, they find inside the stone that is from the future. They fail to stop the disaster, and war commences although a few weeks late, which indicates that the stone is from an alternate universe. (Maybe none of the universes in this story our ours.) What they do find are alternate worlds, with staggering technology and strange cultures and politics that are painfully boring to follow. However I stuck to the end of the book as I am a glutton for punishment. I admired the humans who were brave enough to go back to the earth after the destruction to help the inhabitants rebuild but I thought Patricia, who was supposed to be the savior and heroin, was a selfish self-centered dreamer and a coward to go off looking for an alternate earth where her world was still in perfect order, hoping her alternate self was dead, and her boyfriend was still alive, so she could slip into her identity and have her life back. Well, fat chance of that happening. I'm glad she didn't find it.

It was hard to read, with too many characters. The author approached the act of sex (twice) as something that must be performed once in a while in order for a person to be able to think strait. (That's just insulting.) In reading a book I try to imagine what the author's message is overall. Okay I get it, we are not alone in the Universe, we don't understand the nature of space and time, there might be in infinite number of parallel worlds, and we will probably reek havoc and death upon the earth, but don't worry, life goes on.... somewhere.

title: Avoid Wolfram Kandinsky's Narration Like the Plague
text:
If you enjoy listening to audiobooks, I strongly advise against choosing any that were read by the late Wolfram Kandinsky, unless you feel like listening to Stephen Hawking have a long conversation with himself. That may be a bit harsh, but so was having to listen to him drone on, in this case, for 14 CDs.

I had to take a step back to decide if Herzog would still be just as boring without a narrator who did nothing more than intone the entire novel, but yes, the story itself was still incredibly dry. It might have gotten an extra star out of me if it were provided with a narrator who gave it some emotion because this is a book about a guy who has been in not one but two terrible marriages, the second one worse than the first, so you'd expect there to be a bit of passion in the anger. Yet I felt like I was stuck in one of the most boring college classes ever, falling asleep on my hand and watching the clock.

I didn't know if or how I'd get through the whole book, and I nearly gave up quite a few times, but I'm a completionist and, in Herzog's case, my persistence was of no benefit. Herzog was no more likeable at the end of the book than he was at the beginning, and you're left feeling like if you were his divorce attorney, you'd be convinced that you were the one who was stuck with the crazier client. Madeline doesn't seem all that bad, despite cheating on him, and while I would never condone cheating, it's almost understandable in her case.

Though, maybe I'd have felt differently if I had chosen instead to just read the text. It is for that reason that I strongly suggest avoiding the audio version and picking up a physical copy of the book so that you can form an honest opinion of its plot and what it meant to you.

text: This is one of those books that makes you both relieved to have finished it and surprised that you got through the whole thing.  This is the last time I take a recommendation from the Doubleday Book Club.  "Return to Sullivan's Island" is what every aspiring writer should read as an example of what not to write.  Incredibly bad dialogue that sounds even worse when read aloud, annoying characters that no one can possibly care about, haunted houses, and a ridiculous, drama-packed ending all await you on Sullivan's Island where the moral should be: Mom, don't ever jet off to Paris and leave your idiot daughter in charge - the typical white, rich, moronic damsel-in-distress.  This is the same book where a woman can make a joke about getting raped on a date, yet her mother frowns upon her using the word "hell."  And where another woman can die and be chucked into a freezer, and her brother says that an act like that is "unforgivable."  Really?  Oh, then the entire family will attend her funeral and demand that the closed casket be opened while ass-pinching is going on, then head out to the car for some whiskey afterwards.  But don't worry, all of the major problems that occur in the last three chapters or so (including literal insanity and major fraud) are forgivable, and everyone manages to get their happy ending.  Ugh - I hope I never read a book this bad ever again.

title: obvious & odd
text:
Well, this is a tiny little book, about 3" x 2". It goes from page to page, listing a bad thing about "holidays" (although it seems obvious almost immediately that by holidays they mean Christmas) on one page, and a good thing on the facing page.

The only thing is, the things they list from page to page were, to me, obvious, and not very instructional.

Then, at times, there are places where you are to answer a question they've posed by writing a little list in the book.

Each time they do this, they start the list for you, rather than just having a "for example" at the end of the question, which is how you can tell it's "about" Christmas, as their lists usually relate to that holiday. It turned me off that they began the list each time, as their likes, thoughts, etc., did not match mine, but if I continued it felt as if they were, by default, part of my list, i.e. intrusive. Is this book to be about me, or the Tubesings?

And I was particularily bothered by their "starter" list to answer the question, "As you think over the past year: What experiences are particularly memorable?"

Their first answer? "Mike's suicide."

Now, I'm sure everyone out there wants to contemplate suicide at Christmas. Not exactly, right? Besides, knowing someone who was a successful suicide, I really don't like having the memory randomly thrust upon me by a book that should be discussing de-stressing. And, as I said, were I to fill in my own list there,as I'm clearly supposed to, their friend/realtive Mike's suicide would become a default part of my list.

The back cover states that, "This book is a holiday gift to you-" Some holiday gift.

I think the book is a gimmick-ie little book, and not really valuable for helping re-invent the holidays.

But, I'm sure the Tubesings won't mind a review such as this, as, towards the end of the book, they gave me "permission to feel."

title: Tragic misinformation
text:
I had high hopes for learning about the positives of responsible drug use. As someone who belongs to a social group where responsible, adult drug use of mind-enhancing (low/non-addictive) drugs, I was excited to hear someone speak of this concept with scientific authority! Sadly, the author grossly and irresponsibly promotes highly addictive drugs and seems to pretend that there is no addictive quality. He overstates how big Pharma money and the government have downplayed the danger of these types of substances, especially opioids, instead of explaining the actual dangers. The worst part is that he uses himself and his own experiences as the control for most of his assumptions. Just because he has managed to take opioids including heroin without addiction (yet) does NOT mean that everyone will. And the consequences of being wrong about this assumption are catastrophic.

As the now ex wife of a man who was using opioids and other drugs “responsibly” for a while and who is now an addict whose life is falling apart, I can tell you firsthand that not everyone can do hard drugs responsibly. Hart gives a short disclaimer at the beginning about how the adults who try this should be mentally sound, careful people, which I agree with. But most people don’t know they’re not mentally sound until they find the means to start avoiding life on a destructive scale. He ignores the fact that almost everyone in this entire world has trauma. And that even for the small percentage who don’t, events could take place which would push their use from recreational to harmful. Furthermore, there is no discussion about the real dangers and actual effects of becoming an addict. He completely side steps the ACTUAL, REAL opioid epidemic as if it’s all propaganda and misinformation. I can personally witness that it is not! I kept waiting for him to address this angle on addiction and which substances were more dangerous and likely to be habit forming. But he repeatedly ignores it because HE doesn’t have a problem with it. For that reason I found this book incredibly dangerous and I am disappointed that he published it in the name of science.

title: Waste of money
text:
The book is structured properly; It gives you a chapter summary area where you can write your own summary and what you felt was important (Basically, blank lined pages). However the chapter summary and keyword lists are generic. When I say generic, I don't mean "They're very broad in how they describe the chapter", they're literally generic.

The Landmarks in Humanities book is subdivided into eras / dates / times. An example of how useless the keyword lists are is that within the Renaissance chapter (7), the keyword list is 11 words long. It defines "Fertile Crescent", "Trojan War", "Maya", "Paradise", and "Culture". Now, something like Paradise or Culture may seem to apply if they were defined specifically for the Renaissance except they're very broad generalized definitions.

So if you want to pay $30 for something that probably wouldn't even start a fire, buy this book. Otherwise, buy some lined paper and take notes. You're better off than wasting your time with this.

text:
The storyline is so cut down that it makes absolutely no sense. It is only a total of 5 pages and it completely lacks the necessary character development to tell the story in any meaningful way. The plot line is very disjointed and incomplete.

For example it says "the Grinch hated Christmas, the whole Christmas Season" but without saying "please don't ask why, no one quite knows the reason..." and without the contrast of the whos who love Christmas you are left confused thinking this makes no sense and the Grinch is just bad. Dr Seuss knew that a person would naturally wonder "everyone else loved Christmas; why did he hate Christmas?" and continued to develop that thought, but this book deletes all of that ingenious writing and cuts it down to something incomprehensible.

title: Sorry but no!
text: Starts well enough but before long it goes terribly wrong. I find it hard to believe the many positive endorsements regarding this book. Funny once you realize that the book itself does not have one single credible reviewer. Who are these people singing praises to an otherwise mediocre effort? The story itself is convoluted with pieces of information here and pieces of information there. One moment the victims are these outstanding members of the community, the next there are out of control in remote bars in the middle of nowhere, to the point that besides recognizing the awful crime committed by the guilty party one can not help to wonder if they (victims) did not venture too far into no man's land. I think all the confusion starts with the writer of the book who doesn't seem to know how to lay out the information. Chapters one page to two pages long? Little takes here, repeating themselves in an endless cycle, of the same information during the course of almost twenty years with no added facts. I guess it is safe to say that the story line here is more like short takes on the same subject trying to achieve the distinction of being a whole book. The problem as I see it is that once a reader of this type of book reads authors of caliber and authority, Mr. Tom Henderson's weakness become too obvious to the point of no return. Come on! So if according to the amazon reviewers of this book it deserves almost 5 stars, where does that leave the real serious authors of this genre? 10 Stars? Short of all the reviewers being members of the immediate family and wanting to help the career of this writer as an author, it is inconceivable a 5 or even a 4 star rating for this wannabee. Just to upset the high marks, highly undeserved in my opinion due to the lack of aptitude, I chose 1 star even though 2 stars would have been more like it since he did write 389 pages regardless of the quality of the content. 1 Star.

title: Waste of Paper
text:
I'm truly glad I bought this book used instead of paying full price for it. I'm furious at its content, especially since most books in this series are really good.

It's "encyclopedic" knowledge is absolutely elementary and it includes chalk and pastel pencils as "colored pencils" while completely leaving out oil based pencils such as Faber-Castell. It doesn't go over the usual brands of colored pencils and their differences as most decent books about colored pencils do but it will explain to you quite thoroughly what a pencil sharpener is.

It includes no information on building heavy layers, whitening , blending with a colorless pencil, or blending using solvents (which were the reasons I figured this book would be good since it is supposedly an "encyclopedia") The use of solvent (only turpentine is mentioned which, BTW, is not recommended at all by most artists that use solvents since it is highly toxic. Turpenoid or denatured alcohol are preferred) is shown to spread the color very lighty across the paper with a cloth like watercolor pencils rather than to acheive smooth blends on thicker layers or to rid the artwork of it's grainy paper surface. It mentions the use of blending markers in a tiny corner insert in about 10 words. I've been using professional grade colored pencils and ink for 27 years using burnishing and colorless pencils to blend and only recently discovered blending markers and the use of solvents which really got me excited so I want to know more. I am SO disappointed...

The tiny section on papers doesn't even explain the different effects that can be achieved by using different paper grades with REAL colored pencils. There is no information on color theory. I was hoping to be enlightened in at least one area of colored pencil use but gained NOTHING from this book, and only half of the book is about "techniques". Most techniques have only a single short page devoted to each one. The rest is entitled "Themes" or, basically, what to draw. I could go on for an hour about what a piece of garbage this book is but I'm sure you get the idea.

Do not buy this book unless you're an absolute beginner or don't know what a friggin' pencil sharpener is. Not a wise investment if you know anything at all about colored pencils. I am so angry I could punch my monitor...

title: Not Worth Time nor Money
text:
I believe this is the first "biography" I've ever read obviously written by the subjects of same. The prose was horrible - "the rising sun washed over her makeshift yoga garden, while an exotic flock of birds that looked as if they had just had their tails dipped in pots of colourful paints serenaded her". OMG. Could we possibly try to fool MORE of the public into thinking that Meghan and Harry didn't write this themselves with the help of a PR firm and two enterprising reporters who probably jumped at the chance to participate in such subterfuge. Too bad most people with half a brain will see through this attempt to self-aggrandize.

I admit I could not finish this, at least not without taking a break and getting in touch with reality again. If I had been able to remove the horrible prose, written for someone with an eighth grade education and meant to make them feel "smart", I probably could have stomached part of this. Maybe. Probably Not.

This book was, for the most part, Harry and Meghan's way of justifying themselves to the world. Every single move they made from the moment they met is immortalized in a way to make them appear "right" and the rest of the world appear to be slightly skewed. If, as their numerous and quite public statements said, they did not participate in this farce, then they fed the lines to their friends and allowed them, once again, to speak for the Duchess. My opinion of Harry, allowing his wife to now be his mouthpiece, went so low that I've decided as cute as he was as a kid, he didn't grow up either cute or smart. His mother, the late Princess Diana knew how to play the press, how to take full advantage of them, something at which Harry and Meghan are failing. One cannot, on one hand, want to "explain" oneself constantly, then on the other, complain that they're getting the attention they wanted, except maybe a bit more than they'd planned on.

This book is fluff, nothing more. This tendency to make biographies into "even the score" pieces, or as one biographer in Great Britain called the raft of current biographies, beginning with anything written by Princess Diana, a "vehicle for settling scores". But even as fluff, this book is just downright embarrassing. It is obviously authorized by the Duke and Duchess. Why? Because these people are suing everyone and everyone's cousin for everything. I've never seen a Royal so quick to head to court and air their dirty laundry as these two have been. So, someone writes an UNAUTHORIZED biography and has more detail in it than could possibly be gotten from third party sources, and they DON'T sue? Not likely. In fact, the entire idea that Harry and Meghan would not have been up in arms about some of the details is ridiculous.

The people I feel sorry for are Meghan's former assistant. The book doesn't hesitate to make Meghan right and the assistant wrong. Then the night nurse. Then the Queen's dresser who (gasp!!!) handled the tiaras without gloves (and how would the biographers know that if they weren't in the room, or (another gasp!) Meghan TOLD someone to tell them.

Sorry, this wasn't worth the money I spent, and it irks me that they just put another "nominal" amount into the multi million pound fortune (yea, Meghan, you may want to change that line up a bit - that "nominal" sum you are worth? Trust me, you aren't.). By 50%, the book had made me feel sorry for Harry for getting caught up in this woman's sphere of influence. She stated before she ever met him that she was fascinated by royals and wanted to be a princess. She got her wish. Let's hope she doesn't take Harry down with her. This book should help that a lot.

title: A short story that needs a writer
text:
I read and reviewed the first of this duet, and I'd really hoped, since the first book rambled and really didn't have a plot, that I could find one in this second of the two short stories (because that's exactly what they are, with the author wanting you to buy both so that he/she can make more money).

I would suggest that the author needs to read a few books on writing, or take a class of two. A book isn't just words strung together telling you every move the H and h make. The author needs to understand the arc of a story, the plot and its various dimensions, depth of characters (and in this case, depth of at least one would have been welcomed), and most of all, how to build suspense, because this one didn't do it. A couple of explosions at the end, with no detail, no true action, and a lot of missed opportunities to expand on the suspense and climax, does not a plot make.

It would also help if he/she learned what the term alliteration means. This book needed it, a lot. It also needed a smattering of descriptive phrases in order to turn it into a real suspenseful book, plus, a dictionary (massing isn't a good substitute for massive, if that's even what was meant).

I got these on KU, so it only cost me a few cents this month to read them. The first book I read of Logan Chance? I liked it. No doubt about it. I guess I grew up.

title: Received as a gift.
text:
And I would have told them to send it back, except the money they spent on the book goes to Hurricane victims, I think (although I think someone should be asking them to prove it, because for all the hype for this book is ridiculous). I get that the "author (and I use that term loosely) has no idea what comedy is beyond politics. God bless him, it just gets VERY tiring to know that he's a one-trick pony. But what really bothered me the most was that there are so many really good things we could be teaching our children in subjects that they aren't doing well in, such as mathematics, science, or history, that I find wasting time teaching them HATE isn't what we should be doing for them. I have no love of Trump's mouth but even I have to admit he's creating jobs, and we're doing better than we were (which I suppose is why this book was written in the first place, because when people hate you and you're on top, they have to feel like they can bring you down a peg to make themselves feel powerful).

Overall, unless you want your children growing up to be small-minded, learning hate instead of tolerance, and just generally thinking that it's ok to show disrespect daily, I would suggest NOT spending the money on this book and instead donate directly to the Red Cross, Salvation Army, or The Humane Society of America.

title: Drop the Mic
text:
You know the old saying, "don't judge a book by it's cover"? This seems to be a shining example of that old adage. The cover and title look fresh and new and certainly caught my attention. Then I started reading. It begins with an introduction, which is no more than 2 pages on my iPhone, so very short. Allow me to share two sentences from the introduction...
"A less time-consuming and systematic house cleaning and organizing plan is beneficial not only for housewives, but also for women who have hectic schedules because of their regular job."
It made me pause. I chewed on that line for a moment. At first irritated and then I calmed my mind and pushed on. And then, Introduction pg 2 - "You will surely become the perfect wife after learning about the tips in this book and applying them in real life."

Drop. The. Mic.
WHAT?!
I didn't even begin to read this short little informative book. I get it. Most of the audience for this book WILL be female and possibly married. But, REALLY?! Because I can keep a clean, organized house I'll become the perfect wife?!

I so hope that this Introduction was actually just a joke and had I went on a few pages further Evelyn would have explained what a riot it was to say all these sexist things and make these assumptions. But instead I deleted it from my Kindle as fast as I could.

title: VERY BAD PLAY; HITCHCOCK'S FILM IS SO MUCH BETTER
text: I am a lifelong Hitchcock fan, and I am particularly fond of his version of _Rope_. I have also done a considerable amount of theater, and the film's unique approach to production led me to believe it could be a good work for the stage. I think Hume Cronyn's adaptation might be. But this play is very poorly written. None of the characters are interesting or easy to identify with. Characters other than Rupert talk about whether a murder has been committed, which has a bad effect on the suspense. Usually, I prefer stage plays over film scripts, but it is a testament to Cronyn's writing that he managed to adapt such a bad play into such a good film script.

title: Apple Goes the Way of Microsoft With Constant Software "Updates"
text: It's so sad to see Apple go the way of Microsoft and update its operating software every 15 minutes. I just want my computer to do today what it did last week in the same way it did it last week. The constant needless changes to corporate Web sites is irritating enough without changing how my computer works. My job demands that I stay current in my field, and the last thing I need is to have to learn new software every time I turn around. Tools that take time away from productive work aren't tools; they're nuisances that interfere with productivity. I've purchased a license for Lion, which does what I need it to do without wasting my time figuring out how to do what I knew how to do before all these other animals invaded my world and that all the software I spent thousands on works with. Changes and all these extras are for kids, who do nothing but play with technology. Macs were always known for their ease of use, but this constant software update eliminates that. If it weren't for AppleCare, the Mac advantage would no longer exist.

title: SHAME ON YOU, LITTLE BROWN!
text: Will you textbook publishers THINK? Yes, teaching a live class, profs can switch gears on a moment's notice. But are you even aware of what it takes to put together an online course or to update an existing one? If you can't produce a revision at least a month before the beginning of a standard academic term, wait until the next term. After making this foolhardy decision to completely change a textbook Aug. 11, refusing to supply the previous version during the overlap term is absolutely unacceptable. I had confirmed with my bookstore which text we were using and its ISBN and emailed that info to on students who wanted to purchase or rent books online. Half my students had one textbook, and half had the other. Well, your rush to publish to cash in on MLA changes backfired. I'm producing videos and handouts and using Purdue OWL. Of course, having set my online pages up that way, I will go on teaching without a text, which will mean that at least 100 students a semester who would have been buying your texts won't be. I hope you lose many, many online profs because you had to rush for profits this ONE semester. When will Americans ever learn to think beyond this year's bottom line?

text:
A penny dreadful, with the emphasis on dreadful. Published in 1910. Here's an excerpt:
"It was easier said than done. The chattering bunch of Chinks crowding around offered no help.

"I don't see how in thunder we are going to get the boy up without a ladder," muttered Old King Brady.

"And where will we find one?" echoed Harry.

"That's the point. But here comes a policeman. Perhaps he can suggest——"

Thus far in his speech Old King Brady got when there came another call for help.

He could not exactly make out the words, but it was certainly, also, a cry of fear.

"Let go! Don't you touch me!" they heard now.

The cry came from the hole.

Then all was still below, although above the Chinamen chattered louder than ever.

"By Jove! the Chinks are going for the boy," cried Harry. "He has fallen into one of the secret dens of Pell street, sure!"

It looked like it.

The policeman came."

I think that suffices for a full review.

title: I returned my copy for a refund.
text:
I was sorely disappointed by the actual content- the text, the *words* which were supposed to communicate something of the glory and wonder of science to my children.

The book had promise- I was impressed with a my first glance in the bookstore. It's beautifully laid out- lovely pictures, interesting sidebars- but once I sat down and tried to read the text, those sidebars were horribly, awfully distracting. I don't know who chose the formatting, but it's guaranteed to interrupt any chain of thought a reader might have. At least one 'sidebar' interrupted the flow of a passage in midsentence, then the 'sidebar' continued on, taking up two entire pages before returning to the next word in the interrupted sentence!

It's like a commercial or a video game- distracting to the utmost. I also thought the writing was choppy, a little bit condescending, and very much designed to foster a sort of vacuous, uninformed arrogance in the student.

Ancient history, says a well educated homeschooling father I've read from time to time, should not be taught as 'how the peasants lived back then,' because we really aren't any smarter than those who went before us. We stand on their shoulders so we have more information at our fingertips, information they discovered, but we are not smarter than they. It is a natural tendency to think that we are 'it,' that nobody has thought the thoughts we have, figured out the things that we know, and that we have advanced beyond any society before us. This is a superficial understanding at best, and a broad study of history should go a long way toward correcting that. Unfortunately, Hakim's book encourages that attitude. She does seem to teach science history along the lines of 'how the peasants lived.'

At the beginning of her book she hubristically tells her students that when they finish reading her book they will know more than Isaac Newton. Since he invented Calculus, that's just a bizarre thing to say. She's feeding her readers a false image of what it means to 'know' and what knowledge is, and just who Isaac Newton really was. They will, perhaps, have more facts at their disposal, assuming they remember everything.

They will know more history, since much of what is in her book happened after Newton's death. But will they have more knowledge than Isaac Newton? That is highly doubtful, and it does not do students any favors to confuse knowledge with a handy list of data points.

title: Disappointing in Every Way!
text:
My Min Pin is a German breed and my maternal grandmother was born in Bavaria. I had high hopes, for both my Min Pin and myself, that we would soon be enjoying German cuisine.

I really wanted to like this cookbook and couldn't wait for it to arrive. Now that I have it, I wonder how it got any positive reviews?!

First of all, it is a very small 8"x7" hardback without a dust cover. And it isn't even 1" thick. It looks a bit like a thin children's nursery primer. It's a challenge to read much less keep open to follow a recipe.

The recipes are not well organized, do not have uniform measurements, lack basic baking instructions (including oven temperatures in some of the entries).

There are very few colored photos of cooked items and they appear to be randomly placed in the book. If you are not familiar with German cuisine you will not know what you are looking at--there are no descriptions with the photos.

Most of the recipes are just jammed together on a page. None are easy to make, as advertised, because the measuring systems are a mashup of Eastern and Western and many ingredients are not readily available.

Included are recipes I wish I hadn't seen: Fried Kid, Calf's Lungs, Knuckle Jelly, Calf's Tongue.

The prize-winner for useless is a cake recipe on page 149, Fruit Cake "Egg Weight", where the weight of the eggs used in the recipe are used as a measure for other ingredients. I have no idea how that works.

Nowhere is there a recipe for Black Forest Cake, which is what I was hoping for. And although full of recipes for various animal organs, there is nothing that appealed to my Min Pin either...except possibly the Fried Kid.

The fold-out map is hand drawn and also a huge disappointment. In fact, there is nothing in the cookbook as advertised. The history is unimpressive and scant and the font hard to read.

If you want a German cookbook with recipes that are appealing and easy to follow, then bypass this one and save your money to purchase a quality German cookbook. Sadly, I have not found one to recommend on Amazon. Min Pin and I must look elsewhere.

title: Useless
text:
This book as a whole is poorly done. Its principal fault is that you are simply told what to do, instead of educated what to do. Otherwise the faults are: 1) no diagrams 2) unsatisfactory supporting evidence/explanations 3) omissions 4) useless factoids 5) mistakes. The only useful part is the bibliography.

First of, there are no diagrams in this book! Every aerospace book that I looked at included some kind of diagram about something. The author mentions that he had built models himself, but provides no examples, no designs, etc. This is inexcusable. In the whole book I counted only 4 pictures of model airplanes. The other 14 pictures are of full sized airplanes which didn't show anything useful.

Second. He will tell you his opinion and not explain them well. I didn't know much about airfoils when I started to read this book, so to me when Reyes talked about airfoils it was new information. His general recommendation was to use the GA(W)-2 / LS(1)-0413 / NASA LS(1)-0413 airfoil for the wing because it's popular for general aviation use, and NACA 0012 for the horizontal stabilizer. You're supposed to take his word on this. He then says that at 100,000 Reynolds number (as a hint, indoor models are well below that the rest are about 70k to 200k) or less the NASA LS(1)-0413 airfoil doesn't work so well. Why? I had to find this out in another book. While reading [[ASIN:1619540177 Aerodynamics for Naval Aviators: NAVWEPS 00-80T-80 (FAA Handbooks series)]] I came across a section that explains what happens to an airfoil under high and low Reynolds number. Using NACA 4412 as an example, I could tell from the diagram in the book that at an Re of 9 million the airfoil will develop the highest lift coefficient at an angle of attack of 14 and stall past 15, while at Re of 100000 this will happen at of 8 and 12 AoA. As explained in that book this is because at low Reynolds numbers the flow will become laminar and will not have enough energy to stick to the wing at higher angles of attack. To me this make much more sense than saying that "it will not work as well." I then compared the Clark-Y airfoil against Reyes recommended airfoil LS(1)-0413 that he favors over the Clark-Y, on airfoiltools dot com. To me at Re of 100000 the Clark-Y actually looks like a better choice. While it might look like that the LS(1)-0413 develops a slightly higher Cl(max) overall at 11 AoA, and stalls at 14, the Clark-Y will reach a lower Cl(max) at 12 AoA - but will stall out at 18 AoA. To me that seems like a better deal. A higher max AoA means more room for control error, gusts, etc. A proper book would have provided way for you to make that decision yourself. I then read [[ASIN:1854862707 Model Aircraft Aerodynamics]] and realized that there is also something called a critical Re number. So an airfoil that does not “work well” below an Re of 100000, what that actually means is that the airflow completely breaks down. The critical Re number is the number you want preferably below the stall, not the number the plane will actually fly at!
While the book has many formulas, oddly enough he suggests a cryptic method for calculating vertical stabilizer size by cutting out pieces of cardboard based on side body profile and certain wing area size. I get that there is trial an error involved with reading [[ASIN:1854862707 Model Aircraft Aerodynamics]] in respect to dutch roll and spiral stability, but Reyes seems to suggest that it's easy.
Reyes makes some points on materials, engines, batteries, etc. But In the end I have no idea how any of that goes together.

Third. In the end a wing airfoil is just one part of a wing, yet he doesn't talk about wings themselves. His only wing planform is the crescent shape! What about explaining how different wing planforms effect tip stalls, which is included in every aerodynamics book? Rectangular, delta, swept, etc. There is no mention of flaps besides him telling you that they serve no purpose on a slow flying model.

Fourth. Some of Reyes book reads like some of the first parts of [[ASIN:1600869114 Aircraft Design: A Conceptual Approach (Aiaa Education Series)]]. There are countless small factoids and side points included by Reyes that cover full size airplanes that frankly should have been edited out do to the objective of the book. For example both Authors mention Rutans' VariEze, Raymer mentions that that the winglets on the wings presented a novel dual use design in that they serve as both winglets and vertical stabilizer/rudders, while Reyes mentions that it was the first airplane with winglets. Raymers' point in the context of an airplane design book is interesting, Reyes point in a model design book on the other hand is useless. I expect model specific examples!

Fifth. There are many formulas and some tables with calculated values, but when I tried to use Table 6.1. Scale Factors on page 124 it became apparent that the figures provided for weight % are incorrect. Instead I looked through the Bibliography and started a search for the recommended books instead, and in starting to read some those (Simons, etc) I have to say they are miles apart.

title: Better for historical insights. Not good for children.
text:
Written in the late 1800's, the book "Elsie Dinsmore" offers some fascinating insights into the culture of very wealthy southerners in the post-civil war era. I was interested, for example, when Elise received $50 from her father to buy Christmas presents. That's more than my children in 2014 have to spend. Compare it to the penny Laura received in her Christmas stocking, during this same time period.

Parenting has changed dramatically from that time to ours. The moral lessons proposed in this book do not suit a world in which children need to learn to think for themselves and make good decisions at a young age. Modern parenting books in the U.S., for example, urge parents and teachers to offer choices whenever they are possible, even for toddlers, "Do you want broccoli, or do you want peas?" The book does not sync well with the hopes and dreams we have for our children today. My daughters, age 10 and 12, did not relate to the protagonist, so we stopped the book. Elsie would be seen as weak and incapable of making decisions for herself, into ur world. To view the Bible as the sole source of conduct isn't a lesson I want my children to learn, when I want them to be exposed to the beauty of other cultures, other religions, and other value systems. However, if the book is taken in context, it encourages adults to ask questions about parenting, and why we have changed so much as a culture.

The severe and narrow views on diet, the religious dogmatism, and even the female etiquette standards are difficult to for Americans of the 21st Century to relate to. In one incident, Elsie is sternly punished for sitting on the floor to help younger children, guests in her own home, to build blocks in her nursery,. Her father thought it undignified. The values offered in this book come from a culture that was not exposed to the outside world or to the observed experimentation of scientific research. And Elsie's relationship with her father, so exclusive and possessive, is not something I would encourage my daughters to seek with any person in their lives: male, female, peer, or elder.

I cannot fairly rate this book. For children, it deserves a 1-star. For adults, it deserves a 3-star, or perhaps more for its historical insight. About all I can say for the book is that I enjoyed that the author cares a great deal about her ideas and bringing them out through her characters. She's consistent, and makes her reader feel strongly in reaction to her writing.

I bought the book only because the rating was so high here on Amazon. I did not take the time to read the reviews, as you are doing now! My daughters love books like the "Little House" series, "The Five of a Kind Family" series, and "Old Yeller", for example. And I was excited that maybe I had found a new historical series they would enjoy as much, and something with depth, for my children. Not so.

title: Melodramatic women’s fiction with a retread romantic subplot
text:
Anna Sun is a Chinese-American virtuoso violinist who is suffering from burnout. It is clear the moment that Anna steps onstage that she is autistic, but she doesn’t find this out herself until several chapters into the story through the insight of a therapist she is seeing about her issues with her music. Her boyfriend of five years informs Anna that he wants to eventually marry her, but just to be sure she’s the right choice for him, he wants them to take a break so he can, basically, have sex with other women. When Anna asks if he is expecting her to have sex with other people, too, he laughs at her and says he doubts that she will, because they both know she doesn’t like sex. Anna knows that is true, but she decides to have sex anyway with a series of strangers. Unfortunately for her revenge-sex plot, Anna can’t even force herself to have sex with the first man she goes out with, a gorgeous, sweet-natured, Vietnamese-American man named Quan Diep, whom she is very attracted to and who treats her with tremendous kindness and compassion.

I had quite a few issues with this story that made it a real slog to get through:

1. This is not a romance novel, even though it is marketed as such, and the author has written it in the alternating, first-person points of view of Anna and Quan. In actuality, this is depressingly melodramatic women’s fiction, because the author’s main focus is on Anna’s psychological journey. This consists of several main issues. First and foremost is her discovery that she is autistic—autistic protagonists being the brand of this author. She realizes that she has covered up who she really is all her life via the process of “masking,” that is, trying to look and act “normal,” in order to avoid being bullied by family, friends and strangers. The second and related issue is Anna’s very, very slow growth out of her inability to say, “No,” to anyone, due to the rigid, controlling way she was raised. Unfortunately, a heroine who spends scene after scene angsting over how helplessly, psychologically immobile she is, is inevitably an extremely passive, boring protagonist.

2. Quan is presented as an ideal, Beta male who is endlessly supportive and kind to Anna. I could definitely see why she would fall for him—who wouldn’t? But I could never figure out why he is so wild about her. Does she feel familiar as a woman with autism because—in a huge coincidence—both his best friend’s wife (the heroine of Book 1 of this series) and his own younger brother are autistic? Is it because she is as sweet-natured as he himself? Is it because they both like nature documentaries? Of course he thinks she is beautiful, but what good does his sexual attraction to her do him when she is tragically, sexually dysfunctional? The only thing she can offer him is that she is accepting and non-judgmental about his losing a testicle to cancer—which is just standard ordinary decency rather than a huge virtue. In the end, the only conclusion I could draw is that he is a person who likes to be in the Rescuer role, and Anna is obviously a Victim in need of rescue.

3. The whole subplot about Quan and Michael’s business is a huge digression from the central plot of the mental-health journey of Anna, and it is not even particularly interesting, other than serving as an extended epilogue about the hero, Michael, which fans of the author’s first book in this series might possibly enjoy.

4. There should be a trigger warning in the blurb for this novel. The author shows on the page in vivid detail the kind of sexual trauma that can happen to a woman who can’t say, “No.” Anna has been in a relationship for five whole years with a patronizing, narcissistic user named Julian. Like her, he comes from a wealthy background, and her parents and older sister approve of him. (It is never made clear what Julian looks like and if he is Chinese-American like Anna, but if so, that would certainly be a huge plus to Anna’s family.) Anna and Julian have never lived together, and in one of the earliest scenes in the novel, the author vividly shows on the page how the two of them have been conducting their sexual relationship for the past five years. Julian summons Anna to his apartment several times a week to give him a blow job, complete with swallowing. And during the act, just to make it even more despicable, he shoves on her head to force her to suit his speed and penetration preferences. Anna loathes everything about servicing Julian, but she doesn’t feel she has any right to say so, because it might hurt his feelings. Not only that, Julian makes no effort to offer Anna any kind of sexual pleasure whatsoever during these sordid encounters. Neither of them undresses, and as soon as he’s gotten what he wants, he zips up his pants and starts watching TV. The author makes it clear to the reader that the reason Anna has stayed in this rape-based relationship so long is because she never stands up to anyone, for any reason. Her sister and mother like Julian very much, especially since Anna has never talked to them about how Julian treats her, and she doesn’t want to disappoint them by dumping him. Not that she has the backbone to end this horrible relationship. It is clear that, if not for the fact hat Julian demands “space” from Anna while he screws around with other women, Anna would eventually have married him and been stuck with him for life.

5. I can’t imagine how a child with Asperger’s, who was treated as badly as Anna by their family, would have the ability to do anything but lapse into an unmotivated depression. I don’t understand how such a child could possibly summon up the amount of grit and passion necessary to become a genius violinist.

6. The author never specifically mentions where the money is coming from that supports Anna. Across the entirety of this novel, which consists of over 2-1/2 years in story time, never once does Anna engage in any paid work. Her parents are extremely wealthy, and perhaps she is a “trust-fund baby,” but if so, the author should have specifically said so.

7. Neither Anna’s nor Quan’s age is ever given in the story. Are they in their 20’s? Their 30’s? We are never told, which is extremely frustrating. People are very different in their 20’s than they are in their 30’s.

8. Anna is never described, other than that Quan considers her beautiful, and all we know about Quan is that he has lots of muscles, is heavily tattooed, and buzz cuts his hair. Speaking of which: Why does he keep it that short? Is he going bald? We are never told.

9. The romance plot in this story, such as it is, is a tired retread of the plot in The Kiss Quotient. Quan, as Michael did for autistic Stella, acts as a sex therapist for Anna (though unlike Michael, Quan is not a sex worker who is paid for his efforts). Anna is incapable of expressing what she might enjoy in partnered sex, because she has never experienced affirmatively consensual sex with her only previous lover, Julian, and also because she has never enjoyed anything sexual she has done with him.

10. When Anna’s father has a severe stroke, with zero chance of recovery, her mother completely gives in to the insane logic of Anna’s control-freak, much older sister, Priscilla, as to how Anna’s paralyzed, bedridden father, who is incapable of speech, will be cared for. Priscilla demands that, rather than their father receiving competent hospice care in a residential facility or, since their family is rolling in money, hiring round-the-clock nurses to care for him domestically, that they bring him home where Priscilla, Anna, and their mother will rotate 8-hour shifts acting as his untrained, inevitably inadequate caretakers. This involves the three of them changing his diapers, bathing him, turning him over in bed every two hours to prevent bed sores, feeding him tiny spoonfuls at a time so that he does not choke to death, and giving him a host of medications. Due to the fact that Anna’s mother doesn’t stand up to Priscilla and goes along with her agenda, it becomes obvious that she is almost as much of a doormat as Anna.

11. After an entire book of Anna’s being presented as unable to stand up for herself, because, we are told over and over, that her words are trapped inside her, magically, during the dramatic climax of the story, Anna manages to tell off both Priscilla and Julian. Though it is certainly a relief to see the worm finally turn, the whole thing is ridiculously unmotivated and out of the blue.

12. After a long, dreary slog through Anna’s helpless-hopeless despair during the vast majority of this book, the author tacks on a rainbows-and-unicorns, HEA finale that is irritatingly convenient.

Finally, I experienced this novel as an audiobook. Though the two narrators do about as good a job as possible with the material at hand, I do not recommend the audiobook version of this novel. If you must read this novel, I recommend the ebook version, because it is much easier to skim over the dragging portions of the novel that consist of Anna’s endlessly repetitive thoughts about how powerless she is against her awful fate as a pathetic doormat.
