title: Long, wordy, and poorly plotted
text:
(visual) Stephenson's career, in a nanotech Zodiac, jumping a horde of orphaned Chinese sharks in extreme, ultra, ridiculously, slow motion. (end visual) It's excruciatingly slow, it's wordy, the characters are by courses overdrawn, poorly drawn, or inconsistently drawn, and the plot resolution is both rushed and stupid. The net result is a thin fictionalization of branches of philosophy that probably ought to be allowed to die a natural death, and that surely deserve better than to be buried under a deus ex machina in the end. It's a waste of your time, money, attention, and intellectual consideration.

I had high hopes for this novel. I was disappointed in it, just like his last several. Having cooled off (I wrote the first paragraph above immediately after finishing), my complaints are threefold:
1) Poor plotting. Grafting "The History of Philosophy" onto a Heinlein juvenile is not "plotting". The final resolution is a dumb plot device from a 1950's monster movie, with a PC finish.
2) Excessive size and insufficient editing. 981 pages for a bildungsroman about a philosopher-in-training has a certain irony about it, but it isn't fun to read. Stephenson-as-David Weber is not a pretty sight.
3) Poor character development. The single most interesting character in the entire book, Orolo, disappears off-page, and is eventually killed, without a lot of chance for Erasmus to show the audience what about Orolo inspired him.

Stephenson, IMO, has failed in his past four (7?) books to live up to the bright expectations of his first two big hits, "Snow Crash" and "The Diamond Age". I didn't expect an army of Chinese orphans on nanotech skateboards to show up at the end of "Anathem" with Italian pizza for everyone, but I did expect something more creative than what did.

title: A total miss for me!
text:
I tried several times to read this book, but I couldn’t get past the first few chapters for two glaring reasons.

First and foremost, being from Alaska, I found hundreds of small inaccuracies that I could not tolerate. A sample: school ends before Labor Day in Alaska. In the first chapter, the protagonist talks about sitting in class on a hot June day. Yaaaaaa....so not right. Another sample: never ever would someone use the word “sqaw” to refer to an Alaska Native—more likely than not, kids here wouldn’t even know the word. AK culture is very present in the curriculum (and I have firsthand knowledge of curriculum in three different districts, including Anchorage).

Those are just two glaring inaccuracies that appeared in the first few paragraphs. I just couldn’t go on with this book. I suppose that if you’re not from here, you wouldn’t notice the errors, or assumptions on the part of the author. I, however, did.

The other problem I had with the book was the writing style. The sentences were very short and abrupt. Like this. And this. Perhaps the author does not like commas or is trying to communicate something with the trunctuated style of writing. If so, I did t get the message.

Overall this was a miss for me, as most books written about Alaska by non-Alaskan writers are. Too bad, I had high hopes.

title: Super, super thin card stock.
text:
Holy smokes. I own almost 100 decks, Mass Market and Indie alike. I have to say, this is the thinnest, most fragile card stock I’ve ever seen used on a deck. Think of the card stock you buy at Office Depot to use in your printer, then divide that width in half. That’s how thin it is. The cover of the companion book is actually twice as thick as the cards themselves.

The weird thing... I’m usually the last person to get worked up about crappy card stock. It’s usually not that important to me. But, this is just too silly. It’s basically paper! It’s hard to believe the artist signed off on this as a prototype. It’s terrible. And cheap. And makes the deck impossible to shuffle and therefor unsatisfying to use. I’m super disappointed. I’ll never buy from this publisher again.

title: YIKES.
text:
I’ve been reading Tarot for a long time and own all sorts of decks. But, this is the first deck I’ve owned that chose to forgo labeling the major arcana, in favor of just numbering them. They are numbered 0-21 in Roman numeral on the top AND bottom of each card (why number both the top and the bottom?) Clearly one of those areas could have been used for naming the card (The Fool, The Empress, etc.) I truly don’t understand this decision and think it devalued an other-wise beautifully illustrated deck.

If you haven’t memorized which cards correspond to which numbers in the major arcana, this deck will make reading very tedious; you’ll have to keep stopping to consult the LWB or another guide to figure out which card “XVII” is (for example.) Some practioners may have success reading these cards intuitively, but if you’re like me and use the traditional RWS meanings, the images won’t help you identify the card either.

title: A real slog through this one
text: In my opinion, this is not worth your time.  I had to read it for my book group, but like others in the group, I could barely finish it.  First, it is not well written. It reads like the notes for a high school history report - fact after fact, interspersed with quotes from Ruth's diary.  The character of Ruth Rapport is not fleshed out and never really comes alive.  So  it is boring, boring, boring.  There are some interesting places, to be sure. But even those are told as tho you are reading research notes.  Secondly, Ruth is not a likable character.  She is shallow, selfish and self-absorbed.  I am not sure the author of the book likes her much either.  I didn't enjoy reading about her.  Perhaps this is the fault of the author who could not make her a compelling character.  I don't really know what she did that makes her a candidate for a book, tho her life is unusual in that she was born in Nazi Germany, escaped its horrors when she was young, and worked for the government as a librarian.  None of this makes for a gripping narrative - at least as it is told here. .  I forced myself to finish the book -  get to the end where the author talks about herself more than Ruth.  But it was a real slog and I am glad it is over.  I got this book free from Amazon First Reads, and I am SO GLAD I did not have to pay for it.  Save your money and time and look elsewhere for an interesting read.  There are so many good books out there.  This is just not one of them.

title: Knit the season is disappointing

Too much time is spent recapping the events of the first two books, and there are senseless flashbacks to childhood events that have nothing to do with the story.  I couldn't even finish it.  I think the author needed to turn out a third book - and fast - for her publisher.  And this trite and boring read is what we got.  Too bad.  Save your time and money.  But do take a look at the first two books.  The first book, especially, is a delight.

title: Repetitive and uninsightful
text:
I enjoy reading fiction from China and non-fiction about China. Because of this particular interest, China Tripping stood out to me. It is a collection of anecdotes by Western acdemics, mostly from the US, who visited China. The anecdotes range from one paragraph to perhaps two pages.

Through the first half of the book, almost all of the anecdotes are simple observations about state minders or restrictions placed on the university professors who are visiting the country. The second half of the book is mostly slice-of-life observations about consumerism and daily life. Many of the anecdotes were self-indulgent, despite being a page in length.

Although some of the anecdotes were about interesting topics, they were repetitive and failed to provide the insights that were promised by the publisher and in the introduction.

title: Fraudulent history of Sahrawi independence
text:
“Stories of the Sahara” by Sanmao (real name Chen Ping), is a unique work of travel literature. The book is light and breezy with the exception of two chapters, one about slavery, and the other about the Sahrawi independence movement. Unfortunately, major events in that long, climactic chapter about the independence movement are fraudulent.

Moving to the coastal city of El Aiún (Laayoun) with her husband, Sanmao writes very well about the mundane details of life, such as municipal water delivery, nosey neighbors, and making house repairs. Sanmao also writes about her Bohemian lifestyle, artistic interests, and frequent trips to the beach. Her description of El Aiún as a backwater village in the middle of the Sahara dessert does not mesh with some of the other descriptions she includes. It is a metropolitan city with Spanish and French colonizers, including major contingents of Franco’s Spanish army and the presence of multinational mining interests, where her husband works. Still, Sanmao concentrates on describing the minutiae of life, which is absolutely fascinating.

Sanmao frequently talks about the grooming habits of her Sahrawi neighbors, commenting on their odors and dirty skin. This is a little off-putting, but certainly forgivable. In addition, while she breezes past the subject of slavery in an early chapter, she does return to the subject in a lengthy article whereby she proves her generosity and sympathy.

However, As many professional reviewers have described (such as Miriam Lang in “East Asian History,” 2000), the chapter “Crying Camels” is largely a fabrication. In this intense and energetic chapter, Sanmao meets Muhammad Bassiri, an ethnic Sahrawi independence leader. Although he died in 1970, Sanmao describes hosting Bassiri and his in-town girlfriend Shahida (who is pregnant with the child of another man) as tensions with the Spanish occupiers heat up. Inserting herself in Sahrawi independence matters and claiming to have sheltered and advised Bassiri the day before he was killed is no small matter. It would be odd if a Koranic scholar married a liberal, urbane, Catholic convert in any event, but it is even more complicated because of the fact that Sanmao was in El Aiún for two years, around 1974 and 1975.

Nowhere does the publisher, translator, or author of the forward try to account for these inconsistencies. I only found out about this after I researched information about Bassiri independently. This damages my relationship and trust in the book. I cannot separate the book from other literary forgeries, such as Margaret B. Jones, James Frey, and Nasdijj.

title: Save your  time for something better
text:
I was looking for some writing classes which is how I found Ryan Wiley. I thought that I'd like to see a sample of his writing before I committed to anything, and so I chose this from Kindle Unlimited.

So, the protagonist is 25, has dated Ashley since Junior year of high school, and they've been together for four years. Well, that math doesn't work. It's written in the first-person perspective for no real reason (it's not hard-boiled detective, for example), and the writing is pretty sophomoric.

The story puts a lot of focus on mundane details:

"The Medina Bank and Trust has an old-fashioned feel to it, with a huge chandelier hanging from the ceiling. It makes you feel important just being in here.

"We wait in line, and as we do I look for the candy suckers at the front desk. The last time I was here the bank lady gave me a huge handful of candy.

"Next, please," one of the attendants says.

We step up and my mom says "Hi. We'd like to open . . ."

These details go on in minute detail forever; it's just like watching grass grow.

The plot is weak and there's no real character development. I had no sympathy for the characters and didn't get to know them or really even care about them one way or another.

On the positive side, the dialogue is actually pretty decent and natural.

The events of the story even start out with them doing it. It just wasn't believable and doesn't even work as a romance.

The wider story of it does have some intrigue and has the potential to be a pretty good story. There's a plot to prevent a senator from making a vote that could ruin someone else. This could've made a nice political thriller, but it still needs work.

He is a best-selling author, so maybe I'll give another one of his books a try.

title: Just Couldn't Finish
text:
I had hoped I would enjoy this book since there were so many good reviews on it; however, I only lasted 9 chapters.
Here are a few reasons I quit:

* Even though I had read the first book (several years ago), I was given no idea how old anyone was except that two people had graduated, but I felt as though all the young people acted as though they were 14-15, so that wasn’t any help.
* The author kept tossing in big words that jarred me from my reading and didn’t seem to fit with the rest of the writing style.
* You don’t “bottle feed” baby parrots. I looked it up. You might hand feed them with a syringe, but that’s not bottle feeding. And there was no mention of WHY this would be done, and it took me a few minutes to figure out what creatures needed “bottle fed” since it wasn’t explained.
* If a character was going to a spelling bee, I would have thought she’d at least know some of the basic rules like asking for a definition before you spell anything. That part just seemed odd.
* I can NOT figure out how anyone could not hear or feel an airplane coming up behind you. And what was the matter with the pilot’s eyes? And you can’t get out of the way of something that is going to chop you up in a second. It takes longer than a second to react. That exaggeration, and the airplane’s amazing ability to jump back into the sky in a second or two after it was already almost on the ground if not touching the ground, made me give up. And should I inquire as to why the pilot then landed his plane without his engine on? Did it quit?
* There wasn’t enough setting to feel like I knew where the characters were.
* The whole fasting thing sounded very self-righteous or as though the person was trying to atone for her sin.

After that I decided to stop. There might be some good messages in this story, but I just couldn’t keep reading.

title: Not Worth Reading
text:
1.5 stars
I was hesitant about reading this book to start with because I'm not a big fan of medieval books. After I started reading I couldn't decide if this was really medieval or fantasy. There were no strange creatures or anything, but an island with a rain forest in the middle of it was rather strange, so I'm not sure what genre it belongs in.

The spiritual aspect was good, and for this reason I added the .5 to my rating.

The rest of the story? The writing was a bit on the amateur level. I got tired of the horses being referred to as "steeds" and I'm sorry, but I've never heard so much "sizzling lightning" before! And who wants to sleep on nothing but sand in your house? And a fisherman who goes to sea but "doesn't have his sea legs yet so his son has to take over." What sort of enemy writes a letter to tell that king he is going to attack him if he doesn't leave his castle and land? And of course there was the incredible princess who spend 8 days learning to sword fight, then spends 5 months not even touching a sword, yet is able to hold her own against a trained soldier at the end of those 5 months? Please!
But what gave me the biggest laugh, and I still haven't figured it out, was what kind of powder was in the "powder room" of this merchant ship. There was absolutely no mention of guns of any sort, yet the ship blew up when fire reached the "powder room." One family member suggested it was baking powder. Does that blow up? But another insisted it was powder for the princess to powder her nose. Either way it made me laugh.

Besides all the "exciting" things that happened, I didn't like the fact that for the most part the parents were non-existent. One father was mentioned once, and then not mentioned again for months! The mother was mentioned a few more times, but they weren't involved in the danger and excitement. Yes, the father went with the young people at the end, but he didn't get involved in the fight as he had to stay back with his daughter who was looking after the horses. It was up to the princess and a young man to fight the trained soldiers on their own.

Overall, this is not a book I will be reading again, nor can recommend it others. Sorry.

text:
It’s very difficult for me to make a case for buying any kind of decorating or organizing magazines or books as everything is on Pinterest or IG. Everyone has a blog for this stuff as well. This author had a large following on Pinterest and has tried to parlay that into a book. But there isn’t really anything new here unless you are interested in learning about her life. The tips are basic and old; putting pasta and grains in clear jars on your kitchen counters, using colorful picture frames on your white walls, making a signature cocktail for entertaining. There are hanging plants, antlers on walls to hang things (really???). Nothing I personally find inspiring or helpful.
This is a combo of memoir, self-help, and decorating. Most of it feels dated and regurgitated. Are you rustic or modern? Color psychology, color wheels? It is filler. And there are also 7 blank pages for notes at the end because she still needed more filler. Don’t waste your money. Check the 5 star reviews carefully, there are several that aren’t “verified purchase” and by people who don’t regularly review.

title: just awful
text: This book starts out fine, describing the friendship of Lara and Marija through school up to university in Yugoslavia. Then the war in Sarajevo breaks out and Lara marries an American and moved to the US and Marija who is Muslim, I think, moves to Sarajevo to work as a journalist. The author then skips through most of the war, its just occasionally mentioned when Lara calls Marija. Then when that part of the war ends, Lara discovers Marija's family is killed but Lara's sister tells her that Marija is still alive but was a victim of the rape camps. Again the story just skips along after Lara makes some calls and can't find her friend. Skip ahead to after 9/11, Lara meets a man at a conference in France and starts having an ongoing affair. There is more emotion in Lara when they meet up years later and he has to cut their tryst short because his mother had a stroke and he needs to return to Tunisia, than there is over the loss of her friend. Lara thinks the universe is conspiring to keep her and her lover apart and this is when I stopped reading. The writing and the story are just terrible as is the idea of using the horrible war in Bosnia and Serbia as a back drop for a story but casually skipping past everything. Maybe the author should try writing about something she knows and has experienced. I would not recommend this book to anyone.

text:
If I could give zero stars, I would. This is nothing but a preachy anti-abortion book. Seventeen year old girl's mother kills herself and girl (Nadia) is lost and drifts into a secret sexual relationship with local pastor's son (Luke) who is kind of a loser, gets pregnant and has abortion and goes off to college instead of having the baby of her slimy, secret boyfriend. Boyfriend told her to get an abortion, gave her money to get an abortion but then after she does he ditches her and says "maybe I didn't want you to abort our baby" and then she regrets it only because she now thinks of it as something that would have kept them together. But now her life is empty even though she goes off to college to fulfill her dream.
Her best friend ( Aubrey)knows nothing of this, latter falls in love with boyfriend, he becomes a better person because best friend is a great person and they get married. Girl comes back from law school because her dad was injured. Has an affair with boyfriend, he now wants to leave best friend. Girl says no but knows if she'd had her baby they'd be together (boyfriend grieves over aborted baby though didn't want it until he couldn't have it and obviously would have left her a single mother). Best friend ironically has trouble conceiving, finally does but has discovered the affair. Leaves the boyfriend but eventually goes back because of the baby but knows boyfriend doesn't really love her. Girl never marries, lives solitary existence. Boyfriend is son of a pastor, he and his wife paid for the abortion, once discovered years later, they are ostracized from the community.
Worst book ever, encouraging black women to just procreate and give up their dreams. Having a baby means you can hang on to your man. Writer should be shunned from literary community. Did she write this with Jerry Falwell? It's too bad the story and message were awful because she has some potential but no one wanted to tell her how terrible this book is but it didn't have to be. The parts where Nadia is attempting to learn more about her mom and the choices she made. Nadia wonders if her mom had regrets about getting pregnant at 19 and choosing to quit college and marry Nadia's father. Aubrey is very likable but never deals with her sexual abuse and is just reduced to a jealous wife in this story.
There is very little character development. The Mothers are the elder women of the church and they partly tell the story in an omniscient fashion but they don't really mother either of these girls, it's just a bad writing ploy to fill in the plot. Nadia and Aubrey are connected in that Nadia's mother kills herself though we never find out why and Aubrey's mother chooses her boyfriend over her daughter that he has been raping for years. Aubrey moves to Oceanside to live with her older sister and becomes involved with this church. But the author unimaginatively has them choose the guy over friendship.
The reader isn't even allowed to imagine what happens after the fairly abrupt ending. The Mothers let us know that Nadia is alone forever. What a horrible way to end a story. It doesn't have to have a happily ever after but this had nothing other than the idea that there is no redemption for girls who have abortions but life is fine for the guy that got her pregnant and encouraged the abortion. Just awful!!

title: Save your money
text: These are not Gothic tales. They are random vignettes of vaguely curious incidents. Shame on you Penguin Books. Not the first time you have done this. Gaskell is an excellent writer but these stories weren't meant to go together for you to profit by misleading marketing.

title: rape is rape even if victim is male!
text: This story started out very slowly. The main character, Stevie when she is stripping, Gwendolyn when she isn't, is working as a stripper to put herself through grad school. Her boyfriend, Leo is a sort of musician, who makes very little money. When we meet Stevie, she is stripping and letting one of her regulars touch even though it is against the rules. Then she has some erotic thoughts about another stripper. but then we discover Stevie is pregnant. She became pregnant when she was having sex with Leo while he was asleep. Apparently this is something she likes to do sometimes and I guess the author doesn't consider this to be rape. Which it is. And people would be outraged if it was reversed. I though Stevie was a pathetic pushover so I guess the fact that she is a rapist fits. It is about power not sex. About a quarter of the way through this book, I had enough. It is slow and boring and I'm concerned about what the author considers to be "erotic". Rape isn't it. Don't waste your money or time.

title: I seriously can't understand how anyone could like this book
text: Wow, I seriously can't understand how anyone could like this book. I am a third of the way in and I have to stop I am so disgusted. The two police inspectors are on their way to visit a convicted pedophile, discussing how sad that gay men are now accepted by society but pedophiles will always be outcasts. Then they go visit a pedophile to see if he can help them with their case. He is just a man they can't help but be charmed by even as he talks about his fantasies of abusing boys. He has a calendar with a picture of a hungry African child. The pedophile says he can dream but if he met the child in real life he'd certainly feed him first. The police are still charmed. I'm not reading anything by this author again. I'm just glad I didn't pay for this book but got it free through Kindle Unlimited. Just so wrong!!!

title: This is one of the worst books I have ever read
text: This is one of the worst books I have ever read. The story is obvious and ridiculous. The writing is of very poor quality and the random and overuse of italics just added insult to injury. Horrible, do not read!

title: disappointed
text: I'm not sure if it is a marketing issue or if I just have high expectations but to me this book seemed written for young adults or middle grade readers. It was too simplistic for me as I was expecting more. It isn't because the protagonist was an 11 year old boy. I've read plenty of great fiction with young characters. I just think Mark's young angst and otherworldly adventures would be better aimed towards a younger reading group.

title: Just could not get into it
text:
I tried to get through this book, I really did. I had heard great things about it and was looking forward to reading it.
But it just went so slow. I kept putting it down and picking it up again and having to reread pages. It certainly had potential but the plot just did not move. I wasn't able to engage with the characters quick enough for me to want to stay with the book despite it's slow pace. After about a month of this, I finally gave up. I hate to give up on a book unless the writing is bad but I just as if it wasn't going anywhere. I would not receommend this book.

title: Overdone and unsatisfying
text: This mystery starts with a mermaid reunion and a dead body floating in the water. It leads to crazy golf cart and boat chases, exposes mid-twentieth century racial segregation, and disputed parentage. There's plenty of juicy material. Unfortunately the plot is long and meandering, over-long, in fact. The bigger problem, however, is that most of this book operates in the realm of absurdity. Things are exaggerated for effect, but the effect is so extreme that the tone and prose are cringe-worthy. Everything is overdone. The dialogue is stilted. It feels like it is trying to sound 'southern,' but over-compensating. Every emotion is presented as overwhelming, there's a keystone cop level of physical comedy, and it is just not well done.

title: Give this one a pass
text: This book was a bit too saccharine for my tastes.  This is the sort of book where a few pages in you know that everything is going to turn out just fine.  I am by all accounts not a romance reader.  This book was presented as general fiction, and I was expecting more women's fiction than romance.  But it's a kind of sappy romance that's at the heart of this story.  Both mother and daughter find love, and all turns out a-ok.  I'm not inherently opposed to reading about love stories, but I hate knowing from the first few pages that everything's going to end up great.  In addition to those plot problems, the dialogue is limpid and the characters feel more like caricatures.

title: So many problems
text: If you like angsty teenagers, this is the book for you.  Said teenagers were far too angsty and out of touch for my taste.  It's about a student studying abroad in Lausanne, and it had so many of the hallmarks of books I liked when I was a young teenager, but have little use for as an adult.  The main character, Hadley, is the sort of faux innocent who is ripe to have her eyes opened and her innocence ripped away in Switzerland.  Hadley quickly gets herself a mysterious "bad girl" friend, and is totally infatuated.  Of course, there's also a boy.  Except it's not a boy, it's a man, and HE'S HER PROFESSOR.  Gross.  This whole book seemed to me like the sort of teenage fantasy that every adult knows is a bad idea.  For me, reading this book was a bad idea.

title: Can't recommend it
text: This is one of those women's fiction books that is shallow and underwhelming.  Claudia Silver, the entirely unlikable protagonist, is trying to figure out her life.  She doesn't get along with her family, especially mom, she's in all sorts of dysfunctional relationships, and she gets fired from her job.  This sounds like fairly classic women's novel plot. What makes other novels in the genre better than this one, is that they generally are written with a keen sense of humor or a protagonist with some redeeming qualities.  These things are absent in Claudia Silver.  In all honesty, pick a different book, I can find little to recommend in this one.

title: Awful
text:
This book doesn't work. It just doesn't work. Israel Armstrong travels to rural Northern Ireland to become a librarian. He arrives to find that the library has been closed. His job is to drive the bookmobile, but all of the books have been stolen. It becomes Israel's job to search for the books in a place full of bizarre and unfriendly locals.

There is so much about this book that doesn't work. Every instance of dialogue goes on for far too long. Israel is an absolutely pathetic character. He mopes around being miserable and refuses to do anything to improve his situation. The ending of the book is hardly an ending at all. This is one of those books that made me feel like I had wasted my time by reading it.

title: Annoying Characters
text:
This book features one of the most annoying protagonists I've encountered. Carolyn Emerson owns a pottery shop in a Vermont tourist town. When a dead body turns up in her backyard, the prime suspect is Carolyn's associate, who also happens to be her best friend's son. Convinced that the police are incompetent, Carolyn undertakes the task of solving the mystery.

The problem with all of this is that Carolyn is annoying. REALLY annoying. Her favorite activity is complaining. Carolyn complains about her husband, her customers, the local sheriff, among others. She's downright rude to the sheriff because she thinks he's incompetent (though there's no evidence of that in the book).

Then there's Carolyn's troupe of followers, "the firing squad," a group so devoted to pottery that they're willing to go all out to solve a dangerous mystery. They still take pottery breaks, though. Each of the members of the firing squad is a sort of stereotype, especially the ex-con with the heart of porcelain, and the tough, no-nonsense lady judge.

Honestly, life is too short for books like this. There are more entertaining ways to spend one's time.

title: Unpleasant
text:
I wanted to like this book, I really did. Instead, I found it to be quite offensive.

Loretta Crawford has lost significant weight after a gastric bypass. Life remains a struggle, as she ties to get her catering business off the ground and navigate the dating scene as a thinner woman. Loretta has a terrible self-image, and discovers that life as a thinner woman is not as easy as she expected.

The main problem with this book was the characters. They were at best unlikable, at worst offensive. The worst of the lot is Loretta, who expresses tremendous hatred of fat people. She is constantly criticizing overweight people, including her friends and family. Loretta genuinely believes that fat people do not deserve happiness, and she thinks that her overweight friends and family are disgusting, a sentiment she repeats ad nauseum. She expresses anger and disbelief when good things happen to her fat friends. Loretta Crawford is certainly not someone I would want to be my friend. Hatred of fat women seems to be coursing through this book. The male character who prefers to date fat women is repeatedly described as "a pervert," and treated much more harshly than the male characters who commit rape.

This book also employs a strange dialect. I've lived in the south. I'm used to heavy accents. I've never heard anything like this. Loretta calls everyone "Bub," "Buster," or "Buckaroo." I have no idea what the intention was, but I have yet to hear a Texan speak lie this.

I honestly cannot recommend this book.

title: Problematic in many ways
text: Oh, where to begin? Possibly the most important thing to state for potential readers of this book is that this is not a book about tea. Rather, it's a self-help book that's masquerading as a tea book. There's preciously little information about tea in here, but more on that later. The basic premise of the book is that ideas and principles of tea can be used to affect positive change in your life. Each of these principles comprises a chapter (or "nourishing blend" to use the author's lexicon) and is linked with a similar principle that one can apply to one's life. Some of them sort of work, for example, not all tea should be brewed with boiling water is paired with the idea that living in a constant state of stress is toxic. Other of the principles, however, seem to bear little resemblance to the tea principle in question. Make sure each cup you serve has the same taste and temperature doesn't seem to bear a strong resemblance to seeking balance in life. And that particular point leads to one of the larger issues in the book. There are a wealth of inaccuracies and misinformation concerning tea in these pages. In a number of cases the author states things that are wrong or unresearched. Making sure each cup of tea has the same flavor every time? Most frequent drinkers of green and white teas are well aware that these teas stand up to, and indeed are expected, to go through multiple steepings (particularly if brewing with a gaiwan), and the entire point of the multiple steepings is that the flavors change slightly with each. A number of other examples are found in the health benefits of tea chapter. The author refers to rooibos as "the only naturally caffeine-free black tea." Sorry, but no. Rooibos is an entirely different plant. It does not come from the Camiellia Sinesis plant; it is not black tea. Or what about "lemon tea," which the author describes as "mainly sugar with tea solids." Ummmmm, does she mean Nestea? Seriously? In a book about making and enjoying tea? She refers to it as energizing, in a chapter on tea and health no less. At this point I've started to wonder how much of the issue is bad writing, and how much is lack of knowledge. I suspect there's some of both. The author's bio indicates that she has written other self-help books, but there's not much I can praise on the self-help side either. Most of the suggestions are basic, standard, self-help filler (the challenges and disappointments give life texture, seek balance, etc. etc. etc.) In sum, the tea theme is never well-wedded to the self-help content of this book, making it seem contrived at best. The research, factual, and writing problems only add to the more fundamental problems. The one positive thing I can say about this book is that the pictures are beautiful, but beyond that, there is little to recommend here.

title: waste
text: Slow, painful read for me. It never takes me this long to finish a book. Wish I would not have wasted my time.

title: did not enjoy
text: I found this book difficult to get into. It's one of those writing styles where passages start in the middle of something or apropos of nothing and expect you to read on to figure out what's what. I also found the writing choppy, awkward and difficult to read. Actions and events are stretched out as if paid by the word. Wordy. It was a struggle to read and I just didn't enjoy it.

title: American Kingpin
text:
I read a lot of nonfiction. I know it can be dry, but a good author can liven up the subject matter. The Silk Road seemed like a really interesting subject to me, but I struggled with Bilton’s take on it in AMERICAN KINGPIN.

The book reads like a crime thriller. That’s not a genre I like; I personally would have preferred a straightforward recounting. Not a pseudo thriller by a writer who thinks he has a gift for description. I don’t want dramatized details of how a mail sorter works, or his daily routine. I don’t want made up conversations between Ulbricht and his girlfriend. And so on, for the entire book.

I wanted the facts, laid out in a clear manner. Not … this.

title: Bright Burning Stars
text:
I’ll read just about any “ballet book” but I was super disappointed with BRIGHT BURNING STARS. There’s a lack of development in everything from the characters to the setting to ballet itself. The summary makes the book sound far more magical and compelling than it is.

Marine and Kate have spent most of their lives pursuing a position in the Opera’s corps de ballet; at the end of this school year, only one girl in the class will be chosen. But why do they dance? Marine has musicality and a promise to her dead brother…? Kate’s mother abandoned her and for some reason she took up dance…? I don’t understand. I also don’t understand why, if Kate is so driven to be the chosen girl, she becomes boy crazy and has sex without thinking of the possible consequences. That whole storyline, with the school’s beekeeper??? stepping into help and a lack of reflection or impact… eh. Why go there if you aren’t going to examine it?

And the Demigod thing… I find it hard to believe a girl who has spent years working towards a goal would suddenly “fall in love.” I could see wanting to be his partner for rankings advancement, but Kate felt like a kid to me instead of a teenager.

BRIGHT BURNING STARS could have taken place anywhere. I never really felt like the book was set in France. Sprinkling some French phrases does not make me think of Paris. And how in the heck did American Kate make it into such a prestigious French school?

As for the dancing sections: mentioning the name of a move does not allow me to picture it, or to know how the characters are moving. Sure, I like ballet books, but I don’t know what every single term means. For the longest time, I was confused about the woolen overalls the characters wore, because the author never described them! Amplify that confusion with dance terms like “soubresaut.”

The more I think about BRIGHT BURNING STARS, the more questions I have, which is frustrating for me as a reader.

title: Age of Swords (The Legends of the First Empire #2)
text:
Two years ago, I was super excited after finishing the first book in the new Legends of the First Empire series. I couldn’t wait to start the second, and I was excited to know that the author had already finished all the books in the series. These days, I’m picky about starting epic fantasy series and prefer the chance that they’ll actually be completed.

When I started AGE OF SWORDS, I wondered what I’d been thinking, to rate the first book so highly. I could not get into AGE OF SWORDS. There was no recap, so I couldn’t remember what had happened previously, or why I should care that giants were suddenly attacking the village and so on. The writing and dialogue were painfully dry. I don’t mind basic writing is the story and/or characters are good, but absolutely nothing kept my attention in this book.

title: Hurricane Child
text:
Sometimes I read a book and go to look at other reviews to see if anyone else felt the same way I did. I’m often a black sheep when it comes to disliking books most other people enjoy. HURRICANE CHILD is no exception.

My younger self would have given up on this book without finishing. Caroline is bullied mercilessly by other students and her teacher, her mother has abandoned her (and the reason why, holy cow), and has “inappropriate” feelings for the only girl who is friendly to her. I say “inappropriate” because of course her feelings aren’t, but again she’s mocked for her feelings.

I felt like the author packed too much into the book to fully examine any of the issues or storylines. The ending left me shaking my head and going “What?”

title: When Dimple Met Rishi
text:
At first, I liked WHEN DIMPLE MET RISHI. I respected Dimple’s determination to buck her mother’s expectations for a good Indian girl and follow her dreams of a career in app development. She even convinced her parents to let her go to a summer program for coders. Only to find out when she gets there that her parents have tried setting up a marriage for her, and the guy? He’s at the camp too.

After a few chapters, this book turned into a standard YA contemporary romance with a bit of Indian culture. Despite her dislike of romance and other girls, Dimple quickly focuses on Rishi. The actual purpose of the summer program fades way, way into the background, which disappointed me. I really felt like Dimple deserved to lose, since she and Rishi seemed to put more time into practicing for the talent show and making out than they did working on her app. I couldn’t believe the speed with which their relationship progressed. Basically insta-love, though at least Rishi was somewhat better than a lot of guys in YA. By the time I finished the book, I was disappointed in the whole thing, except for the few encounters between Dimple/Rishi and their parents.

title: Hullmetal Girls
text:
I’d heard good things about the author’s previous books, so I was excited to read HULLMETAL GIRLS. That excitement quickly faded the further I got into the book.

I thought I was getting a science fiction story of superpowered soldiers with implants, and maybe even an f/f relationship between Aisha and Key. Instead, there was a lot of body horror, which is not something I like at all, an extremely slow moving plot, and a few other issues.

If you want a book where a girl is trapped with an exo in her head and a surgically modified body and doesn’t know why, HULLMETAL GIRLS is for you. If you want a book full of science fiction and adventure, this book isn’t for you.

title: Gilded Cage (Dark Gifts #1)
text:
Commoners serving “slavedays” and magical elite ruling England initially drew me to GILDED CAGE. But the execution, slow pace, and multiple characters couldn’t keep me interested. The book was a chore for me to read.

There was a serious lack of worldbuilding or common sense. I can’t get past the Hadley family thinking they’d get to stay together if they served their slavedays as a family. I never understood why anyone would serve their days early, rather than waiting until they were near death. The Hadley family seemed to be comfortable enough (even with the few disadvantages the author mentioned) so it didn’t make sense to me. Even for a fantasy, I need the bones of a story to make sense or I question everything.

title: October
text: I’ve read textbooks that are more exciting than OCTOBER. I was originally interested in the book because it’s described as “the story of the Russian Revolution.” Perhaps naively, I expected an engaging story. What I found was a boring book, overly wordy yet low on actual information. After every chapter, I could barely understand what I’d just read. Maybe if the author had focused on a few important people rather than trying to give so much overarching (and often unimportant) details, I’d have had an easier time following or staying interested in this.

title: The Waking Land (The Waking Land #1)
text:
The longer I slogged through THE WAKING LAND, the less I could remember why the book caught my eye in the first place. The more I read, the less I cared about anything.

The worldbuilding was really lacking. The first few times Ida was mentioned, I thought it was a person! You can’t just toss country names around without establishing any background for them. Elanna’s inner monologue was painful to read. So much going back and forth. I started skimming through her thoughts because it was the same thing over and over again. This book could have been really condensed and not lost anything.

title: Sugar
text: SUGAR is supposed to be a cute, culinary romance. The food descriptions and time in the kitchen were good, but that was it. Unfortunately, there was no spark between Charlie and Kai for me, and honestly, I would have preferred to see Charlie pursue her career -- the career she worked a decade to build -- rather than chase after a guy she’s known for three months. I also didn’t find the reality TV angle to be worked in that well. Charlie’s judgmental attitudes on everything from television to bruising fruit grated on me.

title: In the Name of the Family
text:
IN THE NAME OF THE FAMILY is a continuation of Dunant’s tale of the Borgias. I didn’t know this when I started the book, but it follows BLOOD & BEAUTY. That said, it’s not necessary to have read that, but I think if you like the author’s style, you’ll want to read both in order.

I really struggled with this book. The Borgias are a fascinating family, but in the author’s hands, they were drier than dirt. Only Lucrezia’s passages were halfway alive. I feel the author did a much better job with her perspective than Cesare’s or Pope Alexander’s. Instead of making me feel like I was in Renaissance Italy, much of the book felt like regurgitations of research.

I want historical fiction to excite me and get me invested in a time period I don’t know much about. IN THE NAME OF THE FAMILY nearly put me to sleep several times.

title: Furyborn (Empirium #1)
text:
FURYBORN is a door stopper kickoff to a new YA fantasy trilogy. Books structured with one character in the past and one in the present normally don’t appeal to me, but here I liked the initial descriptions for both Rielle and Eliana. I’m on a big royalty kick lately, so I was especially excited for Rielle’s chapters.

The prologue/beginning was the best part of FURYBORN for me, but in a way, also the worst part. The prologue captured my interest. I instantly wanted to know more about Rielle, her powers, her world, the angels, etc. But the prologue spoils Rielle’s fate. I already knew she would pass the trials, so I didn’t care too much about how she passed them or her feelings for Audric.

I was so bored reading FURYBORN. If I’m going to slog my way through a 500 page book, I do not want to be bored! The book was rushrushrush action yet it didn’t feel like a lot happened. Looking back, I just don’t care about the story or the characters.

title: Forever On
text:
I’m not the biggest fan of social media, so I was intrigued by the idea of Phluttr, a social network that basically knows everything about a user. It knows where you are, what you’re doing, who you’re talking to, etc.

Only … FOREVER ON is a book that meanders all over the place and was a chore to read. When I was a hundred pages in, I wondered when the heck the story would actually start. I’m a story/character reader rather than a concept reader, so I just wanted something to happen! The writing itself didn’t click with me -- the descriptions are odd, there’s misogyny, and the dare at the beginning was just silly.

title: The Evaporation of Sofi Snow (The Evaporation of Sofi Snow #1)
text: I have no clue what I read in THE EVAPORATION OF SOFI SNOW. The author describes almost nothing, which meant I was constantly flipping back to see what I’d missed because I was confused. There was very little background information or worldbuilding, which also left me confused and feeling like I was missing vital details. The characters are bland and underdeveloped, which was the final straw for me, as I’m a character-driven reader.

title: Definitions of Indefinable Things
text:
I liked the first few chapters of DEFINITIONS OF INDEFINABLE THINGS. I liked Reggie’s voice and sense of deadpan humor.

But then Snake seriously entered the novel, and I just couldn’t get over how he acted. He basically bullies his way into a date with Reggie and has no remorse when she learns he’s the father of another girl’s unborn baby. The ensuing conversation between Reggie and Snake felt super unrealistic for teenagers (or anyone of any age, really). Anytime Snake showed up, the book took a negative turn for me, making it a chore to read their pretentious conversations (and Snake’s smarmy behavior).

title: The Fandom
text:
I liked the idea of THE FANDOM. Characters getting sucked into the world of their favorite fandom? Sign me up. But within pages, the characters and writing had me cringing and wondering why I’d fallen into another trap book with a cool idea and horrible execution.

First, The Gallows Dance is … I found it to be really silly. Naturally, Violet has a Very Big Crush on the main guy character, so much that she can’t bear his picture to have a thumbtack hole in it. Then after her presentation, Violet proceeds to have horribly mean and catty thoughts about her best friend. Violet’s narration was painful to read from the start and didn’t get any better.

THE FANDOM combines a bunch of YA tropes, mediocre writing, and underdeveloped characters.

title: My Life with Bob
text:
I was initially drawn to MY LIFE WITH BOB because I too have kept track of the books I’ve read since I was 8 or 9.

But I found this book to be super pretentious and not really about the books the author read at all, but a memoir with some book titles scattered about. I believe the idea of this book started as an essay for the NYT Book Review and was then expanded. It’s my belief it should have stayed an essay, because I felt like the author was just filling the pages by trying to make herself sound like a sophisticated reader who, even at a young age thought librarians would look down on her for reading “juvenile” lit like Judy Blume.

title: Defy the Stars (Constellation #1)
text:
I honestly can’t think of much to say about DEFY THE STARS. I found it to be incredibly bland, a romance in space dressed up with very little science. I didn’t connect with Noemi or Abel at all, the plot was boring, and I didn’t buy the romance.

This is my second or third Claudia Gray book and by this point, I just don’t think her writing style or ideas are for me, no matter how cool the summary sounds.

title: Doctor Benjamin Franklin's Dream America
text:
I’ve enjoyed alternate history books in the past, especially when they’re mashed up with fantasy or science fiction. I usually find it interesting to see the different spins authors put on such eras. So, I was intrigued by the idea of the Founding Fathers having the Internet and social media.

Only to actually start the book and wonder what the heck I’d gotten myself into. Each chapter is about the death of one of the men who signed the Declaration of Independence. I guess they’re dying because of their connection to the Cloud, which is somehow replicating and creating worms and a plague? And then it gets crazier.

To me, this is the sort of book where the author takes a bunch of ideas and concepts he wants to explore, tosses them in a hat, and pulls stuff out at random to include in a chapter. I couldn’t suspend my disbelief enough to rationalize the Internet, smartphones, and computers existing but medicine still being extremely primitive, horses the main mode of transportation, etc.

title: The Tethered Mage (Swords and Fire #1)
text:
THE TETHERED MAGE is less magical fantasy than it is a story about politics with a clueless pawn.

Lady Amalia, daughter of one of the most influential, powerful women in the Empire, accidentally captures a magic user. Literally captures Zaira by slipping a jess (like for a falcon) onto her wrist to keep her from setting the entire city on fire. Zaira, who spent her life living on the streets to avoid the fate of being a Falcon, is captured by rich, privileged Amalia.

Obviously there’s some problems with the premise, but all the same, I liked it and hoped this would be the start of a great fantasy.

Only to be bored and wonder when actual magic would show up again.

The book is from Amalia’s POV, which means a lot of politics and fumbling about. Zaira is trotted out every now and then. Now, I like politics in fantasy, but Amalia was clueless. I expected her mother would’ve trained her better since Amalia is her heir, but nope! What’s character development? Then there’s an instalove romance, which is a peeve of mine. THE TETHERED MAGE read like a lackluster YA fantasy, with a lack of everything.

title: Tempests and Slaughter (The Numair Chronicles #1)
text:
I still remember the magic of reading the Alanna quartet for the first time. Tamora Pierce books will always have a place on my bookshelf, which is partly why it pains me to rate one of her books so low.

But I struggled and struggled and struggled to read TEMPESTS AND SLAUGHTER. Arram is the bestest mage student ever, so talented that he’s continually favored and moved up at the academy, where he becomes friends with a prince and pretty girl, etc etc.

Absolutely nothing captured my interest. Normally I adore all sorts of little details about a world, especially in a school setting, but I was just so bored here. Where is the conflict? What is this book about? Surely more than Arram’s daily life.

title: Caraval (Caraval #1)
text:
CARAVAL bored me to tears.

Because of all the over-the-top and extremely flowery descriptions of everything, it took 75 pages to get to the Caraval. Scarlett apparently sees colors or feelings, which resulted in sentences packed full of colors of every shade of the rainbow, with words strung together because they sounded unusual.

What did I just say? I don’t quite know, but that was what reading the book felt like to me. Sometimes I like poetic descriptions, but not All Of The Time. Purple prose does not make good writing.

Scarlett is incredibly naive, there’s parent abuse for shock value, a lack of worldbuilding/magic, and there’s instalove. I know this is a book that had a lot of hype behind it, but I just couldn’t get into CARAVAL at all.

title: The Bear and the Nightingale (Winternight #1)
text:
I should have really liked THE BEAR AND THE NIGHTINGALE. Russian-inspired fantasy? Rebellious main character? Old gods? Check, check, and check.

Yet I could barely keep my eyes open while I read. The book plodded along at a glacial pace. The first quarter of the book is scene setting/backstory. There are maybe five sections from Vasya’s POV. Instead nearly everyone gets a chance, from the new stepmother to her brothers and even a monk. I think the author was trying to show the world from all angles, but it fell very flat for me.

I was not enthralled by this book, or even interested. I just wanted something to happen instead of turning page after page and waiting for plot to show up.

title: Carve the Mark (Carve the Mark #1)
text:
While I didn’t like Veronica Roth’s first YA series (Divergent), I thought I’d give her books another chance with the start of a new series.

CARVE THE MARK was a snoozefest. Akos’ perspective was as boring as his frozen world. Crya’s perspective was a little better, possibly more engaging because her chapters are in her POV, compared to third-person POV for Akos.

I feel like I read at least half the book before anything interesting happened, which -- I don’t have the patience or desire to sit through boring books full of nothing anymore. The writing, especially for Akos, was so juvenile and stilted. Even when he and his brothers were in danger, I wasn’t excited or invested in their survival. The author didn’t bring the action to life, or even have much of a spark to keep me wanting to read.

title: The Black Witch (The Black Witch Chronicles #1)
text:
These days, if a book doesn’t hook me within 75 pages, I’m outta there. Making it so far in THE BLACK WITCH was a chore. By page 75, practically nothing had happened. For a book that’s 600 pages … look, I like fat fantasy novels a lot, but the author has to intrigue me so I keep turning the pages. Laurie Forest did not intrigue me in the slightest.

It took 75 pages to get Elloren off her family’s farm and into the city, where something will presumably happen. Maybe. If those events don’t get bogged down in overwrought descriptions of every little thing. I was particularly tired of learning the skin color of every single servant and person Elloren met.

I’ve read enough of the online commentary and controversy around THE BLACK WITCH to know there’s a lot of bigotry, casual racism, and worse, and that the author wanted to show Elloren’s realization that what her people think about other races is wrong. I skimmed ahead myself and saw plenty of examples of horrible behavior and thoughts. The intent and execution are so far apart, I couldn’t take much more of the book.

title: Grace and Fury
text:
GRACE AND FURY takes a mishmash of popular dystopian scenarios, throws two sisters into the mix, and hopes for the best. A lot of readers will enjoy the mix of tropes, but I wasn’t one of them.

Serina was raised to be a Grace, to be picked by the Heir to be one of his courtesans; she’s fine with this direction for her life. Her sister Nomi is to be her handmaiden; she’s not fine with this choice. Nomi wants to read, to pick her own job, and to choose her own husband one day, all choices forbidden to women in their country.

I read half the book, went to have a snack, and didn’t care one bit about finishing the rest of it. The characters are caricatures. Nomi is the feisty one who never learns to think. After having her sister thrown in the worst jail possible, you think she’d learn to shut her mouth. Nope. Not Nomi. Heir Malachi is the brooding, scary prince who lusts for power. His brother Asa is the charming spare who wants to help Nomi.

I had problems with almost everything from the lust triangle to the lack of worldbuilding. I had so many “I can’t believe what I’m reading” moments, which I can’t mention because I’d spoil too much. I think I get what the author was trying to do by showing how a “choice” isn’t a choice unless there’s real options, but overall the book didn’t work for me.

title: In Darkling Wood
text: IN DARKLING WOOD just did not capture my attention. I made it a quarter of the way through the book before I gave up in utter boredom -- I didn’t want to know more about any of the characters, the plot, or why there were letters from 1918 scattered in. I felt like I was reading an outline rather than a fleshed out story.

title: Gork, the Teenage Dragon
text:
I was intrigued by the summary for GORK, THE TEENAGE DRAGON, but I noped right out of the book itself after a painful 50 pages. I didn’t expect the mashup of fantasy and sci-fi (dragons in space), or that Gork would have such an annoying voice.

Comedy can be hit or miss for me, and here it was very much a miss. I felt like the author was trying waaaaay too hard to be funny and clever. To me, this book was nothing like the comparisons—it’s definitely no HITCHHIKER’S GUIDE TO THE GALAXY.

If I never read the words “my scaly green” again, it’ll be too soon. The writing was super repetitive. I also felt like the author was trying to outdo himself every chapter, with more and more outrageous events or information. By the time I made it to Gork’s quest to find Runcita, the female dragon he wants to make his mate/queen, I wasn’t invested or interested in the slightest.

I probably sound like I’m nitpicking, but I can’t remember the last time I thought “WTF” so much while trying to read a book.

title: The Visionary Mayan Queen: Yohl Ik'Nal of Palenque
text:
I thought I would like this book because I generally like historical fiction, especially books that are set in time periods outside of the popular ones. And Mayan history has always interested me.

But no matter how hard I tried, I could not get into THE VISIONARY MAYAN QUEEN: YOHL IK’NAL OF PALENQUE. These days, if a book doesn’t hook me in the first 50 pages, I’m likely to give it up, and with this one, I struggled to make 50 pages.

The author clearly did a ton of research to make the book read authentically, and I like a lot of detail, but here I was awash in a deluge of minute details. I don’t need to know what every random person is wearing, or how every single Mayan calendar is calculated. The writing style was too dense for me.

I honestly have no idea what the book is supposed to be about, because in the handful of chapters I read, I could barely pick out the story or main characters amidst the author trying to make sure I knew every tiny detail.

title: No Good Deed
text:
I was originally drawn to NO GOOD DEED because Ellie is an archer. I bought a recurve bow a few years ago and really enjoy it, so I thought, here’s a main character I have something in common with from the start of the book.

But after the first chapter at an archery meet, the book didn’t keep my interest. Even when Ellie was mysteriously pulled back in time to medieval England, I was just skimming the pages for something interesting until I finally gave up.

The pacing was sloth slow. Even though Ellie is caught immediately after going back in time, she escapes. And then she’s caught. And then she escapes. I think. I wanted something of consequence to happen, rather than Ellie luckily being rescued by a knight on horseback.

title: The Wearle (Erth Dragons #1)
text:
THE WEARLE is my first Chris d’Lacey book. I’ve seen a lot of The Last Dragon Chronicles, but that has seven books, so I thought I’d start off with a new series of his. But after finishing THE WEARLE, I doubt I would try anything else of his.

THE WEARLE opens with a cast of characters; I was confused right away because every dragon’s name starts with “G.” I have a good memory for big fantasy casts, but I had to keep referencing the cast of dragons because I couldn’t tell many of them apart. There’s also a lot of made-up words, such as “whinney” for “horse.” Most are easy enough to figure out with context clues; there is a glossary at the end, but I didn’t realize until I finished the book.

This book is aimed at grades 3-7, ages 8-12. Now look, I’m the last person to advocate censoring books for kids, but there’s so much gory violence and senseless murder in this book! Limbs are charred with dragonfire. Eyes get poked out. Someone is impaled. And that’s off the top of my head.

This book also jumps into a lot of different heads and stories. I liked it more until humans or “Hom” showed up. Almost all of the Hom were … violent jerks. Ren was the exception, but I can’t believe how much that boy survived.

title: Warcross (Warcross #1)
text:
Oh, WARCROSS. How I wanted to like you.

WARCROSS is a book with a lot of hype behind it, and as a player of MMORPGs, I was hoping to love it. No book I’ve read yet has completely captured the sense of living to play a game.

WARCROSS didn’t do it for me. For starters, it takes over two hundred pages to show a real Warcross match. For the first half of the book, the reader is constantly told how much people play the game, how they practically live in the virtual world to escape real life, how important Warcross is, etc etc. BUT WHAT IS THE ACTUAL GAME? When the book finally gets there, the Warcross match is the best part of the book.

I gave up on the book soon after reading the game, because nothing else was holding my attention. There’s a lack of worldbuilding/too much hand waving over how the technology works, an insta-love romance reminiscent of Fifty Shades of Grey, and boring filler like reminders about Emika’s rainbow hair, tattoos, or tragic past.

title: Daughters of the Storm (Blood and Gold #1)
text:
Five sisters teaming up against their stepbrother to save their kingdom?

Sign. Me. Up.

Unfortunately, DAUGHTERS OF THE STORM didn’t work for me. I was excited for a fantasy book with so many female leads, and inspiration from Norse mythology. But I barely made it to page 75 before giving up because the book was just not catching my attention.

By then, I still hadn’t met all of the sisters. The sisters I did meet were … one dimensional. I didn’t particularly care for Bluebell, Ash, or Rose, but I don’t always need likable characters. But I DO need a book that moves along at a good clip, rather than saturating me with unnecessary details and a meandering story. By page 75, only Bluebell had made it back home to her dying father’s side, and I just did not care what came next, because the author didn’t hook me enough.

title: How to Be a Supervillain
text:
HOW TO BE A SUPERVILLAIN was a snoozefest for me. Sure, I’m above the intended age range, but I expected a funny book about a kid learning to be a supervillain. Instead, the book is full of Victor’s very unfunny attempts to be bad.

There’s a mix of text and illustrations in the book; I wasn’t expecting this and didn’t care for the sketchy art style. So many illustrations probably make this unsuitable for reading out loud.

Because he’s a good kid, too good to be bad, Victor’s parents apprentice him to the Smear, a supervillain whose power is to make a mess. I almost put the book down at that point, because I just wasn’t getting the humor or the story. I powered through, but I honestly can’t tell you what the book was about today, because it bored me that much.

title: The Call
text:
I tend to enjoy books where the Sidhe are as creepy as they are in the old legends. Wicked, magical, and ruthless, the Sidhe in THE CALL have isolated Ireland and turned it into their own personal hunting ground. Only 1 in 10 teenagers survive the Call, when they are sucked into the Grey Land for a day, or three minutes and four seconds on Earth.

But THE CALL wasn’t a book for me. It was one I struggled to finish. The biggest reason the book didn’t work for me is that I’m a character driven reader, and I just didn’t care about any of the characters at all. I can barely remember most of their names. Nessa did stand out slightly, because she has polio but didn’t let it stop her even though everyone else thought she was useless. Everyone else, though, meh. I have to care about the people I’m reading about, but the author didn’t succeed in making me worry about anyone or care about them. Even when a character was killed, I just wanted to see what new gruesome way they’d die.

I also really disliked the whole Conor obsessing/wanting to hurt Nessa thing, because I am so sick of guys wanting to do horrible things to girls because their obsession isn’t returned. I also didn’t like how Nessa just kinda sat back and let her life be in danger from Conor because she wanted to see another boy she was crushing on. For a girl who wanted to survive so badly, it felt like she just sat back for a lot of the book.

The writing style in THE CALL also contributed to my lackluster feelings about it. It’s written present tense, third person, with some head jumping. Sometimes I wasn’t sure whose perspective I was in, so I’d have to go back and reread. Head jumping like that is a big peeve of mine.

title: The Crown's Game (The Crown's Game #1)
text:
THE CROWN’S GAME has a lot of things I enjoy: a historical setting, magic, a strong and determined female character, and a duel to the death. But I didn’t enjoy the book as much as I’d hoped due to the lackluster romance and sloooooow pacing.

THE GOOD:
--The author was very good at describing the setting and the magic of the enchanters. I could easily see imperial Russia and picture the fantastical magic Vika and Nikolai created.

THE BAD:
--Maybe this is just me, but when two characters are in a duel to the death, playing the Crown’s Game for for their life and to be the tsar’s Imperial Enchanter, I expect a little more… danger. And I guess there’s a little danger, because they make an attempt on each other’s life. But the attempts stop very quickly, because Nikolai and Vika forget everything at stake when their magic touches each other. Cue insta-love and using the game to woo each other and renovate Saint Petersburg, because *that* will impress the tsar.

--The romance. I’m usually picky on romance, but this mess of a love triangle nearly had me fleeing for the hills. I need to believe the characters are attracted to each other. The author just can’t tell me they are because they fell in love at first sight. Here’s what Pasha, the heir, has to say about Vika, “If there were ever a girl a man could fall in love with without knowing, it would be Vika (p. 320, ARC).” Sorry, that doesn’t work for me.

--The magic has very few rules. Yes, I know this is fantasy, but magic has to have a system. As far as I can tell, the enchanters can do almost anything they can imagine. Vika is more talented with the elements and Nikolai with mechanics, but that’s because of their upbringing.

--The story itself was boring and slow. For me, this was partly because there were so many POVs in the book. For example, I would have preferred to read about Vika creating the island, rather than Nikolai waking up and finding it. Because there were so many POVs, good story bits were often just dropped into the text, rather than getting to see them happen. And then that ending… I won’t spoil it, but there’s no way I’ll read book two.

As you can see, THE CROWN’S GAME didn’t live up to the hype for me.

Disclaimer: I received a copy of this book from the publisher in exchange for an honest review.

title: Reliance, Illinois
text:
From the summary, I thought I’d really enjoy RELIANCE, ILLINOIS. Madelyn’s mother, Rebecca, insists Madelyn pretend to be her younger sister, not her daughter, so Rebecca can marry. Madelyn puts up with the charade for a while, but when given the chance to work for the mysterious Miss Rose, the town’s most infamous woman, she goes for it. That all hooked me, as did the mention that Miss Rose is a suffragette who helps provide black market birth control to the town’s women.

I talk a lot about books. But RELIANCE, ILLINOIS is a book I have very little to say about. I have no freaking clue what the book is really about. It’s literary fiction with a thin layer of historical fiction on top. I do not enjoy literary fiction at all, so if I’d known that beforehand, I wouldn’t have read this book.

I can’t figure out what story the author is trying to tell in RELIANCE, ILLINOIS. Madelyn isn’t a particularly likeable character, but that’s the one thing that didn’t bother me. Everything else… there are so many plotlines, many of which are unresolved (a big peeve of mine). That tantalizing bit about black market birth control? It turns out to be a tiny thing. Why did Miss Rose even pick Madelyn in the first place? The writing style threw me too; I can’t remember how many times I had to reread a paragraph to figure out the meaning.

title: Reign of Shadows (Reign of Shadows #1)
text:
REIGN OF SHADOWS is the first in a new YA series by Sophie Jordan. It’s set in a world of darkness where an eclipse has reigned for 17 years. The rightful princess of the land lives in a tower hidden in the forest, waiting for daylight to come back to reclaim her kingdom.

I liked the idea behind REIGN OF SHADOWS -- the world of darkness and the hidden princess. Unfortunately, the author didn’t deliver on anything, from worldbuilding to an actual story. Why’s the world dark? Because of an eclipse. That’s the entirety of the explanation. Where do the dwellers come from? Underground. How can a blind girl run through a forest like she’s Usain Bolt, without tripping or falling?

Yeah. Luna is blind, which could have been very cool, but the author turned her into Superwoman with no basis. I understand that one’s other senses do amp up, but Luna’s abilities are unbelievably superhuman.

Then there’s Fowler, the bad-boy love interest who is incredibly broken. He’s lost too much in life to care about anyone. But Luna’s love fixes him in a matter of days. Every single one of their kisses is good enough to cause a volcano to erupt.

Lastly, what the heck happened in REIGN OF SHADOWS? The book read more like a prequel to a series than a real first installment. I just finished the book, and I’m trying to remember what happened… not much.

I’ve read one of the author’s other books -- UNINVITED -- and had many of the same issues with that book. So, I’m thinking Sophie Jordan just isn’t an author for me. She has cool ideas, but the execution is off and there are just too many cliche tropes in her books for me to enjoy them.

title: Black City Saint
text:
I’m a fan of Richard A. Knaak’s books in the World of Warcraft realm, so I was eager to try out some of his original work. BLACK CITY SAINT sounded quite intriguing, with its mashup of noir, fae, dragons, and 1920s Chicago.

Unfortunately, I was bored by 97% of the book. Every time I picked it up to read, I kept putting it back down and looking at Instagram or Twitter or any other diversion I could find. Part of the reason was the stilted, overly formal writing style, which I think the author used in an attempt to make the book feel more 1920s-ish. But I also know that Knaak can overwrite, so that was part of it as well. I hate when I have to reread sentences 2 or 3 times to figure out what they mean.

My second problem with BLACK CITY SAINT? Nick spends the first half of the book going all over Chicago for no real reason at all. The first few chapters were cool, because they introduced Nick, the dragon, and the author’s version of fae, but then nothing happens. Nick goes here, he goes there, he keeps secrets, he goes here, he goes there, he keeps more secrets.

Third, the author tried so hard to make Nick’s enemy the typical tricky fae lord that I was confused by all the double-crossing, lying, trickery, and secrets. Nick was continually surprised by the villain, which I found hard to believe considering they’d fought before, and he had more than a thousand years of experience. And because he kept getting tricked by Oberon, I found it even more hard to believe that he would eventually triumph.

Fourth, why was Claryce even in BLACK CITY SAINT? All she wanted to do was follow Nick into danger and Nick wanted her to stay behind and be safe. She never listened and he loved her even more for it? Claryce played practically no role in the book, other than a prop to be moved around until the very end. I thought it was lazy the author relied on her past incarnations to develop hints of a relationship between them, instead of just developing it in the here and now.

All of that said, I did like the dragon in BLACK CITY SAINT. Knaak is good with dragons.

Overall, I think BLACK CITY SAINT tried to combine too many things and genres, and tried too hard to be clever. There were some cool ideas, but the execution was off for me.

title: Sisi: Empress on Her Own (Sisi #2)
text:
I didn’t know that SISI: EMPRESS ON HER OWN is actually a follow-up to THE ACCIDENTAL EMPRESS. I learned that only after I went to Goodreads and searched for the author. The summary for SISI gives no clue that it’s a sequel, which is an unfortunate omission.

Because if I’d read THE ACCIDENTAL EMPRESS first, I might have enjoyed SISI more. SISI starts in 1868, with the empress reflecting how much more she enjoys life in Hungary than Vienna. I thought it was an odd place to start her story, as I wanted to know just how she influenced the Austro-Hungarian Compromise, since she didn’t seem to care much about government. I realize now that the events of her early years were covered in THE ACCIDENTAL EMPRESS.

But even if I had read the first book about Sisi’s life, I might not have liked SISI anymore. I wasn’t a fan of the author’s writing style or her uninspiring attempts to bring Sisi to life. I thought the Wikipedia entry was more exciting and educational. I like my historical fiction to educate me, or at least stimulate an interest in a new-to-me figure or time period. If I went off Pataki’s Sisi, I’d think she was a vapid, selfish, irresponsible woman who preferred to fantasize about horses and unavailable men. And yes, Sisi might have been all of that to some extent, but bring something new to her story? Or why not delve into her psyche, really dig into her mental state rather than staying on the surface? At least tell her story in an interesting way, instead of stringing me along for some 460 boring pages of riding and etiquette and stiff, flat characters.

title: Aweeeeesome.
text:
If you're looking for a comprehensive resource for NCLEX prep, look no further...this book is fantastic. Extensive topic coverage complete with rationales for every response. Prefer going online to take quizzes? No problem this book's got that, too. (Although the content online is a tad bit confusing to navigate, once you figure out how to get to the quizzes section, you won't forget.) I have several books for review and this one is my personal favorite. Some of my professors loan this text out to students, but I prefer 24/7 availability in my own home! :-) Happy studying, future nurses!

UPDATE: I saw sooo many reviewers having trouble getting to the online content to take system-specific quizzes that I decided to post instructions here on how to get to the right place.

1) Go to the Pearson Pegasus log-in page once you've set up online access, and log in.
2) Click on the book title on the left side of the website.
3) On the next page, on the left side near the top, you will see a menu bar that has the following options: "Today's View, Course Content, Grades, Communicate". Look just BELOW this menu bar and you will see the following options: "View All Content, Course Calendar, Learning Objectives."
4) Click on Learning Objectives.
5) On the left side, you will see the following options: "Client Need, Topics Areas, Integrated Process."
6) To take quizzes related to your system or topic of choice, click the plus sign for "Topics Areas".
7) Click on your system of choice.
8) On the right side, there are several options for that topic of study. Scroll down to the bottom-ish. You will see a heading called "Self Study" for that topic of study. Click on it.
9) A separate pop-up window will appear so that you may begin your quiz.

I hope this is helpful. If you have any problems or questions, feel free to comment below. Note that the online quiz portion only works with Internet Explorer and certain versions of Firefox, but not with Chrome.

title: Great Story!
text:
Cool Wind's Gate by Wayne Bernard Sr.

Many books and stories written about the antebellum south and Louisiana in particular, usually tell one of two tales... a life of ease and prosperity on a grand plantation or the atrocities committed against those same men and women in bondage whose slave labor enabled the life of ease and prosperity. Cool Wind's Gate though, while still set in pre-civil war Louisiana, gives a different accounting, a better way that could have been, one that I wished as I was reading it were true.
The story of Cool Wind's Gate grew out of the belief that slavery was wrong. Mr. Clem Collins of Wisteria plantation knew that to simply liberate his slaves wasn't enough. Without a means to care for their families and lacking protection from the prejudices and cruelty of the outside world it would do little good to set them free to starve or worse. He had a plan though, a broader vision of how a good life could be had by everyone. A life filled with well-earned respect, dignity and love. And Clem had Will Trahan, who would see to it that the vision of self-sufficiency and autonomy would become the reality.
Cool Wind's Gate is written simply in a straightforward way. I would have liked more descriptive features of the book's characters, but at almost 900 pages, the author gives us a very authentic story.
