Highly recommended for groups wanting to begin a good discussion of this important encyclical.

title: A Delightful and Unconventional Family
text:
I was drawn to this book because I read and appreciated Emma Donoghue's first book, "Room," and I was interested in what she would do in the YA genre. "The Lotterys" is a horse or a completely different color, but it is excellent in its own way, and I enjoyed it very much.

The story is narrated by nine-year-old Sumac Lottery, one of seven children in an extraordinarily unconventional family. The parents are two gay couples, and the seven children, some biological offspring and some adopted, are all named after trees. They all live in a great old house in Toronto, Canada, and because they have won the lottery, they are financially secure and free to pursue whatever interests they have. The children are likewise free, as they do not attend school, to study and explore whatever interests them. The parents are loving and interested in each child, encouraging them to learn and explore on their own. They are progressive, but they do not look down on others, and the children are not self-centered, entitled, or obnoxious. The freedom they have been given makes them tolerant and accepting of almost everything and everyone. In short, this is a kind of fantasy life.

However, reality intrudes when one of the fathers, PopCorn, learns that his own father, from whom he is estranged, has moderate Alzheimer's disease. The older man, named "Grumps" for obvious reasons, lives alone in Alaska and is not eager to leave his home. He is induced to visit his son and his family in Toronto, whom he has never met. One thing leads to another, and the decision is made to incorporate Grumps into the family. Each family member copes with Grumps in his or her own way, but none moreso than nine-year-old Sumac, the narrator, who must give up her room to her grandfather and has a difficult time with him. The novel describes the impact of Alzheimer's disease on both the patient and the family, but never in a preachy or overly medicalized way. The parents are determined to maintain their family values and activities, and though living with Grumps is sometimes quite a challenge, they find that he is a great addition to their family, and the children come to appreciate him as well.

I loved this novel for several reasons. First, I loved the playful way the author had with language. The children, as I noted are all named for trees, with the exception of Brian, whose given name was Briar. She decided that she wanted to be called Brian, and so she was. The dads are PopCorn and PapaDum, and the moms are MaxiMum and CardaMom. The attic is the Artic, because that is where the art room is located. The house is Camelottery, because it is a mythical, idealized home purchased with lottery money. And on and on and on. There is no end to the creative and interesting use of language.

Second, I liked the fact that while Grumps had dementia, he was not portrayed as a wild and crazy person. He was given dignity and value, and he contributed a great deal to family life. He teaches the children to fish, tells tales of life in Alaska, and fills in some of the details of PopCorn's childhood. Each family member gains understanding and compassion from dealing with Grumps.

Finally, I loved the illustrations. Caroline Hadilaksono's depiction of events in family life are terrific. Whether they are full page or even two page line drawings or just simple silhouettes or drawings of a piece of sports equipment or a butterfly net, they are delightful and add a great deal to the book. I found myself going back several times to the drawing at the beginning of the book of the entire family, with each member labeled. When Grumps enters the family, he is depicted in the illustrations as well. In short, the illustrations are one of the best parts of the book.

I recommend this novel to tweens--the narrator is nine, and this is about the right age to begin. However, I think parents will also be delighted, as I was by the values, humor, language and art in this delightful book.

title: Another wonderful book by Elizabeth Strout
text:
I am a big fan of the writing of Elizabeth Strout, and I was delighted at the opportunity to review her latest collection of interrelated short stories, "Anything Is Possible."

First, however, it must be said that in order to fully enjoy and appreciate this book, you really must have read her previous book, "My Name is Lucy Barton." In fact, I think of these two books as companions. In "Lucy Barton," the reader is introduced to Lucy, a writer living in New York City, who is enduring a lengthy hospital stay following complications of surgery. Her mother, from whom she is estranged, shows up one day unannounced and stays at Lucy's bedside for five days. In their conversations, they discuss many people from the past in the small town where Lucy grew up, Amgash, Illinois. In this book, the reader gets a feel for Lucy's traumatic childhood and impoverished family and her remarkable journey to become an esteemed writer.

"Anything Is Possible" tells the reader more about most of the people who were only mentioned in the previous book. It is not a coherent novel with a straightforward plot; rather, it is like a camera giving us a snapshot into the lives of many people from Lucy's past, including her brother Pete and her sister Vicky. It provides us with a backstory on each character, so that what we were told about them in "Lucy" is expanded and fleshed out, making almost all the characters more sympathetic.

I liked all of these stories, but one of my favorites was the first, "The Sign." The main character in this story, Tommy Guptill, whose kindness and compassion are remarkable, is the school custodian who allows the child Lucy to stay after school for hours so that she can keep warm. In "The Sign," we learn about the tragedy that led Tommy to become a custodian, and we see his present day interaction with Lucy's reclusive older brother, Pete. Tommy is one of the most sympathetic characters I have met in a long time.

I also enjoyed "Sister," a story in which the Barton siblings are reunited after many years of not having seen each other. The reader sees how the past has affected each of them and learns new details about the abuse and isolation they endured. I am in awe that they survived at all, given the past; Lucy's panic attack at the end is completely believable.

Strout's writing is wonderful. I am most drawn to the honesty of her observations, her refusal to sugarcoat anything. If you read "Lucy," you will see that this is an obsession of sorts with her, and it is no less evident in this collection of stories. Another collection by Strout, "Olive Kitteridge," is more unified, but given the fact that the unifying character in this book does not even appear in some of the stories, this lack of complete unity did not bother me.

Although I loved this book, I recognize that it is not for everyone. Some members of my book club were put off by the lack of plot in "My Name Is Lucy Barton," and I especially caution readers who have not yet read "Lucy." Yes, of course you can read these stories on their own, but it is hard for me to see what meaning they would have for you unless you had read the previous book. If you are looking for a tight plot, look elsewhere. However, I highly recommend this book for people who appreciate superb, closely observed writing and can tolerate some scenes of almost unspeakable abuse of children.

title: Wonderful new cookbook!
text:
While I am not a sports fan, I do entertain a lot and thought that this cookbook might give me some easy and creative ideas. I was right. This new book by Daina Falk is full of wonderful food photography (some call it food porn, and I can see why) and recipes that range from super easy to somewhat complex, feeding anywhere from two to eighty people.

The salsa recipes are very simple and delicious. The cashew chicken in lettuce cups is much more complex, but definitely worth the time and effort. Most of all, I love the little introductions to each recipe, where Daina gives her observations about the recipe itself or the time she served it--what game was being played, who won, which athlete gave her the idea for a particular recipe, and the like. I am one who loves to "read" cookbooks, and if you are like me, you will enjoy this book.

I noticed this cookbook at our local library, and I urge you to look at it at your library before you buy. Having said that, I think you will likely end up wanting to add this cookbook to your collection--it is that good. Happy eating!

title: A stunning debut collection
text:
I have just finished "Beasts and Children," and I sit here absolutely blown away. I knew at the outset that this was a set of interconnected short stories, and I really enjoy this approach to fiction, a la "Olive Kittredge." However, halfway through the book, I was perplexed: these stories did not seem to be interconnected at all. They are well written, sure, but how did they fit together?

The reader's patience will be rewarded. It is not until the final two stories that all the connections are made, to the great satisfaction of this reader. Not that there is a happy ending, but there is a satisfying ending, and in life, that must often be enough, or more than enough.

The main characters in the stories are two sets of sisters, Carline and Cecilia (and their cousin Danny), and Jill and Mazie; these are rounded out by an immigrant family from Columbia and a boy named Jerry whom you will never forget. The author shows us these characters at different points in their lives: childhood, adolescence, early adulthood, marriage, parenthood. These stories are not for the faint of heart. They involve child abuse, parental neglect, animal cruelty, sexual aberration, and even torture of political prisoners--the list goes on. How then, can I give such a book my highest recommendation?

In a word, writing. I find it difficult to believe that this is the author's first book. At first, you notice magical word choice or effective metaphor or characterization. But the delights of the written word do not end there. The piece de resistance, at least for me, is a stunning letter in the second last story from a mother to her unborn child. I could not help but cry at its beauty and truth. Presented without an ounce of sentimentality, the letter will remain with you forever. (However, if you read this book, don't skip ahead to this story. You need the background in the preceding stories to experience the full impact.)

Thus, I recommend this book for anyone who wants to read about real people dealing with the tragedies life presents to us all, and then some. You will be rewarded with some of the best writing you have ever read.

title: A Stellar Debut Novel
text:
"Make Your Home Among Strangers" is one of the best new novels by a first-time author that I have read. It tells the story of the first year (actually from November to August) of college for Lizet, a bright Cuban American young woman who gained admission to Rawlings, a very competitive liberal arts college (think Williams or Cornell), for which she is woefully unprepared. One strand of the novel deals with her experiences at school, especially her feeling that she just does not fit in and will not succeed no matter what she does. As the novel begins, she is paying a surprise visit to her mother and sister in Miami for Thanksgiving.

Just at this time, Ariel Hernandez (think Elian Gonzales) has been rescued from a raft on its way from Cuba to Miami. Ariel's mother dies on the way, and Ariel's relatives mount a campaign to keep him in America against the wishes of his father in Cuba. Lizet's mother is very interested in this child and his family, and as the months go by she becomes increasingly invested in the fate of little Ariel and his main caretaker, a young woman named Caridaylis. Lizet and her sister Leidy, who has a child, Dante, by her ex-boyfriend, become very concerned about their mother's mental health, as she detaches from her real family to participate in the demonstrations on behalf of Ariel and his family.

This second strand is woven into Lizet's experience as she tries to figure out just who she is and where she belongs. Suddenly she seems to fit nowhere; she has no place to really call home. Her Cuban family and friends mock her intelligence and new interests; they feel that she has "forgotten where she came from" and that she thinks she is too good for them now. Lizet herself is uncomfortable both at home and at school, where people take for granted things she must learn. College is a totally new culture for Lizet, one that she has to navigate in fits and starts.

I have never read a better account of the problems facing young people who transition from one cultural milieu to another. Whether you are a working class white person in an Ivy League university, a young African American from the inner city who attends a private or top-tier public school, or a Cuban or Latin American or Native American student in a similar situation, you will be able to relate to Lizet's anguish as she deals with both college-related and family-related issues. Don't get me wrong: No one is openly racist or mean to Lizet; there are no slurs or put-downs. But there are more than a few misunderstandings that lead to anger and hostility. Lizet is unsure of herself, and her uncertainty makes her defensive; her college friends make insensitive remarks and are oblivious to how they are perceived by Lizet. Most of the students at Rawlings are from privileged upper-middle class or upper class families, and their air of entitlement is both palpable and unconscious.

Book clubs will love this book. So many issues lend themselves to discussion, such as affirmative action, cultural identity, and coming of age. The characters are almost all exasperating, especially Lizet and her sister Leidy, and their mother is beyond the pale in her devotion to the cause of Ariel Hernandez (note that Ariel is a near anagram for Elian). The writing is excellent, and I look forward to reading more of Jennine Capo Crucet's work. I cannot help but think that this is at least in part autobiographical, so well does it express Lizet's experiences and conflicts. I recommend this book to anyone who seeks a better understanding of the cultural differences that we all encounter in our pluralistic society, and especially to anyone who, like me, loves books about school.

title: Not so much about how to die, but how to live
text:
"When Breath Becomes Air" is one of the best books I have read this year. This memoir tells of the life of Paul Kalanithi, the son of Indian immigrants, who attended Yale School of Medicine and trained as a neurosurgeon. On the cusp of an outstanding career, Paul is diagnosed with Stage IV lung cancer.

It is said that "Life is what happens to you when you are making other plans." The first half of the book concerns Kalanithi's "other plans"--his family, childhood, schooling, and internship and residency as a neurosurgeon. He learns not simply the nuts and bolts of his specialty, but how to talk with and relate to people who have just received the news that they or someone they love has a brain tumor. This part is beautifully written, but the reader knows that the second act will bring about Kalanithi's own mortality far sooner than anyone expects.

The second part of the book tells of the cancer diagnosis and how Kalanithi and his family deal with this devastating news. Anyone who has ever dealt with cancer in his or her own life, or even in the life of a loved one, will be able to relate to how difficult it is to deal with all the medical interventions, the shock of family and friends, and the facing of one's own death. How should we treat the cancer? When does the treatment become worse than the disease? How do you find meaning in life? All of these issues are covered in beautiful and poetic prose.

The book is finished by Kalanithi's wife, who is also a physician, an internist. I highly recommend this book for everyone. It is beautifully written and not at all morbid. It deals honestly and forthrightly with end of life issues, especially when you must face them forty years earlier than you expected. The reader is reminded of what makes life worth living, what make "a good life." This is a book to cherish, and to reread on occasion in the years to come.

title: Excellent Help for Owners of iPhone 6 and 6s
text:
My husband and I just purchased our iPhones about a year ago, and we love them. However, we realize that we do not use a great deal of the phone's capability; in fact, we probably use only about 1% of what we could use. In addition, the iPhone 6 does not come with a written user's manual, and I wish it did.

We ordered both iPhone 6s Portable Genius and the Teach Yourself Visually manual for the iPhone 6. While I have to give a slight edge to the Teach Yourself Visually book, the Portable Genius is excellent, too. It does not have as many colored screen shots, but it does have detailed illustrations and step by step directions for any operation you can imagine. Actually, the two manuals complement each other nicely. The Portable Genius has more text, so if that suits your learning style, go with this book. Some of the areas covered in this manual include an overview of the audio features of the phone and an extensive chapter on the camera and all its features. (By the way, if you have not yet purchased an iPhone, you will be blown away by the potential of the camera. It is, by far, the best camera I have ever owned,) You will also learn about the Cloud, and I freely confess that I did not really understand the Cloud until I read this book. The chapter on fixing your iPhone is invaluable. Truly, I am glad we have both books. I give the Portable Genius my highest recommendation.

title: Superb Help for iPhone 6 Users
text:
My husband and I each purchased an iPhone 6 about a year ago. We have grown to love them (these were our first smartphones), but we both realize that we use only about 1% of the phone's capability. Add to this the fact that iPhones come without written instructions. Yes, I know that I can use the phone itself for help, but I am not sure how to do that. The Apple store is wonderful, but I hate to keep going there every time I have a question.

Into the breach comes Teach Yourself Visually iPhone 6S IOS9. My husband and I both love this book. Like all the others in the Teach Yourself Visually series, the book has screen shots in full color so that you can see exactly what you have to do for any given operation. In addition, there are clear and simple step-by-step instructions. You do not need to know anything to use this book. Some of the areas that are covered include getting started with the iPhone, both for experienced smartphone users and for rank beginners like us. You learn how to sync your phone with your computer or tablet. You can find out how to download an app, and how to navigate the APP store. There are suggestions for useful apps, and an excellent section on Siri, which I have yet to explore fully.

The main attraction of this book is its simplicity. In my opinion, it would be hard to make a mistake with your iPhone if you are using this book. The section on troubleshooting is superb, as it is inevitable that various issues will arise. I have never seen a Teach Yourself Visually book that I did not like. I highly recommend this manual for both beginning and experienced iPhone users. You will learn a great deal, and you will likely double or triple the use of your iPhone.

title: A Sensitive and Perceptive Search for Oneself
text:
I have loved Elizabeth Strout's writing ever since I read--and reread--"Olive Kitteridge," so I leapt at the chance to review her new book, "My Name is Lucy Barton." This latest of her books is shorter than the previous two, and I think it is more personal as well, though I have no way of knowing how much of the action, if any, comes from real life.

As the book opens, Lucy Barton, a successful writer, is in the hospital with a mysterious complication of surgery that is never fully explained. She remains in the hospital for nine weeks, largely isolated from the outside world--her husband hates hospitals and rarely visits, and her two daughters are too young to come on their own. Suddenly, Lucy's mother, whom she has not seen in several years, shows up and stays with her in the hospital for five days. During this time, the action alternates between the present and Lucy's past, her childhood and young adulthood, and the reader gradually comes to an understanding of both Lucy and her mother. The two reminisce about various events and persons from the past, and in particular, they discuss the marriages of various friends and relatives. As the book develops, the reader sees that all this talk of other people's marriages is a way for both Lucy and her mother to avoid the elephant in the room, their own marriages and relationships.

Lucy's mother's visit is not all sunshine and roses. In chapters alternating between past and present, we see the truly terrifying past that Lucy has overcome, and her mother's limited awareness of the damage she has done to her daughters and son. Lucy's brother and sister are mentioned in small but important glimpses into the past, and the reader sees the childhood of poverty and abuse that is her heritage. Despite all this, however, Lucy loves her mother and desperately wants her approval. She slowly comes to a realization of who she is--the time in the hospital could be compared to an extended retreat, without the religious element--and we see the results of her epiphany in the last part of the book.

I loved the way this book was written. There is very little action; most of what happens is conversation and memory and conversation about memory. The point of the book is the development of a self, an identity, an awareness of who you really are--thus the title: "My Name is Lucy Barton." The book reads very quickly--it has fewer than 200 pages--but it will stay with you long after you have read it. I recommend this book for anyone who enjoys contemporary literary women's fiction.

title: Charming, Attractive, and Moving ABC Book
text: This is a charming little ABC book for preschoolers.  It is subtitled "A Natural Alphabet," and I found that it was true to that in many ways.  First, the animals and other items named in the book are somewhat unexpected.  For example, E is for egret, and Y is for yellow-bellied sapsucker.  I can imagine kids having fun with the language of the book.  Second, the illustrations are lovely.  They have the look and feel of woodcuts, though actually they are paper art.  Finally, the colors are subtle and beautiful.  There are grays, yellows, blues, browns, pinks--but nothing bright or garish.  (If you want bright colors and cute animals doing human things like washing dishes or cooking, this is not the book for you.)  This book would be a lovely and inexpensive shower gift.  Highly recommended.

title: A Delightful Read as well as a Delicious Collection of Recipes
text:
I love cookbooks and have far too many, even after having donated several dozen to our local library booksale. My favorite kind of cookbook is one that you can read like a real book; one that has comments about each recipe and personal stories to accompany them. "Goldie's Kitchen Cookbook" is exactly the sort of cookbook I love. Written (or collected) by a writer of mysteries whose work I have never read, this cook book connects each recipe with one of the author's works. Each has an introduction detailing the connection with the book, the personal experience of the author with the recipe, and any caveats about challenges you may encounter as you prepare the recipe.

The recipes themselves are not the "simple and easy" kind, but they are not overly complicated, either. The author often urges the cook to use the best and freshest ingredients available, which is a great suggestion no matter what you are preparing. Some recipes are ultra simple, such as Green Beans Amandine, which is exactly what you would expect, a simple preparation with salt, pepper, and butter to add flavor. Others are longer and more complex, such as Shuttlecock Shrimp Curry, but none are truly complicated. I look forward to reading and re-reading this book and to trying out a great many of the recipes. Anyone who loves both cooking and commentary would love and appreciate this book. Highly recommended.

title: Excellent, Absorbing, and Psychologically Astute
text:
"The Year She Left Us" by Kathryn Ma is the story of a multi-generational Chinese American family told from multiple points of view. At the center of the story is the youngest member, Ari (short for Ariadne), a very young adult who is trying to come to terms with having been abandoned as an infant on the steps of a Chinese department store and adopted by a single parent, Charlie (short for Charlotte), a Chinese American public defender with more than a touch of social worker in her. The other major narrative voices are those of Charlie's sister, Les (short for Lesley), a lawyer/judge, and their mother (and Ari's grandmother), Gran. Each of these women is complex and interesting, each strong in her own ways.

As the book opens, Ari has graduated from high school and is on her way to her grandmother's alma mater, Bryn Mawr. She decides to visit China with her closest friend, A.J., who is also a Chinese adoptee, to see the orphanage she was adopted from and to determine whether her birth parents ever regretted their decision to give her up and tried to retrieve her. The reader realizes that this is futile, but it is important to Ari, who is suffering from many of the issues that beset adopted children, especially those of abandonment and the fantasy of "what might have been." In China, Ari suffers what can only be called a breakdown and does something irrevocable to herself, a highly symbolic act that I will not reveal.

Meanwhile, at home in San Francisco, Charlie is living in major denial that anything is wrong with Ari. She wants her to come home in time to get ready for college; she has no clue as to Ari's true state of mind. Charlie has a secret of her own, one that is not revealed until midway through the book, but it has a major impact on all the characters. Les's importance as a character increases as the book proceeds; despite being sisters, Les and Charlie are very different personalities with diametrically opposed approaches to life. Gran has the strongest personality of all. She and her sister left China after World War II, leaving their entire family behind to deal with the horrors of the Communist regime. Gran has more secrets than anyone else, and some are revealed only in the final chapters of the book when she herself returns to China for a visit.

Most reviewers would classify this book as a coming of age story, and indeed it is, but it is also a family saga, a cautionary tale about the corrosive power of the past and its secrets, and the dangers of not dealing with reality. Frustrating as all of these characters are, they are also endearing; the reader cannot help but feel affection and sympathy for each one of them. The writing is superb; if I have any issues, it would be with the pacing of the book about a third of the way through, when it seems just a bit sluggish. The second half, however, is riveting; it was hard to put the book down.

I know personally some young adult adoptees, and the issues Ari is dealing with seem authentic and well defined. I hope to share this book with my young adoptee friends, as well as with their parents and others who are trying to help them deal with their issues of abandonment and identity. I give this book my highest recommendation.

title: Meltdown:  Nuclear and Personal
text:
"Close Your Eyes, Hold Hands" is a book you will not soon forget. Set in the present (or possibly near future) in Vermont, it concerns a meltdown at a nuclear plant (think Japan's Fukushima Dai-ichi in 2011) that has a predictably searing effect on the main character, 16-year-old Emily Shepard, whose parents are implicated in the accident and are both killed. As the book opens, Emily is homeless, living in an igloo she has constructed of trash bags and wet leaves with a nine-year-old companion, Cameron. How she got here is the subject of the book, and it is a coming of age tale for the ages.

I will not spoil the book by revealing too much, but you should know that Emily goes through the tortures of the damned in so many ways: physically, psychologically, spiritually. Imagine months of life on the streets of Burlington for a homeless teenage girl, and you will not be far off the mark. Emily is a marvel, however. She is by turns and all at once insightful, childlike, hopeful, cynical, intelligent, honest, deceitful, passionate, caring, lost, and found. She quotes Emily Dickinson at length and often, and shows uncanny insight. The author, Chris Bohjalian, has a pitch-perfect ear for the bright but disillusioned teenage girl voice, and this is evident from page one. (To be fair, he credits his young adult daughter for her help in achieving this. Still, it is amazing.)

If this book interests you, I recommend that you listen to the NPR interview with the author conducted by Diane Rehm in July of 2014. (You can find it on the Diane Rehm website and listen to the entire thing or read a transcript. I recommend listening.) In that interview, I was surprised to learn that the author did not envision this as a YA novel. Although much of the subject matter is very adult, this is not unusual for today's YA literary scene, and I thought from the first that this book would be the next new thing in YA literature. That said, I can see it as an adult novel as well, one that adults and teens might profitably discuss together.

Hats off to Chris Bohjalian for creating Emily and letting her tell her story. This is a novel you won't want to miss. Highly recommended for everyone from mature teens to adults.

title: Superb and Concise History of Railroads Around the World
text:
I ordered this book because my husband is a railroad enthusiast, and I knew that he would be able to help me review it honestly. In addition, the is a DK book, and for those unfamiliar with DK travel books, they are a delight. Although other books may provide more text, DK books offer a wealth of photos, maps, and drawings.

This book, "The Iron Road" by Christian Wolmar, has exceptional drawings, photos, maps, and graphics, but in addition, it provides a superb and detailed text. The book is divided into five sections, each dealing with an aspect of railroads around the world in chronological order. Many books have examined the engineering of railroads, but this one also deals with the human aspect of railroad construction, especially the intrigue and greed that form the backdrop of many railroads. Most readers, unless they are well acquainted with railroad history, are unaware of the human cost of rail expansion, not only in the United States but around the world. Wolmar recounts this human cost with compassion and insight, never over-dramatizing it, but making sure the reader does not dismiss it.

In Australia, for example, rather than standardize the track width, 22 track widths were used, a case study in how not to create a railroad network. Why did this happen? Every rail baron wanted to be first to get his piece of the railroad action. This greed precluded cooperation and set Australia's rail system back decades.

The transformative effect of railroads on society cannot be overestimated. In addition to travel, industry, and commerce, the impact of railroads on war, especially the American Civil War and in Europe, World War II, is covered in detail. The role of rail transport in the mass deportation of entire populations to prison and extermination camps in Germany, France, Poland, and China is recounted. Railroads in Asia and Russia are significant, too. This book reads more like an adventure story than a history; indeed, if history were taught this way in schools, many more of us would know it and learn from it.

I recommend this highly readable book to anyone who is looking for a good general history of railroads around the world. An expert will likely know most of what is in this book, but the general reader will not. This is a perfect book for the general reader.

title: Beautiful and poetic first novel
text:
I am stunned that this is Celeste Ng's first novel. I was instantly drawn into this book, with its beautifully drawn characters and superb writing. On its surface, the story is a mystery: What led to the death of Lydia Lee, a sixteen-year-old honor student with (supposedly) everything to live for? In reality, the mystery goes far deeper, into the lives of each member of the family. By the end of the book, the reader is fully in sympathy with each character.

The novel, which takes place in the late 70s, begins with Lydia's death. Was it murder? Was it suicide? Or was it something else? The reader spends most of the novel thinking one thing, only to be surprised at the end with the truth. The author delves into the lives of each family member: James, the father, who never felt really at home in any situation; Marilyn, the mother, whose dreams were shelved by the demands of marriage, family, and the times; Nathan, the older brother, whose brilliance is overlooked; Lydia, the golden child burdened with all the frustrated aspirations of her parents; and Hannah, the overlooked afterthought of a child, a silent but keen observer of everyone in her family. (I was torn between imagining the author as Lydia or as Hannah; I suspect she is an amalgam of both.)

Many chapters in this novel focus on just one character, telling the story from his or her point of view. The reader is led to an understanding of just how profoundly even the best intentions can go terribly awry. Once again, we see people living out their own frustrated dreams through their children, who may or may not be on board. The term "helicopter parent" comes to mind, though this idea was not in vogue until the 90s. In addition, issues of race in America and women's roles are explored through the parents, James and Marilyn, who came of age in the 60s and early 70s at the height of the sexual and civil rights revolutions. Even gay identity comes into play, and remember that this novel is set in 1977, not 2014.

I am compelled to praise the writing of this book. Both psychologically astute and poetic, it draws the reader into the story and evokes sympathy and awe. We see the devastating grief that overtakes each member of the family as he or she tries to see why Lydia died and what he or she may have done to prevent it. I also loved the way the author treated memory, that old deceiver, who smoothes out that which we cannot bear to recall.

I do not think this book is marketed as a YA novel, but it is certainly a book that parents and teenagers may profitably read and discuss together. The issues are fresh and relevant, and I can imagine that meaningful discussions and insights may result. Highly recommended for all readers 14 and above.

title: Engaging and compelling
text:
Count me among those who were immediately involved in E. Lockhart's "We Were Liars." Readers both young and old will be captivated by the characters and the superb writing, which combines everyday life with a hint of magical realism.

As other reviewers have noted, the plot revolves around the Sinclair family. When you imagine this family, think of a cross between the Kennedy clan and a Ralph Lauren print ad in an upscale magazine. This is an old money family, with more than its share of secrets, prejudices, rituals, and customs. The patriarch of the family owns an island off the coast of Massachusetts, to which his three daughters and their families come each summer for a golden idyll in a magical place. At least, this is the way it is supposed to be, but that is a lie, and it is just the beginning of lies.

Now think of King Lear, and you will have an idea of the sort of father this patriarch is. The daughters are not exact parallels to Lear's daughters, but there are enough resemblances to keep the reader interested. The focus of the book is on the next generation, the children of the three daughters (and their friend, a contrast both in culture and social status).

I hope no one reviewing this book has revealed the plot in too much detail. You will have to trust me when I say you will not see the final plot twist coming, though when you re-read the book (as you will feel compelled to do), you will see all manner of foreshadowing and hints. This book is an examination of the lies we tell ourselves and each other to live harmoniously on the surface of our world, and the price those lies exact. I am recommending this book to all my reader friends, and I will be sharing it with my nieces, who I am confident will love it.

A final note on style: You will occasionally encounter a disconcerting narration that seems at first literal, but is in fact magical realism. For example, when Cady Sinclair Eastman, the 15-year-old narrator of the book, is recounting her parents' divorce, she describes her father packing his things into his Mercedes. Then you read this: "Then he pulled out a handgun and shot me in the chest. I was standing on the lawn and I fell. The bullet hole opened wide and my heart rolled out of my rib cage and down into a flower bed. Blood gushed rhythmically from my open wound,
then from my eyes,
my ears,
my mouth.
It tasted like salt and failure. The bright red shame of being unloved soaked the grass in front of our house, the bricks of the path, the steps to the porch. My heart spasmed among the peonies like a trout.
Mummy snapped. She said to get hold of myself."

My first thought upon reading this was that Cady's father had lost control and actually shot her. The mother's comment makes clear, however, that this passage is a poetic description of how devastated Cady was at her parents' separation. This sort of thing happens throughout the book, and I came to enjoy the poetic imagery. Just don't take these passages literally.

I hope you enjoy this book as much as I did. Highly recommended.

title: Perfect "Welcome to the World" gift for parents of a new baby
text:
I was confident that National Geographic would do a stellar job in presenting a unique baby book, and I was not disappointed. The photography alone makes this book a treasure, in itself well worth the price; the accompanying quotations and poems are of highest quality as well. Everything you would expect to find in a traditional baby book, you will find here, but without the pastel colors and cute drawings. I loved this book and am looking for an opportunity to give it to parents of a new baby.

Though I think almost anyone would love this book, parents who enjoy writing and reflecting will appreciate it the most,. There are opportunities to reflect on the baby's future as well as on what was going on in the world when he or she was born, and to reflect on many other events in the baby's life, and what these events might mean. For example, one page has a space for parents to write about what they learned from their child. Anyone who has a child knows that they teach us much about life, love, and what really matters.

Parents should think of this book as a gift for their child, to be given when the child asks about his early years and may perhaps be starting a family of his or her own. Well filled out, it will be a testament to parental love, and who would not appreciate that? Highly recommended, without reservation.

title: Fantastic gift for a new baby
text: I absolutely loved this picture book.  With starkly lovely illustrations and a minimum of words, the author takes us through the first year in the life of a baby robin, and by analogy, the growing up and launching of a child.  As I "read" this book, I marveled at the ways a parent or teacher could engage a child in its various aspects.  For example, in the depiction of the parent birds feeding the chick, you could talk to your child about how human parents feed their babies, what foods your child used to like/hate, and how gross it would be if human mommies fed their babies as birds do.  In another picture, the baby is learning to fly, and a cat lies in wait.  Not to fear, however:  the parent birds are there to protect their chick.  I see this as a gentle way to get across the idea that parents always want to protect their children and keep them safe, and are aware of dangers that the child may be oblivious to.  Even the endpapers of the book, huge robin's eggs, could be used for a little elementary math.  I also loved the way the seasons were portrayed in the book, with lovely illustrations that invite the reader to look at nature in a fresh way.  It seems to me that this is a book that invites a parent and child to engage with one another on so many levels.  Mostly, this book is about family bonding and love.  I will be giving this book at the next baby shower or christening I go to, and I give it my highest recommendation.

title: Thank goodness for old textbooks
text: In a recent purge of our bookshelves, my husband, a retired math teacher, donated his copy of this book to our local library.  Of course, six months later he wanted it back, and we were fortunate to find this copy on Amazon.  It has no bells and whistles, no colorful pictures or cutesy approaches, just clear, direct explanations of all aspects of analytic geometry.  He is tutoring students in high school geometry, and although much of the material in this text is beyond the scope of most high school curricula, he is finding it helpful to review some of the principles in this book.  This text is a classic, and it is particularly good in its approach to matrices and trigonometric functions.  It emphasizes the use of matrices in solving equations.  Though this text was written nearly sixty years ago, it is still relevant.  The examples for each concept are clear and the practice problems are excellent, and answers are given for the odd numbered problems.  The section on solid analytic geometry is extensive.  I highly recommend this text to anyone desiring a thorough understanding of analytic geometry.

title: Well-written Hospital Suspense Drama
text:
"Doing Harm" is Kelly Parsons first novel, and it is the best novel I have read since "Defending Jacob."

Steve Mitchell is a chief resident in surgery and is the supervisor of a group of medical students at Boston University Hospital, a teaching hospital associated with BU. Steve, who is in charge of making these students into doctors, is married to Sally, a stay-at-home mom who used to be a high-ranking assistant to the head of Human Resources at the hospital, where the two met.

Sally and Steve go to Dr. Collier's annual cocktail party. Collier is Steve's boss and chairman of Steve's department. Sally wants Steve to become a member of the faculty of the medical school, which would be an enormous advancement for him. She hints at this to Dr. Collier, with whom Steve is scheduled to meet in the next week. At the meeting, it seems that Steve will get his promotion, but then things become a little crazy at the hospital.

Two of Steve's new students are Luis, a very serious and conscientious student, and Gigi (which stands for Golden Girl), a very bright student who is perhaps a little too smart for her own good. After Steve is promised the promotion, very bad things begin to happen. Medicine is not given in the proper dosage, patients go into comas, and some do not ever come out. All of these events are blamed on Steve and his students, and soon, even Steve's favorite mentor will not allow Steve near him in the operating room.

Does Steve get to the bottom of these mysterious events? Is he destroyed mentally and professionally in the process? Read this superb novel and find out.

This is a very well written novel. The characters were very realistic, and it is easy to see that the author has first-hand experience in a hospital. If I could, I would give this novel ten stars.

title: Fascinating book for Everyone
text:
I have been a huge fan of Lonely Planet guidebooks ever since I first ordered one on Rome with kids as the target audience. I like the adult Lonely Planet guides, too, but when it comes to children, no one does it better than Lonely Planet. So when I had the chance to review this book, I jumped at it, and I was not disappointed.

"Lonely Planet Not for Parents Real Wonders of the World" has as its subtitle "Amazing Stuff to Know about the Coolest Places on Earth," and that just about sums up this book. The book is divided into eight major sections, each having seven to nine topics. Some of the major sections are Stupendous Structures; High Tech; Cultural Wonders; Hidden Places; Thrills, Spills, and Games; and Fright Night. Each sub-topic is composed of two pages loaded with a collage of photos and graphics, and while there is some text, it is not overwhelming. The topics are wide-ranging, from Barrow, Alaska, to Pompeii, to the catacombs, to outer space. While the guide is aimed at children (about age 8 and up, I would say), I am convinced that most adults would learn a thing or two from this book.

The book is oversize, so it is not a conventional travel book. Rather, it is a great "Let's find something interesting to read" book, one that I can see kids returning to again and again. It is well made with heavy paper and a sturdy hard cover, so it should last through several children. I give this book my highest recommendation.

title: Excellent guidebook
text:
I ordered this guidebook, Lonely Planet Hawaii, because my husband and I took an all-too-short trip to Hawaii earlier this year, and we are both eager to go back and experience our 50th state in a little more depth than we did the first time around. I was hoping that this guidebook would help, and I was not disappointed.

Hawaii is a beautiful and complex state, and this guide covers just about every aspect of it: people, culture, history, natural resources, ecology, and cuisine, to name just a few. The book helps the reader plan a trip based on his or her individual interests, whether they are artistic, historical, or nature-oriented. There are the usual "Where to Stay" and "Where to Eat" features, as well as some "Don't Miss This" features as well. If you are traveling with children, this book includes several child-friendly attractions to help you plan a trip that the entire family can enjoy. The book includes an up-to-date driving map that includes each island, helping in the planning of an itinerary. It should be noted that the maps are not street maps; rather, they give an overview of each island. If you want a street map, you will need to go elsewhere. (I suggest the Auto Club, which has superb maps that alone are worth the price of membership if you travel a great deal.)

In our previous travels, we have relied on Eyewitness Travel Guides, and if I were forced to select only one guide, I would prefer Eyewitness. I do not know if they have one on Hawaii, but I suspect they do. The advantage of the Eyewitness guides is the superb photography that accompanies many of the cultural and geographic entries. Eyewitness claims to be "The Guides That Show You What Others Only Tell You," and we have found this to be true.

However, this is not to denigrate the Lonely Planet Guide. It too has photographs, though far fewer than an Eyewitness Guide. It includes a wealth of information about Hawaii, so much so that I am convinced that even a native Hawaiian would learn a great deal about his state by surveying this guide. A tourist will find it extremely helpful and informative. Highly recommended.

title: Superb supplement to your new Apple laptop
text:
Like the many other "Teach Yourself Visually" books, "MacBook Pro" is an excellent book for anyone who has or is planning to get an Apple laptop but may want some help finding out about and navigating all that it has to offer.

"MacBook Pro" is set up logically, and the reader can easily find the area he or she wants to learn about and simply go through the step-by-step instructions. The photos are excellent, and they are photos, not diagrams or sketches. The index is easy to use as well, and you will definitely learn a great deal about your new Mac by using this handbook.

Highly recommended, especially for the technologically challenged.

title: Simply fantastic
text:
This is the latest of several "Teach Yourself Visually" books that my husband and I have ordered to help us use our electronic devices more fully. Like the others, "iPhoto for iPad" does not disappoint. In my opinion, these books are all you will ever need to help you use your devices more effectively.

First of all, the book assumes nothing more than that you have an iPad and the you want to work with your photos on it. The chapters are made to order for those of us for whom technology is decidedly not "second nature." They begin at the most elementary level imaginable--looking at your photos and experimenting with different ways of viewing them. From there, you learn how to import your photos and use the Cloud. There is a great chapter on organizing your pictures into albums and editing your photos with special effects. You learn to "photoshop" your pictures and use color and filters. There is a chapter on creating advanced photo effects that I am not ready for just yet, but I look forward to learning about sharing photos and making journals of our travels. We do not have an iPhone, but if you do, you will enjoy the chapter on iPhoto and the iPhone. It is important to note that you do not have to cover all these areas if you are not interested. The book is set up in such as way that browsing and selective learning are easy.

Second, I love that this book has photographs of exactly what you see on your own screen. Not diagrams or sketches, but real photographs. These photos accompany easy-to-follow, step-by-step instructions. They take nothing for granted, which I appreciate a great deal.

Third, I like the use of white space. The pages of this book are not cluttered up with "stuff" on every inch of space.

Finally, I really enjoy the sidebar "Question and Answer" sections that accompany almost every step, and I found the index complete and easy to use.

In short, if you are mystified about how to integrate your photos with your iPad (or even your laptop computer), this is the book for you. I cannot imagine that it would not be helpful to just about everyone. It has my highest recommendation.

title: Heartwarming tales for dog lovers
text:
Anyone who loves dogs will love and appreciate this book. "Devoted" tells the brief stories of 38 dogs and their human companions, and each one celebrates the bond that we humans have with our dogs.

I enjoyed all the stories, but I was especially touched by the story of Schoep (which I think is pronounced "Shep") and his owner, John Unger. Schoep was adopted by Unger from a shelter in Wisconsin, and he was probably the dog most in need and least likely to be adopted. Nonetheless, Unger wanted to adopt a dog that had been abused and help him realize his full potential. Unger worked tirelessly with Schoep and eventually transformed the dog into a wonderful pet. The best part of the story, though, is that, just as Unger had saved Schoep, Schoep eventually returned the favor, as only the thought of leaving Schoep alone saved Unger from killing himself at an incredibly low period in his life. Readers will love the photograph of Unger floating in the water with Schoep lying on his chest, asleep and perfectly content.

This is only one of the many stories of the fantastic intelligence, loyalty, inventiveness, and amusement that dogs offer in return for our custody of them. I was impressed by the variety of dog breeds that were represented in these stories, especially by the number of "pit bulls" that appeared. This breed has an unjustified reputation for vicious behavior, and this little book will do much to help readers overcome any prejudices they have. There were a few greyhounds as well, and as I have a cousin who works with greyhound rescue, I know firsthand how wonderful this breed is as a pet.

The book is replete with beautiful photographs as well: the reader sees each dog profiled and usually his or her owner as well. Each story is short enough to be read in only a few minutes, and each dog has something to offer that will just make you smile. I can see this little book as the perfect holiday gift for a "dog person."

It is hard to imagine that anyone would not enjoy this book. I highly recommend it.

title: Inspiring story of a gifted teacher
text:
Let me say at the outset that I am a retired English teacher, and I love books about school and inspiring teachers. When the opportunity to read an advance copy of this book was offered, I accepted with enthusiasm, and I was not disappointed.

"Drama High" is the story of the kind of teacher any parent wishes their child would have, Lou Volpe, who taught at Harry S Truman High School in Levittown, PA, for over 30 years. It traces his evolution as a teacher and as a person. Volpe's first attempts at theater were not successful, but in theater he had found his life's work, and he never stopped challenging himself or his students with ever more demanding and out of the mainstream drama.

"Drama High" is written by Michael Sokolove, a former student of Volpe, and although the respect and affection he has for Volpe are evident, they do not prevent him from giving a clear-eyed account of a year in the life of this remarkable teacher. In addition, we see the many challenges faced by urban teachers and students today, primarily through the lives of Volpe's cast members. In presenting "Good Boys and True," a play that pushes the envelope in several respects, Volpe knows that he is taking a risk, but that fact does not prevent him from going forward and entering the performance in the International Thespian Festival in Nebraska, the Cannes Film Festival of high school drama. Competition is fierce, and Volpe is facing schools with state of the art facilities and nearly unlimited resources. The story of his journey is one the reader will not soon forget.

One thing I loved about this book is its unabashed assertion that the arts matter. Today's emphasis on testing in schools has all but eliminated many arts programs, sapping the life of the school experience. Drama, music, dance, visual arts, all must take a back seat (if not be thrown out of the bus entirely) to test preparation. This is a terrible loss both for individual students and for society.

If you are interested in reading an excerpt from this book before you buy it, go to the New York Times website and find the Sunday magazine for September 15, 2013. There you will find an extended summation of "Drama High" entitled, "If All We Had Was a Bare Stage with One Light Bulb, We Could Still Do Theater." That title just about sums up Volpe's philosophy: Drama is so important, so central to life, we will do it any way we can.

One more thing: As I read this book, I was constantly reminded of a documentary film I saw a few years ago. "The Hobart Shakespearians" is about another inspiring teacher, this one in elementary school, who brings Shakespeare into his fifth or sixth grade classroom. He, too, was the sort of teacher you hope your child encounters at least once in his or her school career. You can get this film from Netflix, and I hope you do.

title: A valuable tool
text:
I ordered this book because my husband and I are thinking about setting up a living trust, and I was interested in seeing whether or not we could do this without a lawyer. This book is extremely clear and well-written; it does not assume any legal knowledge other than general information, so it is easily accessible to the lay person. It seems to me that this book covers every conceivable question one could have about trusts, from basic questions like why a trust is a good idea and why people set them up, to complicated questions about selling property that is in a trust, revoking a trust, or leaving property to minor children. Each chapter has many concrete real-life examples of each major point the author is making. I especially liked this aspect of the book as it broke up the expository parts with clarifying examples. I was also impressed that with the purchase of this book, you can go online and download, free, any legal documents you may need in order to set up your trust. You also have access to the NOLO website, where you can find out about any changes in the laws regarding trusts.

Now, the ultimate question: Would I set up my own trust after reading this book? To be honest, I am not sure that I would, but that is more about the sort of cautious person I am than about the quality of this book. In my opinion, even if you do end up going to a lawyer to set up your trust, if you read this book you will be far more informed that you would be without having read it. You will be a better consumer, and you will understand far more of what your lawyer is telling you. I have learned so much about trusts from this book, even though I have not read every single chapter. I do recommend this book to any lay person who is interested in setting up a trust. I do not think you will ever regret your purchase.

title: Good for tweens and early teens
text: I did not read these books myself; they were a birthday gift for my 15-year-old niece.  She was absolutely delighted, so on that basis, I recommend them.  I was also impressed that the language is appropriate and that sexual content is virtually nonexistent, based on the observations of other reviewers.

title: Great crime novel
text:
I write here as one who has never read a book by Allison Leotta, but "Speak of the Devil" has made me want to read everything she has written. The main character in "Speak of the Devil" is Anna Curtis, a sex crimes prosecutor in Washington DC, who has just become engaged to Jack Bailey, chief of the DC homicide unit. Jack has a six-year-old daughter, Olivia, and his late wife, Nina Flores, had been killed four years earlier by one of the street gangs of Washington DC. Most investigators believe that that the crime was committed by MS-13, a notoriously violent and ruthless DC gang. The leader of this gang is Diablo, accurately named "the Devil." Diablo's skin is completely covered in tattooed hieroglyphs. His nose is two sunken holes; he has long black hair and two fleshy horns protruding from his forehead. Indeed, he is aptly named.

Diablo and his gang appear throughout the book as Anna Curtis and Jack Flores attempt to solve various gruesome crimes occurring in the DC area. There are many twists and turns, and a huge red herring that comes as a total surprise to the reader in the last third of the book. I really enjoyed this book and recommend it to anyone who likes true-life crime fiction. The author's experience as a sex-crimes prosecutor for 12 years in Washington DC is evident on every page, and she is a superb writer. If I could give the book more than five stars, I would. Highly recommended.

title: Excellent, but for very young children
text: This is one of the best books in the "Dummies" series.  Unlike many of them, it is beautifully illustrated and colorful.  It gives wonderful descriptions of Apps the are appropriate for young children.  I was hoping to find apps that were suited to older tweens and teens, but this book is really for young children and early elementary age kids.  However, if this is the age group you are searching for. I recommend this book highly.

title: An absorbing and quick read
text:
Set in the fictional town of Red Paint Bay, a typical small town where everyone knows everyone else and nothing is kept secret for long, this book deals with a long-buried secret that is about to re-emerge and haunt many, especially one family.

This family is headed by Simon Howe, who was born and raised in Red Paint and is now the editor of the town paper. He is married to Amy, a psychotherapist, who runs the family with an iron hand. Their son, Davey, is a more or less typical teen, but he gets into trouble and is grounded regularly for some pretty bizarre behavior, such as throwing knives at his best friend. Simon and his staff are always trying to think of events to fill their small-town paper. It has been said that when the gods wish to punish us, they answer our prayers, and this is true in spades with Simon. His 25th high school reunion is approaching, and in this town, that qualifies as front page news. It is here that the excitement and horror begin.

Simon has been getting a number of unsigned postcards, the content of which ranges from mundane (Will you meet me for dinner?) to threatening. He decides to meet with the postcard-sender, and though he is instructed to come alone, Amy insists on coming with him. Davey is left alone with strict orders to stay in the house. (Never a good idea in a mystery book.) The mysterious writer is a no-show, and when Simon and Amy return home, they find that Davey has disappeared. The police are called, and Davey is found safe in a treehouse. But how did he get there? There is, of course, a connection with the mysterious postcard-writer.

The story gets better with every page--I challenge you not to finish this book. Many interesting and typical small town characters have their roles to play, and the mystery deepens with each chapter. If you enjoy mysteries with a small town flavor and fast pace, you will like this book. Highly recommended.

title: Great for a select audience
text:
Let me say at the outset that I am a great fan of Cook's Magazine, the magazine whose compiled articles compose this superb cookbook. For those unfamiliar with it, each issue of Cook's Magazine takes a few dishes and explores in excruciating detail how to make each one. For example, take beef stew. The magazine would examine every aspect of several recipes, from cuts of beef to cooking time and temperature, to when to add the vegetables, to how and why to brown the beef, and on and on. After experimenting with several, or even dozens of recipes, the magazine gives the "ultimate" beef stew recipe, one that will produce perfect results if followed exactly, even for the novice cook. Along the way, you get a lesson (or several) in the science of food, why some things work and others do not.

This massive cookbook (486 pages) is excellent, but it was a little overwhelming, even for me. I love reading about food and learning what works and why. And I have never tried a Cook's recipe that failed. However, I can see that this cookbook is not for everyone. If you are looking for recipes with 5 ingredients or less, or that use a lot of processed foods, you will be disappointed.

So why five stars? Because this cookbook does a superb job of what it sets out to do. The reader learns the techniques of food preparation, the science (with accompanying diagrams) of why some things work and others do not, and in the end gets a great recipe for whatever it is he or she wants to make. The book covers all sorts of food, from bread and muffins, to meats and poultry, to vegetables, to eggs and cheese, to desserts--be sure to try the recipe for Perfect New York Cheesecake--the ultimate best.

I recommend this book for people who enjoy the "why" of food preparation, not merely the "how." It will take time to go through the article on even one recipe, but you will be rewarded with not only a great recipe, but with greater confidence in your cooking skills.

title: A "fix" for Randy Cohen fans
text:
I must confess at the outset that I am a big fan of Randy Cohen, and I looked forward to his "Ethicist" columns each Sunday in the New York Times Magazine. When he left a couple of years ago, I missed him, even though I thought his successors did a good job. And I like the current Ethicist, Chuck Klosterman, very much. Still, I was happy to see a book of Cohen's columns compiled and categorized.

The columns are loosely grouped into one of several categories. Some of these are Family, Home, Money, Civic Life, Animals, Sports, Work, School, Arts, Love and Sex, Religion, and Community. What I like especially about these ethical dilemmas, and Cohen's comments on them, is that they make the reader think, and in some cases, vehemently disagree. Most of them would make interesting (if not always convivial) dinner conversation. I almost never go away from a response thinking, "Well, obviously!" So much of what we deal with in modern life is not obvious, and the columns Cohen has selected for this book reflect that in spades.

This book goes beyond a simple compilation of columns, however. First, each section is prefaced by a short essay on the topic in general, highlighting both the topic itself and the author's views in general. Second, a few of Cohen's columns generated much response, for example, a column about whether an IT worker is ethically required to report the presence of child pornography on his boss's computer. In these cases, Cohen describes and quotes extensively from the response(s), which are usually objections to what he has written. He evaluates the writer's point of view, sometimes agreeing at least in part, but more often clarifying his own thinking. In reading these, the reader gets a short course, not just in ethics, but in critical thinking.

I enjoyed this book a great deal, and I recommend it to anyone interested in thinking about everyday ethics in today's world.

title: Tween Horror
text:
"The Cavendish Home for Boys and Girls" is aimed at the 10 to 14 age group, but my guess is that older teens and even adults may enjoy it as well, though not for the same reasons. First, the target audience. This is a horror fantasy, plain and simple. A children's home staffed by monsters masquerading as kindly caregivers, a house that changes shape and comes to life, children trapped with no hope for escape--all of these elements are well integrated in this excellent book. I will not review the plot, as other reviewers have done so quite well, but I think most tweens will be hooked by the strange Harry Potter-esque events that occur within the house, as well as by the efforts of the heroine to save the day.

Now the older readers. When I began this book, I immediately thought it was a sort of Stepford Wives for kids. Children, especially strange or odd children, or those who are for any reason outside the norm, are kidnapped, or disappear, only to (sometimes) turn up weeks or months later, transformed. They suddenly fit in; their odd individuality has been excised. As I read on, however, I began to think of this book as a cautionary tale against conformity, perfectionism, and intolerance. For me, the most insightful lines in the book occur when Miss Cavendish, the villain, says to Victoria, the heroine, "You and I are just alike." And the truth is, they are. As Victoria experiences the house in all its horrors, she realizes her own tendencies toward judgmental condemnation of others and love of doing things "just so," attitudes that can lead, in adulthood, to intolerance and bigotry. In addition, Miss Cavendish cannot enact her villainy without the consent and collusion of nearly all the townspeople. This idea is given expression in a metaphor, that of puppets; each citizen of the town is no more than a marionette. This part is horrifying to any reader.

This is not a light and sunny book. Victoria wins, but only just, and her victory is not a lasting one, as the epilogue of the book suggests. Perhaps we are being set up for a sequel? In any event, readers young and old will appreciate the powerful descriptive passages and superb writing. Five stars.

title: Gripping psychological thriller
text:
I am one of those readers who is new to the novels of Karin Slaughter and her dyslexic hero, Will Trent. Head of the Georgia Bureau of Investigation, Will is a hero with a lot of baggage. He has found love in the beautiful pediatrician Sara Linton, but Sara is justifiably cautious about involvement with a man so damaged as Will. All this is background: readers of Slaughter's other books will already be familiar with it, but I was not.

In "Criminal," the time shifts from the early-to-mid seventies to the present day. Georgia in the seventies was a place teeming with racism and sexism, and the police department was not immune to either. The subject is prostitution, and the story centers on Lucy Bennett, who was unlucky enough to be led into prostitution to feed her increasing drug addiction. Lucy's pimp is the stereotypical bad guy, taken to an extreme. When Lucy decides to run away, she meets up with an even more evil, almost Satanic figure. The reader should be warned that these passages are not for the faint of heart. Slaughter does not mince words or pretty up what she is describing. You will see in detail the sordid side of life.

The conflict is of course between the criminals and the police. The title is ironic in that the police are in many ways criminals themselves. The reader may become frustrated at all the plot twists and seemingly unrelated digressions, but don't worry--everything is tied together in the end, as it should be in a good police procedural.

"Criminal" is so well written that I am determined to get Slaughter's other books and read them in the order she wrote them. If you are already a fan, buy this book with confidence--you will not be disappointed. Highly recommended.

title: Superb help for iPad users of any age
text:
My husband and I purchased an iPad about a year ago, and it has become one of our favorite electronics ever. To help us become acquainted with all that it had to offer, we bought iPad for Dummies for Seniors, which was very helpful. When iPad for Older and Wiser became available through Amazon Vine, I decided to order it to compare its helpfulness with the Dummies book.

iPad for Older and Wiser is excellent, even better than the Dummies manual. It has extremely clear, step-by-step instructions and numerous helpful illustrations. The summaries and quizzes at the end of each chapter were a good way for the reader to see if he or she had gotten the main points, and if you did not, you could go back to review. It is also an excellent reference for each chapter; a sort of mini-index. The format is appealing, with a lot of subtle color and well-designed paragraphs and bullet points. It is wonderful to have this reference handy when I use my iPad and explore all its capabilities.

I recommend this manual to everyone, not just seniors. Unless you are supremely computer-literate, it will help you with your iPad more than any other reference I have found. I am looking forward to reading other books in this series. Five stars and more!

title: A bit slow at first, but ultimately rewarding
text:
I selected "The Unlikely Pilgrimage of Harold Fry" to read and review because I loved "Major Pettigrew's Last Stand," a book to which it was compared in the publisher's preview. And while I prefer "Major Pettigrew" for its pacing and multicultural appeal, I wholeheartedly recommend "Harold Fry." It has charms of its own.

Henry David Thoreau observed, "The mass of men live lives of quiet desperation," and I could not help but recall this quotation as I began Rachel Joyce's lovely debut novel. As the novel begins, Harold is merely existing. The reader is not given many details, but it is clear that Harold's marriage to Maureen is an empty shell, and that there are problems in his relationship with his adult son, David. Then Harold gets a farewell letter of sorts from a friend, Queenie Hennessy, and his carefully orchestrated charade of a life begins to come apart. Queenie had "done something nice" for Harold twenty years previous, and he always regretted not thanking her. Whatever this is is shrouded in mystery, and many readers will suspect a long-past affair. All these questions are a bit disconcerting, but if the reader is patient, all will be resolved.

Harold writes a "pro forma" response to Queenie's note, but as he goes out to mail it, something prevents him from putting it in the first mailbox he comes to. He passes postbox after postbox, and eventually makes an impulsive decision to walk from his hometown to Queenie's hospice, about 600 miles. Thus begins his transformation from a kind of living death to fullness of life.

Readers who are familiar with Joseph Campbell's "The Hero's Journey" will immediately recognize the motif: the hero leaves the world he knows to embark on a quest. Along the way he meets both helpers and tempters, and he eventually returns to the known world with a fullness of knowledge or with something to enrich his community and himself.

Harold Fry fits this motif to a tee. He meets many people and even animals along the way, and he gains something of value from each of them, even those who would deter him from his quest. Meanwhile, back at home, Maureen is undergoing her own transformation as she worries and responds to Harold's calls, postcards, and gifts. Nothing is as Harold or Maureen expect it to be. And the end of the quest is rewarding, but not in the way Harold imagines.

One final observation: This is a beautifully written novel. Most readers will love the use of language, especially in descriptions of the natural world. I am stunned that this is the author's first novel, though she has written many screenplays for the BBC. I hope to read much more of her work.

Most readers will like and appreciate "Harold Fry" if they persevere through the ambiguity at the beginning. Everything falls together eventually, I promise! Highly recommended.

title: Great short stories
text:
I loved "Shout Her Lovely Name," a superb short story collection by Natalie Serber. Each of the eleven stories in this collection explores some aspect of the mother/daughter bond. While other emotional entanglements occur, this bond predominates.

The first story was my favorite. Told in second person, it captures well the utter frustration of a mother whose daughter is struggling with an eating disorder. Neither mother nor daughter is named, and this adds to the universality of the story. The emotions depicted run the gamut from exaltation to utter despair and everything in between. While I am not a parent myself, it was easy for me to believe and relate to each and every line.

The next nine stories are loosely linked. They center around the relationship between Ruby Goddard and her mother, Sally, and eventually to Ruby's daughter, Nora. We first meet Ruby as she is coming home from college for a visit with her dysfunctional parents. From there, the stories explore Ruby as she tries to find herself in several ways: through travel, through study, in various relationships with men, and finally through motherhood. I found each story compelling and interesting, psychologically true and extremely well written.

The final story was, in my opinion, the least successful of the eleven, and I am eager to know what other readers thought of it as well. Longest of all the stories, it introduced new characters and simply did not work well for me, which was surprising as I loved the other stories. Despite this, however, I gladly give this collection five stars, and I eagerly await more writing by Natalie Serber.

title: Engaging book for Disney enthusiasts
text: My niece had this book (and all its companions in the series) on her birthday list.  She absolutely loves the books (I purchased the first three in the series) and stays up late at night to read them.
