I guess I was expecting an anthology of Seattle writing, but what I got was the equivalent of sitting in a coffee shop and listening to writers gossip about the local writer's scene. It was interesting to get this kind of insiders look at what has happened and is happening in Seattle, but make sure that that is what you are looking for.

The book also points out that I don't know much about the Seattle scene beyond Tom Robbins and he was placed right up front in the very first pages. Also they played the Pynchon card at the same time, leaving me with a lot of poets that I didn't know. There is a long litany of name dropping that was pretty much lost on my except for the musical notes. I appreciated hearing that Sleater-Kenny came into a writers bookshop far more that hearing that someone remembers seeing the godfather of Seattle poetry get out of his car once. But I did end the book with a feeling that there was this close knit group churning out writing in the flavor of the northwest. In the end, I envied them for having this community and would love to be able to fit in, know the inside jokes and name drop along side them.

The purpose of the book is to support a campaign to get internationally recognized as a center for literature. It does prove that there is a vibrant community with some chops. But next time, I'm looking for a anthology of writing showing what life in Seattle is like.

title: Decent Book, A Little Dark
text:
This seemed like the perfect book, and I did like reading it, but it fell a little short of my hopes. I was hoping this would be more along the lines of Paulson's Hatchet which my kids loved. And I did find it enjoyable, but it was not quite Hatchet and I don't have the same hopes that they will love it.

At heart this is a good survival in the wilderness book. It has bears, hunger, precious tools, and hope, but it also has an overly angry main character, a not very happy ending and some natural history gaffs that kind of bug me. It really was kind of annoying to have such a stubbornly truculent and bullying character to have the narrator stranded with. Eventually it got absurd that this character, (Frank) who seemed to have all the tools and knowledge to survive would refuse to team with the narrator (Chris.)

The writing is truly decent, I turned the pages willingly but in the end, I didn't find it as satisfying as Hatchet.

title: A like able book with a good message
text: I really wanted to love this book.  I love the idea of a small voice changing the world and I love the theme of mountain top removal in the southeast, so I had high hopes. And for the most part the book lived up to my hopes, but I was a little put off by the style of the writing. I found the writing and dialogue a little choppy and not the strongest writing in general. But it was a likable story for sure.

title: Decent Book, Like that it's a Rapid Fire Series
text:
Well it took a while to get through this book but just finished it on my commute this morning. I was interested in this series for a couple of reasons, first the premise sounded good and I like to get into series that I know my kids will like. But mostly I was intrigued by the rapid fire plan to get all six books out in a year by using different writers for each installment. I had been considering getting the first book at Target when I got the chance to get an ARC of book 2.

While starting on book 2 has some downfalls, I think it does give a good tenor on what the books are about. I definitely feel that book one was an establishing introduction where the characters were introduce, and this book is clearly a transition book to the rest of the series where some major secrets are revealed, and a new set of competitors are introduced that should take the reader through the rest of the series.

The main adventure is not super strong. In each book, the crew needs to find a component for a super fuel to save earth. Due to the limitations on space travel technologies, only humans under 14 can travel, adults cannot survive the process. (Isn't that a stretch for a premise for a tween book?) In this installment, they find that they need to recover some magma from a planet that ends up being the creation of one of the characters in the book, and while the peril is a little light, the purpose of this book seems more aimed at developing the main characters of the book and lay the foundation for the rest of the series.

The writing is decent, it is not the most compelling tween adventure, but it was definitely readable. There are lots of tie ins with contemporary culture, like references to Taylor Swift and games like Simon. This should be appreciated by kids. Much like 39 Clues, there will be interactive tie ins as well to draw kids deeper into the series. Hopefully it will not be totally heavy handed, but there are ads in the books leading you to look into the online game etc.

All in all, it's been a decent book. My kids seem interested in reading it now that I am done and I look forward to seeing how well it gets them engaged.

title: A simple story, good for early readers
text:
This was a cute story, perhaps a little young for our kids (8-14 year olds). It is a second level intro to chapter books. The illustrations are great, but the story is not an award winner for sure. The story is cute and straightforward.

I read it before our 8 year old and she was definitely more taken with it than me. Eventually she re read it aloud to our 10 year old so it did engage them well, but the story did seem pretty disposeable.

So great book in that it kept the kids reading, not a great book in that there are No life changing messages or passages. But it is ultimately like able.

title: A Great Book, But with a Feel of just an Introductory Book
text:
I'm kind of on the fence about this one. The writing is very good, the story line was interesting and it held my engagement. But I can't quite say that I loved it. I did very much like it. The characters were strong, the imagery of the museum was fantastic, the illustrations were scattered but strong and the action was good.

But something about the resolution left me with the same feeling you get when you are watching a movie like the Hobbit and it stops abruptly and you get to wait a year to pick up the story from there. The ending just didn't bring resolution. Actually, I think that is just it, there was no huge transformation in the characters, just an introduction. They did meld as a team of misfits, they did find their place but there was no final victory.

Other than the unsettling lacking of closure, this truly is a well written book. Some of the facts in the mystery are telegraphed. But many are well crafted deductions and surprises. It's kind of Hardy Boys meet Scooby Doo goes to the Circus but darker. There are murders which seemed a little strong for a juvenile lit book, but plenty of grossness and farts for kids to enjoy.

title: A Decent Light Read
text:
This is a very likeable book. It fits well in to the easy reading books that scholastic puts out. In fact, after 40 pages or so, I actually flipped to the publishing page to see if it was a scholastic. The story is unique enough and the writing is good and propelled me through the book.

The story has essences of many books but it reminded me of modern and lighter combination of Narnia and A Wrinkle in Time. I suppose because of the combination of a magic portal and an attempt to rescue a lost father. But the tenor of the book is far more light and whimsical. This is not a piece a literature, but a fun little romp.

My biggest concern is that the son I gave the book to has been having problems staying locked in on the book. He typically inhales books so I look forward to see if this one eventually catches on with him.

title: Good book, but I think the author brought more to the search than usual
text:
I love Paul Theroux. I am amazed how he finds the perfect characters in his travels and how rich they are. I have been in awe of simple Chinese drivers to Polish black marketers and everything in between. But the characters in this book hit to close to home since I grew up int the South. This is not the South I have been returning to which year by year has grown more cosmopolitan.

It seems like Paul has gone in search of the southern stereotype we had in the mid twentieth century. Sure you can find these individuals, but there seems to be a focus to the search, an attempt to push a narrative that he wants to tell. Personally, I wince everytime I head back to the South as I watch the regionalisms die, taken over by ubiquitous American homogeneous. I wish there was as much regional difference as he's finding.

That being said, Theroux is a master of his art and of words. The reading is entertaining and engaging. I still love his prose, just this one didn't seem to ring true on his observations. I just returned from a Chitlin feed and where there once was authenticity, there is now nostalgic window dressings. this book seems more a search for the endangered than unveiling of a character.

title: A Surprisingly Good Book
text:
This was a very surprisingly good book. To be honest I was not sure who would write a book about Noah Webster but I thought my oldest, history loving son would like the book. We both read it and I can say for myself, I found the times he lived in remarkable. He was at the sidelines of our very creation as a nation.

This ended up being an amazing portrait of an amazing individual.

title: Good Book, but less focus on DDay than I Hoped
text:
I got this book trying to get my oldest son interested in a post graduation trip to Europe. He is a huge fan of military history and I hoped that this would help inspire him. I have to admit I was a little disappointed to find that the DDay section was not particularly big or filled with information. But it was filled with practical information for his visit. It has things like opening times and logistics of food and lodging, but will be more important during the planning stages and not so helpful in the dreaming stages. Definitely get other books for learning about DDay, get this one when you are ready to plan your drive.

The quality of the book is good, it has thick, almost cardstock pages so it does not lay open well, but the size is good for travel. The photos are good and plentiful. But this really is a nuts and bolts logistics book. I like that there are several drives, including one to follow Monet's footsteps, which is an interest to me, but an indicator that the focus is not just on DDay.

This is a good book, but know what you are getting. You are getting travel information, you are getting a few pre-planned routes. The information is good, but not comprehensive. And is what you need when actually sitting down to plan your trip.

title: A Good Start to What I Hope is a Great Series
text:
This is a great concept. I love the national park focus and would love to have had these to introduce my kids to parks we were traveling to, and maybe we'll get a chance to have one come out before they are too old. It reminds be a lot of the Magic Treehouse series which educated my kids on all kinds of things. This series has tons of potential to do the same for the parks.

The storyline is OK. I found the time jumping a little jumpy at times and while the narrative was pretty good, some of the time jumps seemed a little out of place. Also, to a degree it read a little like the pilot for a network sitcom. The characters were there and defined, but it just felt that it needed a season of production to find the right chemistry for everyone. I really expect this to be a great series in the end, and I have a huge wish list of parks I'd like to have covered (like Denali where we're going next week.)

I really, really like the premise. The illustrations are decent. The writing was good. Once polished, I think this series will shine.

title: An Okay Book
text:
So I tried to read this book and could not get through it due to time, so I gave it to two of my kids. When asked they gave a rather lackluster, "It's Good." Which is kind of an endorsement, but far less warm than their usual reaction to books. And that was kind of the feel I was getting from it while reading it. It was interesting enough, but I don't know that I feel compelled to finish the story. It was not bad, but it also wasn't great. I am glad that it kept the kids interested enough to finish the book.

The kids were super excited to find a couple more books at the library, but apparently it was to glean codes to put into an online game. As of right now those books have remained unread after an initial flurry to find the codes. I'm not a huge fan of that kind of online tie in or marketing.

title: A Very Likeable Book, if You Can Get Past the Dog POV
text:
Ok, I had a little problem with the juniorization of this book and found the dog's POV strained and a little cliché, but I liked the book. I think I would have much preferred the original better, but I can see that kids could get into the dog's voice better than I did. But it made it a little tedious to hear a young dog experience the mysterious fears and frustrations of the world.

Where the book excels is the actual training and work of a rescue dog. This is what caught me into the book and I think it's what will really make the book for kids. The human plots are OK and tie the book together, but the joy for me were the mini rescue adventures. And here, even the dog POV worked well and I felt it helped get you into the dog's head.

title: A Great Starting Place for Selling a House
text:
This was the perfect introduction for me to selling my house. I'm not planning on selling by owner or earn my own real estate license, I'm just hoping to be informed in choosing a realtor and going through the process with some knowledge. I greatly appreciate that it had lots of hints for getting your house ready and getting the most for it. I feel that I'm in a good location and this is good timing, and this book has prepared me to go into this equipped with the knowledge I need.

One of the biggest things I was worried was how much work to put into the house. The prepping chapter did a lot for letting me know what would have the best bang for the buck, and man hour for that matter. I think I can maximize my efforts now, focusing on decluttering and getting a good return on investment for our efforts.

It's not the end all book, but I'm certainly glad I read it.

title: A Very Good Juvenile Mystery
text:
I really liked this book, but surprisingly it was abandoned by to separate kids. I read it and thought it was a nice little juvenile mystery. I'm not much for literature narrated by the animal characters, but this one seems to handle that very well and where I find a this dog-centric narration tedious and clichéd in most books, it was fine here.

There are plenty of kind of clichéd elements here, orphan rescues an orphaned dog, scoundrel makes good... but there is a sweetness to the relationship and the characters were good. I found the book rather engaging and hope that it is picked up again by the kids as it is a heartwarming little tale.

title: An Engaging Read, Good Suspense, A Simple Tale
text:
I have to admit that this book read a little like an PETA anti-hunting fairy tale, but it was a nice and engaging read. It shows two colliding stories of a boy and an aging wolf with building suspense as the story comes to it's completion. I'm not a huge fan of "talking animal" stories but read a lot of them with my kids and this one works as well as any of them.

The natural history of the wolf pack and animals that they relate with is decent...well beyond the talking part. The images are strong and well described and contrast well with the modern lifestyle of the boy in the story. And I did like how the parallel stories converged.

The books reads like strong juvenile lit, and I did not find it overly graphic or gory, but there is enough here to be careful for more sensitive kids. But I think the author handled the story line well.

title: A Great Idea Generator for Kids Activities
text:
I love books like this. They often give great ideas for engaging you children into different activities. This book has a decent mix of things to do. Some are better than others for sure, but it there are a lot of good ideas. Some are things like, learn your zodiac sign which are a little iffy. But others like create your own newspaper or obstacle course really engage creativity. It actually kind of reads and is used like a scouting badge guide but without the badges. The ideas mostly open ended and can be taken as far as you would like to.

The book itself is well made, playfully illustrated and should stand up to the adventures. Each idea has a completion check off spot with date so you can record your progress through the book. All in all a cute little book.

title: A Moving Book about Family Loss in the Vulnerable Tween Years
text:
This is a very well written book with a couple of rather deep themes. Because of discussion of depression, abuse, suicide and love, this may be a rather mature book for the target audience. But all of these subjects are discussed frankly and meaningfully. And all these issues are authentically filtered through the viewpoint of a tween girl.

I was very impressed with the author's writing style and characters. The writing was clean and easy to read. This was a great debut for the author and I look forward to more strong juvenile literature for it. If I had anything as far as constructive criticism, I would say that the target audience is a little older than tween.

title: A very complete coverage of the Eating Experience.
text:
OK, I'll admit it, the only reason I got this book was to impress a girl with a perfect meal and I was very taken in by the title and description. I was hoping that this book would unlock the mysteries to making the perfect meal. And to a degree it does. It takes a lot of disparate research and pulls it together so show how different senses, beyond taste, that affect the meal.

The book reads like Freakonomics for the kitchen. The research that it pulls is varied and often very surprising. It is somewhat loosely organized around chapters on expected things like plating, atmosphere and the science of taste, and some surprising ones like eating in the dark. Some of the research seems to be tossed into these categories, but the research is interesting.

The reason I didn't give the book 5 stars is because it was a little academic and it didn't really hit the bullseye with me. The chapter on naming and describing food was nice, but for my date night purposes it was not needed. As were all the restaurant and menu specific stuff. But on the other hand much of this book was fascinating and I truly appreciated the chapters on plating, cutlery and atmosphere. I have to admit, I did skip some areas that were very restaurant specific, but got a lot of value out of the book. At the very least it was an entertaining read. But I have a list of things to try on the next dinner date. Wish me luck.

title: I Good Graphic Novel, Hoping it Becomes a Series
text:
I love to get graphic novels for my boys. I feel that they were key to getting them to become life long readers and even though they may not be as mind stimulating as other books, they are engaging and were an entry level into chapter books and beyond. So I was happy to have gotten a review copy of this book.

The illustrations are stylized and consistently strong. There is a little bit of gore in the form of decapitations which parents may want to be aware of. My kids are not big fans of gore and over the top violence, but they seemed to be okay with it, although my 13 year-old kept count of the deheadings and reported them to me. But for the most part the violence was not bad.

The storyline was decent and pretty straight forward. I would not call it a complex plot, but it had a good linnear flow toward vengeance (which is not great surprise.) Dialog was good, and all in all the story was engaging and both my kids got through to book in one sitting.

We are long fans of such series as the Stone Keepers and other strong graphic novels so we have read a lot of very good ones and this one is pretty good. I don't know that it is in the upper crust of the genre, but worth the time to read for sure.

title: A very Decent Book about Studio Photography
text:
I am planning on doing some product photography in the near future so I was really looking forward to getting a copy of this book. And this book proved to be a very decent overview of product photography. It started out pretty basic, even for an amateur like me, but I guess the low end of the audience is someone who is just thinking of getting a camera and looking for the base equipment to get.

The book was well illustrated and well worth my time, but it did not quite live up to the two books I once had on studio lighting. It would have been nice to have more specific shots illustrated to show how the lighting was set up specifically. There are a few good examples but (and I wish I could find it to link to it) not as good as my memories of my old book.

This book however is well worth the money. It is a solid introduction to shooting products and I got a lot out of it.

title: A Decent Book Giving and Overview of the Human Predator
text:
It is amazing that even in the middle of an urban area, there are now conflicts with predators. The topic is becoming more and more important as wolves, coyotes, bears, and mountain lions expand and start to get more and more entwined with human habitats. And this is the time to look at facts and science to see the best way to manage the interactions.

I like that the book goes through most of the dimensions of the dilemma and gives suggestions for ranchers for controlling losses to predators other than wholesale and often misguided slaughter. However I am still leery of rosy stories about the ecological successes in Yellowstone. I think good or bad, the jury needs to be out for at least a couple boom and bust cycles. Even wolves work on S curves of abundance and I wince when I read conclusions so soon after wolves have been established.

All in all, a good book though.

title: A Decent Overview of Mandela
text:
I was really hoping to learn more about Nelson Mandela, and I can say that I did do that. However the format made this book a little less than cohesive when read front to back. It almost reads like a bathroom reader, with shorter digestible essays. This made it a breeze to read, but since from letter to letter the subjects changed greatly, it does not flow well in parts.

The sprinkling of photos is nice. The insights of those who spent a lot of time with Mandela were great. I had high hopes for the book, and while I was not overwhelmed. I do appreciate what I have learned from this book.

title: A Cute Story with Great Illustrations
text:
My son and I really enjoyed this book. The illustrations are fantastic, bright and playful. The text is easily read, rhyming couplets which tell a nice little story of a boy and his father who suddenly find themselves in need of a mechanic and end up being bailed out by some gracious apes.

The book has very high quality paper, dust cover and binding. And while I don't know that we'll be rereading this one much, the book will hold up well over time.

My son appreciated the rebellious ending which finds the boy driving the car from the shop with the support of all the monkeys. So it has enough subversiveness and beautiful illustrations to engage a six year old boy. All in all a very good book but probably not destined to be a classic.

title: A Cute and Decent Book
text:
I have read a lot to my kids, and I have really appreciated all the great children's books that have come out in the last few years. I don't feel that this one is amongst the recent greats, but it is squarely in the pretty good recent group.

The illustrations were cute although not masterworks. The story was cute but not masterful. But the results were what I was hoping for. Several smiles and held attention as we read through the book. The dialogue is standard caveman "Tarzan Speak" which reads humorously.

I hope I am not being too harsh, this really is a good book, and continues the story of Ogg and Bob which was nice. Returning to a series seems to help grab my kids attention and since this book did that and helped continue their path to lifelong readers, I am very happy with it.

title: A Modern Fairy Tale, True to Grimms Brothers style
text:
I really liked this story on a lot of levels. I loved the the premise of Jacob Grimm narrating a story that ultimately was a fairy tale in itself, filled with all the hallmarks and cliches of a fairy tale, but with a brutal, torturous side that sadly could be lifted from some of today's headlines. Even the somewhat brutal ending chapters are reminiscent of the frank brutality of some of the Grimms brothers recorded stories.

I have to admit the book seemed a little long winded in sections, but it pulled me through the story well and kept me going. I have a son who is big into the Rick Riordan books and this fits in with those fairly well. The author does a great job of creating a fairy tale aura for the bad guy while blending in some horrorifyingly modern ugliness to him. I don't want to spoil anything but this book is a very worthwhile read.

title: Updated but Unchanged from Original, Kids Loved It
text:
I have to admit, as a parent who went through all the classic stories, I really like remakes that have great twists like [[ASIN:068981528X The Three Little Wolves and the Big Bad Pig]]. I thought this book might have the potential of being something very similar but it was actually very true to the original tale with just some cosmetic updating. Not that there is anything wrong with that.

The illustrations are great with many humorous details. For example, there is a little side tale of credit card fraud where the bad guys use the emperor's cards to purchase items that are specific to their species. All in all the modernization pulls a little of the power of the original story, but at the same time enliven it with humor.

But the key to how much I like a book is how much my kids enjoy the book and this book totally passed that test.

title: A Decent Overview of iPads
text:
I have to admit that for the most part, the iPad needs a manual about as much toaster does. But there are some things you do need to look up, like where security settings are. It is good to have a reference to find things like this (other than google if you are old school) and this fills the bill for it. It reads like a text book including end of the chapter review questions.

I think I prefer the missing manual over this book, but it does have all the information you will probably need. And most importantly it is well indexed and the table of contents helps you find the information you need. It definitely fills the need for a hard copy manual.

title: A Decent LIttle Bed Time Book
text:
This was not a bad little book. The story is a pretty straight forward child gets lost/reunited story without any real kind of twist. The Illustrations range from great to a little off when the tiger faces looks a little misproportioned, but in general the illustrations are decent. Where the illustration excels are the images of the dusky, frozen and snowy forest.

There were a couple of forced natural history facts like spraying and scratching to mark territory. The species were correct in the book and it has some authenticity, but the storyline was a little too straight forward.

My kids seemed to think it was OK but I could tell it did not capture their imagination or grip their attention. It's OK but there is a wealth of stronger books out there these days.

title: A Nice Read for Bed Time Stories or Early Readers
text:
I can see why this book would be a classic in the early 70's but this book is a little dated when compared to some of the delightful children's books that are coming out now. The first couple of books in this compilation are very straight forward with the staccato delivery of Dick and Jane books, although in fuller sentences. The last few stories have a little more twist to them, but again, pretty straight forward which is great for young readers but a little less than entertaining for the parent involved.

The Illustrations are simple and satisfying. I found the pictures of Ms Monster and Monster's cohabiting kid particularly charming (although a little disconcerting that Monster asks a boy to live with him...)

All in all this is decent early reader and it is great to see it republished for the parents and grandparents who remember this from the 70's. It is cute enough, but with less twists and cute plot lines than I enjoy in the usual books I read to my kids.

title: A great Overview of the Office Products
text:
I recently took a job where I would be supporting Office 2013 a few weeks after I started. I found this book and decided it would be a good overview to help me get up to speed on the products. I was right about that. The book does give a decent overview of the entire office line which was great. At least it helps me navigate the screens well.

Where I felt this book fell short for me was that it does not cover any in depth troubleshooting. Which is fair enough, the book was scoped as an introduction, not a troubleshooting reference. I won't knock the book for what it is, it just wasn't quite what I was looking for or needed. But the book was informative on the level it goes into the products. If you are new to Office, I would highly recommend the book to you.

The only other constructive thing I can think of, is that it did not seem to be the most elegantly designed book. I didn't find it as scannable as I would have hoped. Otherwise, I just have praise for it being a good, but not great book. If you want to be ready to start a new job using office 2013 it's perfect. If you want to start helping 1000 people having questions regarding their problems and training issues, you'll need a little more.

title: A Decent Book, but for Me, not Quite Into the Wild
text:
I figured I would really like this book since I was strangely sucked into [[ASIN:B003TGMFG4 Into the Wild 1997 Anchor paperback by Jon Krakauer]]. That book drew me into the mystery and mystique of Christopher McCandless far more than I expected. Perhaps that set the expectations a little high for this book which is very similar in topic.

I found the book very readable and I liked the details like the woodcuts from Ruess spread throughout the book. But much like McCandless, I don't think I saw a complete genius in Ruess. He did seem sharp and walking to the beat of a different drummer but perhaps I am tone deaf to the call of their lifestyles. But I did appreciate the bravado of his actions, and I envy the sights he must have seen in the southwest.

The Ruess mystery did not seem as tangiable to me. Although I have a connection with Alaska I don't have to the Southwest. This was a very decent book, it just didn't grab me the way that Into the Wild had.

title: Eye Opening for a Beginner iOS Hack
text:
This book is well above my head for many of the things covered. But it did a great job of showing me some of the possibilities I was not even able to fathom. Unfortunately all books for programming have a shelf life, but i have found myself picking this book back up and flipping through it again for inspirations when brainstorming an app.

This book is definitely not iOS for dummies or an intro book. Definitely well worth it for advanced programmers, but it made my head spin how fast iOS 6 came out and relegated this book to an idea book.

title: A Decent Fantasy Book for my Young Reader
text:
We are always on the lookout for a new series to stoke my oldest boys reading habit. This book has a lot of good things going for it, dragons, pegasi, and the whole retinue of other mythical beasts. Also there is a great sense of adventure and some suspense, almost everything a boy can want.

Well maybe a male main character would be nice for my son. I like the idea of a female lead, but it is remarkable boys and girls relate to characters of their own gender. I am totally going to introduce my niece to this series as she gets older. It is nice to have a resourceful female lead.

Otherwise this book read well, it still has to pass the kid test, but it totally passed the parent preview test. I can't say that I like this book as much as the Riorden series, but it was pretty good. I feel comfortable in recommending it to anyone with young readers into the Percy Jackson, Harry Potter genre, especially for young girls.

There is an environmental tilt to this book, and even though I feel very strongly about environmental issues, I often cringe at preachy "environmental" kids books. This one touches on environmental themes and feature an environmental protest, but it does it tactfully.

All in all a decent book.

title: A Good Reference for a Literacy Instructor
text:
I am a huge reader and would love to see my sons follow in my footsteps and be recreational readers as well. This book really caught my eye since my youngest son is in first grade and is just starting his reading career. I was looking for a guide to help teach him to learn and excel at reading.

While this guide has had some insights for nurturing my son's reading, it really is meant for a teacher. I passed it by a friend who teaches in a literacy centric school and she said it was a good synthesis of what she had been studying in graduate school. She said the coverage was good and up to date and a good reference for anyone teaching in the field.

The book has some good exercises and content. I took the suggestion of paraphrasing to get almost instantly get my son to read for content more than he was. I really felt informed for preparing my kids to be lifelong readers and learners.

title: A Great Casual Read for Kids
text:
Our family has read a lot of books like this from Ripley's Believe it or Not, Guiness Books of World Records, National Geographic, etc. These really lock brains into facts about the world around young minds. I don't know that there is any lasting academic gain through these books, but boy do the darndest facts come out of their mouths at the darndest times.

The book tries to push that is full of yuckiness, but it really doesn't push any envelopes. It has a frenetic design, splashed with photos, drawings and infographics across bright backgrounds.

I really like this book, my kids and I had fun flipping through it and after a week it is still being picked up. I'm giving it 4 stars because I don't feel that it's the strongest in the genre. It is not as strongly design as many of the others. The facts are good, but some of the themes are a little weak (pinkest and purpleist) But it does the one thing I hope from any book like this, it got my kids involved in a book and it got them reading. Anything that can help nurture of a love of reading is worth its weight in gold.

title: An OK Survey of infographics
text:
I was pretty excited about the potential of this book, but by about halfway through it seemed like it was just repeating some fairly obvious points. However I do feel like I gleaned some decent information from the book. Some I would guess are design standards like "SMART" objectives to keep you on track (I actually started implementing it.) Also, I loved that he listed a bunch of infographic source websites to look for inspiration. His suggestion of infographics.alltop(.com) was very worthwhile. Within minutes I had some great ideas for illustrating a couple of web projects I've been looking at.

Sadly, I wish the examples in the book were a little stronger. They ranged from brilliant to baffling. I often had to read the explanation of the info graphic before getting it's gyst. One of the strengths of infographics should be clarity, which was often missing.

Since this book was kind of a survey, it seemed to suffer from having to cover all the basics. I have to admit I finally skimmed the chapter on whether you should make infographics yourself or outsource it to pros or students and why. Also, retelling the different places you can publish your infographics got a little tedious. All in all, I think my time on the book was well spent, but I think there is a more inspiring book waiting to be written on the topic.

title: Felt Accomplished in just the first fircouple days
text:
I've played around with my old guitar a few times. Often picking up "teach yourself" books and getting a ways before frustrations, pain, and pressures of life force me to put it away. This book has been far more successful then the others. In just the first couple days of sitting down with the book I felt like I was actually playing the guitar, rather than just plucking a few things.

One of the biggest reasaon was the DVD that came with the book. If I have any complaint about the book, it's that I wish they put in about 400 more videos. I've watched a lot of online tutorials, but found these videos more useful. I think for one thing, they start at such a low level that they were meeting me where I was. Later videos are still beyond me, but I have been able to work about of the examples out (again, feeling like I'm playing the guitar!)

Oh and best thing about the videos, it breaks down things like hammer on and bending strings. Suddenly a whole bunch of the jargon I was hearing or reading means something. This book is truly for Guitar Dummies like me.

As for the book, it is very digestible. If I had a single complaint, I wish the examples could be a little more relavant to my tastes. It dedicates a lot of time to folk, country, classical.... I wish the book came in genres so they could focus on the rock/folk things I want to play. But I guess i can appreciate a survey of music types.

I'm only about halfway through the book at this time, but so happy I had to write a review. It has actually been effective and kept me engaged and moving forward. Now if I can just get some killer callouses.

title: A Wonderfully Illustrated Regionalism of a Classic
text:
This was definitely a cute book. I read a lot to my kids so we have read a lot of regionalized fairy tales and this does a fairly good job. It does feel like the author could have pushed the West Texas accent and vocabulary more throughout the narrative, but there is enough to set the location. It is cute that at least in part, the juke box appears to speak in vintage country music lyrics although that breaks down after a page or two. It would have been nice to have both of these things pushed a little more. Also the story is pretty straight forward, but it was enjoyable to read the book to my 6 year old.

The book is well illustrated in playful pictures that work great with the story. All in all a nice little book, well worth a bed time read.

title: Better than I was Expecting
text:
OK, 365 FAQ's about photography. This had all the makings of a bathroom reader. I was expecting entertaining little snippets, maybe some little hints and tips and not much more. Maybe it would be like a daily devotional giving inspiration to try one thing or another. I couldn't imagine any way they could take this book and make it into an instructive narrative. But I have to admit this has been a very educational book.

Actually this book is kind of a bathroom reader full of quick tips and hints. But I think why I can't help but like this book is because I have been asked about 3/4ths of these questions at one time or another. And I can say without a doubt, they were answered far better, and more correctly here. The questions are timely and relevant and I've learned from this book. I don't know that I would have hunted down a lot of this stuff but it was nice to stumble upon it in bite sized chunks when I had a moment to go through a few pages (like in the bathroom.)

As a reference, the book is fairly handicapped. There is not table of content, no index, and questions are answered in a rough organization (starting with hardware questions kind of bunched, then some camera features explained, then something of a trend toward techniques...it is all very organic. The only real structure it has for referencing now are the postit notes I've put on pages I wanted to show people.

So, it's not a perfect book, and I never thought I would recommend a loose collection of FAQ's. And I have a hard time recommending one now, but this book has been very educational, in kind of a "rambling conversation with a photography expert" kind of way. I'm glad I read it.

title: More of a Glossary of Environmental Science
text:
I had really high hopes for this book. The description described it as a way to help kids digest the concepts. But it looks like the description has been retooled a bit since I received the book. I was hoping for a bunch of interactive exercises to better understand complex concepts in life sciences. I thought it could be a great help in curriculum development, but I was a little disappointed there.

I do think they rewrote the description to put it more in line with what the book is, but I'll try to clear it up a little more. It's not a bad book, but it is what it is.

What this book is.

- A Glossary of the terms of Environmental Science
- A fairly complete but not deep overview of the major topics
- A syllabus of a Environmental Science education

The book does have some great illustrations and it defines topics well, but it doesn't do what I was hoping which was to be a tool to help move into a deeper understanding. Some of the illustrations are fantastic and will be used in presentations and I can see referencing the book for basic definitions, but it will not be shaping curriculum.

So why 4 stars. Because for what it is - a high altitude survey of Environmental Science, it is very decent. Judging it for what it is, it is complete and it is well illustrated and written. But it is not what I was looking or hoping for. So buyer beware, if you are looking for an outline for a Environmental Science course, this might be your book. If you are looking to flesh that outline out, you will need to go to other references.

title: A Decent Portfolio of Good Design Examples
text:
I recently got [[ASIN:1119977428 The Smashing Idea Book: From Inspiration to Application (Smashing Magazine Book Series)]] and really liked it for spurring creativity, so I figured this book would also be perfect. Perhaps it was because my expectations were raised but I was not as thrilled with this book as I was with the Smashing ideas. I'm happy with this book, just not ecstatic.

I'm a big fan of idea books and illustrator annuals. I think they can unlock the mind to possibilities. At best they work as springboards to let designers or students stand of the shoulders of great designers and reach even higher heights. Also, it can work as a group critique when the author describes what a site is doing well. I think that is where this book shines, but it does not do this often.

The organization is a little bit all over the board. It has chapters based on color, theme, artistic style and major graphic elements. The author points out how daunting the task of categorizing sites is, but it seems a little haphazard to jump from one thematic grouping of categories to the next. One thing I did really appreciate were the categories for specific page types like ecommerce, blogs and forums.
That proved that there isn't much you can do to change the look of a forum - but there were some clean examples.

Pros
Tons of thumbnails of great websites - and that's the point of the book

Cons
the thumbnails are a little small
the organization is a little all over the place
does not really teach design concepts with the examples

All in all, it's a good book, not a great book, but worth the time to read/glance through (can be read from cover to cover in a few hours.) I did find some examples which were very similar to my idea for a blog design, and improved it by compositing ideas from a few other examples. So I guess it proved it's merit.

title: A Good Primer to the Basics of Wordpress
text:
I while ago I decided to develop a blog and was looking for a reference to get me started. I think I was looking for a little more than this book, but it definitely got me started on the road to learning Wordpress. I installed wordpress easily with the instructions given in chapter 3. I'm not the strongest linux user, but the install is so easy I'm sure anyone can do it with these instructions.

At times the book did get a little tedious. Often it was just walked your through clicking every button or menu option on a screen, many of which were pretty self explanatory. But over over the course of the first 9 our so chapters, I had the vocabulary down well. Beyond that, I do feel like I learned enough to make the time spent worthwhile although I guess I was looking for more advanced customization information. You have to judge the book for what it is - an introduction. For example, it touches on plugins, it gives some potential troubles and helps you know were to look for other. More of a survey of what is possible.

Probably the best gauge for telling the value of a book like this is whether it can be used as a reference beyond the initial run through. I have gone back to it a few times, but find myself googling more than flipping pages for answers. But all in all, it was worth the asking price and the time spent with it.

title: Another very good memoir of a life spent in pursuit of nature
text:
This book seems to be breaking the series rules a little. To claim the arctic summer and brief fall as autumn did not see quite right. The flash of bright autumn colors last about a weekend in arctic as it moves down in elevation or lattitude so you do have to cheat a little. But the book captures that certain melancholy of the autumn season in ruminations of the autumn of a man's life and the autumn of polar bear existence. And like autumn, which is a time to collect the fruits of summer, Dunne looks back at a life of birding and traveling and appreciates the fruits of living a life in the outdoors.

That's what the book does best, it captures the essence of travel and life in the artic from a series of visits by Pete Dunne and his wife. The book is a collection of travelogues and something of a memoir while walking the themes of Autumn and Artic. If you have read the other books in this series, it fits in well. If you appreciated the first two, you get more of the same to savor. Personally I really appreciate this mix of natural, human and personal history. This is not a reference book on life in the Arctic, it is a collection of essays that gives the texture of one man's experiences there.

title: Very nice guide LITTLE guide to low light photography
text:
I have several books in this series and I appreciate the content of the books. This one is well written and gives a great overview of basic low light photography. I'm especially impressed with the coverage of the post production techniques for adjusting low light images. They discuss the camera settings, concerns and techniques which is what I expected, but what I did not expect is so many post production repair techniques. Probably more than any book in my collection it helps you move from camera to computer, suggesting you shoot RAW for the digital options then walking you through Aperture/LightRoom/Photomatix and more to correct and enhance what you have captured.

So those were the Pros, the few but legitimate cons are, first and foremost, the very small format. While it fits into a camera bag wonderfully, the type is very small and hard on older eyes. (cannot be read in low light either.) Also, it is not horribly in depth in anything, but it is a decent overview of low light photography. It is well worth the asking price for me - one of the most educational photography books I've gotten in a while.

title: Maybe a little too much Dummy, But there is Some decent content
text:
I really like the Dummies series, but this one leans a little too hard in favor of the Dummies. The book literally mentions that access to bathrooms and water fountains may be a concern in pick-up basketball games. In fact, the first few chapters also are a little too dumbed down.

However, there is some useful content, especially when it comes to techniques and practice drills. My nephew is as budding basketball star and we can use several of these to help him continue to develop. I also enjoyed that the book is full of little basketball factoids for the fan. Things like the history of the two towers Olajawan and Sampson and explanations of Hoosier mania for Indiana High School etc goes a long ways towards capturing the mystique of the game.

So the book can get painful at times, but like nearly all the dummies books, if you knew everything in this book your could hold your own with any basketball fan. They really go into the culture of the game, even comparing Kobe to Jordan and teaching you what to look for to fill out your NCAA brackets. It is a pretty simplistic book, but I could see this book helping out new coaches and maybe helping a March Madness widow understand their husbands more.

title: An Entertaining Coffee Table Book, A So So Reference
text:
I have copies of the author's earlier multimedia bird song books and my kids have spent a lot of time playing with the players and flipping through the pages. When I saw that they had produced a "bible" of bird songs I was was pretty excited.

The book itself is impressively huge and heavy. In fact, it is so impressive that it is hard to find a location to put it. the only place I found where it fit well was next to Audobon's baby elephant folio. Otherwise if you can, the book deserves to be displayed on a table top, preferably where kids can take advantage of it.

The images are great. This is not a field guide, the paintings are not necessarily for identification and the illustrator is not intending to display all variations, but just to give an attractive image to go with the cooresponding bird sounds. The artwork is beautiful and the pages are on very heavy, high quality paper. The book itself is a work of art.

But the whole point of the book is the bird songs. The playback mechanism is nice and easy to control. Perhaps my one disappointment is that the book does not quite live up to the "bible" definition. First, the text entries for the individual species do not really say much about the bird songs. Often this can be used to help reinforce learning of bird songs or at least to better understand what you are listening for. Secondly, the bird recordings are often restricted to a single call. For a bird such as the common loon, that leaves a lot of vocalizations left out. Also, there are a couple of North American birds that are missing, like an eider or two.

So take the book for what it is. It is a big, beautiful novelty of bird songs. It is educational, but limited as a reference, but huge on entertainment.

title: Some great information crammed into a very small book
text:
[[VIDEOID:7df4af9f322ab66be9930e7e573597d9]] So here is what I'm looking for in a photography field guide - information that helps me when I need it in the field. I have long owned and treasured [[ASIN:0817435425 Art of Bird Photography: The Complete Guide to Professional Field Techniques (Practial Photography Books)]] and there are a few crucial pages I ended up photocopying and putting in my photograph bag. They have simple graphics for considerations you need to make when photographing white birds against a dark background or vice versa. That is the kind of information I was hoping was in this book. And to a degree it was here.

Due to the small format of the book and the very small sized text, this book should have focused on what is needed in the field. The middle of Bosque Del Apache is not the time to debate .jpeg vs RAW but it is the time to get some quick hints about capturing flight photos. Digital Photography 101 should be left to a bigger book you can enjoy at home with full sized text.

I wish that rather than discussing what to look for in a DSLR, it had an annotated checklist of what to pack for your trip. I'm not knocking the authors for their content, it is all solid, but due to the format I wish they stuck to the immediate field needs. To stereotype, Birdwatchers have aging eyes and it is a slog to read the text cover to cover due to the tiny font size. It would have been nice to find pages on those in the field needs, like those charts in Morris' book, how should I handle a backlit flight shot of a overflying eagle. How should I use fill flash to light a roosting owl. How do I use the histogram (which is covered well in this book.) Also it would be nice to have a cold weather section focusing on camera care and exposure hints to shoot in a snowy winter landscape. Well I guess there is my million dollar idea for what it's worth, a field guide focused on what you actually need when you are in the field.

What I do like is the coverage of post photography. It is complete but not exhaustive. I like that the book is full of beautiful and inspiring photographs, although the book has a European bias in photos and content. And I like the content in general, just doesn't all fit the format.

See accompanying video for details on size.

Summary

A very good book that may not be exactly what I was hoping for, but well worthwhile. Text is small enough to be a chore to read. Beautifully illustrated. With these caveats, I would recommend it.

title: Great exposure to the next level of CSS design
text:
I'm a hack web developer - the kind that lays pages out using nested tables (but I want to change.) So when I read this books overview, with it's 50 pages dedicated to CSS layout, and more on CSS tables, I couldn't wait for it to arrive. But it was not quite what I was expecting.

First I should say that I do really, really like this book, but you have to take if for what it is. Perhaps it explains this somewhere in the book or the Amazon description and I'm missing it, but this is a tips and tricks or ideas book, not a training book. Actually this is exactly the kind of book you get when you take years worth of a magazine's "Cool Tricks" column and try to fit it into a book. The result is a whole lot of disparate tips and gathered loosely into a bunch of themes. This rarely comes out with a flowing style, and this book is no different. It is a bunch of gathered CSS tricks that fall under a handful of topics. So it is not a book to learn CSS with, and for that matter, it is not an easy reference book.

So why do I really like the book? It has some amazing tips and eye-opening examples. In many places it delves into esoteric concepts of CSS that never make it into the "Learn CSS in 24 hours" books. This book has opened whole new worlds of CSS organization and capabilities. Not all the ideas are winners (for my needs anyway,) but there are enough great new things to pay back your time and money.

To give some examples, the book opens with 40 pages of tools. The descriptions are brief, and the packages are somewhat repetitive, but I have pulled a couple of the free tools and they are great. I see them making a big difference. Later he points out validators, another valuable tool. (Remember, I'm a hack, not a pro, but it was great to be introduced to them.) The tips section is kind of a good example of the layout of the book. It is kind of a catch-all for the ideas that don't fit into other areas, so it reads a little jumpy. One by one, the tips range from "not relevant to me" to "Oh my God, I wish I knew that a long time ago!"

I really did like the book, it reads fast and it is probably about 5 of the most valuable hours of research I have done on CSS in some time. But it is not for a beginner looking to learn CSS, more for someone like me who needs to be exposed to the possibilities.

title: A  Fictionalized but Valuable Account of the Anne Frank Story
text:
This book wonderfully augments the Anne Frank diary by giving another perspective to the events in the Annex. It humanizes the story even more and helps bring the reality to life in the readers mind. However the book is a fictional "best guess" about what is going on in Peter Van Pel's mind during their time in hiding. But historical fiction can have great value. My wife is a middle school history teacher who often uses historical fiction to bring history to life and has added the book to her suggested readings for those who have read Frank's diaries.

The book reads well and quickly. I finished it in just as few days of leisurely reading and it kept me engaged, even in suspense at times, despite knowing the ultimate outcome. If I had any criticism of the book, it would be that Peter's ultimate fear of never making love to a woman seemed a little over the top and used these yearnings a little too hard to connect Peter's story with Anne's. As someone who survived the male teen years, I could see his desires being an issue, but not so singular as it becomes in this book. At times the book seems to be a romance for tweens and young teen-agers.

Those mild criticisms aside, the book stands up fine against Frank's diaries in conveying the claustrophobic confinement in the annex. It was interesting to hear another angle from one of those involved (again with a grain of salt as it is fiction, but valuable in that it helps young minds connect to the historic reality.) But where I felt the book truly shone was the section that started after they were discovered. The concentration camp section of the book was a great synthesis of survivor experiences. It covers life in the camps very well for a juvenile fiction audience and even better then the section in the annex, it brought me into the world of the characters.

Great Juvenile Historic Fiction.

title: Great Content, but Field Guide Might be a Misnomer
text:
When I chose this book I was thinking I was going to get a small guide to help me with issues that would come up in the field. What I got was a small book with very small text that covered the entire world of digital imaging from how CMOS and CCD sensors work to post production work flow.. At least I was right on the small size, it easily fits into a field bag, but it is not an in-the-field reference. Perhaps it would be nice to have in your bag to fill your time on airplane rides, but less helpful when encountering an issue in the field.

I'm not knocking the quality of the content, it is solid. However, as it takes on every conceivable subject in digital photography the coverage is not overly deep. It is kind of a primer for the subject, much like [[ASIN:1592006051 Mastering Digital SLR Photography]]. I think everyone should know what's in the book as a base level, even if almost no one will buy a GretagMcBeth color panel and start creating color profiles, it's nice to know it exists.

Pros - good overview of DSLR photography
Well layed out
Very good writing
Very portable
Great Content (if somewhat lacking in depth)
Well illustrated

Cons - text is tiny, not for older eyes
coverage is a little shallow
not a field guide, just a travel sized book surveying Digital photography

All in all, a fantastic resource for the world of digital photography. I don't know if it fits the format, or that it is a field guide. But those are forgivable as a learned a lot from the book. Highly recommend to anyone looking to learn more about their DSLR.

title: Good Learning Tool, but could be Great with a little Refining
text:
I think the author has locked onto the perfect format to teach composition. I learned everything I know about composition from peer reviews in graphic arts classes and photography salons. This book uses hundreds of example photographs, one per page with a short critique of what works and what doesn't work in the photos. It seems like this should be an incredibly effective way of teaching composition by focusing analysis on lots of sample photographs one at a time. Probably the best way to learn is to critically look at thousands of photos, or even better thousands of your own photos. However I feel it needs to be tweaked just a bit to take this book from good to brilliant.

Photos - I didn't find the photograph selections to be the greatest. I do like the mix from classic photos and paintings to snapshots. It is a good idea to show that you should still think composition in point and shoot snapshots, but in general there were a lot of uninspiring photos. Flipping through the photos, there is very little wow factor. While there are a few truly inspiring photos, I think it is possible to create a collection that inspires you so much it literally drives you into the field to start shooting. Also, some of the concepts could be demonstrated with better photos.

Text - The text is very short and concise when getting the point across, however there seems to be a little filler information that seems discordant. Occasionally the narrative is broken to give information on photo content matter like to list the members of the camel family when viewing a photo of a dromedary or the height of Denali. These show up infrequently, just often enough to interrupt the focus.

Exercises - I read the book front to back, but have not done the exercises yet. I really like the suggestions for more classic examples to track down. Also there are some thought provoking questions and some good suggestions to get you shooting and thinking about your compositions.

Overall - I would recommend this book to beginner photographers who are looking for help in crafting their compositions. I would put myself at high intermediate and I don't know how much new information I learned by reading the book, but it was great reinforcement. I would like to see this format revisited again. It is great focusing on so many example photos.

title: Very Informative Book with a Lot of Information that is Glossed Over in the Textbooks
text:
I'm a big fan of the micro-history and loved books like [[ASIN:0140275010 Cod: A Biography of the Fish That Changed the World]] and [[ASIN:0142001619 Salt: A World History]]. Often the most entertaining part of these books is how they myopically distort the importance of their subject, but in this case it's hard to understate the importance of Sugar in the world of the 16th through 19th centuries. As the basis of the triangular (or as this book and other sources say, circular) trade, it drove the economy and human movement of the era.

The facts in the book seem solid and it is well illustrated. Although, and I can't put my finger on it, I found the book a little less than satisfying. The facts were great and I appreciated the Haitian History and the post slavery use of almost indentured Asian labor. I definitely cannot knock the book for being informative, it was well worth the read and had lots of eye opening facts. It just seemed to miss a little focus on its thesis. Maybe it's that micro history myopia made some connections get stretched a little. I was a little less than clear on connection of sugar and equality, seems like enlightenment may have affected sugar industry more than sugar drove enlightenment. Also the connection of Ghandhi to sugar was a little tangential.

Where the book did really shine was the histories of the plantations and the rarely discussed post slavery plantation systems. It is good to see the coverage of the Asian laborers who replaced the slave system. This is a rarely covered subject which deserves discussion.

All in all, It was a very worthwhile read and a great reference text for the era and the circular trade. But like I said, it seem to miss something - some coherence, but this is more than made up for in historic information.

title: What I Wanted but Probably not Everything I Needed
text:
I've been hearing the gospel of HTML 5 for quite a while and heard how it will kill Flash, be fully multimedia, and revolutionize web design completely. Which is then given the caveat, when it is finally released. Well it HTML 5 has pretty much arrived (except for Microsoft IE.)

So I figured it is time to find out exactly what HTML 5 is. And this book does a great job of showing what HTML5 is or will be, but aS a kind of bird's eye overview. Perhaps a little less in depth than I was hoping for, because it really is more of an introduction than a full explanation of each feature.

What the book is: An introductory primer to HTML 5

What it is not: A HTML5 reference you will go back to over and over.

I'm glad I got the book because I now feel comfortable with what HTML 5 will bring, but it also made me decide to stay with xhtml and CSS2 for now. I appreciated the coverage of CSS3, the multimedia capabilities, and javascript chapters. There is a project that runs through all the chapters which give you a little hands on experience. If they read the, a novice would be able to create a website. But the book is of limited value to an experienced coder.

I read the book cover to cover over a couple of days (minus some of the SVA graphics section, which I can't see myself using.) So it reads fast and clearly. Overall it is a good book if you are looking for an overview of HTML 5, a little lacking if you are looking for a deep reference.

title: If you think you have it bad now, try the 1860's
text:
This book does a very good job of opening ones eyes to the differences in rights African Americans have now compared to the 1860's. Just as it opens the eyes to the main character when she is transported in time from modern projects to the Draft Riots of the Civil War. It was interesting to see that even those who were trying to help her still had a subtle and open racism towards her which seems very authentic to the times. While we definitely have a long way to go to eliminate racism, it is nice to see how far we have come.

My one reservation is the somewhat cliched storyline of time travel. It kind of detracted from what was otherwise a great historical fiction book. But, I guess that was needed to create the juxtaposition.

title: The Small Business Legal and Tax answers I was looking for
text:
A long time ago I bought a used copy of [[ASIN:0917510283 Small Time Business Operator, 10th Edition: How to Start Your Own Business, Keep Your Books, Pay Your Taxes & Stay Out of Trouble (Small Time Operator)]] to help me flesh out a small business idea. The book was eye opening and made me realize all the nuts and bolts considerations I had not thought of. But the information was a little dated and I did not feel confident about legal and taxation issues. When I read this book, I found it just as eye opening but more focused on the legal and taxation issues I am now concerned about.

Now I feel pretty well versed in general business lingo. For example, now I can throw around Sole Propriortorships, LLC's and S corporations with the best of them. And more importantly, I know which way I should go with my fledgling plan.

I am hoping to monetize a website and the hobby behind it. The book does a great job of pointing out up-to-date on-line business considerations. I am not looking for a tax shelter or a way to write off toys. I'm just want to take my hobby to the next level while not violating any legal or tax laws out of ignorance. This book really seems to have answered my concerns (as well as make me realize I never want to hire anyone - it gets too complicated.)

If I have to criticize the book in any way, I was a little put off how it sometimes feels like an advertisement for other books and resources in the Nolo series. The book stands well by itself, and it put me off a little to be reminded that you need to buy another resource to go further into a specific topic.

All-in-all, exactly the resource I was looking for. It is too dense to be a quick page-turner, but it had all the information I was looking for, and I have never gone wrong with Nolo books.

title: A Page Turning Immigrant Tale
text:
I wish I could give this book 4 and a half stars because it was very good, but not quite book of the year or life changing. It was great at illustrating a historic period that I do not know particularly well. The images of hunger in the old country where people were extending their food with plaster scratched from their walls vividly brought their desperation to life. I could understand their hope and drive to find a new life in a new land.

The story was gripping, albeit a little predictable. I guess I never felt any huge suspense, it just seemed like everyone was going to come out fine in the end while reading. But is a great story of a kidnapping and how organized crime preys on and terrorizes families. A very good book.

title: A very good memoir of a life around deer and nature
text:
First I should point out that there are two kinds of animal lovers. First, there are those who love nature as an academic pursuit. They read anything they can about nature, conservation, and ecology. Often they are birdwatchers and day hikers who study population trends and field guides while observing animals in the wild, careful not to interfere with their behaviours. Then there is the second kind who knit sweaters for their dogs and feed the local geese through the winter. I squarely fall in the first group and this author falls squarely into the second group.

After reading a couple chapters, I expected to have to grit my teeth through the rest. But a surprising thing happened on the way to the end of the book. I really gained a lot of respect for the author. Her research for this book was essentially a single year of watching the deer she was feeding with an additional sprinkling of a lifetime of anecdotal experiences. But it impressed me how detailed her observation was. Obviously it is not perfect or complete, and there is plenty of guess work and conjecture, but she really did a good job of studying her subjects. Once I stopped judging the book as academic research and started measuring it as a memoir of an amateur naturalist, I was very impressed by what she has accomplished.

The main weakness with the book is that the first half seems like an attempt at an unapologetic explanation for why she decided to feed the deer. It seemed like she was struggling with justifying it to herself and the reader. The struggle tainted the observations she was giving, and it grated on me that she was trying so hard to justify feeding. I almost laughed out loud when she finally finds acceptance and professes to feed until she dies in the epilogue. It seems like she finally finds herself.

Once the struggle with explaining her deer feeding subsided, she did put together a lot decent observation and research from an number of sources. She still had a lot of "Animal Rights Activist" type viewpoints, but to be intellectually honest, I feel that most of her observations are valid. And in what is probably the greatest way of judging a nature book - I feel like I learned a lot about deer and its ecology. I was challenged to look at them in a different way than usually portrayed in books. The author uses a much more matriarchal viewpoint than the typical hunting magazine so it's the most "doe centric" deer book I have ever read.

But where I think the book shines is the final chapter when she drifts away from deer completely and talks about being a naturalist. When she quoted Olaus Murie, a personal hero, I realized she lives his values far more than I do. She keeps her eyes open to nature and I feel like I found a strong common bond of being in awe of nature. So even though she does a few things which I think are a little loony, like feeding deer, and promoting the exotic animal trade by owning parrots, and feeling bad about trapping or poisoning rodents,...I can appreciate her love of nature and I'm glad she shared it.

title: Not your father's Lonely Planet Guide
text:
Decades ago I got my first Lonely Planet Guide to Southern Africa. I remember tips like going to a certain bar and asking for an individual who could take you into Zambia for a fee. The book had the feel of a fanzine, written by a vagabond elite of backpack travelers for their own. Since then I have gotten their Alaskan guide which seems to have moved more towards guides like Frommers. This book seems to have taken the rest of the leap to The Eyewitness guide format. Which is beautiful at the expense of depth.

Not that this change is bad. For one, I am no longer looking for dirt cheap solutions to travel while walking the seedier streets. So it fits my life better. The images are alluring and just flipping through the book makes me want to get on the plane. However, where the series once gave amazingly detailed secrets, this book does not delve so deep. The suggestions are rock solid and if you followed their itineraries, or their top 25 destinations you will have an amazing trip. I was just taken aback how mainstream the book seemed.

There is some great information in this book and the page by page design is impeccable. All in all a great and beautiful guide. The maps are crisp and again beautiful. The writing is clean and readable (I read it cover to cover). I would have given it 5 stars except that it seemed to lack a depth I was expecting. However, there are plenty of insights that will help you prevent scheduling mistakes or to make sure you don't miss a specific highlight, it's just seems a little weighted toward design over written content.

If you do know someone who is thinking about going to Japan, get this book, it will seal the deal. It is a great starting point toward planning a trip.

title: Not the Story You Would Expect It to Be
text:
This book shows the power of not following the standard script in your life. When finding out that her husband was having a relationship crisis, it would have been easier to over react and end the marriage. That is such a typical response that I was amazed when she did not. It went against all expectations when she pulled back and realized she was in charge of her reactions to her husband. I can't even say that I agreed with her decision to just help her husband by just carrying on with their life.

Munson has a good writing style which seems like a conversation with a close friend. Her visuals made me feel like I was in her Montana home at her neatly set table. The writing just put me there. Where many memoirs are overly sad or strive too hard to be ironically funny in every line, this book seemed like a visit with an old friend, talking about what happened in the years apart. I just wish we were given more of the happy times after the crisis. Her husband did come around, but I would feel more comfortable if I felt they were on a very good footing.

The basis of the author's memoir seems very similar to a message Eleanor Roosevelt had (and I am paraphrasing badly.) You are in charge of your own happiness and how you react to situations. This is a perfect book club book, it deals positively with universal relationship issue and would stimulate a lot of conversation.

title: A Decent General Guide to Modo and 3D
text:
The one thing that has been missing from my digital resume is 3D graphics. Since I had access to Modo, I though this would be the perfect entry book into the 3D world, and for the most part it is. I worked through some of the examples in the book, trying to replicate what they were doing with my personal ideas and projects and I do feel that I have a decent understanding of the software and it's capabilities (which are obviously higher than my capabilities.)

The Book is well written and well illustrated and gives a good basic overview. If I had to fault it for anything was that it seemed a little thin in areas such as animation and export/import options. For animation, I will concede that a whole other book would be needed to cover it, and I was able to create some very simple hinged items and get them to move. I just have no idea how to get my simple arm to become a Pixar feature. But the scope of the book is to get a basic understanding of Modo and I do feel that I got that. As for export/import, I obviously need more knowledge about different formats and 3D packages. This book does go into Modo files with Maya, but since I don't have access to Maya I was limited on what I could learn there.

So, it's not horribly in-depth, but it was a great introduction for me to the world of 3D. From everything I have heard, modo is a great entry software package to learn the basics. I really enjoyed going through the use of the camera options and textures and lighting. All of which seem well covered in the book (but again, I'm sure you could write a book on each, but for my entry level knowledge it was perfect. It got me playing with the tools.)

title: A Story of What Really Makes a Hero
text:
First, if you have ever read Ann Renaldi before, this is classic Renaldi. She runs two story lines, one rooted in historical fact and another that is rooted in a spiritual world. In this case the first story is about a civil war era factory town in the south, and the second is a story of Cherokee spirituality. Other themes that Renaldi seems to champion are girls passing themselves off as boys and a happy endings and they are all here. Please don't read this as formulaic or a retread, but it is in the same vein as some of her other books, so if you liked those, you'll like this one too.

The main character is seen as a hero for her attempts to save the towns mill from being destroyed by Union troops by placing a French flag atop its roof (a little advice, do well in advance of an enemy's approach don't wait till the last minute.) However, her sacrifice and effort to help her family is where her true heroism shows.

The spiritual story line weaves through the story and brings a mystical aspect to the book. It seemed a little confusing for me, but did not take away from the descriptions of the historic era. The author brings out a lot of good points about the abuses in the factories. Definitely a recommend.

title: Good Book of Resilient Kids and Kindness from Strangers
text:
This is a nice book similar to [[ASIN:0553494104 Bud, Not Buddy (Readers Circle (Laurel-Leaf))]] or [[ASIN:1416949755 From the Mixed-up Files of Mrs. Basil E. Frankweiler]], where kids take situations into their own hands and use self reliance as well as some help from kind strangers to solve issues. In this case the main character is trying to escape a broken home, bringing his siblings with him. They run from their father and step-family in California and try to get to their deceased mother's sister. The grow along the way and it is nice to see others step up to help them on their way.

One the most intriguing things about this book is that the voice of the writing seems true to the 1930's. It feels like you are pulling an old book written in the 30's off the shelf. I have never read this author before, but I get a sense that she was there. It seems authentic to the times, not a modern book trying to look back.

A good book, it is going into our permanent library and can recommend it.

title: My kids enjoy the series
text:
I have to admit I am not in love with this series as much as my kids are. We got the first book in the series, [[ASIN:1416971483 Big Fun! (Adventure of Meno)]], and they read it over and over. In fact, my 8 year old read to my 3 year old over and over, which of course is priceless.
