Perfect Parks
City of Art
High Time
Barcelona Style
City Surprises
Spotted in the Streets
Spooky Stuff

title: Go High: The Unstoppable Presence and Poise of Michelle Obama by M. Sweeney
text: Terrific coffee table book. 50 full-color photographs with quotations by the former First Lady. I've never been in the cult of the First Ladys but she was admirable and these are a fun remembrance, and she is a person you can point to with integrity, perseverance and good morals.

title: Cruise Ports Alaska (Travel Guide) By: Lonely Planet,
text:
Coverage Includes:
Seattle,
Vancouver,
Ketchikan,
Sitka,
Juneau,
Glacier Bay National Park,
Icy Strait Point,
Petersburg,
Haines,
Skagway,
Whittier,
Seward,
Anchorage,
Denali National Park
First, if you can ever swing the dollars to cruise Alaska you should. We did in 2017 for our 10 anniversary and it was the best money we ever spent, it really was magical. And if you can, get a room with a balcony it makes all the difference sitting on your balcony with the ocean below you and the land in the distance. So I got this guide becuase we want to go back if we can swing it. The first time we took an excursion each time we landed and we were very glad we did becuase it made the trip twice as magical. This time we want to just explore the towns on our own and this guide will help us. This gives us the most up to date info (Next edition due: Jun 2021). This guide will help the first time cruiser to this area in helping select the most interesting excursions (thye vary somewhat by cruise line). I found it helpful in offering a but more info outside the cruise line offered excursion. The only surprise was that for the size of the guide it didn't have more info, for example, our super terrific stop in Ketchikan we booked a Duck Tour excursion, it was a blast and not a mention of it here. It makes me wonder what more is it missing?

title: How to Behave in a Crowd by Camille Bordas, Hardcover – August 15, 2017
text: Quirky novel set in France. Isidore (Dory) Mazal ages from 11 to 14 lives at home with his mother and his frequently away from home on business father he is the youngest of 6 brilliant, highly educated, and still living at home, oddball siblings who barely interact because of their compulsive pursuit of their area of expertise. The story is told from Izzy's POV and it makes all the difference in enjoyment. When the Denise thread went off the rails it was so jarring and off putting I stopped caring where the rest of the book was going.

title: The Martin Chronicles by John Fried,  Hardcover – January 8, 2019
text: 1980s upper West Side Manhattan, Martin/Marty Kelso, and his best friends Dave and Max, ages from eleven to seventeen and along the way finds out that the world isn't like he thought it to be. The cover caught my and and I looked at the summary, I come from the generation before Martin (I don't think I knew anyone younger than my father named Martin), but I did grown up outside NYC and that grabbed me. I enjoyed this book, ten linked stories, much more than Catcher in the Rye which I read in high school; I wonder if I would enjoy that title more now. I think I especially liked that Martin is so average, not an outsider and not the star of the school. Best of all Marty has a sense of humor. This is a dynamic collection of vignettes, The suspense provided because you want Marty to choose the best action but he certainly gets into his share of fixes. His cousin Eve, 4 years older, stands out as a character.

title: Hot Little Hands by Abigail Ulman, Hardcover – May 31, 2016
text: Debut collection of 9 short stories (published between 2008 and 2015) from Australian author Ulman. Set in Australia and America. Seven females ages 13 to 30 years dealing with friendships, sex, disappointments, self-awareness, higher education, music, heartache, pregnancy, politics, religion, immigration, first love, sexual abuse, teenager turmoil and fitting in.  While the cover had no appeal for me the author's being a Wallace Stegner Fellow in fiction sold me. I especially like that 3 of the stories followed one character. Well written I look forward to more from this author. The stories range from sad, to thoughtful, intense, raw, heartbreaking and disturbing.

title: The Unofficial Poldark Cookbook: 85 Recipes from 1783 Cornwall, Hardcover – May 1, 2018
text:
From Shepherd's Pie to Cornish Pasties, a delightful gift for any lover of the Poldark novels and TV shows. From the artwork to the design it is a sumptuous treat and totally gift worthy. Produced by American fans of the show:

Tricia Cohen grew up surrounded by family, food, and love. She is a hostess, gourmet home cook, and sous chef. She coauthored A Thyme and Place and A Thyme to Discover, two books in a three-part historical cookbook series. She lives in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.
Larry Edwards is a classically trained chef and internationally renowned food writer. He is the author of Edwardian Cooking, Style and Spice, and The American Table. His recipes have been featured in the Wall Street Journal, USA Today, and the National Examiner. He lives and works in Tucson, Santa Fe, and San Francisco.

I found the recipes easy to follow and simple to make (even the one that takes 20 hours).

Each recipe had a couple paragraphs reliving moments in the novels when the dish was served that was like watching the series or reading the boos all over again.

title: The Wharf of Chartrons by Jean-Paul Malaval, Paperback  August 12, 2014
text:
Enjoyable novel (published in French in 2002) about the French wine business from 1895 to 1933 as told from a very high level through the lives of two cousins who embark on careers in a joint venture of owning a vineyard. I was never on edge when reading about the cousins or their relationships, they had huge struggles but I never had an emotional attachment whether they suffered or triumphed. It was a very dry telling of their story, it was oddly liberating and gave me the freedom to read the story in the moment and focus on all the details.

One odd thing - Constance sailing 3 thousand nautical miles on page 328 is hardly a day trip on a single crew sailboat. I wonder about that translation?

title: 2019 edition Essential Costa Rica  (Full-color Travel Guide)
text:
I would not use this to arrange my travel, rather this is a lovely guide if you are considering visiting the country. This is a nice starting place, but there really isn't enough information here to confidently book travel, nor are the maps robust enough to use in a country you know very little about. I could bump this to 5 stars once I go over it with a friend of mine who was just there July of 2018 and December 2018.
Things I liked:
The phrases that will get you through for non-Spanish speakers
Information on Medical providers, money, local traditions/taboos, How to stay safe & Packing suggestions
FYI most of Costa Rica does not have high speed wi-fi internet connection.

title: The Spark and the Drive by Wayne Harrison,l Hardcover – July 15, 2014
text: Gritty Waterbury Connecticut in the summer of '85. What if Gatsby and Daisy were working class, married to each other, in love and the world was their oyster; and Nick Carraway was a 17 years old who finally found a home in their circle. And it all goes horribly wrong. That sort of dreamy tragedy is how the beginning of the story felt to me. This is a perfect book club choice.

title: What You Don't Know About Charlie Outlaw by Leah Stewart, Hardcover – March 27, 2018
text:
I hesitated to order this title, I thought it had the potential to be boring, but after reading the opening chapter i was hooked and had to know where this story would take me.

EW called it a 'brutally honest look at the inner workings of fame: What makes actors tick, what it’s like to be inside Hollywood, and what happens when you’ve let the business get the best of you.'

title: Orchid and the Wasp by Caoilinn Hughes, July 10, 2018
text: I HIGHLY recommend you sample the first chapter, you will know at the end f this is the book for you. Set in Dublin, London and New York. The writing is brilliant, the author is also a poet. The novel is character driven with a plot that can be a little out there. I should have read the reviews before I ordered the book because I would have known this isn't the novel for me. The main character has her hands full. The father deserts the family. The mother and brother are getting by, but she wants so much more for them both due to her belief in them, that she goes to extremes and crosses a line. A line that was too much for me.

title: The Drowning King (A Fall of Egypt Novel) Emily Holleman Hardcover – April 4, 2017
text:
As a fan of the 1963 movie Cleopatra I was a sucker for this type of novel and the writing and plot did not disappoint. I also don't think I missed an enjoyment of this novel by not reading the first book. To set up the story: Cleopatra VII was born in 69 BC to Ptolemy XII, her older sister, Berenice IV Epiphaneia was the ruler of Egypt 58-55BC while her father was in Rome (he beheaded her on his return). His younger children are Arsinoe IV, Ptolemy XIII Theos Philopator and Ptolemy XIV. When Ptolemy XII died in 51 BC, he left his eldest son and daughter, Ptolemy XIII and Cleopatra, as joint rulers of Egypt. This is where the story opens up. I enjoyed it very much. I wasn't looking to find a hero in any of the characters and I wasn't disappointed, none of them are admirable but the story is epic. The only thing missing for me is a last chapter.

Book 1: CLEOPATRA'S SHADOWS covers 3 years: The secret beginnings of Cleopatra's epic saga, seen through the eyes of her forgotten sisters. Arsinoe, the bright and incisive eight-year-old daughter of King Ptolemy, awakes one morning from an ominous dream of statues weeping blood to find that her reality is even worse. There's been a violent coup, and she is stranded alone in the palace, abandoned by both her beloved older sister Cleopatra and her indifferent father. The new monarch? Arsinoe's half sister 19 year old Berenice, who has seized the throne and now rules over a bloodthirsty royal court. Arsinoe's struggle to establish herself in this strange new world takes her from the palace to the streets of war-torn Alexandria, where she must cast off her childhood comforts, including her idolization of Cleopatra. Meanwhile, Berenice confronts her own demons--her cruel, dying mother, a pair of fickle husbands, and the ever-present threat of her father's return from exile--as she fights to maintain power as the first queen to rule Egypt alone in a thousand years. When their deposed father, Ptolemy, marches on the city with a Roman army, both daughters must decide where their allegiances truly lie, and Arsinoe grapples with the difficult truth--that the only way to survive her dynasty is to rule it.

title: My Last Lament by James William BrownHardcover – April 4, 2017
text: Historical fiction as told by an elderly woman in Northeastern Greece beginning with the death of her father by Occupying German deliberately starving the citizens to death and when they weren't dying quick enough proceed to shoot them for fun. Only 70 years ago. Good story telling only marred with vernacular I don't see coming from an elderly woman. If you are looking for a multifaceted story you should enjoy this. It has lingered with me after reading it.

title: This Too Shall Pass by Milena Busquets, translated by Valerie Miles,  Hardcover May 24, 2016
text: set in a beach town in Spain. The cover caught my eye as a lighthearted read. I was wrong. Blanca at age 40, her mother has just died. The impact to Blanca has set her adrift. The reader comes to realize that even though she has 2 sons, Blanca has never matured. This is her chaotic journey toward adulthood. Told in a stream of consciousness style with humor and vivid settings. If you can deal with her immaturity and lack of self respect, you can take from it vivid moments of her inner life and relationship to her mother.

title: The Latecomers Hardcover – November 6, 2018 by Helen Klein Ross
text: I'm a fan of historical fiction. There is so much here to like: a 400 page book covering 1899 to 2018, good dialogue and story telling. Highly enjoyable yet strangely frustrating, you just never get the payoff scene like you do in The Thorn Birds between Meggie and her mother or Meggie and Ralph, or Meggie and her daughter. I loved the dynamics of all the characters. I would have enjoyed seeing more of Vincent and Sarah and Edmond's later lives, I felt like I got tantalizing snapshots of them and wanted more because they were such vivid characters.

title: The Worthington Wife, Paperback – December 27, 2016 by Sharon Page
text: I would never have ordered the book based on the summary on the back cover because the main character Cal Carstairs sounds like a complete and utter jerk "Cal has designed the ultimate revenge. Rather than see the estate prosper, he intends to destroy it. .. Unless Cal ends his quest to satisfy his darkest vendetta, he stands to ruin his Worthington wife and all her glittering dreams." how loathsome.  I thought I would give it a shot after seeing so many positive reviews. Lady Julia Hazelton spends her days doing charitable work with war widows after her fiancé (the future earl of Worthington) died in WWI. The new earl is Cal, his lower-class mother was rejected by his father’s family, the Worthingtons, thus the revenge angle.  I thought the writing was well done but Cal never won me over. I did like the ending.  Don't get invested in any of the secondary characters they matter little to the overall story so just enjoy and forget them.

title: Chasing the Sun Hardcover – June 3, 2014 by Natalia Sylvester
text: A character study set in turbulent Peru 1992 when kidnapping was so prevalent and the law so ineffective that people could be readily hired to negotiate the release of their loved ones. A time where the kidnappers were heartless in the treatment of those they kidnapped and ruthless in their ransom demands, resulting in ransoms that wiped out all savings and wealth. The only unsatisfying thing for me was you really don't know why the many characters are acting the way they are until the last couple of chapters reveals their full history, it gave me a very frustrated feeling for the entire read because you keep wanting to ask why they are acting the way they are and by the last page I came away with regret for all but the nameless kidnappers who I would have loved to have seen blown up in their own explosion. This would make a very good book club read.

title: Small Country: A Novel Hardcover – June 5, 2018 by Gaël Faye
text: Fascinating and a tragedy. Told in hindsight by the 33 year old narrator of his youth. The 34 year old author (at publication in 2016) is one of the lucky ones, his parents fled their homeland during the civil war when he was 13, this is his debut  The story is set in Burundi, 1992 where 10 year old Gabriel lives with with his French father, Rwandan mother and young sister. We watch his coming of age through the lens of wealth, his parents crumbling marriage and the savagery of the violence that makes the American civil war 160 years ago look quaint. The Rwandan genocide of April 1994 went on for 100 days 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, were slain. Today 85% of the population are of Hutu ethnic origin, 15% are Tutsi, yet the government is Tutsi controlled. Reading a wiki page on Burundi one group listed it as the most miserable country on earth in 2015. Interesting discovery The difference between the Hutu and the Tutsi? Not so ethnic. 500 years ago the words designated the economic class of haves/Tutsi and have-nots/Hutu. The eruption of violence of 1993 began after a first democratic election brought a have-not to power (Hutu) and was assassinated but the haves/Tutsi.

title: The Heart You Carry Home, November 3, 2015 by Jennifer Miller
text: I got hooked into reading this novel after watching a video of the author discussing and reading from her novel at a local bookstore 'Politics and Prose' Published on Dec 17, 2015. I found the story riveting on many levels. First with the story going back to 1969 Cambodia and revealed in flashback throughout the novel. Then the story of King and how his wife found a way to save his life. The story of Ben and Becca and the Middle East war that continues over 2 decades. I wish there was a book club reading this novel - I would love to discuss so many aspects of the story.

title: She had me at a character named Bea
text:
A terrific name for a strong character. Bea held me in her hands the entire story. Allyn had her issues, big issues and super low self confidence. Her entire self worth was wrapped in her wife and her wife was a narcissistic horror. I really really love how Bea and Allyn meet, and then we learn about their lives and slowly become friends and slowly become more than friends and just when it looks like they have 'a thing' a smoke bomb is thrown into the picture. Allyn makes stupid decisions and luckily for Allyn Bea stills thinks she is something special.

I love the setting of the Pacific Northwest.

title: Terrific thriller
text: The action sequences were super suspenseful - they aren't even alluded to on the back cover but they start in the first chapter so I don't think I am giving anything away and for me they were the best part of the book.

title: Winner 2018 Ann Bannon Popular Choice
text: Its a great feeling being in the hands of an author who has a way with dialogue, making characters come to life and makes a story so compelling you race through to the last page, add to that the suspense of a who dun it you have a pretty terrific read. There are so many reveals in this story that talking about the plot at all will give the story away. Suffice it to say I hope to be at the next bookclub that has this title to discuss. ~ A Proper Cuppa Tea  by KG MacGregor published July 24, 2018

title: Island of the Mad, book 15 in the Mary Russell and Sherlock Holmes Series by Laurie R. King
text:
I have a Sherlock Holmes fan since Basil Rathbone showed up in black and white movies from the 1940's on our 1960's era black and white TV. When I was old enough to read novels I read the complete set of Sherlock Holmes. When American PPS TV present the complete series starring Jeremy Brett my mom and I watched them in complete delight, I even have them on dvd. Long introduction to say this series by Laurie R. King is terrific in its own spin on the character, has been entertaining me for 24 years, and while they have all been memorable some contain less Holmes than others and those just don't grab me as much. In all honesty I didn't care for the last book, The Murder of Mary Russell, at all; this title is much better.

1 The Beekeeper's Apprentice (1994)
2 A Monstrous Regiment of Women (1995)
3 A Letter of Mary (1997)
4 The Moor (1998)
5 O Jerusalem (1999) the events in this book take place after The Beekeeper's Apprentice
6 Justice Hall (2002)
7 The Game (2004)
8 Locked Rooms (2005)
9 The Language of Bees (2009)
10 The God of the Hive (2010)
11 Pirate King (2011)
12 Garment of Shadows (2012)
13 Dreaming Spies (2015) the events in this book take place between The Game and Locked Rooms
14 The Murder of Mary Russell (April 5, 2016)
15 Mary Russell's War And Other Stories of Suspense (2016) 10 short stories
16 Island of the Mad (2018)

title: Cancerland: A Medical Memoir by David Scadden with Michael D'Antonio
text: The author co-founded the Harvard Stem Cell Institute and is Chair of the Harvard University Dept. of Stem Cell and Regenerative Medicine. Cancer, leukemia, impacted my family when I was in college. The whole family learned rapidly over the 5 intervening years how far cancer research had to come, because it was all guess work. In 1983 cancer darkened my family forever when it robbed us of my beloved uncle, his children were still very young. This book covers the coming of age of cancer research as observed and studied by one doctor. Next up for our family when cancer struck again my mother, 9 years after her brother died, mom was diagnosed with multiple myeloma, her initial diagnosis of at best 3 years lasted 9 hard won years, including a stem cell transplant in 1994. So you can see how fascinating the doctors journey was to me and will be to anyone whose life has been touched by cancer.

title: Never Anyone But You By Rupert Thomson
text:
A novel that is neither fully fiction nor fully fact. What an amazing life they led! I am so glad to find that their work is so appreciated today as to have Davie Bowie mount an exhibition of their work.

Marcel Moore (1892 – 1972), born Suzanne Alberte Malherbe, was a French illustrator, designer, photographer, and surrealist writer.

Claude Cahun (1894 – 1954), born Lucy Renee Mathilde Schwob, was a Jewish-French photographer, sculptor and writer.

They met as adolescents and are smitten, eventually becoming lovers, trapped in secrecy until Lucy's father married Suzanne's mother making it oh so conventional for them to spend so much time together. They eventually arrive in Paris at the end of World War I and for almost 20 years live and thrive in the amazing avant garde scene, mingling with all the bright young things until they escape the looming threat of German invasion of all things Europe. By 1940 they are under German occupation where they are compelled to do all they can to undermine and overthrow the Germans.

Compulsively readable.

title: Beauty in the Broken Places, a Memoir of Love, Faith & Resilience by Allison Pataki, David Levy(Epilogue) Lee Woodruff(Forward)
text: I was really looking forward to reading the rest of the story after reading the book summary. By the last page I felt no closer to the subjects as humans than I do after watching an episode of Dateline.

title: THE SPIRIT OF CATTAIL COUNTY by Victoria Piontek
text: A a heart wrenching fantasy suitable for ages ten and up.  I found the gorgeous cover misleading, I don't feel it set me up for all the hurt that would engulf 10 year old Sparrow, and because of the gorgeous evocative writing, it engulfed me too. Hopefully I can be forgiven that by the end of the first chapter I wish it was Aunt Geraldine ( a vile creature) who was swallowed up in the grave, and not Sparrow's mom. I loved the setting, it took me right back to the 22 years I lived in southern Florida.

title: Fun read. I ordered it because the cover caught ...
text:
Fun read. I ordered it because the cover caught my eye, then the story summary caught my attention being a big fan of theatre and cinema and British storylines. I was glad I did. The first half could be a downer to some readers, I thought it set the 2nd half of the book up great. And I am a sucker for malapropisms.

The author has 2 other novels along the same line:

[[ASIN:1408846896 Not Quite Nice]] Theresa is desperate for a change. Forced into early retirement, fed up with babysitting her bossy daughter's obnoxious children, she sells her Highgate house and moves to the picture-perfect town of Bellevue-sur-Mer, just outside Nice. With its beautiful villas, its bustling cafes and shimmering cerulean sea, the village sparkles like a diamond on the French Mediterranean coast. Once the hideaway of artists and writers, it is now home to the odd rock icon and Hollywood movie star, and, as Theresa soon discovers, a close-knit set of expats. There’s Carol, the infinitely glamorous American and her doting husband David; Sally, the erstwhile British TV star; the ferocious Sian and her wayward Australian poet husband; the sharply witty Zoe with her strangely youthful face and penchant for white wine—and the suave Brian who catches Theresa’s eye. As Theresa settles to the gentle rhythm of seaside life she embraces her new-found friendships and freedom. However, life is never quite as simple as it seems and when skeletons start to fall out of several closets, Theresa begins to wonder if life on the French Riviera is quite as nice as it first appeared.…

and it's sequel [[ASIN:1408876949 Nice Work If You Can Get It]] Witty and enchanting, the second novel from the well-loved actress and Sunday Times bestselling author of Not Quite Nice follows the hilarious exploits of retired expats in the South of France. Somewhere on the French Riviera, tucked between glitzy Monte Carlo and Cannes' red-carpets, lies the sleepy town of Bellevue-Sur-Mer. Sheltered from the glittering melee, it is home to many an expat – although it hasn't proved as peaceful as expected. Now an enterprising band of retirees has resolved to show it's never too late to start afresh, and open a restaurant. Snapping up a local property and throwing themselves into preparations, Theresa, Carol, William and Benjamin's plans are proceeding unnervingly well. But when Theresa encounters a mysterious intruder, she begins to wonder what secrets the building is concealing. Meanwhile Sally, an actress who fled the stage to live in quiet anonymity, has decided not to be involved. She's far too busy anyway, shepherding around a gaggle of A-listers including a suave Russian with a super-yacht and a penchant for her company. As the razzmatazz of Cannes Film Festival penetrates Bellevue-Sur-Mer, its inhabitants become entangled in a complex pattern of love triangles and conflicting business interests, and something starts to feel distinctly oeuf. Finding themselves knee-deep in suspicion and skulduggery, the restaurateurs realise they can no longer tell who's nasty … and who's nice.

And one memoir [[ASIN:1444709291 The Happy Hoofer]] 'I've always been wilful... I've always been stubborn and always determined'One of our best-loved actresses, Celia Imrie would rather have been a dancer. As a child she planned to join the Royal Ballet and marry Rudolf Nureyev. Now she has become one of our finest and funniest performers, on stage, TV and screen - adored for her roles in Acorn Antiques and dinnerladies, as well as films including Calendar Girls and Nanny McPhee. In her hugely entertaining autobiography Celia Imrie recounts a life hurtling (not always intentionally) into adventures both on stage and off. Whether it's finding herself on stage with half the scenery stuck to her cardigan, or being kidnapped on her way to location, somehow she emerges from the chaos unscathed. Acting, she admits, is a mad, chaotic profession and it is her refreshing honesty, sense of mischief, fun and almost unruffled determination in the face of it all that makes this autobiography a never-ending delight. One of the UK's favorite comedy actresses—with starring roles in Calendar Girls, Acorn Antiques, and Dinnerladies—tells her extraordinary and highly entertaining life story. Celia Imrie was born one of five children to an aristocratic mother who married beneath her station. Desperate to be a ballet dancer, Celia was told by the Royal Ballet School that she was too big and in a desperate effort to lose weight Celia became anorexic. She underwent highly controversial ECT and brainwashing treatment. It didn't work and she eventually cured herself.

title: The Heat Is On (Next Best Junior Chef) by Charise Mericle Harper  (Author), Aurélie Blard-Quintard (Illustrator)
text:
This is a perfect book for the TV junkie family. For ages 9 to 12. Book 2 in the (Next Best Junior Chef) series, the main characters are pre-teens and are back from book one, except Tate, who was eliminated in the first round *sigh*; so if your child likes this title they will most likely really enjoy another dose via the first book. Frivolous fun with a touch of drama, nothing to get excited about and basically the book blurb tells you everything you want to know.

book 1 was [[ASIN:0544912608 Lights, Camera, Cook! (Next Best Junior Chef)]] "A zesty series for fans of kids' cooking competitions! It's “lights, camera, cook!” for four tween contestants—energetic Tate, charming Rae, worldly Caroline, and hyper-competitive Oliver—who are all about to enter a televised cooking competition. What will the kids cook up? How will they all get along on- and off-camera? Which junior chef will have the grit—and maybe the grits—to make it through each challenge? And which junior chef will have to hang their apron up for good?
Bonus: Includes real cooking techniques for the aspiring young chef!"

title: Ragged Lake: A Frank Yakabuski Mystery by Ron Corbett
text: Over the top violence but will try his next in the series because he is a good storyteller with an appealing main character, Frank 'Yak' Yakabuski. The author writes in a style close to Lee Child. A police procedural set in the forestal wilds of Canada, on an old logging river. The action perks along and then, unfortunately, the author inserts a journal by on of the victims into the story. The reading skids to a stop, disappointed, interrupted, annoyed, The story within the story also makes for good reading, but not in this tense, focused mystery. The journal is really too well written for the character and her desperate situation.

title: The Fourth Figure (The Pieter Van In Mysteries). by Pieter Aspe
text: The plot has to do with Satanism, illegal drugs and psychiatry. There is much activity, none of it compelling enough to keep me interested in the story. .I loved the details about the setting in Bruge, Belgium I disliked the effete main character, Commissioner Van In. Van In and his sidekick, Sargeant Versavel, have a fun relationship and and good buddies. Versavel is gay and in a relationship, Van in is married and his wife is pregnant. Paper-thin characters, a lot of jumping around, and a predictably satisfying ending

title: The Bad Decisions Playlist by Michael Rubens
text: Heading in to senior year of high school Austin (described as a lazy stoner) finds out his deadbeat dad who deserted him at birth when he (Shane) was 20 years is now a has been rock star with 2 hit records. Austin's mom loves her son to pieces and her lawyer boyfriend is crazy for her. Austin thinks the best way to spend his time is to make them miserable. The miserable read (for the adult) was worth it for the last 30 pages (Rick is a keeper!). Teenagers will love it.

title: The Tragic Age by Stephen Metcalfe.
text: Set in San Diego California, 17 year old Billy has the troubles of Job. He has a port wine stain on his face, his twin sister has died from cancer, his parents marriage is crumbling and he hooks up with a bad news new friend. Then it gets worse. He and his peeps start a life of crime, breaking in to homes, partying, sex parties and violence - yuck. Well written, evocative and depressing as all get out,

title: The Sweet Spot (A Willamette Valley Romance) by Heather Heyford
text: 'The Sweet Spot' is the name of the vineyard. I live in the area where the book is set, wine country (Newburgh) Oregon. So I was delighted to order and read the book. I have to say I didn't care for the fate of one of the secondary characters in the book, it just didn't fit for a romance feel good aura. I think the author captured the residents accurately this one tiny exception: I am sure I have never heard any second generation Oregonian use the word 'putz' out here, so that was a lol moment. I thought Jamie's actions the last 30 pages were rather odd. Also, the vapid creature from Colorado (not Jamie) got more unbelievable as the book went along.

title: Book 2 - Ever the Brave (A Clash of Kingdoms Novel) ... Erin Summerill
text:
For the 15 year old and over crowd. Having missed reading book 1 [[ASIN:1328767000 Ever the Hunted (A Clash of Kingdoms Novel)]] I looked up the plot summary (below) to bring me up to speed). This novel was a little slow-going in the first half but picked up later in the story. In this book there is a love triangle that seems to be popular in teenage target fantasy novels. Kirkus Reviews say the first one is better then the 2nd so I may order the first if a 3rd book comes out.

In book 1: Seventeen-year-old Britta Flannery is at ease only in the woods with her dagger and bow. She spends her days tracking criminals alongside her father, a legendary bounty hunter—that is, until her father is murdered. The alleged killer is none other than Cohen Mackay, her father’s former apprentice. The only friend she’s ever known. The boy she once loved who broke her heart. She must go on a treacherous quest in a world of warring kingdoms, mad kings, and dark magic to find the real killer. But Britta wields more power than she knows. And soon she will learn what has always made her different will make her a daunting and dangerous force.

title: #1 Best Seller in Christian Inspirational  Higher Is Waiting by Tyler Perry
text: Part memoir, part Christian homily. I liked this very much and recommended it to a couple friends who have enjoyed his movies as much as I have.What a strong man. I recommend this for any young person ages 13 to 18, a lot of good life lessons about perseverance. It does get better. Tyler Perry is the creative genius of the Madea movies as well as an actor, producer, director, philanthropist.

title: Idyll Fears: A Thomas Lynch police procedural by Stephanie Gayle
text:
I've been looking forward to seeing Police Chief Lynch back in print for the last two years. Set in 1997 small town Connecticut two weeks before Christmas, the new police chief is settling into his new gig after retiring from a 20 year career as a NYPD homicide detective when his first major case outs him as gay. Now he is dealing with the fallout of that revelation from some in the community and on the macho police force. This time out the FBI becomes involved in a search for a missing 6 year old. I love Lynch's wit and way with words.

Book one [[ASIN:1633880788 Idyll Threats: A Thomas Lynch Novel]] In the summer of 1997, Thomas Lynch arrives as the new chief of police in Idyll, Connecticut—a town where serious crimes can be counted on one hand. So no one is prepared when Cecilia North is found murdered on a golf course. By chance, Chief Lynch met her mere hours before she was killed. With that lead, the case should be a slam dunk. But there’s a problem. If Lynch tells his detectives about meeting the victim, he’ll reveal his greatest secret—he’s gay. So Lynch works angles of the case on his own. Meanwhile, he must contend with pressure from the mayor to solve the crime before the town’s biggest tourist event begins, all while coping with the suspicions of his men, casual homophobia, and difficult memories of his former NYPD partner’s recent death. As the case unfolds, Lynch realizes that small-town Idyll isn’t safe, especially for a man with secrets that threaten the thing he loves most—his job.

title: The Vineyard Years: A Memoir with Recipes by Susan Sokol Blosser
text:
Very readable memoir stretching from 1970 to 2016, and never a dull moment, the family and business dynamics were fascinating.. The advent of Oregon Wine of the WIllamette Valley. Solid memoir, I would pair it with a Sokol Blosser 2013 Goosepen Block Pinot Noir which showcases flavors of anise and blackberry with a finish reminiscent of baking spice. I haven't read the earlier title published in 2006 but from the write up it seems like it might cover the same ground plus another 10 years and even more perspective.

From the author of 2014 [[ASIN:B00RU8CNCS Letting Go: How One Entrepreneur Energized Her Business, Empowered the Next Generation]]
At the height of her career, after building and leading one of the most innovative wineries in America, Susan Sokol Blosser made an extraordinary decision - to step away from the work she loved and transition control of the winery to her children. LETTING GO is an engaging account of how she made that decision, the surprising challenges she faced, the unanticipated journey that ensued, and the good life that followed. LETTING GO speaks to universal themes: transforming family dynamics as the older generation cedes power to the younger; thriving as a woman in an era of changing gender roles; facing aging and staying vital while no longer climbing the career ladder. Contrary to the “having it all” mind set, Sokol Blosser’s story proves that LETTING GO can be the most fulfilling life choice.

2008 [[ASIN:0615206387 Gracious & Ruthless: Surprising Strategies for Business Success]]
A small book with large ideas, Gracious & Ruthless gives advice on running a successful business while staying true to your values. While gracious and ruthless are two words not usually used together, this book demonstrates how they not only could but should be combined for success. Twelve short, eloquent essays on topics business owners face. Full of common sense and practical advice, Gracious & Ruthless will inspire and challenge. Editorial cartoonist Jack Ohman's illustrations of the author at work are priceless.

2006 [[ASIN:0520248651 At Home in the Vineyard: Cultivating a Winery, an Industry, and a Life]]
Sokol Blosser begins her narrative in the 1970s, when, as a young, idealistic wife, she helped her husband make his wild idea of planting a vineyard in the Dundee Hills become a reality. By the book’s final pages, she has become president of Sokol Blosser Winery, widely respected for gaining national visibility and for producing world-class wines, especially the elusive Pinot Noir. Along the way, Sokol Blosser tells how she learned to do everything from driving a tractor and managing a picking crew to selling Oregon wine in Manhattan. She also shares some special accomplishments: how she instituted values of environmental sustainability and social responsibility at the vineyard, integrated family and business life, and successfully brought the second generation on board.This moving, evocative memoir, woven with lyrical descriptions of the sights and smells of vineyard life, tells the inspirational story of one woman's journey to success in an industry run mostly by men. At Home in the Vineyard, filled with colorful characters and unexpected experiences, brings a local rural community vividly alive as Oregon wine pioneer and industry icon Susan Sokol Blosser recounts how she fell in love with a vineyard, learned how to run it, and ultimately achieved her vision of producing Pinot Noirs to rival those of Burgundy. An intimate family story, At Home in the Vineyard also gives a candid insider's view of Oregon's flourishing wine industry.

title: Be Fierce: Stop Harassment and Take Your Power byGretchen Carlson
text: On July 6, 2016 the author filed a lawsuit against then Fox News Chairman and CEO Roger Ailes claiming sexual harassment, because she stood up dozens of other women also accused Ailes of harassment and he was forced to resign. A less then awesome book considering what happened but Hat's off to the author, she certainly doesn't need the money that the book sales will provide. Carlson does touch on a couple of instances when she was harassed in her career but her $20 million settlement with Fox News prevents her from going into detail regarding her own situation. It helps to be wealthy because you know you will lose your job and figures like her package are extremely rare, just look at Fox News, Bill O'Reilly is already back on as a guest, no sign of Carlson on air *sigh*. Disgusting, isn't it?  Maybe she will enter academia, Carlson graduated from Stanford University and spent a study-abroad year at Oxford University.

title: The Vanderbeekers of 141st Street by Karina Yan Glaser
text: The line drawings in the book are a total treat. Interesting story for kids who have always grown up in a non-rental home. An engaging read for kids who have grown up in a rental home. I rented a home for 9 years and while I never came to care for the home as this family (12 year old twins Isa and Jessie, 9 year old Oliver, 6 year old Hyacinth, and 4 (going on 5) year old Laney) does their rental  I was still charmed by their machinations (and their Thanksgiving culinary skills) to find a way not to leave it. Set in Harlem (between 110th and 155th streets) NYC.

title: Addicted to Americana: Celebrating Classic & Kitschy American Life & Style by Charles Phoenix
text: The book delivered on it's premise: Lots of Americana. It also has lots of Charlie Phoenix that I found a bit of a distraction. Both the 50 and 70 year old in the family say it brought back lots of happy memories.

title: I focus on collaboration and because of this I meet amazing people who look at youth culture in ways I ...
text:
For Grades 6-12. The Owning Up Curriculum teaches students and educators to take responsibility as bystanders, perpetrators, and victims of unethical behavior. First published in 2009 [[ASIN:0878226095 Owning Up Curriculum: Empowering Adolescents to Confront Social Cruelty, Bullying, and Injustice (Book and CD-rom)]]. It's odd that such a topical subject has only 4 reviews in 8 years. You would think it would be a standard curriculum. After going through the website and reading the book I can see that it would be an asset for any school or school system, especially ones that have suffered the suicide of a child.

From the author: My name is Rosalind Wiseman and I am an educator, writer, and founder of Cultures of Dignity. For over two decades I have been talking with, listening to, and occasionally arguing with young people about everything and anything that’s important to them. I have authored five books -- two of which hit the NYT Bestseller List. My non-fiction books are titled, Queen Bees & Wannabes, Masterminds & Wingmen, The Guide, Queen Bees Moms & King Pin Dads, and the Owning Up curriculum. I also wrote a young adult novel titled, Boys, Girls and Other Hazardous Materials. This fall, I re-launched the Owning Up Curriculum, a comprehensive social emotional learning program for grades in partnership with the Association of Middle Level Educators. I write a monthly column for the Anti-Defamation League called Rosalind’s Classroom Conversations where I write about common challenges educators face in talking to young people about youth culture, bigotry, discrimination, and social media. I also write articles for major publications, blog and tweet frequently on a wide variety of topics but always feel I should be writing more often. By far, what I appreciate the most about my work is that I am constantly learning. I have been invited to speak at all kinds of venues: from federal and state initiatives, corporate board rooms, advocacy organizations, national conventions, public schools, charter schools, and private schools of diverse affiliations. As a teacher, I focus on collaboration and because of this I meet amazing people who look at youth culture in ways I haven’t thought about. My work is informed by integrating my expertise with the lived experience of others. I have served on many nonprofit boards but currently only serve on one—the US Health and Human Services Substance and Mental Health Administration. I support many non-profits in smaller ways because these organizations do the work that tirelessly advocate on the issues I care about most. Personally, I enjoy eating really good food, drinking really good bourbon, listening to great music, dancing until my feet hurt, and politics that make me think. I have been married for nearly 20 years and still wonder how I met someone at such a young age that I could walk through life with. On the other hand, I have two sons who are 13 and 15… they are my everyday challenge. My favorite child is my dog, Layla, who is always by my side and has never rolled her eyes at me. I lived in Washington DC for most of my life until I moved to Colorado in 2012…and yes it was a culture shock but I am getting used to it and happy to be living in such a beautiful place with really nice people who never honk at you.

From her publisher's page: Rosalind Wiseman has had only one job since she graduated from college - to help communities shift the way we thk about children and teens' emotional and physical well-being. As a teacher, thought leader, author, and media spokesperson on bullying, ethical leadership, the use of social media, and media literacy, she is in constant dialogue and collaboration with educators, parents, children, and teens. Most famously, Rosalind is the author of Queen Bees and Wannabes: Helping Your Daughter Survive Cliques, Gossip, Boyfriends, and the New Realities of Girl World - the groundbreaking, best-selling book that was the basis for the movie Mean Girls. The fully revised third edition was published in July 2016. Rosalind's other publications include Masterminds and Wingmen: Helping Our Boys Cope With Schoolyard Power, Locker-Room Tests, Girlfriends, and the New Rules of Boy World, which was awarded Best Parenting Book by Books for a Better Life in 2014. She is also a regular curriculum contributor to the Anti-Defamation League. From teaching in the classroom to large keynote presentations, each year Rosalind works with tens of thousands of students, educators, parents, counselors, coaches, and administrators to create communities based on the belief that each person has a responsibility to treat themselves and others with dignity. Rosalind has presented at the White House, the American School Counselor Association, South by Southwest, the Game Developers Conference, the International Boys' Schools Coalition, the American Association of School Administrators, and countless schools throughout the United States and abroad. She is an advisor to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. A native of Washington, D.C., she currently lives in Colorado with her husband and two sons.

title: The Reluctant Highlander by Amanda Scott
text: Medieval historical fiction with not enough romance between highlander Sir Àdham MacFinlagh and lady-in-waiting Fiona Ormiston the daughter of a loyal border lord during the rule of James I, King of Scotland (Reign‎: ‎4 April 1406 – 21 February 1437).  I was hoping for another Roberta Gellis but it wasn't to be.

title: It All Comes Down to This  by Karen English
text: 1965 Los Angeles and 12 year old African American Sophie moves with her family to a all white neighborhood. Right there you know disaster is imminent. Tack on that Sophie's parents marriage is crumbling and her sister is leaving for College, the Watts riots, racism, internalized racism and I gotta wonder what 12 year old in 2017 is going to understand all the dynamics? But this middle school novel was given starred reviews by both Kirkus and Publisher's Weekly. Did my 12 year old grasp all the issues? Yes but the issues are so huge I wonder if their being in a middle school book lessens their import.

title: Empire Made: My Search for an Outlaw Uncle Who Vanished in British India by Kief Hillsbery
text: Titled 'The Tiger and The Ruby' in Great Britain. I loved it but I am a history buff and this is so much more than tracing an ancestor, the author opens up the British Raj for 275 delicious pages. 20 year old Nigel Halleck a distant relative of the author traveled to India 175 years ago. An employee of the British East India Company, which was currently ruling India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. 36 years later he died in Nepal in 1878 this is the story of tracking his history down and hopefully his grave. The reader learns more about the period then the uncle but I went into it with modest expections that the relative could be revealed in total. The only thing missing for me, and maybe it will be in the final print, are copies of 170 year old letters home.

title: VENTURESS by Betsy Cornwell Age Range: 12 - 16
text: Should have ditched the romance(s) it distracted from the story. Other than that a total winner. Loved the characters, the writing, the story and the end.

title: The Streak: Lou Gehrig, Cal Ripken Jr., by.. John Eisenberg
text: A worthy gift for anyone who loves the history of the game. As told by Baltimore sportswriter, they are the only two players to appear in over 2,000 consecutive major league baseball games - Ripken over 17 season from age 21 to 38, and Gehrig from age 22 over 14 season until ALS struck him down in his prime at age 35. It was a fun read at over 250 pages. The only thing I would have enjoyed is more pictures.

title: The Waking Land  by Callie Bates
text: Huge potential that died about 100 pages in.  In this fantasy, 19 year old Elanna Valtai, the daughter of royalty, tells her story (first-person, present-tense) of being a hostage since childhood by King Antoine, who has raised her as if she were his daughter as a way of keeping her dynasty from rebelling against his dynasty's rule over the lands. King Antoine is murdered, with Elanna the suspect. She escapes by letting loose the magic she has over the natural world which she has kept hidden. But magic has been outlawed for 200 years so she is now on the run.And then it slows down. And never picks up. *sigh*

title: EMILY AND THE SPELLSTONE by Michael Rubens suitable for ages 8 - 12
text:
12-year-old Emily Edelman has just moved to a new town with her older sister and six year old brother. She is treated like an outsider and is a target of the local bully. Interesting times float her way via a local beach and a odd shaped stone

Top reasons to love the book:
1) Mrs Hallgren the librarian
2) Angela Rodriguez
3) Gorgo - trust me on this one lol

title: THE EVAPORATION OF SOFI SNOW by Mary Weber Age for ages: 14 - 18
text:
Our 15 year old thought this a rip roaring tale heavy on story but a bit light in character development which he found no problem at all with such a original story. In post–World War 4 Manhattan Sofi Snow and her team of gamers are competing at the arena "Fantasy Fight Games". Shilo, her younger brother is blown to pieces by another player. Sofi escapes and is thought dead, she is kept in hiding by her community of underground hackers. Sofi thinks Shilo is not dead, but is taken prisoner by "the Delonese" who inhabit an ice plant orbiting Earth for the last 11 years. Sofi reaches out to the ambassador to the Delonese, Miguel, for a way to get transport to the Delon ice planet. Interesting side not that government is run by corporations rather than elected government officials.

Book # 2 - Reclaiming Shilo Snow: Sequel to The Evaporation of Sofi Snow will be available March 6, 2018

title: While a fun read it didn't strike me as being equal to ...
text:
The Jensen Brand (Book 1). Author of 200 books, William Wallace Johnstone (October 28, 1938 – February 8, 2004) was an American author, mostly of western, horror and survivalist novels. Since his death over 13 years ago 100 titles have been published under his name with J.A. Johnstone who was assistant, typist, researcher, and fact checker to his uncle William W. Johnstone.

This novel is set 35 years after the first Jensen book (1865 and Smoke is a 16 year old Missouri farmboy whose family was decimated in the Civil Ware) and covers the family dynamic of of the 2nd generation of Jensens. While a fun read it didn't strike me as being equal to the first title published, maybe it is just my take but the people seemed to have a more modern sensibility that I don't get when reading the 1984 title

The character of Kirby "Smoke" Jensen was originated in 1984: [[ASIN:0821714805 The Last Mountain Man]]
