title: A disappointment
text:
I was drawn to this book because of its timely subject matter, online bullying and harassment. It does cover that subject in excruciating detail, but it has several flaws as well.

"Too Close to Home" is set in the south of England in the present day and centers around a family of six: Jenna and Jack, the parents; Paige, Jenna's teenage daughter by a previous relationship; and three younger children who are the offspring of Jenna and Jack. There are three major strands to the novel: Jenna and Jack's new business venture and its start-up struggles; Jack and Jenna's marriage and its breakdown after he is unfaithful; and Paige's difficulties at school with a "real-life" teenage bully and a mysterious online manipulator whose machinations are almost sociopathic. All of these strands are explored in great detail, and the book is overlong by at least 150 pages.

One problem with this book is the writing. Everything is spelled out very explicitly. It is as if the writer never heard the maxim, "Show, don't tell." This author "tells" everything, making obvious observations that are annoying and almost insulting to the reader. It is as if she does not trust the reader to draw even the most obvious conclusion for him or herself. Both the subject matter and the writing made me think that this is a YA novel, but it is not marketed that way. It is recommended for people who love Jodi Picoult, but my guess is that Picoult's fans will not be complimented by that recommendation.

The book explores the topic of cyberbullying in great detail, and if this topic interests you, you may enjoy this book. The characters, however, are two-dimensional; they never really come alive. For me, the book was a disappointment, though the topic is timely.

title: A disappointment
text:
I was drawn to this novel because in our family we have three wonderful adopted children (now young adults), all from Russia. I was interested to see how the author would handle the topic of international adoption in a fictional setting.

The novel is set in an upper middle class suburban community in the Northeast and revolves around four families. The narrator, Nicole, is married to Jay and has two young sons. The action begins when Gene and Paige, one of the couples in their circle of friends, announce that they are planning to adopt a child from Russia. They travel to Russia with their young son, Cameron, to pick up four-year-old Winifred (Winnie).

From the start it is obvious to the reader that this adoption was a terrible idea. Paige is far too controlling, the kind of person who thinks family life should look like a Hallmark movie, and she will do anything to make her vision a reality. Certainly Winnie has her problems--who of us does not?--but Paige's incessant demands on her and on the rest of the family are too much for these relationships to bear. Nothing good comes of this, and the novel ends tragically.

I was disappointed by this novel for several reasons. First of all, I did not like any of the characters. The husbands/fathers are one-dimensional at best, and the mothers are often selfish, self-centered, and downright mean. They want to create an idyllic life, failing to see that such a life does not exist. They are woefully inadequate as parents, and more than once I wanted to shake them. When they are not controlling their children, they are over-indulging them. Nicole cannot even manage a baking session with her seven year old without completely decompensating. Paige is downright abusive to Winnie, the most sympathetic character in the book.

Second, several plot lines were begun and then simply dropped. There is a pretty important subplot concerning Nicole's relationship with her adult sister, who is an alcoholic and possibly a drug addict, and her mother, who cannot carry on a civilized conversation without screaming and slamming down the phone. Nicole has several interactions with both her mother and sister over the course of the book. It is obvious that she wants to create a life that is the exact opposite of those of her mother and sister, but there is no resolution to this plot line at the end; it is simply never mentioned again.

Finally, the style of writing is annoying to this reader. Serling uses sentence fragments. A lot. For effect. Knowing she is doing it. Hoping it will work. Failing. (See how annoying this is?) A few sentence fragments are one thing, but this book's primary style is the sentence fragment. There are literally hundreds, and perhaps thousands of sentence fragments in this book. No, I am not exaggerating. Sadly, the author does show a lot of insight into some of her characters. The content of the sentence fragments is fine. Even when she is doing exactly the wrong thing, Nicole sees what she is doing. She feels remorse and shows insight, but the way she expresses herself is distracting. I think the author may have wanted to create a stream-of-consciousness effect, but for me at least, the style simply does not work.

Even after all that, I did not hate this book. It has some interesting parts and partially developed characters. But I cannot recommend it.

title: A well written but flawed book
text:
I am very conflicted about this novel. In some ways, I liked it very much. The point of view is interesting, and the writing is good, especially the rendering of nature.

However, this novel could not make up its mind what it wanted to be. Is it a domestic family tale, the story of an abusive husband stalking a wife desperate to get away? Is it a tale of small town gossip and politics, of characters good and not so good, each contributing to the stew that is small town life? Is it a ghost story? Is it a mystery? In the end, I thought it was a tale of parallel escapes and restorations, and though I was intrigued by this premise, in the end I found the execution unsatisfying.

"What Becomes Us" is narrated by one of the unborn twins within Evie Rosen's womb. This is an interesting device, and perhaps it is the cause of some of the thematic chaos. An unborn child is the quintessential unreliable narrator, and I found myself questioning every mysterious event and observation. Did such and such an event actually happen? Or did the narrator misconstrue what he witnessed? The narrator is tied in with the title, since the story covers the nine months of Evie's pregnancy. Everything that happened to Evie, also happened to her twins: the events of the novel "became" the babies born at the end. However, the babies were not the only ones gestating; Evie herself is undergoing a gestation of sorts, one facilitated by her escape from her husband and her "birth" into the life of the small town and her new identity as a mother.

No one could say that this novel is uneventful. Between Evie's job as a substitute teacher, to her menacing, shadowy husband, to the married man she is infatuated with, to the challenging students in her class, to the interesting cast of characters that make up the town--something is going on all the time, and often the reader does not know what is real, what may be a dream, what may be a vision, or what is simply an illusion. Indeed, I often felt that if one were teaching magic realism, this might be a good novel to illustrate it.

In the end, however, I could go only so far with this premise. I recognize that the writing is very good, but I was eager to finish the book. I wish I had cared more about the characters; though I wished them well, I did not feel really invested in them. And one last thing: I do not like to see simple errors in books, errors like "I used to teach a forth grade class." This book could have used a good editor; there are far more spelling errors (or maybe they are typos) than I can easily tolerate in a finished book. The copy I received was not a proof, it was a final product.

I have tried to describe this book as objectively as possible. If it sounds appealing to you, by all means, buy it. However, I cannot recommend it with any enthusiasm.

title: A Flawed Book
text:
"Don't You Cry" is a psychological mystery narrated by two young persons. Quinn is a young woman in her early twenties living in Chicago whose roommate has gone missing. Alex is a teenager whose mother abandoned him when he was only five and whose father is an alcoholic; he works in a diner in Michigan. The story is narrated in alternate chapters by these two characters, and for most of the book it is impossible to see the connection between them. Both narrators, for different reasons, are unreliable, and this makes some of their conclusions and judgments erroneous. The two strands come together at the end of the novel, and mystery fans will like all the twists and turns, all the false clues and misleading observations.

I, however, was very frustrated by this book. It was neither the subject nor the structure that troubled me; indeed, I really like the dual narrator device when it is skillfully done. What annoyed me repeatedly was the writing, which was not uniformly terrible, but which had frequent moments that gave me pause as a reader.

First among these was the author's frequent use of the pathetic fallacy, or the attribution of human emotions to nature. In one scene, the sea comes on shore, grabbing at the ankles of a person standing near it, inviting her into the deep. In another, the "deranged November air" dislodges a tin can from a trash barrel. This sort of thing occurs all too often for my taste.

Second is the tone. I realize that the author is trying to convey the affect of young people, but the tone of both narrators is smart aleck-y and flippant, a "too cool for school" attitude. Both narrators are irreverent and cynical, and if you were given a chapter without knowing whose point of view it was, you would be justified is guessing either one. There should be some differences between a college-educated young career woman in the city and a disaffected and somewhat lost adolescent boy, but with respect to tone, there are none.

Finally, the author makes frequent use of metaphors that are imprecise and distracting. For example, when Quinn is trying to find her missing roommate's cell phone by calling her number, she describes it thus: "I . . . continue to search, tracking the subdued ringtone as Hansel and Gretel tracked bread crumbs through the deep, dark, woods." Alex describes the waitresses who use their break time to smoke cigarettes this way: ". . . the two of them teeter-tottering all day on their rotating smoke breaks." Both of these metaphors are ridiculous if you think about them in any depth, and these are only two examples. I love these use of effective metaphor, but most of the metaphors in this book were ineffective and annoying. (If you are interested in an author whose metaphors are superb, read Amy Parker's new book, "Beasts and Children.")

So here is my advice for anyone who is considering buying this book. Read some of the positive reviews, of which there are many on the Amazon site. It may be that what detracted from my reading of this book would not bother you at all. Then make your decision.

title: Somewhat tedious; not amusing
text:
As a retired English teacher, I am always looking for interesting and amusing ways to teach language concepts. The title of this book, "My Teacher Is an Idiom," suggests that it will introduce young children to the concept of idioms, and indeed it does. It describes what an idiom is, gives many examples, and even investigates the idea that different languages have different idiomatic expressions.

Where it falls down, however, is in the "interesting and amusing" category. Perhaps second graders will be captivated by the borderline cruel Patrick and his hapless victim Richard, but that may be too much to hope for. The third main character, Sophie, a transfer student from France, is better, but only somewhat. The two boys run afoul of school rules and are required to do a presentation about good manners. If this does not sound particularly interesting or amusing to you, that is because it is not. I have a feeling kids will be bored with this book and set it aside about a third of the way through.

That said, it is easy to read, written on a very basic reading level. I cannot in good faith recommend it, but if you decide to get it, it will teach your child about idioms. There are, however, far better ways to accomplish this.
I

title: Very difficult
text:
This is an excellent geometry text for honors and advanced placement students. It is extremely challenging and provides in-depth learning for students who enjoy the challenge of math or who have access to a teacher or tutor on a regular basis. It is far too difficult, however, for the typical high school geometry student. It is very proof-oriented, and the difficulty may discourage the student who may like math but does not want a career that is dependent on it. For the budding engineer or scientist, this book is a great choice, but it is not for everyone.

That said, I want to point out one aspect of the book that is great. Each chapter has three levels of practice problems, labeled A, B, and C. The A problem set is for everyone, and B and C levels are for those who want a greater challenge. I wanted this book to use for a geometry course for home schooled students, who meet with me only once a week. This is not nearly often enough, given the difficulty of this book. However, in a school, where students and teacher meet five days a week, the levels of problems provide the teacher with great flexibility. I could see the book being used at several levels.

In short, this is a great book, but it is not the best choice for me. However, if may be a good choice for you. I suggest that you buy a used copy so that you can judge for yourself before you invest in the entire course.

title: Ambivalent feeling toward this one
text:
The premise of "Afterwards" by Rosamund Lupton is similar to that of "The Lovely Bones": a dead (or nearly dead) person communicates with others in an attempt to uncover a crime. In the case of "Afterwards," the crime is arson, and the beginning of the book is well done--fast-paced, interesting, and engaging. The main character rushes into a burning school to save her teenaged daughter. Both mother and daughter are severely injured in the fire, and their spirits communicate with one another as they lie in comas in the local hospital. Then minor characters (father, son) become involved as Mom tries to discover who set the fire and why.

After this superb beginning, this novel simply bogs down. It is too long in the middle, and there is far too much psychological analysis for my taste. Of course the reader wants to know underlying complexity of motivation, but too much is too much. Mother and daughter communicate, and parts of this section are confusing. It is occasionally difficult to know who is speaking. Mom finds out things she never knew about her family--surprise, surprise--and the incredible and undying love of a mother for her child is repeatedly reinforced.

In the end, the reader discovers who set the fire, and the answer is very unexpected. There are any number of likely suspects, and the motivations of each are explored, but most readers will not guess the identity of the arsonist.

To sum up, this was a good story, but not great. I notice that many other reviewers have mentioned Lupton's other book, "Sister." I plan to read this book to see if I can get a better handle on her storytelling. For now, count me in the ambivalent category.

title: Some satisfaction; some mystery
text:
"The Cottage at Glass Beach" by Heather Barbieri is set on the coast of Maine, an inviting setting if ever there was one. The back story is fairly straightforward: Nora goes with her two young daughters to the cottage on the beach to escape the incessant pressure of the press resulting from a scandal involving her husband and his mistress. In addition to this major conflict, issues arise as the older daughter blames Nora for her father's infidelity and Nora herself has to resolve issues with her own mother.

So far, a pretty typical summer read, right? Now comes the mysterious part: A stranger appears seemingly out of nowhere to entwine himself into Nora's affairs. This touch of magical realism surrounds the story of the selkie, seals who shed their skins on land and become human. Unfortunately, this aspect of Irish folklore is never fully explained, and the mysterious stranger seems jarring to the plot.

Despite this, however, I suspect that this book will find a wide readership. It is a satisfying beach/summer read, but I urge readers to familiarize themselves with the selkie myth before beginning the book. You will appreciate the story far more if you do.

title: Challenging and slow to start
text:
"An Uncommon Education" by Elizabeth Percer traces the life of Naomi Feinstein from early childhood through her college years at Wellesley and, briefly, beyond. Though there were moments of lovely writing and insight, I found much of this book a tough go.

The reader can look at other reviews for a summary. I will try here to describe the strengths and weaknesses of the book. First, some of the writing is excellent. The book is slow-moving, especially in the first half, and much of the writing describes the thoughts of a sensitive, intelligent child dealing with a loving but depressed home life and the pain of being the odd man out at school. Naomi's insights are beyond her years, and her struggle to make even one friend is well-documented. The pace of the book picks up when Naomi finally goes to Wellesley, fulfilling her father's dream for her (and, she thinks, her own dream). At Wellesley, surrounded by other highly intelligent and driven women, she begins to find her true path. The second half of the book is much more satisfying than the first, much better paced and far less ruminative. Naomi's friendship with a Japanese economics student, Jun Oko, is central to her becoming the person she is meant to be.

But there are other aspects that are problematic, at least for me. First, the book begins with a long treatise on Naomi's father's near obsession with Rose Kennedy (and Naomi's fascination with Rose's daughter Rosemary, who was lobotomized in her early 20s and never recovered). It is Rose, however, who is the father's real obsession, especially with respect to her frustrated desire to attend Wellesley, which was sacrificed to her father's political ambitions. He thinks of all Rose could have been with a Wellesley education, and Naomi is encouraged even at age six to aim for Wellesley. The first scene in the book has Naomi as a child getting sick at the Kennedy house in Brookline, Massachusetts. This entire theme recurs again and again, and I found it annoying, repetitive, and pointless.

I expected to love this book. I enjoy coming-of-age stories, and I loved Curtis Sittenfeld's "Prep" and the film version of "Dead Poets Society," and when I read the advance information that this book would appeal to fans of these works, I enthusiastically ordered it. I have to say, however, that it was a disappointment. I wondered at times if it were more memoir than novel, and I think it would have worked better as memoir. Most readers will be put off, I think, by long passages describing every thought and every nuance of every thought.

I hate to be so critical of a author's work, especially a first novel. I know how hard it is to write, and I think this author has great promise. I wonder if, years from now, this book will be re-issued as a "first novel" by a great writer whose later work is far superior. I can see that happening, and I hope it does.

title: Difficult to like
text:
I hate to give books I review three stars--it seems so wishy-washy. But "This Beautiful Life" by Helen Schulman has forced me to do just that. The cover art for the book is inspired--the "beautiful life" that the Bergamots have worked so hard for is a house of cards, one that comes tumbling down at the first storm.

I will begin with the positives. Schulman has written a devastatingly accurate portrayal of the nouveau riche of New York City. Their obsession with money and status is well drawn, from the boss who deserts Richard Bergamot at the first sign of trouble, to the shallow and gossipy "friends" who do the same to his wife, Lizzy. The reader cannot but despise these people, and one would think that he or she would find him or herself automatically in sympathy with Richard, Lizzy, and their teenaged son, Jake.

However, one would be wrong. Though I wanted to like these characters, I could not. The parents leave a perfectly wonderful upper middle class life in Ithaca, New York, where each has a satisfying career at Cornell University, for the seductive bright lights of New York City, where Richard has been offered a dream job at a university that sounds a lot like Columbia. Lizzy gives up her career to manage her children's lives, "the deal," as Richard characterizes it, which ultimately leads her to frustration and substance abuse. The son, Jake, is typical of his age (15), but not all that likable either. Five-year-old Coco Bergamot, adopted from China, is by far the most attractive member of the family, but the reader wonders how long her irrepressible spirit can last in this land of spiritually dead or dying people.

The book is a fast read, and I think it will find a wide readership, since the central incident, sexting, is much in the news today. There are glimmers of excellent writing, but the overall impression is just appalling. I found the book's end ambiguous, filled with regret over opportunities lost. The book is a cautionary tale of what happens to people who make money their god. They are sorry in the end, but it is too late.

title: good but short
text: My five-year-old nephew is a truck fanatic, so I bought him this book for his birthday.  My only complaint is that it is too short.  He really enjoyed the book, but there just was not enough of it.

title: The Gilded Age railroad boom and bust
text:
The book, by Jack Kelly, describes in great detail how the railroad boom during the Gilded Age, featuring George Pullman, crashed in 1893, with the ensuing labor crisis and depression, resulting in an almost nationwide labor strike, headed by union leader, Eugene Debs. Besides these two men representing unregulated capitalism and the wealth it created for some versus jobs for everyday working people, was President Grover Cleveland who had to contend with possible anarchy.

The book brings relevance to the US economy now, with great income inequality and the strain it’s putting on the working class.

I recommend the book, with a caveat. The book was more detailed than I wanted, so I did a lot of skimming, but the detail does seem valuable for those wanting it.

title: An important topic
text:
First off, I have a problem with the author calling finance an evil. Sure, as the author describes, human rights are too often the casualty, but, as have been said by many others, the arrow of history points forward. Specially, world poverty has been minimized coincidental with finance, so, likely because of finance; human beings run finance and are neurologically wired overwhelmingly for justice.

That being said, I agree with the author that more can be done to further human rights, like with better regulation and redistribution, and the book does offer many ways to do this.

Throughout history, the wealthy always have had advantages, however excessive wealth doesn’t always bring happiness. There, the author seems to ignore.

Anyway, I do recommend the book because finance is an important topic, especially since the Great Recession and income inequality is perhaps the biggest casualty of the recovery.

title: A biased, but helpful, look at our economic system
text:
The authors and most of the contributors are British and this book focus on Britain's problems post financial crisis 2008, while expanding it to be basically a manifesto against capitalism.

On almost every page, the book uses the words neoliberal or neoliberalism

The book presents an alternative, not an improvement. As such, it is better to use the book as a way to consider improvements. It offers worthy considerations such as sustainability and environmental improvements, as well as social improvements which would make for less greed and for a society less concerned with consumption.

It also mentions that this alternative should be global, but since the crisis some coordination has been achieved.

Further, in the US where the crisis began, better regulation has been achieved via Dodd-Frank, increased FDIC insurance, etc.

It should be remembered that the world is the most peaceful (% dying from war), prosperous (% above poverty), healthiest (highest life expectancy), educated, etc.in history. So, I recommend this book, only with the condition that it be read for ideas on how to improve our current economic system.

title: Original and wonderful story, but a little hard to follow at times....
text: Thoroughly enjoyed the storyline of this book, but the way it was told made it really hard to get through. I liked the way the stories intertwined, but I just couldn't follow parts of the wartime story. I can't put my finger on exactly what made it hard to follow, but I enjoyed the story enough to push through it and get to the end.

title: Fun little series
text: My 4 year old grandson enjoyed having this book read to him. I was surprised how often he asked me to read him another chapter. I enjoyed reading it to him and discussing it with him, but towards the second half, we both lost interest in the story. It was fun learning about all the different Quirks in the beginning. It's worth reading to find out if it's a book you might enjoy.

title: OK
text:
This book is pretty good in describing the steps which led Europe to its current problems and juxtaposed America's handling of its financial mess which also became part of Europe's mess.

Anyway, the book does think pretty much all financial markets have been tampered with such that their future directions are more uncertain than usual. As for Europe, more planning for the Euro should have happened especially since there are significant problems remaining, mostly political. Weak nations can be bailed out, but it is doubtful politics will allow that, so probably too much austerity will still lead to real recovery being delayed. The author does think it would be wise if a few of the smaller/weaker nations left, but that still would leave Spain and Italy, two nations too large to leave but with much different politics than the strongest nations. So, it is hard to see things working out well in the foreseeable future.

So, a good book in laying out what has happened, but it doesn't seem to me there are any great revelations as to what might happen.

title: OK for informing investors of a decent strategy
text:
I'm conflicted on this book. If one wants to use options and ETFs, this book details how to use them in a pretty good way. However, I think there is a better way to invest in stocks, just buy stocks of great companies with sterling balance sheets (little debt) which have services or products which will always be in demand and with a long history of paying good dividends and raising them each year. And, only buying them when they are off their highs and at reasonable prices and valuations (PEs, etc). Plus, always have some cash, cash equivalents or other assets in reserve for when there is a market collapse, etc one can treat such as a gift to buy more of one's portfolio of stocks at bargain prices. This way, these stocks and the way of investing in them essentially have their own built-in hedges. Plus, by holding them for the long-term, one can still make periodic buys and sells to take advantage of specific situations. Plus, using derivatives as the book recommends, adds a lot of complexity and confusion, rather than just focusing on the stocks. Plus,I see options and ETFs as unnecessarily adding to commission costs, plus certainly with ETFs, a product which is still fairly new and hasn't been well-regulated.

Anyway, if one is interested in using options and ETFs, these are things worth noting from the book.

1.The authors have 22 years experience. Much with an an online broker, but that might bias them as such brokers make oodles of money from options and ETF trading.

2. It is difficult to beat the market and difficult to stay disciplined with an investment strategy. The authors have never met an investor who beat the market without being disciplined.

3. Derivatives exist to control risks/emotions, especially "loss aversion," which studies show investors are wired to be, like not selling a losing stock. Fear is a stronger emotion than greed. Hedging is the cure for loss aversion: set your maximum loss so never ride a loser. Hedge funds, because of their 2%/20% compensation structure encourages risk taking, not controlling risk.

4. Never forget why you invest - realizing your life goal, a long-term approach. Hedges are best suited for long term. Preservation of capital is important - hedges do that. Best investors have used stop and stop limit orders and/or options for capital preservation.

5. Investing is competitive - individual investors are at a disadvantage against institutional firms which have more information, but the individual investor has an advantage because these firms increase volumes of trades and therefore make the market more efficient. The authors see three strategies used by the firms - indexing, asset class allocation and defensive hedging. So, individual investors can also do this.

6. Taxes matter - long-term capital gains, qualified dividends and 401Ks/IRAs.

7. Types of hedges discussed - married put, collar, ITM options, puts and calls, portfolio hedges using ETFs.

8. Risk metrics are discussed and hedge correlation. Diversification of portfolio can be done using ETFs.

9. Book advocates harvesting gains and losses as target prices are met. Don't use fortune telling.

10. If want to speculate, suggest using OTM calls.

11. Some advanced tactics - vertical spreads, diagonal spreads.

12. Manage cash - using a married put with a fixed income ETF. Also describes ways to manage tax efficiency .

So, overall, a decent book if one subscribes to the book's approach to investing. What I learned mostly is that I am quite satisfied with the way I invest and the book convinced me to concentrate on what I do and adding their approach wold add too much confusion, extra commissions and give me less time dealing specifically with the stocks in my portfolio. But, now I am a better informed investor.

title: OK, but for statistic wonks
text:
This book is very good as a reference book for those who want to follow China's economic data closely. Some things of note, besides descriptions of, and explanations, to better understand and value the specific statistics like GDP, etc are....

1. Mainland China's equity markets are moved more by economic data than by profit/loss of companies. Plus, the Hong Kong market moves with mainland China's, as do Japan's, Korea's and Singapore's, and also can affect US's.

2. China is changing fast, with many new products, etc, so it means collecting data is extra hard.

3. Small businesses keep three sets of books, making data not very trustworthy for them.

In conclusion, the book is valuable as a reference for those who want to keep a close eye on China's economic data, especially those who want to invest in China. For other investors, as China becomes an even more important and larger economy, it is also valuable. And, certainly for any investor, at least reading the book is worthwhile. For me, I'll probably stick with US investments, especially when so many already do business in China, and probably the biggest takeaway from the book is to be extra cautious about any economic data released from China and make sure I do look for reliable analysts of China's economy.

title: Dated, but some helpful writing tips
text:
Although the book is dated and of little help to a serious genealogist, it does have some helpful writing tips like:

1. We are our stories.

2. A memory is a story with a beginning, middle, and end.

3. It is helpful to provide some historical background when describing a family event.

4. Always remember the audience. Think of your book as a gift to the family.

5. Every writer has a style. Make sure it is appropriate for the audience.

6. The most important part of a book is the opening/beginning. Make sure you have a 'hook' in the beginning to keep the reader interested in reading more.

7.Go for a word 'picture', a vivid image.

8. Highlight the most interesting ancestral moment.

9. 'Media Res' - it is OK to begin in the middle, if that is where the best 'hook' is.

10. Model the ancestor - like being an immigrant.

11. End the beginning with a transition.

12. Tossing out stuff is important.

13. Rewriting is the secret of great writing.

14. Two reasons for a new paragraph: 1) new idea 2) give the reader a break.

15. Stay away from quotation marks, except when quoting a person. Also, avoid 'deflators' which reduce the impact of a sentence.

16. If a subject is important: 1) long, several sentences are OK. 2) position at the beginning of a paragraph and remember the end of the first sentence has the most impact and 3) repetition is OK, here.

17. Proofread a lot.

title: Evolution explained well
text:
"Your Inner Fish" looks at how humans evolved. I was hoping the book would have been more insightful like, 'OK, we evolved from earlier life, but what does that mean, besides where we came from?' Anyway, the book covers evolution well, mentioning things like this:

1. 99% of species which ever lived are extinct.

2. Fossils are one of the major lines of evidence we use to understand ourselves.

3. About 375 million years ago appeared the first intermediate form of life in fish which led to the appearance of a land animal. Specifically, this is when fish fins began having bones like in our upper arm, forearm and parts of the wrist.

4. There are exceptional similarities among creatures as different as frogs and humans.

5. Genes are switches to make fingers, arms, toes, etc.

6. Teeth are important to study - likely evolved when animals began eating other animals - feathers, scales, etc became necessary because of teeth.

7. The head is made up of plates, blocks and rods. No developing living thing begins with a head. Stages of development for every creature are similar. There is an 'organizer cell'.

8. Collagen is important for body development - it comprises 90% of a body's protein, by weight.

9 Probably, when oxygen first appeared in the air, did land animal bodies develop.

10. Since soft tissues in bodies don't fossilize, that is why DNA is so important to study the history of bodies.

11. The sense of smell developed as a tool for survival. DNA is present in every cell, but certain genes are only turned on in certain cells, like only in nasal cells, here. Sense of smell genes make up 3% of the human genome, but most are inactive/useless unlike other animals which needed better senses of smell to survive. Likely, most of such human genes are inactive because they weren't needed as the eye was developed so well in humans. Likely, the eye developed the ability to see in color when so many different colors of plants/food emerged.

12. The bottom line is that every living thing has parents, the operative term being 'descent with modification.'

title: Moderately interesting
text:
The book is pretty good at going into the scientific details which explain questions people ask, however, I really can't say I was that interested in wanting to know the details for many of the questions. But, some were interesting, like:

1. Why do darker alcoholic drinks produce worse hangovers? Because of the methanol they contain, as opposed to lighter drinks' ethanol.

2. Why do people have eyebrows? Besides diverting sweat droplets, perhaps mostly to express emotions - like telegraphing friendly intentions for survival.

3. How fat would you have to be, to be bulletproof? Although the human body could never be totally bulletproof because of certain tissues and appendages, about 24 inches of flesh would protect against a 9-mm handgun.

4. How can a person reduce cellulite? By reduction in calories and exercise, that's it.

5. Does beheading (like with a guillotine) hurt? Yes, a few seconds.

6. Is green potato skin toxic? Although the color is harmless, chlorophyll, it is a warning of a toxic level of solanine. A lethal dose for a 160 lb. person would be about five pounds of such potatoes.

7. Does anything eat wasps? Yes, what doesn't, is a better question. Frogs, goldfish and spiders do.

8. Does pickling cause vegetables to lose nutrition? Not much.

9. Why do incandescent lightbulbs turn grayish over time? Evaporation of tungsten from the filament.

10. Why does sea look blue? Seawater absorbs all wavelengths of light except blue, which is scattered.

11. Can two galaxies collide? Although space is expanding, galaxies have their own trajectories which are pulled about by the gravity of other galaxies, and therefore, can collide.

12. Why is it colder at the South Pole? Because of the high mountains.

13. Since wheels are so efficient in getting around, why didn't they evolve in nature? Although bacteria have flagellum and there exist tumbleweeds in nature, for humans - every part is either connected to or communicates with other parts, so wheels would cause all kinds of entanglements. However, with humans, evolution has allowed them to make wheels.

So, for me, the book does make for a fun read, as long as I skimmed over several of the questions and their answers.

I was interested because I've had students learning English as a Second Language who've become mute for an extended time, (Chinese and Vietnamese) for a year or two before they started talking 👄. A fellow volunteer in the Peace Corps who was Vietnamese American said it took him 7 years before he finally began speaking. They had some delayed response in a silent period. title: Some Concerns in the Author’s Views.
text: I thought this book would be better than it was. The author name drops some famous names in TESOL at the beginning, her methods and advice for teaching ESOL students ignore important facts. She stresses throughout the book that speaking English in the home is important but sees the native language as a detriment to learning English. It’s not true. In fact cutting off the native language can be very detrimental to learners of English. She also is not willing to allow writing that isn’t grammatically correct or a bit easier in vocabulary. Grammar and vocabulary are learned in listening and reading. Speaking and writing will lag behind and can’t be forced forward without falling into a trap of being incomprehensible and essentially written by the teacher or directed by them. The comprehension hypothesis by Stephen Krashen. I felt that students were missing from this book although there were many scenarios on almost every page. It was cold and inauthentic.  The best progression for English language learning is the bond between student and teacher, staff, fellow students and school. This book is highly clinical and misses the ballpark.

title: Basic Family Recipes for Air Fryers
text:
Air fryers provide fried-food flavor, but the cooking method is healthier than deep fat frying or pan frying. The reason is that air fryers require a very small amount of cooking oil or fat. If you love your air fryer, this cookbook, EVERYDAY FAVORITES AIR FRYER COOKBOOK: 115 RECIPES MADE EASIER AND HEALTHIER, will expand your inventory of family recipes beyond those found in the cookbook that came with your air fryer.

Of course, no cookbook can solve the basic disadvantage that is built into most air fryers--these appliances can handle very limited amounts of food. To serve a family, the cook must remain in the kitchen and prepare multiple batches. This is especially true of foods like French fries that most people consume in quantity.

The cookbook includes a very general discussion of the different types of air fryers currently available. It does NOT provide adequate information on how to choose the brand or type of air fryer that is right for you.

title: Simple Unexciting Recipes Take Time to Prepare
text:
THE ELECTRIC PRESSURE COOKER SOUP COOKBOOK: 100 FAST AND FLAVORFUL RECIPES lives up to its title--it contains many simple recipes for soups that can be easily prepared in an Instant Pot. The recipes follow a standard pattern: (1) saute ingredients like onions, garlic, ground beef; (2) add broth, veggies, spices; (3) pressure cook for a specified number of minutes; (4) release pressure, stir, and serve. Sometimes ingredients are added after the pressure cooking is done, and the soup is simmered briefly to blend the flavors in. Some soups require finishing with an immersion blender (e.g., Butternut Squash soup).

The recipes themselves are NOT particularly exciting, perhaps because of the emphasis on “simple”. The recipes include French Onion Soup, Chicken Noodle Soup, Butter Bean Soup With Cabbage and Ham, Unstuffed Pepper Soup, Turkey Pumpkin Chili, Lasagna Soup, Salmon Chowder, and many more.

Because I have similar recipes in my other Instant Pot cookbooks, this is a cookbook that I don’t need. The recipes are simple, but they aren’t “quick”. They involve the usual amounts of Instant Pot preparation and cooking time.

I had hoped for recipes that could be quickly prepared for my soup-loving husband’s daily lunches. This cookbook does NOT satisfy that need.

title: Recipes for Baking Bread the Old-Fashioned Way
text:
EVERYDAY BREAD BAKING: FROM SIMPLE SANDWICH LOAVES TO CELEBRATORY HOLIDAY BREADS is misnamed. It is NOT about “everyday” bread baking. Instead, it is about baking bread “from scratch”, using all of the classic time-honored--and time-consuming--steps (mixing, kneading, rising, folding, baking).

The book contains “Master Recipes” for flatbread, no-knead sourdough, sweet Levain rolls, whole wheat, rustic sourdough, challah, baguette, and brioche breads. These recipes are followed by chapters of recipes for “Everyday Breads” (sandwich loaf, lemon-herb focaccia, ciabatta, tortillas, etc.); “Entertaining and Special Occasions” (cinnamon rolls, fougasse, doughnuts, etc.); and “Holidays” (cinnamon wreath, pumpkin rolls, star bread, etc.).

The author seems to really understand bread baking, and the recipes all look like they will produce excellent bread. A nice feature of the book is the “Troubleshooting Tips” that follow each Master Recipe and answer questions such as “Why did my brioche come out tasting dry?” There are also good photos of the steps involved in making the Master Recipes.

However, if l want to learn how to bake bread the old-fashioned way, I’m going to turn to a classic work like James Beard’s [[ASIN:B004JHYSAI Beard on Bread]]. And if I really want to bake “everyday breads”, I’m going to rely on the recipes that came with my bread machine, or on the excellent [[ASIN:1250018285 Artisan Bread in Five Minutes a Day]]. While this is a worthy book, it doesn’t offer anything that is new or different about bread baking.

title: Hard-to-Follow Cozy Mystery Includes Suspenseful Hurricane Scenes
text:
DEATH ON TUCKERNUCK is hard to follow, and was not a particularly enjoyable read for this cozy mystery lover. The novel has a cast of thousands--Merry’s incoming wedding guests; assorted Nantucket police and support staff; two different US Coast Guard rescue crews (one helicopter, one cutter); two caretakers for Tuckernuck Island (and their helpers); Tuckernuck residents requiring evacuation; three people from a grounded yacht; more helpers; a bereaved parent; and even a pair of beautiful Palomino horses.

The timeline gets wonky in places, especially at the end. For example, it’s unclear exactly when the caretaker’s daughter is finally discovered, amidst all the hospital interviews; the internal police department developments; the unmasking of the perp; and the wedding arrangements--all of these things are packed in after the hurricane abates. There are just too many things going on simultaneously in the plot for the author to be able to handle everything smoothly.

The characters take crazy risks that would never happen in real life. I can’t imagine that a Coast Guard captain would agree to winch an untrained person (even if she is a detective) down to a grounded yacht to gather crime scene evidence when a hurricane is about to hit. Similarly, I don’t believe that an experienced person would swim to a skiff in order to moor it properly, when the seas are treacherously high due to an incoming hurricane.

In the novel (which fans of the Merry Folger series won’t want to miss because of Merry’s wedding), Merry’s elaborate wedding plans must be postponed and drastically altered, because Hurricane Teddy is headed straight at Nantucket. As if the hurricane weren’t enough, a yacht is grounded on Tuckernuck Island with two people on board who have been shot. Merry takes on the investigation, and has to deal with Chief Pocock--who makes the worst boss you can ever imagine seem like a pussycat.

The secondary plot, involving the Tuckernuck Island caretakers (Jack and Dionis Mather), takes over most of the novel. Dionis and Jack must unexpectedly evacuate Tuckernuck and board up all the houses. As Dionis is making a final run to Tuckernuck in roiling seas, she encounters a wounded stranger who needs her help--but who may also be a killer.

This was my first Merry Folger mystery, and I suspect that it is NOT the best one in the series. The novel works all right as a standalone, but it didn’t really hold my attention. There are some well-written, suspenseful scenes where the humans are fighting the weather, but it definitely is NOT a page-turner. The outcome is telegraphed early on, and the denouement holds no real surprises.

title: Mildly Amusing Historical Cozy Featuring Bored Housewife in 1893 Poland
text:
MRS. MOHR GOES MISSING (A ZOFIA TURBOTYNSKA MYSTERY) is an historical cozy mystery set in 1893 in Poland--specifically in provincial Cracow during the time of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Thus the novel abounds with aristocrats (countesses, baronesses, etc.), professors, and peasants, and the story describes a society with strictly defined classes.

The main character (Zofia) is quite well-to-do (a university professor’s wife). She is basically a bored housewife, but is also an avid social climber, and a devoted reader of mystery novels. In this mystery--well-translated from the Polish--Zofia is attempting to improve her social position by performing charitable works.

In the course of organizing a raffle to benefit scrofulous children, Zofia learns that a wealthy resident of Helcel House (a nursing home run by the Sisters of Charity) has disappeared. Zofia visits Helcel House, surreptitiously interviews staff and residents, and causes the discovery of the missing woman’s body. Zofia is convinced that the woman was murdered, and eventually unravels the mystery surrounding the murder, a subsequent murder, and a subsequent disappearance.

The novel is amusing, because of (1) Zofia’s forceful opinions; (2) her manipulation of her husband, of a terrified nun at Helcel House, of her servants, and of everyone else she finds useful; and (3) her intense focus on seeing--and being seen with--the creme de la creme of Cracovian society. However, Zofia’s social-climbing becomes tiresome long before the Helcel House mystery is solved.

The characters’ long Polish and Hungarian names add some difficulty for the reader. However, the worst thing about this novel is that the plot seems to be a very conventional mystery plot that is mechanically superimposed onto the researched historical setting. The disconnect made me lose interest in Zofia and the story about halfway through. The ending is satisfying enough, but I didn’t like the book well enough to want to read any more Zofia Turbontynska mysteries.

title: Dissatisfying Ending Ruins Otherwise Excellent Mystery Novel
text:
TRACE ELEMENTS: A COMMISSARIO GUIDO BRUNETTI MYSTERY is the 29th entry in this immensely popular mystery series, but it works fine as a standalone. (The first “Guido Brunetti” mystery is [[ASIN:0330337726 Death at la Fenice]]). I loved the Brunetti character, the wonderful descriptions of Venice, and the leisurely plot. However, the immensely dissatisfying ending destroyed all my accumulated pleasure in reading the book.

In the novel, Brunetti responds to a dying woman’s plea to speak with the police. The woman (who is in hospice care) can speak only a few words at a time. She communicates to Brunetti and his colleague (Claudia Griffoni) that her husband (who died in a motorcycle accident about a week before) was murdered. Brunetti is profoundly affected by the woman’s passing (in his presence), so he investigates.

The husband was a technician for a company that provides drinking water to a region of Italy. He was a scrupulously honest man, yet he was involved in something that yielded “bad money” that his dying wife refused to use for her continued hospital care. Brunetti, in his dogged fashion, utilizing the extraordinary (and somewhat unbelievable) system-hacking capabilities of the Vice-Questore’s secretary (Elettra Zorzi), eventually unravels the complex sequence of events that led to the husband’s non-accidental death.

Astute readers will quickly surmise, as soon as the water-supply company is introduced, that the novel’s plot will involve important environmental issues. Apparently the series plots often require Brunetti to make difficult, pragmatic choices when it comes to obtaining justice for victims and punishment for the guilty. However, in this novel (my first Brunetti mystery), the Commissario makes an extremely wrong choice at the end. The fact that the legal process moves slowly is an inadequate justification for his decision.

Perhaps I would have found the ending more satisfying if the book hadn’t ended so quickly, with Brunetti’s choice made on the final page. But as the novel stands, it appears that the author created a dilemma that even she couldn’t find a reasonable way out of, and that’s too bad. Other than the ending, the novel has great characters, a fabulous setting, and excellent writing, and it makes me want to read more of the Brunetti series.

title: Disillusioned Maggie Becomes Bomb Defuser
text:
THE KING’S JUSTICE: A MAGGIE HOPE MYSTERY is the 9th “Maggie Hope”, but it works fine as a standalone. Maggie is a likeable, reasonably believable character, even though she’s recently become somewhat self-destructive, and a heavy drinker. Presumably it’s her disillusionment with the British Special Operations Executive (SOE) that drives her reckless behavior—having left the SOE, she has accepted a new job as one of London’s elite defusers of unexploded German bombs.

Whether Britain actually had female bomb defusers during WWII, I do not know. However, the historical setting of WWII London generally rings true. The novel addresses, among other things, the extreme prejudice exhibited by home front Londoners against young men who were conscientious objectors. The “white feather”, a symbol of cowardice carried forward from WWI, figures prominently in the plot.

In the novel, Maggie is following the sentencing and hanging of “The Blackout Beast”, a serial killer she helped to capture—and who nearly killed her—in series book 6, [[ASIN:0804178720 The Queen’s Accomplice]]. She is also teaching a young conscientious objector (Milo) how to defuse live bombs. The training is strictly on-the-job, so Milo must learn by standing beside her and watching her defuse them. When Maggie takes Milo along to a pub for a celebratory drink, he is hassled by a group of young women who present him with a white feather.

Maggie and her friend Detective Durgin soon become involved with investigating a new series of murders. Beginning shortly after The Blackout Beast is sentenced to death, suitcases filled with human bones begin to wash up on the shores of the Thames. The bones have all the flesh boiled off, so there are no clues to the manner of death. Ominously, the suitcases all contain white feathers . . . .

The novel is well-written, but rather wordy and slow-moving. Still, fans of the “Maggie Hope” series won’t want to miss it, as it explores Maggie’s continuing romantic relationship with Durgin.

title: Of Interest to “Magic Men” Series Fans; Not a Standalone Novel
text:
NOW YOU SEE THEM (Magic Men Mysteries) is definitely NOT a standalone mystery. The story is almost entirely about the relationships among the established series characters (Max, Edgar, Emma, Sam, Ruby), and you probably won’t find the characters at all interesting unless you know their backgrounds as developed in the previous books.

I’ve read and enjoyed all of the earlier “Magic Men” novels (the first one is [[ASIN:B00QPIGTOM The Zig Zag Girl]]), so I recommend the series. But even I found NOW YOU SEE THEM to be frequently (ack!) boring, generally slow-moving, and weakly plotted.

The book is basically about former detective Emma’s dissatisfaction with her wife-and-mother existence--she and Edgar have three children now. (Why has it taken her this long to get bored?) Emma is unhappy at the beginning of the book, and is still unhappy at the halfway point, without having done any freelance detecting. (To be fair, hardly anyone has done any detecting in the first half of the book.)

In the novel, a teenage Rodean schoolgirl, Rhonda, has disappeared. Superintendent Edgar must find her, but his investigation soon expands to include two other missing girls. (Emma’s reporter friend Sam has noticed similarities in the three cases, and tells Emma.) Edgar’s new 19-year-old detective, Meg, goes undercover (as a Bobby Soxer), and learns that before Rhonda disappeared she was hanging around a London theater in hopes of meeting the latest teen idol, Bobby.

One of the missing girls turns up dead--wearing Rhonda’s Rodean uniform cloak--and the search for Rhonda becomes urgent. But then Ruby (now the famous “Ruby Magic”) disappears, too. Is Ruby’s disappearance connected to the other three? Will the Magic Men (Edgar and Max) be able to find Ruby and Rhonda before something really bad happens to them?

Series readers will want to read this book to find out how the familiar characters are doing. However, if you’re going to skip one of the series books, this is the one to skip.

title: Boring Police Procedural Is Deservedly Optioned for TV Series
text:
TIN BADGES: A NOVEL has been optioned for TV by the producer of “NYPD Blue”, and it should make a terrific TV series. In the novel, a retired detective (“Tank” Rizzo), his disabled former partner (Pearl), an off-duty NYPD Chief of Detectives (Ray Connors), Tank’s computer-whiz teenage nephew (Chris), and a squad of street-smart misfits make up a team that solves NYPD cold cases (cases handed off to freelancer Tank by Connors). What a TV series framework!

As a novel, though, TIN BADGES is boring and predictable. Tank gets a not-so-cold case involving the brutal rapes of two women (prostitutes, maybe?) that the NYPD doesn’t want to handle. It’s likely that the women are connected to an NYC crime boss (Gonzo), who exacts swift and terminal retribution against anyone who knows too much about his operations.

When Tank gets onto Gonzo’s radar, it endangers not only his team, but his girlfriend (Connie Tramonti) and her father (Carmine). Connie and Carmine are the co-owners of Tramonti’s Italian restaurant/bar/jazz club, which Carmine established when he retired from running a major organized-crime numbers operation. The restaurant is now neutral ground for cops and criminals alike.

The 14-year-old nephew Chris has just lost his parents in an automobile “accident”, and is living with Tank only because it’s better than entering the foster care system. Chris hates Tank because Tank and his father had become estranged, and had stopped speaking to each other. Tank keeps the reason secret until the very end of the book, and the reveal isn’t worth the wait. Happily, the secret doesn’t affect the plot of this novel in any significant way.

The novel’s title is based on the fact (?) that retired gold-shield detectives who freelance like Tank are known as “tin badges”. The novel is decently written. The characters are mildly interesting in their cliched fashion (e.g., tough-talking Tank, Bruno the former boxer with a heart of gold, Chris the teenager with mad computer skillz, Connie the sensible and understanding love interest, etc.). The plot is a perfectly ordinary police procedural plot. More books in the series are promised, but I think that I’ll pass on them, even though I’m looking forward to the TV series.

title: Rex Stout Might Think He’d Written This “Nero Wolfe” Mystery
text:
Rex Stout himself might be unsure whether he had written DEATH OF AN ART COLLECTOR: A NERO WOLFE MYSTERY--Robert Goldsborough is that good at emulating Stout’s style and getting into Archie Goodwin’s viewpoint character. However, this new “Nero Wolfe” series entry has an extremely thin plot. The one thing that sets the novel apart is that Wolfe finds it difficult to solve the murder mystery, and needs a little luck to wrap up the investigation and preserve his reputation.

In the novel, Archie escorts his girlfriend Lily to a dinner that offers a “sneak peek” at the still-under-construction Guggenheim Museum. They are seated at a table for a wealthy art collector (Arthur Wordell), his daughter (Nadia), and four of Wordell’s art advisors (biographer Faith Richardson, artist Zondra Zagreb, curator Henry Banks, publisher Emory Sterling). When the MC prematurely announces that Wordell is giving his fabulous art collection to the Guggenheim, Wordell nearly walks out of the room. He is notorious for preserving his privacy in all matters related to his collection.

A few weeks later, Wordell is killed by a fall from a windowsill in his office building. The windowsill is hundreds of feet from the ground, but Wordell was in the habit of perching on it with his feet dangling out, to take in the sights and smells of Midtown NYC. Daughter Nadia asks Wolfe to investigate Wordell’s death--she is sure that Wordell was pushed.

As Archie investigates per Wolfe's directives, it becomes clear that Wordell was disliked for his “art hog” buying tactics, but not really hated by anyone. Yet almost everyone who is interviewed agrees that Wordell must have been pushed from the windowsill. So who was it that pushed him?

It’s fun to follow Archie’s antics, but his interviews of the suspects are repetitive, and eventually become tedious. The individual suspects aren’t that interesting as characters (except for the colorful Zagreb), and their possible motives for murder overlap a lot. The ultimate solution is briefly exciting, but not particularly satisfying.

Rex Stout Might Think He’d Written This “Nero Wolfe” Mystery

title: Disappointing, Thinly Plotted Addition to Series; Advances Bruno’s Romantic Relationships
text:
THE BODY IN THE CASTLE WELL (Bruno, Chief of Police Series) is disappointing addition to this generally entertaining series. The “Bruno” novels are always about French cuisine and wines, the lovingly described Perigord region, and WWII history, but there is little else to be found in this one. The mystery plot is extremely thin. Was the young, wealthy American student who is found in a negligently sealed well murdered? If so, who did it? And what was the motive? Unfortunately, the answers are telegraphed well in advance of the final few chapters that wrap the mystery up in record time.

In the novel, a gifted art history student (Claudia) is found drowned in the Limeuil Castle well. Evidence suggests that Claudia may have fallen in while attempting to rescue a kitten, but the death is suspicious. Because Claudia is the daughter of a wealthy, influential financier who has the ear of the U.S. President, Bruno must follow every lead, and use extreme delicacy and caution, in pursuing his investigation. The American ambassador, a PI sent by Claudia’s father, Claudia’s divorced mother, and French authorities at every policing level are actively involved, because the Americans want some heads to roll. The suspicious death takes some time to resolve, because Bruno is uncharacteristically slow in putting together the bits of evidence that are right in front of him.

The novel advances the reader’s knowledge of Bruno’s love life--his relationships with Isabelle and Pamela. There’s also a lot of character development of the politician/songbird Amelie, and of course dog Balzac and horse Hector make regular appearances. The novel works as a standalone, but it’s slow-moving, short on plot, and generally boring unless you’re already interested in the Bruno series.

title: Duplicates Prior Series Novels; Develops Ruth/Nelson, Judy/Cathbad Relationships
text:
Until now, I’ve enjoyed each new entry in the “Ruth Galloway” series. The novels are pleasant “cozy police procedural” mysteries about an archaeologist, now a single mother, who consults with local police whenever bones are discovered in henge sites in England’s North Norfolk salt marshes. However, most of this 11th series entry, THE STONE CIRCLE (RUTH GALLOWAY MYSTERIES), is duplicative of the earlier novels, and the new material about The Great Circle of stones at Stanton Drew is thrown in at the end and almost irrelevant to the solution of the main mystery.

In the novel, a second stone circle is discovered at the marshy henge site explored in the prior novels. This one includes a stone cist (a grave), but Ruth finds, once again, that the bones in it are recent--definitely not Bronze Age like the henge. Ruth’s detective contact (Nelson), her daughter Kate’s father, is once again receiving anonymous letters with literary references that urge him to investigate circumstances related to the child’s bones buried at the henge site.

A prime suspect in the burial is the look-alike son (Leif) of the deceased author of the letters Nelson received in the previous henge investigation. The bones are soon identified as probably belonging to a 12-year-old girl (Margaret) who went missing in 1981. But where were the bones kept, before they were reburied in the newly discovered cist? Who was responsible for Margaret’s death? And who reburied her bones in the cist?

Most of the novel deals with Ruth’s star-crossed relationship with Nelson. Nelson is married with adult daughters, and hasn’t informed his family of Kate’s paternity. He does have a regular visitation arrangement with Kate, so that one wonders why they don’t seem to suspect that he is Kate’s father. The novel also ties up a lot of loose ends from the original henge investigation--it’s basically a reworking of the original henge plot.

The novel does NOT work as a standalone. It’s extremely slow-moving, and the plot and ending are unsatisfying. Read it if you’re interested in following the latest developments in the Ruth/Nelson and Cathbad/Judy relationships.

title: Farcical Mystery With Unpleasant Darkness Underneath
text:
I ordered A SHOT IN THE DARK: A CONSTABLE TWITTEN MYSTERY because a national newspaper reviewer labeled it “the funniest mystery of the year 2018”. Well, it’s written as a farce, and funny at times, but it has an unpleasant darkness underneath that destroys the humor and fun. I shouldn’t have ignored my personal rule, which is to always avoid novels that borrow their titles from other famous literary, dramatic, or comedic works (e.g., [[ASIN:6305308713 Peter Seller’s “A Shot in the Dark”]]).

In the novel, a too-clever-by-half young constable (Twitten) arrives in Brighton, where the police (Steine and Brunswick) are in total denial about the existence of crime in the seaside resort. When crimes are reported, they dismiss them as too baffling to be solved, or accept any faked evidence that will allow them to close a case.

Twitten annoys his superiors and upsets the comfortable status quo by easily solving all the outstanding cases. In the end, he is outsmarted by an equally clever Master Criminal, and the status quo is restored by (1) an unbelievable event that removes a threat to a main character; and (2) the machinations of the Master Criminal.

The novel ends with a mild cliffhanger that suggests there may be more “Inspector Twitten” novels to come. If there are, I won’t be reading them. The novel is professionally written and plotted (with elaborate plot twists), but there isn’t a single character that I really liked.

title: Quality Wall Calendar; Ice Cream Cone Photos Are So-So
text:
This ICE CREAM 2019 WALL CALENDAR is decorative, and has date boxes with enough space for recording your most important events (e.g., medical appointments, birthdays, etc.). However, there isn't enough space for recording an entire family's important events. Major U.S. holidays are shown on the calendar; mainly it's a calendar to glance at quickly to check the day of the week and the date.

The ice cream cone theme is nice, but I think the photographs could be better. Some cones aren't very colorful (e.g., September’s is avocado green and white), and some cones don't look all that scrumptious (e.g., May’s has brown and black things stuck onto it).

This is a nice, well-printed, standard wall calendar. However, I’m not sure that I want to look at each of these ice cream cone photographs for a full month.

title: Llewelyn Heads Investigation Into Bombing That Seriously Injures Barker
text:
BLOOD IS BLOOD: A BARKER & LLEWELYN NOVEL is the 10th novel in the “Barker & Llewelyn” series, but the first one that I’ve read. It works fine as a standalone, but it didn't hold my interest--I just couldn't warm to the priggish, self-important, unimaginative Thomas Llewelyn (Cyrus Barker’s associate). This time out, Cyrus is hospitalized, so Thomas must handle the inquiry-agent investigations by himself, with some help from Cyrus’ long-lost, American cowboy brother (Caleb Barker), and a hired female inquiry agent (Sarah Fletcher).

In the novel, a bombing at the inquiry agents’ offices sends Cyrus and Thomas straight down to the cellar. Cyrus lands beneath a heavy desk and a pile of debris, and is seriously injured. Thomas rides down inside a rolltop desk, and escapes injury. After Cyrus is rescued and transported to a hospital, Thomas sets about reassembling the office files. He compiles a list of individuals who might have been responsible for the bombing, and submits it to Scotland Yard for assistance in finding the ones that are currently out of prison.

Caleb shows up unexpectedly, and supplies the investigative acumen and big personality that Thomas lacks. Caleb is an experienced tracker, and is employed by the famous Pinkerton agency. Thomas’ involvement is complicated by the need to get everything finished before his fast-approaching wedding to Rebecca.

The novel is very slow-moving, in part because of the extra descriptive passages and formal prose style that the author employs to make the plot believable as a historical “Victorian” mystery. I didn't find the Victorian atmosphere very convincing (though the characters do travel around in hansom cabs).

The characters are shallowly drawn, and Caleb is a sort of caricature of an American cowboy turned Pinkerton agent. Perhaps I would have liked this book better if I had already been acquainted with Cyrus and Thomas, and with their working methods.

title: Well-Written, Engaging Novel
text: CIRCE is a well-written novel, and the story engaged me as a reader from the very beginning.  However, I still prefer to read the classical versions of the Greek myths, which can hardly be improved upon.

title: Well-Written, Divided-Plot Novel About Cold War CIA Operations
text:
SAFE HOUSES: A NOVEL is another one of those mystery/thrillers that tells a story via a divided plot with two timelines. There’s a present-day (August 2014) mystery: Why did gentle, developmentally-disabled Willard murder his parents? And there’s a long-ago (Berlin 1979) mystery: What is the meaning of the coded message overheard by Willard’s mother (Helen), and why did Helen leave her job with the CIA after hearing it?

The novel starts with the Berlin story (chapters 1-4), then switches to the present-day story (chapters 5-8). It then returns to the Berlin story (chapters 9-11), and to the present-day story (chapters 12-14). And the pattern repeats throughout the book. Information about what happened to Helen in 1979 is revealed gradually, as are events in the ongoing investigation of Helen’s murder (conducted by CIA contractor Henry and Helen's daughter Anna). As it progresses, the ongoing investigation increasingly indicates that the motive for the parents’ murders is rooted in the 1979 Berlin events.

I have no patience with this divided-plot style of novel-writing. I generally forgo the cliffhangers and skip ahead to the next segments of one story until I tire of it; then I go back and catch up the segments of the other story, ditto.

In this novel, the overall story turns around Helen’s past and present-day efforts at thwarting a powerful, dangerous CIA agent (code name Robert) who rapes his female informers in safe houses. I didn’t find Helen’s story or the novel’s ending believable, and thus I didn’t care for the novel. However, it's a well-written novel, and readers (especially those with feminist leanings) who like mystery/thrillers about Cold War spying operations will probably enjoy it.

title: Slow-Moving Cozy Mystery Featuring Drab British Ex-Pat
text:
DEATH IN PROVENCE: A NOVEL (PENELOPE KITE) is a slow-moving cozy mystery with a drab, boring amateur detective (Penelope) and an uninteresting plot. Especially at the beginning, the narrative is weighed down by many untranslated French phrases that are presumably inserted to establish the Provence setting. I guess they’re needed, because other details regarding Penelope’s run-down stone cottage and its environs are fairly generic.

As for Penelope, she’s a middle-aged, divorced British ex-pat, with unappreciative step-children and horrible, insulting step-grandchildren back in England. She used to work for a medical examiner, which gives her limited forensic knowledge (e.g., the number of hours required for rigor mortis to wear off). She’s rather unsure of herself, which probably explains why local authorities don't take her very seriously when she shares her forensic theories about the murder of a local drunk found floating face down in her swimming pool. There's a love interest for Penelope, in the form of a dishy middle-aged mayor who seems to find her attractive.

The plot turns around some problems regarding the title to Penelope’s newly acquired dream home. Ownership became murky after WWII, when the property was first occupied by a French family suspected of collaborating with the Germans during the occupation. Penelope leans very heavily on the real estate agent (Clemence) who sold her the cottage. Clemence provides support far beyond what might be expected, including offering Penelope temporary shelter after the body is discovered, lining up repairmen, translating to supplement Penelope’s faltering French, and providing introductions to all the important local people.

Nothing about this novel makes me want to read any more of the series. Generally I love any and all cozy mysteries, but this one just falls flat.

title: Slow-Moving Psychological Thriller--NOT a Ghost Story
text:
THE NEW NEIGHBORS is a rather slow-moving psychological thriller. In alternating chapters, two viewpoint characters (Jack and Sydney) recount the mysterious things that happen to them after they move into their new house. Some of the events are creepy (e.g., the discovery of something decomposing in the attic, a hand on the woman’s face at night). However, as Sydney says in an early chapter, it isn't a ghost story. It’s about hidden familial relationships, and about Jack’s and Sydney’s differing interpretations of shared events.

In the novel, Jack and Sydney (as yet unmarried) acquire and move into their hoped-for “forever home”. It’s a bargain-priced, 3-bedroom, detached home in London. It’s also packed with the previous owner’s furniture and junk. That owner left suddenly for Australia, leaving all his possessions behind.

Jack and Sydney have been in the house for a few weeks before they notice “the smell”. It’s emanating from the attic, and Jack climbs up to investigate. He’s shocked to find that the attic is empty--in stark contrast to the trash-filled rooms below--except for the disgusting source of “the smell” and a child's treasure box that has a name he recognizes scrawled inside. From then on, things can only get worse ….

The writing is pretty good, and the suspenseful story is told well enough to keep the reader reading if he/she has plenty of leisure time. The novel is pretty decent for summer or beach reading. However, the characters and the plot aren’t particularly memorable; and it’s unlikely that anyone could have pulled off the grand scheme that’s revealed at the end.

title: Snail-Paced Procedural About Hunting Incident on Maquoit Island
text:
STAY HIDDEN: A NOVEL (MIKE BOWDITCH MYSTERIES is the 9th series novel, but my first. It works okay as a standalone, but I felt like I was missing something important because it never explains anything about Mike’s estrangement from the daughter of his father-figure/mentor (Charlie). The novel is a snail-paced police procedural (game warden investigator procedural, to be more precise).

In the novel, newly minted warden investigator Mike is assigned his first case--the fatal shooting of a woman who was hanging white laundry on a clothesline on isolated Maquoit Island, which is located off the coast of Maine. The first reports suggest that a hunter mistook the white fabric of her laundry for a white-tailed deer.

However, forensic details at the incident scene, and the general secretiveness of the island residents (especially the secretiveness of take-charge-guy Harmon Reed) make Mike suspicious about the “hunting accident”. His further interviews and investigations prove out his suspicion that it was murder. Mike successfully identifies the killer, but nearly loses his own life in the process.

If I liked the Mike Bowditch character enough to want to read further series novels, I would definitely start with the first one, [[ASIN:1250161657 The Poacher’s Son]]. I’m sure that it’s more interesting than this one, which has a predictable plot and is best described as tedious. The Maquoit Island setting rings true, and I hope that the islanders will deal with the deer/tick problem soon (if it really exists). Series followers will probably want to read this for the information about Mike’s ongoing relationship with Charlie.

title: Run-of-the-Mill Cozy Mystery Lacks 1913 Greenwich Village Atmosphere
text:
MURDER IN GREENWICH VILLAGE (A LOUISE FAULK MYSTERY) is a decent but run-of-the-mill cozy mystery. It’s supposedly set in Greenwich Village in 1913, but there isn’t much of an historical atmosphere. References to new buildings (e.g., the electrified Woolworth Building) are dropped in; and male figures (especially the police detectives) are predictably patronizing of the female amateur detective (Louise). However, the story doesn’t have much to do with the time period chosen for the setting.

In the novel, Louise (from Altoona, Pa.) is working for a NYC publisher, having landed the job with the help of her wealthy aunt (who writes popular fiction). Louise shares a Greenwich Village apartment with another girl (Callie), and with Callie’s unwelcome, sponging cousin (Ethel). Louise and Callie return home one night and discover Ethel’s body with a butcher knife buried in it.

Callie and Louise lie to the police, by withholding information about admirers who happen to match the description of a man seen on the apartment stairs shortly after Ethel arrived home. Louise ends up spending lots of time at the police station, talking to Detective Muldoon, for various reasons. Eventually Louise figures out who the killer is, forms her own (highly illegal) plan for trapping the killer, and ends up in mortal danger herself when the plan doesn’t succeed as expected.

The novel is well-written, though rather wordy. The plot is nothing special. Amateur detective Louise isn’t very interesting, and is likely to become even less interesting if she pursues her announced desire to become the first female homicide detective in NYC.

title: Second Book in Series About Investigators’ Hunt for Cult Leader Quinton Zane
text:
PROMISE NOT TO TELL is the second novel in the “Cutler, Sutter & Salinas” mystery/thriller series about a trio of private investigators who are hunting a charismatic, manipulative cult leader (Quinton Zane). It sort of works as a standalone, but it’s hard to commit to if you don’t know the backstory. (I did not.) If you’re interested in the series, start with [[ASIN:0515156353 When All the Girls Have Gone]], because the second novel is chock full of spoilers.

In the novel, a reclusive survivor of Zane’s cult (Hannah) commits suicide after spotting a person that she believes is Zane, who is apparently returning for the key to a cache of hidden cult money. Before she dies, she paints a picture on the wall of her cabin, photographs the painting, mails the camera to another cult survivor (Virginia), and torches the cabin. Virginia, who is an art gallery owner, subsequently hires the Cutler, Sutter & Salinas PI firm to determine whether Hannah was murdered, and to help unravel the meaning of Hannah’s final painting.

What follows is an extremely convoluted investigation, every bit as complicated as the one in [[ASIN:0307474275 The Da Vinci Code]]. The book is well-written, but the characters spend a lot of time sizing one another up, talking about motives, and discussing relationships. Also, the story skips forward and back, and repeats itself, which can be confusing to the reader, and which makes for a slow read.

The plot has lots of action, and the many threads are tied up more or less satisfactorily at the end, despite the story’s ending with a cliffhanger. However, I didn’t like any of the characters well enough to want to read any more books in the series. Jayne Ann Krentz may be a best-selling author, but I don’t care for her mystery/thriller writing style.

title: Pedestrian Cave-Exploration Thriller Gets Reality-TV Host’s Dialogue Exactly Right
text:
THE ANOMALY is a rather pedestrian ancient-cave-exploration thriller about a fifth-rate-documentary-filming team’s discovery of actual buried secrets. The irony of it all is that afterwards the team can’t tell anyone about the discovery. Again and again, the author absolutely nails the phony on-screen dialogue spewed by the on-camera “explorer” (Nolan). For example, “Will we find the cavern? I don’t know. But I do know this: in the search for truth, it matters not whether we find. It matters only that we continue to seek.”

I hate those empty reality documentaries that air all the time on cable channels, so I didn’t enjoy reading Nolan’s glib pronouncements one bit. However, the Nolan character himself isn’t bad--Nolan and his producer (Ken) are both cynically aware of the emptiness of the documentaries that they make to sell to a gullible public.
