The plot takes off from a real April 1909 newspaper story (reproduced in the novel) about a cavern supposedly discovered in the Grand Canyon by explorer G.E. Kincaid. The story has all the stock elements of an archaeological thriller: a huge stone rolling down a passageway, explorers trapped by blockage of the only exit, discovery of mysterious writings, emergence of frightening creatures, secret society conspiracy, and so on. Some of the film team members live, some don’t.

This is a rather slow-moving novel, and I just couldn’t warm to it. It’s okay if you like any and all thrillers belonging to the “Indiana Jones” genre.

title: Weird, Philosophical Novel About Torture and Walking
text:
THE MIRANDA is a weird, sort of philosophical novel about torture and walking. Although it’s a book that I wish I hadn’t read (at least I refrained from Googling “the Spanish boot”), it has a sort of horrid fascination, and probably has some literary merit. It’s written as a first-person narrative, almost but not quite as stream of consciousness. There is structure to the story that the narrator tells.

In the novel, a psychologist (Joe) burns out at his job as a U.S. government torture-resistance trainer. He quits, but knows full well that one day some of the civilian “volunteers” that he legally tortured (to make them less likely to break if captured by enemy combatants abroad) will come after him to even the score.

He divorces his wife, and eventually purchases a house with a backyard containing a 100-yard circular path. He decides to use the path to walk a distance equal to the circumference of the Earth, by walking 25 miles a day (about 8 hours a day) for 1000 days. He hires an aspiring bartender (Miranda) to do his shopping, and devotes himself to walking.

While Joe is walking, he meets his suburban neighbors, and philosophizes. He also quietly fixes problems--such as the riff-raff with vicious dogs next door--in brutal but effective fashion. And he’s at home in his house with the path when someone from his past does finally show up . . . .

The novel is well written, and interesting in a way, but one wonders what inspired the author to create such a novel. Readers take note: the novel contains torture scenes, although they aren’t excessively graphic.

title: A Real Slog--But With Important Romantic Developments for Ongoing Characters
text:
Although I’m a fan of author Elly Griffiths and the “Magic Men” series, I found THE VANISHING BOX (MAGIC MEN MYSTERIES) to be a real slog (unlike the other series books). If I hadn’t already been committed to the characters, I probably would’ve abandoned it about a third of the way through. This is the 4th novel in the series, which starts with [[ASIN:0544811879 The Zig Zag Girl]].

In the novel, detective Edgar investigates the murder of a young woman (Lily) whose body is posed like the figure of a young woman in a famous Victorian painting. The murder seems to have a connection with a variety show that is playing at the Brighton Hippodrome. Magician Max Mephisto and his magician daughter Ruby (Edgar’s fiancee) head the bill, but the secondary attraction is a “living tableaux” act where nearly naked women pose motionless as famous women in history (Cleopatra, Elizabeth I, etc.).

When Lily’s murder is followed by the murders of a tableaux actress and the tableaux act’s organizer (Vic), the pressure really mounts on Edgar and his team (especially Emma and Bob) to stop the killer. Then Emma disappears, and it looks like she may become the next victim, unless Edgar and Max can reach her in time.

Series readers won’t want to miss THE VANISHING BOX, because (1) Max finds a serious love interest; (2) Bob gets romantically involved with a tableaux girl; and (3) Edgar and Ruby finally straighten out their engagement and wedding date. (Note that the book’s description, as of September 2018, erroneously states that Ruby (not Emma) disappears.)

title: Easy-Reading, Entertaining Thriller If You Like Paranormal Stuff
text:
SCHOOL FOR PSYCHICS: BOOK ONE is an easy-reading, entertaining thriller, if (like me) you have a taste for supernatural/paranormal stuff. I really want to believe in the existence of people with actual psychic powers, so I enjoyed reading about how the novel’s colorful characters employ their differing skills (starting fires, communicating with animals, receiving death warnings, telepathy, telekinesis, etc.) at their government-sanctioned school for psychics. A plus factor for this S.F. Bay Area resident is that the school is supposedly located on lovely Angel Island (in the middle of San Francisco Bay).

Unfortunately, the novel reads like it’s intended for a young adult audience. That’s okay with me, but I got awfully tired of main character Teddy’s plotting with her “team” to break into locked school offices and break any and all school rules. She’s a 20-something (really too old for that kind of thing), and her crazy schemes shouldn’t succeed as well as they do. Also, she keeps getting caught doing things that should get her expelled, but she’s allowed to remain at the school anyway.

The plot is pretty thin. Secrets are being kept from adopted Teddy (about her birth parents and the real purposes of the school); and the competing intra-school squads of Alphas and Misfits hate each other, even as individual members struggle to develop and master their personal psychic skills. All of the “recruits” are being groomed for jobs with the FBI or Homeland Security.

The 20-something kids remind me of the Scooby Gang in “Buffy the Vampire Slayer” (which I loved), but the novel isn’t as well done as the TV series. Nor does it have the charm of the Harry Potter books. SCHOOL FOR PSYCHICS Book One ends with a cliffhanger of sorts, although most of the threads are tied up enough to create a reasonably satisfying, if unsurprising, ending.

Although I enjoyed the novel as extremely light reading, neither the characters nor the cliffhanger is interesting enough to make me want to read Book Two.

title: Detailed Account of Reddit-Related Activities of Alexis Ohanian, Steve Huffman
text:
WE ARE THE NERDS: THE BIRTH AND TUMULTUOUS LIFE OF REDDIT, THE INTERNET’S CULTURE LABORATORY is a very long and detailed account of the Reddit-related activities of Alexis Ohanian and Steve Huffman, the original founders and current leaders of Reddit, the so-called “front page of the Internet”. It’s a book about people, based on many personal interviews.

The book doesn’t provide much, if any, insight into what Reddit is or why it became so wildly popular. Read it if you enjoy biographies of individuals who made millions from Silicon Valley/Internet startups.

title: Biography of Winning Trainer of Famous Racehorse Stymie
text:
OUT OF THE CLOUDS: THE UNLIKELY HORSEMAN AND THE UNWANTED COLT WHO CONQUERED THE SPORT OF KINGS is a biography of the trainer of the famous racehorse Stymie (Hirsch Jacobs) and of the trainer’s moneyman (Isidor Bieber). Other than in a short prologue, the colt Stymie makes his first appearance at the end of Chapter 9 (p. 153 of 285 pp., or more than halfway through the book).

The book is mostly interesting for the history of how horse racing and race tracks in America developed and prospered from the 1920s through the 1950s. As biography, the book is interesting because Hirsch Jacobs, a multimillionaire who started with nothing, was, at the time of his death in 1970, the winningest trainer of all time (3,596 career wins).

title: Odd Erotic Romance Between Self-Involved Student, Merman
text:
THE PISCES: A NOVEL is something of an oddity--an intellectual’s erotic fantasy romance. I enjoyed the ruminations of the selfish, self-involved viewpoint character (Lucy), as she tried to understand why she couldn’t let go of her long-time boyfriend (Jamie), and why she couldn’t make any progress on her dissertation about Sappho.

However, I found her intense physical relationship with a merman (Theo) to be creepy, even though I appreciated the excellence of the accompanying erotic writing. This novel is so far out of my wheelhouse, I don’t know how to rate it. However, I suspect that it will appeal to college-educated women with a taste for erotic fiction.

title: Quasi-Historical Novel About New York Mob, Garment Industry
text:
BUTTON MAN is NOT the mystery/thriller that I expected. Instead it’s a quasi-historical novel about a garment manufacturer (Morris Raab)--a self-made man of great integrity who stands up to the New York Mafia and homegrown gangs of the Prohibition Era (the 1930s). Among the real historical figures appearing in the novel are Lepke Buchalter, Legs Diamond, and Dutch Schultz.

I don’t know whether there is a real person or persons that Morris Raab is based on. In the novel, Raab’s life is entangled with the mob figures because he grew up with them in Brooklyn, and because his brother Harold hangs out with, and runs errands for, the local mob.

This is a well-written book, but it isn’t the sort of thing that I enjoy as escape reading. It has serious themes that don't interest me, because I’m a mystery/thriller fan with very plebeian taste in fiction.

title: Exhausted Vic Pursues Dual Investigations Into Affairs of Powerful People
text:
SHELL GAME: A V.I. WARSHAWSKI NOVEL is the 19th V.I. Warshawski novel. I’m a fan of this generally excellent series, but SHELL GAME is very slow-moving, and has a downright silly ending. Private detective Warshawski (Vic) is always a reckless risk-taker, and we see plenty of risk-taking during this “adventure”. However, the ending (which has Vic paddling down a Minnesota river on an ice floe) is totally unbelievable and over the top. In addition, Vic engages too many times in extended feminist and political rants.

In the novel, Vic investigates (1) the disappearance of her all-but-forgotten, former niece-in-law (Reno); and (2) the connection between her dear friend Lotty’s grandnephew (Felix) and the body of a murdered man (Leroy aka Lawrence) that was found stuffed into a hollow log in a Chicago-area forest preserve.

Reno worked for a corporation (Trechette) that specializes in payday loans to the working poor. Something made Reno want desperately to learn the name of the corporate CEO, but that information is so closely guarded, neither Vic nor her reporter nemesis (Murray) can find it anywhere. Reno’s lawyer uncle (Richard), who is also Vic’s ex-husband, is representing Trechette, seems uninterested in Reno’s disappearance, and won’t talk to Vic about Reno or Trechette.

Felix is an engineering student at IIT. He’s involved with an Arabian girl (Rasima) who’s also an engineering student. His address was found in the dead man’s pocket, although he never met the man. Because of Rasima, federal authorities conclude that Felix is a terrorist. To make matters worse, some powerful person seems to be pressuring local authorities to convict Felix of the man’s murder despite no evidence.

Vic’s investigation is further complicated by a pair of gigantic Russian thugs who attack Reno’s twin (Harmony), and later come after Vic herself. Adding to the confusion, there is an ancient Sumerian artifact, a fish-man (Dagon) figure, that is mysteriously delivered to Chicago’s Oriental Institute and then almost immediately stolen. Felix and Rashima may have some connection with the artifact. The demands of the two investigations, plus working for her regular clients, leaves Vic so exhausted that she starts making uncharacteristically stupid mistakes.

If you’re already a Warshawski fan, you’ll want to read the book, because it has great repartee between Vic and her ex-husband, and it introduces a new love interest for Vic. If you’re new to the series, you should start with a different one (e.g., the first one, [[ASIN:0440210690 Indemnity Only]]), even though this novel works okay as a standalone.

title: Impressive Contemporary History of Dark Times in Colombia
text:
THERE ARE NO DEAD HERE: A STORY OF MURDER AND DENIAL IN COLOMBIA is a readable, but highly detailed account of interconnections between murderous Colombian paramilitary units and the Colombian government and military forces in the period from 1996 to 2010. It’s an impressive contemporary history of an extremely dark time for those living in the South American nation.

However, the book isn’t really something that a history buff or a true crime aficionado (like myself) will enjoy. It’s mostly about Colombian politics and law, and thus it’s a book for political science students and other individuals who have a special interest in the history and government of Colombia.

title: Novelized Account of Two Ships Lost During Hurricane Joaquin
text:
INTO THE STORM: TWO SHIPS, A DEADLY HURRICANE, AND AN EPIC BATTLE FOR SURVIVAL reads like a novel, even though it’s intended as a nonfiction account of the loss of two ships (El Faro and Minouche) during Hurricane Joaquin in September 2015. The U.S. Coast Guard rescued the 12 men on Minouche (by helicopter); the 33 men aboard El Faro perished.

The story has a lot of detail, and moves very slowly. For example, the description of El Faro’s sailing into bad weather doesn’t begin until Chapter 7 (of 17 chapters); the description of Minouche’s encountering difficulties doesn’t begin until the middle of Chapter 8.

To make the account readable, the author uses the “fly on the wall” technique, and recounts the happenings on the two doomed ships by means of invented conversations. (The shipwreck stories are mostly told through quoted dialogue involving crew members. However, the statements attributed to the captains and sailors aren’t really exact quotations, but are the author’s reconstruction of what the people probably said to each other.)

The author informs us that the crew member quotes from Chapter 7 came from the El Faro’s voyage data recorder, NHC’s archives, and the Coast Guard’s MBI report. Information about crew conversations aboard the Minouche are apparently based on interviews with survivors.

In my opinion, what is known about the tragic loss of the two ships is insufficient to warrant a full-length nonfiction book. It seems that the author has worked hard at stretching out the narrative to fill the pages, with the result that the story as a whole is boring. Also, as a novelized nonfiction work, the book doesn’t really qualify as a solid history of the events.

title: Ruth Galloway Sorts Love Life While on Holiday in Italy
text:
The “Ruth Galloway” series falls in between the “police procedural” and “cozy” mystery genres, if the two “Galloway” novels that I’ve read (books 9 and 10) are typical. They feature an overweight, frumpy, but highly intelligent archaeologist (Ruth), and a stalled-in-his-police-career detective (DCI Nelson); the plots are as much about personal relationships as they are about solving crimes. I like the unpretentious, solitary Ruth character very much.

In THE DARK ANGEL (RUTH GALLOWAY MYSTERIES BOOK 10), Ruth is a happy single mother who’s still in love with daughter Kate’s married father Nelson. Nelson is unhappy, torn between his two families--pregnant wife Michelle and adult daughters Laura and Rebecca, and his true love Ruth and small daughter Kate. Things are complicated, because Michelle’s baby may not be Nelson’s, and the baby’s father may be a black man.

When Ruth is asked by a former lover (Angelo) to consult on skeletal bones from a Roman dig site in Italy, she leaps at the chance to have a working holiday abroad. She and close friend Shona travel with their small children to (fictional) Castello degli Angeli in the Liri Valley, and land in the middle of the town’s buried secrets.

The Roman bones that brought Ruth to Italy are insignificant, but after the beloved parish priest is murdered and an earthquake unearths some much more recent bones, the four English tourists find that their lives are in danger. They welcome the arrival of Nelson, along with Ruth’s nutty friend Cathbad, to help figure things out.

The 10th series book is primarily a vehicle for Ruth to sort out her love life, though her situation is still unresolved at book’s end. (There’s even a cliffhanger involving somebody from Ruth’s past named Frank.) The plot is rather boring--not much to be investigated--and the ending is contrived and unsatisfying. Like Nelson’s daughter Laura, I ended up liking Nelson’s German shepherd Bruno best of all the characters involved in the final scenes.

Unfortunately, the murderer is easily guessed, too. If you already know and like Ruth Galloway, you’ll want to read this book; otherwise, you should probably choose a different novel from this generally interesting series.

title: Primarily Valuable for Politically-Charged Images
text:
THE FEMINIST REVOLUTION: THE STRUGGLE FOR WOMEN’S LIBERATION is a contemporary history of feminism, commencing with the year 1966, the year that the National Organization for Women (NOW) was founded. To the extent that it’s a serious history, it merely describes what feminists and anti-feminists were doing and saying in the years from 1966 through the 1980s. The text portions are based for the most part on newspaper, magazine, and journal articles.

To my mind, this volume is a picture book, primarily valuable for the scanned, politically-charged images of protesters, advertisements for feminist events, political cartoons, newspaper stories, magazine covers, and the like. Indeed, the images overpower the accompanying text, which is set in small type and often displayed on colored backgrounds (as if no one is really expected to actually read it). The oversized, square book format also detracts from the readability of the text.

The subtitles of the chapters are generally a better guide to the topics than the actual, politicized titles (e.g., ch. 1 “‘Sisterhood is powerful’”, subtitled “How the movement mobilized”). The subtitles are as follows: (1) How the movement mobilized; (2) The struggle for liberation; (3) Civil rights and liberation; (4) Reclaiming the physical and mental treatment of women; (5) Sexuality and lesbian feminism; (6) Reinventing culture in and out of the workplace; (7) Publishing and the media; (8) Music and the arts; (9) The anti-war and anti-nuclear debate; and (10) Radicalization, fragmentation, and educating the next generation.

The history is very fragmented--for example, Ms. Magazine, which caused many 1970s women to wake up and become feminists (remember the “clicks”?) doesn’t appear until ch. 7 (page 154 out of 220-plus pages). Also, the choice of mostly politically-charged images makes the whole book seem biased and “shrill”, even though the text itself is written with a balanced, neutral tone.

title: Book About Data Analytics Has Misleading Title
text:
The title of this book is highly misleading. THE HIGH ROLLER EXPERIENCE: HOW CAESARS AND OTHER WORLD-CLASS COMPANIES ARE USING DATA TO CREATE AN UNFORGETTABLE CUSTOMER EXPERIENCE contains almost nothing about the special perks (high-roller experience) provided to VIP customers at “world-class” companies.

Instead, the book is all about data analytics, and how big companies can use data to design the most effective customer loyalty rewards programs. The main message is that rewards programs should be tied to the profitability of types of customer behavior, rather than to the dollar-amounts spent by individual customers. For example, slot machines are more or less profitable (by the casino’s share, or “hold”), depending on the customers’ machine choices. Thus the casino’s loyalty program should be designed to reward the customers who use the profitable types of machines, rather than to reward the customers who spend the most dollars.

The book appears to be sound in its analytics, and will no doubt be of considerable interest to business people with customer rewards programs, and to data analysts in general. However, it’s of no interest at all to casual readers who would like to know more about the perks actually extended to Las Vegas’ regular high rollers.

title: Mildly Interesting Collection of Stories About Female Detectives in Civil War Times
text:
THE PINKS: THE FIRST WOMEN DETECTIVES, OPERATIVES, AND SPIES WITH THE PINKERTON NATIONAL DETECTIVE AGENCY is a mildly interesting collection of stories recounting the exploits of the first female detectives employed by the world-famous Pinkerton Detective Agency. As biography or history, the book is limited in scope, because many of Pinkerton’s early case files were destroyed in a fire in the early 1930s.

Thus the women’s stories are episodic--compiled from newspaper articles and various agents’ memoirs as supplements to surviving case files. The stories involve the female detectives’ activities in the 1860s, and mostly their activities are related to the Civil War.

There are three things that I dislike about this book. First, it’s written in very simple language, as if intended for a young adult audience. Second, it reads like an extended advertisement for the Pinkerton Detective Agency. Over and over again it heaps praise on Allan Pinkerton for his progressive hiring policies and good judgment in selecting operatives and choosing their assignments. Third, the women’s stories aren’t particularly inspiring, perhaps because Pinkertons generally kept themselves in the background.

The “Pinks” featured are as follows: Kate Warne, Mrs. R.C. Potter, Hattie Lewis, Mrs. M. Barkley, Vinnie Ream, Elizabeth Baker, Mary Touvestre, Elizabeth Van Lew, Dr. Mary Edwards Walker, and Miss Seaton. These women didn’t operate wholly on their own, of course, but had a lot of support from male Pinkerton detectives.

title: Lots of Flashbacks; Teaser in Prologue Poorly Resolved
text:
COLORADO BOULEVARD: A CRUSH MYSTERY is the third “Crush” novel, and it works fine as a standalone, except … as a reader, I just couldn’t accept the Crush (Caleb Rush) character as real. Crush is a he-man, physically huge and powerful, able to charge in and take control of any situation, and just a little too much of everything.

A large part of the novel’s story--which is moderately interesting and entertaining--is told in flashbacks. The prologue about Caleb’s being enlisted to drive a float in the Rose Parade after the float’s driver is inexplicably shot in the head is part of the flashback plot; the main plot is about Caleb’s stepbrother K.C. Zerbe’s being kidnapped and Crush’s recovering him.

The part I was most interested in--the prologue’s Rose Parade float mystery--turns out to be incidental to the main story, and isn’t resolved until nearly 100 pages have gone by. (The resolution is a letdown.) I generally dislike plots that rely heavily on flashbacks, and I really hate teasers that are designed to keep the reader reading while some not-very-interesting groundwork is laid down for the main story.

Probably you need to have read the previous novels, and developed a liking for the Crush character, to appreciate this one.

title: “Historical” Mystery Lacks 1894 Atmosphere, Details of Everyday Life
text:
LAST STOP IN BROOKLYN: A MARY HANDLEY MYSTERY is set in 1894, but lacks the atmosphere of the time, and the details of everyday life back then. Except for Mary’s traveling about in a rented horse and buggy, and the historical name-dropping (Teddy Roosevelt, Jacob Riis, Russell Sage, Oriental Hotel, etc.), the story could be set in the present day.

In the novel, Mary investigates a series of brutal, Jack-the-Ripper-style murders of prostitutes around Coney Island. She stumbles onto a conspiracy among New York City police and the city’s wealthy elite--a conspiracy that has covered up the murders in order to protect a man belonging to the elite class. Mary has her work cut out for her, to put everything right, because the prostitutes are nonentities whose deaths don’t matter to the people in power.

The plot incorporates a real historical incident, a bombing at Russell Sage’s office that killed the bomber (Henry Norcross), Sage’s stenographer (Benjamin Norton), and seriously injured a visiting bank clerk (William Laidlaw), while leaving Sage (the actual target) unharmed. To me, this was the most interesting part of the book, but the incident isn’t woven into Mary’s story--it’s just recounted and included as an appendage.

I don’t think that recounting an actual incident from 1894 is enough to transform this novel into an “historical” mystery. In addition, the story (Mary’s investigation) just plods along, and the writing is mechanical and dull. This was my first “Mary Handley” mystery, and I liked the character reasonably well, but not well enough to want to read any more of the series.

title: Easy-to-Guess Perpetrator, Unbelievable Plot
text:
In DARK TIDE RISING: A WILLIAM MONK NOVEL, Commander Monk returns to miserable Jacob’s Island, and it isn’t kind to him. I don’t like author Perry’s “Monk” series nearly as well as her “Pitts” series, and this “Monk” novel was extremely disappointing. I guessed the identity of the perpetrator within the first quarter of the book, and the plot winds up with a highly contrived, Perry-Mason-like courtroom scene.

In the novel, Monk is summoned by his friend, Sir Oliver Rathbone, to organize a ransom-payment and kidnap-victim-recovery operation at Jacob’s Island on behalf of Rathbone’s client, Harry Exeter. Exeter’s adored wife Kate has been snatched, and Exeter is willing to pay everything he has to get her back. When the Jacob’s Island recovery turns into a disaster, Monk has a new problem to solve--which one of his most trusted men was the one who betrayed his well-laid plans to the kidnappers?

The novel is well written, and nicely develops the character and backstory of Monk’s right-hand man, John Hooper. However, the plot isn’t believable--the perpetrator’s scheme was far too risky at the outset, because it depended completely on what certain other people might do and think after the initial kidnapping happened.

The novel works fine as a standalone, if you’re new to the “Monk” series. Author Perry really knows how to incorporate all the necessary details from earlier novels into later ones without giving away any prior plot endings or boring the reader with long passages of backstory.

title: Good Job of Presenting Arguments For and Against National Educational Standards
text:
This readable book, COMMON CORE: NATIONAL EDUCATION STANDARDS AND THE THREAT TO DEMOCRACY, does a good job of presenting the arguments for and against the project aimed at achieving standardized education in U.S. The big problem is that standardized “common core” education seems to go hand in hand with standardized tests. Thus, what gets taught is what is on the tests--students are only taught the things they need to know to pass or score high on the tests.

Recognizing the sincerity of author Nicholas Tampio’s arguments against the imposition of common core standards, I fear that that boat has already sailed. I think that this book is mainly preaching to the choir.

title: Activity Book for Very Young Readers
text:
JUNIOR MAKER is an “ activity book” for very young children. The target age isn’t given, but the book seems to be intended for young readers (2d or 3d grade?). There are some projects that might be fun (e.g, making a Roman mosaic from colored paper squares, or building a pipe cleaner frame for blowing square bubbles, or making a hanging bird feeder from gelatin and birdseed).

However, the projects are tied to very general topics (space, nature, history, animals, science), and seem too random to be teaching much of anything. Mainly the book seems to be a “keep the child busy” book, perhaps intended for use over summer vacation?

title: Reacher Searches for His Roots
text:
PAST TENSE: A JACK REACHER NOVEL solves a mystery surrounding Jack’s parentage--who, exactly, was Jack’s father, a guy who could never remember his birthday? Reacher fans will want to read this novel to find out. But otherwise, except for the dramatic ending scenes, the novel is just plain boring.

In the novel, Jack starts to hitchhike from the East Coast to San Diego, but takes a side trip to Laconia. NH, his father’s birthplace. He visits various public records offices, and gets a lot of help from the locals when dad Stan Reacher doesn't show up right away in the town’s 80-year-old census records.

At the same time, a young Canadian couple has car trouble, and ends up at a remote motel near Laconia. They can’t leave, because the weird motel owners keep making excuses for not calling a mechanic or driving them to town to get a tow truck. Eventually the couple finds themselves imprisoned, because the motel owners have secret plans for them.

SPOILER ALERT: Naturally the two plotlines--Jack’s search for his roots, and the couple’s predicament--merge, but only in a superficial way. The couple’s plotline is basically “Psycho" meets “The Most Dangerous Game", and it isn’t even close to the quality of either one. The motel owners’ intentions are easily guessed, long before the reveal.

This novel is the latest in the long, popular Jack Reacher series, and it works fine as a standalone. It’s well-written, but, as previously mentioned, darned boring.

title: Scholarly Monograph About “Bioinformation”
text:
BIOINFORMATION (RESOURCES SERIES) is a scholarly monograph about “bioinformation”--what it is, where it comes from, who owns it, and who consumes it. The monograph also discusses the Big Data revolution, and some of the concerns that arise from “the datafication of everything”. For example, Big Data analytics may be used in diagnosing illnesses, recommending treatments, or identifying criminals, but may also result in “algorithmic branding” of certain individuals, to their detriment (as in charging them more for medical insurance).

The work is readable, but scholarly in tone. Its purpose, according to the authors, is as follows: “(O)ur intention here is to elucidate … how bioinformation is abstracted (its messy corporeal existence) and rendered as notated sequences, photographic images, x-rays, slides, or written or digitalized clinical, criminal or credit records--in short, as highly accessible, readable and manipulable distillations of bioinformation (data and aggregated big datasets) that now have tremendous commercial and economic value.”

This book isn’t intended for the casual reader who is interested primarily in the ethical and privacy concerns surrounding the unauthorized use of biological samples and data. I’m not sure who the intended audience is, but am guessing it’s primarily of interest to people involved with the actual buying and selling of bioinformation.

title: Q&A Format Detracts From Use as Legal Reference
text:
THE LEGAL GUIDE FOR WRITERS, ARTISTS AND OTHER CREATIVE PEOPLE: PROTECT YOUR WORK AND UNDERSTAND THE LAW provides a pretty good “plain English” summary of current intellectual property law. However, the area of law is not only technical, but it’s largely determined by individual case rulings (which are based on specific legal factors and facts). Thus the book is hard to understand unless you have some legal training (e.g., paralegal, law student, lawyer); and the book won’t give you answers to your specific questions about your own intellectual property rights, unless your questions have already been ruled on by the courts.

The subject matter is presented in Q&A format, which makes the book difficult to use as a legal “nutshell” reference. (For instance, the four “fair use” factors of copyright law are listed under the question, “Did Congress Provide Any Guidance?”.)

The summarized areas of law (see chapters 2-6) are as follows: (1) Copyright and other legal rights; (2) Libel, Privacy, Obscenity, and other possible legal risks; (3) creator’s rights in Cyberspace; (4) Contracts involving creative people; and (5) Business and Tax matters affecting creative people.

title: Well-Thought-Out Technical Knitting Book, But Silly
text:
ARM KNITTING: 30 NO-NEEDLE PROJECTS FOR YOU AND YOUR HOME is a perfectly decent technical knitting book, but it’s just plain silly. Why would you want to knit with big loops of thick yarn on your arms rather than on big knitting needles? And what do you do if nature calls while you’re still all wrapped up—quite literally—in your knitting? (The book is silent about removing loops to stitch holders.)

The looping techniques (cast on, knit, purl, bind off) for arm knitting are the same as for ordinary two-needle knitting. The techniques are clearly explained, and illustrated with step-by-step photos. There are 30 well-thought-out projects, ranging from scarves (of course) to hats (ditto) to pillow covers (natch) to throws (yes) to rugs (practical). There’s even a sweater and a vest.

Try this niche knitting technique for fun, but don’t take it very seriously. It’s NOT easier than knitting with needles—it’s just different and a lot less efficient.

title: Lincoln Defends Unpopular Accused Killer in Springfield in 1838
text:
FINAL RESTING PLACE: A LINCOLN AND SPEED MYSTERY is the third novel in this series, which is loosely based on the actual close friendship that existed between Abraham Lincoln and Kentucky native Joshua Speed. The story is set in 1838 in Springfield, Illinois, at a time when Lincoln had an active law practice, was running for the Illinois state legislature, and was engaging in debates with Stephen A. Douglas (the “Little Giant”) on behalf of the Whigs.

The plot takes elements lifted from real people, real events, and a real trial, and mixes them up to create a wholly fictional, new murder mystery that has Lincoln (1) endangered by a mysterious enemy, (2) defending an unpopular accused killer at trial, (3) debating Douglas and his Democrats, (4) courting local belle Margaret Owens, and (5) serving as a second in a duel. The genuine history is fully explained in the author’s concluding “Historical Note”, although this note is rather light on the true history of Lincoln’s love interests.

Generally I’m not crazy about historical mysteries that take as many liberties as this one does with the real events, but my main quarrel with the novel is that it’s slow-moving and mostly boring. The conclusion is especially disappointing—too many plot threads are tied up in too few pages, and Lincoln’s last-minute rescue at the very end is NOT believable. (No spoiler here—of course Lincoln survives the events of this book, because he wasn’t assassinated until 1865.)

I enjoyed the previous series novel, [[ASIN:B01H082E5I These Honored Dead]], but after this one, I’m no longer interested in the series. Still, I am greatly indebted to this novel for the quite curious historical fact that the highly respected Douglas had a habit of sitting on other men’s laps while arguing courtroom cases!

title: Archeological Alien Horror Fantasy—Total Bloodbath of a Novel
text:
FORSAKEN (A UNIT 51 NOVEL) is the second “Unit 51” alien archaeological horror thriller (for the first, see [[ASIN:0786041587 Subhuman]]), and it works reasonably well as a standalone. However, the series ought to be be read in order, because FORSAKEN is a direct continuation of the first novel (in which Unit 51 scientists in the Antarctic discover a flooded pyramid beneath an icecap, unwittingly “activate” the pyramid, and by so doing spawn a horrific creature that seems bent on killing every human researcher it can find).

In FORSAKEN, a few of the Unit 51 survivors (along with a lot of newly recruited researchers) have returned to the Antarctic, drained the pyramid ruins, and resumed their study of the ancient civilization that built the pyramid and decorated its walls with picture writings. Central to their research is the now-caged creature, which survives on a diet of live pigs, and spends its days in total darkness, writing something mysterious on the walls of its super-protected underground prison. The Antarctic research site is atop a tangle of unmapped underground tunnels.

Other surviving Unit 51 researchers have scattered to Nigeria, Stonehenge, and Teotihuacan, where they are studying jungle ruins, crop circles, and the brutal murals inside a pyramid that contains a labyrinth of unmapped, flooded, booby-trapped tunnels. A series of simultaneous events in Antarctica and at the other sites causes the remaining survivors (except for those in Mexico) to return to the Unit 51 site In Antarctica, where events even more horrible than before await them.

FORSAKEN is a total bloodbath of a novel, where the thin “exploration” plot is driven by one bloody encounter after another between unwitting researchers (or their highly trained but ineffective military protectors) and bloodthirsty, semi-human creatures (or the creatures’ human worshippers). With each encounter, it’s mostly a matter of which character gets killed next, as nearly everyone gets killed eventually.

The book isn’t an easy read, because the bloody happenings are occurring simultaneously at two very different pyramid sites, and happening to two different teams of people—and the events are related from the individual viewpoints of different team individuals (e.g., Anya, Kelly, Barnett, Roche).

Thus the story is told in chapters that rotate among individual sites and the viewpoints of individual researchers at each site. Toward the end, I gave up and read all the chapters about the Evans team in order, then went back and read all the chapters about the Roche team in order, to make it easier to follow the events at the different sites.

The novel has a horrid fascination, and is exciting—though the writing is less than stellar. You’ll enjoy it if you have a taste for bloody archaeological alien horror fantasy. For me, one Unit 51 novel was interesting, but I’ll stop with one.

title: Unlikeable “Girl Reporter” Investigates Jockey’s Murder in 1962 Saratoga Springs Area
text:
A STONE’S THROW: AN ELLIE STONE MYSTERY is a competently written mystery/thriller—your basic PI procedural. The PI is “girl reporter” Ellie Stone, a surprisingly thin-skinned Jewish lass (she’s outraged by fairly mild anti-Semitic jokes, and disapproving of any and all bad language). Her thin skin is surprising, because she drinks like a fish (there’s always a bottle of Dewars handy), and she considers herself “a modern girl” (she’ll sleep with a strange guy she met only hours before).

In the novel, newspaper reporter Ellie is drawn into the world of horse racing, as it supposedly existed around Saratoga Springs circa 1962. When covering a fire at an abandoned horse barn, she stumbles upon two burnt bodies. A fragment of unburnt racing silks on the jockey-sized male, and bits of red hair and fur on the normal-sized female, are just enough to launch Ellie’s quest to identify them. Autopsies reveal that the pair were murdered. Ellie uses her contacts with local police, gangsters, racehorse owners, track habitues, and addicted bettors to stay one step ahead of everyone else in getting the facts and publishing her stories ahead of the competition.

The writing is fine, but the plot is just barely interesting enough to keep the reader reading. Ellie herself isn’t particularly likeable (the drinking doesn’t help). Her behavior is often reckless (for example, she goes alone into the basement of a remote, derelict cottage), yet she’s constantly fearful that a stranger may break into her home. Ellie does find a racehorse (the handsome Purgatorio) that takes a shine to her; but this isn’t very believable, given that Ellie knows next to nothing about horses or thoroughbred racing.

Perhaps the other novels in the Ellie Stone series are better, but this one’s a snooze. It works fine as a standalone.

title: Readable Narrative Woven From Archival Records of Contracts, Financial Transactions
text:
THE QUEEN’S EMBROIDERER: A TRUE STORY OF PARIS, LOVERS, SWINDLERS, AND THE FIRST STOCK MARKET is a remarkable accomplishment: a readable narrative woven from myriad archival records of financial transactions and contracts executed in France between 1604 and 1790. It’s a chronicle of the rise and fall of two money-grasping families (the Chevrots and the Magoulets) during the reign of Louis XIV.

Unfortunately, all the detail regarding apartment rentals, “legitimizing” of children born out of wedlock, bad debt complaints, corrupt tax collectors, legal actions, etc. finally overwhelmed me about one-third of the way through the book. Neither family captured my interest sufficiently to warrant plowing through the full 323 pages.

Serious historians will no doubt find this to be a valuable work. I suspect that it provides new perspectives on the historical period, as it teases a human story out of existing archival records. However, I can’t really recommend it for pleasure reading by casual historians like myself.

title: Modern Retelling of Shakespeare’s “Macbeth”
text:
When I ordered MACBETH (HOGARTH SHAKESPEARE)—which is described in the marketing material as “a heart-pounding new thriller”—I thought (silly me!) that “Hogarth Shakespeare” was the name of a character in a mystery/thriller series. Instead, Hogarth Shakespeare is a publishing project, launched in October 2015, that “sees Shakespeare’s works retold by acclaimed and bestselling novelists of today”.

Thus, this novel by Jo Nesbo consists of a modern retelling of Shakespeare’s “Macbeth”. The story is set in the 1970s in a nameless Nordic town where police and drug traffickers are locked in a life-and-death struggle for control of the unemployed, addicted populace. Nesbo does a terrific job of novel-writing. However, the reader needs to be familiar with Shakespeare’s play to make sense of the novel, and if the reader IS familiar with the play, then much of the suspense is lost. (One knows already what happens to Duncan, Banquo, Duff, Lady, etc., so the only reason to read the novel is to see how Nesbo handles the plot threads and specific details of their fates.)

Novels that use classic authors’ characters and/or plots just aren’t my cup of tea. I prefer mass market thrillers with little or no literary merit that are written solely to entertain. This novel is a literary exercise, and it’s well done, but it’s NOT the thriller that I was expecting.

title: Boring Mystery About Crime Reporter’s Investigation of Mother’s Murder
text:
THE ECHO KILLING: A MYSTERY is a competently, professionally written private investigator mystery, but it’s just plain boring. Also, the basic premise, that two murders committed 15 years apart must be linked because the crime scenes are almost identical, is weak and unconvincing from the get go.

In the novel, a journalist (Harper) investigates a career woman’s murder. The woman’s nude body was discovered on her kitchen floor by her 12-year-old daughter who had arrived home from school. Harper can relate to the girl, because the exact same thing happened to her when she was 12 (she discovered her mother’s nude body on the kitchen floor after school). The crime scenes are eerily similar—from the body’s unposed position on the floor to the fact that all of the evidence (clothing, fingerprints, blood, residue under fingernails) was removed.

Harper, hoping to finally identify her mother’s killer, is driven to investigate, and uses her special police reporter privileges to access evidence boxes, old and new police reports, etc. The investigation is a slog, as Harper manages to slowly recover various significant photos and documents. The only relief is provided by Harper’s illicit, white-hot relationship with an undercover police detective (Luke), who saves her life from time to time.

POSSIBLE SPOILER ALERT: The perp is guessable, though the perp’s motivation isn’t particularly believable—it’s wildly inconsistent with the perp’s character. There are a lot of reasonably well-drawn characters in the novel, but none of them stand out as memorable—not even Harper.

title: Disappointing Gourmet Chocolate Series Is Continuation of “Home Repair Is Homicide” Series
text:
DEATH BY CHOCOLATE CHERRY CHEESECAKE (A DEATH BY CHOCOLATE MYSTERY) isn’t really the first novel in a new series. Instead, it’s a continuation of the author’s “Home Repair Is Homicide” series—same Eastport, Maine setting, same characters. The difference is that Jacobia and Ellie have opened a chocolate-specialties bakery, named, so unoriginally, “The Chocolate Moose”.

I loved the “Home Repair” series, and read all 16 books (starting with [[ASIN:B002RLBKSG The Dead Cat Bounce]]). It was refreshing to have a cozy mystery heroine who could teach the reader how to handle tools. It’s too bad that the series theme has now shifted to the execution of fancy chocolate recipes. The cozy mystery world doesn’t need another gourmet detective—and this novel is generally disappointing. It’s wordy, and the oft-repeated details of baking-cheesecakes-on-a-deadline are tiresome. I now know how to bake a chocolate cherry cheesecake, and I wish I didn’t.

In the novel, Jacobia finds a man’s body in the bakery’s kitchen, with the head submerged in a bowl of melted chocolate. Her friend Ellie is the prime suspect, because she hated the victim. He was trying to close down “The Moose” for health violations.

But it’s the Fourth of July weekend and Police Chief Olson is too busy to investigate the murder right away, and “The Moose” must deliver dozens of freshly-baked chocolate cherry cheesecakes to an auction to raise money for the annual Eastport fireworks display. Thus, even though Ellie and Jacobia’s usual snooping around to find a killer is particularly urgent because of Ellie’s imminent arrest, their investigation has to be worked in around all the baking. They also have to snoop around in terrible weather (a hurricane is headed directly at Eastport).

As usual, the plot is intricate, and Jacobia and Ellie take foolhardy risks while investigating. They are threatened with knives and guns, nearly swamped by a boat, nearly run off the road by a pursuer, kidnapped, and almost drowned. The ending sort of wraps everything up, but isn’t particularly satisfying.

I think that the characters deserved something better than this “new series” about their new jobs as bakers. Because I like them a lot from the “Homicide” series, I’ll probably look at the next “Death by Chocolate” book. However, I probably wouldn’t bother if I weren’t already familiar with the characters and setting from the previous series.

title: Peculiar Crimes Unit Investigates Series of Murders in London’s Parks
text:
The “Peculiar Crimes Unit” mysteries work as standalones, but they’re kind of an acquired taste, because of the unusual methods of the octogenarian detectives (Bryant and May). While the Unit itself is kind of peculiar (staff and office always in disarray), the Unit is actually named for its mission—to investigate crimes “peculiar to London”. Thus WILD CHAMBER is about a series of murders committed in London’s parks, squares, and gardens—aka “the lungs of London” or “London’s wild chambers”.

In the novel, an elegantly dressed woman (Helen Forester) is murdered in a private garden that requires a key for admittance. Her body is discovered by a gardener, who snapped a photo of her, just moments before the killing. The photo may show her killer, caught on camera by accident, but the image is indistinct. The murder is a real “whodunit”, and more murders follow, but Bryant visits London’ parks until he is able to identify the killer. As usual, the story contains a lot of humor, mostly at the expense of the clueless PCU head (Raymond Land).

This novel includes a lot of description of London’s squares, parks, and gardens (history and monuments). Not being at all familiar with London (and not planning to visit London soon), I found this tedious. This book was slow going, even for a PCU novel, but the mystery itself was interesting enough to keep me reading to the solution at the very end.

I did love a passage about mystery writing, spoken near the novel's end by a popular writer being interviewed by Bryant: “The traditional rules of fair play demand that the criminal must be someone we’ve met. There can be no supernatural elements, no secret passages, no imaginary poisons, ..., no twins, no mystical intuitive powers, …. To them I would add several further moratoria: no more alcoholic policemen with dead wives, no autistic idiot-savant crime-scene specialists, no oppressed female detectives derided by sexist colleagues, no overweight computer nerds in dimly lit rooms, no erudite killers arranging corpses in tableaux reminiscent of medieval paintings, no renegade detectives sharing a psychic bond with the killer, no cryptic messages hidden in museums by victims, no opera-loving loners who solve mysteries because without them their lives would have no meaning, and absolutely no more reinventions of Sherlock bloody Holmes.”

Wouldn’t it be wonderful if today’s mystery novelists would abide by those rules?

title: Great Concept, Poorly Executed
text:
RETROGRADE has a great concept, but it’s poorly executed. The concept: The international (U.S., China, Russia, Eurasia) colony on Mars is prepared for absolutely everything that can go wrong on Mars, but is totally unprepared for anything to go wrong on Earth. So when nuclear war breaks out, with no one knowing who fired the first missile, the colonists are left in an impossible situation. They must cooperate to survive—their resupply ship has just sailed right on past Mars (failure of automated braking rockets)—but they don’t trust one another.

This is a wonderful plot idea, but the story gets bogged down by far too much detailed description of the layout, construction, and environment of the colony itself. Plus the characters talk, talk, talk about what alternative actions are available, and why each alternative won’t work (e.g., the Russians won’t go for it), but are very slow to start doing anything. When the characters aren’t discussing matters, and worrying about the fate of loved ones back on Earth, the lead character (Liz) is thinking about everything around her, and describing whatever is before her eyes in minute detail (e.g., the wheat growing in the common area shared by all the colonists).

To my mind, there simply isn’t enough action to drive the plot. I can believe that the detailed description of what a Mars colony will be like is technically and scientifically accurate (or as much as it can be in 2017), but it’s just too much information piled into a thin story. Also, I think the novel would be far better with a male lead, because Liz doesn’t ring true to me as a female researcher/adventurer.

In the novel, when it becomes clear what started Earth’s nuclear war, the plot becomes more interesting. However, the whole story has a hurried finish that needs an Epilogue to tie up the many loose ends, and in one important aspect the story has been done before.

title: Readable “As-Told-To” Confessional About Doping in Professional Cycling
text:
DESCENT: MY EPIC FALL FROM CYCLING SUPERSTARDOM TO DOPING DEAD END is an “as told to” confessional--unlike many of these, it's not overly self-serving, and it's a decent, fast read. Former superstar cyclist Thomas Dekker takes responsibility for his illicit use of Dynepo and blood-doping, and doesn't whine “why me?” over getting caught.

Even though everyone (including Dekker and author Thijs Zonneveld) agrees that Dekker was an arrogant, self-centered guy with delusions of cycling grandeur, the reader can't help feeling sorry that such a promising young cycling talent was lost to the sport. When Dekker became a professional, nearly all of the top cyclists (Armstrong, Ullrich, etc.) were doping, and their teams simply looked the other way. Dekker’s team doctors at Rabobank picked up early on his doping, and merely offered to monitor him closely so he wouldn't get caught and reflect badly on the team.

Why did Dekker cheat? Because he wanted more--more wins, more money--and because the doping made him feel on top of the world during events. Did he know the doping was wrong? Absolutely.

In the end, this book doesn't plow any new ground re the doping problems in professional cycling, even though it names some names. It's mildly interesting for the details of Dekker’s travels to store and receive blood. There's nothing in it regarding the physical dangers of EPO and cortisone shots, so it's hardly a cautionary tale for aspiring pro cyclists.

Much of the book describes Dekker’s repeated self-destructive behavior, which includes skipping secondary school final exams, engaging in dissolute high-living (drinking, brothel visits, etc.), and letting family and cycling teammates down.

title: Literary Novel by Author of Wallander Mysteries
text:
AFTER THE FIRE is Henning Mankell’s last novel (he passed away on 10/05/2015). It's a well-written literary effort, written in the first person, featuring a 70-year-old retired surgeon whose settled life is turned upside down by a fire. It's an arson fire that he barely escapes from alive; it totally destroys the home that originally belonged to his grandparents, and he loses everything inside.

As you would expect from a novel written by the author of the [[ASIN:1400031575 Kurt Wallander series]], the surgeon is a man given to personal and philosophical contemplation, and the story includes a mystery. The mystery of the arsonist’s identity is a thread that runs through the plot, although it doesn't really drive the plot.

A continuation of [[ASIN:0307472248 Italian Shoes]], this is an interesting novel, but hardly a remarkable one. The language is rather lifeless--whether this is the fault of the author or the translator, I do not know. For me, the novel was slow-moving, and I never really engaged with the surgeon as a character. I enjoyed the Wallander novels much more.

title: Art Expert Seeks Priceless Titian, Engages in Thuggy Budapest Intrigue
text:
The fictional heroine (Helena) of the THE APPRAISAL is an art expert, a master of disguises, a burglar, and a dangerous martial-arts-trained killer. But what else would you expect from the daughter of a skillful painter of fake “Old Masters” and easy-to-fake Corots?

In the novel, Helena is hired to buy a priceless Titian painting (a fictional depiction of Christ’s Entry Into Jerusalem) that was bartered for food during WWII by a starving refugee, now her wealthy American employer. Once Helena arrives in Budapest, she finds she is being watched by local police, and that there are competing bidders (including some Ukrainians) who will stop at nothing to obtain the painting.

Even if Helena succeeds in buying the painting, she must figure out how to ship it to America, because Hungary--like so many European nations--won’t allow “Old Masters” paintings to be removed from the country. Will Helena, who is the foremost expert in Titian’s oeuvre, be able to use her impeccable credentials to engineer the painting’s exit?

The novel is suspenseful, but fine art plays a very minor role in it. The plot is mostly about thuggy intrigue in Budapest. As a character, Helena isn't very believable--she's a highly credentialled art expert, yet she takes on the very dangerous task of extricating an Old Master for a fee from a dodgy private purchaser. I prefer the much lighter art-forger’s-daughter series by Charlotte Elkins (starting with [[ASIN:1612182739 Dangerous Talent]]).

title: Well-Written Novel About CIA Analyst and Russian “Sleeper” Spy
text:
The well-done FX television series, “The Americans”, does a terrific job of humanizing a murderous Russian “sleeper” spy couple, so it's hardly surprising that novels about Russian sleeper-cell spies have begun to arrive. NEED TO KNOW: A NOVEL is so well written, it is probably among the best of these.

However, the plot is fantastical: a CIA counterintelligence analyst (Viv) develops software for tracking Russian sleeper-cell networks, and her first success turns up a photograph of her husband (Matt) in a five-person sleeper cell. Confronted by Viv, Matt freely admits that he’s been working for the Russians for many years. (This all happens in the first 27 pages; in Chapters 1 and 2). The remainder of the book is about Viv’s efforts to preserve her family, while still working for the CIA, and remaining loyal to her country.

The novel is suspenseful, if you care about Viv, Matt, and their beautiful children. However, I couldn't connect with them, and I kept thinking as I was reading that this plot idea had already been adequately explored by the FX TV series.

title: Grisly Murder of Ethnic Hungarian in Victorian England
text:
AN ECHO OF MURDER: A WILLIAM MONK NOVEL is the 23rd entry in the William Monk series. It's slow-moving in the extreme, filled early on with Commander Monk’s ruminations about pure hate as the likely motive for the grisly murder of a bayoneted Hungarian businessman. The presence of 17 candles at the dreadful murder scene, their wicks dipped in the dead man’s blood, also suggests to Monk that a secret society may be behind the murder. More similar murders follow.

I enjoyed the author's previous novel, [[ASIN:0425284980 Murder on the Serpentine: A Charlotte and Thomas Pitt Novel]], but didn't care for Commander Monk at all. His enlightened attitude toward bigotry in Victorian England is admirable, but seems a little far-fetched--did Victorians give any thought at all to being fair to ethnic minorities? Probably this novel was just a poor choice for someone who was new to the series.

title: Hugo Investigates Murders Relating to Spy Camera in Romance Writer’s Paris Hotel Room
text:
THE SORBONNE AFFAIR: A HUGO MARSTON NOVEL is the 7th police procedural novel featuring former FBI profiler Hugo Marston, who is currently the head of security for the U.S. Embassy in Paris. It's extremely slow-moving, despite the added subplot that perhaps explains why Hugo (and his best friend Tom Green) left the FBI. The “Sorbonne” in the title isn't the landmark university building, but a fictional luxury hotel.

In the novel, a best-selling romance writer, an American, seeks Hugo’s help after discovering a spy camera hidden in a painting in her hotel room. The camera is aimed at the desk of the writer (Helen Hancock), so she’s convinced that someone is trying to plagiarize her novel-in-progress. Multiple murders follow, including a hotel staffer and one of Helen’s writing workshop students. Hugo's investigation is severely hampered by the characters’ lies regarding the true nature of their relationships with Helen and one another.

In the subplot, Hugo and Tom are threatened by news of the early release of a bank robber who has vowed to kill them both. The story of the robbery-gone-sideways is told in flashback chapters sprinkled throughout the main narrative.

The writing is good, but the main plot is boring and filled with too many red herrings. Also, there are poorly-integrated references to Sherlock Holmes and Agatha Christie novels that don't really advance Hugo’s investigation. The person behind the murders is guessable, and the ultimate resolution of the subplot is both silly and a letdown. I really liked the previous Hugo Marston novel, [[ASIN:1633881776 The Paris Librarian]], but was disappointed by this one.

title: Decent Literary Suspense Effort by Laurie R. King
text:
LOCKDOWN: A NOVEL OF SUSPENSE is by Laurie R. King, and she's such a good writer, you can't ever go too far wrong with one of her novels. However, the problem with LOCKDOWN is that it isn't particularly suspenseful. It's the story of a disadvantaged middle school’s “Career Day” event that ends in a shootout and a school lockdown.

The story is told through shifting viewpoints: certain students (Chaco, Brendan, Mina, Nick, etc.), the principal (Linda), the principal’s adventurer husband (Gordon), a cop (Olivia), a janitor (Tio), a parent (Thomas), the school itself, and others. The school is struggling, and the mood of students and teachers alike is negatively affected by the recent disappearance of a female student (Bee).

The point of the story is to show the threads of different ethnicities, races, sexes, family backgrounds, and whatever that weave together to create the tapestry that is a school’s identity. The ending is exciting, and the shooter’s identity is a surprise. However, the plot is slow-moving, the characters aren't particularly memorable, and the novel is much more of a literary effort than a suspense novel.

title: Maggie Seeks to Learn Fate of Compromised SOE Spy
text:
THE PARIS SPY: A MAGGIE HOPE MYSTERY finds Maggie in WWII occupied Paris, seeking to learn the fate of a Special Operations Executive (SOE) spy who stopped including security checks in her transmissions to England. The 7th “Maggie Hope” novel, this one continues from where [[ASIN:0804178720 The Queen’s Accomplice]] left off. It starts slowly, and it doesn't work well as a standalone.

This is a thoroughly researched historical novel that is based on all the facts presently available about the sadly compromised SOE project that lost--or intentionally sacrificed--many brave young female spies during WWII. At times it reads almost like nonfiction, and I found it very hard to separate the likely historical truths from the novelist’s fictional speculations about (1) the motives and loyalties of the crucial characters, and (2) what was really going on inside the SOE and the war effort.

For example, the novel includes imaginary “fly-on-the-wall” scenes from Churchill’s top-secret war council meetings, at which the PM personally chooses the invasion site (Normandy) and says that deception to keep the secret is England’s highest priority. The scene establishes the importance of Maggie’s extremely dangerous mission, and rings more or less true, but of course we cannot know what anyone said at those meetings or what England’s priorities were. There are also fly-on-the-wall scenes featuring Hitler at Wolf’s Lair.

Maggie’s foolhardiness in jumping into her situation (as established in the previous novel) undermined my sympathy for her fears and her general plight. It also wasn't very believable that the French Resistance could supply her with a trunk full of perfectly fitting designer clothes to support her cover persona.

The novel is well-written, with strong characters, and it is a solid addition to the “Maggie Hope” series. Maggie’s fans won't want to miss it.

title: Impossibly Cluttered Plot; Highly Disorganized Female Investigator
text:
MURDER IN SAINT-GERMAIN is my first “Aimee Leduc” novel, and I suspect that it's NOT among the best in this long-running series. (It's the 17th “Aimee Leduc Investigation”; the first is [[ASIN:1616957301 Murder in the Marais]].) Aimee comes across as a dismayingly disorganized private investigator (surely she's not just inept)--her transportation is an unreliable scooter, she can't ever reach her business partner when she needs to, she takes on complex new assignments when she's already strapped for time, and she's constantly scrambling to find trustworthy caregivers for her infant daughter (Chloe).

In the novel, Aimee runs two concurrent extra investigations atop her contracted computer systems security work at the prestigious Ecole des Beaux-Arts. The first investigation begins as simple scanning of the art school’s emails on behalf of a famous professor (Jules Dechard); it eventually uncovers clandestine sexual liaisons and blackmail threats that threaten the school’s very existence. The second investigation requires locating a presumed-dead Bosnian warlord who may or may not still exist; the warlord or someone else may be plotting to murder Aimee’s extremely busy counterterrorism investigator friend (Suzanne).

Does the plot sound complicated? You bet it is. Plus Aimee herself becomes a murder suspect, gets imprisoned, constantly fends off colleague’s entreaties to visit her dying former mentor (Morbier), and tries to handle her former husband's suspicious insistence on babysitting Chloe.

The investigations are resolved by novel’s end, but the story nevertheless ends with a significant cliffhanger involving Aimee’s back story. This was annoying, even for someone like myself who was ignorant of the back story. The Paris setting is described with considerable detail, and is probably accurate. However, I found the plot to be impossibly cluttered, and I never could warm to Aimee (who carries wigs and other silly disguises around for use at a moment’s notice).

Series fans will of course want to read this book for the information about Aimee's ongoing personal and work relationships.

title: Scholarly Analysis of External Factors That Contributed to Austen's Popularity
text:
THE MAKING OF JANE AUSTEN is a rather tedious academic analysis of the external factors (book illustrations and illustrators, parlor dramatizations, stage performances, famous movies, biographies, close relatives’ activities) that supposedly transformed the spinster author into a literary icon. To my mind, it minimizes the intrinsic merit of Austen’s novels, by settling on canny publicity and advertising as the primary explanation for the author's popularity.

Personally, I think that the novels remain popular because of their great charm, strong characters, and close observation of human foibles. One of my all-time favorite scenes comes from PRIDE AND PREJUDICE, where Elizabeth’s friend Charlotte confides that she encourages her husband, the dreadful Mr. Collins (whose marriage proposal was rejected by Elizabeth), to spend as much time as possible outdoors in his garden. The scene is timeless, and reveals so much about the people themselves.

THE MAKING OF JANE AUSTEN is a book for Austen scholars, NOT for Austen fans like myself who simply love the novels, and the movies and TV series based on the novels.

title: Routine Police Procedural Spends Too Much Time on Medical Issues
text:
Early in THE DYING DETECTIVE: A MYSTERY, the detective (Johansson) has a stroke. The novel gets the stroke symptoms, rehab, and treatment right, but this material fills far too much of the book. And it's depressing to read about a main character who is supposedly dying, even though it's the man’s lifestyle (and resulting heart disease), not the stroke itself, that's killing him.

As a mystery, this is a very ordinary police procedural. Johansson's physician (Ulrika) hands him a cold case involving a murdered child, and he is able to identify the likely suspect very quickly because no one pursued the original investigation very seriously. Johansson gives fact-finding assignments to various helpers, including a couple of caregivers (Matilda and Max). When the suspect’s guilt is proved, Johansson and his helpers must find an unorthodox way to bring the man to justice--because the statute of limitations on the child’s murder has expired, making the murderer immune from normal prosecution and trial.

The translation from the Swedish is good, but this is a slow-moving story without much plot. A moderately interesting subplot--connected with the murderer’s ability to escape detection for more than 25 years--involves sexual abuse of children in Thailand by pedophile tourists.

title: Richly Descriptive Literary Novel About Veterans With PTSD
text:
THE STANDARD GRAND: A NOVEL is an impressive example of what I see as moderately “experimental” fiction. There is a story, but the vivid, descriptive words just pile up, and pile up, until the reader is nearly exhausted by the weight of all the language. The prose makes me think of Proust or Joyce--it's actually too rich for me.

The story is a fantasy about U.S. war veterans, both male and female, who are coping with post traumatic stress syndrome after completing tours in Afghanistan, Iraq, etc. The “Standard Grand” of the title is a private rehab (survival) camp in the Catskills, where some extremely damaged vets go to find a structured existence.

It's an interesting book, and the prose is a treat for lovers of the English language. The novel is serious literature, and I suspect that it will find its way onto many a college class reading list.

title: Run-of-the-Mill Thriller With Exotic Settings, Fantasy Elements (Man-Made Weather, Quest for Ark of the Covenant)
text:
THE DEVIL'S TRIANGLE is my first Catherine Coulter thriller, and it doesn't inspire me to read more of her novels. Fourth in the "Brit in the FBI" series (the first is [[ASIN:B00C5R7H70 The Final Cut]]), it works fine as a standalone. However, it's a plodding, run-of-the-mill thriller in which a team of nearly immortal (you-can't-kill-'em-but-maybe-you-can-wing-'em-if-you're-really-lucky) covert FBI operatives save the U.S. Government and the world once again. Neither the exotic settings (Venice, Rome, the Bermuda Triangle), nor the fantasy elements (the evildoers' ability to control the weather, thanks to notes from Leonardo da Vinci; the evildoers' mad, obsessive quest for the Ark of the Covenant) are sufficient to lift the novel above the ordinary.

In the novel, a professional thief (Kitsune aka "the Fox") delivers to anonymous clients in Venice an artifact (Aaron's rod) that she stole from the military-guarded Topkapi Palace. Instead of paying
Kitsune, the clients send death squads after her. Kitsune enlists the aid of her FBI enemies from prior series novels (the "Covert Eyes" team of Michaela "Mike" Caine and British-raised Nicholas Drummond), by persuading them that a massive Gobi Desert sandstorm--currently burying Beijing and killing thousands--is not a natural weather phenomenon, but is a man-made event.

After Mike and Nicholas arrive in Venice, their meeting with Kitsune is thwarted by a shootout in the Piazza di San Marcos that leaves seven bad guys dead and one FBI team member (Lia) seriously wounded. Eventually Kitsune successfully contacts Mike and Nicholas. With her help and with help from the FBI team's incredibly skilled teenage computer expert (Adam), Mike and Nicholas identify Kitsune's clients as the evil, "identical" Korath twins (Ajax and Cassandra). They also figure out that the mad twins are seeking the Ark of the Covenant. Mike and Nicholas and Kitsune head off to beard the twins in the Koraths' castle stronghold near Rome, and kill a bunch more bad guys on their way. The novel goes on from there, with more killings and close escapes--it's a very long thriller at 512pp--and eventually the team winds up on an island in the Bermuda Triangle.

The well-written novel has lots of action scenes, even though it's not really a page-turner. It's a decent read, as thrillers go, but nothing to shout home about. I expected much more from an established, popular writer like Coulter.

title: Northern Ireland Detective Duffy Is Targeted by Post-Troubles Death Squads
text:
Because I loved [[ASIN:B013NI8W4G Rain Dogs]] (the previous series novel), I had high expectations for POLICE AT THE STATION AND THEY DON'T LOOK FRIENDLY. But this novel begins with a prologue--Duffy is about to meet his maker--and the prologue's action isn't picked up again until page 212 (of 321) in my reviewer's copy of the book. This is a long time to make the reader wait! I generally dislike prologues, because they are such an artificial device for generating reader suspense, and in fact I found it very hard to get interested in the story's events up until the plot resumed after the prologue's cliffhanger.

When the story resumed, I liked the novel a lot. I admire detective Sean Duffy for his dogged determination to do his impossible "peeler" job during and after the time of the "Irish Troubles". EVERY time Duffy gets into his official BMW, he must check underneath for bombs, because peelers who skip this safety check don't survive.

In the novel, which starts with Duffy digging his grave in preparation for execution by an IRA death squad, Duffy angers a lot of people by investigating the oddball crossbow murders of two low-level drug dealers. He ends up targeted by the local IRA, by the local paramilitaries, and by his own RUC (police). All three groups have powerful members who want the investigation permanently buried. Even as Catholic Duffy is dodging death squads, he is trying to hold onto his tough but terrified Protestant girlfriend Beth, and to keep both her and their baby daughter Emma safe.

As previously mentioned, the final hundred-plus pages are exciting and entertaining. There are a lot of surprising twists, and the resolution of the whole complicated plot situation is satisfying and reasonably believable. U.S. readers should be warned that this Sean Duffy novel is set in Northern Ireland in the year 1988, and that the police procedures and organizations are those that were in effect in Northern Ireland at the time.

title: Extremely Poor Mystery, But With Darned Good Recipes
text:
BANANA CREAM PIE MURDER (A HANNAH SWENSON MYSTERY) doesn't work very well as a standalone, unless you're mainly interested in the many scrumptious dessert, cookie, quick-dinner, and snack recipes. It's puzzling that newlywed Hannah doesn't know much about her husband Ross' likes or dislikes; and that she's apparently seeking a subordinate wife's role in their marriage. Hannah's confusion about what's expected of her in her new daily routine weakens her previously established character as a strong, independent, happy-though-single businesswoman.

As a reader, I couldn't help wondering whether author Joanne Fluke is already regretting having married Hannah off? (This happened in the previous novel, the 19th novel of the series, [[ASIN:1617732184 The Wedding Cake Murder]]. I probably should have read it before this one, though the novels are usually okay as standalones.)

In the novel, Hannah's mother Delores hears a scream from the luxury condo below hers, the condo owned by her close friend Tori. When Delores investigates, she discovers that the former actress has been murdered. Delores calls in detective Mike (oddly keeping back Tori's appointment book, an obviously important piece of evidence, to show to Hannah, who is due back from her honeymoon).

Hannah takes over the amateurs' murder investigation, using overheard grocery store conversations, as well as tips from local gossipy waitresses, and some breaking and entering, to move the investigation forward. Hannah gets help from Delores, Doc, Michelle, Norman, and other friends and relatives. Food is featured in almost every chapter as the family shares meals; or as Hannah bribes sources with Cookie Jar cookies; or as Mike shows up at the Cookie Jar for coffee and goodies, and to warn Hannah to stay clear of his murder investigation. As Hannah's investigation advances, Ross becomes somewhat distant, and Hannah begins to doubt his love for her.

As a mystery, this is an extremely poor effort, but the recipes are darned good. (You do need to enjoy reading about food to be able to enjoy this cozy mystery.) Hannah's existing fans will certainly want to read this book to find out about the honeymoon, and to keep up with the ongoing events in Hannah's somewhat weird extended family. However, I hope that the next series book will be a much better mystery.

title: Most Designs Use Garter Stitch in Traditional Ways
text:
Where is the garter stitch "revival"? Alas, most of the patterns in GARTER STITCH REVIVAL: 20 CREATIVE KNITTING PATTERNS FEATURING THE SIMPLEST STITCH are for cowls, ponchos, shawls, wraps, shrugs, and scarves--all fairly-easy-to-knit wearables that traditionally incorporate garter stitch, because they're good beginner projects, or require knitting a lot of fabric.

I'd hoped that this book would change my mind about garter stitch (which I've never cared for), but that didn't happen. Of the 20 designs in this collection, the only one that I might want to knit is the intriguing Brioche Boardwalk Cowl (a cowl with a sectioned band of reversible stripes done in orange and blue, by Jessie Ksanznak; see my customer photo).

The book's "garter stitch" designs are divided into three main categories: Garter Stitch Details (6 designs); Garter Stitch in a Supporting Role (7 designs); and Garter Stitch All Over (7 designs). The designs in the first two categories use garter stitch, but not enough of it to make you think of the finished items as garter-stitch knits.

The Garter Stitch All Over section includes only two sweaters: the Festival Halter Top (a very plain, sleeveless tee, by Sachiko Burgin), and the Autumn Evening Shrug (by Melissa LaBarre). Both are decent knitted garments, but the fabric looks like ordinary garter stitch.

The Garter Stitch Details section has three sweaters with garter stitch decorative elements: the Seashell Dolman Tee (garter stitch columns at the waist, by Kiri FitzGerald-Hillier), the Asymmetrical Cropped Jacket (garter stitch back panel and button band, by Toby Roxane Barna), and the Just Peachy Saddle Shoulder Cardigan (wide garter stitch bands at waist and cuffs, by Kristen TenDyke).

The Garter Stitch in a Supporting Role section has two sweaters with garter stitch yokes and bands that contrast with the fabrics' main stitches (e.g., lace, brioche): the Cotton Candy Mosaic Yoke Cardigan (colorful garter stitch yoke in Greek key mosaic bands, by Amy Gunderson), and the Santa Monica Cardigan (long cardigan with garter stitch back, by Holli Yeoh).

The book cover photo shows the Arrowhead Stole (by Courtney Spainhower), which is one of the many included shawl, cowl, and wrap designs.

As you would expect from an Interweave Press book, the designs have both written-out and charted instructions, accompanied by schematics. In my opinion, the book's overall design isn't up to the usual Interweave Press standards, although the multiple photographs of the finished items are of the high quality you always expect from this publisher. The skill level for these designs is probably intermediate to advanced intermediate; a few of the scarves can probably be knit by adventurous beginners.

title: Collection of Garment Designs Using Simple Textured Stitch Patterns
text:
TEXTURE: EXPLORING STITCH PATTERNS IN KNITWEAR is basically a collection of garment patterns (mostly cardigans), rather than the technical knitting book that I expected. The textured stitches featured in the patterns are pretty basic (e.g., broken rib, moss stitch, horseshoe cable, honeycomb), and the garment designs are kept simple (basic shapes without any unusual collar, cuff, or edging treatments).

In the introduction, designer Hannah Fettig explains: "I have been designing simple, wearable knitwear almost exclusively in Stockinette stitch since the beginning of my career. In 2010, I designed a sweater called the Rocky Coast Cardigan, which featured an all-over cable pattern. This was a departure for me, and knitters went crazy for it! ... I have continued to design in my beloved Stockinette stitch .... Meanwhile, I was still thinking about that cabled sweater. What if I did an entire collection of all-over textured knitwear? And what if I ... helped knitters take the leap from simple knit to textured stitch?"

This, in a nutshell, is the story of this book. The textured garment patterns are accompanied by modest technical designing instructions and tips (e.g., choosing yarn, measuring gauge in textured stitch pattern, reading your knitting, increasing and decreasing in stitch pattern, etc.). These are the important things that Fettig encountered in moving from stockinette to textured designs, but advanced intermediate and expert knitters will already be familiar with the technical material. There is NO glossary of textured stitch patterns.
