The written-out (not charted) garment patterns are as follows: Pretty Little Cardi, Eventide Cardi, Jennie Drop Shoulder, Supermoon Kerchief, Boatyard Pullover, West End Cardigan, Wharf Street Pullover, Textured Hats and Mitts, Pierside Cardigan, Art Walk Cardi, Morning Jacket, Big Cable Cowl, and Big Texture Cowl. The patterns should be suitable for adventurous beginner or intermediate knitters. Because the patterns involve texture, they are mostly knit on US size 5 or size 6 needles.

Two of the designs, Boatyard Pullover and West End Cardigan, feature all-over moss stitch--something that you probably won't want to knit more than once in your life, even though moss stitch looks lovely!

If you love Hannah Fettig's design aesthetic, you'll want this book, but none of the designs appeal to me. The garments are too simple to be inspiring, and none look like they would be particularly interesting or challenging to knit.

title: Well-Written But Formulaic Assassin Thriller
text:
GUNMETAL GRAY is a well-written but formulaic thriller--professional assassin (Courtland Gentry, aka "the Gray Man") accepts a "mission impossible", but carries it off, because he's the best gol-darned assassin ever hired by the CIA or by any other world-class spy organization. It's a long book (over 450 pages), with plenty of exciting, moderately believable, fight-to-the-death scenes.

The trouble is, when a main character is constantly fighting his way out of mortal peril, a novel can become tiresome. Especially when, as with this novel, a gazillion lucky coincidences are needed to both extricate the character and to point him toward the location of his next big fight scene. (No spoilers, but I'm thinking now about Courtland's second exit from the "dive bar", and about the "informer" he ran into while escaping--this happens about a third of the way through the book.)

In the novel, a young, top-level Chinese computer intelligence expert (Fan Jiang) goes on the run. The Chinese, British, Americans, Russians, and every other world spy organization that hears about him is after him--the Chinese to kill him, the rest to capture him and mine his knowledge of Chinese intelligence operations.

Starting in Hong Kong, it's Courtland's job to capture Fan Jiang for the CIA, and also to extract Courtland's former British employer (Sir Donald Fitzroy) from the clutches of the murderous Chinese colonel (Dai Longhai) who is pursuing Fan Jiang. The ongoing casualties are huge--Courtland personally contributes quite a few bodies, and the pursuers contribute many more. There is a sprinkling of mercilous torture.

As thrillers go, this one is decent enough. The plot has a lot of twists, and there is fairly constant action, plus liberal use of modern weapons and electronic surveillance equipment.

title: Slow-Moving Thriller About Quest for Antidote to Radiation Sickness
text:
THE BOY WHO GLOWED IN THE DARK is the third book in the "Nadia Tesla" series (the first is ASIN:1612186084 The Boy From Reactor 4); and it doesn't really work as a standalone. Without knowing the backstories, I found it difficult to get involved with the characters and plot. The early chapters are slow-moving because the basic plot line (acquiring the second half of a world-changing chemical formula) has to be explained to the reader; and later chapters aren't much better because of the wooden writing.

In the novel, the boy (Bobby) has just been released from jail. He finds emails from a mysterious "GenesisII", sent from Japan during his imprisonment. The emails suggest that a person exists who may possess the second half of a chemical formula for an antidote to radiation poisoning. Bobby has a locket with the first half, so he and Nadia set off for Japan to obtain the second half before an unscrupulous country or individual can get hold of it. A country that possesses the formula can use nuclear weapons at will, because its own citizens will be protected from radiation sickness. From the outset, Nadia and Bobby are pursued by Slavic-looking men who appear to be Ukrainian thugs bent on getting the formula.

The book seems to finish off the series, although it is followed by a prequel about Nadia (ASIN:1477827978 The Altar Girl).

title: Thin Prequel Describes Police Chief Craddock's First Case
text:
AN UNSETTLING CRIME FOR SAMUEL CRADDOCK is blessedly short, and a fast read, but it's thinly written. It's set in a small, segregated town in Texas, sometime after JFK's assassination. I couldn't place the actual time period, and the town and its citizens' attitudes seemed impossibly quaint for a post-1960s setting. I kept thinking that the novel belonged in turn-of-the-century (1900s) historical detective fiction.

The characters are one-dimensional, and I didn't care for the young, newly-appointed, totally inexperienced Police Chief Craddock at all. The plot hook--the discovery of 5 children's bodies in a burning house in "Darktown"--failed to grab me. Craddock fans will no doubt enjoy this prequel that describes Craddock's first real case, but it doesn't inspire me to read the other five books in this series. (The series begins with [[ASIN:1616147997 A Killing at Cotton Hill]].)

title: Another FBI Profiler Novel Featuring the Wooden Karen Vail
text:
As hard as I try, I simply cannot warm to the Karen Vail character. She's an FBI profiler, she investigates serial murders, she cares about the victims, she wants to stop the killer before he/she kills again, and she's very, very good at her job. She's a gorgeous redhead, and she's willing to risk her own safety to capture a killer. But there's something very wooden about Karen, and the plots seem to just plod along--even when they're intricate, with surprising twists and turns, as in this novel, THE DARKNESS OF EVIL.

In the novel, Karen goes against the wishes of her new section chief, and takes steps to protect a serial killer's adult daughter (Jasmine), after the daughter receives a threatening letter from her imprisoned father. Jasmine provided the evidence that led to her father's arrest and conviction for the "Blood Lines" killings, and has written a book about the crimes. Dad isn't happy about Jasmine's upcoming book tour. When he pulls off a bloody prison escape (two more bodies), and Jasmine goes missing (yet another body left behind), Karen's work is cut out for her, trying to capture Dad before he kills his daughter.

The book is well-written, with unusual plot twists; although the twists may test readers' willingness to suspend disbelief. Karen Vail fans will probably enjoy this 7th series book (the first is [[ASIN:1497692040 THE 7TH VICTIM]]), but I'm done with this series after two books. This novel works fine as a standalone, but it isn't even as good as the previous series entry ([[ASIN:162467271X SPECTRUM]]).

title: Scholarly, Revisionist Biography of Disgraced Bureaucrat Charles Forbes
text:
A TIME OF SCANDAL: CHARLES R. FORBES, WARREN G. HARDING, AND THE MAKING OF THE VETERANS BUREAU is a scholarly (but reasonably readable) biography of Charles R. Forbes, the thoroughly disgraced bureaucrat who established the U.S. Veterans Bureau, but later served time in Leavenworth prison for rigging government hospital-construction contracts. In this account of Forbes' life, author Rosemary Stevens questions whether he was in fact guilty of defrauding the U.S government of more than 200 million dollars.

Because the papers of President Harding and Forbes himself are missing (and presumably destroyed), Professor Stevens bases her revisionist biography on new material found in "the papers of significant figures, military and civilian personnel records, records of the Veterans Bureau and Department of Justice (including the FBI), congressional and court records, prison records, and more".

Like so many histories written by academics, this one has long, long paragraphs that are filled with every factual detail that the author uncovered during her research. It's a standard biography with Forbes' story told in more or less chronological order.

While I'm sure that Stevens' revisionist take on "the Harding scandals" (Veterans Bureau and Teapot Dome) is of great interest to scholars of the Harding/Coolidge era of U.S. politics, it's a real slog for someone like myself who has only a casual interest in learning more about the scandals themselves. I rate A TIME OF SCANDAL at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Entertaining Cozy Mystery/Romance With Many Flaws
text:
SOMETHING BURIED, SOMETHING BLUE is a mildly entertaining, spiritualist-themed cozy mystery set in Lily Dale, NY (a real-life center of the Spiritualism movement). For a novel, it's oddly written--the actions of the viewpoint character (Bella) are described in present tense (e.g., "Wearing comfortable old jeans ..., Bella steps out the front door of Valley View ...") as if they were stage directions in a play, or as if the reader were an outsider looking on. This is the second book of a series, but it works fine as a standalone.

In the novel, Bella is persuaded by a local medium (Odelia) to organize a "destination wedding" for a young couple (Johneen and Parker) at Valley View Guesthouse. Beautiful Lily Dale is not anyone's dreamed-of "destination" (it's no Paris or Cabo), but if Bella can pull off the wedding, she may be able to stay at Valley View year-round as the events manager. This would be wonderful, not only for the penniless, recently bereaved Bella, but also for her young son (Max) and for Chance the cat and her eight tiny kittens. (Yes, the cats play a significant role in the story.)

Johneen is the worst sort of "Bridezilla", but Bella must deal with more serious complications. Odelia is telling Bella that Spirit is uneasy about the bride's safety. A letter arrives, warning Bella to stop the wedding. And Bella's mother-in-law (Millicent, but "Maleficent" to Bella) shows up without warning, determined to rescue Bella and Max from the Lily Dale "cultists".

As a cozy mystery (with a sizable dollop of romance novel), the story moves along pleasantly enough. Unfortunately the perps can be identified early on, and the ending is silly. At many points, I wanted to strangle Bella, who is generally likable, but overly timid and suggestible. There were also too many temporary "disappearances" of key characters, employed to add suspense to the plot. Because SOMETHING BURIED, SOMETHING BLUE is entertaining despite its many flaws, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Well-Written Historical Action/Adventure Novel With Outlandish Plot
text:
RT Book Reviews got it exactly right, in describing THE SMOKE HUNTER as "Indiana Jones Meets Lara Croft". It's an historical action/adventure novel, with lots of detailed description of the historical setting and times; and with a plot that is over-the-top outlandish. There's no history in it--it's just a made-up account of a bold female heroine's 1898 adventure--her search for the lost city of El Dorado.

In the novel, the heroine's search begins with her finding an Inca artifact secreted in an old Psalter that she steals--with appropriate self-justification--from a desk in the British Office of Public Records. The artifact is accompanied by a map of the New World, as it was when the Mission of San Pedro de Flores was founded. The Psalter also contains letters saying that a half-crazed friar brought the artifact out of the jungle, and died soon after. So the heroine sets out to find the city that the friar babbled about.

Author Jacquelyn Benson is to be commended for her writing skill and mastery of this genre. It's hard to believe that her polished work is a first novel! However, it's not my kind of book--all of that rich, detailed description adds up to a 436-page novel, and I strongly prefer mystery/thriller to action/adventure anyway. Basically I ordered this book by mistake, so I rate THE SMOKE HUNTER at a neutral 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Well-Done Flashback Novel; Superficial Cincinnati Setting
text:
FRACTURED is a very good novel, but the plot is the type that I always lose patience with. At the beginning, a life-altering, tragic event is hinted at. Then the actual details are dribbled out in the remainder of the novel, through one or more viewpoint characters' flashbacks that recount the events that produced the tragic one. This type of plot must be extremely difficult to write well--and this skillfully written novel is an example of how to pull it off--but as a reader I prefer a more straightforward plot, without flashbacks.

In the novel, the author of a best-selling first novel (Julie) relocates her family from Tacoma to Cincinnati, because she needs to escape the attentions of a particularly troublesome, threatening stalker (Heather). Julie and her unemployed, married neighbor (John) are attracted to each other, and the attraction sets in motion the events that result in tragedy for all.

John, Julie, Julie's attack dog (Sandy), and Julie's twin children all run afoul of the ever-changing "neighborhood rules" written (and emailed) by an officious neighbor (Cindy). Cindy, the self-appointed neighborhood leader and organizer of compulsory monthly block parties, is both amusing and frightening. John's teenage son (Chris) and Cindy's teenage daughter (Ashley) also figure in the complex plot. Ultimately, neighbors end up confronting neighbors both in civil court and in grand jury proceedings.

The Cincinnati setting, in Mount Adams and Eden Park, is incidental to the plot. (This was a disappointment to me, because I was interested in reading about the Cincinnati locale.) The characters are well-drawn--Cindy is particularly memorable, as the type of well-meaning but overbearing person who always seems to turn up in neighborhood groups. Because FRACTURED is well-done, but the kind of novel that I find tedious, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Designs Don't Cry Out, "Build Me!"
text:
I love LEGO books, but GEEKY LEGO CRAFTS: 21 FUN AND QUIRKY PROJECTS is kind of hard to love. The building instructions are clear enough, but the projects don't cry out, "Build me!"

The basic designs resemble low-resolution screen displays reduced to individual pixels. You have to sort of squint to see what they're supposed to represent--for example, the zombie face on the "Zombie Pencil Holder"; the cassette on the "Cassette Letter Holder"; the trophy deer head in the "Mounted Deer Head" (shown on the book's cover).

Assuming that you want items that generally look like resemble vintage floppy disks, Tetris squares, or pixellated Santas and skulls-and-crossbones, the actual projects are impractical. Typical examples are the "Hazmat Place Mats" (a large studs-up platform with a flame or a skull-and-crossbones design) and the "Space Invaders Space Savers" (upright invader-shaped blocks with basins for paperclips or highlighter pens). Food is going to get stuck on the placemats, and the footprint of the space savers is large compared to their capacity.

Many projects (for example, the "Cassette Letter Holder" require a lot of LEGO blocks, so they represent a small investment in money as well as time. The "Fridge Magnets" fail to specify what sort of magnets to use, or where to purchase them.

The projects in the book are as follows: Space Invader Space Savers; Cursor Bookends; Rubber Ducky; Flying Ducks; Christmas Decorations; Flame Toast Rack; Zombie Pencil Holder; Hazmat Place Mats; Hanging Ghost; Floppy Disk Coasters; Cassette Letter Holder; Sword-in-the-Stone Paperweight; Retro Controller Phone Station; Lady Liberty Fish Tank; "Fuzzy Dice"; Giant Key Holder; Mounted Deer; Fridge Magnets; Bearskin Rug; Grenade Planter; and Robot Wine Bottle Holder.

Because the book is mildly interesting to look through, even though I wouldn't want to build any of the designs, I rate it at a very generous 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Good Job, But Gear S2 Owners Don't Really Need This Manual
text:
SAMSUNG GEAR S2 FOR DUMMIES does an excellent job of explaining how to set up and use the Gear S2 smartwatch. The book describes in detail every preinstalled app and setting. It gets you quickly up to speed on handling telephone calls, text messages, and emails. It has good chapters on troubleshooting, and on finding online help and support. Surprisingly, it even has a chapter on designing, developing, and selling your own Gear S2 apps.

However, I question whether any new owner of a Gear S2 really needs this book. The Gear S2 is a rather simple device, and the interface is quite intuitive to use. I figured out the watch features fairly quickly (all by myself, without benefit of any detailed manual) just by rotating the bezel and tapping on the icons to see what they did.

It did take me a while to realize that the Gear S2 does NOT run wholly independently of an Android smartphone (e.g., an interactive NBA watch face on my Gear S2 stopped updating game scores whenever my phone went to standby mode). This book would have saved me some troubleshooting time in that area--it tells you on page 2 that you need a smartphone running to make full use of the watch.

Switching the watchbands is very tricky, and this book has photos and step-by-step instructions that show you how. However, there is a Samsung video available online that demonstrates the method. There is also a complete Gear 2 User's Manual available online from Samsung that explains all the apps, settings, and capabilities of the device, just as this book does.

Without a doubt, author Eric Butow does a fine job of covering the S2 Gear in this "Dummies" book. It's not his fault that the Gear S2 is limited in things it can do, so that there isn't a whole lot for him to write about. However, at its current Amazon selling price (about $23 in paperback format), I don't think that this book is enough of an improvement over the Samsung User's Manual to be worth the money. I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Excellent 1963 Chicago Ambience; Ho-Hum Plot
text:
You should read MY KIND OF TOWN for the excellent 1963 South Side Chicago ambience and for the amusing portrayal of a self-centered but generous Frank Sinatra, but NOT for the ho-hum plot. The basic "locate Al Capone's lost treasure" concept has been done to death, and even the accomplished writing of this novel cannot rescue that theme. This is the second Joe Buonomo mystery (the first is ONE FOR MY BABY). The novel works pretty well as a standalone, but it's kind of short on explanations for why Joe stayed away from his family for so long.

In the novel, tough guy WWII flying ace Joe Buonomo answers his good friend Frank Sinatra's call to act as bodyguard for Frank's upcoming private command performances for Chicago gangster Sam Giancana. Frank's debts to the gangster are quickly squared, but Joe decides to hang around Chicago for a little while longer to reestablish ties with his warm, close-knit, Italian family.

Joe discovers that (1) his old Italian neighborhood is threatened with destruction due to Mayor Daley's ambitious building plans (historic Hull House is already under the wrecking ball); and (2) the local mobsters think he knows where Capone's missing millions are stashed (he doesn't). Joe gets involved with the local "save our neighborhood" group, takes his new girlfriend Claudia on a tour of Chicago's landmarks, and agrees to follow the leads on an Irish chieftain's Capone treasure map. The map quest requires him to visit many of Capone's old stomping grounds.

Despite the good writing, the likable Buonomo and Sinatra characters, and the fascinating Chicago local color, I tired of reading the book about two-thirds of the way through. The final third failed to rekindle my interest. I rate MY KIND OF TOWN at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Lincoln Is Mostly Absent; Historical Setting, Characters Don't Come to Life
text:
THESE HONORED DEAD: A LINCOLN AND SPEED MYSTERY is loosely based on historical fact--accounts of Lincoln's early Illinois trials, and of his close friendship with a Springfield general store manager, Joshua Fry Speed. However, Fry is the viewpoint character, and the events are imaginary, so the "Lincoln" part of the subtitle is misleading, in that Lincoln barely contributes to the murder mystery investigation.

In the novel, a young woman is murdered (stabbed to death) in a town close to Springfield (Menard), and her body is discovered by her aunt (the Widow Harriman). Fry and the Widow are paramours. When the Widow becomes the chief suspect in the police investigation, Fry launches his own investigation to clear the Widow's name. More murders follow.

Fry's sister joins him in Springfield (having travelled from the family home in Kentucky). Fry spends a lot of time riding his horse (Hickory) between Springfield and Menard. Lincoln offers advice to the Widow, who declines his legal services. A former Harvard German-language tutor, and the keeper of an early form of insane asylum, also figure in the plot.

The book is well written, and the plot has unexpected twists and turns, but it's rather boring as a mystery story. As historical fiction, the book fails to bring the historical setting and characters to life. Lincoln is mostly absent, and Fry comes across as a rather naive, immature young man. For these reasons, I rate THESE HONORED DEAD at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Another Damaged Detective; Too Much Oakland Police Procedure
text:
THRILL KILL: A MATT SINCLAIR MYSTERY is the second “Matt Sinclair” novel (the first is [[ASIN:1629533734 Red Line: A Matt Sinclair Mystery]]). It’s set in Oakland, CA, and certainly gets the geographical setting and the Oakland police procedure right—as it should, given that author Brian Thiem spent 25 years working homicide cases in Oakland.

In the novel, homicide detective Matt Sinclair is called to a murder scene where a naked woman is hanging—posed like a dancer—from a pair of trees in an Oakland park. Matt recognizes her as a prostitute/call girl that he tried to help many years before. As he investigates, Matt must deal with post-traumatic-stress syndrome that he’s trying to keep secret from his partner and departmental colleagues. He’s damaged by not only by PTS, but also by his former alcoholism.

The plot takes Matt all around Oakland, meeting all sorts of street characters. It incorporates bits of Oakland’s recent history regarding demonstrations that result in destructive vandalism, the “Occupy” movement, and the “Black Lives Matter” movement and fringe groups. It incorporates some out-of-control “Grand Theft Auto” gamers. It ensnares Matt in local politics.

The plot has a lot of twists and turns, but it includes too much police procedural detail, and the story isn’t a page-turner. I never came to care about Matt or the prostitute victim, or Matt’s partner Cathy, or anyone else in the novel. The parts about Oakland’s history seemed unnecessary to the plot, and added to my overall boredom. I rate THRILL KILL at a generous 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Filled to Overflowing With Exciting Action Scenes
text:
If you read thrillers for the thrills, then THE DAMASCUS THREAT: AN ICE THRILLER is the book for you. Author Matt Rees has totally mastered the art of writing action scenes, and this book is filled to overflowing with them. So much so, that the plot material connecting the exciting hand-to-hand fights, executions, explosions, car chases, foot pursuits, nerve gas attacks, etc. is often rather carelessly written. Although there is a fairly solid plot, vital details are left out of the material that drives the investigation that produces the action.

In the novel, a United Nations weapons monitor (Dr. Weston), just returned to NYC from Syria, is murdered on her way to speak with ICE agent Dom Verrazzano. As she dies, she hands Dom some map coordinates, and tells him he has only a short time. A short time to do what? Dom quickly tracks down Dr. Weston’s murderer, but the bad guy kills himself without elaborating on a statement that “the four-ten” is killing him.

Dom quickly figures out what “the four-ten” must be—a highly toxic poison. As he follows up on Dr. Weston’s lead, it looks like she was warning him of a deadly terrorist attack. In Syria? In New York City? Before long, Dom flies to Damascus, and engages in a race against time to contain a toxic weapons stockpile, and to thwart the money-making scheme being carried out by U.S. military contractors and mercenaries.

The action scenes in THE DAMASCUS THREAT are extremely well done—they had me on the edge of my seat—but there are so many that the details seem awfully repetitive by the end of the novel. Also, Dom and his ICE colleagues seem virtually indestructible, even as they leave body after body behind. Dom seems like a good guy, but I didn’t like him enough to want to read the next book in the series. For these reasons, I rate this unquestionably exciting thriller at 3 stars (“It’s okay” on the official Amazon scale).

title: Inspector Sejer Investigates Double Murder Perpetrated in Dilapidated Caravan
text:
HELL FIRE: INSPECTOR SEJER MYSTERIES is my first "Inspector Sejer" novel, and it certainly works as a standalone. It's not much of a police procedural, though. The story is told mostly through flashback chapters describing events in the lives of two single mothers--strangers to each other--who both have extremely close relationships with their sons (one aged 21 years, one aged 4 years). Interspersed with these chapters are chapters describing Inspector Sejer's ongoing present-time investigation of the bloody double murder of one mother and son.

The identity of the murderer is telegraphed early, so one reads the book to find out what caused the convergence of the two mothers' lives. The Inspector's criminal investigation is routine and not particularly interesting. I don't know whether this is a standard format for Karen Fossum's "Inspector Sejer" series, but if it is, I don't want to read any more of them.

In the novel, a mother and her 4-year-old son are found murdered--stabbed to death--in a dilapidated caravan (a trailer home) in a farm field. The victims were sleeping there overnight, with the farmer's permission, apparently on a whim. Their killer took nothing, but apparently targeted the pair. It's a sad story, because the dead mother was a lovely person--a hard-working 'home help" worker who always got stuck with the most difficult old people, because she cared and would meet their unreasonable demands without complaining.

The book is well-written--the flashbacks are handled extremely competently. There are interesting vignettes about providing for the needs of aging citizens, and about the trauma experienced by a young child left in daily nursery care. There are some memorable characters (Bonnie, Simon, Eddie). However, because HELL FIRE is not much of a mystery novel, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Accessible, Anecdotal History of MacMillan's Abortive Expedition to Explore Commander Peary's  "Crocker Land"
text:
A WRETCHED AND PRECARIOUS SITUATION: IN SEARCH OF THE LAST ARCTIC FRONTIER is an anecdotal history of Donald MacMillan's abortive 1913 expedition to explore "Crocker Land" (the unknown arctic land mass reported on, and named by, Commander Robert E. Peary in 1906). Historian David Welky's narrative is well-written, in an easy, journalistic style, and it reads almost like a novel.

However, the story simply includes too much information. What I'm interested in, and want to read about, is the expedition itself--and especially about new facts and insights to be gleaned from "the trove of unpublished letters, diaries, and field notes" that the book is based on (according to the publisher). But after reading 115 pages (of 440 pages; or of 492 pages if notes, bibliography, and acknowledgments are included), I've only reached the point where the expedition departs from Labrador's Battle Harbor.

A couple of things that I've learned, though, are that (1) MacMillan was an extraordinarily fit athlete who could jump straight up and out of a chest-high barrel; and (2) members of a Peary expedition learned to use a whip to control a dogsled by laying out dead sled dogs as if they were harnessed to a sledge, and repeatedly flicking the dogs until mastery of the whip was achieved. Those facts are kind of interesting, I suppose (at least they stuck in my memory), but the story would move along so much better, if they were relegated to footnotes.

Finally, I lost patience with all the detail, and Googled "Crocker Land" to find out what happened on MacMillan's expedition. The Wikipedia article satisfied my curiosity--and I don't recommend doing it before you've finished the book. The article will definitely spoil David Welky's story, if you don't already know what MacMillan discovered.

Because it organizes facts in a way that makes history accessible, but includes too much detail in the main narrative, I rate A WRETCHED AND PRECARIOUS SITUATION at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Literary Science Fiction--All About Love and Relationships
text:
VALLEY OF THE MOON: A NOVEL is a reasonably well-written literary effort, but I don't understand it at all. The plot is basically science fiction, but it's all about love and relationships.

In the novel, a single mother (Lux) of a mixed-race son (Benno) goes on a solo camping trip in Sonoma County's Valley of the Moon (VOTM) in the year 1975. On that trip, she stumbles on a fog-shrouded breach in the very fabric of time.

The breach, created by the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, allows her to pass back and forth from the present day to the distant past--where a farm community that was located at her campsite in 1906 is still operating. The farm inhabitants are trapped by encircling fog (the breach is open in only one direction), but they always welcome Lux warmly on her recurring visits. Time flows at different rates in the past and present-day locales, so that Lux needs to sort out events at both ends of her passages through the breach.

Why this book was written eludes me. I think that my baffled state is caused by the author's very poor handling of the time-and-place transitions in the writing. The story is told in alternating chapters from the viewpoints of two main characters (1906 Joseph) and (1975ff. Lux). However, the narrations of both characters are frequently interrupted with flashbacks to past events in the characters' widely disparate lives in non-VOTM locales. The reader needs the chapter name-and-time labels to even begin to keep track of the novel's overall timeline, and, the reader's job is made even more difficult by the fact that the flashbacks within chapters are indicated only with white-space breaks in the text.

There are a lot of important subsidiary characters (e.g., Rhonda, Beth, Martha, Fancy) that are introduced within each main character's narration by name-dropping--well in advance of the reader's discovering that the character is a significant one. Frequently I had to go back and search for introductions, to find out what the secondary characters' relationships were to the main characters.

Except for those flaws, the writing (e.g., the general prose, the dialogue, the descriptive passages) is pretty good. I was interested in the book because of the VOTM setting--the Jack London State Park area, which is close to where I live, is indeed magical and romantic. However, the lack of a real plot was disappointing, so I rate the book at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: History of How Modern Forensics View of Crime Scene Came Into Being
text:
MURDER AND THE MAKING OF ENGLISH CSI reads like someone’s Ph.D. thesis (and for all I know, that’s exactly what it is). It’s clearly an academic work, not something written to appeal to a mass audience made up of “CSI” television fans, true crime fans, or forensic documentaries fans.

This slender volume (230 pages, including footnotes) is indeed a history of forensics, but the focus is on how early ideas about close observation of crime scenes came to be applied in practice to crime scenes. Thus there is a lot of recounting of exactly how pioneering crime scene investigators conducted themselves. For example, one investigator (Thorndyke) used a knife blade to scrape a sample of sand from a murder victim’s pillow into a seed packet to preserve it for laboratory analysis; another investigator (Spilsbury) would walk through rooms with hands in pockets to avoid disturbing anything.

The book includes many excerpts and diagrams reprinted from groundbreaking handbooks for criminal investigators. For example, there are descriptions of how to walk a crime scene (on a sort of grid) to avoid missing tiny details; and there are passages that emphasize the importance of, and methods for, securing blood-stained items or clothing to avoid subsequent contamination.

The methodology of the actual, lengthy forensic investigations of a couple of famous English crimes (the 1924 murder and dismemberment of Emily Kaye; and the 1953 discovery of John Christie’s “murder house”) are discussed in considerable detail. The chapter on the “murder house” includes photographs of forensic investigators digging up bones. Other chapters have photos of bone fragments, skulls, hair, murder victims’ bodies in situ, and other evidence uncovered by close forensic examination.

The book is of mild interest to forensics buffs, but it would be misleading to describe it as anything other than boring. The authors say that the book is intended to show how the modern forensics view of a homicide scene “as a highly choreographed space of investigation” came into being. I guess it succeeds at that, and so I rate it at 3 stars (“It’s okay” on the official Amazon scale).

title: Cozy Mystery Is Spoiled by Forced “Alice in Wonderland” References
text:
The “Alice in Wonderland” references in A MOST CURIOUS MURDER: A LITTLE LIBRARY MYSTERY are so forced, they eventually spoil what might otherwise be a reasonably good cozy mystery.

A major character, Zoe Zola, is a highly intelligent “little person” who is writing a nonfiction book about Lewis Carroll’s famous work. Zoe generally talks in riddles sprinkled with quotes from “Alice”. She also loves fairies and has a gorgeous flower garden ornamented with “fairy houses”. Yes, she’s an eccentric character—the sort of character you generally expect, and appreciate, in a cozy mystery. However, Zoe’s disjointed speech patterns don’t make her loveable—they’re just confusing, and they slow down the story. Worse, Zoe’s “Alice” references are dropped in so frequently, and with so little connection to anything in the plot, they ultimately come off as a mere book sales gimmick.

The other major character, Jenny Weston, is reeling from a recent divorce, and has returned to her mother’s place in Bear Falls, Michigan. Jenny is all wrapped up in how she’s been dumped by two men--her former husband and her high school sweetheart. The former sweetheart is married, still living in Bear Falls, and obviously a train wreck that Jenny was lucky to avoid. Still, Jenny spends much of her time brooding about her romantic misfortunes and her lingering feelings for the sweetheart. Otherwise, she renews a lot of her old acquaintances with long-time Bear Falls residents.

In the novel, there are two mysteries to be solved: “Who murdered the spiteful old curmudgeon found dead in Zoe’s fairy garden?” and “Who hacked apart the ‘Little Library’ book exchange box that stood for years in the front yard of Jenny’s childhood home?” Rather inexplicably, the local police chief focuses on Zoe as the major suspect in the curmudgeon’s murder. No one has any idea who murdered the book box. Both mysteries are eventually solved.

The murder mystery plot was fairly interesting until the ending. But the ending is marred because all of the plot threads are wrapped up too quickly in the final few chapters. There isn’t enough preparation for the “reveal” of the murderer; the book-box-destroyer’s motivation is extremely weak; and the incredible, timely return to Bear Falls of a long-missing resident conveniently solves a mystery from Jenny’s past that didn’t even need to be solved.

Because of the gimmicky "Alice" aspects, and the disappointing ending, I rate A MOST CURIOUS MURDER at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Entertaining Thriller With Conventional Plot Features Military War Dog
text:
WAR HAWK is an entertaining thriller with a rather conventional plot--conventional in the sense that the good guys (Wayne Tucker and friends) repeatedly enter into impossible search-and-rescue or search-and-destroy missions, but repeatedly triumph against all odds. They lose some people along the way, but the core group always survives through lucky coincidences (including the happy acquisition of an opponent's advanced military weapon).

What sets this thriller series apart is that a main character (Kane) is a Belgian Malinois (a type of shepherd dog). A highly trained military war dog, Kane is outfitted with a protective vest, a night-vision camera, and an earpiece. Kane's handler Tucker uses hand signals and voice commands to direct Kane on advance scouting forays. The special equipment allows Tucker to see things through the dog's eyes and ears, and Tucker's missions would NOT succeed without Kane's help. Kane is also a weapon in his own right. He's highly intelligent, and able to deviate from Tucker's orders whenever it's necessary to take down an enemy with jaws and teeth.

In the novel, a powerful media magnate (Kellerman) uses privately-designed, computer-controlled drones to influence an election and to start a war. His hoped-for rewards are lucrative licenses to exploit oil resources and to mine rare earths. The ruthless Kellerman is willing to murder his own scientists and to order the destruction of villages filled with unsuspecting civilians in order to achieve his objectives. An underlying theme is that Kellerman's advanced drone warfare technology is based on a theory advanced by codebreaker Alan Turing during WWII.

This is the second book chronicling the adventures of Tucker and Kane (the first is KILL SWITCH). Dog lovers will no doubt find this series particularly enjoyable. The novel is well-written (except for the unconvincing italicized passages written from Kane's viewpoint). The plot has lots of exciting action scenes, but the book seemed long, and the story didn't sustain my interest for extended stretches. In my opinion, there are too many happy coincidences, and there is too much description of man/dog bonding. I rate WAR HAWK at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Pleasant "Coming Home" Novel About Unsolved Disappearance of 2-Year-Old Twins
text:
ARROWOOD is a pleasant mystery/suspense novel that's hard to characterize. The story revolves around a 17-year-old cold case, the disappearance of the 2-year-old twin sisters of the main character (Arden Arrowood). It stars an old house (Arrowood, Arden's family home in Keokuk, Iowa), which the family abandoned, along with all its furnishings, shortly after the tragedy. There's also a dollop of romance, as Arden seeks to rekindle an old relationship with her first love (Ben).

In the novel, Arden "comes home" to Keokuk after more than a decade's absence. She has inherited Arrowood from her father, and moves into the house, which has been maintained by a creepy handyman (Dick Heaney). Almost immediately, she is contacted by a true crime writer (Josh) who's investigating Iowa's famous unsolved crimes. He has new, never-published evidence that disputes Arden's memory of the day the twins disappeared. Reluctantly, Arden joins Josh's investigation, and she turns up additional new evidence by interviewing old neighbors, reading documents still stored in the house, and following up watery clues provided by the (apparently haunted) house itself.

The plot has a lot of twists, and I was enjoying this "cozy suspense novel" until everything kind of fell apart in a tacked-on "action" ending. The Keokuk setting is interesting, although I couldn't tell whether the description of a slowly dying Mississippi river town was imaginary or was a reflection of the present-day state of the real Keokuk. I did like Arden fairly well, and the other characters are not cardboard characters, although there isn't a whole lot of depth to them. The actual writing is skilled, making this a slow-paced but highly readable book, great for summer vacation reading. Because of the unsatisfying action ending, I rate ARROWOOD at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Biography Focuses on Exterminator's Trainer, Owner, Stablemate
text:
As a child, I read and loved [[ASIN:B005CM1M1W Old Bones the Wonder Horse Kentucky Derby Champion]], which is all about the horse Exterminator (and even written from the horse's viewpoint!). This is why I wanted to read a biography of the famous Kentucky Derby winner that was written for adults. However, I was disappointed by HERE COMES EXTERMINATOR!, which doesn't really focus on Exterminator, and which glosses over most of the gelding's specific races without giving any detail other than that the horse lost or won.

HERE COMES EXTERMINATOR! is actually a recounting of the early history of American thoroughbred racing--before, during, and after World War I. During the war, there was a lot of political emphasis on developing strong thoroughbred bloodlines for the "remount" program--which involved breeding and supplying horses to the U.S. and other nations' military cavalry divisions. After the war, the emphasis shifted, more to racing for racing's sake, because horses were no longer needed to fight wars, pull trams and milk trucks, etc.

The book contains a great deal of biographical information about Exterminator's trainer (Henry McDaniel) and his owner (Willis Sharpe Kilmer). Kilmer was a man made rich by marketing his family's patent medicine (Swamp Root), and was an extremely difficult person who had more money than he knew what to do with.

The horse that is really featured in this book is Exterminator's stablemate, Sun Briar, who was Kilmer's great favorite. McDaniel acquired Exterminator as a workout horse to challenge Sun Briar, and ended up running Exterminator rather than Sun Briar in the Kentucky Derby. It was a surprise to everyone when Exterminator won the Derby. In fact, Sun Briar was another great racehorse (who happened to have a bad year as a 3-year-old). Modern-day thoroughbreds that trace their lineage back to Sun Briar include Secretariat, Native Dancer, Seattle Slew, Funny Cide, California Chrome, and American Pharoah.

This is a well-researched, readable, history of early thoroughbred racing in America, with decent biographies of the people surrounding Exterminator. However, because I was looking for a book with more about the particular horse, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Good "Magical" Cocktail Recipes, Interesting Single Concept, Thin Plot
text:
LAST CALL AT THE NIGHTSHADE LOUNGE is a pleasant urban fantasy novel. It's based on the concept that bartenders (in Chicago) not only protect their customers from themselves (by limiting their drinks) but also from fearsome, night-prowling beasts (the Tremens) that just love to eat humans. It's a fun concept, but not terribly well executed, because the repeated idea gets tiresome over the course of the book.

In the novel, an aimless Ivy-League business grad (Bailey Chen) finds work as a "barback" (a bartenders' assistant) at her neighborhood bar (the Nightshade Lounge). At closing one night, she mixes herself a Perfect Screwdriver, which glows because it's made with oddball "CC" vodka. On her way home, Bailey encounters her very first Tremens, which she is able to dispatch (and live to tell the tale) because of a temporary superpower (extra weight) given her by the magical cocktail.

Bailey's encounter with the Tremens leads to her becoming a novice bartender for the Cupbearers Court (source of the CC vodka and other magical liquors). Initially apprenticed to an old high school pal (Zane), Bailey discovers she has a crush on Zane. The remainder of the novel proceeds as a light romance superimposed upon a series of exciting action encounters with various Tremens. The Tremens are defeated when CC bartenders imbibe the cocktails described in the CC bartenders' manual ("The Devil's Water Dictionary", which is reproduced in the novel). The cocktails grant the CC bartenders superpowers that range from invisibility (the Martini) to mind-reading (the Chimayo).

The included recipes will make very good cocktails, though the reader will have to locate CC liquors in order to make the magical, glowing ones! The novel is reasonably well-written, but the plot is very thin, and the main characters (Bailey, Mona, Zane, Bucket, Garrett, Vincent) aren't particularly interesting or likeable as individuals. For these reasons, I rate LAST CALL AT THE NIGHTSHADE LOUNGE at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Readable But Extremely Lengthy Biography of Famous Soldier
text:
DOUGLAS MACARTHUR: AMERICAN WARRIOR isn't a good choice for someone like me, who merely wants a readable, fairly complete biography of the famous soldier. The book is 834 pages long, without counting the footnotes, bibliography, index, or other extraneous material!

The text IS readable, but it's simply too much unless you have a serious amateur historian's interest in the life of the late General MacArthur. I haven't read any other MacArthur biographies, so I can't attest to this one's accuracy, or to whether it contains new material, or to whether the author's take on MacArthur's persona is intriguing. However, in looking at the book as a historian might, I'm bothered by the author's decision to present so many real-life conversations as if the reader were "a fly on the wall" at the actual event.

The conversations sound like they were taken verbatim from a Movietone newsreel, or a tape, or a transcript of the actual event--but the passages are NOT footnoted with specific references to the source material. Presenting the conversations in this manner makes the book feel more alive and current (and certainly adds to the overall readability), but it seems to play fast and loose with actual facts. I never feel that I can trust a biography as a reference, when it includes conversations with words in quotation marks, without nailing down the factual sources.

A random example of what I'm talking about is this (from Chapter 15): "The general drew himself upright. 'Don't you know,' he said in his sonorous voice, 'the Japanese haven't yet made the bomb with my name on it?" This sounds like the biographer is describing something seen in actual photographic footage. However, the footnote (#22 in my Advance Reading Copy) says "Quezon, Manchester, 255"--which suggests that the conversation is not necessarily verbatim, because it is based on something this biographer found in some other biographer's book (in this case, a biography by Manchester). Whether the actual words were ever spoken depends on where Manchester got them from, and what he cites as his source.

It may well be that the footnotes will be fleshed out in the final version of this biography (to be released on June 14, 2016), so that my problem with the citations to the source material will be corrected. Nevertheless, I believe that the usefulness of this biography as a reference book is substantially limited by the author's decision to present so many conversations as if they were "overheard". For this reason, I rate DOUGLAS MACARTHUR: AMERICAN WARRIOR at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Novel Brings Exotic Ghana Background to Life, But Investigation Just Plods Along
text:
GOLD OF OUR FATHERS is the fourth "Darko Dawson" mystery (the first one that I've read), and it works fine as a standalone. Set in Ghana, the novel really brings this exotic (to U.S. readers) background to life, with its widespread poverty, corrugated-tin-roofed buildings, and police stations so underfunded that detectives must hire taxis to reach crime scenes. As one character notes: "This is Ghana. You do whatever you can to get money." Unfortunately, as a police procedural, the novel is a plodder, as it follows the likeable Chief Inspector Darko Dawson from place to place and interview to interview.

In the novel, Dawson is unexpectedly transferred, for one year, from the Criminal Investigations Division at Accra to the position of supervising Crime Officer at Obuasi, a backwater even by Ghanian standards. Upon his arrival, he finds that the police headquarters is a disorganized mess, and that its undisciplined officers seem to have forgotten the Ghanian Police Service motto ("To Protect and Serve with Honor").

On Dawson's second day, two "galamsey" gold miners discover the mine's Chinese owner buried in the gravel pit they are working. The owner was tied up, wrists to ankles, and buried alive. By the time Dawson reaches the scene (by hired taxi, fee negotiated), the body has been dug up, removed to a shack, and washed. Also, the crime scene has been thoroughly trampled by curious onlookers. Dawson's investigation is further complicated by language difficulties--knowing no Chinese, he must interview suspects and witnesses who speak neither English nor any Ghanian language.

Dawson also encounters hatred--by Ghanians for the immigrant Chinese who are destroying the Ghanian landscape with their illegal gold-mining operations; by the Chinese for the Ghanians that they see as "lazy black people wanting money for no work"; by the mine workers for their cheating bosses who make them wait for their daily pay. Naturally the highly competent detective Dawson finds a way to solve the crime despite all these obstacles.

GOLD OF OUR FATHERS is well-written, but in rather formal English. That, along with all the attention the author pays to describing the Ghanian locale, and the author's decision to sprinkle in authentic Ghanian words to add verisimilitude, makes for an extremely slow-moving mystery novel. (There is an excellent glossary of Ghanian words, with easy-to-understand definitions, in the back of the book; there is a map of Ghana and a helpful cast of characters in the front of the book.) The plot is complex and satisfying; but because the narrative just plods along, I rate this novel at a somewhat stingy 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Scholarly History of Rise and Expansion of For-Profit Learning Institutions in U.S.
text:
DIPLOMA MILL$: HOW FOR-PROFIT COLLEGES STIFFED STUDENTS, TAXPAYERS, AND THE AMERICAN DREAM is a scholarly, footnoted history (from colonial times to the present day) of the rise and expansion of for-profit colleges and universities (FPCUs) in the United States. It focuses on "the long history of interplay between national policy and predatory behavior critical to understanding current debates over the for-profit industry." The book's goal, the author tells us, is "producing a substantive history with an eye toward the long view that could help us put recent events within their broader context."

The book achieves this goal, but it's a dry-as-dust, boring history. I was expecting to learn details about how specific fraudulent schools operated (e.g., how they recruited students, how they manipulated financial reports to keep government funds coming, what kind of lasting damage they did to their failing students, whether they helped any students). Unfortunately, there is little anecdotal material about the exploited students themselves.

Information about the FPCUs' actual fraudulent practices is usually presented in a detached, generalized fashion--for example, "Along with canvassing, FPCUs recruited students by printing false or misleading advertising in local papers and periodicals. Proprietary schools often marketed themselves under the employment sections of newspapers." There is a lot of description of government programs, such as the G.I. Bill and the Health Education Act of 1965, though not much explanation of how the FPCUs managed to take advantage of particular legislation.

As a scholarly history, DIPLOMA MILL$ is probably a worthwhile book. However, because it pays so little attention to the impact of FPCUs on the exploited students, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Literary Mystery Set in 1942 NYC Weaves Actual Events Skillfully Into Intricate Plot
text:
THE LETTER WRITER spends so much time re-creating the historical setting--New York City as it existed in 1942, right after the luxury liner Normandie caught fire and sank in the harbor--that it becomes a long, slow-moving, literary mystery. This is true even though the rather well-developed characters (detective Woodrow Cain, Jewish letter-writer Danziger, girl friend Beryl) engage in a substantial amount of evidence-gathering and crime-solving in the course of the novel.

In the novel, detective Cain (newly arrived in NYC) is assigned to investigate a "floater" pulled from the Hudson River. Against protocol, he examines the body, and discovers a ticket stub from Yorkville (an area of the city that is populated by immigrants who sympathize with Germany's ongoing cause in Europe); a tattoo reading "Sabine"; and several cigarette burns suggesting torture. Mistaking a newspaper reporter for the coroner's representative, Cain gives these details to the reporter, who publishes them in a news story the next day. When letter writer/information specialist Danziger sees the story, he realizes that publication of the details has placed both Cain's and his own life in danger, and contacts Cain..

The intricate plot proceeds--through alternating chapters told from Danziger's and Cain's separate viewpoints--to reveal a corrupt NYC police department that "loses" crimes as political favors; a secret spying collaboration between U.S. government and military officers and the NYC underworld; and many sordid details of both Cain's and Danziger's past lives. Cain's detective efforts are hampered by Danziger's unwillingness to share information except in tiny "need to know" bits, by a hostile police captain who gives him punitive make-work assignments, by his influential father-in-law's spying, and by his own troubled past (in which he shot and killed his partner, who was his wife's lover).

The novel is extremely well-written, and the plot is successful at providing a convincing imagined explanation for certain very real historical events. (The author's Afterword explains clearly what is real, and what is the author's invention.) However, because the novel is too literary and slow-moving for my taste, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: More Travelogue Than Mystery Novel; Short on Oliver's Bone Analysis
text:
SWITCHEROO, the 18th "skeleton detective" novel, is mostly a travelogue set in Jersey (in the Channel Islands). The mystery plot is thin, and the story is padded out with a lot of descriptions of archeological sites, present-day buildings, unusual geographical features (e.g., tar pits), and restaurant meals enjoyed by the characters. The mystery itself has an historical background, loosely tied to the German occupation of Jersey during World War II.

In the historical part of the novel, two Jersey families agree to swap their infant sons, so that the more sickly child can be evacuated to hoped-for safety in England until the coming German occupation is over. Only the families and their lawyer know about this arrangement. After the war, the evacuated parents return with the child to Jersey, and the parents who remained behind make good on their promise to deed over Jersey property in return for their child's safety. The children grow up, but both are murdered (the bones of one are recovered from a tar pit), and their murders remain unsolved.

In the present-day bulk of the novel, a bored Gideon Oliver is recruited by a high-ranking Jersey politician (Rafe Carlisle) to examine the tar pit bones (which are purported to include some of his father's bones). Rafe is a wealthy forensics enthusiast, and is curious to know what bone expert Oliver will have to say. From the outset, Oliver is suspicious of the official findings--which determined that the tar pit bones were the bones from two persons of specific ages--because specific ages cannot be determined from the examination of bones alone.

As always happens in mystery novels, it would have been best if Rafe had let sleeping dogs lie. Oliver's investigation naturally leads to another murder. In the course of his investigation, he sees a lot of interesting Jersey buildings, eats some excellent Jersey food, and learns a lot about the history and political structure of Jersey. Eventually Oliver solves the old, cold case, and the guilty present-day murderer is brought to justice.

I have read all, or nearly all, of the Gideon Oliver books, and found all of them, including this one, to be enjoyable. However, SWITCHEROO is definitely NOT one of the best of the series. Because it is slow-moving, has a thin mystery plot, and is somewhat lacking in Gideon Oliver's trademark skeleton analysis, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Thinly Fictionalized Account of Cambodian Kidnapping of Italian/American Spy
text:
SUPERNOTES, co-authored by "Agent Kasper" and Luigi Carletti, is a "thriller based on the true story of Agent Kasper." It's well-written, but it reads more like a nonfiction memoir than a fictional thriller. Given that "Agent Kasper" is supposed to be an alias of "a top-level undercover spy who worked for both the CIA and the Italian intelligence services", the reader is probably safe in assuming that this "thriller" is, in fact, a thinly fictionalized account of an actual kidnapping and lengthy Cambodian incarceration of an Italian/American spy.

Being a news/information junkie, I found this book highly disconcerting to read. I really don't like filling my mind with suspect facts, and this book lacks an "Author's Notes" chapter--included in many historical-fact-based thrillers (e.g., [[ASIN:1250058449 The Patriot Threat: A Novel]])--to help the reader sort out fact from fiction. If the authors wanted the world to know about, and believe in, the "explosive secret" that Kasper uncovered, it might have been better for them to write an openly nonfictional account.

In this book, the Italian owner (Agent Kasper) of a Phnom Penh bar is warned by a Cambodian senator that he needs to get out of Cambodia immediately. Unfortunately, the warning comes too late, and Kasper is captured/kidnapped by military personnel at the border. His Italian family's wealth saves his life--as long as they can make payments to the captors, Kasper will be allowed to live.

Kasper is beaten and tortured, and imprisoned under the worst possible conditions. He has been working with "the Americans" to discover the source of the "supernotes" (nearly perfect forgeries of U.S. currency) that are flooding Southeast Asia. However, the Americans have callously abandoned him. Italian diplomats merely look the other way, when informed of the Cambodians' kidnapping of an Italian citizen. So it is up to Kasper's family, and the doggedly persistent lawyer that they hire, to obtain Kasper's release and his safe return to Italy.

Because SUPERNOTES isn't much of a thriller, and makes no attempt to help the reader sort fact from fiction, I rate it at a rather generous 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Manual Barely Scratches Surface of Complex Office 2016 Applications
text:
Like all of the Teach Yourself Visually computer books, TEACH YOURSELF VISUALLY OFFICE 2016 is aimed at novice users. It uses exact screenshots to explain even the simplest procedures (e.g., "Create a New File", found in the opening overview section titled "Office Features").

The screenshots explain every icon, button, tile, screen area, and procedure. They show exactly what the user should be seeing on the display, if the user correctly follows the detailed step-by-step written instructions for the procedure (e.g., "Change Word's Views"; "Create a Pivot Table" (in Excel); "Add and Edit Slide Text" (in PowerPoint); "Create a Database Based on a Template" (in Access); "Create a New Contact" (in Outlook); "Swap Pictures" (in Publisher); and "Navigate One Note"). The screenshots are overlaid with lettered and numbered circles that help the user shift back and forth between the written steps and the appropriate navigational buttons and menus shown in the screenshots.

Although this is a technically sound book, and should be somewhat helpful to rank beginners, it barely scratches the surface of each Office 2016 application (Word, Excel, Powerpoint, Access, Outlook, Publisher, One Note). Thus it is of quite limited value, even to novice Office 2016 users.

I think that beginning Office 2016 users would be better off investing in the individual manuals for the applications they use most, as the manuals become available (e.g., [[ASIN:1119074665 Teach Yourself VISUALLY Word 2016 ]] ). For this reason, I rate TEACH YOURSELF VISUALLY OFFICE 2016 at just 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Terrific Forensics, Too Much Romance in This Complex Literary Mystery/Thriller
text:
In the tradition of Henry James' THE TURN OF THE SCREW, Jonathan Moore's THE POISON ARTIST is a literary mystery that keeps the reader guessing as toxicologist Caleb Maddox assists the San Francisco medical examiner in solving a series of diabolical murders. The killer tortures his victims, but only after drugging them so that they will experience maximum pain. Happily, the reader is spared the details of the torture and the victims' final agonies, as the plot focuses instead on the forensics and police procedures involved in identifying and arresting the killer.

Caleb has broken up with his girlfriend Bridget, who signaled the end of their relationship by throwing a heavy glass tumbler at his head. Escaping her wrath, Caleb leaves home with a head wound and his wallet, and books a room at the famous Palace Hotel. In the hotel bar, he meets a fascinating woman in black, and becomes obsessed with her. Thus the plot splits into parallel threads, tracing (1) the murder investigation, and (2) Caleb's romance and clandestine meetings with the mystery woman.

The San Francisco background is authentic, with accurate descriptions of the western end of Golden Gate Park, downtown San Francisco, the Haas-Lilienthal House, and other Bay Area locations. The forensics are terrific, with discussions of mass spectrometry that ring true to this decidedly nonexpert reviewer. However, there is far too much description of the details of Caleb's romantic interludes (especially the woman's perfume).

The romance causes the plot to bog down, though the pace picks up at the end with an astonishing, exciting finish. Because this mystery/thriller is too literary for my admittedly plebian tastes, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Disappointing Inspector Van Veeteren Mystery, With Boring, Predictable Plot
text:
HOUR OF THE WOLF, the latest Inspector Van Veeteren mystery, was a disappointment. It's boring, and the plot is totally predictable. I correctly guessed every single important development well in advance. The most satisfying aspect of this well-written novel is the way that Chief Inspector Reinhart and his team brainstorm in order to figure out the killer's motives and the nature of the crime--even though they have barely any clues and hardly any help from the all-but-retired former Chief Inspector Van Veeteren.

Readers who are interested in exploring a parent's feelings when a grown child predeceases the parent may like this novel more than I did. However, there are some memorable Van Veeteren musings, particularly this one about the nature of a heinous crime: "There is a sort of twisted logic which is often easier to discover than the logic that governs our everyday actions. As we all know, chaos is the neighbor of God: but everything's usually neat and tidy in hell . . . ."

In HOUR OF THE WOLF, an upstanding citizen hits and kills a teenage boy while driving drunk. He stops at the scene, then leaves. However, he has been witnessed by someone who recognizes him and demands money for maintaining silence. When the blackmailer arrives to pick up his cash, the hit/run driver kills him--except that victim is NOT the blackmailer, but only a courier. Unfortunately for the killer, the murdered courier is a very important person, and the case becomes a must-solve case that receives the attention of all available police resources.

Because the plot is so predictable, I rate HOUR OF THE WOLF at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale). Although I like Chief Inspector Reinhart, Van Veeteren's replacement, I much prefer the series novels where Van Veeteren runs the show and does the detecting.

title: Romantic Historical Mystery With Amusing, Eventful Plot
text:
Sometimes you order a book from the publisher's description, and it turns out to be a decent, well-written book that just isn't your cup of tea. For me, that's THE SECRET LIFE OF ANNA BLANC. It's amusing, has an eventful plot, and is a fast, easy read. But I simply cannot warm to Anna--a wealthy, spoiled, over-protected, turn-of-the-century banker's daughter who will do almost anything to escape from her controlling father's influence and her extremely-well-provided-for but stultifying home life.

This is a romantic quasi-historical mystery. It's a fine novel, if you never think about whether 1907 Los Angeles society could actually produce an independent, rebellious, adventurous young woman like Anna; or whether it would be possible for a young woman with Anna's upbringing (and naiveté) to actually get a job with the police department and proceed to do the things she does. Purely as a matter of personal taste (because I don't care for romantic fiction), I rate this book at 3 stars ("It's okay on the official Amazon scale).

title: Elizabeth I Depicted as Exceptional Ruler, Not as Exceptional Woman
text:
ELIZABETH: RENAISSANCE PRINCE is a readable biography of Elizabeth I that strives to depict the queen as she saw herself. In the Introduction, the author informs us that "Elizabeth was not, primarily, an exceptional woman; she was an exceptional ruler . . . ." Thus, the thesis of this new biography is that Elizabeth descended from a European tradition of ruling women ("princes" despite their gender), and that she thought of herself, first and foremost, as a ruler (a "Renaissance prince").

I cannot quarrel with the thesis (which I would more mundanely state as "Elizabeth thought like a man"), but I don't think that Elizabeth's seeing herself as a "prince" (in the Machiavellian tradition) changes much about our understanding of her as a historical figure. Of course Elizabeth saw herself as a ruler or a potential ruler! After all, she was educated alongside and received the same classical education as Edward Tudor, who was being groomed to become the next king of England (Edward VI).

Thus, for me at least, this biography doesn't seem to plow new ground. (Hardly surprising, given how many books have already been written about the Tudor rulers and about Elizabeth herself.) This "portrait" is presented chronologically (which is reasonable enough in any biography or history book, but hardly exciting). The prose is readable (not overly scholarly), the text is footnoted and indexed, and there is an extensive bibliography of sources.

The illustrations--contemporary drawings and paintings of Anne Boleyn, Elizabeth (from princess to old woman), Edward VI, Mary Stuart, Dudley, Wyatt, Cecil, Phillip II, Machiavelli, and other important personages and items--are well worth looking at. The reproductions of paintings are good to have, because the author frequently introduces into the text her personal interpretations of the portraits and their iconography (e.g., the Pelican as a symbol of Elizabeth's motherly love for her English subjects).

This is a well-done biography of Elizabeth I, but the "Renaissance prince" theme seems like a gimmick to sell books, and I question the need for yet another more-or-less-standard biography of the Virgin Queen. I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Tinker's Cove Inhabitants Plan Silly "Giant Pumpkin Fest" Events
text:
Usually I love cozy mysteries, but CANDY CORN MURDER is mostly cozy, little mystery. The writing is excellent--how many authors can so vividly describe a vandalizing that transforms straw-stuffed, pumpkin-head figures into pornographic displays?--but the story is mostly about the rather mundane daily lives of the inhabitants of Tinker's Cove, Maine, and is very slow-moving.

The story opens with a 1979 crime (an abused wife is clobbered (maybe killed?) with a jar of candy corn). The scene then shifts to present-day Tinker's Cove, which is preoccupied with staging tourist events for its annual Giant Pumpkin Fest. The events include a giant pumpkin weight competition, a pumpkin-throwing-accuracy contest, displays of stuffed pumpkin-head figures, a disk-jockey-managed children's party, an underwater pumpkin-carving contest, and a boat race in carved-out pumpkin vessels. The main character, Lucy Stone, is not only helping to plan the events, but is covering the festival for the local paper.

At first, the only crimes are the "murders" of the leading local growers' giant pumpkins that are damaged prior to their weigh-ins, and the vandalizing of the pumpkin-head-figure displays. But eventually a body is discovered, and Lucy's husband Bill becomes the prime suspect as the person who last saw the victim alive. In the end, both the 1979 murder and the present-day murder are solved, and the perps are more or less brought to justice.

This is my first Leslie Meier cozy mystery, and it certainly did NOT make me want to go back and read the earlier books in the Lucy Stone series. I didn't care for Tinker's Cove or its inhabitants, there wasn't much action, the silly pumpkin festival events were too contrived, and the feminist subtheme dealing with abused wives seemed dated. Also, the ending was very, very easy to guess. I rate CANDY CORN MURDER at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Jitpleecheep Encounters Political Intrigue That Reads Like Science Fiction
text:
Sonchai Jitpleecheep, the only policeman in Bangkok who isn't on the take, is one of my favorite detectives. Forced to work for the utterly corrupt Colonel Vikorn, he performs the tasks that are assigned to him with long-suffering good humor; and he solves crimes, because he is one of those rare policemen who thinks outside the box.

Unfortunately, THE BANGKOK ASSET takes Jitpleecheep through a plot that is more science fiction than mystery/thriller. Jitpleecheep is assigned to investigate the brutal murder of a child whose head was wrenched off by a killer apparently possessed of superhuman strength--perhaps an alien. As it turns out, that is very, very close to the truth. As Jitpleecheep investigates, he quickly finds himself in the middle of high-level political intrigue that involves the auction of an advanced new military weapon--a "transhuman" possessed of such enhanced mental and physical capabilities that the once-merely-human individual relates to ordinary humans in the same way that ordinary humans relate to dumb animals.

THE BANGKOK ASSET is a well-written book that is entertaining to read. Jitpleecheep performs expertly, detects many things, finally learns the identity of his father, and handles himself extremely well (as always). The fictional explanation for the development of the new weapon (the race of transhumans) is fairly plausible and carefully plotted without leaving a lot of loose ends. But at the end, Jitpleecheep is still caught up in the science fiction situation. Apparently the author couldn't think of a way to end the book in a way that would be satisfying to a mystery/thriller fan like myself.

Because the extremely far-fetched plot is complex, full of twists, and entertaining, I rate THE BANGKOK ASSET at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale). But instead of looking forward to reading the next book in this series, I'll be headed back to read the older ones that I've missed so far.

title: Literary Fantasy Mystery With Echoes of "Warehouse 13"
text:
THE BEAUTIFUL BUREAUCRAT is a literary mystery, or more precisely, a literary fantasy mystery. The main characters have relocated from "the hinterland" to find jobs, which clues the reader to the fantasy. The novel touches on "big" universal topics (e.g., spousal love, survival, death, procreation, individuality of souls), but doesn't really say anything memorable about those topics. This novel left me extremely dissatisfied--if it amounts to more than just a story (with some anagrams and number sequences employed as a trick to advance the plot), then the deeper meaning went over my head.

In the story, a young husband and wife relocate from the hinterland in search of a better life. Both find jobs, but the wife's job is a mind-numbing data-entry position. She sticks with the job because the couple is desperately poor--they've been evicted from one place, and are now moving from dreadful sublet to dreadful sublet with little more than the clothes on their backs.

The wife's immediate superior is a faceless bureaucrat memorable only for her terrible bad breath, and for her ability to walk into the wife's windowless cubicle whenever the wife isn't working. The wife must enter dates from stacks of files into a secret database that she doesn't know the purpose of. The job ruins her eyesight and complexion, and the wife becomes paranoid--a paranoia fueled in part by her husband's occasional failure to come home from his job, which he won't discuss, and by his unintelligible cell phone messages. The wife desperately wants a child, and this need, plus her insatiable curiosity about the purpose of the database, are what sustain the mystery.

The novel is well-written (if not particularly quotable), and tightly plotted. It has echoes of the TV series "Warehouse 13", but isn't nearly as entertaining. I rate THE BEAUTIFUL BUREAUCRAT at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Thoughtful Sociology Text--or Protest Organizers' Handbook
text:
If you're thinking of starting, or getting involved in, a contemporary protest movement, then you probably ought to read PROTEST: A CULTURAL INTRODUCTION TO SOCIAL MOVEMENTS. It presents a thoughtful, complete analysis of modern social movements, and is valuable for the "dilemma" sidebars that describe the inevitable problems that accompany organized protest movements, and that must be dealt with by protest organizers.

The dilemmas are:

Janus (do you encourage a collective identity that emphasizes members' similarities, or their differences?);

Dirty hands (will you use deception or money or other suspect tactics to achieve your ends?);

Character work (will you portray your protesters as victims or heroes? will you portray your opponents as villains or clowns?);

Innovation (how far or fast will you push societal boundaries?);

Media (how will you use the media to get attention without being portrayed badly or suffering backlash?);

Organization (how will you keep rules aimed at sustaining the organization from becoming ends in themselves that will destroy your mission?);

Extension (how do you find the right size for your movement to be maximally effective?);

Naughty or nice (how do you choose between tactics that make you appear morally upright and tactics that make you appear stronger and more threatening?);

Identity (how will you manage the collective identity so that subgroups won't split off?);

Band of brothers (how will you keep face-to-face bonds from crowding out the larger group?);

Powerful allies (how can you keep politicians, etc. from twisting your movement to their own needs instead of using their power on your behalf?);

Audience segregation (if you convey different messages to different audiences, how can you avoid being seen as deceitful?); and

Articulation (how do you avoid demobilization resulting from achieving a clearly stated goal?).

PROTEST is, in essence, a textbook for a sociology course--more analytical than practical--though it also functions to some extent as a protest organizer's handbook. The reason I was interested in this book, was that I hoped it would provide some insight into local, recurring protests in Oakland, CA (e.g., Occupy Oakland, multiple ad hoc protests over police brutality in Oakland and other cities), and perhaps offer some explanations for why these protests so often result in looting and vandalism of local businesses. Unfortunately, this topic ("naughty or nice") was barely touched on, and the discussion of Occupy Oakland was extremely superficial.

As a sociology text, PROTEST probably merits 5 stars. However, it was too theoretical and "above the fray" to be of value to me. I rate PROTEST at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Skeleton With Porcelain Teeth Proves Difficult to Identify, Pulls Highly-Placed Belgian Officials Into Van In's Inquiries
text:
FROM BRUGES WITH LOVE is a Belgian police procedural. It has an interesting plot that sustains reader interest, but it's NOT a page-turner. The story constantly switches from the good guys' actions to the bad guys' actions (by following several parallel story lines within each chapter along a fairly straight time line). The story is so cut up, I constantly had to flip backwards to locate the pages where this or that character had been introduced or had last appeared. It didn't help at all, that most of the important characters have names that sound very similar to a U.S. reader like myself (e.g., Van In, Vandaele, Vervoort, Provoost, Vermast, Versavel).

In the book, a child discovers a skeleton (with a pricey set of 24 porcelain teeth) in the back yard of her parents' decrepit home. Unbeknownst to the parents, the property (the Love) had previously housed a whorehouse for rich and influential Belgians, including civil servants, ministers, political party leaders, and businessmen. Because of the porcelain teeth, Inspector Van In expects the skeleton (nicknamed "Herbert") to be easily identified. But Herbert's identification proves elusive, and Van In's investigation stalls. Many of Van In's police and government bosses were once regulars at the Love, and their unwillingness to risk public exposure ties Van In's hands. Also, the man who operated the Love (Aerts) has disappeared. Is Aerts alive? Or is he on the run?

As Van In continues to investigate, he is assisted by his gay partner (Guido), and his beautiful, pregnant wife (Hannelore). Hanne, a deputy public prosecutor, attempts to keep Van In's inquiries within legal bounds. Using some questionable police interrogation tactics, Van In obtains a list of the Love's former clients, and learns that many are now involved with a charitable organization (Helping Our Own) which runs Care House (a property that supposedly houses needy families).
