Helping Our Own is heavily endowed, but has an almost invisible public profile. Could it be that Herbert, the Love, and Care House are all connected? Eventually one of the principal characters is murdered in a most unpleasant way--and this proves key to Van In's eventual unraveling of the case.

Unfortunately, this book's slam-bang ending, which includes a very dangerous undercover operation that is casually assigned to a young, untrained policewoman by Van In, is quite forced and unbelievable. Also, if Belgian law (as described in the novel) is to be believed, then no one in a position of influence in Belgium is ever brought to justice for even the most heinous of crimes. For these reasons, I rate FROM BRUGES WITH LOVE at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale). This is the third Van In novel to be translated into English (for the first, see [[ASIN:1605984469 The Square of Revenge]]).

title: Biographies of Players Who Developed, Popularized MP3 Standard
text:
HOW MUSIC GOT FREE is basically a series of biographies of the players (audio software engineers, music company executives, music pirates) in the development and adoption of the mp3 audio standard that "obsolesced" the compact disc. It's well-written--entertaining and fast-reading, if you like biography--but constantly gets bogged down in too much detail. For example, does it matter that music pirate Dell Glover lived in a rented trailer in the back yard of his mother's home, and left broken parts from his computer repair business out on the trailer's kitchen table?

This well-researched book seems kind of irrelevant, at least to someone like me who has only a casual interest in the history of computers and the Internet. In the Epilogue, author Stephen Witt has this to say about his personal collection of bootlegged mp3 files:

"It had taken me 17 years to amass all these files, but the rise of cloud computing made the whole thing pointless. My hoarding instincts were fading, curating the library was growing more tiresome by the year, and the older drives didn't even work with modern systems. Finally I caved, bought a Spotify subscription, and accepted the reality: what I'd thought of as my personal archive was just an agglomeration of slowly demagnetizing junk."

For me, that statement kind of sums up the history of the mp3. I rate HOW MUSIC GOT FREE at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: An Author's Lifelong Love Affair With Sherlock Holmes
text:
THE GREAT DETECTIVE is a readable, freewheeling account of author Zach Dundas' lifelong love affair with Sherlock Holmes. To write the book, Dundas set out on a personal expedition to discover all there is to know about the great fictional detective. Now he takes his readers along with him on that entertaining journey, and shares all that he found out. His flippant prose is replete with little-known facts: facts about the birth of the detective story; Arthur Conan Doyle's early, poorly compensated efforts as a hack short story writer; the number of replicas of Holmes' rooms at 221B Baker Street in existence around the world; and many, many more.

In theory, the book is a work of literary criticism (because it analyzes the "essential" Sherlock Holmes stories, and is the product of genuine research, if not exactly rising to the level of serious scholarship), but it reads more like a memoir (because it spends so much time on Dundas' boyhood discovery of Holmes' adventures, and on descriptions of where and how he found his facts, and employs such a casual, serendipitous sort of organization). For serious Sherlock Holmes fans, this book is probably immensely entertaining. For more casual Sherlock Holmes fans (like myself), it's a decent summer read. I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Dated Fictionalized Account of Leopold & Loeb's "Thrill Killing"
text:
Meyer Levin's COMPULSION, written in 1956, is a nonfiction novel based on the famous 1924 "thrill killing" committed by Nathan Leopold and Robert Loeb. So much has been written about this particular crime, it's hard for a "true crime" aficionado like myself to accept Levin's portrayal of Leopold and Loeb as fictional characters (as Judd and Artie, respectively) with complicated thoughts (as imagined by Levin) that describe their motivations and feelings during and after the crime.

The book (reissued in modern format) is very well written, but Levin's 1950s style is wordy, resulting in a book that is 456 pages long. It tries the patience of a modern reader accustomed to "sound bites" and fast-reading thrillers. Because it is so speculative, and devotes so many pages to Judd's and Artie's not-very-convincing inner thoughts, COMPULSION doesn't work for me. If I'm going to read about Leopold and Loeb's crime, I'd much rather read a nonfiction account. I rate COMPULSION at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: All About Bernie Gunther's Efforts to Stay Alive During WWII
text:
THE LADY FROM ZAGREB was my first "Bernie Gunther" novel, but it's actually the 10th series novel (for the first three novels, see [[ASIN:B006LFO1DA Berlin Noir]]). As a standalone, it didn't work well for me. I was expecting a mystery/thriller involving an ordinary detective/policeman working at solving crimes in Nazi Germany during WWII--sort of the flip side of the BBC's "Foley's War", I guess. What I got, was a story about a Nazi detective (admittedly not a very good Nazi) who is working the inconsequential Berlin night shift, doing precious little detecting, merely trying not to make waves and to stay alive until the end of the war.

Without a doubt, author Philip Kerr has thoroughly researched his WWII Germany background. My frequent googling verified the details of Nazi uniforms, buildings, and organizational structure, and the biographies of famous Nazi officers. The story in this book begins shortly after the death of Reinhard Heydrich, who (in this fictional series) pulled Gunther (unwillingly) back into the Berlin police forces, and made Gunther an officer in the SD (also unwillingly).

For a new series reader, there isn't much of a story, even though Gunther is a likeable enough character (as a very, very poor Nazi). Early on, Gunther meets with a lawyer who is helping the young widow of a disgraced German industrialist in her attempts to recover her property held by German authorities. When Gunther returns for a second meeting with the lawyer, he discovers the lawyer's body. Sort of out of his jurisdiction, he hands the investigation of the lawyer's death off to someone else. By the end of the book, Gunther discovers the identity of the murderer, as well as the motives of the murderer, but the book itself isn't about the investigation. It's about Gunther following orders and doing whatever it takes to stay alive until the war is over. I did like Bernie Gunther well enough to want to read some of the earlier books in the series.

Because it doesn't work as a standalone, I rate THE LADY FROM ZAGREB at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Rock-Thriller Fiction for  Rolling Stones' Fans?
text:
Author Greg Kihn--whose band has toured with and opened shows for Journey, the Grateful Dead, and the Rolling Stones--puts his insider's knowledge of the 1960s rock-music scene to use in his "Dust Bin Bob" rock-thriller series (which begins with [[ASIN:1497660998 Rubber Soul]], a novel featuring the Beatles). In PAINTED BLACK, Bobby Dingle ("Dust Bin Bob") takes on the hopeless task of trying to save Brian Jones, the deeply troubled founder of the Rolling Stones.

As Kihn states in a preliminary Author's Note: "None of it actually happened. I took all the facts about Brian Jones and fit my story on top of it. . . . Dust Bin Bob, Clovis, and their wives are obviously fictional . . . . At the end of my last novel, . . . I didn't want to let these characters go, . . . so I just kept on writing." Like the author, I really love the delightful Bobby, Clovis, and Erlene characters.

But I didn't love the cardboard famous-name characters (John, Anita, Mick, Keith, Marianne, Jimi, etc.); or the tiresome descriptions of the characters' wild parties and drug trips; or the insider's references to famous performances or pieces of rock memorabilia; or the weird, meandering plot that culminates with Brian's staring into a shaman's magic mirror. To appreciate this novel, I think you must be a rock-music-history buff, or a Rolling Stones' fan. I am neither, and I rate PAINTED BLACK at a generous 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Thin Story--Padded With Repetitive Architectural Description--About Gigantic Mansion's Forgotten, Doorless Room
text:
THE FORGOTTEN ROOM is mostly boring--the first 90 pages consist largely of landscape and architectural description, and the remaining 200 pages are liberally salted with more of the same. Yes, the novel is about a sealed-up, doorless, "forgotten" room, but it would be nice to have more action involving people. There are a couple of vividly described, quite gruesome "incidents" involving suicidal "think tank" researchers, and there is a concluding "escape-from-the-mansion" sequence that doesn't lack for excitement. But the oft-repetitious descriptions of a gigantic mansion's interior hallways, load-bearing columns, piles of renovation tools and debris left abandoned, seldom-accessed vista spots, expensively-appointed private living quarters, and original/altered architectural plans are not interesting enough to carry the story.

The novel is set in Newport, RI, in a gigantic castle-like mansion that houses a long-established "think tank" named Lux. (The building is modeled on England's Knebworth House, which is worth a Google, to get the "big picture" of what the Lux mansion and setting is supposed to look like.) Enigmalogist Jeremy Logan (an expert in the study of enigmas) is summoned to unravel the mystery behind the inexplicable, violent, gory suicide (caught on surveillance video) of a formerly quiet, unassuming Lux researcher, Dr. Willard Strachey. Shortly before his difficult-to-watch suicide, Strachey appeared to be hallucinating, was covering his ears to block out sound only he could hear, and was shouting about voices in his head.

Logan soon learns that Strachey was overseeing the long-postponed renovation of the West Wing of the Lux mansion. Strachey halted the project--immediately discharging all the workers and sending them home--only a few days after discovering the existence of a puzzling, doorless room. Telling no one at Lux about the room, he resealed it, and subsequently committed suicide. When Logan, who is an empath, rediscovers the room and enters it, he feels a malignant presence and hears faint, disturbing piano music. The centerpiece of the spotless, dust-free room is a strange coffin-like apparatus, encased in beautiful rosewood, that has all sorts of odd appendages. Logan's unraveling of the mystery of the room's construction and the machine's purpose (a ghost detector? a summoner of evil spirits? something else?) constitutes the remainder of the story.

Lincoln Child is an accomplished writer, who knows how to write dialogue and description, develop characters, and tell a story. However, the story of the "forgotten room", with all of its architectural-detail padding, is just too thin to support a full-length novel. Also, the supposedly menacing paranormal elements of the story aren't very scary (unlike the details in Preston & Child's [[ASIN:B00FIL1UNM Relic (Agent Pendergast Book 1)]], which is one of the scariest books I've ever read). Not only did I consider not finishing THE FORGOTTEN ROOM, I was also disappointed by the ending, which has rather mundane explanations. Because it is generally so well-written, I rate THE FORGOTTEN ROOM at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Slender Plot Featuring One-Dimensional Serial Killer Who Carves Up Victims' Faces
text:
THE HARVEST MAN is the fourth book in the "Scotland Yard's Murder Squad" series, which begins with [[ASIN:0425261271 The Yard]]. It seems to be a close continuation of the previous series book, which featured Jack the Ripper ([[ASIN:0399166432 The Devil's Workshop]]). This fourth book doesn't work well as a standalone, because a new reader (1) doesn't at all understand the hold that "Saucy Jack" has over Inspector Walter Day; and (2) doesn't know anything about what put the "Harvest Man" into a lunatic asylum or how he escaped from the asylum. (Given the cliffhanger at the end, the fifth book in this series probably won't work as a standalone, either.)

The Harvest Man--who hides in unsuspecting victims' attics (like the harvest spider he is named for)--is murdering married couples, after first carving up their faces. Someone else (could it be the escaped "Jack the Ripper"?) is killing and removing the internal organs of local "working women". The first investigation is being handled by Inspector Tiffany, who reluctantly consults with the deskbound Inspector Day, at Dr. Kingsley's insistence. The second investigation comes to light through former Sergeant Hammersmith's private efforts toward collaring Jack, and also involves Dr. Kingsley and Inspector Day. Most of the plot events center around the activities of Inspector Day's family and friends, and around the activities of two boys and a young wife who have seen, and narrowly escaped from, the Harvest Man.

The book is set in London in the Spring of 1890, though it's somewhat lacking in the historical detail that would firmly anchor it there. In fact, the leisurely murder investigations seemed curiously modern to me. Although the investigators are limited to communicating in person or by messenger, I kept wanting them to pull out their cell phones and get on with it! As previously mentioned, the characters' qualities, backgrounds, and motivations seem to have been developed in earlier series books. I liked Claire, Fiona, Henry, the doctor, and the detectives, but I know little about them beyond their activities in this book. The one really good character is the deaf shopkeeper who insists to everyone that "you don't need to shout". The Harvest Man himself is totally one-dimensional--just a lunatic driven by a single mad obsession that forces him to carve up and remove his victims' faces.

Some reviewers have complained that the crimes are described with too much grisly detail. It's true that the crime scenes are bloody messes, but none of the victims are tortured. The reader isn't subjected to graphic descriptions of a victim's pain or of a sadistic, psychopathic killer's pleasure in inflicting it. For me, grue (lots of blood) is to be expected in a mystery/thriller novel, and it doesn't bother me.

But in my opinion, THE HARVEST MAN isn't worth the time it takes to read it, if you're new to the series. The basic face-carver plot is too slender to justify a full-length novel, and you need to be familiar with the good-person characters already if you're going to care much about what happens to them. Also, I was baffled by the inclusion of several poems from Robert Louis Stevenson's [[ASIN:1402750625 A Child's Garden of Verses]]--were these intended to enhance the historical atmosphere? For these reasons, I rate this mystery/thriller at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Hopelessly Outdated, "The Saint" Belongs to Era of Pulp Fiction
text:
Leslie Charteris was a talented writer, and his memorable character ("the Saint") certainly deserved its immense, long-running popularity. But "the Saint" belongs to the era of pulp fiction--when heroes in thrillers could be painted in very broad strokes, and plots could allow heroes to always wriggle out of ropes, escape from death traps, or save the day by showing up unexpectedly in an airplane with a machine gun at the last possible moment.

It seems pointless to try to revive "the Saint" for today's readers of thrillers. Trash-talking, for "the Saint", means insulting bad guys by addressing them as "precious" or "sweetheart", or by taunting them by "coolly and sweetly" predicting they will lose because he's a superior being who always wins. "The Saint" beats up bad guys because the bad guys deserve to be punished, and because he enjoys it. "The Saint" has four helpers (his "haloes") who do his bidding because of "the Saint's" sheer force of character. Whenever "the Saint's" implausible plan goes awry, he thinks up another implausible plan, which works. When bad guys tie up "the Saint", they always overlook the throwing knives that "the Saint" wears strapped to a forearm and an ankle. "The Saint" has a "signature" (a little stick drawing of a man with a halo) that supposedly strikes fear into the hearts of bad guys who receive the drawing by some means. But for today's readers, the stick figure's oddly feminine pose totally destroys the effect.

Because the three included novellas are mildly entertaining but hopelessly outdated, I rate ENTER THE SAINT at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the Official Amazon Scale).

title: Delightful Aunty Lee's Second Investigation Is Entertaining, But Not a Standalone
text:
AUNTY LEE'S DEADLY SPECIALS is entertaining and fun if you've already read the first "Aunty Lee" ([[ASIN:0062227157 Aunty Lee's Delights]]), but it's not really a standalone. And it's not nearly as well-written as the first book. It seems hastily thrown together, as if to meet a publisher's deadline. This second book lacks the charm, careful writing, and precise plotting of the earlier book, although Aunty Lee herself remains the same--a delightful force to be reckoned with. "Commissioner Raja caught her eye but said nothing. Stopping Aunty Lee was like trying to stop ice melting . . . It's going to happen anyway, you just try to put the bucket in the right place."

In AUNTY LEE'S DEADLY SPECIALS, a big-time lawyer (Mabel Sung) hires Aunty Lee to cater a brunch in celebration of daughter Sharon Sung's elevation to full partner in Mabel's famous law firm, Sung Law. On the menu--at the client's request--is a traditional chicken dish that incorporates black nuts containing cyanide. The dish is poisonous unless all the cyanide is properly removed, and of course Aunty Lee knows how to prepare it right. But naturally the worst happens: Mabel and her generally disliked son Leonard die after eating Aunty Lee's chicken, and Aunty Lee's food shop is closed down while the police investigate their untimely deaths that look suspiciously like murders.

Aunty Lee investigates along with the police (Commissioner Raja, Inspector Salim), and with some help from her illegal foreign "maid" (Nina), and her new "drinks business" partner (Cherril Peters). Aunty Lee's inquiries are also helped along by her extensive contacts among Singapore's well-established elite families, and by her married gay friends (Otto and Joe). All of these are carryovers from the first book. The inquiries eventually involve Aunty Lee with a prayer group that seems to be arranging organ transplants for its members!

The first Aunty Lee book, [[ASIN:0062227157 Aunty Lee's Delights]], sets out many important facts about Aunty Lee that are buried or altogether missing from this sequel. To mention a few: Aunty Lee cooks superb Peranakan food (a special kind of Singaporean cuisine); her bottled delicacies are well-known and admired in Singapore; she's an indefatigable busybody; and she cooks for her friends and family in order to manage them all to her own best benefit.

Because so much of what makes Aunty Lee a memorable character is missing from AUNTY LEE'S DEADLY SPECIALS, and because this book seems so hastily written, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale). As an Aunty Lee fan, I enjoyed the mystery--and I don't want to miss the next Aunty Lee book. However, if this were my first and only Aunty Lee book, I wouldn't be wanting to read another.

title: Bones Never Lie, But This Novel Is Short on Bones
text:
It may be true that BONES NEVER LIE, but there aren't many bones to be analyzed in this latest Temperance Brennan mystery. Of course, the story is all about Tempe--she's pulled into the investigation of a series of Charlotte, NC child abduction/murders because the murders are chillingly similar to three Canadian child abduction/murders that Tempe successfully linked to the despicable Anique Pomerleau after analyzing the buried skeletons of Pomerleau's young victims.

Pomerleau is the perp who got away--and the perp who nearly killed Tempe by lighting her on fire during a dramatic escape. Now Tempe is certain that Pomerleau has relocated to Charlotte, NC to taunt Tempe by murdering more children to commemorate the anniversaries of the earlier children's abduction/murders. Instead of analyzing bones, Tempe's role this time is analyzing the statements of Pomerleau's relatives and of the new and old victims' relatives, in order to track down Pomerleau herself. In one instance, Tempe literally dreams up an interpretation of a few sentences obtained from an old woman with advanced Alzheimer's (and this significantly moves the investigation forward).

The book is properly described as a "page-turner", but only because author Reich has mastered the technique of ending each chapter with a puzzling statement or event that makes the reader want to know what happens next--always ending with something that seems likely to be explained in the very next chapter. So the reader keeps turning the pages, and the story keeps plodding along.

There is hardly any character development--although there is a lot of description of the hard-working Detective Skinny Slidell that might possibly pass for character development. Fans of the entire Temperance Brennan series will want to read this offering for the updates on Tempe's mother and on Tempe's relationship with the emotionally wounded Detective Andrew Ryan.

This is a well-written novel, but it's just a simple mystery story with a little bit of forensic stuff about X and Y chromosomes and about preservation of bodies without embalming fluid. "Heart-pounding" this novel is not, except near the end when Tempe must almost-single-handedly try to prevent the murder of yet another abducted child. Because the novel makes for decent escape reading, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Author Demonstrates Complete Mastery of "Da Vinci Code" Formula for Exciting Page-Turner
text:
THE LINCOLN MYTH demonstrates author Steve Berry's complete mastery of the [[ASIN:0307474275 Da Vinci Code]] formula. To wit: An investigator (Cotton Malone) learns that a widely accepted idea (that under the Constitution, states cannot secede from the United States without permission) is false, and that the long-suppressed truth can be discovered by finding secret documents that were hidden long ago (at the time of the Civil War and the Mormon migration to Utah) by governmental and religious conspirators (early U.S. Presidents and Mormon Church Prophets). The book's plot then tells the story of the investigator's progress toward finding the truth (as he/she uncovers, and pieces together, small bits of information found in obscure, widely separated geographical locations), while overcoming the massive opposition of modern-day descendants of the original conspirators who want the truth to remain hidden from public view at all costs. (In this case, the conspirators want to expose the truth, and the investigators want to keep it hidden--which is an interesting variation on the formula.)

To my mind, there are three good reasons to dislike this book. First, wasn't one [[ASIN:0307474275 Da Vinci Code]] enough? (Well, maybe not--the book is a pretty good read.) Second, the book teaches bad history, by adding a few wholly fictional but convincing documents for the purpose of altering the interpretation of many very real, existing historical documents for the purpose of advancing the plot. (One needs to remember after reading this book that no lost document from the original Constitutional Convention actually exists; and that no "eyes only" letter was ever passed from George Washington to each new President until the practice was ended by Lincoln's assassination.) Third, the book comes across to me as a possible attempt to discredit the worldwide Mormon religion (the Church of Latter-Day Saints), by using Mormon theological documents that the church repudiated long ago for the purpose of advancing the plot. (Very near the end, the book's characters admit that the theological documents have been repudiated, but throughout most of the book, the Mormon religion and certain of its leaders are the evil villains.)

President Lincoln, at least, comes through relatively unscathed, although his reputation as "The Great Emancipator" (a label applied posthumously) is hardly furthered by the book's quotations from Lincoln's pre-Civil-War statements about the rights of slave owners. The novel observes that U.S. schoolchildren are incorrectly taught that Lincoln freed the slaves, and that the Civil War was fought over slavery. I agree that those statements are incorrect, but I certainly hope that schoolchildren aren't still being taught those things. Regardless, the "Lincoln myth" that is the focus of the book is NOT about Lincoln's views on slavery, but about his views on the Union and States' Rights--especially a state's right to secede from the United States.

For lovers of historical fiction who like to keep their historical facts straight, I have a suggestion: Start by reading the "Writer's Note" at the end of the book, in which author Berry promises "to separate the real from the imagined". I found the author's note to be incomplete and often confusing, but his explanations saved me some time. Before I found the "Writer's Note", I spent a lot of time looking up historical facts on the Internet (checking on the authenticity of documents mentioned in the novel that I'd never heard of, or that didn't comport with my existing historical knowledge).

If you like the [[ASIN:0307474275 Da Vinci Code]] type of book, you should enjoy this. It's a skillfully written, extremely well-plotted, fast-moving page-turner of a novel. However, for the reasons stated above, I rate the novel at only 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Female P.I.'s Sugar Addiction Detracts From Reasonably Interesting Story
text:
IDENTITY is a good female P.I. novel, but not a great one. For some 450 pages, private investigator Fina Ludlow interviews (and re-interviews) one person after another, until she collects enough information (sometimes from accidental or coincidental disclosures) to be able to solve the crime. This may accurately reflect what private investigators do, but it's not exactly edge-of-your-seat reading.

The crime in this mystery/thriller is the bludgeoning death of a self-made, high-tech billionaire. It's sort of a locked-room mystery, because the crime happens in the parking garage of the security-conscious billionaire's office building, in an area NOT covered by the building's security cameras. No suspicious persons are caught on the cameras that cover the garage entrances and exits. The suspects are the billionaire's former spouse, his trophy wife, his business partner, the many "cryokids" he fathered in his youth as an anonymous sperm donor (to the Heritage Cryobank), and the Cryobank's employees.

Fina becomes involved in the case because her rich superlawyer father (Carl) is hired by a political activist (Renata) to sue the Cryobank for refusing requests to disclose the identities of its anonymous sperm donors to the donors' cryokids. Fina quickly uncovers Renata's anonymous donor's (the billionaire's) true identity--starting from the minimal information about the donor's age and education that Renata was given when she conceived her daughter (Rosie). After the murder, Fina is hired by the billionaire's acknowledged son (Michael) to investigate and identify the killer. Fina is also involved in parenting her niece (Haley), whose mother was recently murdered, presumably in the first series book ([[ASIN:0425268527 Loyalty (A Fina Ludlow Novel)]]). In the course of the murder investigation, Fina is attacked a couple of times, and Haley's safety is threatened.

Because Fina is the rebellious product of a dysfunctional family, there is much made of her mutual-dislike relationships with her parents. Her father employs her in "the Ludlow family business", so she isn't hurting for money; however, father and daughter barely tolerate each other. Her mother (Elaine) constantly criticizes her eating habits, which seems pretty reasonable. Fina not only doesn't cook, she survives almost entirely on food cadged from interviewees and friends (chocolate mousse, diet soda, salmon filet, vegetarian smoothie, whatever is available); and she supplements this with fluffernutters for breakfast, coffee-shop donuts, machine-dispensed candy bars, pantry-stocked peanut butter cups, and still more diet soda. Reading about this unhealthy, unbelievable "all-sugar diet" is kind of sickening, and interferes with identifying with her as a strong female protagonist.

This well-written story was interesting enough to keep me reading, but the book failed to spark interest in the "Fina Ludlow, P.I." character, or in prior or subsequent books in the series. I rate IDENTITY at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Victorian Detective's Confusing Investigation Into Details of Poet Shelley's Household Life
text:
In A FATAL LIKENESS, Victorian-era detective Charles Maddox is hired by Sir Percy Shelley (the son of romantic poet Percy Bysshe Shelley and Mary Shelley) to spy on his mother Mary's step-sister (Claire Clairmont), and to negotiate a deal for any papers Claire may possess that would tarnish the poet Shelley's character and/or literary legacy. In the course of his investigation, Maddox uncovers horrifying facts about the poet's household--the true stories behind the suicides of the poet's first wife (Harriet Westbrook) and his second wife's half-sister (Fanny Imlay), and the infant deaths of the poet's first three children (an unnamed girl, William, and Clara).

Although I loved the first Charles Maddox novel, [[ASIN:0345532422 The Solitary House]], I had a hard time warming to this one. Lacking familiarity with the details of Percy Bysshe Shelley's life, I was frequently confused by the plot as it was slowly revealed through documents discovered by Maddox. Every now and then, Maddox would read something and experience an epiphany of sorts, even as I was left wondering what Maddox was seeing that I couldn't see. My confusion persisted to the very end, and not even the author's interesting closing biographical comments could clear things up satisfactorily. I do applaud the author's decision to include the poet's genealogical chart at the novel's beginning, as this helps the reader to keep the characters' confusing relationships straight.

Sadly, A FATAL LIKENESS lacks the "authentic" Dickensian flavor of the first Charles Maddox book. The focus is almost entirely on Maddox's investigation of the details of the poet Shelley's relationships (although there is some exploration of happenings in Maddox's own household), so there is little descriptive detail about Maddox's Victorian surroundings. The all-knowing author viewpoint that I loved so much in the first novel is still there, but in a disconcerting way. Is it really a good idea for an all-knowing author to step in and talk about 20th-Century forensic and medical developments (e.g., DNA, genetics) in the midst of a Victorian mystery, even though the author observes that Maddox could not have known about these things?

Because the author's mystery story--which attempts to explain various unusual occurrences and gaps in what is known about Percy Bysshe Shelley's life--doesn't work for me, I rate A FATAL LIKENESS at 3 stars ("it's okay" on the official Amazon scale). However, I'd still like to see more of detective Charles Maddox. If there are sequels, this book is a must-read for Maddox's fans, because of the extremely important personal events that occur within Maddox's household.

title: Cheese Lover's Breezily Written Travel Memoir, With Factoids
text:
For some reason, I expected THE WHOLE FROMAGE to be a reference book about French cheese. Indeed, the book includes (1) a short appendix that lists six Parisian fromageries, (2) a short glossary of fromagespeak, (3) a brief bibliography of eight cheese reference books, and (4) a substantial number of footnotes. But it's definitely not a reference work: it's a cheese lover's breezily written travel memoir, gussied up with a gazillion cheese factoids.

The book devotes a chapter to each of several types of French cheese (Salers, Maroilles, Chevre, Camembert, Beaufort, Comte, Roquefort, Langres), and talks a lot about traditional methods of cheesemaking (and how the old ways are falling by the wayside). However, the narrative seems to be organized largely by the author's free association; in particular, the copious factoids are dropped in all over the place, apparently whenever the author happens to think of them.

Although it's interesting to know, for example, that the stinkiest French cheeses are formed by a process that uses the bacterium that causes human foot odor, it's hard to take away any real understanding of French cheese from this author's style of narrative. THE WHOLE FROMAGE is probably best viewed as an "entertainment" for cheese lovers who enjoy reading about food. For this reason, I rate it at 3 stars ("it's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Well-Written Novel, Easy-to-Guess Ending
text:
THERE WAS AN OLD WOMAN is creepy, at least at the beginning. A young museum curator (Evie) returns to her childhood home to deal with the affairs of her elderly, alcoholic, terminally-ill mother. Evie is astonished to find that her mother's house has become virtually uninhabitable. A few months earlier, at Evie's last visit, the house was merely disorganized and cluttered. Now the rooms are entirely filled with hoarder's debris, the plumbing is leaking below the foundation, the porch steps are rotted, the bedding is filthy and disgusting, a broken upstairs window is letting squirrels in, roaches and rodents have taken over, and the car in the garage is leaking gasoline.

Yet Evie's mother has plenty of cash and a brand-new HD television set. What earthly--or unearthly--presence could have caused such a rapid deterioration in the house and in Evie's mother in so short a time? Then, as Evie seeks answers, strange things begin to happen inside the home of the elderly woman (Mina) who lives next door. Whatever happened to the papers that Mina quickly hid under the sofa cushions? Why are Mina's gas burners and smoke alarm suddenly malfunctioning? Why doesn't Mina remember previously confronting her across-the-street neighbor about polluting the nearby marsh? And how can it be that Mina's elderly neighbor up the street has passed away so suddenly and unexpectedly?

In this book, a deteriorating urban neighborhood, filled with older homes populated by long-time inhabitants, is beautifully described. Perfectly ordinary homes (the homes belonging to Evie's mother and Mina) are at times transformed into truly frightening places. The difficulties that a daughter encounters in accepting a mother's terminal illness, in making end-of-life-care decisions, and in settling a parent's estate are skillfully handled. The problems that inevitably arise when an elderly population is "aging in place" are sympathetically portrayed, and are shown as potentially dangerous and life-threatening.

However, despite all the interesting questions posed early on, and despite the excellent writing about important and timely elder care issues, THERE WAS AN OLD WOMAN failed to capture and hold my attention. It began as a mystery/thriller page-turner, but quickly turned into rather insubstantial literature, and I correctly guessed the ending about halfway through. Because the book doesn't deliver as an entertaining mystery/thriller, I rate this book at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Collection of Patterns for Reasonably Cute Toys
text:
KNITTED CATS & KITTENS has patterns for some reasonably cute knitted toys, but most don't look much like cats or kittens to me. My favorites are: "Fluffy Cat" (a fairly realistic kitten, knit in white angora yarn); "Floppy Moggy" (a fairly realistic "longhair" kitten, knit in black fur yarn); "Doorstop Cat" (a brown knitted doorstop); "Monster Cat" (a turquoise alien cat with wide-open red mouth); and "Cosy Toes" (a cat-shaped hot water bottle cover, knit in fur wool yarn).

A cute twist is the inclusion of patterns for "accessories" for the cat toys: a scratching post, a cat bed, balls for batting around, and tiny mice. There is also a kitten in a Christmas stocking with a mouse on the toe, to be used as a tree decoration. As knitted toy patterns go, these patterns don't look particularly difficult. However, they do require knitting a lot of small, shaped pieces that must be seamed up, stuffed, and sewn together.

Because I don't like any of the designs well enough to want to knit them, I rate KNITTED CATS & KITTENS at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale). The "Look Inside This Book" feature shows all of the included designs as a gallery in the Table of Contents. Cats seem to be difficult to translate into knitted toys, but if you're looking for patterns for knitted cats, you might want to consider [[ASIN:1579128939 Knit Your Own Cat: Easy-to-Follow Patterns for 16 Frisky Felines]], a book of patterns for small "pedigreed" cats to display.

title: Collection of Randy Cohen's Advice Columns From the New York Times
text:
BE GOOD is a collection of ethical advice columns that author Randy Cohen wrote for the New York Times (as "The Ethicist") between 1999 and 2011. The gnarly ethical dilemmas submitted by NYT readers are interesting, but I wasn't particularly impressed by Cohen's analytical replies. Quite frequently, I disagreed with Cohen's ultimate conclusions about what would constitute ethical behavior, and I often felt that the arguments he raised were illogical, or strayed too far off topic in an effort to find "a way out" of a reader's basically impossible situation.

For example, parents asked about allowing a teenage daughter to see her boyfriend in their home, when the boy's parents forbade his dating, and the boy was using their telephone to lie to his parents about his whereabouts. Cohen tells the parents they aren't responsible for enforcing other parents' rules, but that they are teaching the kids that it's okay to break parents' rules that seem unfair, if only the kids can locate parents with more permissive rules. Cohen's eventual conclusion is that the parents should tell the kids they can continue to see each other in public places but cannot continue to meet in the parents' home.

I wonder what Ann Landers might have said about this? Probably she would have given a black-and-white answer that I'd be more comfortable with. In this case, I worry that if the parents follow Cohen's advice, the kids will simply find another semi-private or private place to meet, keeping their relationship secret from all four parents--and how can that be right? Obviously, if you question many of Cohen's arguments and conclusions, as I do, he is not your first choice among advice columnists. However, if you're generally interested in unraveling ethical dilemmas, Cohen's columns will give you plenty of food for thought.

Cohen has organized his NYT columns into chapters (Family, Home, Doctors & Nurses, Civic Life, Money, Animals, Sports, Work, Arts, Technology, Community, School, In Transit, Love & Sex, Religion, and 9/11, Iraq, Afghanistan). He has also added introductory material to each chapter that raises one or more timely ethical issues that are related to the general topic. For example, in the introduction to the Doctors & Nurses chapter, he talks about the ethics of imposing a government tax on sugary beverages in order to combat the current "epidemic" of obesity in America.

I rate BE GOOD at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale). However, I think that new, current, and long-time readers of "The Ethicist" column in the New York Times are likely to enjoy this collection of older columns very much.

title: Collection of Patterns for Fibre Company Yarn
text:
KELBOURNE WOOLENS VOLUME 1 is a collection of patterns written for Fibre Company yarn. There are some shawl patterns that I like ("Linden", "Mountain Ash", "Springtime Bandit"), and the photos are nice, but this is basically another yarn company pattern book. For this reason, I rate it at a generous 3 stars ("It's OK" on the official Amazon scale).

If you're looking for a specific design that you want to knit, this book includes the following patterns:

"Alice" scarf by Antonia Shankland
"Give a Hoot" mittens by Jocelyn Tunney
"Hawthorne" cardigan by Courtney Kelley
"Hiker's Waistcoat" vest by the Fibre Company Design Team
"Kiva Hattu" hat by Courtney Kelley
"Linden" shoulder shawl by Courtney Kelley
"Mountain Ash" half-circle shawl by Kate Gagnon Osborn
"Selbu Modern" hat by Kate Gagnon Osborn
"Springtime Bandit" triangular scarf by Kate Gagnon Osborn
"Springtime in Philadelphia" hat by Kate Gagnon Osborn
"Winthrop" open-front sweater by Kate Gagnon Osborn

title: Dolls That Illustrate Six Favorite Fairy Tales
text:
Generally I love Fiona Goble's books with designs for knitted toys, but I definitely do not care for FAIRY TALE KNITS. It's a collection of little knitted dolls that recreate the characters from "Little Red Riding Hood", "Rapunzel", "Hansel and Gretel", "Goldilocks and the Three Bears", "The Three Little Pigs", and "Beauty and the Beast". The figures are pleasant enough, but I can't imagine what I would do with them after putting in the effort it would take to knit and stuff them. A gift for a child? A "Rapunzel" diorama? A teaching tool in an elementary classroom?

Some of the Goble books that I really like are these: [[ASIN:1908005483 Knit Your Own Zombie]], [[ASIN:1449411312 The Twelve Knits of Christmas]], and [[ASIN:B006CDDABK Knit Your Own Royal Wedding]]. All of these have characters that I think would be fun to knit and would make interesting displays. Because I can't see the need for dolls that illustrate these six well-loved fairy tales, I rate FAIRY TALE KNITS at 3 stars ("It's OK" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Another Collection of Previously Published Patterns From Vogue Knitting Magazine
text:
THE ULTIMATE HAT BOOK is another collection of patterns that were mostly published previously in Vogue Knitting magazine: this time the focus is hats. Perhaps to justify the "ultimate" title, the editors have added 10 pages of "Hat Basics" at the beginning of the book. The "Basics" topics are: History of Knitted Hats (interesting, but only 2 pages); Anatomy of a Hat (definitions of "visor", "band", etc.); Types of Hats (cloche, chullo, etc.); and Basic Techniques (knitting in the round, knitting back and forth, yarn selection, etc.).

The "Hats Off to Knitting" introduction states that the editors culled the magazine archives for "favorite and most enduring" designs, and also asked current designers to submit new designs for "their perfect hat". Unfortunately, there's no way to tell which designs are new, and which are reprinted (short of pulling out your old magazines). Some of the reprinted patterns were originally written for now-discontinued yarns, so the editors have substituted available yarns. To the editors' credit, the discontinued yarns are fully described in the "Helpful Information" at the back of the book.

When the VK magazine patterns were originally published, the hat designs were fresh and fashionable. However, as collected in this book, the reprinted patterns seem dated and somewhat dull, and the new patterns don't stand out from the rest. The book's layout doesn't help. A colored band on each right-hand page lets you fan the book pages to find the pattern categories (Basic Shapes, Cables, Lace, Color, Embellishments), but this restricts the full-page model photos to the left-hand pages, resulting in a predictable, boring presentation.

The patterns have clear, written-out instructions supplemented by charts as necessary. There aren't any patterns for very simple, basic hats (which I think should be part of any "ultimate" hat book). I like some of the hat designs very much--for example, "Brioche Swirl Hat", "Plaid Tam", "Cabled Pillbox", "Hood" (but my goodness, all that moss stitch!), "Beanie", and "Bowler". Nevertheless, because I simply can't get excited about this collection, I rate THE ULTIMATE HAT BOOK at 3 stars ("it's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Collection of Patterns for Rowan Tweed Yarns
text:
Martin Storey is one of my favorite designers, but this collection has only two patterns that I would consider knitting: the Skye Poncho (with an elaborate interlocking cable in front), and the Cromarty (aka "Aviemore") coat (sideways-knit, with Fair Isle fronts and collar, and fishtail triangles in back).

Apparently the book is titled SCOTTISH KNITS because the designs are named after places in Scotland ("Aberdeen Argyll", "Caithness Socks", etc.), and are accompanied by uncaptioned stock photos that probably were taken in these locations. The knitted models are NOT photographed on location. Generally the designs include "Scottish" elements, such as tartan patterns, Aran cables, and Fair Isle colorwork motifs. I have no idea what the "Twist" mentioned in the book's subtitle might be, because none of the cabled designs seem to use any new or unusual knitting techniques. There is minimal description of each pattern, no discussion of "Scottish" knitting per se, and only a very general two pages of "knitting know-how" at the back.

The book cover shows two of the prettier sweater designs ("Portree Sweater" and "Ross Cardigan"). The colorways in these sweaters are typical--overall the colorways used in the book's designs seem rather odd to me: gray and black; predominately pink and green; large areas of red, green, gold, and white. Because SCOTTISH KNITS strikes me as just another pattern collection intended to sell Rowan yarn (Fine Tweed, Felted Tweed, and Tweed), I rate it generously at 3 stars ("it's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Delivers on Devil Creature, But Mostly Describes Life in Locked Mental Institution
text:
THE DEVIL IN SILVER is more a critique of the American mental health treatment system than a work of fiction designed to entertain a reader. I was intrigued by the publisher's book description about a devil "with the body of an old man and the head of a bison", and expected this lengthy 406-page novel to be a fantasy/science fiction or mystery/thriller book. However, although the book delivers on the bison-headed devil--it's truly a creature of nightmares--the book is mostly devoted to chronicling the indignities and activities that are experienced daily by mental patients who are confined to a locked ward.

In the plot, the main character, a big man who is a furniture-mover (Pepper), is dropped off at New Hyde Hospital for a 72-hour hold after assaulting three cops while resisting arrest. He is greeted by Dorry, a permanent inmate who knows all the ropes, who takes him under her protective wing. But Pepper soon gets into a fight with another inmate, is subdued by the staff, and heavily "medicated". A few months later, he wakes up from a drug-induced haze, and finds himself upgraded to an "involuntary admittee" who cannot be released without the indifferent staff psychiatrist's approval. Lacking anyone on the outside to go to bat for his release, Pepper is stuck.

The rest of the plot is driven mostly by character development. Pepper, Dorry, Loochie, Coffee, Josephine, Frank, and Xiu are all fairly memorable. Otherwise, the plot is taken up with the inmates' daily routines, their methods of protecting themselves from the murderous devil, and their schemes for finding a permanent solution to the "devil problem". One full chapter recounts the life of the famous mental patient Vincent Van Gogh.

In describing Pepper's lengthy stay, the book touches on the many unpleasant realities of life in a mental institution: inadequate food; lack of telephone access; the staff's "herding" mentality; dispensing of severe punishments (e.g., restraints, withholding food, heavy medication) for minor rules infractions; the staff's inattention to serious inmate health issues and injuries; sluggish investigative response to incidents resulting in inmate deaths; the "hardening" of nurses who were once caring individuals. Author Lavalle achieves this in part with an "all-knowing author" viewpoint: the viewpoint focuses on Pepper, but sometimes shifts to reveal the thoughts of other inmates and psychiatric unit staffers; and sometimes the author inserts a "news report" explaining how the fictional situation in the plot is a situation that actually exists in present-day American mental institutions.

The plot isn't very exciting, and I nearly stopped reading THE DEVIL IN SILVER at the end of the first 109 pages (Volume I, "Intake"). But the book got better, so I finished it. Because this novel is well-written but dull, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

title: A Study of Relationships--Not Much of a Thriller
text:
If Val McDermid weren't known for her thrillers, I would classify THE VANISHING POINT as chick lit. Although there is a kidnapping at the beginning, and some murders surface toward the end, nearly all of the book is devoted to describing the unlikely bonds of friendship forged between a ghost writer (Stephanie) and her reality-TV-star client (Scarlett).

When Stephanie's ward (Jimmy) is kidnapped before her eyes, Stephanie's emotional response causes U.S. airport security personnel to detain her as a terrorist. By the time they recognize their mistake, the kidnapper and child are long gone. Worse, the kidnapping investigation is handicapped by the nearly total absence of suspects. Jimmy's parents (Scarlett and Joshu) are dead, his grandparents aren't interested in him, and the most likely suspect is Stephanie's old stalker boyfriend (Pete).

To further the investigation, Stephanie participates in hours of interrogation by the airport security chief (Vivian). Thus, almost entirely in flashback, Stephanie recounts how she met Scarlett, how their friendship blossomed, how they helped each other through their various personal crises, and how Scarlett came to name Stephanie as Jimmy's guardian after Scarlett developed terminal cancer. The story is moderately interesting, although I only lasted for 197 pages of this 434-page novel before I read the ending to find out whether the rest was worth reading. The ending was good enough that I read the intervening 200-plus pages, but this was still a very, very long book.

The story includes a lot of description of (1) strategies for becoming a reality TV star, (2) methods used by a successful ghost writer, (3) undermining tactics used by a controlling boyfriend, (4) ways that the rich and famous deal with paparazzi, (5) evading a stalker boyfriend, (6) the inability of lawyers and law enforcement officials to help a stalker victim absent clear-cut threats, and (7) the terrible effects of chemotherapy and cancer. Not surprisingly, Stephanie's soul-baring to security officer Vivian during the grueling interrogation fails to advance the official investigation. Eventually Stephanie solves the kidnapping mystery with self-help measures--and the assistance of a handsome, unattached police officer (Nick).

If you're a Val McDermid fan, I'd say wait for the paperback; if you're not already a fan, I'd suggest you start with one of McDermid's more typical (and excellent) thrillers (e.g., [[ASIN:B003J5UJ5O The Wire in the Blood]], which inspired a TV mystery series). Because THE VANISHING POINT is well-written and sort of interesting, but more of a psychological relationship study than a thriller, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's OK" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Good Reference for Moderately Knowledgeable Knitters
text:
Lori Ihnen, the author of COLORWORK FOR ADVENTUROUS KNITTERS, is clearly an expert knitter who thoroughly understands colorwork knitting. In each book section (stripes, slipstitch/mosaic, stranding, intarsia, duplicate stitch/embroidery), she touches on all of the important technical issues, such as fixing "jogs" in striped or stranded circular knitting, or carrying colors in Fair Isle (stranded) knitting so that the motifs will stand out from the backgrounds.

However, I don't believe that Ihnen's step-by-step technical instructions are systematic enough or complete enough to teach new knitters all the things they ought to know when learning to do each type of knitting. For example, in talking about intarsia knitting, Ihnen notes that the "[t]he main technique with intarsia is the twist or interlock of one color to the next", and that "[i]f you do not interlock your color changes, you will produce holes in your work." She then goes on to talk about making yarn butterflies, without ever explaining what is meant by "twist or interlock". On a following page, "interlocking" is illustrated with photos of actual knitting, but I know that I would find the author's accompanying written instructions very confusing if I were just learning to do intarsia knitting. When I was starting out, I was mystified by instructions that mentioned "twisting" the yarns--and only after taking some knitting classes did I understand that the yarns are not "twisted" at all but only laid across each other at color changes.

COLORWORK FOR ADVENTUROUS KNITTERS has beautiful, full-color photographs of a limited number of colorwork techniques, some nice colorwork design patterns, and some simple colorwork projects. Overall, the book seems like a very good set of knitting class notes--if you already know something about colorwork knitting, then it's an excellent reference that includes many advanced tips that are easy to forget when class is over. I rate this book at 3 stars ("It's OK" on the official Amazon scale).

If you're a new knitter who wants to learn to do colorwork knitting, there are several books that I would particularly recommend. The classics are [[ASIN:B0006S8CGK Intarsia: A workshop for hand & machine knitting]]; [[ASIN:0486472183 Alice Starmore's Book of Fair Isle Knitting]]; [[ASIN:094201815X Mosaic Knitting]]; and [[ASIN:1883010322 Slip-Stitch Knitting]]. In addition, there are a couple of recent, very good comprehensive books that I like much better than this one: [[ASIN:1603420401 The Essential Guide to Color Knitting Techniques]]; and [[ASIN:0307586502 Mastering Color Knitting: Simple Instructions for Stranded, Intarsia, and Double Knitting]].

title: Recipes for Cooking With Commercial Pantry-Shelf Foods
text:
SIMPLE RECIPES FOR USING FOOD STORAGE is an attractive, spiral-bound recipe book. It includes many very basic recipes for cooking with standard dried and canned pantry-shelf foods (e.g., cracked wheat, powdered milk, vinegar, dried beans, dried pasta, canned fruits and vegetables, canned tuna). The recipes are all for ordinary ingredients and dishes that many cooks will already know how to prepare (e.g., Basic Cooked Cracked Wheat, German Pancakes, Refried Beans, Tuna Noodle Casserole, Baked Rice Pudding, Ham Hock Soup, Apple Crisp).

The book has a couple of fairly useful tables: (1) substitutions for recipe ingredients (e.g., corn syrup), and (2) food shelf life (e.g., sugar keeps for 20+ years). This book might be good to store with a household emergency food supply made up of commercially dried and canned foods. It also might be useful to a busy person who doesn't do much home cooking but keeps the pantry stocked for occasional "eating in". Because SIMPLE RECIPES FOR USING FOOD STORAGE is nicely designed and printed but duplicates the recipes and information found in most general cookbooks (e.g., [[ASIN:1588168131 The Good Housekeeping Cookbook]]), I rate it at 3 stars ("It's OK" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Well-Written Mystery Set in 1925 Shanghai and Cambodia
text:
THE MAP OF LOST MEMORIES is a very well-written book, but the story is something of a snooze. Set in 1925, the plot centers on Irene, a former assistant Seattle museum director and expert on Cambodian art--particularly Khmer art (e.g., the temple at Angkor Wat). After losing a promised museum director promotion and resigning in disgust, Irene receives an antique missionary's diary from a wealthy mentor/father figure. The diary, which includes a hand-drawn map, reveals the possible location of 10 storied copper scrolls that purportedly contain the entire lost history of the Khmer civilization.

Funded by the mentor, Irene sets off to Shanghai to assemble an expedition to find the remote temple in the Cambodian jungle where the missionary said he saw the scrolls. Following the mentor's advice, Irene recruits four key persons for the expedition: Simone, a female Chinese Communist revolutionary; Marc, the mentor's barely-acknowledged son; Louis, the official curator of the Angkor Wat ruins; and Clothilde, the mentor's nurse. Each has plans for the scrolls that widely diverge from Irene's own plans.

In chapter 16 (of 26), Irene and Simone finally board a slow steamer, the Alouette, which carries them to Saigon. In chapter 18, Irene's expedition finally moves forward into the Cambodian jungle, and subsequently encounters various more-or-less expected obstacles which threaten the success of their expedition of discovery. Their ultimate discoveries are intriguing, although borderline believable, and rather anticlimactic.

The bulk of the book deals with Irene's gradual discovery of long-hidden family secrets. Much is made of Irene's deep-felt attachment to the Khmer and the Khmer civilization, but the book never quite sold me on the idea that this sort of attachment could actually develop in a child growing up in the United States. What is most interesting about this book, is the descriptions of early-20th-century Shanghai, Saigon, rural Cambodia, and the accommodations available to European travelers in the Far East at that time. Also interesting is the general background regarding the French colonial rule of Cambodia. All of the historical backdrop seemed quite plausible to me, though I know little about Shanghai or Cambodia at any time period.

Because I can't see myself recommending this book to a friend, even though I enjoyed reading it in leisurely fashion, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's OK" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Fewer Snowflakes Than Expected
text:
When I ordered 100 SNOWFLAKES TO CROCHET, I expected more snowflakes, and fewer motifs. My idea of a crocheted snowflake is a delicate, six-armed figure with irregular outside edges. Although some real snowflakes are simple hexagons, so that any six-sided crochet motif can reasonably be called a "snowflake", this book's many hexagonal figures with straight outside edges don't look much like snowflakes to me.

However, the book has at least 37 pretty snowflake patterns, and 63 attractive motif patterns. The motifs can be joined together into lacy table coverings, scarves, or other traditional items. There are simple instructions for blocking and stiffening the snowflake figures, and some suggestions for using them to decorate clothing or pillows, in framed wall decorations, to construct a mobile, or to make simple hanging decorations (like tree ornaments).

All of the designs have both written out and charted instructions, and are shown with clear, close-up photos. Because this is basically another book of nice crochet motifs, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's OK" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Pretty But Time-Consuming Patterns for Knitted Gifts
text:
I really liked designer Lucinda Guy's earlier book of Scandinavian knitting patterns, [[ASIN:1596681713 NORTHERN KNITS]]. This sequel, NORTHERN KNITS GIFTS, isn't nearly as interesting. Because the book is published by Interweave Press, it has beautiful photographs, lovely charts, and clear pattern instructions. But there are only a few designs that I would actually want to knit--and nearly all of the complex designs require much more knitting time and effort than I would be willing to invest in "gift" knitting. Many are charted Fair Isle designs, and most are knit at 5-7 stitches per inch, so they're NOT quick knits.

The designs I liked best are the Tovio Mittens and Hat (Fair Isle knitting, shown on the book's cover), the red-and-white Freja Twined Scarf (two-ended knitting), the delicate white Dimitie Scarf (Shetland lace, shown in "Look Inside"), the Birta Twined Hat with simple flower-design border (Sweden-inspired), the stylized hen-shaped Oluffa Doorstop (Faroe Islands, shown in "Look Inside"), the colorful lice-patterned Onni Child's Sweater and Hat (Finland, shown in the "Look Inside" photo montage), and the felted brown Noomi Slippers with classic Norwegian star on the instep (Norway).

Not so successful (to my eye) are the Liisi Open Cardigan (Estonian knitting, with nupps and flowers on the shoulders and lace body, shown in "Look Inside"), the shaped, drab ecru/white Marna Woman's Cape (Faroe Islands), the plain gray man's Fridmar Hat (Iceland, shown in "Look Inside"), the oddly colored Mootie Fair Isle Socks (Shetland, shown in "Look Inside"), the bird-motif Ida Icelandic Lace and Patterned Mitts (lace and Fair Isle knitting), the French-knot-embroidered Asa Mittens (Sweden, shown in "Look Inside"), the white and gray Nanna Twined Mitts (Norway), the brown-and-white Oda Baby Blanket with rows of stylized Fair Isle hearts and stars (Norway, knit at 4 stitches to the inch but still a large project, shown in the "Look Inside" photo montage), the little girl's stuffed Annelli Doll (Estonia, shown in "Look Inside"), the damask-patterned Adda Socks (Denmark, shown in the "Look Inside" photo montage), and the strangely-shaped Rya Flower Cushion (Denmark, shown in "Look Inside").

If you want a book of patterns for 2012 holiday gifts, you should probably select something else (for example, Ann Budd's excellent [[ASIN:1596680911 Interweave Presents Knitted Gifts: Irresistible Projects to Make and Give]], or Debbie Bliss's [[ASIN:1570764611 The Knitter's Year: 52 Make-in-a-Week Projects-Quick Gifts and Seasonal Knits]]). Because none of the designs in NORTHERN KNITS GIFTS particularly inspire me to grab my knitting needles, I rate this book at 3 stars ("It's OK" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Templates Do the Pattern-Writing Math for Different Yarn Gauges
text:
The NEW KNITTER'S TEMPLATE is a book of charts intended for experienced knitters to use in designing various styles of garments, in yarns of different gauges, to fit bust/chest sizes 30" to 60". The book is not so much about achieving custom fit, as it is about telling a knitter how many stitches to cast on, increase, and decrease to obtain the desired size and shape of a standard knitted garment component (e.g., back, front, sleeve) when using different gauges of yarn.

The authors provide a schematic "Style Diagram" drawing showing basic knitted garment styles (e.g., straight body back, v-neck front, cap sleeve). This schematic is used in conjunction with a "Blank Pattern Worksheet" and "The Templates" to create garments with specific bust/chest measurements using yarns of different gauges. The knitter takes her/his body measurements, selects a style out of the possible components, and then chooses a bust/chest size depending on the amount of ease desired. At this point, the knitter goes to the template for the yarn gauge (e.g., 5-1/2 stitches and 7-1/2 rows equals 1 inch), and finds the column headed by the selected bust/chest size (e.g., 36 inches). The knitter can then find the number of stitches to cast on, increase, and decrease (including number of times to increase and decrease) for each standard-shaped component part for the selected style. The knitter then writes these numbers down in the appropriate areas of the pattern worksheet. Voila! The knitter now has a pattern for the project.

Basically, the templates do the math for the knitter. They substitute for a software "sloper" (e.g., Cochenille's top-of-the-line "Garment Designer"), which will write out knitting instructions after the knitter selects a style and inputs figures for body measurements and yarn gauge into appropriate fields. But unlike the software programs, the NEW KNITTER'S TEMPLATE does NOT give templates for garments that will "custom fit" persons with "non-standard" body measurements (e.g., small bust, wide hips). Instead, the templates are based only on bust/chest size and standard garment component shapes. If a knitter has wide hips and simply follows the directions for the bust/chest measurement, the knitter will end up with a garment that is too narrow at the hips.

The NEW KNITTER'S TEMPLATE does include a few pages of general discussion about adding ease to various styles, to help the knitter choose the appropriate template to follow in compensating for different body types. However, I found the book to be difficult to use, and to be little more than a collection of pattern-writing charts. For these reasons, I rate it at 3 stars ("it's okay" on the official Amazon scale). If you're looking for a book that will really help you achieve a custom fit, by making a personal pattern based on your specific body measurements, then you might want to consider Jean Frost's excellent [[ASIN:193306420X Custom Knit Jackets: Casual to Couture]].

title: Cute Toy Patterns, But Not an Ark's Worth of Animals
text:
Generally I love Fiona Goble's books of instructions for knitted toys, but this one was a disappointment. I was expecting instructions for an ark full of animals, and instead got instructions for (1) Noah, (2) Mrs. Noah, (3) elephants, (4) lions, (5) monkeys, (6) tigers, (7) crocodiles, (8) giraffes, (9) zebras, (10) polar bears, (11) penguins, (12) rabbits, (13) tortoises, (14) goats, (15) pigs, (16) a raven, and (17) a dove. Lots of animals, to be sure, but mostly exotic ones, and no dogs or cats!

There is a pocket in the back cover that contains a cardboard ark. In the book are instructions for cutting it out and assembling it. This is a cute touch. The book's full color photos and drawings are attractive, the patterns give you cute but realistic-looking animals, and the pattern instructions are clear. However, because of the limited number of animal patterns in NOAH'S KNITS, I rate this otherwise very good book at 3 stars ("it's okay" on the Amazon scale).

Two of Goble's other books that I really like are [[ASIN:0764164597 'Twas the Knits Before Christmas]] (highly recommended), and [[ASIN:B006CDDABK Knit Your Own Royal Wedding]] (dated now, after the Prince's wedding, but still fun).

title: A Knitting Project Book for New Knitters
text:
Claire Montgomerie's spiral-bound KNITTING ENCYCLOPEDIA is not really an "encyclopedia" at all. It has knitting history (4 pages) and basic knitting instructions (71 pages) at the beginning, as well as a stitch directory (39 pages) at the end, but the bulk of the book is devoted to knitting project patterns for basic items (97 pages).

The project patterns are pleasant enough. Simple-to-knit patterns include a garter stitch scarf, fingerless gloves, a beanie hat, a striped pillow, a small bag with shoulder strap, a patchwork baby blanket, a slash-neck child's sweater, a shrug, a cowl, a beret, a chevron baby blanket, and a man's crew-neck sweater. Intermediate patterns include a double-breasted cardigan, mittens in the round, a round-yoke cardigan, ankle socks, a ribbed sweater, a felted bag, a basic lace scarf, a cabled hat in the round, Fair Isle mittens, an intarsia pillow, a cabled hot-water-bottle cover, and an Aran tunic sweater. Advanced patterns include lacy socks, a child's Fair Isle yoke sweater, lace panel gloves, a Fair Isle woman's cardigan coat, a lace stole, and a cabled afghan.

The technical information in the book is competent, but none of the projects are interesting enough to make me want to knit them. The matte photos are nothing to shout about. Basically, this is a knitting instruction book for new knitters, and there are many better general instruction books available (for example, [[ASIN:193154316X Vogue Knitting: The Ultimate Knitting Book]], [[ASIN:0762102489 Knitter's Handbook : A Comprehensive Guide to the Principles and Techniques of Handknitting]]. As for knitting history, or just reading about knitting, a couple of good books are [[ASIN:1931499373 A History of Hand Knitting]] (an out of print collector's item), and [[ASIN:1933027614 Vogue Knitting Knitopedia: The Ultimate A to Z for Knitters]]. Because I wouldn't have purchased this book if I'd seen it first, I rate it at 3 stars ("it's okay" on the Amazon scale).

title: Too Many Graphic Descriptions of Senseless Torture Murders
text:
At a fertility clinic, many women seeking artificial insemination may select, as the potential father of their hoped-for children, the same handsome, high-achieving sperm donor who lists multiple athletic, educational, and professional accomplishments. But what happens if this man is a serial killer with a dominant gene that makes all of his many artificially-conceived children into serial killers? And what happens if a government learns about the sperm donor's serial killer gene, and decides to exploit that gene to combat or advance terrorism?

An interesting theme! Unfortunately, EXTENDED FAMILY explores this theme only shallowly, and focuses mostly on providing shock value. Much of the novel consists of a mysterious researcher's "journal" entries that graphically describe the highly creative, often motiveless murders that are perpetrated by the serial killer's deadly progeny. The killer's children cannot help but commit murders--serial killing is "in their genes", along with the desire to torture, dismember, inflict great pain on others, burn victims alive, and commit mass murder. Worse, the children will remorselessly kill men, women, and even children.

As I was reading this book, I kept wondering (1) how any author could invent so many gruesome, shocking crimes; (2) why any author would feel the need to include so many crimes, described in such terrible detail, in a single novel; and (3) why any author would expect to find an audience of any size for such a novel. Without question, Patrick Kendrick is a skilled fiction writer who knows how to tell a story that will keep his readers reading. But his talents are simply wasted here--in a novel that seems to have been written for its shock value.

I cannot recommend to anyone that they go out and read EXTENDED FAMILY. However, because the book is well-written and well plotted, and a page-turner at times, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the Amazon scale).

title: Historical Account of Thompson/Lowden Political Rivalry
text:
Historian Gary Krist is a painstaking researcher, and an accomplished writer of readable, accessible history. He is extremely skilled at marshaling the known facts surrounding a collection of historical events, and then presenting everything in a polished, seamless narrative that reads more like a novel than nonfiction.

Nevertheless, CITY OF SCOUNDRELS is something of a snooze, even for a "Second City" fan like myself. The book chronicles, in detail, the events of a 12-day period in Chicago's history (July 21, 1919 to August 1, 1919) that included an unusual number of "disastrous" events. The events include the unfortunate crash of the blimp Wingfoot Express in the midst of the Loop (13 deaths, 27 injured), the mysterious disappearance/abduction of a 6-year-old schoolgirl, the public suicide of a municipal court judge, the crippling citywide transit strike, and the well-documented Chicago race riots. The events are described, more or less in chronological order, as they were reported in the Chicago daily newspapers, with some supplementation from contemporary diaries.

Unfortunately, it's hard to see how the unrelated events of this 12-day period "gave birth to modern Chicago." What CITY OF SCOUNDRELS is mostly about, is the bitter political conflict between Chicago's mayor, the unethical "Big Bill" Thompson, and Illinois' governor, the aspiring Presidential candidate Frank Lowden. Both men struggled mightily during the 12-day period to get headlines and political credit for settling the Chicago transit strike and for containing the race riots. To me, what was most interesting about the entire Thompson/Lowden rivalry, was that it ultimately led to the Republicans' infamous "smoke-filled room" nomination of Warren G. Harding for President (in June 1920, nearly a full year after the 12 days in question).

CITY OF SCOUNDRELS is carefully footnoted, includes a map of 1919 Chicago, and has an excellent index. Because it is a well-written book on contemporary political history, I award it 3 stars ("it's okay" on the Amazon reviewing scale).

title: San Francisco Bay Area  Setting Is Not Enough
text:
The San Francisco Bay Area setting is not enough to salvage this thriller. In it, Harlan Donnally--yet another retired homicide detective turned vigilante--decides to honor an old friend's deathbed request and deliver a letter to the sister the friend abandoned at a Berkeley commune in 1965. When Donnally learns that the sister was murdered 10 years later, he embarks on an investigation of the more-than-30-year-old "cold case". Soon he uncovers a terrible act of deceit: a violent, mentally ill man was falsely accused of the murder, declared incompetent to stand trial, and committed to a mental hospital to keep the case from ever going to trial or being fully investigated.

Donnally's investigation turns into a travelogue of sorts: it takes the detective from Mt. Shasta to downtown Berkeley, courthouses in San Francisco and Oakland, a homeless encampment in Golden Gate Park, Hunter's Point, a Ft. Bragg commune, a home in Hollywood Hills, a Vancouver religious community, and a Cancun sex-traffickers' complex. As the plot unfolds, Donnally learns that the act of deceit was perpetrated by powerful local individuals who were engaged in recruiting young boys who were already victims of sexual abuse as prostitutes. Donnally's complicated relationships with his long-time girl friend and his famous Hollywood filmmaker father are explored in subplots.

Author Steven Gore is a competent thriller writer who knows how to keep his readers turning the pages. However, the story jumps around a lot, and can be hard to track because of the myriad of characters that figure significantly in the plot (Mauricio, Anna, Sonny, Charles/Rover, Father Phil, Brother Melvin, Trudy, Bear, Perkins, Pipkins, Blaine, Sherwyn, R2T2, Gregorio, Jago, Lalo, Beto, Janie, and a few others whose names I can't remember right now). Also, Donnally has hard-to-believe, near-superhero abilities, when it comes to escaping a hit man, carrying out a burglary, and rescuing someone from a criminal complex that has military-level security.

Because the plot was interesting enough to keep me reading, I give this book 2.5 stars, rounded up to 3 stars ('it's okay"). Probably I won't bother to look for the next "Harlan Donnelly Novel", though, because I didn't find the Donnally character to be particularly interesting.

title: Row-by-Row Instructions for Beaded Covers for Glass Ornaments
text:
This is a 24-page booklet with 12 patterns for knitted, beaded covers for 2-5/8" glass Christmas tree ornaments. For each ornament cover, the beads are pre-strung on yarn, then knitted in, according to row-by-row instructions that produce various beaded designs (e.g., lattice, windowpanes, Fleur de Lis, zig zag, Christian cross, diamonds, vertical stripes, hearts).

The covers are knit using double-pointed needles. When finished, they are slipped onto the ornaments and drawn snug around the glass necks. When the ornaments' metal caps are replaced, they hide the covers' drawstring closings. The patterns are simple, and easy to follow. Even a brand-new knitter should be able to make these ornaments, because they require only knitting, purling, and simple knitted increases. There are brief, but clear, instructions on how to use double-pointed needles.

Creative knitters can no doubt create gorgeous tree ornaments by using designer yarns and varying the bead and yarn colors. However, I found the photographs of the ornaments in the booklet to be rather uninspiring, and for that reason I rate the booklet at 3 stars ("It's okay"). One recent book with patterns for Christmas ornaments, which will probably interest moderately experienced and experienced knitters, is [[ASIN:1570764875 55 Christmas Balls to Knit]] (charted designs for knitted, stuffed Christmas tree ornaments).

title: Explains Why You Should Worry About a Vitamin D Deficiency
text:
If you regularly use sunscreen to protect against sunburn and skin cancer, or if you live far from the equator, or if you always cover up with clothing when you go outdoors, you are at risk of developing a Vitamin D deficiency. As this book explains, adequate Vitamin D ("the sunshine vitamin") is manufactured by the body whenever the skin receives sufficient exposure to the sun's ultraviolet rays. But if you don't get enough exposure to the sun--and don't take Vitamin D supplements--then you may develop serious bone diseases (such as rickets, osteomalacia, or osteoporosis); and you will definitely lose out on the many likely benefits of having an adequate level of the active Vitamin D hormone (calcitriol) in your bloodstream.

As this book explains, recent research studies strongly suggest that the Vitamin D hormone does far more than help build strong bones by regulating calcium in the body. Calcitriol seems to play a role in protecting the immune system (including protecting against autoimmune diseases); preventing cancer (especially colon and breast cancer); improving heart health; avoiding diabetes and asthma; treating psoriasis; preventing brain diseases (such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, autism, depression, and seasonal affective disorder); and managing your weight. The book describes all of these diseases and their symptoms, and how calcitriol levels may relate to them.

Written by a physician, the book explains in easy-to-understand language exactly how Vitamin D and calcitriol are known to function in your body, and how these substances operate to prevent bone disease. However, the bulk of the book consists of educated conjecture about the possible preventive and protective effects of calcitriol that are merely suggested by recent studies of the Vitamin D hormone. Because the book has so much repetitive conjecture, I rate it at 3 stars ("it's okay"). Nevertheless, the book is an excellent choice if your doctor--like mine--has recently ordered you to be tested for a Vitamin D deficiency, and you are wondering why Vitamin D testing has recently come into such vogue with family doctors.

title: Overdone Exhibition Catalog for Textile Art Enthusiasts
text:
This is a museum exhibition catalog--an overblown, overdone one--that was first published in conjunction with a 2007 exhibition, RADICAL LACE & SUBVERSIVE KNITTING, that was organized by the Museum of Arts & Design (New York City).
