title: Flavorful, mostly meat recipes but no photos and it takes more than 30 minutes
text:
This cookbook is thin but is packed with flavorful recipes that use herbs and other spices to achieve a balanced dish. The dishes have salt shaker icons on them to denote low, lower, and lowest sodium. I made the lowest sodium black bean soup dish. It came out very flavorful but watery. However, from prep to completion of cooking, it took me 75 minutes and not 30 minutes and that does not include serving the dish. Both my boyfriend and I love this.

Note that the recipes sometimes call for frozen, canned, or already cut up ingredients. I followed the recipe to a tee and it did not change the timing. Also, note that there are no photos of any of the recipes in this book.

There are actually a lot of recipes I would make in this book. Most of the recipes are NOT a full meal but part of a meal, such as soup, fish, etc. In most cases, several recipes would have to be combined to make a full meal unless one is only having fish or just soup for a meal.

I do wish there were photos. I attached a photo of the black bean dish both with and without the optional sour cream and cilantro.

title: Guides others to see the positives of the unknowns written like an academic textbook - 2.5 stars
text:
The text is very dry and difficult to read. This book is written as if it were an academic textbook that makes the subject matter un-engaging when it needs to be the exact opposite.

The authors both live in France and this guide is an attempt to clarify that, although uncertainty is very real, we can see the positives in that unknown and actually turn something that is uncertain into something very successful, positive, award winning, etc. They do provide examples throughout the text but almost every example was either unknown to me or unrelatable that it made it impossible to remember. They must have picked only those that are visible in academic circles or on their side of the world. Examples such as Feringa and how he created molecular machines 10,000 times smaller than a human hair or Werner Heisenberg having a "breakthrough insight that laid the foundation of quantum mechanics," etc.

What I got out of this book is that people have to evaluate their choices in the face of uncertainty and reflect on what is right for them, decide if they will have regrets if they do or don't do XYZ, find a way to flip their fear into a strength, determine what their values are and align their outcome to that, etc.

I read the book from cover to cover but it was so unengaging and dry with unrelatable examples, that I can barely remember what it taught me. It is for this reason, this gets 2.5 stars rounded up to 3 stars from me. This is a valuable topic but the delivery fell incredibly short.

title: Dish I made is worthy of a high-end restaurant; only chapter photos; recipe timing is understated
text:
I have over 550 cookbooks and particularly have an interest in books with healthy recipes. Even though I love the idea of eating an anti-inflammatory diet, I ordered this because I feel it would have recipes that would interest me.

I read this from cover-to-cover and many of these recipes I would not make because they have ingredients either I do not use much or do not use at all such as vinegar, mushrooms, monk fruit extract, etc. Nevertheless, I did find about eleven recipes I would try.

Note that there are only a few pictures in this cookbook and that is at the start of the chapter. I do wish there were more pictures. Despite this, I decided to try the roasted red pepper soup with basil and goat cheese (pictured). I did add slightly more peppers, garlic, basil, and goat cheese than called for but not much more. The prep time took me about 60 minutes but the recipes said it is only 5 minutes. The cooking time also said 15 minutes and that was close but then the blending part with the immersion blender takes longer.

The resulting soup was stupendous. My boyfriend and I wanted to lick the bowl. The soup was so good. Of course, I did attach a photo of bread with the recipe. Bread is not part of an anti-inflammatory diet but it goes incredibly well dipped in the soup.

With regard to the anti-inflammatory part of this cookbook, there is a two-week plan included. Also, there's an intro on how to set up one's kitchen, etc. that coincides with the anti-inflammatory theme of this book.

In summary, this book is a keeper because I know there are at least two good recipes I would make. However, it is not my favorite because of the 100 recipes included, there are only 11 I would ever consider trying. The recipe ingredients are healthy in my opinion and this book does not only have to be for a follower of the anti-inflammatory lifestyle. I give this about 3.4 stars even though the recipe I made tastes like something that came from a high-end restaurant. I think this book mostly achieves its goal but will not satisfy everyone.

title: For meat lovers with time to prepare & marinate; many dishes are Asian inspired
text:
I am mostly a fish eater but I do eat meat once in a while. I thought this book would inspire me to elevate some simple meat dishes. Unfortunately, this is not for me. I have had this book since December 5, 2020 and today is February 13, 2021 and I still am not inspired to make anything in this book. I did mark off a few recipes but still cannot bring myself to make even one. This cookbook is more for those who are incredibly into their meat dishes and have time to prepare and marinate their cuts.

Here is why I find this cookbook uninspiring in the order of importance to me:

1 - I eat chicken, filet mignon, and lamb chops only. On rare occasions I eat ground beef. There are zero recipes for filet mignon and two recipes for lamb chops. There are some chicken recipes that appeal to me and a couple of ground beef ones. However, practically all take more time than the author says and many include making marinades or have a lot of ingredients.

2 - There are too many recipes that call for ingredients I do not normally have. I do not drink alcohol, so for two tablespoons of this or that I would have to buy pinot grigio, dry white wine, brandy, whisky, Shaoxing wine,  etc. Some non-alcoholic ingredients that I would have to buy are Hawaiian sweet rolls, Katsu sauce, food coloring, Worcestershire sauce, masa harina, sesame oil, dark soy sauce, regular soy sauce, sriracha or sambal oelek, meyer lemons, greek seasoning (although a substitute can be created from regular ingredients), etc.

3 - A lot of dishes are Asian inspired. There is nothing wrong with that except that is not typically what I eat. This means there is a lot of salt and spices in the recipes.

3 - There are only four recipe photos in the entire book. There are also some other photos at the start of a chapter. I would have liked more recipe photos.

In summary, this cookbook is not for me. I read it from cover to cover. I like the introduction into each section explaining the cuts of meat but not much else. I am disappointed there is absolutely no filet mignon recipe. Although the author includes the prep, cook, and marinating times, I know for a fact it would take me longer than instructed. This book includes a lot of recipes for beef, lamb, veal, and poultry (meaning only chicken and turkey) as the title suggests. However, most of those recipes require a lot of ingredients that I do not use in my normal cooking, so I would have had to make a significant investment in alcohol and sauces for two tablespoons of this or that which would just be wasted unless I made the recipe every week. Nevertheless, for those who are hearty meat eaters that love to experiment with flavors and like Asian-inspired dishes, then this might be a wonderful addition to that cook's library. For me, it is a struggle to even make one recipe in this book even though I marked off several potential ones and I usually do not review a cookbook without making one recipe. Unfortunately, this is the exception where I have not even made one dish from this book.

title: Good but basic advice in part one; reference in part two & most is common sense
text:
This book is broken up into two parts. Part one is more foundational and about eating right, sleeping, history of natural medicine, etc. I enjoyed the first part but it was too short and also very basic. 

Part two, which is the main section of this text, covers a couple of pages on various diseases and ailments. It provides a very brief synopsis of symptoms, root causes, treatment, lifestyle changes, and herbal supplements to help in controlling or alleviating some of the symptoms. Unfortunately, I consider part two more like a quick reference. Although I read this from cover to cover, the gist of the book is to eat clean, get enough sleep, and exercise. There are supplement suggestions thrown in as well. 

Unfortunately, I did not feel I learned much from this text and the book was not what I expected. I thought it would be more focused on creating natural concoctions to help various ailments but it was not that at all.

This book really was not for me. I enjoyed part one even though it was basic but I could have passed on the rest.

title: Coffee table book full of photos of one man’s obsession with European Junk Cars
text: Rudi Klein, a now deceased a German Immigrant, maintained a European car salvage yard in California that his sons now own. There is a short story about the stubborn and ornery Mr. Klein which hinted that he made his fortune selling these cars and car parts. Ninety percent of this book are just pictures of the scrap heap of cars on his property with a short caption of what one is looking at. This book held my interest but the photos are not particularly enticing to me. I would have preferred more story and more complete car photos than rusted parts. The current price of $35 is typical of coffee table photo books; however, unless one is into European cars, this will not hold much interest.

title: This should have been titled "How to Live with MS for Dummies"
text:
I am disappointed in this book because, based on the title, I automatically assumed there would be an initial chapter on MS Symptoms and the disease itself. This book does not include that at all. I learned about the symptoms piecemeal by reading the various coping strategies in this book, such as when one has to tell their child why they walk like a drunk or what it feels like to be spastic and so on. This is a text dedicated to teaching an MS sufferer how to cope in life with MS, how to handle bladder issues, how to talk to the children, how one can have a child, and much more.

It is not a bad book but when I read books on diseases and autoimmune disorders, I want to immediately learn in the first few chapters what the disease is about and what the symptoms are. I do not only want to learn how to cope with the disease.

PS I attached a picture of the "contents at a glance," however, the Amazon system is currently turning all photos upside down and putting them out of order.

title: No simple carbohydrates, no beans, no dairy, & no grains; meal-plans barely enough to sustain life
text:
I love cookbooks and even though I am not someone who eats a paleo-only diet, I believe almost every cookbook is a complement to a well-stocked library and contains recipes one can enjoy.

From a paleo perspective, this book meets its goal as it focuses on whole and unprocessed foods devoid of simple carbohydrates, beans, dairy, and grains. It spotlights fats and oils, fresh fruits, meats, fish, pure unfiltered honey and maple syrup, and fresh vegetables. However, the problem I have with this book is that the meal plan samples barely have enough calories or food to sustain life and some recipes are so simplistic that they appear to be page fillers. For example, one meal plan calls for warm water for a morning boost, then meal #1 as blueberry pancakes and bacon, meal #2 as zesty italian chicken and "rice" casserole, evening meal of 3 bacon slices, and final drink of herbal tea. Basically there are only two skimpy meals per day and barely any fluid. The "rice" in the casserole is actually grated cauliflower and the maximum calories are below 1200 per day based on the sampling I did. Second, there are some recipes like sweetened coconut water (water, honey, and coconut water) and bacon-wrapped asparagus (bacon and asparagus) that appear to be more like filler recipes.

Since I am not a person that follows paleo, there are only about five recipes I would make in this book. There are others that I would need to change to accommodate my style of eating. I almost never use honey or maple syrup in my recipes or sugar in any form. Nevertheless, any book with two or more good recipes is a keeper to me, so this stays on my bookshelf.

I did make two servings of the garlic, spinach, and kale omelet and both my boyfriend and I really enjoyed it. The only thing is that it was a bit watery and it was hard to tell why; perhaps it was due to the sauteed onions. I attached a few before and after pictures. Note that I did add canteloupe on the side but the recipe did not call for that.

In summary, this book achieves its goal. I do think there is some filler in this volume and I the meal plans are unattainable except for the disciplined eater who wants to starve themself and is not athletic. I commend anyone who can eat this way and eliminate beans, grains, and dairy from their diet which I personally feel is a healthier alternative. Despite this, these recipes can be used as a complement to a full meal for almost any person's meal plan.

title: Recipe I made was deeply flavorful; prep time is for Iron Chefs; book has confusing info & mistakes
text:
Cookbooks that are dedicated to help relieve the symptoms of a disease are generally ones that are full of healthy recipes. This one is no exception. I love healthy and wholesome whole foods and have been eating that way most of my adult life. Although I do not have rheumatoid arthritis, I do suffer from inflammation and wanted a guide that has a meal plan along those lines.

I read this from front to back and, although there are over 20 recipes in this book I would make, some information given at the beginning of the book is contradictory. For instance, page 16 states that the recipes feature whole foods, yet anti-inflammatory smoothies are on the menu. Even though a smoothie features whole foods, those foods are more glycemic since they are basically pulverized. On page 55 she mentions the flare-soothing meal plan will not include ingredients like honey. However, honey is included on page 57 on the flare-soothing plan shopping list. For the "Basil Pesto Pizza with Mushroms and Spinach" recipe on page 111, the spinach ingredient in the name of the recipe is not listed in the ingredient list--instead the recipe calls for chopped artichokes. I am unsure if spinach should be included with that or in place of that. Also, page 12 ends with the word "These" as the start of a sentence where the rest of the sentence or paragraph is nowhere to be found. There is only one sentence for the entire section and after reading that sentence, I felt like I was missing something when it ended on that one word.

Despite the above, the recipes read like they would be fantastic--flavorful and healthy. I decided to make the "Italian Sausage and Kale Soup" and the depth of flavor was out of this world. I attached a sequence of before and after photos. However, the prep time must be for an Iron Chef because it said it would take me only 15 minutes to prep and it took me about two hours. I admit I am slower than most because I like to lay all my ingredients out, but it definitely was not a 15-minute prep for anyone but the most advanced and speediest cook.

In summary, there are just so many recipes I would make in this book. Even if one does not have arthritis, this is a great addition to any cookbook library despite my three-star rating. I was going to rate this book four stars but the reason I lowered it to three is because of the contradictory information in the front. For someone who has rheumatoid arthritis, it is important that the information presented in such a book be clear and not contradictory or confusing. Also,there are only about three recipe pictures in the book and the few other pictures are just of ingredients like garlic or lemon. If a cookbook is going to include pictures, it is important to include a picture of the finished recipe. I would have liked to see more photos. Nevertheless, the recipes themselves appear to be great (excluding the one with the editing error). I know the resulting end product in the recipe I made was out of this world in a flavorful, scrumptious, wholesome, and supremely satisfying sort of way.

title: One woman searches out her family Holocaust history and family tree
text:
I read several Holocaust memoirs over the years and have come to learn two things. First, they are all different as some are written by survivors and others by those longing to know their heritage. Second, it seems speaking about the Holocaust is taboo and so many descendants have a longing for knowledge that is not satisfied by their parents who unwaveringly refuse to speak.

This book is of the second variety. Esther was born of parents who fled the Holocaust and a father who was saved by some man agreeing to hide him. Her memoir is about researching her family history and the trials and tribulations of that research. Although, the story is interesting, it was hard for me, as a reader not to be confused as I did not understand, nor could I follow, all the family relationships. Someone who is related to this family or is in search of their Holocaust family lineage may be more intrigued but this was not the book I expected it to be.

title: The message is simple but the text is long winded – 2.5 stars
text:
This book's message is very simple to me. The idea is to project positive energy and set the tone for yourself which, in turn, sets the tone in meetings and with others. In essence, one's energy or lack of it is contagious. It requires one be self-aware. She coins the concept IEP (Intentional Energetic Presence). The idea is to use this to rise above OPPPE (Other People's Problems, Projects, and Expectations).

Paraphrasing from the book, "there are three parts to the IEP method - 1) reboot your presence, 2) build a strong and energetic foundation and field, and 3) create intentional impact." There are a few poignant points one of which is that anyone can transform bad into a good by changing their thinking by learning "how to reframe, use, and partner with bad things for good." We cannot change others but we can change ourselves. By being contagious, we can effect good change in others most of the time. If we cannot, we can either work around those negative energy people or remove ourselves from that situation. This was the essence of the entire book to me.

I felt that most of the pages between 65 to 195 were worth the read but what came before, after, and somewhere in the middle felt like a sales pitch for the book and the process, a mishmash of questions and exercises, and unorganized and unnecessary fluff to add to the volume of this text. For instance, in the center of pages 65 to 195, the author decides to talk about neuroscience and the brain (ATP, glutamate, etc). I felt this science had no place in this book and did not add to the message. The beginning of the book had a lot of praises for this text and the end contained a bunch of case studies that sound more like praise and offered nothing for the reader, in my opinion.

I am obviously the odd one out here considering everyone else loves this. I love the message but I honestly could not wait for this book to end once I finished the few inspiring sections.

title: Nice mix of low carb recipes but results look unappetizing even though they taste good
text:
I do not follow any specific diet. Instead I use books like this to find dishes that complement a meal. First, I really like the Ninja 101 section in the intro. Second, I found 18 recipes that I would consider trying, until I made one of them.

I did make the chicken tortilla soup (note there is no tortilla in the recipe) and was surprised at how awful looking the soup turned out. It was certainly unappetizing visually and looked nothing like the picture in the book (see photos). It looked more like a dirty consomme even though I added more chicken than the recipe called for. Nevertheless, it was delicious. Therefore, I have very mixed feelings about the results and am a bit leary of trying another recipe.

Some recipes are super easy like parmesean asparagus (unlike the one I made), which makes me wonder why recipes like that are in the book.

The final chapter includes sauces, guacamole, and dressing. There is also a shopping list in the back which I consider book filler. I do really love the Ninja Foodi charts in the back, however.

In summary, this cookbook does have a generous offering of low carb recipes. I am concerned about each recipe's visual palatability based on the result I got from one recipe where the dish looked like a different item altogether. I eat not only with taste but also with my eyes. Although, this book has some good Foodi tips I have mixed feelings about how valuable this will be in my library. After trying this, this is not a book I would run out and buy, but it is also not a book I would throw away either.

title: Vegan cookbook w/o oil, salt, sugar but heavy on maple syrup (which is sugar) & low on flavor
text:
To me this WFPB (whole food plant based) diet is a lightly processed vegan diet without oil, salt, or sugar. Although it says sugar is not allowed, there are many recipes that call for maple syrup (like half a cup). I personally would not make a steady diet of recipes with maple syrup in them because that is sugar. There are about 100 grams of sugar in half a cup of maple syrup.

Now I have other vegan cookbooks that I would cook from. However, this book only has eight recipes I would ever consider making. 

I made the lime mint soup and put that over brown rice (see before and after photos). I did substitute chicken for vegetable broth because I am not only a plant-based eater and I have no interest in eating vegetable broth which tends to be very bland. The soup was okay over the rice but was still a little bit bland. The flavor of the lime sort of overpowered the dish. I wound up draining out all the liquids and only eating the solids over the rice due to the overpowering flavor. Mint and lime just does not go together for me.

There is an introduction and basics section up front before the recipes. I like the section on how to "cook the basics" such as rice, quinoa, potato, etc. However, I was surprised the steam cooking method was not even mentiond here.  I also like the "instead of this, eat that" section.

I am unsure yet whether this book will remain in my library. It probably will not get much use simply because most of the recipes I would not make and those that I would make have to be doctored up for flavor. Nevertheless, if one is interested in a less-processed vegan method of cooking, this is one book that can be tried. For me it is somewhat of a disappointment.

title: The truth about the abysmal US healthcare system but reads like a policy document
text:
I learned some things about healthcare that I did not know from this book but, unfortunately, this reads like some sort of government policy document. He also uses unrelated analogies (such as Lincoln's Gettysburg address to indicate emancipation of healthcare) to try to get his point across that actually made me question, why am I reading this.

I learned that the reason our insurance is supplied by our employers is because they get a tax break that corporations would not get if they had raised wages instead so that we could buy our own insurance. I personally never understood why insurance has to be tied to our jobs and now I do. His suggestion is to eliminate this tax break for corporations.

Although the author has done his research on healthcare, I just do not feel he goes far enough and I found his message sometimes hard to grasp. For instance, there is no argument for eliminating insurance companies completely except for maybe establishing large muti-speciality physician groups people can belong to.

The American Healthcare System is totally broken and destroys lives, causes death, and promotes sickness and does this at an unaffordable price not commensurate with the care received. I understand his solution to this is to eliminate the corporate tax break, establish full-risk contracting where the balance of risk and service is shifted form healthcare providers (companies who are providing the insurance) to the healthcare service purchasers (the users of this healthcare). Using an unrelated analogy like the author does throughout his book, it is like he is suggesting eliminating defined pension plans (where the ultimate user has no say or stake in the decisionmaking) in order for the employee to manage his own retirement via a 401K. In this case, the users of the healthcare would shop around for what they need and assume the risk and buy the level of care they need. I still believe the user could be in trouble if they did not buy enough. I do agree, however, that we (the user of healthcare), should not be so removed from the true cost of the care.

On another note, there are alot of acronyms thrown around this book and defined once or twice. Since this was more like reading a text book, I would have loved to see a glossary in the back that included what the acronyms stood for so that the reader could consult it once he or she forgot.

SOME OF WHAT I WOULD INCLUDE IN A GLOSSARY:
BCBS - Blue Cross Blue Shield
CHIP - Children's Health Insurance Program
CMMI - Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation
CMS - Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services
ED - emerency department
FFS - fee-for-service
HCAHPS - Hospital Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems
HHS - Health and Human Services
MA - Medicare Advantage
MHI - medium household income
PBMs - pharmacy benifit managers
TPAs - third party administrators

In summary, I totally agree with one of the doctor reviewers (Rushika Fernandopoule, MD) who said "We need to restore the humanity in healthcare." However, I am unsure if the suggestions in this book are complete enough to do that. This was an interesting, confusing, sometimes dry, and sometimes enlightening read and only mildly worth reading for me.

title: LOVE in business means taking care of your customers and employees
text:
This book is an enjoyable read. However, I still find it very difficult to explain the message within. To me love is common sense in business. I do not believe one can be truly successful unless they genuinely love their customer, company, employees, work, and themselves. 

I actually did not realize that the author was touting a LEAP Model until the end.  LEAP, in this business context, stands for love, energy, audacity, and proof. A business leader must cultivate a caring environment for their customer, company, employees, work, and themselves. Love also means the leader may need to make tough decisions. For instance, someone who loves their company may need to to fire someone who is not up to muster in order to maintain a healthy culture within their firm. A business leader must also generate an environment whereby their employees can get behind their vision, be shameless in achieving their goal with love, and provide evidence of success day after day by making what they do better and reaping the rewards.

If a leader is genuine and truly cares and then motivates their employees, the proof of customer satisfaction will be evident via the results achieved (monetary or otherwise).

The above is what I inferred from the examples in the book but was not specifically spelled out. It was a good read and there were many examples incorporated  throughout the text; however, I did not feel the information provided was concrete enough for me to sink my teeth into or describe to someone else. I feel love in business is just plain common sense in that one reaps what they sow and if the sow well, they and their customer and employees will be rewarded. It is also important to be genuine in achieving that goal.

title: Jason’s autobiography of unusual money-making schemes which helps the reader think
text:
This book reminded me a lot of [[ASIN:1559500883 The Art and Science of Dumpster Diving]] except for two things. First, there are fewer lessons for the reader. Second, it started out great but then fizzled for me toward the end.

To me this was more like the author's autobiography of unusual money-making schemes than it is a self-help or good advice book. It does get the reader thinking, however.

The author talks about selling his future, selling sponsorship in having a others watch him write a book live online, selling his last name for a year, an IWearYourShirt for a different vendor every day of the year, etc. He never gets into the how behind his successes or failures but he does provide a few snippets of good advice like not waiting for the perfect time, embracing fear but doing it anyway, etc.

This story is very entertaining at the beginning but then it felt a bit repetitive. The main premise of this text is to get the reader to think outside the box and to be themselves, have integrity, and be consistent. The idea is to not just work a 9 to 5 job, have that white picket fence, and the 2.5 children but to carve out a life that is yours alone.

This delivered on the weirdness but not on the self-help side of things for me. I definitely enjoyed the first two thirds of the book and feel it is worth the read but not necessarily worth the current purchase price of $16.50.

title: Thought-provoking narrative; mostly focuses on black/white racism; message was confusing at first
text:
This was a long read for me as I had to re-read sections of this book to try to absorb the message being delivered. The theme of the book is about racism but focuses mostly on black and white racism particularly because that type of racism can be seen.

This text certainly highlights that racism is alive and well in America unlike in Europe. It also is a good read for opening the discussion about these issues.

I love the ending in how the author elaborates on five kinds of cross-racial friendships.

1 - bubble friends
2- fantasy friends
3- calendar friends
4 - fellowship friends
5 - heart friends (the stage we should all be at)

I observe the racism that exists today between blacks and whites just when I go to high-end craft shows. Whenever there is an African American vendor, it is rare to find their booth crowded. I can see where they are ignored and there is a lack of patronage. If I like the product they are selling, I have no hesitation to buy it or even browse those booths full of wonderful art. However, there are definitely racial issues prevalent as I can feel it and find it very disturbing.

I also agree that cross-racial friends are necessary if only for just fostering an understanding of how another group of people sees things differently. For instance, I use to commute with a Chinese fellow. One time we were talking about American cars and how unreliable they generally were and how we both loved Japanese cars. The discussion then drifted to other products and I made the comment that Chinese products are garbage and their dishware is chipware because it always chips at the slightest touch. He was immediately offended and said it is not the fault of the Chinese. It is because Americans want cheap products and they ask the Chinese to make them. I never looked at it this way. If it were not for him "opening my eyes" (so to speak), I would not know this viewpoint. Now I realize that we have asked for the garbage.

I rated this book 3 stars only because it was difficult for me to understand what resolution the author was touting until the end of the book. At one point, I got the impression that she was advocating for everyone to stay within their racial boundaries simply because that is what we gravitate towards. I also felt the message was not organized in a way that describes what actions should be taken. However, at the end what I understand is this. We will always feel more comfortable within our own racial group but we need to have "cross-racial heart friends" so that we can understand our differences and respect them. We certainly have a long road ahead to get there.

title: Snippets of Rwandan life & culture during the 1960's genocide
text:
This story is set in the 1960's in Rwanda and is told through a young daughter's eyes. The daughter mostly talks about how her mother protected her children due to the genocide that was going on around that time.

I learned a little about her culture and beliefs which was very interesting. The narrative is really snippets of thoughts and flashbacks woven into a non-sequential story. It is for that reason, I had trouble connecting the dots. I was even unsure if the daughter was a Tutsi or Hutu until the end where I believe she is a Tutsi. I thought it was the Hutu who were committing the slaughter during that time but I also could not tell from the story. It is because of this lack of clarity from my perspective that I did not enjoy this narrative as much as I could have. Nevertheless, it is still an interesting and relatively quick read.

title: I found the content of this text too overwhelming as it relates to the criminal justice system
text:
It has taken me several weeks to read this book and the content was mostly overwhelming to me and not that easy to understand as the author writes about the inadequacies with the criminal justice system.

The main gist of the book, in layman's terms, is that the criminal justice system is screwed up. What we think of as justice is actually injustice. There are prejudices throughout, ridiculous laws (basically every one of us has done something illegal), people who do not have the legal education who are making decisions for the judges, police who continually use excessive force, government who cannot be held accountable for their misconduct unless they agree to be held accountable, ordinary citizens who have their property seized even before being proven guilty, evidence which is not foolproof being considered the holy grail of proof--even the biological kind ("meaning forensic science is a witness with an agenda"), etc., etc., etc.

SOME EXAMPLES

- If you pet your dog during a car ride you are breaking the law in D.C. and will be fined.

- If you do not have a law license or training, you can still work in a judge's chambers as a clerk and "deny a prisoner's rights, draft a death penalty opinion," etc.

- "The prosecutor has more control over life, liberty, and reputation than any other person in America."

- In one police raid mentioned, an innocent stepfather was killed because police used excessive force when they raided a house where the illegal step son lived. The cops firearm went off and the policeman was not held accountable.

I tried to put what was said in layman's terms as I understood it. In reality, however, the text was too intense for me to grasp. We all know our justice system fails us and this book intended to prove that. However, it was proven in a way that was most difficult to read and which made it hard to remember. I can only recommend this for someone who is in the legal field or someone who has an acute interest in the criminal justice system and can handle a book with thousands of well-researched facts strung together in a somewhat informative way for an incredibly overwhelming subject matter.

title: This was more of a reminder to me of why I pursue my passions than a self-help book
text:
To me this book is full of common sense because it has been the way I conduct my life since youth. I found this more of a reminder of how passion can be either fulfilling or destructive. The reminders in the margins are excellent and the conclusion chapter is really what the book is about in two-pages.

EXAMPLES of REMINDERS:

- "The best route to making your passion a bigger part of your life is to do so gradually."

- "Someone who embodies the mastery mind-set judges herself not on whether she accomplishes her goal but rather on how well she executes on her process."

MY UNDERSTANDING:

The sentences below sums up what this book is to me and not necessarily what was exactly said or meant in the text:

- Pursuing an interest and becoming a successful master (or mistress) requires being intrinsically motivated to achieve results rather than being externally motivated on reaching the goal. In other words, satisfaction and passion must come from within otherwise it can become toxic.

- One must be self-aware and re-evaluate their passion.

- Pursuing a passion means life is unbalanced by default but if we look at our entire life as a whole, we are usually balanced.

- We must be patient and keep striving toward our passion to achieve success.

- Some of us may have many passions and choose to re-evaluate where we are at different times in our lives so as to re-direct our passions.

- What helps us to achieve the life we want is to think about death, This helps us realize there is only so much time that we have so we should be doing what moves us.

- There is a fine line between passion and obsession.

In summary, this felt like a pep-talk and a reminder of how I already live. I was not personally enlightened although I did appreciate the inspiring notes in the margin.

title: A cathartic sexual abuse recovery story for the author with some self-help guidance for the abused
text:
The author was "temporarily" sold into a sex traffic ring when she was seven years old by her nanny. However, there is nothing temporary about the lifelong pain that results of such a despicable situation.

In this book, I feel that she is working through the pain via artistic pursuits, spirituality, and her poetry peppered throughout the text. She had to go through bad relationships and learn to honor herself and understand that she is worthy to really heal. Honoring herself is a way to get justice for the perpetrators who will never serve a day in jail.

The author is obviously a talented poet and very spiritual but I had trouble relating to a story told in this manner. Part two is much better and is less poetic and part three provides questions the abused can use to heal. In the end this is both a very personal story and one offered up to help others similarly abused.

title: This is not my kind of book but the recipes are good & the one I made was delicious & healthy
text:
I love health and recipes books that talk about well-being and super food ingredients. However, I have been reading this book on and off since early November and the first section was disorganized and wandering to me which made it an uninspiring read.

The first few chapters talk about a healthy gut, fermented foods, setting personal goals, morning routine, 3-day gut reset, becoming a wellness babe, etc. However, I felt it was overly wordy, did not get to the point quick enough for me, and I am not a fan of meal plans.

Nevertheless, once we get into the recipes, there are about six that I would make even if I had to substitute some ingredients. I made the smoked trout and lentil salad but without the vinaigrette because I like my salads dry or just with olive oil and rice vinegar. Nevertheless, it was absolutely delicious--see photo. I did have trouble locating the smoked trout. It took me over one week to find it and that really annoyed me. I did not want canned trout. However, I discovered packaged smoked trout is not an ingredient stocked in any of my local stores. I finally found it at Wegmans forty miles away from me as the store about 14 miles away did not have any in stock.

For me the recipes are five stars but the first half of the book is one star, hence my three star rating. It is only a keeper due to the good, healthy recipes included.

UPDATE 1/26/19 - I also made the Hearty Winter Stew and it came out delicious--see last two photos.

title: Quick read, nice to glance through, but not much inspiration to me
text:
I like to visit kitschy stores and antique and collectible shops and during one of my travels, I purchased this book at full price thinking it was right up my alley. I enjoyed reading it from cover to cover and even liked the pictures. However, there is not much inspiration to me here and some advice is what I consider "half-baked."

For instance, one idea they proposed was to pile up a bunch of pallets and put a mattress on top for a "fabulous" bed. However, when looking at the pictures, one can clearly get splinters from these pallets just by getting into bed. Another idea is how to to glue pine cones on top of a four poster bed as "fancy finials." However, there is absolutely no mention that these pine cones have to be fumigated first as there are always bugs in pine cones.

Overall, I did enjoy reading this and looking at the pictures. Most of what they propose I would not do; like make a newspaper wreath, cut a sleeve off a sweater and make a dog coat, etc. It is not a book I am keeping and I feel it was not worth the price I paid. I should have gotten this out of the library or ordered it on Amazon used.

title: Hodgepodge book for those who love dessert, sugar, fats, cheese, & fried foods for "breakfast"
text:
This breakfast book is totally not what I expected. I expected some really good deviations from healthy breakfast foods that included eggs, vegetables, quiche, crepes, and lean meats.

The first section of the book is somewhat entertaining with how to soft-boil an egg, what certain brands of coffee taste like both hot and cold (hilarious write-up actually), how to make candied bacon, why diner toast is so damn good, etc. However, after reading the rest of this book and reviewing those recipes, I had to suppress some dry heaves. There's recipes for doguhnut hole croquembouche, DIY toaster strudel, velveeta chex mix nacho dirtbag casserole, doritos quiche, yogurt bark, pop-tart haus (looks like a candied gingerbread house), egg-in-a-doughnut (which is 4 donuts piled on top of each other with egg yolk running down the outside and center--SUPER DRY HEAVE for me), etc.

Nevertheless, I decided to try two recipes that I thought I could stomach and only one of them I found good. However, my boyfriend loved both of them. Note that he is a man who could eat dessert for breakfast, lunch, dinner, and snack--so this did not surprise me.

I made the "10-Minute Asparagus Brunch for Fancypants People" which came out good. Both my boyfriend and I actually loved this. He asked me if there was a sauce on the asparagus which their was. He said it "elevated it to another level" and I agree. (See first three pictures - not as pretty as what is in the book, unfortunately.)

I also made the "Cornmeal Pancakes with Mascarpone and Jam Because Why Not." Note that it was not easy to assemble as all the jam and mascarpone required caused the layers to start sliding around. My boyfriend actually had to hold the stack in place until it solidified a bit and it cooled down. My boyfriend loved this dish, although he did say he would never want to eat it again. He had seconds; I did too only because I did not want to waste it. However, I was not as enamored with this recipe. In fact, after I was done, I felt nauseous. It is definitely not a "breakfast" I will make again. (See last two pictures.)

In summary, this book is full of some interesting tidbits of breakfast information, including alcoholic drinks. There are only a few recipes I would ever consider and the Fancypants one above is one I would make again. Nevertheless, this gets 2.5 stars from me because overall this is NOT my kind of book and it is not how I eat. I suspect a college kid or bachelor living on chips and dip would adore this recipe book. Breakfast may be the most important meal of the day but this is full of the "heart-attack-on-the plate" stuff that is rarely in my repertoire.

title: Easy and relatively plain recipes; I made 5 of the 75
text:
I have had this recipe book since September 24, 2018 (over two months) and have been going through it since then. I read this book from cover to cover and highlighted all the recipes I wanted to make before I assessed this book.

“Authentic Italian Desserts” is full of simple recipes. As I was reading through it, I was so excited that they were not high in sugar. I really dislike cloyingly sweet desserts and it was clear that these are more on the "non-dessert" end which is exactly what I was looking for.

Normally, when I review a cookbook, I make only one or two recipes. However, I was so excited about this one that I made five of the seven recipes I picked out as listed below. I also attached pictures (in the same order shown below, from before baking to plated).
1. semplice torta allo yogurt (a.k.a. simple yogurt cake)
2. torta di pere (a.k.a pear cake)
3. biscotti al caffee (a.k.a. coffee cookies)
4. torta alla ricotta (a.k.a. ricotta cake)
5. semifreddo alla pesca (a.k.a. peach semifreddo)

Every recipe came out looking exactly like the picture in the book. Note that practically every recipe picture in the book is non-descript; all of them are various shades of brown or tan or yellow. Nevertheless, good things come is boring packages.

The yogurt cake was nice but almost tasteless. Since I used a lemon yogurt it did have a mild lemon flavor. I think I will add lemon zest to it next time in addition to the lemon yogurt. I actually liked this cake as a breakfast cake. It did come out somewhat dense. My boyfriend tried it and did not care for it much. I actually liked it and would make it again but would not say it is outstanding. It is more on the bland side and needs to be spiced up with something like fruit, whipped cream, jam, etc. However, I prefer to eat it plain. This recipe was my third favorite.

The pear cake was extremely dense, super tasteless, and took over 30 minutes more to bake than stated in the recipe. My boyfriend hated this cake and I seriously disliked it. This one was next to my least favorite recipe.

The coffee cookies were beyond terrible. I threw them out. It really irks me to throw recipe ingredients, out but these were horrific to my taste buds. Also, the recipe is unclear. It states 2 tbsp of coffee. Is that brewed coffee, instant coffee, espresso powder, etc.? I used brewed coffee but I suspect (after tasting the cookies) that I was supposed to use unbrewed instant coffee. This was the worst recipe and most likely the fault of unclear instructions. However, I doubt it would have been much better even if I used whatever coffee that was wanted but not listed.

The ricotta cake is absolutely wonderful. I could not stop eating it. The orange zest makes it flavorful yet it is not sweet at all. Once again, the recipe left off the last ingredient which was to dust the cake with powdered sugar as shown in the picture. I also wish it said what type of milk to use (skim, 2%, whole). I used 2% and it came out fine. This recipe is one of my favorites.

The peach semifreddo is also divine. Not sweet but perfect for a summer evening. Once again, the recipe ingredients left off the mint that is shown as a topping in the picture. Also, it did not mention what type and flavor of Greek yogurt to use. I used vanilla-flavored non-fat Greek yogurt. Even though vanilla is also one of the recipe ingredients, the vanilla was not overpowering. This recipe is also one of my favorites.

In summary, out of the five recipes I tried, two were excellent for my tastes, one was good, and two were terrible. I always follow instructions precisely, so it is not me. I attached 18 pictures of the recipes in the order below.

The instructions in this book are very easy to follow and the recipes are easy to make. Some instructions left me wondering what ingredient I needed to use. This is not a high-sugar cookbook and not what one would normally expect from desserts. I do not consider any of the ones I tried decadent. Nevertheless, that is not what I was looking for. For me this book is a keeper because I found 2-3 recipes I will make again and I will eventually try others. Due to how horrible two recipes were and some incomplete instructions, this book is just okay as it stands today.
