title: Heartwarming story about Homer the blind cat who lived through another Christmas, but...
text:
I read the author's book [[ASIN:B002LLRE50 Homer's Odyssey: A Fearless Feline Tale, or How I Learned about Love and Life with a Blind Wonder Cat]] back in December 2015. That book is an incredible and relatively lighthearted read about a blind cat who shared his home with the author.

This book provides an incredibly brief snippet of that same blind miracle cat. Homer defied the odds in every way. His first miracle was finding a home with the author when others passed him over and then immersing himself in life. Second, and what this story is about, is by surviving for nine months longer than he was expected to live--living through another Christmas and New Year after his deathly diagnosis.

Homer and The Holiday Miracle would make a great stocking stuffer for a young adult. It is a sweet story and somewhat positive considering we know how it ends. However, I wanted so much more.

Note that 10% of the royalties from this book go to organizations that serve abused, abandoned, and disabled pets.

title: A business woman's autobiography that attempts to teach through her mistakes; it lacks the business inspiration I expected
text:
This is more like one person's corporate autobiography than a self-help business book. I somewhat enjoyed reading about how Beth Comstock (former head of marketing and innovation at GE, who also worked at NBC, etc.) brought about change in corporate thinking and challenged the norms. I particularly like how she took chances such as selecting an ad after September 11, 2001 with the Statue of Liberty running that says "We will roll up our sleeves. We will move forward together. We will overcome. We will never forget. ...... A message from GE." This ad went against the stiff corporate culture of GE yet the public loved it.

Throughout this book, the author describes meetings, encounters, challenges, etc. but nothing that I found earth shattering or super interesting. It was somewhat mundane reading.

Interspersed through the text are pages that provide some pointers such as:
- "Success correlates as closely with confidence as it does with competence."
- Get a coach
- Create a monthly bucket list - hold yourself accountable to do things that are outside your comfort zone.
- Build team trust - trust must be earned one action at a time.
- "In change, people have to find their own path. You can't mandate how that happens."

In summary, had I purchased this book, I would have been disappointed. It is not full of the business inspiration I expected. However, as a autobiographical business read it is somewhat interesting even though it was mundane in spots. This gets 2.6 stars (rounded up to 3) from me.

title: Cooking with Ziggy Marley's Coco'Mon Coconut Oil; recipes may be flavorful but it's not my cup of tea
text:
This recipe book should have been named "Cooking with Ziggy Marley's [[ASIN:B0195NFLWY Coco'Mon Coconut Oil]] because practically every one calls for that ingredient.

I read this cookbook from cover to cover and the menus are supposedly all about healthy eating "Rasta culture style" which includes a lot of juices, greens, and nuts--although I only found two recipes with nuts in them ("oatmeal" and "almost coconut smoothie"). Practically every recipe called for his coconut oil or an equivalent. There were also some other ingredients I don't like such as pomegranate seeds, okra, curry powder, Guinness, golden syrup, molasses, etc. I would be hard pressed to include these items in any recipe of mine. As a result, this left me with only a couple of menu items I would even venture to try.

I made the "frittata" because the recipe allowed for the substitution of oilive oil. It was absolutely delicious. I had to stop myself from eating the entire creation. The first picture is the frittata after it came out of the oven. The second picture is a piece of the frittata on the left with a salad of my own creation on the right. The recipe says it can be served with a side salad and their apple cider or simple lemon dressing (neither of which I made because I also dislike dressings).

I may try the "ALL GREEN" juice recipe but other than that and maybe one other recipe, there's not much in this cookbook I would ever make and most of that is due to the fact that practically every recipe calls for coconut oil. Based on the one recipe I made, I have no doubt the resulting food is flavorful. However, this book just isn't my cup of tea and will rarely be used in my house.

title: The main message of this book is to STOP RUMINATING (worrying or catastrophizing) as STRESS IS OPTIIONAL
text:
I am not as enamored with this book as the other reviewers. The premise of the entire book is that stress is optional and is caused by rumination. There’s a four step process of waking up, controlling attention, becoming detached, and letting go that builds resilience which leads to a life without stress.

Below is what I understood the author to be saying:
- Rumination refers to unnecessarily worrying and emotionally hashing out details over and over.
- Waking up is the ability to be present in thought and not drift off in thought to the past or future.
- Controlling attention is the ability of being in the moment and aware of what is around you.
- Becoming detached is the ability of maintaining perspective.
- Letting go is the ability of not staying locked into one scenario or emotion.
- "Resilience is the ability to negotiate the rapids of life without becoming stressed." Resilience is also enhanced by one’s sensitivity which requires one to quickly and accurately assess how others feel.

Although this text included some other gems of information such as describing the two Rs of leadership (leaders with “relationship” and “requiring” skills), I found that “Work Without Stress” could have been summed up eloquently in less than 50 pages.

I felt this book only started to address the leadership side of the equation from Page 59 onward as Pages 1-58 were more background in nature about rumination, stress, resilience, etc. Also, pages 169 to 198 contain the Appendix which describes the science (or studies) behind the theory and that text wasn’t as interesting to me.

Overall, this text captured my attention sporadically. I found it to be repetitive and a bit unorganized. It is definitely a worthwhile read but I do not feel that I learned much other than what I highlighted in the above list. The main message is “STOP RUMINATING.”

title: Bird behavior studies, facts, and details
text:
I spent over 17 hours reading this book because it was such a tedious read for me. I actually expected this to be a lighthearted and entertaining book about the author’s observations of bird behavior but it is not really about that. Instead it is an in-depth diatribe of facts based on research by biologists, animal behavior specialists, ornithologists, psychologists, and other scientists and researchers.

For instance, I learned that:

- Bird brain size correlates with how long the bird’s juvenile period is.

- Scientists related structures in the bird brain to parallel structures in the mammalian brain for comparison purposes. For instance, “nerve cells in a mammal’s neocortex are stacked in six distinct layers like plywood, those in the bird’s cortex-like structure cluster like cloves in a garlic bulb.”

- New Caledonian crows are the only birds that craft their own complex tools, including hook tools, to get at food.

- Many birds are extremely social such as the belted kingfisher and the scissor-tailed flycatcher (also called the Texas bird of paradise).

- Ravens remember their friends and humans too.

- Pinyon jays make a determination on the social status of “stranger” birds based on the way those birds behave.

- Birds are conformists like humans.

- Birds from the same US state, but which are from a different area of that state, may sing entirely different tunes.

- Bowerbirds use extravagant objects to woo a female. Sometimes they allow juvenile males to watch their performance as a test drive prior to trying to lure a female. This is beneficial for both males.

- Humans are driving the specialist-type birds to extinction, meaning the ones with old bird lineages.

I also learned that researchers do awful things to study birds. For example:

- In one study, they removed the inner ear of homing pigeons to see if it had an effect on their ability to home. It had “no effect on their ability to home.”

- In another study researchers “cut the nerve that runs from the beak to the brain, the so-called trigeminal nerve, which is thought to transmit magnet information to the brain.” The warblers whose nerve was cut “lost their ability to fix their position;” meaning they lost their ability to navigate via what we call their map sense.

This book is packed with scientific and researched facts and in some cases just hypotheses that are yet to be accepted or proven. For me, it was a marginally dry read and not what I expected from this book. I believe this book is an ornithologists or animal scientists dream as I suspect they love to devour data. I, on the other hand, was looking for more of a good observational story on birds than this text provided.

title: This is one of seven books I read on Parkinson's Disease
text:
For the past 14 years an extremely close friend of mine has had many unexplainable symptoms (lack of smell, muscle cramping, choking, extreme abdominal pain with nausea after eating fiber or fat-rich foods, etc.) This November 2015 I noticed a resting tremor in the arm on his left side. This was the first time I suspected his issues were related to one disease which might be Parkinson's Disease (PD). However, I still dismissed this possibility because tremors can be related to other medical issues (one of which is benign) and he has only had this tremor three times. Periodically over the past several months I noticed him walking slower, a frozen facial expression, and his right hand curled in front of him as if he had a stroke. On Dec 5, 2015 he really exhibited the slow walking, frozen face, and curled hand and he took forever to dress that morning. Later that evening I became certain (in my opinion) that he has PD due to his telling me about a change in his handwriting which I did not witness. Unfortunately, he refuses to go to the doctor or seek medical help from a neurologist even when I told him I believe he has PD. On extremely rare occasions he'll go to see a particular specialist for whatever ailment is almost killing him at the moment. As a result, since December 2015 I've completely immersed myself in learning about PD with some cursory investigation of illnesses that exhibit Parkinson-like symptoms because I wanted to be sure I was on the right track.

Besides searching the Internet for information, I purchased seven (7) books on Parkinson's Disease (PD) of which this book is one. My review is written from the perspective of someone who does not have PD but wants to learn about what the signs of PD are, what a person's life will be like, what are their challenges, what they should do about it, what is their life expectancy, etc. This book is in the list below. I've listed the books in the order of value to me and not in the order that I read them. I also put the copyright date of each book in parenthesis as well as my star ranking based on its usefulness to me and a short few sentences of what the book was about. If I had PD myself, I would rank them in a different order. I posted the same review to each one of these seven (7) books. At the end, I wrote a summary of what I think about PD and listed seven (7) other books I may one day buy and read.

[[ASIN:0470073950 Parkinson's Disease For Dummies]] (c 2007) (4.5 stars) - Although this book does not have the latest developments or information on PD or Lewy Body disease (dementia included), it was invaluable in helping me understand what PD is in the most simplest terms. It helped me understand what to look for in a person with PD and what challenges they face. Since we are in 2016, the information on treatment is somewhat outdated. This book is great for someone who suspects they have PD or just got diagnosed because it clarifies symptoms in easy-to-understand language. It's a great resource for the newly diagnosed PD patient and those preparing for their first appointment. It also has information on Young Onset Parkinson's Disease (YOPD) and a chapter (sections of which I skipped over) full of exercises for the PD patient.

[[ASIN:0446678902 What Your Doctor May Not Tell You About(TM): Parkinson's Disease: A Holistic Program for Optimal Wellness]] (c Feb 2003) (4 stars) - This is like a textbook on Parkinson's disease with case studies from actual patients and information on alternative therapies such as acupuncture. This book appears to outline all the symptoms of Parkinson’s, including ones not in other books such as Seborrheic dermatitis and stuttering (which is also in Wilson's disease). This book discusses everything from A-Z, like complementary medicine (homeopathy, acupuncture, etc.), issues for caregivers, etc. Case studies are interspersed throughout the text to give the reader a general idea of a PD person's experiences. It even mentions Mucuna pruriens which is a bean sold in supplement form and has high levels of levodopa that could be of help to PD patients--of course, only take this with supervision of your doctor.

[[ASIN:193260393X A Caregiver's Guide to Lewy Body Dementia]] (c 2011) (5 stars) - this broadened my horizons about PD because it described the symptoms related to two very similar diseases and was co-written by someone whose spouse had dementia with Lewy bodies. PD is a Lewy Body disease where abnormal proteins show up on the part of the brain that controls movement. However, it is closely associated with Lewy Body Dementia that has abnormal proteins on the cognition part of the brain. Both diseases have many of the same symptoms and depending on which symptoms appear first that determines what the disease is called. It is either dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) or Parkinson's Disease with Dementia (PDD). The diagnosis is critical because medications for one disease can have adverse effects on those with the other disease or on those with Alzheimer's. Some DLB patients are misdiagnosed with Alzheimer's and those medicines are contraindicated in most cases for them. It was this book that helped me realize the symptoms I was seeing was the same with my friend and also easily explained what a caregiver needs to do.

[[ASIN:1630261297 Living Well with Parkinson's]] (second edition) (c 1991, 2005) (5 stars) - This book was originally written by a woman who had Parkinson's Disease but who died on November 25, 1998 from a heart attack unrelated to PD. It was revised in 2005. This book is phenomenal in my opinion because it supplied me with an excellent narrative of what it was like to live with Parkinson's and how to make that life worth living. The chapter on "Medications and Therapies" provides a list of diseases that can resemble PD. The chapter on "Is There Life With Parkinson's" is a positive narrative on how the author lived very well with the disease.

[[ASIN:1478325844 Parkinson's Humor - Funny Stories about My Life with Parkinson's Disease]] (c2012) (4 stars) - is a lighthearted book written by someone who has PD. The book, although not very funny to me, educated me on what day-to-day life is like to live with PD. For instance, Beverly mentioned how sometimes she felt starched when describing the rigidity PD patients experienced. Except for [[ASIN:1630261297 Living Well with Parkinson's]], this book was the only other uplifting book. All the others books were way too serious and sobering. At a time when I am new in trying to understand PD and PDD, reading a text like this or the one above was critical especially since I was overdosing on the subject. This book provided the mental break I needed, was slightly educational, and an extremely easy read.

[[ASIN:0671768190 Parkinson's Disease: The Complete Guide for Patients and Caregivers]] (c 1993) (3 stars) - this book is similar to [[ASIN:0446678902 What Your Doctor May Not Tell You About(TM): Parkinson's Disease: A Holistic Program for Optimal Wellness]] but it's 10 years earlier so the information is dated. For example in one chapter on how to cope with Parkinson’s there's a suggestion to use a Dictaphone if you can't write. It has a short first section on symptoms of the disease and then goes into history, treatment, etc. There are three sections, however, that I found worthwhile. The Chapter on "The A to Z Guide to Symptoms and Side Effects," "Planning Your Financial Future," and "Diseases That May Resemble Parkinson's Disease" which is in the Appendix II are invaluable. One thing I did not like about this book is that it was very negative describing more than once about the disabling effects of PD and how you have get your affairs in order, etc. Except for the three worthwhile chapters, I feel I did not need to purchase this book to get the information I was looking for.

[[ASIN:0374116172 Brain Storms: The Race to Unlock the Mysteries of Parkinson's Disease]] (c 2015) (4 stars) - the author is actually a PD patient and this book covers the most recent research on PD. It was not as helpful to me because it talked more about the latest developments in the search for a cure as well a brief glimpse at tests and drugs for PD patients. If I were a person with PD, then this book would probably be second in value in my list. For me, I could have done without purchasing this book.

In summary, what I discovered is that a PD patient does not die from their disease and they can have a normal life expectancy. PD is a slowly progressive disease, that is not usually hereditary, and which affects each patient differently. Not all PD patients have visible tremors. The disease definitely changes the patient's life and the lives of those closest to them but it sometimes does this for the better because the patients re-evaluate their lives and how they want to spend their time. For many, the disease will be an inconvenience that the patients and caregivers can learn to live with. There are no tests that can definitely determine someone has PD while the person is alive. A definitive diagnosis can only be made with post-mortem brain analysis. PD is determined via a process of elimination of testing for other similar diseases, observing arm muscle reactions during a test a doctor may try, and observing how the symptoms respond to Carbidopa / Levodopa drugs. It is critical that patients seek help immediately and partner with a doctor (or several doctors such as physical therapists, speech therapists, etc.) to seek a diagnosis and develop a treatment plan. At the early stages of PD, no drug therapy may be involved; it might me more of a wait and see approach. The positive attitude of the patient along with eating right, exercising, partnering with a healthcare team, and having a good support network provides the best outcome for the patient to have a fruitful life with only some limitations and modifications.

Please understand that no one book provided all the information I needed or wanted. I discovered information has to come from several sources, including the Internet and PD support groups. For instance, one PD symptom not mentioned in any of these books is gastroparesis. I found that one by searching the Internet with the word Parkinson's and abdominal cramping with nausea and the likes. I did these searches years ago, but at that time I did not suspect PD so Parkinson’s was not part of the search criteria. I do hope my friend will seek the help of a neurologist, detail all his symptoms, and let me tell the neurologist what I have been seeing. Could I be wrong about believing that my friend has PD. Absolutely, I could be wrong; even doctors misdiagnose patients. However, after reviewing Internet sources for the other diseases mentioned in these books, the only other diseases that come close with his symptoms are a brain tumor or Wilson's disease. However, with Wilson's disease his eye doctor would have noticed the copper ring (known as Kayser-Fleischer Ring) around his cornea during his eye exam.

Although I am on PD overload, below are seven (7) other books (not listed in any particular order) that I might purchase in the future to learn more. The first one is on a disease with very close PD symptoms and the other six are on PD or a person’s experience with PD.

1. [[ASIN:1401029043 Wilson's Disease for the Patient and Family: A Patient's Guide to Wilson's Disease and Frequently Asked Questions about Copper]]

2. [[ASIN:0763772534 The Muhammad Ali Parkinson Center 100 Questions & Answers About Parkinson Disease (100 Questions & Answers)]]

3. [[ASIN:0801878888 A Life Shaken: My Encounter with Parkinson's Disease]]

4. [[ASIN:0786888741 Lucky Man: A Memoir]]

5. [[ASIN:1421410761 Parkinson's Disease: A Complete Guide for Patients and Families (A Johns Hopkins Press Health Book)]]

6. [[ASIN:067401751X Parkinson's Disease and the Family: A New Guide (The Harvard University Press Family Health Guides)]]

7. [[ASIN:0966437004 Eat Well, Stay Well With Parkinson's disease]]

title: A good story inspires and motivates people to action; many storytellers are made and not born.
text:
Carmine Gallo attempts to explain how good stories are created and inspire through the examples in this text. He makes it clear that most great storytellers are made as a result of struggle or tragedy in their lives that they turned into victory.

The author breaks down the types of stories as follows:

- Storytellers who ignore our inner fire
- Storytellers who educate
- Storytellers who simplify
- Storytellers who motivate
- Storytellers who launch movements

There's no doubt parts of this book are inspiring and that this author has proven his point through the stories of some notable people like Howard Schultz (CEO of Starbucks), Joel Osteen (American preacher), Richard Branson (founder of Virgin Group), Amy Purdy (world-class Paralympic snowboarder), Oprah Winfrey (talk show host), Winston Churchill (former Prime Minister of the United Kingdom), etc., etc.

For instance, Steve Jobs (co-founder of Apple) used a violation of expectations when he announced in a presentation "We have three products...The first one is a widescreen iPod with touch controls. The second is a revolutionary mobile phone. And the third is a breakthrough Internet communications device." He repeated these three products again and then he violated everyone expectations by saying that they were not three devices. He said, "This is one device. And we are calling it an iPhone."

Although this book is spot on with how certain people inspire, motivate, and exert a powerful influence through a great story, I did not find reading this a page turner because it was repetitive, long-winded, and the "secrets" were pigeon-holed into five different types of stories almost all of which could have fit any type of story. To me every story in the book educated, motivated, and simplified the message into something the audience could understand. The author, in my opinion, failed to heed his own advice of simplifying the story and instead crafted a message at least 50% longer than it should have been.

So........ here is my story:

I am an avid consumer who has become weary over the inferior consumer products that I wasted my money on and which have ended up in landfills. Therefore, as a hobby I decided to combine my love of writing with my desire to review products in order to empower others in making informed purchase decisions and spend dollars wisely in the hopes that they not lose money like I have.

Please note that I received a pre-release book. In its current state, I feel this book is one that should be borrowed from a library. If the story were tightened up by about 50% (which I doubt it will be), then I might consider this worth the purchase.

title: Tasty recipes with sometimes unusual ingredients that are not always so simple to make and an overall Asian flare
text:
I belonged to a CSA for three seasons and discovered ingredients I never heard of such as garlic scapes. Lucky my CSA provided me with recipes on how to cook and use some of these ingredients.

Therefore, I expected a lot from this cookbook but it deviated substantially from my expectations. On the positive side, it is really a beautiful looking cookbook and there are certainly plenty of tasty recipes. I made the guyere grilled cheese with chard and caramelized onion except I substituted kale (because that is what I had on hand). I also used a Lean Mean Grilling Machine as my panini press instead of the two baking pans she suggested inside the oven. The recipe came out spectacular. My boyfriend's exact words were "MY GOD, this is excellent."

Despite having such splendid results with this one recipe, this book is not totally what I expected for several reasons:

- Many recipes have an Asian flare like the swiss chard summer roll with citrus soy-marinated tofu; stir-fried snow peas, pea shoots with sesame ginger vinaigrette; yardlong bean curry with wilted spinach (recipe calls for coconut milk); oyakodon-style omelette with spring onions, Vietnamese carrot and daikon pickles; spicy stir-fried sweet potato leaves (recipe calls for 1-1/2 pounds of sweet potato leaves); watermelon rind kimchi; bottom-of-the-box bibimbap; etc.

- Things that I would throw away or consider part of a compost pile are actually used, such as tomato leaves, kale stems, sweet potato leaves, etc. For example, my CSA gave me tomatoes, but I never got any leaf with that. I doubt others get tomato leaves as part of their CSA allotment.

- There are some unusual ingredients that are not provided in any typical CSA I know. (My friend also joined a different CSA in another part of the state and never got these.) For example, kale buds, Padron peppers, fresh wild mushrooms, daikon pickles, radish pods, pea sprouts, tomato leaves, sweet potato leaves, etc.

- Also, many recipes are spicy like the spicy stir-fried sweet potato leaves, spicy fermented summer salsa, spicy minty tomato sauce infused with tomato leaves, etc.

In summary, I think this is a beautiful looking cookbook that does have some great recipes. I like the introduction to pantry ingredients and tools in front. I also think the recipes are well-thought out. However, this is not a book I would purchase for someone who joined a CSA because many ingredients are not even provided with a typical CSA and this is more for someone with a desire for Asian and spicy cooking. Also, many of the recipes require time to make with lots of ingredients (most of which have to be store bought). Overall, it's a great cookbook but the title of it is misleading and it's for that reason I give it 3 stars. If it were called Asian inspired cookbook with farmer's bounty and other unusual ingredients, then I would have rated this 4 or 5 stars. It is certainly a nice complement to my cooking library but not one that I will use extensively.

title: Know your PWR score for leadership success
text:
There are many leadership books on the market touting formulas for success. This book is one of them. The formula in this case in knowing your Power Score which is defined as P x W x R =. A perfect score is 1,000 with a typically good score being 9 x 9 x 9 = 729.

P is for PRIORITIES. Are they clear, connected to a mission/purpose, and correct (ones that are achievable based on the goals)?

W is the most important ingredient and that stands for WHO. This is about building the right team based on the job that needs accomplishing. Sometimes it means moving the jobs (products, etc.) around to the right people who can get them done. It's important to determine if the employee has the right SKILL and WILL to do the job and that that person FITS with the position he or she is filling.

R is about building the right RELATIONSHIPS that matter to the company's success and involves coordination, communication, commitment, and challenge (motivating someone to be their best self).

= means EQUALS; this is the P, W, and R multiplied. Each element is rated on a scale of 1 to 10 and multiplied to determine your leadership success.

I wanted to really love this book. However, I felt only the chapter on the WHO was the best. The P and R chapters meandered and were sometimes muddled. For example, in the final chapter about the overall score, the authors mention a Social Worker named Reggie who was emotionally touched by the pain on a girl's face as she was removed from her parents. It was clear that Reggie's success or failure as a social worker meant life and death in situations like this. However, the authors never clearly explain how this scenario plays out. Instead they say it plays out by delving into an explanation of how the team comes to a conclusion on their power score. I personally could not relate to how this discussion on their score helped this little girl in any way.

In summary, although the PRIORITIES and RELATIONSHIPS sections of the book are mediocre and long-winded with some filler prose, the chapter on the WHO has some excellent advice on interviewing candidates (screening interview, who interview, referral interview, etc.) and other tidbits for building a great team. It is based on this chapter alone that I feel this book is worth the read and a quick read it is.

title: A clinical look at what companies might do to help practitioners (cops, pilots, nurses, etc.) responsible for a tragedy
text:
I selected this book for review because I was interested in user stories of how people get through being a second victim. For instance, my best friend in the whole world committed suicide and at one point I felt guilty I could not prevent that. An acquaintance of mine was brutally murdered (stabbed over 41 times) and I wanted to understand all the emotions a parent goes through. Also, while on the way work one day, a middle-aged man ran in front of a truck (suicide) a few minutes before I passed him as a passenger in a bus. I always wondered how the truck driver coped.

Nevertheless, this book is not about any of that. It's a clinical look at what companies might do to help practitioner (doctors, pilots, nurses, cops, etc.) second victims cope with a tragedy they caused without blame or with minimal blame. There are some brief stories of these second victims which I found to be the highlight of this book because I could get into the mind of the second victim but that was to support the argument of why it second victims should be treated differently. Societies put blame on second victims and have drifted away from calling things accidents. As a result, corporations and facilities do not learn from their mistakes.

The book talks about the clinical implications of trauma, guilt, investigation, justice, retribution, etc. In summary, this 100-page text is a good read but it really was not for me. I'd believe people who are treating second victims would find the most benefit from reading this (5 stars). People who are the second victims themselves might find a benefit (3-4 stars). However, people like me who wanted a text that delved into the mind of the second victim would probably rate this (2-3 stars). At the current price of $31.93, I also feel this book is three-times what I would have paid had I purchased it. It is well-written, I liked it, but it did not achieve the goal I expected. What I learned from this book is that society, corporations, medical faculties, etc. do not want to learn from their mistakes. Instead they are more likely to blame the second victim and seek to punish them without providing them the support that is desperately needed.

title: Several great letters and stories among many cryptic ones
text:
I commend the author for compiling a book of letters and stories that are intended to help the victims of sexual violence. There are 21 short letters and more than 25 short stories in this text.

I found letters 1, 3, & 6 and the story "You Don't Owe It to Anyone Else to Report" to be absolute gems. In fact, a couple of letters can apply to anyone who has experienced any type of abuse, not only sexual violence. However, the rest of the letters and stories are very cryptic and all over the place.

I also felt sort of left out reading the text. The reason is that this appears to be written more for poor black, ethnic, and lesbian survivors rather than white females. Terms such as "brown on brown, African, black, baby mama throughout the text made me feel I was in the minority. There is nothing wrong with this per se because many survivors do come from ethic and poor backgrounds. However, because most of the stories and letters seemed to lean this way, it gave me a "hard to relate" vibe.

Also, the reason I say most of the letters and stories are cryptic is because many read like poetry, one is written in Spanish, one is purposely written with no sentence capitalization, another is written with partial sentences joined together by & for the entire story, etc. I know that abuse in any form leaves one in a topsy turvy state and perhaps it was the intention of the author to reflect this. Nevertheless, I'm not so sure that most victims will understand the message and support that is trying to be communicated.

If these letters and stories were less poetic, less cryptic, and less inconsistent in their content, then I would have rated this book 5 stars. Although there were some gems like I mentioned above, the rest were all over the place which made "Dear Sister" just okay and not great for me personally. Obviously, I'm in the minority based on the other reviewers but I can only relate how I felt reading this book.

title: What makes a leader who they are?
text:
I was captivated with this book starting with the first paragraph in Chapter 1. Why did President George W. Bush react the way he did when he heard about the September 11th WTC disaster while in a classroom full of students? Or, did why British Prime Minister Tony Blair act the way he did when he received the news about the terrorist tube train and bombings in the midst of chairing the G8 summit? After reading the entire book, I never did understand why in their particular case.

The author provides examples of certain aspects or qualities of leadership and tries to interweave various leaders' stories (Ernest Shackleton, Duke Ellington, Hitler, etc.) to fit those aspects of leadership. Some aspects or qualities discussed were:

- SPQ = Situations, Processes, and Qualities
- DDD = Destiny, Drama, Deliberation
- CLR = Critical Leader Relationships
- A model of Self-Regulation (battle for purpose, control, truth, identity, performance)
- Games Leaders Play, such as to be driven by desire, imprisoned by experience, etc.
- Three levels leaders can command are self, people, and the environment.

Let's take the situation character of SPQ. Its components would be to read the situation, consider the range of options, pick an option, and execute. Now if we look at the truth model in self-regulation, it would be the leader's vision of what is real and in some cases that is distorted. For instance, Steve Jobs strongly believed a vegan/fruit diet "immunized him from body odor and the need for regular bathing." In essence, this was a leader who had to be told to take a shower.

According to the author, a "Leader's answers to the "who am I?" question are critical to their actions and effectiveness." I could not agree more. Nevertheless, I did not feel the author answered this question in a cohesive fashion throughout the book.

His interjection of SPQ, DDD, CLR, etc. throughout the chapters while describing or providing examples of different leaders and how this applied to them, served only to confuse me. The book vacillated between how one becomes a leader to how we might apply those characteristics to each of the leaders described. I would have preferred a summarized view of what makes a leader a leader upfront without all the jargon and then an in-depth look by perhaps dedicating individual chapters to each leader instead of using examples periodically throughout the book.

It is really who we are that determines the basis for a leader's path forward. Then other elements such as situations, drive (deliberation), etc. alter that to make all leaders different and effective or ineffective even though no two are really alike. The author is a great writer and he certainly has the ability to captivate the reader with his leadership stories but I actually felt he took the "I" out of leadership by interjecting the various strategies, aspects, or qualities of leadership in a book that fluctuated between excellent stories and a leadership textbook.

title: Leadership transformation through the use of 7 metaphors but without the supporting examples I expected
text:
I received a pre-release copy of Leadership Transformed which is a book about using metaphors to explain how extraordinary managers become extraordinary leaders.

A metaphor is a word, phrase, object, activity, or idea that is used as a reference point to suggest one thing with the intention of symbolizing something else. Dr. Fuda defines 7 Metaphors for Leadership Transformation in this text. They are:

1. FIRE
2. SNOWBALL
3. MASTER CHEF
4. COACH
5. MASK
6. MOVIE
7. RUSSIAN DOLLS

All these metaphors are interrelated with FIRE being the center force. Although the application of these metaphors differs for each leader, this is my interpretation and oversimplification of the seven metaphors presented in this book --> To bring forth extraordinary leadership one has to have a strong goal and burning ambition (FIRE) to create the momentum (SNOWBALL) to propel change forward through the artful application of frameworks, tools, and strategies (MASTER CHEF). This is accomplished with a team that helps coach (COACH) one another toward their aspirations by unleashing their authentic selves (dropping the MASK), editing and directing their performance (MOVIE), and enhancing their effectiveness through a complimentary alignment of goals (RUSSIAN DOLLS).

Leadership Transformed was definitely an interesting read and I liked that the author presented a very different leadership viewpoint. Nevertheless I was surprised by the highly-rated reviews for this book. Although the ideas presented are easy for everyone to understand, I did not feel his supporting examples were validation enough for each metaphor. For example, in the Russian Doll chapter he talks about Mike who chose to keep a low profile on an investment he was making until it showed promise rather than try to align his superiors with his leadership agenda. To me this was contradictory to the inherent meaning of the Russian Doll metaphor he was describing. I would have rated this book five stars if the author spent more time driving home the specifics of each metaphor, which would require a step-by-step model, and had provided much clearer and additional examples supporting these metaphors.

This book does not outline a step-by-step model for creating extraordinary leaders; however, it does get one thinking about how they might apply the above principles to achieve their goals.

PS Quadrant 3 of the "FIRE" matrix presented in the book was incorrect but that is expected since the copy I received was a pre-release version. The author also refers the reader to his website, which is also pre-release (although the "FIRE" matrix is correct on that site). His website looks extremely promising but at the present time the audiovisual tools and some of the content for each metaphor exercise he refers the reader to was missing.

title: Two different women with different philosophies; both can have a successful life
text:
Before this book I never heard of the famous Italian designer Elsa Schiaparelli. "Shocked" is about the differences between the author Patricia's mother Audrey Volk and Elsa Schiaparelli. Audrey's husband buys Schiaparelli's perfume "Shocking" for his wife's birthday every year. Patricia outlines in extreme detail nuanced differences between the way her mother conducted her life and the way Schiap (short for Schiaparelli) conducted hers. The author goes into detail about everything. She dedicates paragraphs and pages to describing the way her mother applies makeup or perfume to the darning of her husband's socks or to the way Schiaparelli lives her life. I started out liking this book but in the end I felt it was just okay. I was confused by the story because after finishing the book I still do not understand the relationship between the author, her mother, or Schiap other than the author's mother was a customer. In my opinion I felt that Patricia was describing in conflicting detail how confused she was by her up-bringing and the differences between these two women. However, in the end she realized it does not really matter how she conducts her life or what she believes because "anything is possible."

PS - The sketches in the book are exceptional and my favorite is the one depicting the living room designed by Salvador Dali for Schiaparelli that was furnished by Mae West's face.

title: Mostly British with some esoteric ingredients
text:
I read this entire book from cover to cover with the exception of the recipes which I just scanned. To me the author tries to cover a lot of ground and focuses on reducing the baking times by keeping the techniques and recipes he mentions short and very sweet.

I did learn a few things from this book; however, this cookbook is not the star player I thought it would be in my cooking library.

What I like is:

- He focuses on pretty much ignoring the kneading part of bread making and instead prefers to use time to do the trick in making the dough rise.

- He mentions how to add steam to an oven.

- He suggests adding a crushed Vitamin C tablet to whole-wheat flour to keep the dough stretchy

- He sometimes provides recipes for expansive ingredients or hard to find ingredients such as marzipan and sweet choux paste

What I don't like is:

- A lot of recipes call for hard-to-find-in-the-US ingredients such as creme fraiche, European butters like Lurpak and President, rosewater, suet, psyllium husk powder, etc.

- I was surprised he did not provide a recipe for super-fine sugar or creme fraiche. For example, creme fraiche is so easy to make yet so expensive and hard to find here. To make one cup of creme fraiche all that's needed is 1 to 2 tablespoons of buttermilk to 1 cup of heavy cream and let it sit at room temperature for 8-12 hours until thick then refrigerate. I've made creme fraiche before after buying it once and I could not taste the difference between store bought and homemade. Apparently to make super-fine (caster) sugar, just take refined sugar and blend in food processor with cutting blade.

- More than a few recipes call for alcohol such as rum, cognac, orange liquers such as Cointreau or Grand Marnier, Pedro Ximenez sherry, champagne, white wine, brandy, Marsala, etc. For someone like me who does not drink alcohol and only uses Vodka for Vodka sauce and making my own vanilla extract, calling for alcohol in a recipe beyond wine means it's something else I have to buy and store. Therefore, this is more off a turnoff for me.

- He does not do justice for sourdough breadmaking. Instead he includes a quick overview of his ideas in an effort to keep it short and say he addressed sourdough bread.

- Most of the recipes are not ones I would normally make such as Victoria plum jellies, black millionaire's shortbread, rye hazelnut brownies, cider vinegar muffins, little prune and cognac pies, etc.

- The "sugar sugar" chapter of the book should really be labeled the caramel section because it's mostly about making caramel and caramel-flavored recipes. I do realize sugar turns into caramel but more can be done with sugar than just this. How about a recipe for flan which is quick and easy to make?

- The pictures in the book are great but none of them are captioned so in some cases I was not abel to determine to which recipe they applied.

- Most of the recipes call for super-rich ingredients, so this is no diet book nor is it meant to be that. Also, except for the bread and supper chapters, most of the recipes in this book seem to be ones that will come out on the sweet side. However, I suspect the end result of following these recipes should be good to great.

I baked the pumpkin ginger cupcakes and they were good. Even though the recipe said they were cupcakes, the directions said to prepare a muffin tin. Instead I used 2 cupcake tins and came out with 23 cupcakes. Since the recipe said I would get 12 cupcakes, I guess it meant that they were really supposed to be muffiin-sized cupcakes. Had I used that tin, I believe the cakes would have been a little bit more moist. Of course, I could have reduced the baking time to accommodate the smaller tins. The results were good but not as good as they could have been. Also, the icing was very sweet. Many would like this but I prefer subtle sweetness in my desserts.

Despite this good result from the one recipe I tried, the likelihood of my making more than five recipes in this book is almost nil. I still do think this baking book is a good compliment to my cookbook library because of the tips provided, but it will not be my main goto book. It is apparent the author put a lot of work into this compendum but for my purposes it is just okay.

UPDATE April 9, 2013 - I ate 5 of the 23 pumpkin ginger cupcakes and decided to bring the other 18 into work. My colleagues loved them. One person even ate 3 cupcakes and another ate 2 cupcakes. They were all devoured.

title: A year in the life of Scott County basketball players
text:
This book is mostly about the Cardinals, a small town high school basketball team from Scott County Kentucky, and their coach Billy Hicks during the 2009 to 2010 season. It was during this season, when America was in a state of financial depression, that the players were focused on winning. Their season-end goal was to play at Rupp Arena in an effort to try to win the state championship--what I would call the "Super Bowl" of basketball.

The author not only details what it took to play the game from the eyes of each player but he also wove in the story of their lives and struggles. In addition, he spoke about several coaches motivations and the successes and failures of other teams the Cardinals were playing against. In this sense, "Outside Shot" is more than just a basketball story. It is inspirational from the point of how the coach and the players morphed their lives into something better than where they came from.

From my perspective this was an okay read.

title: Best read by religious husbands in a religious marriage
text:
I read this book because I wanted to determine if the advice being given to men is really reasonable from a woman's perspective.

"Date Your Wife" is more like a small pamphlet than a book. It strongly preaches religion and how Jesus is in your life and your marriage. Combined with Jesus' presence and teachings in your marriage the author guides the husband on how to date their wife.

In general, I do believe most of the author's advice is sensible and would work on me from my perspective as a woman or as a wife. It is even more reasonable if you are religious. Since I'm not religious at all, I had to sift through all the "religiosity" to get to the core of the message.

Despite what the author says, I do not agree that everything is the man's fault or that to change a marriage you must change the man. Marriage always takes two people in my opinion; however, if I were to sum up the author's message to men it's this:

- Men take the lead and pursue your wife after you are married.

- Follow the same game plan you did when you were courting your wife. Don't get married and then think you can "relax" from the perspective of guarding, cherishing, caring for, loving, dating etc. your wife.

- Plan to cultivate your marriage like you plan for your business. For instance, you can create an annual plan by setting dates for you and your wife for the next 12 months and then sharing that with your wife. Don't change those plans. These plans could be a small weekend trip or a short getaway.

- Plan to cultivate your marriage daily. Say "I love you." Praise your wife or tell her you are sorry for something you did. Cuddle with your wife, stroke her hair, take better care of yourself, etc., etc.

All of the above (and more) is the good advice I understood from this book.

"Date your wife" ends with the pastor's wife providing a few words of wisdom to the wife such as "be datable." This means making an effort to smell and look good. "Spend daily time together." Etc. The 100 ideas the author lists at the end on how to "date your wife" is a good starting point of ideas for the man.

In addition, I loved the comment a 90-year old man made in the next to last chapter. He said, "Someone defined love as 'placing the welfare of the other ahead of your own.' That's the kind of love that pays great dividends. Careful now: you don't love for what you get out of it. What happens is that genuine love--a life invested in another--simply works out that way." I'd have to say I agree as long as the husband takes the lead and the wife is a willing participant along with him.

If I were religious, I probably would have rated this book 4 or 5 stars. Those who are religious will probably love it or like it. I enjoyed the book and do think it offered some great advice although it is too overboard for me on relating religion to how to "date your wife." In general, I suspect the man that reads this type of book does not need this advice anyway; it's the ones who really need the advice that probably won't pick it up.

In summary, this is a decent, easy-to-read book that's too religious for me but still has some great advice for the husband. As a woman, I think most of the advice given is very smart indeed.

title: Unusual memoir that was interesting in places but did not always hold my interest
text:
I will only read non-fiction books. As a result I find myself sometimes being drawn to memoirs as this is my way of getting lost in a type of book that can contain all the suspense and drama of a novel yet because it's real provides me with either a learning experience or the ability to live vicariously through someone else.

"The Great Northern Express: A Writer's Journey Home" is an unusual memoir in that it was interesting in places but did not always hold my interest. I did not feel like I was taking the journey with the author.

This memoir is about a writer who at the age of 64 gets prostate cancer and after his treatments are over decides to set out alone on a cross-country book tour from his hometown in Orleans Vermont. His intention is to tell funny stories about the experience. During this tour in his twenty-year-old beat up Chevy that is more dead than alive, he reflects back on his life.

There is more about his life than the road trip such as the mention of the "abusive sex shows and barbaric cockfights" in Vermont, the elderly couple who lost their farm after 60 years in Vermont, and the wonderful lady Margery Moore who was very helpful to his family. The only story that was funny to me was (when on the road) he was mistaken for a homeless man and given a broom to sweep up at a cafe where the proprietor served him some food for the completed chore. This and a few other stories held my interest but, in general, each different short story (some of which were so oddly told) disturbed the flow of the overall journey.

The other reflections he had on the road were so confusing that I found myself drifting off and having to re-read parts of a chapter. For instance, he talked about the West Texas Jesus and sometimes I thought this was a real guy but then he kept popping in and out of the story at different locations on the book tour that were so far from each other that it didn't make sense. Now I realize it was someone he made up to talk to in his head while on the road like he talked to his father's best friend Reg (who was dead) but who he considered an uncle.

There are 65 chapters of 2-5 pages in length so it was easy to put the book down and start up again because to me each chapter (except for a few) could stand on its own. Overall, I can't say that I recommend this book even though it was interesting in places. It took me a lot of time to put all the pieces together to even write this review which is how confusing this book was to me.

title: Excellent dangerous plant book that is lacking in two areas
text:
"Wicked Plants" is a pocket-sized 235-page book that is very entertaining, enlightening (for example, red kidney beans are poisonous if not cooked thoroughly), and easy to read. The author covers some of the common plants, fungus and other related genre of the natural world that are deadly, dangerous, or just irritating to humans and animals. She also talks about some of the myths and truths associated with some of these plants.

I consider "Wicked Plants" an excellent reference except for two drawbacks. First, it doesn't have an index. If, for example, you remember that XXX was dangerous you'd have to flip through the entire book to find it. Second, there are no color photos for the plants discussed, only pencil sketches are shown.

In summary, this book is not a complete reference nor is it a typical book either. However, "Wicked Plants" balances entertainment, fact, and myths about plants and related "items" of the natural world in one neat little package.

I gave this book three stars because of the absence of an index and no color pictures. However, I still consider this a worthwhile purchase. If it had these items, I would have given it 4-1/2 to 5 stars. If you have a Kindle, then the Kindle edition would resolve the lack of an index because of its search capability.

title: Como is a normal dog with a neurotic and pessimistic "dad"
text:
Como is the author's teenage daughter's dog. The author sets the stage for the title of the book in the first chapter and then describes his and his family's life "before Como" in the next 40 pages. The rest of the book describes how the author and his family went about Como's adoption and the subsequent life and antics that followed during their first two years together. The book's last chapter ends six years after Como's adoption.

On the positive side, the author is an absolutely phenomenal writer. The way he describes some of Como's antics and his response to them were sometimes so funny that I almost peed in my pants from laughing so hard.

BUT........................

On the negative side, his story can make a devoted pet lover SCREAM "ARE YOU CRAZY and that NAIVE"? For instance, he mentions how he enticed Como to eat a piece of a chocolate power bar so he could catch him on one of his wild escape escapades. Every dog owner should know that chocolate can kill a dog yet he makes no attempt to even acknowledge that he made a mistake. Perhaps he still doesn't know chocolate is dangerous to dogs.

I am not sure if the author is really as disturbed and negative as he makes himself appear to be in the book or if he is just purposely over exaggerating and saying things in "jest" just to create a good read. Much of the story makes me want to strangle (figuratively speaking, of course) the author and his wife (less so for his wife) for how naïve they are about pet ownership. The only one who seems to know how to take care of a dog is their daughter Phoebe who reads many books about dogs that apparently they never read.

In my opinion, Como is a normal dog adopted by parents who do not have a clue about pet ownership. An uninformed person who is thinking of becoming a pet parent can get the wrong parenting message from this book. It is mainly because of this that I rated this book three stars. Had he redeemed himself in the prologue or conclusion of the book by explaining the things he did wrong (like the chocolate) and acknowledging that he now knows how to be a pet parent, I would have given the book four stars. Instead the author's last three chapters are boring and erupt like a VERBAL VOLCANO about anything and everything mostly unrelated to Como.

"Come Back, Como" is a bit drawn out for what I consider normal pet ownership issues. Nevertheless, the author's colorful writing style makes the story an entertaining read up until the last three chapters; although, those who question his pet parenting skills may writhe in anger.

In essence "Come Back, Como" is an extremely subdued version of [[ASIN:0061687200 Marley & Me: Life and Love with the World's Worst Dog]].

title: Cutesy book written in "dog-speak" about living life joyfully
text:
The book is a nice tribute to Trixie, Dean Kootnz's former dog (now deceased). The pictures and antics in the book are adorable and the lessons in life written from a dog's point of view are worth noting. Some of the text in "Life is Good" is funny as well.

You'll learn:
- patience is important
- the good times will follow the bad
- what dogs really like (hot dogs, sausage, peanut butter, etc.)
- to sit back and smell the roses
- etc.

I was so tempted to rate this book higher because everyone else rated it five stars but that would be untruthful as this is not how "I feel" about this text. This book reads more like a children's book and can be read by most people in under 20 minutes. The sentence structure is odd like - Dog. Good Dog. Eat sausage. etc. although that is to be expected from a dog and this type structure was mentioned in the product description.

"Life is Good" is certainly a conversation piece, a great tribute to a wonderful dog (Trixie), and the entire proceeds from the sale of this book goes to the charity Dean adopted Trixie from. The pictures and sentiment expressed in the book are definitely five star quality; but the text and limited content of the book left me wanting more.

title: Decent Recipes but Cookbook has Misleading Subtitle
text:
This cookbook has a nice variety of recipes. However, the subtitle and the back jacket which states they are 5 ingredient, 15 minute recipes is misleading. It really means each recipe either has 5 ingredients or has more ingredients but takes 15 minutes to prepare.

However, this isn't even true because some recipes take more than 15 minutes to prepare and the ingredients border on the absurd. For instance, a recipe can call for pre-packaged chopped onions. My supermarket doesn't sell this, does yours.

Although there's variety in every category (soups, sandwiches, salads, vegetarian, fish, meats,and poultry), I don't think every cook looking for a fast meal would be satisfied with this cookbook, since preparation might take longer than expected or the prepackaged ingredients difficult to find.

If you don't mind spending a little more time than 15 minutes cooking and don't mind chopping your own ingredients or adding Campbell's canned soup to a recipe (although I wouldn't call that "fresh"), then this book might be for you. It certainly has enough variety and interesting tidbits for the average cook. My two most favorite characteristics of the book are the gorgeous pictures of each recipe and the calorie, fat and protein breakdown of each menu. These two charactistics are five stars and the two recipes I tried were also tasty. However, due to the misleading subtitle (as well as the word Fresh in the title--canned is not Fresh) and some of the absurd ingredient suggestions, I have to give this cookbook three stars overall.

title: Too extreme for my taste
text:
I felt like a voyeur reading this book. Since the text is sprinkled with cuss words and EXPLICIT sexual escapades and drug episodes in all its virtual detail, you will feel as if you are a "fly on the wall" watching his life play out. I have to commend the author for his forthrightness (whether some of it was embellished or not) as some would have been highly embarrassed to describe all the intimate details in the way he did.

At first I found the text hard to follow because it reads like a chat session vacillating from one subject or thought to the next. However, the details got clearer as the author's life unfolds from college on into a professional legal career and marriage. This is one person's story told as a participant in his own life as well as an observer to his friends' lives. You will find some interesting details about what some women think is the typical male mind as well as what some attorneys are all about. The "lawyer side" of things is what I found most interesting.

To me this book is controversial because reading it will offend some and enthrall others. People who read non-fiction, dislike crude language, or dislike reading about someone's immaturity will probably begrudgingly accept this book but be disappointed by the language and explicit sexual detail. These types of people like to learn something from books and this text will not provide much learning experience. People who are young, crazy, and live life with immature wild abandon or who once lived life like that will probably love this story. Also, people (especially males) who like to read about other people's lives no matter how sordid will also enjoy it.

It definitely was not my kind of book, but was still sufficiently interesting enough to finish reading.

title: OK book with some mistakes
text: The book is small and does have some useful information on Yorkies.  However, I found the text to be more generic in the sense that it looks like the author copied a lot of the information from another generic dog book.  Also, there were more errors in the text than there should have been for such a small book.  For instance, on one page it mentioned how well a tick will show up on the dog's white coat.  Yorkies don't have white coats.  In addition, a lot of contradictory information was presented.  In some parts of the text it mentions one thing while the boxes on the side said something else.  To me the book was acceptable.

title: No Laughs
text:
This fictional book is about a cat, nicked named Callie, in session with a human therapist. Callie is there to get over her mother abandoning her and many other idiosyncrasies common to a cat, such as excessive hairball production, peeing inappropriately, etc. Although the author captured a cat's behavior well (except for the human aspects such as the Internet gambling addiction), I wish I could say that I found this book funny; but I didn't. I was hoping I'd at least laugh once at Callie's antics, but I just didn't find the story funny and I'm a cat owner for over 20 years. However, I'm glad others were able to. Remember that laughter is subjective and unfortunately my experience differs from what the other reviewers encountered.

On another note, the publishing of the book was substandard. For example, the font type printed in the book sometimes varied in size on the same page. Pages 16 and 42 (and almost every other page) provide good examples of what I'm talking about. These changes were distracting. I'm not referring to the italic font used to indicate the author's private thinking, but the apparent use of a font size 12 one paragraph and then a font size 10 in another paragraph and halfway through the sentence back to another font size 12. In addition, some incorrect wording was left in the text. For instance, "abandoned" instead of "abandonment" should have been used on Page 43; "tone down" instead of "tone done" should have been used on Page 48. There were other proofreading errors throughout the text, such as on Page 49 where one sentence picks up several blank lines down. Nevertheless, this did not cause me to lower my rating as the shoddy publishing is the publisher's responsibility. Most people probably wouldn't notice or even care, but as someone heavily into documentation, all these publishing mistakes broke my focus from the narrative a little bit. I read many books and a few errors are only normal; however, it is unusual to find a book so messy with proofreading errors.

In summary, I found the book to be just okay. The story was cute, silly, and a lighthearted read but not the comedy I was expecting and this is why I rated it a 3.

title: A fact book on adventurous women from history
text:
For the first 50 pages or so, the author, talks about different ladies and different travel facts in practically every other sentence. With her method it's more like you are reading a dictionary than a novel. Because there is so much history compacted into a few pages, you never quite get engulfed in the story of the moment. Instead, you are given the name of each woman and the book(s) she wrote and only a tiny bit about her travels.

At the beginning I rated the book a 2. However, the author changed her style in the later pages and the book moved up to a 3 and finally an 4 with my looking forward to reading it in the evening. In fact if I read it again, I'd probably enjoy it more and increase the ratings.

As the story progresses, she elaborates on the travels of some of the women so that you can get a better understanding of the hardships and in some cases, the enjoyment, they endured. I've learned that the Sandwich Islands are Hawaii and that many women were really pioneers in the way they traveled back then. Many endured diseases and actually died during travel. Others weren't lone travelers; sometimes traveling as a result of a husband's wishes. However, I really can't remember a single female name because there were so many. Those who are interested in historical facts, names and dates would love this book.

"No Place for a Lady" turned out to be a very interesting read but did leave me wanting for more. It is extremely evident that the author did tremendous research and reading in order to produce this work. I suspect one would get more appreciation for what women travelers encountered if they read each book the author did during her research.

title: A book I wanted to love. But… !!!
text:
Having an avid baseball fan of a brother expecting his first born son this year.. the book idea was a perfect gift to let him ready for his roll as a dad who’s dreamed of passing on his love of baseball to a future little league player.. Ha! His 2 dogs Fenway + Wrigley are ready to share in the dream as well..!!

This book is BiG- thick as can be full of stadiums old and gone.. and stadiums that remain. What I cant figure out at all- is why so many iconic parks are not included? I’m so uncertain of criteria the author used to decide how one made the cut.. but, I feel as if the author is too?! Trust me.. It’s not an algorithm one can figure out w/ any purpose. Not chosen by age or specific locales.. and leaving out half of the 50 states with great ballparks makes no sense at all?? Not to mention it feels a little biased. Not decided by size nor, any of the architecture. It’s not even by championships won/lost. I appreciate what is included.. I’m just disappointed to what is not!!

Book is full of photos and tidbits but using photos most of us have all seen numerous times.. it’s not original and lacks a lot of creativity. It doesn’t bring you closer to the park being featured. I’d love to see a view from the cheap seats or behind home plate right through the fence iron.. photo of ticket, hotdogs, scoreboard.. vendors- anything iconic about the ballpark that would transport the reader to feel as if they’ve gotten a glimpse of what being there truly felt like.. especially if one isnt fortunate enough to go in person.

Overall, photos and images included are nice.. the fact it feels generic or surface may let some avid fans down. This is more in line for a beginner- or even one out of country, bc of famous names and pic.’s they may recognize. The random inclusivity- would be better if it was titled “My fav. Ball parks” as that would at least explain why/what is chosen or excluded.. Hoping info helps your decision- stay safe everyone.. and play ball!
