title: The intent was there, but the pull into the story was not consistent
text: I really wanted to love this book, as the storyline intrigued me.  The story is split into three sections, the present time of their meeting in their 60s, and then two parallel timelines of their separate lives after they split up in college.  I loved the present time section...i felt the energy and was fully drawn into the story, but I couldn't get into the other sections, the writing and energy felt different, too logical, too matter of fact.  It was a labor of love to read the whole book.

title: Pace was a little slow moving
text: I am biased as I love my thrillers, but I also love learning about an era, gone by, and the pre and post war Shanghai is one of my favorite time periods.  This story is based on a pianist, classical trained, and the one job offered was to play jazz in Shanghai ...err, he had to relearn and given that most of the audience had minimal experiences..he got away it, although his band was less than impressed. So the life of a jazz player and the life of men who choose to make a living here, married or not, the human body so desired...and mingled in the story of late night jazz are all the characters of the local people, the Chinese government, he Japanese invasion.  An easy read, but not as a pace mover though.

title: Cute read about daughter and father
text: Wouldn't it be a wonderful idea to spend a few weeks with your father, but then he and his mates are about to sabbatage your one chance with mr gorgeous?  And yet all your friends are short of throttling his neck as he meddles when he shouldn't?  A real cute book that is a quick read and you may find the father either annoying or cute!  Either way, the author sure made his character get under your skin.  But was there a happy ending?  :)

title: Lost in translation
text: I loved the first book, but this one took me a long time to get into and I believe the translation was not as good, which surprised me.  If you get past the first third of the book then the story starts rolling with the suspense I was hoping to have grabbed me at the beginning.  Good ending, but you need a little patience to move through the inertia of the story line at the beginning of this book.

title: Family caught in the cultural revolution
text: I am a big fan of the author, but for me, this novel left me a little disappointed.  Why, maybe it had something to do with the characters' stories are told in chapters, and that each chapter felt a little too short to allow me to really get into the characters, into the emotions, into the story?  A good book and insight of what would happen if a member of your family is caught on the wrong side of the communist government, the fear, heroism and cowardice.  It is worth a read, but don't expect to experience a page turner sensation.  The story is about one family affected by the cowardice of another family member, and how each of the three generations cope, and there is an extended family too.  A meh feeling when I finished the book.

title: A snap shot of colonial india and discovery of the camera
text: You have to bear with the rather long introduction to the book before you get to experience the life and time of British colonization of India and what it could have looked like through the experience of a colonial family and their one India servant boy.  It is a captivating story of how one colonial family, to keep up appearances had to come into debt with another more powerful colonial family.  Debts had to be repaid and with the head of the family fallen ill, the rather flamboyant wife whose duties were less bound to her family, so it seemed at the beginning has fashioned her belief in the new technology of the camera and trying to instill a permanency 'on film'!  The Indian boy servant played a very strong role in portraying the hate that the local Indians had for the colonials and you see their side of the story, which I found it all very educational and also how painstaking the process was for the first 'photo'!  There is drama, love, despair and hope.  This is a 3.5 star book.  It needs a little patience from the reader to begin with, but it was worth it in the end.

title: The suspense kept piling on, and when you thought you had the answer..
text:
...the suspense stepped up to a huge new level. I was intrigued to read this thriller,partly by the endorsement from one of my favorite authors, James Rollins. Like james' new release, the Devils colony, the thriller is based upon nano particles, but it is used as a mind bender. One man, Tom Candrall, the eldest in a long linage in old town of LA is suddenly caught in a family sage, not with just one member, but with all of them? Who could he trust? Now the secret police, a woman he wanted to love and to trust: who is really in control. Family members drop like pawns and could Tom be next? I dont know, but it seems like in all families, the eldest seems to be the sensible one and takes on resolving all the burdens of other family members! The first third of the book threw you into all the characters, then the rest of the book began ot speed up and as much as I thought the situation was resolved, you were thrown down another rabbit hole: the hole was not there a minute ago. Did it feel like the novel disjointed, no, but it obviously left a lot of unanswered questions and the last page, well read it, and you know there is a sequel. And yes, I am vested and I need to know the answers, but will I ever get them? properly not, just another rabbit hole.

I am an avid reader, i am a tough rater, to get a four, you have to keep me turning the page and staying up late. To get a 5 you have to be teaching me something and give me a whole new twist/insight. A three star means it is still very good, worth reading!

title: Just was not my biorhythm
text: I so wanted to love this book as the description was posing a compelling and rich novel.  I think I needed to be on Prozac to get on the same wavelength as the author.  I found i was thrown into a 50 ft well with all the richness of music poses (helps if you love music and have some background to enjoy all the technical terms) and then thrown sideway with the communist environment that these young musicians find themselves: raw, gritty and that hard?  I found it tough to believe that a 16 year old had such awareness of his surrounding and how dark his thoughts were for such a young age: too precocious.  I had to keep reminding myself that i am reading about a 16+ year olds experiences and not someone who may be 40?  This is where I found the novel unreal, the author is a great writer in delving into the darkness of mankind, but if he had an older character then it may have been more believable.  The pace ranged from what seems like 12 hours of details over a 2 hour plot and then the pace jumped where the author appeared to have no interest in throwing you 50 feet of dark thoughts and events.  This book is not for everyone and you will need to be patient to plough through it.

title: Chinese Culture: Another Culture that shapes American History
text:
If you are interested in the history of early 1900's and how the Chinese population was shaped by the law of the land, which were driven mainly by fear, the local `white' population, segregation, and the suppression of fundamental rights for local born citizens that included the right to schooling and voting. The author provides a good historical account of the main events, contributions by the Chinese culture, leading Chinese and non-Chinese figures at that time based on historical records. Although the author tired to humanize the period of time by focusing on one family: the Tape, which appears from public records to have the most noticeable success in `fitting in' and Americanizing the off springs as much as possible, but yet profiting from the Chinese population from bond money required if you were classified as having no records for permanent abode, through arranging train tickets and transportation. The Tape family made good money because they had the `contacts'. Since most of the information about the Tape family were from public records or family recounts, the author had to surmise and speculate on what it might have been like for the Tape family, which made the reading choppy from recounts that had strong backing to what Mary Tape may have done at that time/event.
One thing for sure, whilst reading this recount, I can not help but compare it to where we are today: immigration issues, boarder controls, rights of illegal immigrants and what suppressing employment. It all sounded too familiar with what the Chinese as one culture had to endure in 1900's. To parallel run all the other `minorities' at that time: American Indiana, the African Americans, the Jews, the Japanese, the list continues.

I enjoyed reading the history of what shapes America today, and cant help think that immigration continues to shape America and how much of that shaping still stems from fear.

title: Cocktail of the chairman mao revolution, chinese society and the women in it
text:
A very adult rated book that explores human lust, sexual awareness blooming in young adults, the intricacy of the Chinese culture of your standing in society marred by the stance of the Chinese revolution under Chairman Mao. Although the exact period is not spelt out in the novel, but you get a sense the people's revolution has been in place for a while, late 70's to early 80's, where the story follows one family, the Wang family, and the story really explores in depth the three of seven daughters: Yumi: the eldest, the one who had the responsibility of looking after the family and siblings and how her quick mind maneuvered to ensure the family's face is saved in on so many occasions because of her father's wondering eyes and her third sister who shared the same `wild' genes; Yuxiu: the third daughter who is her father's favorite daughter has to deal with the humiliation of an event that is considered a big no-no for Chinese girls, and then having to show humiliation when she escapes to live with Yumi, who has resurrected her life as a married woman to a senior general. Then you have the seventh daughter (7 girls and the 8th was the boy), Yuying: who managed to be blessed to have none of the responsibilities of her older sisters and was able to attend an elite school for budding teachers. Her tale follows her through the communist part approach to loyalty to the party, the need to sneak on each other that lead to the discovery of a relationship between student and teacher!
I am not sure whether it was the intention of the author to depict how women are treated in Chinese society as third class citizens or whether it reflects his unconscious thought due to his own up bringing? The treatment of women certainly comes across as being quite harsh, but descriptive to be interesting to read about their struggles and how they view themselves in a male dominated society and the importance of a male child to carry on the family name. this novel is not so dated in that it is that far removed from what is still happening in today's society. An interesting read.

title: Quaint and enjoyable
text:
The novel is set in 19th century England and told through the eyes of two women: one who moved to lyme regis with her sisters to retire (as it was the norm for women who did not find a husband) and a young girl, born lyme regis and the common interest that drew them together was fossils. A lively story told of women in those times and although we take it for granted all the liberty and freedom ofmovement, at that time, many of those actions were unheard off: in that way it was refreshing to be reminded how far we have come,but in some ways there are still a lot of things that remain the same!

Dont expect an action pack story: the pace of the novel reflects the time of the characters: gentle, but yet reflective of what true friendship means. Human emotions remain the same and there plenty of women hormones roaring from disappointment, innonence, jeaousy. Austin-style it is not, but none-the-less very entertaining. A good read for those lazy sunday afternoons.

title: Haunting
text: I am not sure the description provided for this book is accurate: Cressida is forced to grow up quickly within a world that was created by her mother.  How, choices made by her mother changed Cressida's life from a normal childhood where her innocent was drawn into a complicated world of adults and their selfish needs. I dont think Cressida knew of her magnetism amongst the world of adults and as a result, she threw away what kids her age would normally experience for what she thought she really wanted for herself.  This novel was well written and delved into the deep human pain of needs, emptiness and the need to please in the midst of Cressida's sexual awakening.  Although once one of the main character died, she was at last free, but older than her years.  The references to WWII was more of a background noise than critical to the gritty history of a young girl growing up to the needs of unfulled adults.

title: A fun book about new beginnings
text: A witty and British-humor based novel at its best.  Despite the title of the book, the plot was not so much based on the knitting club (a shame), but laid the ground work of one woman and her two sons, supported by gran and friends to enbark on a new life following the death of her cheating husband.  Her gift of a new life came from gran who handed over her wool shop in a little seaside town.  This book very much lays down the plot and  the characters for a sequel.  This book makes a charming light read and you'll love the Britishness of the dialogue -it is not all tea and crumpets! Great for a beach vacation read as the plot is not so heavy that you cant pick it up at any time.

The book could've and should've been a celebration of these bands instead I feel it was mostly mocking,  and making fun of the music I love most.

title: Too bulky
text: Just to note—- all Brain Game books have puzzle on right page and word list on left page! Fine if you do them on a table but inconvenient on your lap or holding up in bed!

title: these didn’t come with the binder rings to keep together!
text: Not happy with the fact they didn’t come with the binder rings to keep them together. Can’t find any large enough to hold them all anywhere!

title: Not his best Mackenzie.
text: I had a hard time getting into this book. Quite unusual for a Housewright book. The characters seemed somewhat wooden. It also seemed to lack the humor normally found in the books along with the warmth. Overall, I found it rather disappointing.

title: Pretty good, but.....
text: I enjoyed where the novel took place and the quirky characters. Enjoyed the dog. The author's obsession with the main character's smoking habit, became old and tiresome very quickly, as it was mentioned ad nauseam. It really detracted from the story.

title: An OK Book
text: This wasn't as good as I was anticipating. The writers style is not very fluid and easy to read. He would also have benefited from a good editor, wrong words etc., and occasionally, things didn't hang together all that well. But it was still a pretty decent read.

title: OK
text: It's okay...not as good as the other classic "I Can Read" books.

title: These are sewn...beware!
text: The binding has visible thread showing how the books are literally "sewn" together.  This works for now, but I'm not sure how long these books with last with my kindergarten students!

title: Kind Of Boring
text: This book isn’t particularly insightful. It was rather a drag to get through. Mostly just generic self-helpism. There is nothing here that you don’t read in a dozen blogs.

title: Not My Favorite
text: I usually love Crossway Bibles, but this one just leaves so much to be desired. I really prefer the Family Devotion Bible from Crossway. It is similar to this one, but the Family Devotion Bible has more extras, not just the pictures, and is larger. This is a small Bible. The only "kid" aspect are some full color Bible story pictures. The font type is pretty small for a kid. I would have hoped for a larger, more readable font and more spacing between lines.

title: Not As Great As Uglies
text: Uglies was such an iconic series and this addition just was a let down. It felt very forced. Westerfeld just seems off these days. I think he peaked and is now just trying to force the same magic out. Imposters is just incredibly forced. The story was moderately interesting. The characters were poorly developed. You hit the big twist and literally didn't care what happened to any of them. The relationship development also fell completely flat. You didn't believe either of them deeply cared for the other at all.

title: Somewhat Helpful but Largely Disappointing
text: I was expected so much from this book. I've been in pastoral ministry for the better part of 20 years and have served as a senior pastor for over 14 (12 where I'm currently serving), and I was truly looking for some fresh, helpful perspective from this book, especially considering the compilation of writers and the various "portraits" being painted. In the end, I found some help but was largely disappointed; the book as a whole just lacked direction and depth. I'm not even sure who thought of those specific "roles", but some of them seemed either forced or far too generalized. Of special note: "The Pastor as Church Historian" was very interesting, helpful, and well-written while "The Pastor as Theologian" was perhaps the most disappointing portrait of the book. It was hard to see how this chapter was specifically about the pastor being a theologian in particular. Great idea for a book that is much-needed, but man, was this a letdown.

title: Good for Classroom
text: This is a good resource for a classroom teacher who needs some additional help. It is not for a homeschooler and for a kid learning or being tutored outside of the classroom. It is more of a teaching aide than anything.

title: Not Super Helpful
text: As a homeschool mom, this book just wasn't very helpful to me. Even in a classroom setting, I don't see it as being very helpful. It is more of a "how to teach math" type of thing than a workbook. I think the Facts That Stick series by The Well Trained Mind are more concise and helpful.

title: Shallow
text: This book was so superficial and not helpful in any way. It was just cliche sayings and then expounding upon them. There just wasn’t any real meat to it.

title: Not The Best
text: I don't really know what is best, but the entire time reading this book, I kept thinking there had to be a better book on cross-cultural psychology that I could read. It is packed with lots of information. It does have critical thinking style questions throughout the book. It was just too much conflicting information in an attempt to cover all side. And there were numerous errors in the book (quoting the wrong numbers for research studies and such). So, while I didn't hate it, it isn't the best read and there has to be something better out there on the topic.

title: Math
text: These math books don’t work as a full curriculum. They are more additional worksheets. Yes, there is an entire plan to teach them, but it doesn’t work for us. (We are homeschoolers.) I have found more comprehensive math helps, so I’ll stick with those.

title: Quick Read
text: This was a very quick read. It was decent, but didn’t feel like a fully formed book. The small group questions felt like a stretch. I did not read this with a small group and cannot really imagine it being very beneficial as a small group study. It just isn’t meaty enough for that. I don’t regret spending the time reading it, but it definitely didn’t feel like a significant amount of time or effort went into writing it.

title: Helps Some
text: I don’t know what I was expecting, but this wasn’t it. It does have activities for kids to help them become more aware of their person, which is what I was needing- but it also includes a lot of things for various issues, not just being aware of your person. So, only about a third of the book is even aimed toward my ADHD child. Only about a third of that is useful for us specifically. So, it provides a couple helps for him, but wasn’t as comprehensive on self-regulating and mindfulness as I needed it to be. Definitely a help, but not as much as was needed.

title: Good Book, Bad Theology
text: I desperately wanted to love this book. And I absolutely love what she said about hospitality. That main theme of the book resonates with me. Her personal testimony I so touching. However, her theology was off. She is very reformed and I am of the holiness persuasion. So, a lot of statements she made about God willing people to sin and fall- no ma’am. I did, in the end, appreciate the book for the challenge toward radical hospitality.

title: Cutesy Pictures
text: My kids are very into Fallacies and logic. I thought they would really like this book. The illustrations are cute. The writing is pretty subpar. It isn’t well organized and doesn’t feel well written. It doesn’t explain the fallacies very well. It offers a few snippets of information and a quote. It seems very haphazard. The Amazing Dr. Ransom’s Bestiary of Adorable Fallacies is a far superior Fallacy picture book.

title: Board Book
text: This book is cute, but not extremely well written. If you love fairies, I’m sure this will be right up your alley. If you’re just into cute board books, this may not be what you’re looking for. I figured the entire book would be about saying goodnight to the fairies, but that is only the last page. It isn’t a bad board book, just not a favorite around our house.

title: Thin Paper
text: I have purchased quite a few adult coloring books. This one has pretty crummy paper. Some of the pictures are funny. Lots of fart jokes. One side is a coloring page, the opposite side of each page is dark wood grain print. The paper is just on the thin side. You will definitely have to use colored pencils because this paper will not hold up to markers or paint. As a joke type gift, it is fine. As an actual coloring book, it is pretty disappointing.

title: For Fun
text: This workbook is designed to be used along with the Bob readers. They turn the Bob readers into an actual reading program. I like the readers. The workbook, well, it is okay, but it isn’t really the best. It seems more like busywork than anything. They follow the layout of the books, so for the alphabet books, they combine letters in the lesson and it makes it a little confusing. It also introduces them in alphabetical order. The work feels more like busywork than actual learning. If you’ve got a kid who just loves workbooks for fun, this might be perfect. For an actual reading program, no. My 4 year old likes it, but it isn’t enough to be a phonics program, even with the Bob readers.

title: I Like The Higher Grades
text: This is intended for classroom use. I am not a teacher. I'm a homeschool mom. This book does give permission to make copies for class use. I don't think these books are effective as a full language arts curriculum. I think they are good for additional language arts practice. Each week has one worksheet, front and back. I don't know any Kindergarten kid who could do the worksheets at the front of this book in the beginning of Kindergarten. Maybe by the end of Kindergarten, but not the beginning. Kids would definitely need help on this. I also don't think the beginning of Kindergarten is a good time to be testing reading fluency. So, I think the expectations in terms of the work are way off. In my opinion, this is a good book to keep up skills and such over summer. Of course, there are 40 "weekly" pages here. There also isn't enough room for the picture drawing. I like the higher grades, but the lower grades seem off in their expectations. Like they are trying to make 5 year olds fit a system they developed for 10 year olds.

title: I Did Like It
text: While I enjoyed this book, I’m not going to stay it was a good book. This book is really a random assortment of what honestly should be blog posts. And as blog posts, I would likely “like” each an every one. But is that where we are going in books? There was no real cohesive purpose for the book. Nowhere it was going. No topic it was sticking to. By the title, I thought it would be more focused on our love for people or what the love of Jesus calls us to and compels us to do. That was not the case. Instead, “for the love” is used as an idiom. Like, “for Pete’s sake!” Again, it isn’t that I didn’t like the content. It wasn’t what I was expecting. The book has really funny parts and very relatable parts. I just feel like this book was kind of slapped together because the publisher knew the name would get books sold, even if the book wasn’t actually a book just a collection of blog posts. So, while I enjoyed each chapter, I feel like it wasn’t actually a good book. They were good blog posts that were sold as a book. And maybe that is where books are going now. But I still feel like you could make a collection of essays into a book with a theme or subject running through it. There were also several places where she contradicts herself. I get it, some topics, you can see the problem, but you also see the problem with the solution. Stuff is messy. But these things weren’t close enough that I think the contradictions were even apparant to the author. The book is essentially a brain dump, so I can see how this would happen.

title: Incorrectly Marketed
text:
This book is beautiful. It definitely is a cover that draws you in. I think the premise is a good one, but there are things I dislike about the layout and the marketing.
First, this book has nothing to do with women other than it was written by a woman. The content isn’t women focused. I don’t know why they chose to market a book on the Psalms gererally to women specifically. It doesn’t make sense.
Second, the book doesn’t feel finished. I feel like I got the author’s notes on the book and not the book itself. It just didn’t feel quite finished.
Third, I felt like they should have included the actual Psalm for each chapter with the notes on it. Let me have all the things in one book. It isn’t set up like a Bible study book, but they kind of treat it like that. I would have just loved to have the Psalm printed and then the information about it. Perhaps a left hand on the page is the Psalm, right hand is the information.
You can use this book with any age group or setting. You can use it for a small group or family devotional. And it isn’t that the content is bad, it just isn’t well written. The content itself is good. It just wasn’t ready to print yet.

title: Not Durable
text:
My son loves this book! He struggles with Phonics, but loves Batman. So he loves using this book even though it isn’t a subject he enjoys. He also really likes the reusable aspect. I do have a couple issues with this book.
The book can only be used as a dry erase book. Dry erase markers are the very worst things to put in the hands of a child. It is worse than a permanent marker. Know how you get dry erase marker off your walls? You have to paint over it. And these are not exactly dry erase. They need water to erase. Like the overhead projector markers.
The book is not very durable to be reusable. The pages will water Log quickly. You have to use water to erase the markers. Don’t let the kid do it. If they use too much waster, the book is toast. It is just frustrating that it isn’t more durable, since it was made to need water and heavy use.
The pages rip out really easily. You’d think the lamination would help, but it just doesn’t.

title: Very Beginner Level
text:
I was a little on the fence about buying this book. I am not a Bible journaling newbie, so I was hoping it would maybe give me some new ideas- expand my abilities a little. There is a very specific art look to this book- very Zentangle type art and lettering.
If you are completely new to Bible Journaling, this book might be helpful.
Page 8-11 is basic information. What is Bible Journaling- if you didn't know, would you buy the book? And how to choose a Bible for Bible Journaling.
Page 14-39 are basic art techniques for Bible Journaling. These were pretty basic. Stencils, stamps, colored pencils, watercolor, acrylic, stickers... Just pretty straight forward and basic art techniques.
Page 40-45 is on lettering. If you want information on lettering, a hand lettering book is going to be a better source. But this is enough to get you started.
Page 46-51 are on layout issues. Where to put the words, which words to make bigger, and illustrations.
Page 54-99 are artists biographies. Why they Bible Journal and how.
Page 102-123 are pictures of Bible Journaling projects. Some of them aren't actual Bible Journaling. And there are also plenty of pictures throughout the rest of the book, as well.
The stickers included in the book are matte, which aren't my favorite style of sticker. Included in these stickers are Bible tabs. I wouldn't say any of the stickers make me really excited to put them into my projects. They are just pretty plain and boring.
So, most of this you're going to be able to find online for free. YouTube, Pinterest, and blogs are going to have all the small information. However, if you're to a computer person, have no internet access, or you need this for your church library, it may be great for you. However, for most people, the book is going to be redundant and quickly dated information. I'm not saying the book is bad. It isn't. I've just seen all of this before. I would hardly call this a "complete guide". It isn't. It is a very basic starting point for brand new beginners to Bible Journaling.

title: Too Much Story
text:
While I liked the basic storyline, it desperately needed some editing and simplifying. There were several story parts that were unnecessary to the story and not completely flushed out that should have really been stories the author saved to write at another time. (Swanny’s entire back story should have been another story entirely as I don’t think her condition or unique story line add much to this story. It would have been enough for her to be herself without her medical condition or the condition of the soil in her county.) The dragons actually play a very minor roll in the story. I hated the main characters, but I am pretty sure they were intended to be hated. I really don’t fault the author for the main issues I had with the book, though some of it could have been alluded to in a much less crass fashion, I really fault the editor. The story needed to be told. It just wasn’t as refined and “done” as I think it could have been.

Also to note: not a book for teens or young readers. I don’t think it technically falls into the YA category, but if you are a parent wondering about your teen reading it: it contains a lot of profanity, drug use, prostitution, suicide, sex, and more.

title: Good Information Poorly Organized
text: This is more of a booklet than a book. It is very all over the place with the information. It is like they weren't quite sure what they wanted the book to be- a resource or comfort, so they haphazardly mixed the two. Some of the book is good information for grieving families. The practical, logistal stuff you might not think of in this scenario or in grief. Some of the book is letters from parents and grandparents to their lost children. You have some poems sprinkled in randomly, as well. I would have liked for the information portion of the book to be beefed up a little. And the comfort/inspirational type stuff saved for a different book. It would have been more cohesive that way.

title: Nothing Spectacular
text: This is not my favorite doll making book. It is just kind of bland on the options. You make two dimensional stuffed dolls with felt and make basic clothing from scraps. I can find most of the things in this book for free on the internet. There is really nothing special or spectacular here. It is hand sewing, so it can be done by a child, which is the only redeeming quality of the book. The pictures are lovely and fun. But the actual projects are very basic and boring. All the dolls are female. And all the dolls are just regular people dolls- no fairies, princesses, mermaids- just ordinary girls. 75 projects and most of them are similar to the others. Just small felt dolls and clothes.

title: Not My Thing
text:
I usually only read teen paranormal stuff, but being an avid Empire Records fan, when I saw it compared to THAT, I figured I'd give it a whirl. It lacked the things I loved about Empire Records and left only the edgy teen angst bits. I just, well, wasn't into it at all. It isn't my usual read and wasn't an enjoyable one for me. I'm not really a fan of teen melodrama.

Parental blurb: Since this is Young Adult, I'll give my parental spill for parents. Rated ages 14 and up, which is pretty accurate, I'd say. Some cursing. Some sexual references, but nothing explicit. (Unless you count using the "f" word explicit.) Some drinking mentioned.

title: Not So Great For Hippie Kids
text: I purchased this book for my 8 year old daughter. She is very inquisitive and loves reading, so it seemed like a good starting point for some of the questions she was having. I wanted to love the book. But it fell short for this family. We're more on the crunchy, granola side of life and this book was too medical and mainstream for us. It recommended a girl see her doctor for EVERYTHING. And we're just not doctor seeing people. (Sure, we'll go in an emergency. But acne isn't an emergency here.) I felt like I had to go behind the book and tell her some of the more natural remedies for issues and steer her away from this overly medical mindset. While I do appreciate the way the book was laid out and presented, it was not a good fit for us.

title: Cute Pictures
text: This little board book has cute little pictures. Though graphically, they are difficult for a baby or toddler to grasp. The doodle nature of the images doesn't really make it easily visible or identifiable. There is no story. Just random phrases containing the word "so". The last page is a mirror, which delights young ones, but annoys me. Sticky toddler fingers quickly make the cheap book mirrors disgusting and unappealing. I enjoyed the pictures. Not really typical of Warhol's style- more like doodles. There are certainly better board books, even containing real art, on the market.

title: Easier Than Figuring It Out On Your Own
text:
Photoshop does not come naturally to me. It is so ridiculously difficult for me to wrap my brain around. This book is easier than trying to figure Photoshop out on your own, but I am still having trouble figuring it all out. I think I need an actual person to sit down and teach me. I hoped this book would be like a person sitting and teaching me, but it really isn't. It is still so foreign to me that even picture by picture instructions don't help.

If you are okay with the Photoshop concept, then this is the book for you to master Photoshop basics. I am just so hopelessly lost that this doesn't even help me much.

title: Not Expected
text: Given the book description, I was anticipating something along the lines of [[ASIN:1442419814 Uglies (The Uglies)]], [[ASIN:014241977X Matched]], or [[ASIN:0439023521 The Hunger Games (Book 1)]]. I expected something political, some hidden system that was the reason for these people now dying so young. This book is not that. The writing is actually a lot like Susan Pfeffer (author of [[ASIN:0152061541 Life As We Knew It: Life As We Knew It Series, Book 1]])- very wordy, very slow, somehow boring despite the awesome material. And the book felt more like [[ASIN:0375828257 The People of Sparks: The Second Book of Ember (Books of Ember)]], very rural and chaotic, not very political. (Though I would argue the Books of Ember are much better written than this.) Overall, the book just doesn't move as it should. It is too wordy on things that don't matter and not wordy enough on things that do matter. And though I know this is a young adult book, this one feels really young. Not an awful read, but certainly there are better books out there.

title: A Tale of Two Irresponsible Dog Owners
text:
My kids thought the book was cute. They enjoyed the superficial feel goodness of the story.

I, on the other hand, wasn't impressed. Essentially, a family decides to take their family dog to the animal shelter because the dog was annoying and they felt another dog would be better suited for their family. Now, in a very non-realistic turn of events (because let's face it, the realistic outcome would have been that the family pet would have been put to sleep) the family picks a new dog and their dog is chosen by the family of the new dog (who also took their dog to the animal shelter to trade it out for something better). Now, animal shelters are not dog trading businesses. The new dog is depressed, which the parents love because who doesn't want a dog that just lays around all day? The kids don't like the new dog because it doesn't "do" anything. So, they end up getting together with the old dog owners, who now own their old dog, and they end up trading dogs because the dogs they had to begin with were best for their family. Unrealistic happy ending, but whatever. The parents are hard noses in the beginning, then push overs in the end. (Isn't that the way children't stories seem to work?) The dog that was so unbearably annoying that the family would risk it being euthanized ended up being the beloved member of the family.

title: Just Not Into It
text:
This book is of the incredibly mundane variety. Justin goes to camp. That is about the gist of the whole book. He isn't a funny kid. Nothing extraordinary happens to him. He just goes to camp and breaks his flip flops. That's enough to keep a 7 - 9 year old plugging away at reading this book, right? Wrong. It makes a terrible read aloud. It is just too boring. Justin is a likable enough character, but the story just doesn't move and flow.

Now, the grammar is awful. I understand that it is written from the perspective of a 9 year old, but I loathe having children read books written incorrectly, even if on purpose. I realize that doesn't bother everyone, but it does annoy me.

title: Better Than The First
text:
I expected The Dead and Gone to pick up where Life As We Knew It left off. It didn't. Which was probably a very good thing. The Dead and Gone is a story of another family during the same apocalyptic event as the first book in the series. Different city. Different characters. Same end of the world. While the second in the trilogy was better than the first, it was still extremely boring. The world should end with a bang! Right? Well, not in these books. In these books they (SPOILER ALERT) starve and freeze to death. How exciting! (That last bit was in sarcastic font.)

Honestly, don't waste your time with these books unless you've reached the end of all of apocalyptic fiction out there, then maybe read these. While, yes, this is probably the most realistic of apocalyptic tales, it isn't the most exciting. The moon moves closer to the earth. Floods. Volcanos. Earthquakes. Colder than normal temperature. No food. Starving. Freezing to death. Everyone gets the flu.

Parental blurb since this is a young adult book- It's pretty safe. No sex. No drugs. Mentions of legal alcohol use. No cursing. Nothing too graphic. People die, but it is the end of the world, so someone has to die, right?

title: Some Good
text:
In reading parenting books, you rarely find one you'll agree with 100%. The trick really is to take the good and leave the bad. The book is a good book if the good outweighs the bad. Raising Our Children, Raising Ourselves did contain quite a bit of good. However, it also contained, in my opinion, an awful lot of bad.

I'll start with the good this book had to offer. It is true that far too many people do not view children as people. Our society tends to place them somewhere around a well loved pet, not a fully formed person. For some reason, the trend has remained that magically at 18 a child becomes a person, capable of having their own opinions only at that magic point. However, that isn't as it should be. This book offers great perspective on treating children as persons, equal persons. Considering their needs and desires as you would the needs and desires of any other person in your life. I wish that message could be sung from the rooftops. Respect children! Treat them like people!

"Many small events... don't require solutions even if the child reacts with tears or rage." (p.100) What a great point! I don't have to rescue my child simply because they are upset. If I'm there, that is all that the child needs. It is not my job, place, or duty to "fix" everything for my child, even if they react negatively. I think that many parents fail to see the value in letting a child be mad and not trying to "fix" them being mad. This book was great at pointing out that children should be free to express all emotion, even negative emotion, and there isn't something you need to do in letting them express their emotions other than simply listen. "We cannot stop the rain for out children and it wouldn't be good for them if we could." (p.145)

I also found many of her communication techniques to work wonders. Simply listening and validating my children has been a big game changer around here. I am listening, I am there for them, but their feelings are their own. I feel that they've been owning their lives more and relying on me a bit less to provide them their happiness or solutions to their negative emotional state. I've noticed a particularly evident change in my older daughter (she's 6) that she feels more "at home" expressing herself these days, good or bad, and she doesn't blame others for her feelings so much. She's also gotten much better at her problem solving skills since I'm not jumping in with suggestions every time she encounters another child who doesn't want to play with her or some other disappointment.

So, there is a great amount of good that can come from this book if you have the particular ability to take the good and leave the bad. If you are one that fixates on what is wrong with a book, then this may not be the book for you.

Most of the personal stories given in the book seem outright fake. The interactions between parent and child or counselor and parent just don't feel real to me. Perhaps much was condensed so that the point was easily displayed, but the stories just didn't sit right with me.

I often felt Naomi Aldort went too far. That she had a good point and I was with her, until she went too much to the extreme and threw the point off a cliff. It seemed many of her points went from me nodding in agreement to saying, "Whoa Naomi! Too far. Too far!" I feel like I took her basic points and then had to throw the rest out of my head.

I felt like she was asking the impossible at times. I get that "power games" (where a child empties the garbage over and over while you pick it up while play acting that is is a big deal, but not trying to stop the child) can be a good tool for kids who are feeling a bit helpless, I just don't have the time or the energy to play anytime my kids says to. I cannot possibly come up with the energy to chase my 3 year old around every evening at bedtime so he can feel powerful. Often I just don't have the time for a game of throw the sippy cup on the floor. There were multiple point like that that could make a parent feel like a big, fat failure because they just can't do that today or right now.

Dr. Aldort and I also disagree on expectations. I know that my living room being relatively clean is my goal. Dr. Aldort feels that as such, it is my responsibility to keep it that way and should my child trash it, I can verbalize my wish that it be clean, but I cannot expect them to help clean it. In my world, family just doesn't work that way. We all have to pitch in and do what helps the whole. There are many goals that my children have that I help meet. Likewise, I expect their participation and cooperation with some of my goals. I don't expect them to steam clean the carpet or keep all the toys on the shelves at all times. I do expect that they pick up their own things when they are done with them and that they pitch in on family cleaning day for the good of all. Mom is not a slave. Community works when everyone works for all, not just when they personally see benefit.

I was also very confused when Dr. Aldort told me I should not praise my children. She seems to believe scolding nor praise should take place. Everything should be matter of fact and avoid trying to steer them on way or another. I want praise when I accomplish difficult things. I anticipate my children wanting the same. I think this is just one instance of Dr. Aldort throwing out the baby with the bathwater. Some people use praise to coerce their children toward certain things. So, no one should praise their children. I think that is very short sighted. I think praising a child in the things the child is proud of or does well is a good thing. And I can't imagine stopping myself from telling my daughter the picture she spent hours making is lovely because I don't want my daughter to think I only want her making such pictures. That's just silly.

So, if you can leave the bad and take the good, read this book- it will do you good. If you are one that fixates on the bad- avoid this book, you'll hate it. If you are a slightly insecure sort of parent who easily feels they fall short of expectations- avoid this book, it'll make you feel worse. If you can read her expectations and feel they are silly and not feel personally assaulted- the good in this book could outweigh the bad for you.

title: A lot of filler, a little story
text:
First, I'm quite tired of the series bit. I mean, some books naturally lend themselves into a series, but suddenly EVERY book is part of a series. Obnoxious.

This book is the first in a series. Honestly, a lot of it feels drawn out and like filler to make a full book, which you run into a lot when authors try to stretch one story into a full series. It really did drag on and on and not to the benefit of building the story.

I did like that it was a different concept. Fated goes the Native American route, which hasn't been touched on too very much in recent young adult paranormal books. I'm confident I would have loved the book if I didn't feel it was half filler.

Since this is a young adult book, here is my parental blurb: teen sexuality, underage drinking, mentions of drug use, gruesome images, and cursing. Also there is one mention of rape, though it is presented in a negative context.

This book was given to me by the Amazon Vine program in exchange for my review. Clearly, I am not required to provide a favorable review.

title: Eh...
text:
As a long time Blogger, I was excited that this book would give me something new to get me beyond my current plateau of readership. If I was just starting a blog, this book would have been very helpful. (Though the information is pretty dated, so I wonder if they'll update it annually. It is pertinent now, but in a year, I'm not sure it'll be so helpful.) Most of what I read in this book were things I already do or already know. Some were things that I'm just not going to be able to implement, since my blog is old and already has a pretty set system.

And I found it extremely funny that they say not to accept free products for review when I got this book free for review! Ha! Funny, funny.

If you are just starting a blog, then pick up this book. If you already have a blog, well, this book isn't going to be very helpful. Well, it isn't going to be very helpful if you are a Mom blogger. If you're a technical blogger or news blogger, then you'll get more out of this book.

title: Not As Good As The First
text:
The third book in the "Then Sings My Soul" series. This book contains more than a few obscure hymns and ranges from the ancient to the very modern. There seems to be more "other" reference in this book than the previous books. (Information on hymn writing and history.)

I enjoyed the first book more than I enjoyed this one. Maybe that is always going to be the case with such things. I also found this book to be less devotionally motivated and more informative about the hymn writing process. I cannot say that hearing the story behind "How Deep The Father's Love For Us" makes it any more worshipful. In fact, the backstory to that one makes the hymn feel more flat. ("I decided to write a hymn!" Wow. Really? Good for you, I suppose.)

Of course, the book looks nice. It is a nice coffee table book or generic gift book. But if you're looking for something soul stirring, look elsewhere.

BookSneeze provided me a free copy of this book for review.

title: Good Content, but Shallow
text:
I'm not usually of books like this. This one, while not great, was not as horrible as I anticipated. There were a lot of good points made. Many things that I think many Christians today do need to hear. However, it was still shallow and seemed to linger on long after the point was proven. The small group questions were completely useless. They were really not good small group questions, in my opinion. If I were doing this book with a small group, those questions would keep the conversation moving for about 10 minutes, then we'd be done. This book would be a good devotional or small group book for established, but still shallow Christians.

The forward by Bill Hybels was actually a turn off for me. It didn't say much of anything about the content of the book. It read like a job reference, not like an actual forward that contributes to the book. It was very clear that a bigger name was wanted for the book, so Hybels wrote a quick note about the author so they could put his name on the cover and add credit to the otherwise little known authors.

I received this book free from the publisher through the BookSneeze Blogger program. I am not required to write a favorable review (clearly).

title: Small and Easy
text: My 2 year old loves I Spy books. I bought 4 of the board books, since he can be a little hard on books. (That might be the understatement of the year.) These books are similar to their big brother, but they are so easy. It is difficult to hold his attention when there are only 2 objects to find on the page and they are very prominent. I was hoping for the I Spy book in just a smaller, more durable package. I mean, it makes sense that they would be easier, since board books are for younger kids. If your child had never done I Spy books before, this would be a fabulous introduction to the game of finding the hidden picture. But if they've been working on the "big" books, they'll likely be bored by these board books.

title: Not As Expected
text: I purchased anew paperback copy of this book. The pictures are pretty terrible. They are grainy black and white photos that you'd see in a cheap newspaper. It covers a wide variety of topics, but did not have quite the detail that I needed on any one particular subject. I do like the premise of the book and it has some neat information in it. I was hoping to use it for introduction to botany with my kids (homeschooled) but it didn't contain the information we were looking for.

title: Rambling
text:
I really love the pictures in this book. They are beautifully done. Soft and imaginative.

I do not like the "story" itself. It is just rambling about stars. Sometimes the rambling children's book is funny. It provides a bit of humor and wit in it. This isn't one of those books. It is just rambling. There is no real story plot. No characters. It is just a rambling book on the topic of stars, particularly fixated with cutting a star out and putting it in your pocket.

I can see this book being fun when mixed with the craft of making a star and putting it in your pocket, or glueing it to a stick to make a wand (as the book suggests). But it is not one of those books you'll want to read over and over. You'll look at the pictures over and over. But the kids won't be begging for this one at bedtime. They won't say when they are older, "Mom, remember that "Stars" book we used to read?"

title: Half The Church?
text:
First, let me say that I had high hopes for this book. I have not read anything by Carolyn Curtis James before, but loved the premise of the book. I was not prepared for the graphic stories in this book. This book tells stories in just about every chapter about atrocities done to women and girls around the world. Nothing in the description of the book prepared me for that possibility. I do not think such stories should be quieted, however, a warning to readers about such things would have been nice.
After reading the book, it seems I should have read [[ASIN:0307387097 Half the Sky: Turning Oppression into Opportunity for Women Worldwide (Vintage)]]. Carolyn Curtis James seems to reference this book in almost every chapter, telling you something else she read in that book.
This book felt very disjointed to me. Carolyn doesn't do a very good job of making clear, concise points. In fact, I had a hard time figuring out just what she was getting at constantly. I don't think the book accomplished it's purpose, which would be to "recapture God's global vision for women." There was nothing clear about what women should be doing that they are not currently. No insight into the cultural vs. Biblical tug of war we find ourselves in.
What this book did do was start an internal dialogue for me. It started me toward thinking about where women are in my own church. It prompted me to begin thinking about how I am using my gifts for the Kingdom.
I do see that half the church is left out, or sold a smaller version of the gospel. I see that women are not given the ministry opportunities within the church. I do see how the church's view of women can harm our evangelistic efforts. However, this book didn't give me anything to rectify the situation in my life or in my circle of influence. It only gave me points to begin thinking on.

title: Cute, But Boring
text: This book has very cute illustrations. And it contains recipes, which adds to the cuteness. However, the story itself is pretty boring. My daughter and I loved looking at the pictures, but when it came to reading the book, she wanted nothing to do with it after the first chapter. I really can't say I blame her.

title: The Story Was Decent ...
text:
For the first 3 or 4 chapters of this book, I was so certain I would never rate it above 2 stars. Once the story actually started unfolding, it was much more interesting and I was actually able to get through the entire book. (I was having some serious doubts that I'd be able to force myself through all of it.) The story itself was interesting. I don't think the author really knew where she was going with the story, it seemed it took half the book for her to decide what she was going to do with the story. The main character was not very well developed. It was really all over the place and you never really could get a feel for "the real" character. She seemed to change and shift with the story. It was all very melodramatic. It was pretty obnoxious, actually. There wasn't even a really good description of what the main character looked like. It was the typical "I'm not popular. I'm so unique." set up with no real description of the character, so she could have been any "outcast" girl.

For Parents: I do not think this is a teen book at all. It contained regular cursing, though probably on a PG-13 level. It contained talk of cutting. (And while it did not condone it, it did not really speak against it. It mainly just put it as a phase of life- the cutting phase.) It also has lots of mentioning of teen sex, underage drinking, and drug use. It also contains some level of gore, since there is murder involved and it does go into a bit of detail about that.

title: Just okay...
text: I was given this book when I had my first child. I did find it informative, but not necessarily helpful. This book did help me get started on my breastfeeding journey, but I needed more to complete the journey. I found the information a bit too clinical and it didn't provide me much help to my issues. In addition, it didn't make me feel very encouraged to continue on. Had I had this book coupled with a good lactation consultant or local support group, it could have been enough. However, I didn't have those resources at the time. I only had the book. [[ASIN:0345518446 The Womanly Art of Breastfeeding (La Leche League International Book)]] was a much better breastfeeding book that encouraged me in its wording and point of view and helped me deal with with the issues I was having.

title: An Interesting Life
text:
I absolutely enjoyed reading the story of Saint Francis. I found it intriguing and thought provoking. This biography is written in chronological order. It is also not a lofty book, but written for the lay person. I enjoyed both the story and tone of the book.
I did not enjoy the writing itself. It flipped back and forth between a typical biographical view, citing previous biographers, and a narrative voice, which was much more readable and better for the target audience of this book.
I do find this book to be a good addition to my library. I am happy to have it and have read it. It could have been done better, but I can appreciate it as is because of the story it tells.

title: Not As Good As I Hoped
text: My children love hearing stories about real people. I had hoped this book on young Albert Einstein would be up their ally. It was not. It is big on information, but not on entertainment value. It also really pressed that Einstein was not good in school, which I understand may be the case, but it seemed to be giving a lot of excuses for his poor behavior that children may want to imitate. And let's face it, most children that do poorly in school are not geniuses. It seemed to give a lot of excuses for neglecting to learn the things you don't deem important. I thought the issue of his poor performance in school could have been shown in a different light, rather than the negative one the author chose. It is a children's book, after all.

title: A Few Good Names
text: I really wanted to love this book, but in the end it was just average. There weren't as many names in the book as I would have liked. Some of the classifications were witty, while others were a bit of a bore. I think this book is really lacking in the boy name department. It was an okay book, but if you are only going to buy one baby name book, don't make it this one. Buy one with more options. The names do range from extremely common to who-names-their-kid-that.

title: Science Fun For Adults
text: As an adult, I got a kick out of this book. It is funny and whimsical. I like it. However, the children were bored. Not only did they have no clue what it was about, but it was too wordy for their liking. The pictures are fun, but not enough to hold their attention while reading the poems. I was also less than appreciative of the evolution and big bang stuff that found its way between these pages. I think it could have been a fun and educational book, but it is lacking, for kids, in both of those areas. However, it would be a great gift for an adult science nerd!

title: Okay, I Guess
text: I really hoped to love these books. Perhaps I will like the actual readers more than these alphabet books. The books are dinky. They are small, not well bound, paperback books. They looks really cheap. They are arranged alphabetically, which you think makes sense, but since each booklet covers a couple letters, the system doesn't work well if you aren't teaching the letters in alphabetical order. (We are using The Ordinary Parent's Guide To Teach Reading.) When we are covering the letter A, I have to read the AB book, instead of just A.

title: Fertility Foods and Exercise
text:
I was expecting a book about which foods boost fertility and which foods inhibit fertility. What I found in this book was a diet and exercise program for optimizing fertility. This disappointed me because I did not want a program, just knowledge about food related to fertility.
I will say it does have some good information, even if you are not following their plan. I'm not sure how the plan works, since I have not tried it.

title: I Liked It, But...
text: I really enjoyed this book. It has beautiful pictures and is so funny, even with just a few words. However, it was a bit scary for the kids. (And I had unfortunately selected it to read before bed.) My children (ages 2 and 4) found some of the images a little frightening before bed, but they laughed out loud at other images.

title: Beautiful Artwork!
text:
The artwork in this book is lovely. It is bright and colorful. However, the bright artwork, plus the crazy fonts make for a challenging read. The story is mediocre- it really could have been better. My children were impressed by the bright colors, but got tired of the book quickly. The font and the pictures leave you feeling very scatterbrained.
Boris the cat is homeless. He falls asleep in a box. He is shipped over and over, each time the recipient of the box doesn't want Boris. He finally finds a home in the end. No turns, no twists, just a cat in a box.

title: Just Okay
text: This book is mediocre. The pictures are cute. The actual writing isn't great. The repeated phrase in the book just isn't that catchy, especially not for young children. If that one line had been a bit more clever, this book could have been a good book. It just falls a little flat.

title: Bad Habits? Or Playful Imagination?
text: I love imaginative play. I love kids dressing up and pretending to be anything their little minds can think of. This book is about just that! Minerva makes a monster mask and is a monster for a day! My only "issue" with the book, is her parents let her get away with some pretty bad behavior, since she is a monster and no longer Minerva (whatever it is that Minerva is). She refuses to clean up her crayons. She refuses to help when her mother asks. She hides under the table to eat dinner after she has once verbally refused to eat. In the end, yes, Minerva decides to become herself again and go to bed on her own terms. But pretend play is not exactly a way to do anything you want. And those crayons never did get put away!

title: Disjointed, But Fun
text:
Arthur doesn't turn in his homework, then lies to his teacher about it. For this, he must visit the principal's office ... tomorrow. That night, Arthur dreams of a pickle world because of the pickle he is in. He wakes from his dream, does his homework, admits he lied, and turns it in a day late.
The actual writing is disjointed, as most popular character books are. This didn't seem to bother the kids, since they asked for it to be read several more times. It would be a hard read for a very beginning reader, as it is a level 3 reader.

title: Good
text:
This book was entertaining. I enjoyed the story, but sometimes the writing felt disjointed. The climax of the book seemed a little anti-climatic- it really wasn't as big as it could have been. I think a better job could have been done developing the story a bit more so it felt more complete and real. It leaves you hanging on several characters, and the plot twists seem minute and unimportant. It is very predictable from beginning to end.
For parents, the book contains only kissing, in terms of sexuality. There are brief mentions of spirituality, but nothing delved into too deeply. As far as I can recall, there isn't much (if any) bad language. Fairly "safe" in terms of teen books.

title: Interesting, but Lacking
text:
I will admit, this was an interesting read. Once I began, I had to finish the book before putting it down. It was a very typical zombie book. I enjoyed Carrie Ryan's story telling.
The book could have been so much better had it really gotten into the vast conspiracy that was "The Sisterhood." Instead, it is pointed out that it was a conspiracy, but it wasn't really explored. Exploring that aspect would have made the book more than the typical zombie story.
It would have also been great if more history had been given. "The Return" of what? What happened that spurred these zombies?
The book was simply okay, but could have been great.
For parents- the book is a bit gorey in the zombie details, but that is about it. The main character in the book does loose faith, but the starting point of her faith seemed lacking, so it did not seem like a direct assault on religion or Christianity, specifically.

title: Dated Information
text:
I purchased this book, hoping for a little more insight into herbal use during the childbearing years. The information in the book is dated. The book was written over a decade ago, and as far as I can tell has not been updated. The herbal information in it is still pertinent. The dating wouldn't be an issue if the book stuck to strictly herbal remedies, as you'd think it would, but it delves into newborn care- which is where the information is useless. (Example: The author says that if you have a son in the United States, he will automatically be circumcised- which is not the case anymore.)
I was anticipating a little more on the fertility side. However, the fertility portion of the book is miniscule. Most of the fertility chapter is about birth control, permanent sterilization, and abortion- all of which I am morally opposed to, so the book offers me little personally useful information on that end.
The book is a little hokey. It is beautifully written, very poetic and beautiful. But feeling for the energy in a dried herb just isn't my thing.

title: Good Information, Dated Projects
text: I found the information in this book very useful after first getting a serger. I found the book to be extremely dated and would never even consider making any of the projects listed. With this book, plus your serger manual, you'll be using your serger in no time. I just wish they would make a completely updated version of this book.

title: She Had Fun
text: My daughter adores Fancy Nancy. I like that Fancy Nancy is increasing her vocabulary. She loved this book. I did not find the stickers to be "reusable" at all. They are just regular stickers (a two page spread) that you stick throughout the book. I do like that the book had its own story. I did not like that the stickers had very specific places they were intended to be used, but didn't clue the child in on where that would be. (That was pretty frustrating for my almost 4 year old, when she didn't know which pants went on which girl on which page.)

title: She Loves It
text: My daughter is a huge Fancy Nancy fan. She adores anything seemingly fancy. And I love that she loves Fancy Nancy, since Fancy Nancy is increasing her vocabulary exponentially. This book has two "paper dolls" on the back cover that you "pop" out. Then, you must carefully cut the outfits out to fold onto the paper dolls. She loved playing with it, but it was really a one time activity. We tried saving it in an envelope for future play time, but manipulated paper only goes so far. She had a fabulous time with her paper dolls, but I was a little sad to see them so easily used and gone.

title: The Fortunate Son is still whining after all these years
text: Bought the hardcover edition about six or seven years ago and broke it out recently for a bit of a re-read as I'm culling through my rock 'n' roll library and deciding which books to jettison.  So long, Fortunate Son.  If John Fogerty was indeed the Grand Poohbah be all of CCR as he consistently contends, why have none of his solo records come close to the brilliance of the Creedence catalog?  Even if they were only taking Fogerty's musical orders as he would have you believe, they all brought something special to the sessions or there wouldn't be such a glaring drop-off in quality between the band's LPs and Fogerty's solo efforts.  For such a purist when it comes to his story and his career, the ever-whining Fogerty depends on the hoary "as told to" format in sharing his rock 'n' roll tale of woe and redemption.  Thank you, Jimmy McDonough.  Two-and-one-half bad moons rising and recommended strictly to unquestioning diehard Fogerty fans.  Me?  I'm looking for a more rounded, less ego-driven history of the great CCR.

title: Change Partners: Definitely not the definitive Stephen Stills bio
text: While this book is definitely not the definitive Stephen Stills biography its title claims it to be, it's still a whole lot better than the many negative (one- and two-star) reviews posted on Amazon.  The book is actually a collection of cut-and-paste information gleaned from decades of music magazines, radio and television interviews, and previously available CSN (&Y) books and retrospectives.  That they're collected, collated, and presented together in one convenient place, and lovingly so, can only be considered a plus.  David Roberts makes it clear from the get-go that he's a lifelong Stills fanboy, seriously, and that's all right with me because he's being honest and up-front about it.  Just don't call your book STEPHEN STILLS CHANGE PARTNERS THE DEFINITIVE BIOGRAPHY, okay?  Hopefully, one day Stills will eventually take pen in hand and tell his own tale about his extraordinary rock 'n' roll life, with none of the usual as-told-to nonsense.  Three-and-one-half stars for a basically good read and a lot of great musical memories.  Mildly recommended, until a truer bio or a Stills autobiography comes along.

title: Graham Nash has some tales to tell, for sure
text: Wild Tales, for sure.  Graham Nash, rock 'n' roll veteran of the Hollies, CSN, CSNY, CN, et al, has a lot of tales to tell and he tells quite a few of them here.  And he tells them with care and a certain British flair in this enjoyable rock star memoir.  A quick, breezy read, Wild Tales touches on the highs, lows, and in-betweens of the rock star life, and Nash is absolutely the right person at the right time to tell the tale.  Its conversational tone works wonderfully well in this setting.  You'll feel like you're having a long chat with an old friend, one who just happens to have led a wonderful life with the rock arena as its backdrop.  This is the CSN(Y) middle child / mediator Nash, before the well documented falling out with Crosby and the sad divorce from his decades-long wife Susan.  The good guy Nash.  The guy who wrote and sang Our House and Teach Your Children and Just a Song Before I Go and Wasted on the Way and seemed to mean every word in every one of them.  Yeah, the good ol' Nash that we thought we knew and thought the world of.  Things change, yeah?  Three-and-one-half stars for the good times and recommended to nostalgic CSN fans from the day.

title: Not a patch on what came next ... the great Daisy Jones and Malibu Rising
text: Well-written and very filmic, but not a patch on the same author's Malibu Rising, let alone the wonderful Daisy Jones & the Six.  While it's kind of fun to cast the characters in your mind's eye while reading, The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo has a specific agenda and sticks to that agenda throughout -- making it all too predictable, front to back.  All men are self-absorbed, undependable louts, unless they're gay, and gay and lesbian love are the only genuine, true loves.  Some of us may beg to differ.  I still love Daisy Jones & the Six and I also continue to recommend Malibu Rising (although it's not quite as absorbing as Daisy, imho), but I'm far less enthused about Evelyn Hugo.

title: Their cheese!
text: Purchased for my Eagles-loving niece who, three generations down the line from the original band, really liked it a lot.  To this original (since 1972) fan, it's pure cheese.  Stick with the music and / or Ben Fong Torres' excellent hardcover group bio.  Combining my low score with her high marks assessment, three stars.

title: Why isn't JR in the R'n'R Hall of Fame??
text: The story of Johnny Rivers needs to be told, but not like this.  Thin on facts and/or new information and  often lame in the telling, this piece barely skims the surface of a truly wondrous career.  A well-done and presented bio may finally open the doors to the Rock Hall for this most deserving artist.  Hopefully, one will show up before it all becomes a moot point.  An autobiography, maybe, Johnny??

title: Long-winded roundabout version of The Association's history
text: Had to force myself to slough through the last third of this one.  Started off promisingly enough, but author Malcolm C Searles gets bogged down in the muck and mire of the group's seemingly endless personnel changes about 2/3rds of the way through.  Spending more time on original recording sessions, songwriting, and touring in their heyday would've been preferable.  A lot of the info included has already been made available elsewhere, and some points are made more than once (more than twice, actually); some serious editing would surely have tightened things up considerably.  I bought it to fill in some of the gaps left by Russ Giguere's far superior (and insider) Along Comes The Association memoir and, though stodgily, it did to a certain extent.  But if you're looking for a single book encompassing the history of the band's golden period (1965-1972), well-told and breezy, Giguere's is the one to buy.  This one?  Two and 1/2 stars, tops.

title: Gallows Hill suffers from the sophomore slump jinx
text: Something of a disappointment, following Professor French's far superior first novel, Maledicus.  The situation brings to mind the old record industry phrase "the sophomore slump," describing a drop-off in quality and/or sales for a second album release after an artist's particularly impressive debut.  Gallows Hill: The Investigative Paranormal Society, Book 2 lacks the tension and suspense of  Maledicus, although it remains character-driven (by an extremely likable, well-defined group of friends/cohorts).  There are unresolved subplots (erstwhile Atlantic City mob boss Michael Flannery and his plans for casino expansion in PA, which involves the IPS); far too much use of foul language, especially the F-bomb, which comes across as inappropriate when used too often among the IPS members, even more-so in the 1800s flashback sequences, and is rather awkwardly handled in the teen- and young toughs- sequences. That just may be a sort of compliment to Professor French, who is perhaps too well-educated and genteel a fellow to deliver such harsh dialogue as natural language.  Docked one star for poor editing and proofreading.  I realize this book is independently published, but mixing up character names page-to-page, repeating portions of sentences from one graph to the next, and poor punctuation throughout (most glaring example: placing a comma at the end of the book's dedication!) -- inexcusable. Still, there's enough imagination, interesting turns-of-phrase, and colorful characters at work here to make me look forward to better things in IPS, Book 3.

title: The Beach Boys (and their fans) deserve better
text: Kind of cheesy and definitely disappointing.  More than 250 pages, but absolutely nothing new.  As an unofficial follow-up to the Boys' short-lived reunion tour and LP (That's Why God Made the Radio), I had high hopes and expectations.  I should've known better.  Fool me once ...

title: Decent
text:
Interesting book. Quick read. Not overly complicated just Entertaining!! I plan to find the other books in hopes of more entertaining reads.,
,

title: best movie ever
text: nice calendar,  not one of the better ones I have purchased and smaller than most.  Being a GWTW fan I will use it.. but not recommend it

title: Good but Shallow Overview
text:
Perhaps this is a tribute to how simple Microsoft Teams is, but I can't say that I got a lot of insights to the product from this book. Usually I say that if you know everything about the subject covered in a For Dummies book you can work tech support for something. Perhaps this is true, but there was little in here that I did not know from using hte product for a while. Perhaps it would be good for someone who is just starting out to give a jumpstart. But to be honest, after reading through most of the book, I think it shows that Teams on the surface truly is just that easy.

I did apprecieate Chapter 8 - Taming the Noise, because as an IT worker, I am in way too many teams and there is way too much noise. At least it showed me how to mute some of the more obscure teams I had been added to for administration purposes. I can't say this is a bad book in any way, but it probably was not the book I needed.

title: Not Quite my Spirograph Memories
text: I enjoyed sharing one of my childhood memories with the kids.  This is basically a spyrograph from the 70's but it is not quite the same quality that I remember.  Also, this set did not seem complete as we needed to find some map pins and make a carbboard backer to draw on.  The end effect was the same, although kids these days don't know how good they have it.  Or maybe they do because this did not really hold their attention like the spyrograph did for use.  Good nostalgic journey for me though.

title: Our Kids Loved the First of These, but Love is Wearing Off
text: We got the first book of this type a couple of years ago and our kids really liked it and worked through it in a couple groups and alone.  They had just been playing a little of D&D and that might have been part of the appeal.  When I got another chance at a reviewer book in the series, I was surprised that the interest just wasn't there. It is still well illustrated, and filled with the same tween humor and grossness that was there before, but for the most part they just flipped through it and set it aside. I was a little surprised and disappointed.  Perhaps they have just outgrown the genre.  But for the right age and kid, these are a great, interactive idea.

title: Oof, Instantly Obsolete
text: I feel for the authors, the change from Chapter one to Chapter two instantly made a good amount of the information obsolete.  The content is good, the photos are good, but with the new release, they are dated.  It's a hard job to make a Fortnite book that can keep up with the changes as the game needs to continually change to keep player interest.  There is some good ever green information such as building techniques and ideas for improving.  But sections on weapons, maps and other time specific information has become outdated.  Some of it is permanently so, other information may be relevant in the future as weapons are unvaulted.  Sadly, book form may not be the best way to learn about Fortnite.  It is a great looking book, well designed, but behind the curve.

title: OK but very formulaic
text: This was a very formulaic plot, kind of Harry Potter meets the X-men in a not great way.  It did have a good plot twist but probably not enough to save the book for us.  The writing was fine for a middle schooler but we weren't overwhelmed by it.  Both of us did make it to the end which says something as my partner is quick to abandon a book but for some reason this one never hit a chord with either of us.

title: On OK Air Fryer Cookbook
text:
We "inherited" and air fryer and have been searching for a use for it. To be honest we were intimidated to even try it without any real idea how to use it.
