I got a chance to get a reviewer copy of this cookbook and we were pretty excited. It did do a good job at teaching us the basics, but I am not overly impressed with the recipes themselves. Most are pretty generic - Fried Chicked, Fries, ... Some did not seem to be an improvement over grilling - Jalapeno Poppers in the air fryer, and some were genuinely good and interesting - honey air fried pears.

Most of the recipes though are simplistic, there are photos for most but not all recipes. The instructions and writing are good enough. It definitely got us up to speed with possibilities but did not push any evelopes. Glad we got it, but wish it was a little more inspirational.

title: Subtle, Dry Humor
text: This reminded me a lot of a comic that used to run in the Onion when it was just a small newspaper out of Madison.  It is so subtle and dry in its humor that it almost raises it to an art form...Almost. These strange things live in a post apocalyptic world, which is almost hinted as having been caused by them.  They are tormented by mysteries of what happened to the humans and unstable human like emotions and frustrations.  It's cute, its a quick read, but in the end it only seemed to be OK.  I would like to know the full answers to the glass house that appears to have been designed to keep them out, and to find out why snakes got sick from hanging out with these things, but not enough to go too far out of my way to find out.

title: Writing was Good but didn't like the character or plot
text: I never really got close to the main character of this book.  I kept finding her whiny and was a little unable to accept that a tween could run away from her family and lie about what she was doing.  The writing was fine but the story seemed a little weak.  I just could not get over how self centered the main character was.  Not sure that this will go on my recommend list.

title: Did not catch on in our household
text: Out of three people who started this book in our house, only one finished it.  Our daughter finished it but did not praise it at all.  My partner finished about six chapters and said she could not go on as the characters did not mean anything to her and she did not like the writing, and I got a chapter in, meaning to go back to it but have not been able to.  We have seen that this book is getting a big push for the book and we had high hopes, but we could not plow through it.

title: Inspirational Story, Had a Hard Time Getting Engaged Though.
text: I got this to read with my partner who has been a Girl Scout Leader for years and I thought she would appreciate reading the story.  She actually ended up abandoning it part way through saying that she did not like the writing style.  I pushed through it and found the story to be inspiring, but like her I found the writing less inspiring.  Her story was good and I am glad I read it, but I had imagined more, including having her pass it around her scouts to spread the inspiration.  Not sure that will happen.

title: Our Youngest Found this to be OK but hard to Follow
text: It never seemed to really catch her imagination and the only kid that picked it up abandoned it a little ways in. It did not get a recommendation from our sixth grader.  She said it was better than nothing, but not great.

title: Did not capture our kids imagination
text: We  got this for youngest daughter. And although she Read it she said it was just OK and would not recommend it to her brothers.She felt it was worth the time but really not her type of book. She said the story just didn’t really go anywhere or do anything super exciting.

title: Adorabale Book, but my family can't seem to get into it
text:
I thought this book was a can't miss for most of my family, but it seems to be striking out. My partner who loves animals found it inane and abandoned it after a couple chapters, our youngest daughter, aged 10, finished it but said that it was just ok "It was ok that I read it, but I don't want to read it again, it was just OK." and everyone else is unwilling to try it.

I flipped through it and it looks like the illustrations will be wonderful, but I have to admit that after reading a few pages I also realized that this is not the book for me. We often read books as a family and they are all passed around based on recommendations but this one couldn't find anyone to endorse it. Perhaps it needs a audience younger than tween audience.

title: Sorry, could not get into this one
text:
I got over my head on this one. I have been reading Spanish books to gain vocabulary and unfortunately this was too advanced for me. I'm back to Narnia books etc.

I did get the book in English from the library and made it through. I figure Isabel Allende, how could I lose, but I just never could get into the book. Abandonded about half way through.

title: Hmm... Don't think I'll Pass This One to the Kids
text:
We love to read books as a family, passing it from one person to the next, parent to child to sibling. I think this one if stopping with me. It was ok, it had some twists, one big and seemingly inevitable, but I don't think it is one for the kids. To be honest, I don't know that it has enough action to keep them moving through it, I was ready to retire it a few times myself.

The story premise is ok, boy from wrong side of tracks dates girl from the right side of the tracks. Grass is always greener. Money is not happiness... In the end humans are humans and everyone has skeletons in their closets. These are not bad themes and all the ground you need to write a classic. This one just isn't a classic.

title: It's Decent and has Value for Kids with a Good Deal of Scratch Experience, Good for Begginners too.
text:
I like the theme and the material that is there. My oldest sone has been somewhat active with Scratch and he went through this book and basically recreated the jet pack game but using simplistic sprites to get the gaming controls down. Initially I scoffed at complaints that there should be downloadable sprites as I could find thousands of star wars sprites with a single google search. But it turns out nothing truly fit the examples here. It truly would have been a better thing to have those sprites available.

Otherwise, the examples are decent for explaining scratch coding. There is some areas that you need to do a little independent figuring when the instructions were a little less than exact, but we were able to recreate and expand on the game we attempted. I do like the layout of the book and would like to see more in the format.

title: Valuable Information, Just a Little out of the Wheelhouse of my Interests
text:
I have to admit it took some effort to get into this book, and I never felt completely engaged despite what I do believe is an important message. It reads something like a socioeconomic manifesto, which is again is good in that it's arguments are valid, but I guess my interests are less in the sociological side of environmental issues. That being said it was a mildly interesting subject to look at, just didn't have the arresting interest that a more biological book would have for me.

The text is readable and the political and economic facts were laid out logically and well, it just didn't strike a chord and it took me literally months of fits and starts to get through it. So for me, it was just OK.

title: Bright, Edgy, But just OK
text:
I love the bright colors of this book. It is flashy and would appeal to any child, except that it is anything but a children's book. It has a lot of adult themes from abortion to drug addiction so it is definitely for a mature audience. The author doesn't go over the top, but he definitely skirts the edge of tact. The humor is like Mad magazine at its raunchiest.

It is a very quick read and while I definitely can't say that I did not like the book it probably will not have lasting effects on me. It was OK.

title: Heavy book for juvenile lit
text: This book was a little confusing, it definitely has a young reading level, but it has a darker story line that I would not associate with a children's book. I'm not exactly sure who it is written for, the themes of war and loss are rather strong here and may not be great for younger readers.  Also, I found the ending a little unsatisfying as it is not exactly clear what the actual truths are.  It was worth the time to read, but not on my recommendations list, especially for young readers. I had high hopes as we have a couple unicorn/Pegasus fans in the family.

title: Good Facts,
text:
This has turned out to be a rather slow slog of a book. I had high expectations since I am one of the few people who would be more interested in the park policy more than the glitzy excitement of the bear attack.

Word for word, the writing is not bad, but I have never felt engaged to help pull me through the pages. I appreciate the facts about fire suppression but the joltiness of the topics makes it feel like a collection of essays. I see the arc over the whole book, but it doesn't seem to create a journey of reading.

title: Perhaps I should have started with Book 1
text:
For some reason I have had a real hard time getting into this book. It has been a month and I have not been able to get into a page turning rhythm on it. One of my sons picked it up for a while and said it was OK but also abandoned it. I have read reviews that this is a true sequel to the original and maybe reading the first book would make this one easier to get into. This might be so. I actually like being emerged into a strange story and have to glean facts but I found myself lost in this storyline and didn't feel motivated to figure it out.

I guess my best advice is that if you are thinking of reading this and haven't read the first book in the series, that is the better starting point. I'm not one to abandon any book, but this one just never seemed to engage me despite decent writing.

title: An OK Book that is Hurt by Stilted and Jumpy Narration
text:
So, I read books with my kids a lot, it is nice to have read the same books then talk about them. And for some reason we have been on a kick of animal narrated books which is not my favorite genre by any means, but we have found some really good ones. Unfortunately this book is not in the really good category. Unless the author was trying to tell the story from a dog who is stricken with ADHD, in which case, this review will not reflect the genius of this book.

The main problem I have with this book is that ADHD flow of the narration. Literally, 50 pages in I had no idea what the plot was. I did get a sense that I was clumsily being caught up to speed on book one of the series, but the story was not being propelled on. I found it hard to get into the story, again because the flow didn't engage me. It seemed to keep haltingly insert facts and characters which only started to make sense much later in the story.

The kids verdict was "pretty good" but without a torrent of conversation about the book. I would put it more at, it's OK.

title: Passable Overview
text:
I have to admit this book was a tough read and was not quite what I was expecting. With the subtitle or "A practical guide to a useful, beautiful design," I expected a beautiful book with beautiful examples. The book is pretty Spartan in it's illustrations. There are only a utilitarian figures, wireframes, and graphs. It is not poorly designed, just underwhelming.

The information is ok but it covers a huge scope. If I had to pick a theme for the book it would be more usability design than aesthetic design.

I can't slam the book but I can't really rave about it. It is not one of those books that pulls you through page by page. It was and informative but dense slog to get through.

title: Not sure who this one is for, Kind rambling survey
text:
I'm a little lost about how to categorize this book. I'm looking to move into HTML5 web and hybrid app development on a amature level and I have been thinking heavily about moving into mobile website design. This book sounded good, but I was worried about the jQuery and Sench Touch focus. The first few chapters are a passable survey of html5 at a fairly low level. I really appreciated the sample examples of pages made on smart phones although they are mostly more for illustration than inspiration.

Where I was kind of lost was the different development platforms the book introduces. They are quite a bit more advanced than the HTML5 section but they don't seem to get beyond a survey of what is available. I wish the book would have pushed the html development on mobile devices more and made this section even more of a "other things available" section. I don't feel like I can actually develop in any of the tools based on what was in the book, but my eyes have been opened to some possibilities such as Phone Gap, which seems intriguing.

I guess I would invest in other references.

title: A Primer for Hiding a Sexual Affair from Your Parents
text:
Unfortunately when this book was listed for 14 to 17 year olds I started to read it through the eyes of the middle school kids my wife teaches history to. My wife and I are avid readers of historic fiction and the idea of a child living in the canal zone during construction sounded like it would have great insights. However I was put off by what turned out to be kind of a smutty tale of a 17 year old girl hiding an affair with an older man. I'm not a book banning type, but the story line does not seem appropriate for 14 year olds, maybe it's target juvenile audience should be moved up a few years.

Otherwise the book did deliver on painting a picture of the construction conditions in the canal zone. There is a good sense of the complexity, difficulties, and grandeur of the project. The plight of the common workers is well handled and much of the historical background is credible and illustrative of the time. However, there were a few too many historical coincidences. The main character goes from living next door to the Wright brothers in Ohio, to the jungles of Panama where she meets the childhood friend of a Spanish prince. It borders on too much, and hurts the credibility a bit.

Otherwise the only thing that kind of stuck out was a shallowness in the main character. She rails against girls who care only for boys, then gets involved in a steamy relationship with an older man who pretty much tells her what her political views should be. Sadly this is probably pretty authentic, but it would have been nice to have a story where the main character forms her own convictions from her own observations and thoughts.

It is an OK book, but will not be added to our library. I do have to warn parents who are looking for a historic fiction books for kids on the lower end of its age range, it does have mature sexual themes.

title: Loved the premise, Less in love with the result
text:
My wife and I love historical fiction. We both jumped at this book when we saw it because the premise of a 14 year old boy in World War I sounded perfect. Even, better it seemed to resonate with the idea of child warriors which have sadly become fairly common in our time. However we never seemed to be able to get into the character. The book seems choppy and disjunct. Maybe this is due to the translation, but the flow seems interruptive, unplanned.

The main reason I read historical fiction is an immersion into the events of the time. It is a way to bring text book history to life in a way that can touch students far more effectively than a chart of stats, a few dates, and a couple of dry facts. Here the book did fairly well, such as the description of Hells Gate and trench life. However a few facts seemed to sit a little awkwardly - like the concept of Lebensraum which seems almost vernacular to the characters in the book. I have always been under the impression that Lebensraum was held secret in World War I as a political goal to be brought out after a German victory. It was a social idea at the time, but not as widely spread as this book portrays. Definitely the idea was championed in World War II under Hitler. Little things like this seemed to block my trust in the portrayal. But I will look into some of the facts that troubled me.

The best thing I took away from this was a fact I had not known, that the author included in his notes. The inventor of many of the poison gases used by Germany later won a Nobel Peace Prize for his work with fertilizers. That is the kind of facts I hope to find in historical fiction.

title: Our three-year-old loved it, unfortunately to a quick death
text:
I have a Toy Story obsessed three-year-old who was extremely excited to see this arrive in the mail. We spent the better part of two days swapping the cards out, which was a little beyond his coordination level. The 3-D effects are pretty good, but not earth shattering.

The unfortunate things about this book is that once you remove the 3D cards (which is a little difficult in itself) there is no where to store them. They quickly got separated from the books and at this time most are lost. Also the cards themselves are not particularly sturdy and several were quickly bent, one of which bent so as to lose a large part of two images, leaving it kind of useless.

The stories are abbreviate plots for the original and the first sequel. I would have liked to see new story lines, but they were abridged fairly successfully. But as a parent, I would love to read something other than a rehashing of the movies (again) and better thought out than most of the Toy Story books we find.

All in all, fun, but not lasting.

title: Cute, well illustrated book, Grammatically (and tactfully) Challenged
text:
The best thing about this book is the art work which is bold and clean. Book construction is high quality as well. But I was taken a little back by the words. Apparently Aliens speak much like Tonto or Tarzan, dropping articles like "a" and "the." Not so good for a kid who is forming speech.

I originally got this for my three-year-old, but it did not hold his attention. We tried reading it together twice but never got to reach the Big Fun the book was building up to before he ran off. In fact it wasn't until my wife, 8-year-old and three-year-old read it together that they got to the climax of the book.

**************SPOILER ALERT *************

"Big Fun" turns out to be flatulence. This may have gone over our three-year-old's head, but it fell in the dead center of our 8-year-old's sense of humor. My wife was a little put off that I got our boys a book that celebrates, breaking of wind but then she has always been pretty classy.

Then to make matters worse, the authors' included a song, which is clean for the most part. However it does reference, Meno's smelly friend. Again the song's gaseous subtleties hit my older boy's funny bone so we got serenaded with this song many times over the next week. Always to a different melody (should be twinkle twinkle little star.)

But here is the shining highlight of the book. Our older son has read this book to our younger son many times, which has been wonderful to watch. But if they ever manage to express Big Fun on command, my wife may disown me.

In all, it's a cute book, a little fluffy, a little naughty, and topped with horrific grammar, but the art work is strong, and is perfect for young boys who can see the humor in a fart.

title: A Book that Didn't Live up to its Cover
text:
I am not sure what William Weir's history teachers were teaching him but there was nothing all that startling in what his book had to say. Many of his topics like the Jesse James Gang, the Earp Gang and John Dillinger are not in history books anyway. They are part of a pop history, but I guess not the biggest history lies.

His first myth busting is about Emperor Nero fiddling while Rome burned. He actually helped people then, however, the guy wasn't all that nice and so those who wrote the history, created the myth. OK he argues this reasonably well, but, it is not exactly a lie that changes my views on the world.

I think his hope was that this book would be in the realm of [[ASIN:1595583262 Lies My Teacher Told Me: Everything Your American History Textbook Got Wrong, Revised and Updated Edition]] & [[ASIN:1592332994 Failures of the Presidents: From the Whiskey Rebellion and War of 1812 to the Bay of Pigs and War in Iraq]]. But it's not. I read it, some of it I enjoyed, but I was misled by the title. There was not a lot of real myth busting going on. I was a little bit let down by judging this book by its cover and title. It is an ok read - perhaps a historical bathroom read. I just had higher expectations.

title: An OK (not great) book, but at times disturbing.
text:
I guess I made the mistake of judging this book by its cover. We read a lot of books to our children and they really enjoyed [[ASIN:0060001569 Diary of a Fly]] and [[ASIN:0439639042 Super Fly Guy]] so this appeared to be a sure winner. The illustrations are fantastic and I have never seen a better constructed children's book. Looking and flipping through the book, it is very impressive.

But the problem is that the story never really caught the my imagination or our kids'. We almost always end up re-reading books and put new books into heavy rotation. Yet, I actually couldn't even get mine to allow me to re-read this one. It was definitely a disappointment there.

More disturbing, there is also one small section that compares the fly's life to farm animals life which ends with "Slice! You become someone else's meal" next to a sort of startling image of a butcher holding a bloody knife and wearing a bloody apron. We're not Vegans or PETA members but it seemed a little out of place in a children's book. Otherwise the story is a little rambling and incohesive. I would have given it one or two stars except it is such a visually well designed book.

title: Nice Book, Nice Pictures, Nice Tourist Souvenir
text:
This book was created to fill a niche in Gift Shops more than to be a field guide for Alaskan Birds. It is nicely laid out and well illustrated, but it is just something of an abridged version of Robert Armstrong's Birds of Alaska. If you are a birder and are looking for a book about Birds of Alaska, get the full version. But see my review of that book before buying it. I recommend getting Birds of Alaska, but not as the only field guide you take with you.

I'm not knocking this book, it is nice, but not complete enough to satisfy serious birders.

title: Three Stars
text: A bit like the popular TV series "Bloodlines." A good summer read.

text: Some of the pictures don’t scratch well and ruin the pictures.

text: The book was very good, except it kept going back and forth from one time period to another and changing people.  I prefer books that continue with one story without going back and forth.

title: Large print is relative
text: I buy word search puzzle books for my 85-year old mom...she loves them.  Large print is the key.  We were disappointed when we discovered that the type, though larger than book type, is not LARGE.  We compared it to the last books I bought at Amazon and the type in this book was half the size.  So if large type is very important to you, you may want to consider a different book.

title: Cherokee America by Margaret Verble, Hardcover – February 19, 2019
text: Gorgeous writing but the story lost me at the man on horse action.

title: Naomi Wolf’s Publisher Cancels U.S. Release of ‘Outrages’ effective October 21, 2019
text:
I was not familiar with the best-selling author of 'Vagina, Give Me Liberty', and 'The End of America' but the premise of gay history—'how a single English law in 1857 led to a maelstrom, with reverberations lasting down to our day' seemed interesting, if rather flamboyant. I made the mistake of ordering the book before researching the author, something I should always do when reading non-fiction. Wolf received her Bachelor of Arts in English literature from Yale and was a Rhodes Scholar at New College, Oxford so color me very impressed. Her Doctor of Philosophy degree in English literature, supervised by Dr. Stefano Evangelista of Trinity College, formed the basis for this book. So much the better!

Lack of fact checking seems to have begun in the author's very first book where she accepted a figure of 150,000 deaths a year from anorexia when the actual figure was revealed to be 400. You might think more rigorous fact checking would be a staple going forward. Sadly this terrific read is now marred by another error. The author interpreted a 19th century legal term of "death recorded" to mean a convict was executed, which it does not. This was a powerful point but not the major premise of the book. The majority of the book comprises so much more evidence of profound injustice, but the thing is, the stand out error makes the reader question the rest of the results. It's a shame because the majority of the book is powerful on it's own and compellingly written. Outrages: Sex, Censorship, and the Criminalization of Love by Naomi Wolf, Hardcover – June 18, 2019

title: Top Gun: 50 Years of Naval Air Superiority by Dwight Jon Zimmerman,  Hardcover – May 7, 2019
text: I think this is for anyone other than a hardcore aviator.  This is not solely about the TOPGUN US Naval Fighter Weapon School (NFWS). It's more about US Aces from WWI to today. Lots of great pictures. Lot's of interesting trivia. Several chapters about the 1986 movie. Totally gift worthy. If you are looking for something other then a textbook this is for you. I enjoyed it very much. The only disappointing thing was I don't know how much of the information is accurate after seeing on page 41 a picture and caption of Douglas Fairbanks Sr. next to a poster for the movie The Dawn Patrol featuring his son Douglas Fairbanks Jr, and the author text stating that Douglas Fairbanks starred in the movie.

title: Swimming Home by Mary-Rose MacColl, A Novel Paperback – June 20, 2017
text: First published in Australia in 2015, this is the author's fifth novel. The cover art grabbed my attention. The setting of 1925 with the conflict between an London based Aunt and her Australian niece recently orphaned piqued my interest. I think the the book, for me, started to go off the rails with too many jarring side stories. I very much enjoyed the history and the settings, I just never engaged with the characters, I found them irritating.

title: Minister Without Portfolio by Michael Winter, Hardcover – August 27, 2013
text: The author is a Canadian writer of five novels and three collections of short stories, he has been published since 1994.  A Bildungsroman, "a novel about the moral and psychological growth of the main character". It was difficult for me to care strongly for Henry, anyone who goes to Afghanistan not expecting to have their life blown to shreds is not living in the real world, and then it happens to him. It also kind of creeped me out how Henry inserted himself into the former life of a friend who died in Afghanistan with Henry as witness. What I enjoyed was that most of the novel is set in Newfoundland, a place I have never been and it really came alive for me. and what was with the beaver at the end? I will say this it is an excellent book club pick because there is so much to get passionate about.

title: Kilometer 99 by Tyler McMahon : A Novel Paperback – June 17, 2014
text:
Malia tells us her story which opens with her taking an epic wave in January 2001 El Salvador where she and her boyfriend Ben have lived for a year as Peace Corp volunteers, working during the week inland and meeting up on weekends at the coastal town of La Libertad. Decisions and luck weave the story and this is a gritty story. My best advice is to read the 2nd chapter and if that appeals to you, knowing it will get darker and still end in darkness. And then decide. Malia and Ben are complex people who you will come to know very well. Vivid compulsive writing.

The author worked as a Peace Corps volunteer in El Salvador, was a surf instructor and lives in Honolulu with his wife.

I was surprised that the surf town La Libertad is an actual town. It had a population of 35,997 in 2007 and is today one of the main tourist attractions in the country.

title: Visible Empire  by Hannah Pittard, Hardcover – June 5, 2018
text: Equal parts appalling and entertaining. It is nothing like the blurb. Instead the author takes an actual event, a plane crash that took place in 1962 killing 130 of 132 people on board. 122 from Atlanta and it's suburbs, and turned it into a comedy thrill ride. With the Mayor of Atlanta and his wife as comedic Greek Chorus. They are such a joke I am surprised their descendants haven't sued. They appear to be the only real people the novel uses. It was into that milieu the author adds the civil rights movement, the KKK, a young black man who you fear could be murdered at several moments and actually is roughed up and terrified, I was appalled at how the author used him, even if he is the only almost realistic character.

title: If I Could Tell You  by Elizabeth Wilhide,  Hardcover  March 22, 2016
text: Anna Karenina 1939 English Village to 1945 London. The cover caught my eye and the blurb caught my attention. The descriptions of life in England during these devastating years was so evocative, it was as if the author set you down there. I really feel I know so much more about what was like for the English during this period. The characters themselves were pretty one dimensional.  Actions and people that were sympathetic and understandable in 1870 Russian society just are not worthy in 1939. 30 year old Julia's actions with Dougie and Richard and her son are nothing to be proud of. Richard and their marriage are summed up for me in one action: his wife of 10 years is filmed briefly in a movie scene, when he learns of this he calls the movie director, Dougie, without telling him wife, and tells him not to use her in his film. Dougie is a stereotype, the name is perfect for him.  I am still trying to figure out the need for the ending it was both anti-climactic and served no purpose. The first 2/3 of the book I kept wondering aloud "what was she thinking?" but I don't think she was thinking except for living in the moment until more then half way through the novel.

title: Do This for Me by Eliza Kennedy, Hardcover – May 15, 2018
text: It slowly went down hill for me after chapter 10, up til then it was wildly improbable and laugh out loud funny with so much to hold on to and enjoy in a bombastic story. I loved ever single element until the story started to go off in so many directions and people became real and they stopped being funny and started to be pathetically foolish and sad. I also didn't care for the ending, it just didn't match, for me, how the Raney in chapter 1 would be or maybe how I hoped she would be. I will read more by this author, she has oodles of talent

title: False Witness: A Novel (Detective Cooper Devereaux) by Andrew Grant  Har,dcover – January 2, 2018
text:
Set in Birmingham Alabama. I wounder why the author chose Birmingham over any other American city? I have never been and I don't feel like the novel utilized it all that much. On to the characters, I didn't find them all that interesting. I also didn't find them to be decent people. I also didn't find Deveraux's baby mama or her story-line all that interesting. Same goes for the blackmail thread, they both were distracting and overwrought.However if you are looking for a lightweight quick police procedural you could enjoy it.

Detective Cooper Devereaux series:
False Positive (2015): Alabama detective Cooper Devereaux makes no apologies for his luxe lifestyle or the way he does his job. Most cops haven’t lived the kind of life he has—starting out as an orphan, raised by a grizzled cop savior—and most don’t use his kind of high-risk tactics. But he may have met his match in fellow detective Jan Loflin, who’s fresh off a long undercover stint in Vice when they’re partnered on a case that will test them both beyond their direst nightmares. A seven-year-old boy has disappeared from his home in the Birmingham suburbs. But the more Devereaux digs into the missing child’s background, the more he discovers about his own, eventually shaking loose a series of harrowing truths—about bloodlines, mass murder, obsession, and what two damaged detectives have in common with the innocent victim they’re so desperate to save. This twisty page-turner—the debut of the Detective Cooper Devereaux series—hurtles at a mile a minute through an action-packed search for a missing child, culminating in an ending that no reader will see coming.

False Friend (2017): An arsonist is targeting schools in Birmingham, Alabama—with devastating effect. Detective Devereaux—a man you can’t quite trust and should never ignore—must put a stop to the elusive pyromaniac’s reign of terror before more damage is done. Or worse, before students’ lives are lost. But as Devereaux sifts through the ashes of the case, a grisly discovery at a burned-out school sends the investigation spiraling in a new, terrifying direction. The detective and his partner are dragged into a nightmare world by revelations of gruesome rituals, the disappearance of local citizens, and allegations against city officials of shocking crimes that stretch back decades.
With innocent lives on the line, progress is hampered by friction between the police department and the FBI, and interference from factions of the local underworld complicate matters further. Devereaux doesn’t make excuses for his willingness to work outside the lines, but just as he needs to be at the top of his game, he’s rocked by echoes from his troubled past that threaten to engulf his daughter and girlfriend—and fracture the life he’s only recently begun to rebuild.

title: The Madonna of the Mountains by Elise Valmorbida Hardcover – June 12, 2018
text: Set in the Veneto region of Italy, from 1923 to 1950. We follow 25 year old Maria through decades of privations, poverty, violence and 5 children. I was looking for the Italian A Woman of Substance or Thorn Birds but this was a struggle to finish. I came away thinking I am so glad I wasn't living in the Veneto region in those years (fyi 3 million Venetians left between 1861 and 1961 to escape poverty that half the population), and that I was so glad I wasn't a woman living at that time where beating your wife was a way of life. I am especially thankful I was raised a Catholic in the US where Mary was all about mercy, this Mary was all about creating guilt where none belongs.

title: Go Ask Fannie Hardcover – April 10, 2018 by Elisabeth Hyde
text: A good dysfunctional family story; at times zany, at times real, at times mysterious and in moments tragic. I can totally see this being made into a movie, I think a good cast could make it entertaining. I thought the siblings came across as fresh and interesting but it's not a story that will linger because they never seemed like completely real people to me. It reminded me in some way of the characters in the movie This-Where-I-Leave-You/dp/B00K2CI008.

title: The Lesser Bohemians by Eimear McBride September 20, 2016
text: told in a style of stream of 'preconsciousness' that I easily got used to after a few pages. Winner of The James Tait Black Memorial Prize for literary fiction written in the English language, it's awarded by the University of Edinburgh in Scotland, the prizes was founded in 1919. This is the kind of novel to read when you have the whole weekend uninterrupted, it's as far away from a tight police procedural or romance as can be. Be prepared for a lot of excitement, passion and angst, basically you are stepping into the head of an 18 year old and her older lover. By the end I was just thanking my luck that I was never either person nor dated them. If you are intrigued by sexual, physical and psychological abuse of children and adolescents, anorexia and self-punishment this would be the book for you.

title: Shakespeare and the Resistance:  By: Clare Asquith
text:
The Earl of Southampton (1573-1624), the Essex Rebellion (1601), and the Poems (1593 and 1594) that Challenged Tudor Tyranny is a lovely academic work by Oxford scholar of whose other work was published in 2005: Shadowplay The Hidden Beliefs and Coded Politics of William Shakespeare. I just couldn't get in to reading it for pleasure. After trying repeatedly for 6 months I finally put my college student hat on an grasped my highlighter to read to the end. I recommend Alan Corduner's recording of the book for audible, he creates a compelling listen in just a 5 minute sample of the author introduction.

Let me recommend an author interview you can listen to on line: Ep #22: Clare Asquith on Shakespeare and the Essex Rebellion, by Cassidy Cash, September 17, 2018.

The poems were published while the plague ran it's way through London. The following is a timeline showing where these poems were published in relation to Shakespeare's other works:

title: 2019 Wall Calendar, Herbarium,  by Caz Hildebrand
text: My favorite graphic was the cover.  I should have looked at the other graphics because none of them thrilled me as much as the cover. They struck me as more 'flat' than I like.  I am sure most buyers will be thrilled, the artist is the award-winning designer of sumptuous best-selling cookbooks by Nigella Lawson.  FYI each month has an anecdote or quote and tips for the featured herb. If you like this calendar you will love the book [[ASIN:0500518939 Herbarium]] .

title: From the Corner of the Oval: A Memoir ... Beck Dorey-Stein
text: This could have been awesome, until it bogged down into a reality romance *sigh*. I was a summer paid intern on Capitol Hill back in 1982 and I was really looking forward to reading about the job and the c-workers and the life, but this just faded into the background. Bummer.

title: Mother American Night: My Life in Crazy Times  by John Perry Barlow  with Robert Greenfield
text:
I had never heard of John Perry Barlow (October 3, 1947 – February 7, 2018) the internet says he was born into a Wyoming Mormon family and his father was a republican state legistator living on a 22,000 acre family cattle ranch, he was an poet and essayist, a political operative working to elect Dick Cheney to Congress, he's associated with both the Democratic and Republican parties, a lyricist for the Grateful Dead, a suicide survivor, a cocaine dealer, and at the end of his life needed go-fund-me type contributions as he battled health care needs.

A lot of what I read I could also find on the internet. There is a bare mention of his family, that would have completed the picture of the man.I am still glad I had the opportunity to read his memoir. WIRED has a lengthy review of the book: The Ghost of John Perry Barlow Lives in His Posthumous Memoir.

title: Buried Truth (A Siren Cove Novel) by Jannine Gallant
text: Living on the Oregon coast I am a sucker for any novel that is set here, and am only disappointed when it is clear the author has never been here or can't write a story worth telling. I enjoyed the story of Ryan & Leah, high school sweethearts who went their separate way and meet again 12 years later. That they fall into bed soon after seeing each other again seemed real, I remember being 30 and single. The tea cozy mystery was fun if not suspenseful. I was disappointed in Leah, I think she was a fool. I didn't care for the type of bad guys, perverted characters in a romance turn me off. the Oregon coast never came alive so I would have to take a pass on any further books in the series.

title: Sucktown, Alaska by Craig Dirkes
text:
What our teen liked: the whole story, beginning with Alaska, and Eddie who screws up big time and flunks out of the first semester of college.

What I liked:Taylor (she’s Yup’ik, Italian, and Swedish, the high school valedictorian, and when Eddie tries to hit on her, the result is hilarious) and Alaska, and nothing else. I didn't care for Eddie, the drugs, and the story just rubbed me the wrong way..

title: Fairy Mom and Me by Sophie Kinsella adventures of a mother-daughter fairy duo!
text: Do you remember the TV show 'Bewitched'? Do you remember Samantha's great-aunt Esmeralda? Ella's mum is a young Esmeralda. She doesn't get her spells quite right. I imagine she would have struggled mightily at Hogwarts. Our 8 year old was mildly amused.

title: All Three Stooges by Erica S. Perl
text: Noah and Dash are 7th grad BFFs until Dash's dad dies, a suicide and Dash shuts down emotionally. Noah is hit hard on many levels, loss of Dash and loss of Dash's dad, Noah has two mothers and Dash's dad was a strong adult male figure in his life. On top of that Noah has to deal with the homophobe kid in his class. Noah then makes a huge error in judement and morals that hurts Dash and gets his Bar Mitsvah postponed. Sprinkled with comedy routines and comedians that held no interest to my 12 year old but may to yours.

title: Come, Let Us Adore Him: A Daily Advent Devotional by Paul David Tripp
text: This week it is the Amazon #1 Best Seller in Christmas books.  Daily lessons for the month of December selected by the author of  [[ASIN:1433502305 Whiter Than Snow: Meditations on Sin and Mercy]]. This is a less opulent, less beautiful book than I would select as a gift. It's a very nice devotional, just not one I would choose when browsing in a bookstore. - I also like having Scripture verses printed in full, in this case they are just cited.

title: Protected by the Shadows (An Irene Huss Investigation)  by Helene Tursten (Marlaine Delargy,Translator)
text: This is the final in The Irene Huss series,a swedish cozy with violence and many police meetings. The writing, or translation, is light and simplistic. I usually like Scandinavian police procedurals but Irene Huss, the main character, is portrayed as such a flat, disagreeable character that she sours the series for me at times, also the narrative is awkward and repetitive. I usually do finish the books if only for their predictability, the locale, and a kind of boring familiarity I find comforting.

title: Misadventures of a City Girl by Meredith Wild & Chelle Bliss
text:
"Hollywood" caught my eye, "swanky retreat in Northern California" kept me interested, wondering how the author could make a character like "Luke Dawson lives off the grid, preferring solitude to society" work led me to order the book. Turns out lots of sex - lol. More plot and character development would have made it better.

"Misadventures is a romantic series comprised of standalone novels, each written or co-written by authors selectively chosen by Waterhouse’s founder, author Meredith Wild, based on works she’s read and loved. The series concept was originally inspired by a casual co-writing project that Wild undertook with an author friend—a low-pressure, high-steam romance that they could pen between their other more heavily plot-driven novels. “As authors, we work incredibly hard on our stories, and the process can be an intense and often stressful undertaking,” Wild says. “With Misadventures, ‘keep it fun’ is the driving philosophy. The resulting stories have been scandalous, refreshing, and, of course, incredibly sexy. They’re the perfect bedside read, a ‘quick blush’ for the reader who loves a page-turning romance.”"

title: Fairytale by Danielle Steel
text:
I am a life long reader of Danielle Steel, from 1978 [[ASIN:B001LQNNWE The Promise]], and while Fairytale is a well written novel with the prose of a Danielle Steel novel it wasn't a Danielle Steel romance. The romance started on the last page, so go into this knowing the lack of romance and you will not be disappointed. Fairytale is a story of a beautiful family of 3 that by the end of chapter one has been torn apart. Told in the prose of a fairytale the story was more simplistic than I was hoping for and Camille was the only one who is fully developed.

I think this is her 110th novel - amazing!

title: Things That Happened Before the Earthquake by Chiara Barzini
text:
Great cover. Great dialogue. I ordered the book because of the cover and the premise and it was listed as a story for teen to young adult. At this point I am not sure who the target audience is. This story is every parents fear. Sex, lots of sex, drugs, lots of drugs, everything including murder. The author speaks with authority having fictionalized and dramatized her own youth. Then there is the death of the donkey. *sigh*

a good read for Ages 18 and above.

title: WITCHTOWN by Cory Putman Oakes
text: Adventures of a 16 year old targeted for 12 year old readers. To me that is such a vast expanse of life experiences. Kids are growing up so quickly that I am pretty happy about my kid experiencing life as a 12 year old that I think I am going to hang on to this book until she is a bit older, say 14 years old but I think by that age the writing level will feel too immature for her. Fyi -  For one thing, the 16 year old and her "mother" are grifters and witches *sigh*. Plus there is a romance to muddy the waters.

title: Lights, Camera, Middle School! (Babymouse Tales from the Locker) By: Jennifer L. Holm, Matthew Holm
text: I thought our middle schoolers would love it - final comments from both boy and girl were "I'm just not that into you".  I would highly recommend using the look inside feature on the hardcover preview, because I can see that my kids are in the minority.

title: WILDERS by Brenda Cooper suitable for ages 16 and up.
text:
In the Pacific Northwest of the future, Seattle and Vancouver Canada are united as the domed city SeaCouver. When she was 16, Coryn's parents left her an orphan after their double suicide, her older sister, Lou, abandoned her to pursue a career far away, emailing Coryn occasionally as if she were a school acquaintance. Coryn turns 18 and goes in search of her sister with the help of her personal computer robot, Paula.

The story never came alive for me, I felt like I was reading a fleshed out outline instead of a complete novel.

title: ... I am too much of an earthling to ever enjoy a book after that happens) and things get worse ...
text:
Earth is destroyed at the end of book two (I guess I am too much of an earthling to ever enjoy a book after that happens) and things get worse before they get better. The ending was upbeat and I enjoyed the characters of Skylar, Win and Jule. Thlo/Ibtep was so wooden to the point of being boring.

[[ASIN:1477847847 Earth & Sky (The Earth & Sky Trilogy)]]17 year old Skylar has been haunted for as long as she can remember by fleeting yet powerful sensations that something is horribly wrong. But despite the visions of disaster that torment her, nothing ever happens, and Sky’s beginning to think she’s crazy. Then she meets a mysterious, otherworldly boy named Win and discovers the shocking truth her premonitions have tapped into: that our world no longer belongs to us. For thousands of years, life on Earth has been at the mercy of alien scientists who care nothing for humans and are using us as the unwitting subjects of their time-manipulating experiments. Win belongs to a rebel faction seeking to put a stop to it, and he needs Skylar’s help to save the world and keep the very fabric of reality together. A mind-bending journey through time with a cast of unforgettable characters.

[[ASIN:1477829121 The Clouded Sky (The Earth & Sky Trilogy)]] Skylar escapes the time-bending Enforcers who secretly control Earth, her troubles have just begun. She and her friend Win take refuge on Win’s home space station with his fellow rebels, but the fate of Skylar’s planet still spins out of her control. To avoid detection, Skylar poses as the Earthling “pet” of Win’s rival, an arrogant boy named Jule. Homesick and faced with a cool reception from the other rebels, she throws herself into the group’s mission: assembling a weapon to disable Earth’s restrictive time field. Gradually, Skylar’s skill for detail gains respect—even from Jule, who is more vulnerable than he lets on. Yet challenges spring from every side. Not only must Sky navigate the muddy waters of romance, but suspicions of betrayal grow among the rebels as their work narrowly misses sabotage. Skylar must expose a traitor before time runs out and Earth is destroyed.

title: Taking Hold: From Migrant Childhood to Columbia University (published 2015) by Francisco Jiménez
text:
A huge hit. The story of an impoverished illegal immigrant making good on the american dream and going to an Ivy League school then sharing that success by a career in academia. You can go online to NBC News "inspiring-memoirs-tell-journey-child-farm-worker-academic" and The NY Daily News "hold-migrant-worker-turns-ivy-league-scholar".

It just didn't work for me. The story of illegal immigrants, breaking the law to cross a border in search of prosperity. I kept waiting for the author to achieve his success in America and return to his country and make that a better place and end the cycle. I guess I am a dreamer.

title: Our Chemical Hearts by Krystal Sutherland
text:
Grace walks with a cane, wears oversized boys' clothes, and leaves grooming to the other girls (ok I am already turned off).

Henry is a bit introspective, he thinks a lot about having never been in love even tho he is still in high school. His other two priorities are getting into a decent college and being named editor to the school paper. His parents are having marriage issues that are not resolved in a way I would hope. Then Grace and Henry are both named editor in chief of the paper.

The ending was not a Happily Ever After. There is also sex between teenagers. The best part about the book was Henry's older sister Sadie - everything about her was priceless.
.
Debut Australian author.

title: The Loose Ends List  by Carrie Firestone
text: Life is going along splendidly for 17 year old Maddie O'Neill Levine. She is head to college and her summer looks golden. She'll be spending time with her fabulous grandmother too, except not as she originally thought. Her grandmother is diagnosed with terminal cancer. Her one wish is to go out on a high note taking the family (Gram’s boyfriend, Bob Johnson, Maddie's parents & brother, cousin Janie, aunts and uncles) a 8 week cruise, a death with dignity cruise that allows her to die on her terms.  A very unique story and truly fits the phrase 'what a way to go'. The really creepy part (for me) was that people choose to die before the cruise ends. I actually didn't give the book to our teen - I didn't like how uncouth the people could be (Grandma talking graphic sex with her teenage granddaughters as if she were a teenager herself - it just kinda creeped me out).

title: Burn: The Rephaim Book IV by Paula Weston
text:
Ooops! I didn't see this was book 4 in a series before I ordered for our teenager to read. If you are in the same boat I included the previous book summaries below. Apparently the 4 books combined take place over only 11 days. I give it 3 out of 5 stars - I can handle the foul language and the sex it was the vivid violence I could do without.

Book 1 [[ASIN:1770495479 Shadows (The Rephaim)]] It's almost a year since 18 year old Australian Gaby Winters watched her twin brother die. In the sunshine of a new town her body has healed, but her grief is raw and constant. It doesn't help that every night in her dreams she fights and kills hell-beasts. And then Rafa comes to town. He looks exactly like the guy who's been appearing in Gaby's dreams, he tells her things about her brother and her life that cannot be true, things that are dangerous. Who is Rafa? Who are the Rephaim? And who is Gaby? The truth lies in the shadows of her nightmares.

Book 2 [[ASIN:1770495509 Haze: The Rephaim, Book 2]] Gaby is one of the Rephaim - a wingless half angel, descended from the Fallen. Demons exist and they are hunting her. She knows she's alive when she's meant to be dead. And that means maybe Jude is too. So why isn't she out there looking for him?

Book 3 [[ASIN:1770498486 Shimmer: The Rephaim, Book 3]] Gaby can just about cope with being one of the Rephaim--a 139-year-old half-angel--whose memories have been stolen. She's even coming to grips with the fact that Jude, the brother she's mourned for a year, didn't die at all. But now Rafa--sexy, infuriating Rafa--is being held, and hurt, by Gatekeeper demons. And Gaby has to get the bitterly divided Rephaim to work together, or Rafa has no chance at all.

title: Soldier Sister, Fly Home by Nancy Bo Flood
text:
Sadly the story lost me at the butchering of a ewe - it was just a little too vivid for a middle school novel (I only wish that in reality all animals raised for food were treated as respectfully as depicted in this book). After I finished the book I learned the author lived and taught on the Navajo Nation for 15 years,

Set against the never ending American involvement in the war in Iraq, 13 year old Tess, half-Navajo/half-white, feels like an outsider in both cultures.She attends a boarding school in Flagstaff Arizona - a town I visited in 2006 and cherish the memories - I would love to go again, it should be on everyone's bucket list.. Tess spends a lovely summer with her Navajo grandmother and it was beautifully depicted by the author.

title: Surface to Air: A Malko Linge Novel #192 by Gérard de Villiers, originally published April 2012
text:
The king of pulp novels, from 1966 to 2013 the author wrote 4 to 5 international spy thrillers a year! I ordered [[ASIN:B011G3HBVA Lord of the Swallows: A Malko Linge Novel]] and Surface to Air at the same time then read them back to back. I had never heard of the author (b.1929 – d.2013) until I read a fascinating interview that you can read on line in the NY Times Magazine titled The Spy Novelist Who Knows Too Much, By ROBERT F. WORTH published JAN. 30, 2013.

I can totally see how in the countries where these novels have been best sellers for decades (France, Germany, Russian, Turkey and Japan) the macho male reader would gobble the Malko Linge novels up - Malko is like James Bond to who lives in the political present day but who never grew out of the 1930's. Malko is an Austrian prince and CIA agent. In this case, which you do not need to read any of the others in the 200 volume series to understand what is going on, he takes on intrigue a little too far fetched for 2012 but I can see easily happening in 2017, A FBI sting uncovers US citizen wanting to shoot down Air Force one with the president in it, using a Russian surface to air missile, The FBI pose as Russians to arrange it thinking they will arrest him when the deal is made, but they need the missile, so the FBI involves the Russians, who make plans of their own, luckily the CIA get wind of this and not having the wherewithal to control the situation themselves involve a Austrian playboy prince to oversee that no harm comes to anyone. Wow.

for newbies like myself this list of Recurring characters may prove helpful:
Alexandra Vogel: Malko's "fiancee".
Elko Krisantem: Turkish servant of Malko Linge. He used to be a killer.
Samantha Adler: A German arms dealer.
Mandy Brown aka Mandy la salope (Mandy the b***h): An American "maneater".
Frank Capistrano: Special adviser to the White House.
Milton Brabeck & Chris Jones:CIA agents who protect Malko on several missions.

title: Lord of the Swallows:  Malko Linge #186  by Gérard de Villiers first published February 2011
text:
The king of pulp novels, from 1966 to 2013 the author wrote 4 to 5 international spy thrillers a year! I ordered Lord of the Swallows and [[ASIN:080416939X Surface to Air: A Malko Linge Novel]] at the same time then read them back to back. I had never heard of the author (b.1929 – d.2013) until I read a fascinating interview that you can read on line in the NY Times Magazine titled The Spy Novelist Who Knows Too Much, By ROBERT F. WORTH published JAN. 30, 2013.

I can totally see how in the countries where these novels have been best sellers for decades (France, Germany, Russian, Turkey and Japan) the macho male reader would gobble the Malko Linge novels up - Malko is like James Bond to who lives in the political present day but who never grew out of the 1930's. Malko is an Austrian prince and CIA agent. In this case, which you do not need to read any of the others in the 200 volume series to understand what is going on, he takes on intrigue involving Russian sleeper agents in the US going back 25 years (a ripped from the headlines case where Alexi Krenkov is inspired by the 2010 case involving Alexander Poteyev,) of course this led me to the real story as profiled in the Guardian "The day we discovered our parents were Russian spies" by Shaun Walker published May 7, 2016.

for newbies like myself this list of Recurring characters may prove helpful:
Alexandra Vogel: Malko's "fiancee".
Elko Krisantem: Turkish servant of Malko Linge. He used to be a killer.
Samantha Adler: A German arms dealer.
Mandy Brown aka Mandy la salope (Mandy the b***h): An American "maneater".
Frank Capistrano: Special adviser to the White House.
Milton Brabeck & Chris Jones:CIA agents who protect Malko on several missions.

title: Best to read this series in order to reap a ...
text:
Best to read this series in order to reap a total rewarding journey. In fact book one is a 5 star read - book two is a 4 star read. Book three was disappointing in that is lacked most of what I loved in book 1 - the relationship of Andrea and Per. There was also too much world building, 3 worlds in 500 pages while gorgeous and rich in detail pushed the people and their relationship to the sideline.

book #1 published by Scholastic UK in 1998 [[ASIN:B01H13AUSA The Sterkarm Handshake]] A twenty-first-century corporation invades the domain of a warlike sixteenth-century Scottish clan in this “brilliantly imagined” time-travel adventure (Philip Pullman). The miraculous invention of a Time Tube has given Great Britain’s mighty FUP corporation unprecedented power, granting it unlimited access to the rich natural resources of the past. Opening a portal into sixteenth-century Scotland, the company has sent representatives back five hundred years to deal with the Sterkarms, a lawless barbarian clan that has plundered both sides of the English-Scottish border for generations. Among the first of the company’s representatives to arrive from the future, young anthropologist Andrea Mitchell finds herself strangely drawn to this primitive tribe of raiders and pillagers who, not surprisingly, view her as magical. As translator and liaison, she becomes enmeshed in the personal lives of these proud, savage folk, developing an especially strong emotional bond with Per, the handsome son of the ruthless Sterkarm chieftain, Toorkild. But the Sterkarms’ welcome does not extend to the FUP corporate despoilers from the future—and soon a fragile agreement between the untamable Scots and the interloping “Elves” begins to crumble. Suddenly war looms on the horizon, and when treachery on both sides ignites a firestorm of violence, Andrea will have to choose where her loyalties truly lie: with her coldhearted employers or with the barbarous kinfolk of the man she has come to love. The Sterkarms have plundered the border between Scotland and England for generations. Suddenly intruders, calling themselves Elves, want the Sterkarms to stop their violent ways. The Elves, time travelers from the 21st century, have found a way back to the 16th century and plan to do their own plundering of the land's rich natural resources. Their only mistake is foolishly underestimating the Sterkarms themselves. For Andrea Mitchell, an anthropologist working among the Sterkarms, none of this matters. In love with Per -- a young Sterkarm warrior -- and feted as a beautiful Elf-May, she's never known such happiness in her own time. But when Per receives a deadly injury, Andrea's decision to take him into the 21st century to save him has explosive results. Per, seeing how powerful and destructive the Elves truly are, swears to keep them from his land forever. And in the bloody battle that ensues, Andrea must finally choose whose side she is on. A winner of the Guardian Fiction Prize and a finalist for the Carnegie Medal, called “enthralling” by Philip Pullman, the author of the His Dark Materials novels, Susan Price’s Sterkarm Handshake is a masterful blend of historical and science fiction critics have called “dazzling,” “exciting,” “memorable,” “thought provoking,” and “a thumping good page-turner.”

book #2 [[ASIN:0060721979 A Sterkarm Kiss]] Andrea Mitchell once found acceptance and love among the Sterkarm clan in lawless 1500s Scotland when she gained access to Great Britain’s past via the FUP Corporation’s “Time Tube.” Since her return to the present, she has been unable to readjust to twenty-first century life. So when the company’s CEO, James Windsor, offers to send her back to the violent, colorful era—and her beloved Per Sterkarm—Andrea eagerly agrees. The past she reenters, however, is not the one she remembers. To avoid potential catastrophic effects on the future, FUP has sent her to a different dimension and an alternate sixteenth century. Here, she is a stranger to her former friends, including her onetime lover Per, who is preparing to marry a daughter of the hated Grannams, the Sterkarms’ sworn enemies. But the union is part of FUP’s insidious plan to plunder the past of its natural wealth. When the wedding goes brutally, tragically awry, Andrea finds herself caught in the middle, a pawn in a violent endgame devised by Windsor and his greedy cronies. And this time there may not be sanctuary for her among the proud, primitive folk she once admired—or even an escape forward to the future where she truly belongs. Andrea Mitchell has never felt as if she belongs in the 21st century. She's too fat, too clumsy, and too plain. So when she's offered the chance to take the Time Tube back to the 16th century -- and back to Per, the young Sterkarm warrior she fell in love with once before -- she doesn't hesitate. The lovely, boisterous, and crude Sterkarms have always made her feel welcome and at home. Maybe this time she'll even stay for good. But things on the 16th side are not what Andrea expected them to be. Per doesn't know who she is, and a wedding between the Sterkarms and their enemies, the Grannams, ends in bloodshed and confusion. Even when Andrea discovers it's the Elves who have betrayed them all, no one wants to believe her. She may have made the biggest -- and the deadliest -- mistake of her life. In this blistering sequel to her award-winning The Sterkarm Handshake, Susan Price weaves a riveting tale of revenge, deceit, and love, set against a backdrop of warring clans and brutal passions. Susan Price’s The Sterkarm Handshake was awarded the Guardian Fiction Prize. In A Sterkarm Kiss, the Carnegie Medal–winning author once again ingeniously blends historical and science fiction in a masterful time-travel adventure as thrilling and unforgettable as its acclaimed predecessor.

title: Dreaming the Bear by Mimi Thebo
text:
Somewhere between OK and I didn't like it. Very odd mix of fantasy and reality. I think the intended target age is 12 - 14 years old and our 14 year old did not finish, our 11 year old did finish it but she found it odd. She also didn't like the main character, Darcy, who recently moved from England to Montana with her family and has not acclimated (Darcy has my total sympathy there) but she is a bit of a Wendy-Whiner. Darcy is recuperating from pneumonia and her woe-is-me story telling gets old, especially considering her parents and brother come off as so nice and caring. The magical realism comes to play when Darcy collapses while snowshoeing, finds a cave to refuge in that happens to have a hibernating grizzly bear that does eat her and is ok with a little cuddle. hmmmm. Really don't want readers thinking that can happen. You would be Bear kibble pretty quick. The story moves on from their with Darcy caring in secret for the bear who is hurt. And it doesn't get better.

On the other hand - I read a online review in the Guardian newspaper "dreaming-the-bear-mimi-thebo-review" and the reviewer loved it.

title: City on Edge by Stefanie Pintoff
text: From the Edgar Award Winning author for "Best First Novel by an American Author".  This is the 2nd Eve Rossi novel, 2015’s Hostage Taker was the first. This wasn't appealing to me (and I love police procedurals), Written like she is following a "how to write a mystery thriller by number". For example the last sentence of each chapter is supposed to grab you and keep you reading into the next chapter, but the was the author does it is obvious and doesn't work,  I loved the NYC setting and seeing behind the scene at the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. The author introduces characters not by letting the reader get to know them but in 'dossiers' so that I didn't get to know them and felt no connection to them. The characters seemed flat, lifeless to me.

title: Lost Stars by Lisa Selin Davis
text: I am not sure who the audience is for this book. It is set in the 1980's and had zero interest, after several chapters, for our teen. I read it, it's my generation, but the story never grabbed me.  Teenage Carrie has suffered more than a person should. Her beloved older sister, Ginny, has died, she exhibits her despair in uncontrolled rage, her mother never comes home from a retreat, her father and younger sister, Rosie, carry on, badly. Her sister's friends let her hang with them and get her messed up with drugs and booze. It gets worse before it gets better.

title: The Leaving Season by Cat Jordan
text: best for ages 15 to 18 — 17 year old Meredith aka "Middie" Daniels and her boyfriend, Nate, are separated when Nate graduates - his plan is to take a year of volunteer work and return for Middie so they can go to college together. Middie has never thought much Nate's slacker best friend Lee but he becomes her rock in the months ahead. The outline of the story had potential but the reading of it seemed rather banal - it was nice but that was it.I never really felt like they were real people.

title: Revenge, Ice Cream, and Other Things Best Served Cold (A Broken Hearts & Revenge Novel)  by Katie Finn
text:
Book 2 of 3 in the Broken Hearts & Revenge Series. If Mean Girls was a reality show. Loathsome 16-year-olds summering and simmering on the Hamptons in an unbelievable plot, acting like spy vs spy from poor behavior dating back to when they last met at age 11.Take a look at the below summary for book one before you go any further.

Book #1 - [[ASIN:1250063051 Broken Hearts, Fences and Other Things to Mend (A Broken Hearts & Revenge Novel)]] Gemma had her summer all planned out, but it takes sharp turn when she gets dumped and finds herself back in the Hamptons after a five-year absence. Being there puts her at risk of bumping into Hallie, her former best friend (that is, before Gemma ruined her life). But people don't hold grudges forever. Do they? Gemma intends to make amends, but a small case of mistaken identity causes the people she knew years ago―including Hallie and her dreamy brother Josh―to believe she's someone else. As though the summer wasn't complicated enough already. Can Gemma keep up the charade? Or will she be found out by the very people she's been hiding from?

title: A few months on a luxury cruise liner--how bad can it be
text:
Young Adult apocalyptic horror (think murderous children and babies being killed). They almost lost me at a guy named Shy. Shy is the main character's name. Every time I read it, it took me out of the book *sigh*

Book #1 - [[ASIN:0385741219 The Living]] Shy takes the summer job to make some money. A few months on a luxury cruise liner--how bad can it be? Bikinis, free food, maybe even a girl or two . . . every cruise has a fresh crop of passengers, after all. He'll rake in the tips and be able to help his mom and sister out with the bills. But then, an earthquake more massive than any ever recorded hits California and Shy's life is changed forever. The earthquake is only the beginning. Twenty-four hours and a catastrophic chain of events later, Shy is lost at sea, fighting to survive--and stuck with 'her'. She's blond and she's rich, and never in her life would she have dreamed she'd be adrift in the Pacific Ocean, surrounded by death and completely dependent on a guy like Shy. And Shy hasn't even faced the worst yet.

Book #2 - Shy, Carmen and Marcus survived the tsunami that sank their cruise ship, escaped the deadly island they hoped would be a refuge and almost perished while adrift for 36 days at sea, The book opens with them making it back home to apocalyptic California. they head to Arizona hoping for sustainable living. I didn't pass it on to our teen, with a wealth of reading out there the subject matter would need a lot more depth. The character Shy ended up being the best thing in the book.

title: Snitch (The Bea Catcher Chronicles) byOlivia Samms
text:
Book 2 in a two book series. Really good potential but fell flat for me, the teenager in the house thought the dialogue didn't sound like a teenagers. The main character, and her BFF Chris, are 18 years old working with Sergeant Dan Daniels on a gang-related murder.

Book # 1 [[ASIN:147781650X Sketchy (The Bea Catcher Chronicles)]] - Bea's life has been a mess ever since she got kicked out of private school and sent to rehab. Now clean, Bea is starting over at Packard High School, in a city shaken from two assaults on young women. The latest victim, Willa Pressman-the one who survived-doesn't remember a thing. But Bea has a disturbing new "skill": she can see-and then draw-images from other people's minds. And when she looks at Willa, Bea is shocked by what she sketches. Bea might be the only one who knows Willa's secrets-and who can take down the killer before he strikes again. Bea's drawings are illustrated thoughout the book.

title: THOSE GIRLS by Lauren Saft
text: Three 16 going on 17 best friends each tell their own stories. It delivered on what I bought it for, the inner thought of girls growing into women. I just don't remember sex being so pivotal when I was a junior in High School - I would be wary of my 16 year old reading this with out discussing the events in the book with a responsible adult. major plot points: sex, jealousy, drugs. Mainly redeemable for showing teens that everyone has insecurities.

title: Glory (The Dust Chronicles) byMaureen McGowan
text:
Book 3 of 3 in the Dust Chronicles Series (the adult in me wanted to add "one person's story of using Pledge in her quest for a clean home').

Book 1 [[ASIN:1612183670 Deviants (The Dust Chronicles)]] - In Glory's world, different means deviant—and dead. In a post-apocalyptic world, where the earth is buried by asteroid dust that’s mutated the DNA of some humans, an orphaned sixteen-year-old, Glory, must hide and protect her younger brother. If their Deviant abilities are discovered, they’ll be expunged—kicked out of the dome to be tortured and killed by the Shredders. Glory would give anything to get rid of her unique ability to kill with her emotions, especially when Cal, the boy she’s always liked, becomes a spy for the authorities. But when her brother is discovered, and she learns their father, who was expunged for killing their mother, is still alive, she must escape the domed city that’s been her entire world. Outside in the ruins, they’re pursued by the authorities and by sadistic, scab-covered Shredders who are addicted to the lethal-to-humans dust now covering the planet. Glory’s quests to transport herself and her brother to safety make up the thrilling and fascinating first volume of The Dust Chronicles.

Book 2 [[ASIN:B00HFRLJ7E Compliance: The Dust Chronicles, Book 2]] Haven Equals Safety. This slogan is emblazoned on the minds of every Haven employee. But for Glory, life inside Haven is anything but safe. Most of all, she must keep her special "Deviant" gift - the ability to kill with her eyes - a secret from those who would want to expunge her. Far from her family, Glory faces danger at every turn as she trains to be a Compliance Officer - to terminate her own kind - while she works undercover to rescue as many Deviants as she can. When people she trusts turn against her and a powerful member of Management takes her under her wing, Glory questions everything in which she believes and can no longer tell her allies from her enemies. For Glory, life inside the domed city is anything but safe. After rescuing her brother, Glory returns to Haven as a double agent to locate and save fellow Deviants.

Our teen thought the last book had more romance than one boy can handle.

title: Crystal Fire byJordan Dane
text:
Book 2 of 2 in a series [[ASIN:0373210760 Indigo Awakening (The Hunted)]] and picks up where book #1 ended.

Book #1 "Because of what you are, the Believers will hunt you down. Voices told Lucas Darby to run. Voices no one else can hear. He's warned his sister not to look for him, but Rayne refuses to let her troubled brother vanish on the streets of LA. In her desperate search, she meets Gabriel Stewart, a runaway with mysterious powers and far too many secrets. Rayne can't explain her crazy need to trust the strange yet compelling boy--to touch him--to protect him even though he scares her. A fanatical church secretly hunts psychic kids--gifted "Indigo" teens feared to be the next evolution of mankind--for reasons only "the Believers" know. Now Rayne's only hope is Gabe, who is haunted by an awakening power--a force darker than either of them imagine--that could doom them all. They are our future--if they survive."

Indigo kids are highly intelligent, psychics with a “indigo” aura, see angels, communicate with the dead, and are on a mission to save the world.
Gabe becomes the most powerful and is forced to become a leader to prevent their annihilation by the Believers, an Los Angeles based powerful organization medically experimenting on Indigos.

This title was a little heavy on the romance and our teen lost interest half way through.

the author's 2011 novel is completely different and a hit [[ASIN:0373210299 In the Arms of Stone Angels]]

title: The Last Time We Were Us ... Leah Konen
text: The cover graphics was the best thing about the book. The synopsis tells the whole story and there isn't much more. Liz is not appealing, in fact no one is everyone is a self absorbed narcissist. The most interesting part for our 14 year old was the story behind Jason's incarceration and learning the full story.

title: The Ice Beneath Her by Camilla Grebe, Elizabeth Clark Wessel (Translator)
text:
An experienced writer but a disappointing storyteller. I found it long and drawn out. All first person narration multiple narrators which makes it difficult to know who is speaking, The transitions are non-existent. Everyone is depressed and I can't distinguish one personality from another. The crime GRUESOME (a woman is found beheaded), but, for a mystery there is more about relationships and self analysis than solving the crime. The depiction of Sweden is evocative.

Murdering Emma's cat was the final straw.

On the other hand Kirkus gave it a starred review.

title: Who Watcheth (the 9th Irene Huss Investigation novel) by Helene Tursten, Marlaine Delargy (Translator)
text:
Helene Tursten is a very reliable author of Swedish police procedurals and an expert at sketching characters quickly and memorably. The sporadic first person narratives of the serial killer are off putting, unsettling, and did nothing for the story. And why must the main character, Irene Huss, be a victim too? I found the solution predicable, and using the term 'nut-job' more than once took me right out of the story.

With these negatives it was still a good read but a bit sloppy, and the ending was awesome. Perhaps the writing or translation were hurriedly completed?

*You can read an excerpt now that the publisher's website penguin randomhouse..

title: Pilgrimage: My Search for the Real Pope Francis  by Mark K. Shriver.
text: Reads like a New York Times Magazine cover piece, very factual and received a starred review from Publisher's weekly. I am practicing Catholic and a huge admirer of our current pope (while I refer to his predecessor as he-who-shall-not-be-named). The author did a terrific job of sharing his tremendous amount of research, meeting so many people who know the pope well, many who have known him for decades. From these reminiscences I feel I got to know the pope as a man better than any 30 minute interview the author may have been granted.  For me, in the end, the author was not as enthralling a story teller as I would like and I got a little tired of the name dropping. I did come away with a greater understanding of our pope and for that I am grateful to the author.

title: Claws and Effect (Secret Smithsonian Adventures) Chris Kientz & Steve Hockensmith, Lee Nielsen (Illustrator)
text: Not a big hit with the home crowd the 10 year old flipped through after the first couple chapters, the 9 year old did the same, tried reading it to the 7 year old and 5 year old and they haven't asked for it again. The summary posted on amazon basically sums up the story.

title: Bright, Precious Days  Book 3 in the Corrine and Russell Calloway saga.
text:
as the saying goes, I'm just not that in to you. I so wanted to be. I'm a Jersey girl who loves NYC, or 'the city' as I knew it growing up. I love reading Vanity Fair, Vogue, the NYT Magazine. I especially like a well written book. I hav ebeen meaning to try Jay McInerney for decades. This story and the writing just didn't grab - I wanted to like or loathe the characters instead it was a struggle to finish. I am totally in the minority here - this author is so well regarded I think any reader should at least give it a try.

Brightness Falls (published May 26, 1992): 'The story of a disintegrating marriage set in New York in the frenzied few months leading up to the Wall Street crash of 1987. A sort of BONFIRE OF THE VANITIES with the added advantage of believable, likeable characters' INDEPENDENT ON SUNDAY Their moment was of the brief, shining sort when everything seemed possible. The gold rush of the 1980s, when the best and the brightest vied with the worst and most craven for riches, fame and the love of beautiful people. With all the force and cunning enterprise of Manhattan itself, BRIGHTNESS FALLS captures lives-in-the-making - men and women confronting their sudden middle-age with wit and low behaviour, fear and confusion, and occasionally even a little honesty and decency. None of them, ever, would be the same again. As he maps the fault lines spreading through the once-impenetrable marriage of Russell and Corrine Calloway and chronicles Russell's wildly ambitious scheme to seize control of the publishing house at which he works, Jay McInerney creates an elegy for New York in the 1980s. From the literary chimeras and corporate raiders to those dispossessed by the pandemonium of money and power, Brightness Falls captures a rash era at its moment of reckoning and gives reality back to a time that now seems decidedly unreal.

The Good Life (published January 31, 2006) Clinging to a semiprecarious existence in TriBeCa, Corrine and Russell Calloway have survived a separation and are thoroughly wonderstruck by young twins whose provenance is nothing less than miraculous, even as they contend with the faded promise of a marriage tinged with suspicion and deceit.
