title: Missing Some Necessary Details
text:
I’m a long way off from retirement but I am already thinking about what I want to do when I no longer participate in the work force. I selected this book as more of an idea book and a starting point, to get some idea of what I might want to do later. This book is stuffed full of ideas but there are some oversights that I think merit mention and could use a revisit.

The book boasts 150 ideas for trips and activities to do when retired. There are some simple and easy ones in there, such as hiking domestic trails or getting iconic meals in different areas of the country. A good number of them, though, require international travel and a good deal of money. There are a lot of ideas that are simply out of reach for the average retiree. That’s not necessarily a bad thing, though it should be more clear.

Where this book does drop the ball is in the lack of necessary details. For example, on page 41 the title of the adventure is “Learn North African Cooking in Marrakech”. It presents the idea and gives all of the positive points, such as what you’ll be doing, what you’ll learn and so on. What it does not tell you is what travel preps are needed – like a passport, travel visa and immunizations – and it gives no clue how much this trip might cost. It avoids mention of any possible travel restrictions, potential hazards and more. This is true on all international suggestions, not just this one. In fact, even the domestic journeys lack much detail in that regard.

This is an idea book more than anything, though it is lacking in important details such that it is of diminished usefulness. This is particularly true of any suggestions that would take the reader abroad. There are some fine domestic ideas, though, so all is not lost.

title: Heavy Reliance on Unusual Ingredients
text:
I selected this cookbook with minimal knowledge of low-lectin eating, more out of curiosity than a desire to eat healthier. To be sure, I do have an interest in a healthier lifestyle so this book had some appeal there. It looks like a good book and there are some positive things I can say about it, but it is likely a book I will use rarely due to reliance on ingredients that I do not have readily available.

The author does a nice job of explaining the problem with lectins and the health issues that arrive from consuming them. There aren't too many references to reputable sources, but the explanations make sense. It puts the whole situation in layman's terms.

There are twelve chapters in this book and there is a broad coverage of recipe types - breakfast, desserts, main dishes and so on. There's a little something for everyone here. And, the book has a lot of full-color photographs which make finding something that looks appealing much easier.

Where this book fails me is in the ingredients for the recipes. In almost every recipe there is at least one (usually more) ingredient that I would otherwise not buy or of which I had not heard prior. Many of these I have never even seen at my local market and I am not close to a health food store or gourmet shop to acquire these ingredients.

This appears to be a nice book and a good bit of effort went into creating the recipes and binding the book into an attractive volume. For me, though, it is not practical.

title: Fine Book but Strays from the Stated Topic
text:
Radically Whole is marketed as a book that addresses the [common] phenomenon of a divided heart - a heart that wants two things and wants the best of both without the consequences of being divided. The focus of this book is centered around the book of James and it takes a fairly deep dive into the Scripture. However, it strays from the stated mission in the title of being just about dealing with double-mindedness and turns more into a deep study of James as a whole. While there's nothing wrong with this, it's a bit off the mark from the stated purpose.

As another reviewer has said, this book doesn't just address the problem of a divided heart. Yes, it does cover that as the primary topic and emphasis, but it also goes into more generalized study of James. For the reader looking for a direct book on a specific subject, this isn't the book.

All of that said, this is actually a good study of James. Each chapter starts with a lengthy passage of Scripture, and the following writing analyzes it well. The author uses copious amounts of Scripture in reference and he makes his points clearly. I am enjoying the book and though I am not done with it I am definitely learning.

I wanted rate this book much higher but I cannot. It's actually a very good book and is worthwhile material for a good analysis of the book of James. The problem is that it is not focused on the topic for which it is marketed - dealing with issues of a divided heart and how to address having a foot in the world and an eye on spiritual things.

title: Boards for the Sake of Boards
text:
"Boards" is currently a trending thing in cooking and it seems everyone is slapping stuff on a board and wrongly calling it "charcuterie", and often writing a book about it or posting online about it. To her credit, the author does not call her collection charcuterie, but it seems like using a board for serving was more of a marketing point than a technique. That said, this is not a bad book at all and if you look past the board it's a good collection of entertainment recipes.

Many of the recipes in this book are well-suited for serving on a board - dips and crackers, breads, small bites of things and more. That's great stuff. However, a good portion of the recipes are not well suited for this kind of entertainment - noodles, puddings and salads jump out at me immediately. All have one thing in common, though: these are all good recipes for entertaining a group, some small and some large.

The book is not packed with color photos but there are quire a few. It would be nice if there were more.

I have mixed feelings about this book. On one hand, this is a good one to have around if you are looking for a collection of recipes for entertaining. On the other, though, it is not a collection of board-specific recipes as one might think. It has a feel of trying to capitalize on a trend in food right now, though it is not a perfect fit.

title: Nice Reference Bible; Not Exactly Suitable for Journaling
text:
I like the English Standard Version (ESV) and it is my translation of choice (and has been for many years). Journaling in a Bible is something that I am not in the habit of doing but I see the value in it, so this seemed like a reasonable choice for me. It's a good idea but there is some room for improvement.

I'll start with the positives. I like the leatherette cover, which is a reddish color with an embossed pattern that makes this volume stand out and also has a nice, tactile feel to it. I prefer this type of cover to paperback and hard cover, especially since it seems to last longer than most. The inner pages are single column with a wide, ruled area for writing and journaling.

There are a couple of negatives that could be improved upon to make this volume better. The font size is small - 7.5pt - and that's uncomfortable for people with bad eyesight. It doesn't bother me, but it won't work well for those who need a larger font size to read comfortably. And, the ruled lines, which are supposed to be for journaling, do not leave enough room for actually journaling but are better used for a few sparse notes.

Overall, making this Bible larger would solve the two issues - more room to write and easier font to read.

I do like this Bible and I can see some use for it, but probably not as it was intended. It's fine for taking notes and I think it's fine for a reference Bible when traveling, but I would consider something larger if you truly want a journaling Bible.

title: Not Ideal
text:
America’s Test Kitchen (ATK) cookbooks have a very consistent format that I like with well-tested recipes that produce predictable results. I like their books and have several of them, and so far very few have been less than ideal. This is not one of my favorites, though it is a decent collection of recipes when used as a normal cookbook instead of a weekly meal planner.

Every other ATK cookbook I have used until this one has included a “Why this Recipe Works” section with every recipe. This is interesting and useful information that explains the goals the chefs were trying to accomplish, what worked and what didn’t, and sometimes even suggestions on substitutions. In this particular book, though, these are absent, and instead each meal plan gets a “Why This Meal Plan Works” section. This section serves more as an introduction than as a helpful guide.

This book lays out roughly 6 months of weekly meal plans, complete with grocery list and mains for each weeknight. Every week has one “Pantry Meal” listed which is basically a hodge-podge of recipes assembled in a chapter later in the book. Each meal plan suggests one, but neglects to offer a page number though that’s not difficult to find using the index.

In practice, I don’t find this book all that helpful or useful as a meal planner. There’s not too much negotiating room for substitutions unless you want to rely on the pantry recipes, and there is a significant number of recipes in this book I likely would never prepare (for example, anything with eggplant will never hit my table). Every recipe serves four; for a family of four, that means no leftovers so lunches get packed separately from the meal plan. Since the meal plans cover five days, not seven, I see a problem with the meal plans with no leftovers.

Oh, and there are no desserts.

All is not lost on this book, though. There are quite a few good recipes I have either tried or earmarked for trying later, and as always the recipes seem to be well-tested and come with full-color photos.

As a normal cookbook this one has some nice ideas and good recipes that work out well. As a meal planner, this one doesn’t quite work for me.

title: Mainly an Italian Cookbook
text:
Mediterranean cuisine encompasses a number of different nationalities and styles. This includes Italian, Spanish, Greek, northern African cuisines like Moroccan, and a few others. I looked to this book as a good overview for Mediterranean. This book does have coverage for a number of different cuisines that would be considered Mediterranean, but it focuses heavily on Italian dishes, While that’s not necessarily a bad thing, it does mean that this book misses its intended mark.

The book is divided into seven chapters: “Where to Begin”, Three-Ingredient Snacks and Cocktails”, “Salads and Soups”, “Beans, Grains and Bready Things”, “Colorful Pastas”, “Gathering Dishes” and finally “Desserts”. For the most part the recipe division is logical and makes good sense. There is obviously a little overlap between chapters which is to be expected. Now, that said, if the breakdown was by nationality instead there’s be a large chapter for Italian dishes and a scattering of others.

So, distribution aside… The recipes in this collection are good, at least the ones I have tried. These aren’t all simple and easy ones, though, and some take some fiddling or require ingredients that are less common than what you may typically have on hand (at least that’s the case in my kitchen). This should not come as a surprise, though, as such cuisine is often seafood-based or uses seasonal vegetables that aren’t always available year-round.

The book is full of nice, full-color photographs. Not every recipe has a picture with it, but most do and this really makes this book a pleasure to browse and to get ideas from. There’s a saying that you eat with your eyes first, and that is certainly true with this book.

This is not a bad cookbook. It’s actually a good cookbook, but it does not cover the Mediterranean cuisines as evenly as it could. It is mainly an Italian cookbook with a few other recipes thrown in here and there.

title: Very Interesting Approach to Bread Making, Just Not for Me
text:
I have been making breads for my family and friends for over 20 years, and this includes sourdough and other slow-rise breads. Based on just the title, I assumed this would be another book on sourdough but it quickly became obvious that this is a completely different approach to making bread.

Before this book, I had never even heard of botanical fermented starters. It’s an interesting approach to making a starter – using fruits and vegetables to make a yeast starter. This is different than using a sourdough starter which is a flour based starter and sometimes is spiked with yeast initially to get it going. The botanical approach is a fascinating and at the same time makes good sense.

The problem I have with this book is that the majority of the recipes in it are not ones that I would ever make for my family. Breads made with flower blossom yeast, fermented vegetable water and others might appeal to some, but not to me. That said, I like the science behind the process and I have enjoyed learning about an aspect of bread making that I had not previously considered.

This is certainly not a bad book and I can’t knock it for the method and writing. It is well-written and it covers ground I have not seen in any other bread book. That said, this one is just not for me. If you are very serious about bread making and like to take the road much less traveled, this is a different approach to bread making not found in other books.

title: This is No Diet Book
text:
I love my air fryer and I use it almost weekly, though admittedly the majority of its use involves reheating and crisping foods that are already made and finished. I have a couple of air fryer books and the recipes therein typically make good alternatives to more traditional fried foods. However, reduced fat does not always mean low fat and low calorie. I looked to this book with the thought of getting a better selection of lower fat/calorie foods, and to some extent that is what I got. But, to say that this is a diet and weight loss book is not accurate.

The advantages of using an air fryer are well advertised – use less oil, cook faster, crispy results, and so on. Using an air fryer *can* make preparing foods a lot better for you. A case in point is breaded onion rings – almost no oil is needed to get crunchy and juicy onions rings which is a big drop in calories and fat. Sausage patties, though, are barely better off (if at all) when done in an air fryer than when using a non-stick or cast-iron skillet.

This book is full of great recipes that work, and it definitely has some fantastic replacements for their more fat-laden counterparts done in more traditional ways. However, many recipes aren’t that much better. For example, the recipe for Baked Potato Breakfast Boats is basically a loaded baked potato skin with traditional breakfast foods like eggs, bacon and cheese. According to the recipe these have over 330 calories per serving, never mind the fact that practically every healthy diet plan out there anymore lists potatoes in particular as forbidden food (high starch and full of carbs as a result). Another questionable inclusion is Eggroll Pizza Sticks. This is another higher-calorie recipe with questionable ingredients, just air fried instead of deep fat fried.

There are a lot of good recipes in this book that actually are healthy, such as Sweet and Spicy Broccoli and other vegetable-based dishes where the air fryer has the opportunity to reveal it’s prowess in cooking healthy foods for you.

A reduced-fat diet is not a weight loss diet when sugars and carbs and starches are used in place of the fat you’d otherwise use. The problem with this book is a marketing issue – it is not a weight loss book at all. I would rate it higher if instead it billed itself as containing lower-fat alternatives to more traditional foods the recipes attempt to replace.

title: Creative Counting
text:
I have a couple of different cookbooks that are marketed as collections of recipes that require 5 or less ingredients, and the result of these recipes is often disappointing. I was hopeful that this collection would fare better. In one sense it does and the recipes I have tried have turned out reasonably well. However, there is some creative counting going on here.

I will start by saying that this is a relatively small collection of recipes, approximately 60 recipes total. If you are looking for a large collection of quick and easy recipes, this isn’t it.

One of the things that has always bothered me about the Joy of Cooking is that it is filled with recipes that are based on other recipes which in turn are based on still more. As a result you end up making things going 2-4 recipes deep to get what you want. This cookbook does some of that too, and it lists the result of one recipe as one single ingredient. More obvious is that some ingredients like salt, pepper and butter aren’t counted at all. Why not? This might be a relatively minor complaint but the collection claims 5 ingredients, not 5 main ingredients plus 2-3 more that “don’t count”.

Creative math aside, this is a reasonable collection broken down into several chapters: quick dinners, breakfasts, soups/salads, vegan/vegetarian main dishes, poultry/seafood, beef/pork, snacks/side dishes, desserts, and finally spice blends. I have not tried too many of these but those I have tried have turned out well and I have earmarked a few others. Each recipe is clearly labeled with special attributes of the recipe – vegan, freezer-friendly, gluten-free, etc., which is helpful for those looking for special preparation styles or have dietary restrictions.

This is not a bad collection but the creative counting methods are deceptive. In many cases, “five” means 8-10. This is a marketing issue, and the cookbook would have been better marketed as a collection of simply and easy-to-prepare recipes instead.

title: Just not My Thing, I Guess
text:
I selected this title because I like ATK cookbooks and I was interested in learning more about the current “bowl trend” in meal preparation. This is an interesting book with some good information in it but it is likely not one I will use much. It seems like many of the recipes have been adapted to be served in a bowl instead of on a regular plate.

So, what kinds of meals do you serve in a bowl as an all-in-one-dish meal? Usually what comes to mind is cereal, soup, salad, and sometimes dessert. This book covers all but the desserts in some detail. But it is more than just that relatively narrow view. It details making dishes that have meats, vegetables, sauces, and grains, all together in a bowl but often separate (not stirred together). I am not sure I see how this is much different than a plate.

To this book’s credit, it does go into some detail on how to build up combinations of flavors without specific recipes. That’s a more useful approach, but even so it is often not necessary to cram all of this stuff in a bowl, specifically.

Some things are perfect for bowls – like soups and cereals. This does give some coverage to those.

While certainly not a bad book, I question the true usefulness if looking at it in terms of “how is this innovative?” Others may find it to be an invaluable resource; I personally find it to be of limited use. I suspect other book on bowl dishes are similar though I have not basis against which to compare. For me, this book was most helpful in satisfying the curiosity.

title: Gets Too Abstract
text:
This book is a very similar to a writer’s resource of writing prompts, though it is designed to be the same for an artist or doodler. It is an interesting concept, though it is a little too abstract in some cases to make sense.

The book is basically empty. On each page is a large drawing area with a prompt for what to draw. This is not a bad thing, though at first it may seem a little disconcerting.

Where I think this book fails is in the abstractness of some of the prompts. Some are great and make perfect sense – draw some physical object, a place, or even people. However, some of the prompts direct the artist to draw emotions, thoughts and other very intangible things. Those types of things are better exercises for journalers. Some of the abstract ideas aren’t going to make sense for some, reducing the value of this book.

I like the concept of this book, but the execution leaves something to be desired. It definitely succeeds in being a creative workbook, but the abstract ideas make it difficult (at best) to follow in many cases.

title: Decent Articles, but More About People than Food or Culinary Interests
text:
I love to cook and I love making food discoveries, so I had lofty expectations for this book, a collection of articles relating to the culinary industry and trending foods. I came away with some disappointment.

One of the great annuals is “The Year’s Best Science Fiction”, a great collection of short stories and articles in the science fiction realm (I am going somewhere with this, please stay with me here). The compiler of the anthology introduces each story, the author, explains where the article appeared initially and gives a very high level synopsis or the story. It’s a good formula that works very well, even if you’re not a science fiction fan.

This compilation, however, doesn’t follow that. Instead, there is a table of contents and each article is presented without any introduction at all other than to name the author, name the original publisher and name the article, with no background information at all and no synopsis. It reads a lot more like a novel broken up into disjoint chapters, or a magazine with loosely related articles. For me, this doesn’t work so well as a collection.

Unfortunately, many of the articles focus on people in the culinary industry rather than culinary trends, gadgetry or even cuisines. That’s really of limited interest to most people who might be looking for a collection like this. Food Network magazine has a column where they highlight a chef’s or restaurateur’s home kitchen and provide a shopping list where you can get all of the furniture, appliances and gadgets in that kitchen – not useful to the average individual – and many of the articles in this collection are about as relatable. I would have liked to see more about individual restaurants or food-related establishments, dishes and cuisines.

This isn’t a bad book and the collected articles are well written. That said, it’s hard to believe that a lopsided number of good articles written relating to the culinary industry specifically deal with individual people.

title: Very Poorly Edited
text:
I recently got my first air fryer and I have been looking for good cookbooks to give me ideas of what I can do with it. I have had some limited success with it, but without a couple of good recipes to get me started I am a little limited. In looking for cookbooks I found this title, and based on the mostly positive reviews I decided to order it (I have ordered others as well). It might be a good book but it has to be one of the most poorly edited books I have ever seen (not just among cookbooks - any books). I never enjoy writing critical reviews, particularly about books because a lot of time and effort goes into writing them, but this is one of those occasion where I need to do so.

Let me cover the good parts first, before I get into my complaints.

This book has a nice collection of recipes, logically broken up into sections: Breakfast, Meat, Poultry, Seafood, Sides, Snacks/Appetizers and Desserts. While that’s a reasonable breakdown, I probably would have sectioned it a bit differently. That’s a personal preference, though - the sections make sense, and each contains a good collection of recipes.

The book starts with a discussion about air fryers and how to choose one, even offering up a selection of summary write-ups about several different brands. That’s a great start and while not meant to be exhaustive it will get you going in the right direction.

A lot of these recipes require a larger model air fryer that can handle baking trays and the like. I have not seen any collection that gives you any kind of indicator of what size fryer you need with the recipes, this book included. It would be a nice addition to include such, which would be a great time saver and would elevate the collection over the competition.

This is a self-published book, which is not a problem if you either take the time to polish your work or if you have a decent editor that takes the time to go through and make corrections. It appears that the only editing that this book received was getting fed through an automatic spell checker. There are so many typographical errors, but not misspellings - this is a case of the wrong word being used. For example, in the recipe for Pesto Sirloin Steak, the instructions say “Preheat flyer to 350 degrees F.” The recipe for Orange Pecan Crusted Lamb says “Season the lamb into the fryer...” (more subtle). Some recipes have all the ingredient names capitalized, most do not. Page 1 of the introduction starts a sentence with “The unfortunate truth us that...”. There’s even an error on the back cover - an extra blank line in the middle of a paragraph. I could go on for a while here, naming many more errors, but that’s not productive. None of these render the book useless or unreadable but they make the book seem more like an uncorrected proof than a completed book.

In light of the numerous errors I am having trouble recommending this book. It’s not bad, and it’s clear a lot of effort went into the writing, but it is so riddled with errors that it’s difficult to rate it any higher. There are better edited, more polished books on air frying available. I can only hope the Kindle version is better than the paperback.

title: For the Absolute Beginner; No Technical Detail
text:
I am an amateur photographer and I have spent a good bit of time learning to get better, see creatively and improve my skills. I have a number of very good books on the subject, and I am always looking for more. I had the opportunity to review this little book and I got the impression from the description that this book is less technical and more creative, like an idea book. I was close. This is more like a field guide. It has its uses but it is most suited for the creatively inept or the absolute beginner.

There is very little technical information in this book; instead, it is full of ideas and suggestions on things you can do with your camera, creative ideas for interesting photos, and generalities on possible issues and approaches on fixing them. For someone who knows more than nothing about photography, this is going to be really disappointing as there’s no meat. However, for someone just starting down the road of photography beyond the odd selfie and the occasional quick snap of the family cat, these suggestions will get the reader thinking about what to do. There are some good ideas in here, and some of the tips do touch on more technical aspects of photography, an example being a discussion about focal lengths and varying them.

I can’t call this a bad book at all, but it’s beneath the majority of readers. Chances are if someone is buying a book on photography to learn, this is not the one they would choose unless they’re an absolute beginner with extremely limited knowledge. That said, for the right reader, it’s a good starting point and it has some good ideas in it.

title: Not to My Tastes
text:
I selected this title thinking it would be a fun read and interesting graphic novel. I will confess I came away disappointed. Some readers will enjoy this little book but it’s not something that’s for me.

This little book is about Leroy the Bear and Popo the Dinosaur. These two remind me of two adolsescent males with shallow interests typical of the age. This will work for others in that age range, but this doesn’t quite suit me. These two are certainly not role models, and that’s not necessarily a bad thing, but I can’t find much about them to like. I consider that a personal taste, not a fault.

The artwork is slightly amateurish, and when taken in context it is probably very appropriate with the story. I have seen a lot of graphic novels with much better artwork, though I have also seen worse.

I did not find the story to be particularly interesting, probably because I am way outside the target audience. The story seemed very shallow.

Some good effort went into this little book and that is not lost on me, but it just isn’t my cup of tea. In the right target group this might be an enjoyable read, but for me it wasn’t which is unfortunate.

title: Answers "What" and "Why". The "How", Not So Much.
text:
There are plenty of devotional books on the market designed to help the Christian find encouragement, improve their walk, find answers to really tough questions or even help the non-believer come to an understanding of who Jesus is. Based on the title, this book holds some promise but it falls a little short. It’s good for explaining the “what” and the “why” but not the “how”.

The premise of this book is broken down into seven primary chapters, one for each day of the week. Another reviewer suggested that this book can be read in 7 days, one chapter per day, or it can be slowed down to 1 chapter every week. I fall into the latter group and took longer to work through the book. The seven chapters are Hope, Life, Truth, Freedom, Humility, Greatness and finally Glory.

Each chapter starts with a scripture verse with a repeated theme, “follow me,” as spoken by Jesus. The following paragraphs tell narratives, offer more scripture, tie the narrative to the Bible and offer some encouragement. This is all well and good, and everything is very, very well written and clear. What is missing, though, is the “how”. The “what” is easily explained through the scripture references. The “why” is expanded through the discussion and narratives as well. But the author offers little in terms of “how”, meaning there isn’t a lot to explain how to implement these ideas and incorporate them into your daily journey. So, you’ll know what to change, but you’re on your own for figuring out how make those changes.

This isn’t a bad book and it makes a fine academic study of the “follow me” statements made by Jesus. It’s a little soft on the practical application though. A good effort, but it needs more for the Christian looking for real change.

title: Missing an Important Point
text:
Mission trips usually have two important, simultaneous outcomes. First, those to whom the missionaries minister are blessed and they get encouragement, which sometimes leads into a lifetime of ministry. Second, and probably more reliably, the missionaries themselves go through a transformation through the act of service and ministry (well, if they go for the right reasons), resulting in more spiritual maturity for the missionaries. This book covers both to a point but is heavily lopsided towards the latter. While this is the general idea with this guide, it’s a little too unbalanced.

This is a mission leader’s guide.

The guide is broken down into five major sections which I will paraphrase as follows: 1. The call to go on a mission, 2. Preparing for the trip, 3. The experience and service of the trip, 4. Immediately after the trip ends, and 5. Continuing the journey. Each of these sections is very well written and includes excellent information, solid preparatory advice for preparing missionaries for the field service, study topics and more. From this perspective, it seems to be decent and has a lot of good ideas and material.

However, it over-emphasizes the expected changes in the missionaries to the point that it feels like this is the sole objective in places. Perhaps these changes are the intended purpose, but it crowds out the point of reaching others and bringing them into relationship with God. Sure, it’s there, but it seems very secondary and almost an afterthought. Doesn’t seem like much salt to me.

I struggle with this book. It does have some excellent study helps and is a good preparatory guide for missionary training and building, but it does so by grossly under-emphasizing the need to reach others. A mission trip where there is little attention to reaching the lost is not a mission trip, it’s a church retreat.

title: A Mixed Bag
text:
The two main tests that college-minded high school students take when preparing to go off to school are the SAT and ACT exams. Both have their uses. On the east coast it appears that the SAT is more prevalent where the ACT is more widely used as you head west. There are a number of good practice and study materials for these tests, and this one is a decent preparation for the ACT. That said, there is room for some improvement.

This book has 8 complete practice exams and covers a lot of ground. It hits the major subjects covered and it gives a student some practice at taking timed exams when following the timing requirements. From that perspective, this is a useful book and it is very good preparation material. It also brings up a lot of material that will serve as a nice review for the student.

Where this book drops the ball is in the depth and scope of questions. It does not provide a really strong representation of the actual ACT exam and is a lot easier than the real deal. That is, a student can work through this book and do well on the practice exams, but be unprepared for how deep and comprehensive the real exam will go. Don’t get me wrong, it’s good preparation, but it does not go far enough in preparing the student for the actual exam questions.

This book is a mixed bag. On one hand, it has fine coverage of the exam format and when following the time controls will give a potential exam taker a good expectation of HOW to take the ACT exam. But, the real exam is much more difficult than the practice exams in this book and if the student has relied solely on this test book to prepare the real ACT may come as a rude surprise.

title: Good Materials, Bad Format
text:
I selected this book because it looked like it might be a helpful resource in our work environment, where prototyping is not in as widespread use as it could and probably should be. Building a prototype is a good proof-of-concept first step, and sometimes knowing where to start is enough to motivate a team to building a workable solution. This book does what it is supposed to do. That said, I dislike the format and the book has a feel of being more like a webpage set to print instead of a published book.

There is a logical ordering to the material that makes sense. There are eight chapters in this book: “Defining the Case for Prototyping”, “The Prototyping Process”, “An Overview of Prototyping Tools and Techniques”, “Paper Prototyping”, “Creating Clickable Prototypes from Designs”, “Integrated Tools for Drawing and Creating Prototypes”, “Building HTML Prototypes”, and “Using Prototypes in Your Project Workflow”. These do cover the material well, but they are also fairly concise and to the point which is refreshing when compared to books that ramble on for 300+ pages and have double the words to say the same things.

The book uses examples and use cases to make its points. It uses a lot of images and pictures.

This little book goes into details about several prototyping tools and explains how to use them. If the issue is getting started with a particular tool, this is a good starting place to get you off the ground and working.

My whole issue with this book is not the material. It is the format. It has the feel of being a web page that was printed on non-photo paper then bound for distribution. Instead of feeling like a book (and a somewhat expensive one), it feels more like an internal report intended for a presentation. This format does not work for me and unfortunately I can’t get past it, especially at the asking price. I would be much more forgiving if this was an uncorrected proof – that is not what I have here.

This is not a bad book. It’s a good book on the business of building prototypes for your projects and how to go about using the various tools available to you to get there. For me, the format and layout is not good at all, but others may find it more to their liking.

title: Artwork is Ok; Storyline is Very Predictable
text:
A good graphic novel is not easy to create and there is a good number of them that are less than stellar. There are two areas where they can fall flat - the graphics and the story line. This graphic novel is among that group for the latter reason. The artwork is decent whereas the storyline is rushed, predictable and a little cliche.

This is the apparent start of a series so it ends leaving the reader wanting to know more. This is fine for this type of book, though frustrating if you do not read many graphic novels. The story does not finish at the end of the book so it is not a stand-alone novel - not at all unexpected.

I have seen novels with better artwork, but I have seen worse too. This one is not bad at all for the artwork. I would say this one is very middle-of-the-pack in terms of the quality and detail of the drawings. It’s slightly different than most manga I have seen, but this is neither good nor bad unless you are a purist.

Where this novel fails is the storyline. It is a fairly predictable vampire story and I found myself knowing what was coming as I worked through, even on very minor details. It also feels very rushed and tries to cover too much ground too quickly. It would have been much better if the author had slowed down, planned for a longer series and stretched it out a little. When I finished it, it did not leave me with a burning desire for the next book.

This is not a bad graphic novel, but it is not a particularly good one either. If you are very serious about graphic novels then this one is likely to be somewhat disappointing; if you are new to the genre, it’s not unacceptable.

title: Good Value but Misses the Mark
text:
I love card games and I have a couple of books on different games that can be played either in groups of 2 or more or as solitaire games. I also like the Dummies series of books which, to be honest, generally presents far better books than the name suggests. In this case, this volume misses the mark and is not what I had hoped. It's a decent book, if you are big into poker and gambling, but one of the included volumes doesn't even have anything to do with cards at all.

This volume is a collection of six books: one on basic card games such as rummy, three on poker, one on bridge and finally one on casino games. Just for the collection of material, this book represents a great value.

However…

Emphasis has been placed squarely on poker and gambling games with four of the six volumes dealing with these topics. That's all well and good, but there are a lot of other games that are not covered in this volume that would have made this so much better. For example, there are exactly 14 pages dedicated to solitaire games, yet there are hundreds of variations on solo games that can be played with cards. There are also dozens of multi-player card games that are simply not in this book (Gin and King's Corners come to mind as examples). To be fair, this book does cover the mainline games that commonly get played such as Rummy, Euchre and children's games like Go Fish and Old Maid.

The book on Bridge is by no means comprehensive though it will give a good, solid introduction to the game. It's a good starting point for learning and will turn you into a good casual player, but it does not cover enough to prepare you for tournament play and it does not aspire to this so it's ok.

Puzzling is the inclusion of the book on casino games. It covers dice games, roulette and more. Why is this included in a volume that is supposed to be specifically about card games?

For a book that is supposed to be an all-in-one for cards, this volume doesn't make a lot of sense. There are some omissions, there is material that does not even cover card games at all and the majority of material is poker- or gambling-related. This is not a bad book and is a great value (hence the three star rating) but it misrepresents itself and could have been a lot better.

title: Interesting Start of a Series, Marred By Flat Characters
text:
Alien Honor, the start of a new series from Vaughn Heppner, is inexplicably named. While aliens eventually make their way into the story, their actions are neither honorable nor dishonorable. It's somewhat refreshing that their motivations aren't the same as that of humanity - by all means, let's make aliens truly alien, rather than humans by another name. The greater problem is that all of the human characters, including Cyrus Gant, the protagonist, lack emotional depth. There are many good reasons for almost all of the characters to affect a stoic outlook, but the descriptions of the characters' emotional states seem somewhat removed, as though they are observing the predicaments that they are in without being a part of them. Cyrus' continued ruminations on Spartacus sound like an academic reading about Rome rather than someone who sees himself as a slave longing to rebel.

The book does a good job of setting up a future history that reaches back before the start of the story, and I especially like that the mechanism of superlight speed requires a rare human with psychic powers, in conjunction with advanced artificial intelligence. This effectively removes probes and superlight communications from the story, as any message or probe requires a human to act as a courier. And while Cyrus does have the psychic powers needed to power interstellar travel, he is the weakest psychic of the Earth ship, rather than the most powerful.

Alien Honor ends abruptly, with the promise of a sequel to continue Cyrus' plot and bring in another plot that's touched upon in the prologue and a couple of short interludes. That book will either make or break the series, and until then, Alien Honor comes off as incomplete.

title: History Advances; Temeraire's Story Remains Stagnant
text:
The latest Temeraire story by Naomi Novik continues the Napoleonic Wars from where she left off in Crucible of Gold. Captain Will Lawrence and his dragon Temeraire return to Asia from their adventures in the Incan Empire, and we get a chance to see how humans and dragons interact in two more cultures (Japanese and Russian).

Unfortunately, much of the first half of the book is Lawrence repeating the same character development that we already saw in His Majesty's Dragon. It also brings into relief the tension that Novik has had between paralleling the Napoleonic Wars, but with dragons, and maintaining an original story. Both Lawrence and Temeraire (especially Lawrence) have been reacting to events rather than driving the story since Empire of Ivory, and it feels like Blood of Tyrants sets up for the conclusion of Napoleon's story rather than Lawrence and Temeraire's.

While much stronger than Victory of Eagles, Tongues of Serpents, or Crucible of Gold, Blood of Tyrants still hasn't recaptured the strength of the first three books of the series.

Minor spoilers below:
The book opens with Lawrence suffering from trauma-induced amnesia as he washes up on Japanese shores, and much of the first third of the book is devoted to his travels across Japan as Temeraire and the rest of the British dragons and people try to reunite with him.

The book hits its stride in the second act when the group returns to China and Lawrence and Temeraire are forced to prove their worth to the Emperor in exchange for support against Napoleon's Grand Army. When Lawrence is shoved into a position of greater authority, he has to rise to the challenge rather than dithering.

The final third of the book reveals how Russians treat their dragons (unsurprisingly, much more poorly than the Chinese or Japanese) and sets up for the final battle in the next book. I am somewhat curious to see how the remaining story becomes a full-length novel, given that this book ends with the start of the Russian winter.

title: Garden of Stones: Good Try, Fails to Live Up to Potential
text:
The Garden of Stones gets off to a fast start, dumping the reader into the middle of a centuries-long dynastic battle in an original fantasy world. One family struggles to find a cure for their patriarch's illness, as well as gain the power that dubious prophets have promised them. The patriarch's daughter is torn between her family and her sworn duty to protect the current ruler... and her attraction to a handsome man with ties to one of her father's enemies.

While that story could be compelling, it takes too much effort to try to piece it out from the actual novel. Too much time is spent building up the world, with a lot of extraneous details that don't serve any purpose other than to emphasize how alien that world is. For example, almost all of the characters are non-human, and have fangs and strangely colored eyes. Beyond that, though, they're basically humans. Barnes also has a penchant for splashing in random diacritical marks on his proper nouns. The novel did inspire me to find out what a macron is, so that's something new.

Many epic fantasy novels use a relatively young or inexperienced viewpoint character to introduce the reader to the setting (think Bilbo in the Hobbit, or Vin in Mistborn). In the Garden of Stones, we're introduced to the setting by Indris. Indris is the main protagonist (the aforementioned handsome man). Indris is also followed the most of the three viewpoint characters, which is a shame because he is also the most boring of the three. Most of his faults are of the form "he loves too much" and "he's too loyal to people", with the big exception being "gets tired of being asked to save everyone all the time, but then does it anyway". He has so many magical powers that even the author doesn't seem to remember them all, as well as partial amnesia so that even Indris doesn't remember everything that he can do. He's essentially the most complex character from a world-building perspective, and the simplest one from a story perspective - the exact opposite of how it should work.

Other reviewers have already commented on the sheer number of characters, and while the appendix's Cast of Characters is some help there, the Garden of Stones would have been better served with a tighter story that didn't need all those people. A promising start turns out to be biting off more than the author can chew.

title: Interesting but Limited Introduction to Edible Wild Plants
text:
I selected this book because I learned an appreciation for the outdoors from my father who did not miss a chance to point out different types of trees and leaves to me. While I can easily identify things like poison ivy and I can differentiate between red oak leaves and white oak leaves, I never really knew much about what was really edible and what to avoid. My hope was that this book would be useful to that end, and it is - to a point.

The book is a little more than just a book on wild plants you can eat. It goes into some detail on plants you must absolutely avoid, such as poison ivy/oak/sumac and the different species of hemlock. This section is an important addition to this book as it shows in full color what to expressly avoid.

There's a good collection of plant species in this book and each one identified has a beautiful, full-color photograph. When there is some confusion that could be made between species, it is highlighted. Some of these come with preparation instructions so that more can be done beyond just digging up the plant and eating the leaves/root/whatever.

There are two shortcomings of this book. First, this is a book that appears to be more regional (Eastern US) than national. Second, even for the focus area this is not a comprehensive collection. Now, with that said, it does cover the major species that can be found in that region, which makes sense based on the title - "Quick Guide to Wild Edible Plants", but this does not make up for the fact that a good portion of the country does not get similar coverage.

This is not a bad reference book. What is there is good material and it will definitely come in handy for the hiker or camper looking to forage. Unfortunately, this book really is not very complete.

title: Beautiful Bible, But...
text:
I like Bibles and I am always looking for new Bibles to enhance study time. I was unsure of what to make of this particular Bible - based on the description alone it did not sound like a study Bible though the idea of including the prayers of past presidents is an intriguing concept. I don't think the execution quite works, though.

Indeed, this is not a study Bible at all. It is a straight reader's copy of the NIV translation, which is good in itself if you are a fan of the NIV. It is beautifully bound with buttery soft leather, which is in my opinion superior to hard-cover bindings. It lays flat too which is very nice when reading. The whole Bible is about an inch thick, though, and inside the reader will find very small print. This may not work out so well for readers with poor vision, though the smaller print does not bother me personally.

This particular Bible has redline, a feature that some Bibles have and some do not. I happen to appreciate redline so I regard this as a plus.

The distinguishing feature of this Bible is, as advertised, the inclusion of the prayers of past presidents. These are all very inspiring, and it's fascinating to read how our previous leaders believed based on their prayers. That said, the way these have been included makes little sense. They appear as special pages, of a different paper type, jammed into the other pages but with little or no relation to the surrounding text. For example, the entry for James Polk refers to Psalm 111, yet it appears in the middle of Isaiah. Worse, there is no index to these special inserts so if the reader is looking for a particular insert then it's a matter of either hunting for it or memorizing where it is once found. This gives the feeling of a project that was not really well thought out.

I question why these prayers are inserted in a Bible at all, to be honest. I think this idea would work better if they were in a separate booklet. If they are included in the Bible regardless, they should probably be grouped together, and in present form should at a minimum be indexed.

Based on the binding alone this is a nice Bible that would make a nice gift. I cannot say the concept of including presidential prayers, especially as executed, works very well. This particular Bible probably needs a rethink.

title: Well organized but poorly proofed
text:
Modern Chess Openings has been one of the major players when it comes to books that deal specifically with chess opening theory. In the age of database-oriented training and the availability of online resources that are available for little or no cost it is important to make sure that printed editions of books like this are as close to flawless as possible. This book is far from flawless though it has its merits.

In my opinion, the very best attribute of this book is the organization. The openings are divided into king-pawn openings, queen-pawn openings, Indian openings and other logical groupings, and each of those sections is further divided by the name of the openings and the many, many variations and sub-variations. Each opening gets a page or two of descriptive explanation, and each variation is further documented with references to past games with frequent evaluations. This format works well for me. I have little issue finding what I need quickly and working through variations as I try to learn.

There are two issues with this book that counter the layout. First, the explanation of each opening could be better. That is, there is an explanation for the overall opening but then the variations are presented just as lists of moves. Some of the variations could use a little more explanation, particularly when the variations have been named. The variations exist for a reason and it would be helpful to know why.

The more grievous issue is that the book is not edited very well. As many other reviewers here have noted, there are typos that seriously take away from an otherwise good book and as a result there are some questions that arise - are the variations accurate? How well checked was each variation? In one particular case I found an error that made one variation literally impossible, and I suspect that the issue was that a move or two was omitted. As a result I have to cross-check with other sources. A book like this is not very helpful when questions of its trustworthiness arise.

For chess opening study I am a little hesitant to recommend MCO. The flaws - in particular the typos that make it inaccurate - raise questions about its trustworthiness. There is some value in this book, but it falls short of where it should be.

title: A Good Book on Bread, but Flawed
text:
I have looked at this title many times and talked myself out of buying it repeatedly until I finally caved in and treated myself to a copy. It's a respected title in the field of bread baking and I was eager to try out several of the recipes therein and to compare results with breads made from different authors' methods and formulas. While the results are usually outstanding, this particular cookbook suffers from some editing issues that make it feasible for experienced bakers but not so good for beginners.

I have made several of the loaves described in this book and each time the final product was well worth the effort. My favorite thus far has been the Oatmeal Potato Bread which is a good daily loaf and is suitable for gifting. Although the author does not subscribe to the mindset of slow-rise bread baking the resulting loaves are usually full of flavor and have good crumb.

There is a problem, though. Each recipe I have tried has been flawed in one way or another. For example, the very first recipe in the book (White Mountain Bread) requires quite a bit more flour than specified - more than can be explained away by changing measuring method - and bakes up better in 8"x4" bread pans than the specified 9"x5" plans. This is minor but will result in disappointment for the baker just starting to work with breads. A more glaring error occurs in the Oatmeal Potato Bread recipe, which calls for chopping and boiling a potato and THEN peeling it to remove the skin. It also calls for 9"x5" pans when 8"x4" pans result in a more attractive loaf after baking.

I have been baking breads for my family for close to 15 years and I have learned a lot about the process. I know how to adjust on the fly and I know how to deal with imperfect recipes and instructions. Someone just learning how to make bread for themselves, however, could run into some difficulties that may prove to be very discouraging. If I had started with this book, I likely would have decided that I lacked 'the touch' and would have given up (or just used a bread machine).

The Bread Bible isn't a bad cookbook. It's actually a good book with some really good bread recipes. Unfortunately it needs to be edited better before it can be a truly awesome book on bread.

title: Heavy on Opinion, Light on References
text:
I am writing this review with a different emphasis than most people who might choose to read this book. I am going to shy away from the political aspects and I am going to leave my opinion of both the author and the President out of it. Instead I am going to talk about the writing and the research. In a nutshell, this is a well-written book but it does not (outwardly) rely very heavily on references.

I have read books by pundits in the past, and in almost every case the writer cites a litany of resources used in the assembly of the material. Use of references when writing a book like this is essential; every point (especially when controversial) needs to have some source from which the writer can draw conclusions. Some pundits have lists of references so long that they take up as many pages as any given chapter.

This book lacks that kind of reference list. My first observation when working through is that there was no source quoted in the introduction, which in itself is not necessarily a problem but it drew my attention to the bibliography. Combing through the bibliography I discovered that some chapters in the book have no references quoted at all, and those chapters that do have sources listed have precious few.

Even if the points made in the book are all easily verifiable by doing a little independent research, that defeats the purpose of this kind of work. Most readers will not take the time to do additional research to verify anything, and the transition between reporting and opinion becomes blurred and indistinct. Opinion then becomes quoted as fact.

The writing itself is good. The author is good at making his point, he writes very clearly and he uses excellent grammar in most places.

I confess that I did not finish this book. I could not get past the fact that there were just not enough sources referenced when writing this book. To me, a book written by a pundit should drip with research and should showcase the references used, and this book just doesn't take the reader there. Instead, it leaves too much leeway for opinion without verification.

title: Disjoint and Confusing
text:
I am writing this review for the audio version of Palimpsest, so there are two elements to this novel for which I must comment. While the audio aspects are excellent and it is well-narrated, the actual story itself is very disjoint and difficult (at best) to follow.

Palimpsest is a magical place where people are transported and branded after a night of sex with others who have already visited. Every visitor receives a map of the city somewhere on their body, and there is no choice as to where it goes (one visitor gets her mark on her face). Traveling back once a visitor leaves requires another round of sex.

To be very honest, the concept itself is very interesting but the actual execution is unpleasant and hard to follow. The transitions back and forth are frequent and jarring, making following what's happening a struggle in its own right. Many reviewers have described this as an adult version of Alice in Wonderland and I partially agree - it is a hybrid mix of Alice in Wonderland, the X Files and a cheap romance novel with the romance removed and the sex left behind. I am not a fan of sex fiction (even very brief and lightweight depiction) so to have it frequently presented is a turn-off for me.

On the plus side, the narration is superb. The novel is narrated by Aasne Vigessa who does a fabulous job with employing accents and voice inflection at the right places. She reads clearly, at the right speed and with enough voice variation that she would have kept me interested in almost any other novel.

Unfortunately I did not like Palimpsest and cannot rate is too favorably. The narration of the novel is above average and drives up my opinion of the actual audio product but is insufficient to compensate for the story itself.

title: Good Idea, Bad Implementation
text:
I am a fan of good Bibles and I am always looking for better ways to reach people that need help. I had hoped this Bible might be a good tool for ministering to those who are struggling with difficult issues. While the highlighting of specific Scripture verses is a good idea toward that goal, this Bible falls short.

There is no introduction that explains why this particular Bible is available save for what's on the dust jacket. If the dust jacket is gone, one might not realize why there are some verses highlighted and what might set this Bible apart. Most people do not read the introduction included in Bibles, but one here is really needed.

There is a small index near the end of the pages that lists certain aspects of God's character and where to find verses that describe Him. This is helpful but something more complete and more accessible would be an improvement.

My biggest complaint with this Bible is that is it billed as a Bible designed to help hurting people find hope, yet the extent of that help is in highlighting verses here and there. There really needs to be more than that - short studies on God's character, His love, His mercy, etc. would add so much more to that end goal.

All is not lost on this Bible, though. The NIV is a popular translation and is quite readable, and Zondervan has chosen a very easy-to-read typeface that makes this particular Bible a little easier on the eyes. This is not to say it's a large print, of course, but it is a little larger than average and makes for a nice "reading Bible".

The Find:Hope Bible is a good idea with the feel of being poorly thought out. There are better resources that accomplish the same intended goal.

title: An Idea Book, Not a How-To
text:
I selected this title with the expectation of getting an introduction on game design. The title and description suggest that this is a book about designing games (strategy, behind the scenes architecture, etc.) and not a tome full of code and snippets. As it turns out, it is neither.

The book goes into various descriptions of what types of gameplay are out there in popular games, digging in right off the bat with Windows Solitaire and moving on to other games such as Fallout 3, Tetris and other hits. The author lays out not so much game design but playability concepts such as 1st-person shooting, drag-and-drop (such as card games), and other gaming ideas that have captivated audiences. This is true all the way through the book, and I found no instance where the author explains (even in general terms) HOW to implement these concepts.

From a designer's perspective this book will help to identify what kind of game will reach your target audience and will guide the decision process at a very high level. It is a far cry from a book about game design in the sense that it will not provide any guidance on how to get past the concept stage.

I give this book 3 stars based on the fact that it is well written and it does contain some interesting ideas on what kinds of games are out there and what general concepts in usability and playability exist. I cannot recommend this book as a reference for technical game development or design, however, because it really isn't that kind of book .

title: Didn't grab me
text:
I have tried several times to really immerse myself in this book. I love medieval-style literature and it was my hope that this would take me on an excellent journey down a new path. I came away disappointed.

The writing is good and the story has some interesting elements to it, but it never really hooked me. I did not care for the main character, and as a result this book took quite a bit longer to wade through than it otherwise could have. The main character could have been much deeper and richer (in character) but I found her to be rather predictable and, sadly, on the more shallow side.

This book offers an interesting alternative to the typical King Arthur literature that is out there, painting a new what-if scenario. For those that love this kind of story, it's a keeper. For me, though, I didn't care for it and will likely not revisit it.

title: Sticky sweet readalong without a book
text:
This audio CD recites the two children's rhymes "On the Night You Were Born" and "It's Time to Sleep My Love". Tracks 1 and 2 are the former, and tracks 3, 4, and 5 are the latter. Though the stories themselves are sweet, the execution of this CD leaves much to be desired.

The first track is a recitation of On the Night You Were Born, and it is read in an insipid, sticky-sweet manner that will grate on the nerves of anyone over the age of 2. Because if this track I almost didn't listen to the rest of the CD.

Track 3 recites It's Time to Sleep My Love and the reader's tone is similar, but not quite as grating.

The real failing of this CD is in tracks 2 and 5, which are meant to go with books. There are no books with this CD yet the listener is instructed to turn the pages at various points. I am guessing the intention is to have the books as separate purchases and then have the CD to read along.

The one saving grace for this CD is the background music and track 4. Track 4 is It's Time to Sleep My Love set to music and it's well done. It would work well as a lullaby for a young child or for someone who is preparing for parenthood.

Overall, this CD is a disappointment. The stories themselves are very nice, but the reading is grating and the lack of the books to go along with this read-along make it a frustrating product.

title: A beautiful beginning that gets lost
text:
I Came All This Way to Meet You, this memoir started like my favorite book of the year. The author is a gifted writer and writes with power, honesty, and passion. She crafts a sentence like a Ginsu knife until she lets emotional pain drag her gift too deep. The gifted writer within goes missing.

The first ten chapters were a 10 star act. Then her story became one that no longer intrigued me. It bogged down with her uncertainty about life. She labored over a physical abuse that traumatized the rest of the book and her life.

She began disclosing her fascination with death, ghosts, and drugs, including cocaine, alcohol, and poor relationships. I felt like I was put into a world of absolute insanity. I wanted to reach out and move the bad away and recover Jami's greatness, but Jami never seemed to recover.

The assault was not rape, but a terrible choice to hold her down where she couldn't move? I didn't understand the reason the young man assaulted her, but later in the book, we learn he too is mentally plagued by something he can't control. That assault became the pivotal moment in her life and stunted her existence and progress.

I wanted to find Jami a great therapist. Maybe send her to Dr. Phil or Iyanla. The tragedy is she began life without much motherly input but was clearly loved. I felt like she tried too hard to find herself, and sadly I think she is still running, looking for answers that are deep within.

She writes like a sad friend afraid to experience life, and the book never recovered its greatness. It fizzled fast, and I wish someone would have taken her hand and got her some mental help instead of letting her bleed her life out on the manuscript.

I think a memoir has the right to have the hard parts of life displayed if it helps the writer, reader and serves a greater purpose. That was not what happened here and truly Jami is a intelligent and gifted person who got lost in her own difficult story.

I hope she keeps writing and finds her way. It is a difficult book to rate and even harder to finish. Please note that there is a scene about her suicide attempt and it could be triggering. Because of the fascination with death, ghosts, drugs and the suicide, I'm not sure who to recommend this book too.

title: Disappointing
text:
From These Roots was Somewhat Informational but mostly name dropping, family and friend mentions, and surface talking. I wanted to hear her life-touching moments. Instead, I heard backstage issues, a few bad choices, disappointing career points, a few historical references, but nothing of genuine substance—disappointed 7 hours of kitchen table talk.

Every place where this biography could have popped and drawn the reader in missed its mark. She skims over the death of Kennedy, King, Sam Cooke, and other notable people with little reference to how it touched her spirit. Even when her mother dies in the middle of her book, it was covered with little emotion. Areas where landmarks like her father's church were destroyed received little mention. It feels like I wasted 7 hours listening to a tabloid.

title: Brilliant and witty until chapter 8
text: The book until about hour 5 was brilliant and humorous. Even with fast-forwarding past offensive and bad language in chapter 8, 5-10 minutes or so, he begins the next chapter with excessive reference to the N-word. I refuse to listen to any more of this book. The fact that the author thinks constantly cursing & saying N-this and N-that in a book is necessary or beneficial is appalling. Whoever published the book should have considered how the general public would receive these two issues. I am offended and disappointed that this disgusting behavior is hidden under the guise of ”teaching grammar.”

title: Story line has too many gaps
text:
I always pre-read the books I order for my 5yr old granddaughter. This story is poorly written which is surprising since this is a Disney Press book. There are too many gaps in the storyline from page to page, making it difficult to follow. Very disappointing. I was distracted, mentally filling in the gaps as the pages jumped from once scene to another. No way a youngster could follow this story without a lot of explanations along the way. 2 Stars for the story.

5 Stars for the seller. I purchased this hardcover book, used & the condition is exactly as described. Also, they shipped it right away & it arrived earlier than expected. I would definitely buy used books from this seller, again.

title: Sugar in most recipes
text:
This book if loaded with great info regarding the genuine Mediterranean Diet. Great prep tips, specifically about how to create wonderful sauces while veggies are cooking.
The reason I am giving only 3 stars is:
1. Almost every recipe calls for added sugar
2. Grams of Sugar per serving are not listed in the nutritional info of any recipe.
Since the author is specifically adding sugar to her recipes she should include Added Sugar in the nutritional info

I realize we have the option to not include the sugar when preparing the recipes, but it just strikes me as an intentional decision not to be forthright by adding sugar to the nutritional info

title: Arrived used & dirty

My frustration was opening the box & finding a book covered in dried spilt milk, inside & out. I had to use Lysol Wipes to clean every page, the spiral binding & front/back covers. I was shocked that this was returned by another customer in this nasty condition, then shipped out to me. Shame on you, Amazon.

title: Cute books - poor case design
text: These 12 mini board books are really cute. Perfect size for 6 mo old. They each contain the first couple of stanza’s of the nursery rhyme. Not the complete rhyme. The design of the case makes it very difficult to remove a book. As an adult, I struggle to pull 1 out. There is no way a young child could remove a book from this case. I am going to have to cut out the center cardboard piece from the case. The case does have a nice magnetic close and an articulating plastic handle. Cute books. Incomplete rhymes. Case design needs work.

title: Three Stars

title: this is a nice beach-read book
text: To me, this is a nice beach-read book. Easy to read.  It keeps your interest with no real surprises. Set in New Jersey, the author's style of writing leans towards a heavy use of stereo-typic language and descriptors which is not something that draws me to an author.  Liked the the book well enough but will not be purchasing more books by this author.

text: A good compilation of Dr Fung's online information regarding obesity, diabetes, insulin resistance and the physiological effects of fasting. Not much of a 'guide' to implementing the fasting protocols. Expected a detailed guide/roadmap for each of the fasting protocols, relative to various health issues and goals.
