title: Didn't Enjoy This One As Much
text: This is one of Higgins's earlier novels, I think. I've read two other later ones, and I really enjoyed the stories, characters, and humor. Fools Rush In was an OK story. Not as funny as some of her others. The leading lady was a bit pathetic in her quest to be noticed by the man she's wanted since high school, the one she has come to believe is her Mr. Right. Higgins's leading ladies always seem to have the same quality that makes you want to slap them silly as they hunger to find the right guy who they believe will complete them. They come across as needy and sometimes pathetic, but it is the quirky characters and the laugh out loud humor in her books that keeps me wanting to read [and finish reading] them.

title: Three Stars
text: no pictures

title: Not a hit for me
text:
The heroine, Honor, just got too much on my nerves. Wasting her young adult life pining away and being the "friend with benefits" for some self-centered jerk, not the type of character I like to read about. I loved the humor in the story, but I cannot stand a heroine who throws herself at a man who is no where near worthy of her. It colors my impression of the entire book.

I like much of Higgins' work, but The Perfect Match falls flat for me.

title: The next step in the Shannara series
text:
I've been a fan of the world of Shannara for over 30 years now. I was really looking forward to learning more about the other Elfstones, & what happened to them. I also always wanted to know the history behind the Ellcrys, how & why it was created. The Dark Legacy of Shannara did all that for me, and I'm happy about it.

What I'm not happy about is the paths where some of the plot went. We already did "Elf girl makes grand sacrifice" with Amberle. It was nice to know why they do that, and why the Elessedils are chosen. However, a change-up would be interesting. I think it would have been fitting & interesting to have Edinja be the next Ellcrys. I feel that the descendants of Aleia Omarosian have paid, and paid, and paid. It's time for someone else to give back for the damage they have caused.

I'm also a little done over with the druids being destroyed again. It's time for something else. Also with love interests being tragically snuffed out. Some of it was just too much rehash of earlier books, just with different characters. However, I will always give any future Shannara book a try so I'm definitely interested in what else Brooks has in mind. I just hope we'll get some treats in storyline.

title: Frustrating inaccuracies but still an enjoyable read
text: After greatly enjoying "Figures in Silk" I was looking forward to "The Queen's Lover." I did like the novel, but like other reviewers have mentioned, there were quite a few situations in the story that jarred me from the read because they didn't seem plausible. Royal children dressing as servants for an adventure may be OK for a fairy tale, but not for a historical novel that is supposed to be based on fact. So that did bother me. I did find Catherine's struggles to raise her son while being controlled by the English lords, & being consistently treated like a "fish out of water" to be really interesting. However, I was frustrated that there seemed to be so little devoted to her romance with Owen Tudor. Once it got interesting, the book was over. I would have liked to see more.

title: An enjoyable but problematic read
text: I do like a good historical fiction, especially if it's set around the Civil War. I did enjoy Hick's "A Widow of the South" so I thought I'd like this book as well. I did, but not as much as I'd hoped. Because the book started off with the deaths of Hood & his daughter, it was difficult for a few chapters to get into the story. Eventually it picked up and I did become more interested, but I would have really preferred a different beginning. Some of the story seemed stilted and didn't make sense. Such as similar to what another review mentioned, how is Hood able to dance with his extensive amputation? That kind of inconsistency tends to jar the reader away from the story. But overall it was an interesting story.

title: I liked it, but the end left me wanting
text:
Warning spoilers ahead!

Sarah's story drew me in and kept me interested, but fell flat in the ending. I was sad for her when her relationship with Jack fell apart, and rooted for her during her courtship & marriage to John Daunt. But when Jack returned, asking her to go with him to tell her niece's family the whole story of what happened to the niece, I was disappointed. Sarah's not to blame for her father & step-mother's behavior, and after the way Jack left her so hatefully he had no right asking her for a glass of water, much less asking her to take a long trip. It annoyed me. I would have rather Sarah tell Jack no, wish him well, shut the door in his face and go back to her husband & child. Instead, she put that at risk for something she shouldn't have been accountable for, even just as the messenger. It didn't sit right with me and affected my enjoyment of the book.

title: Too much fluff, not enough substance
text: I really like a good Tudor historical fiction, so I was looking forward to reading from the perspective of Madge Shelton. But honestly, this one read like one of those old "bodice ripper" Harlequin romance novels from decades ago. All mopey soap opera fluff and no substance. Basic girl meets boy, falls in love, "Big Dramatic Situation" keeps them apart, and then they are reunited in the last chapter, happy ending! Yawn. The sex scenes were fun and all, but the book left the Tudor fan in me wanting more.

title: More miss than hit for me
text: After reading "Bearers of the Black Staff" I was eagerly looking forward to reading the conclusion. I've been a fan of Brooks' worlds (both Shannara & Landover) for three decades. The end of "Measure of the Magic" left me wanting and somewhat disappointed. It seemed to me missing something that I'd previously enjoyed when visiting the Shannara world, I'm not even sure what that really is. All I know is when I finished the last chapter, I set down the book with a sigh of discontent. I've never had that happen before with one of Terry Brooks' novels, so I really do hope it's just a one-time thing.

title: Nan's story fell flat for me
text: I really enjoy historical fiction, especially the Tudor era. But I just couldn't get into this book. My biggest problem was the main character, Nan Bassett. She didn't seem so much "strong and independent," rather self absorbed and immature instead. I couldn't bring myself to like her much, which made it difficult to motivate myself to finish the book. It's a shame because I have enjoyed other books by Emerson, but Between Two Queens just didn't do a thing to capture my interest.

title: Good story but I'm tired of it being dragged out
text: I do enjoy Hobb's writing, I really do. Her worlds are richly described and her characters fascinating. That being said, I'm really tired of the current trend of pulling out a story through multiple volumes. It's not just Hobb, many other authors are doing the same thing. It may be more profitable for them, but it's increasing my annoyance and frustration. Just about the time things get interesting, oh, just wait! Check back in when the next book is out and be sure to buy it to find out what happens next. It really detracts from the enjoyment of the story.

title: Interesting, but difficult for me to finish
text: I really did want to like this book. I'm a big fan of historical fiction, but I found myself repeatedly putting the book down after a few chapters. I think perhaps the main characters were not likable enough for me, just a matter of personal preference I think.

title: Lost interest
text: My daughter has enjoyed other books by P.C. Cast so I'd hoped she'd enjoy this as well. But she never made it past the first few chapters. She told me that the storyline just didn't keep her interested enough to finish it. She doesn't have much interest in centaurs, although she did like the pagan aspects otherwise. For teens who are more into ghost or vampire paranormal stories, "Elphame's Choice" might not be for you.

title: Interesting to read, but had some difficulties with the book
text:
The subject matter was fascinating, and would make for great material in a history class. The information contained in the book is a valuable supplement to a study of early American history. But I had some issues like the other reviewers that made it difficult for me to enjoy the book.

The sidebars need to be separated more clearly from the rest of the chapters. Otherwise, it's difficult and confusing to find where the chapter picks up again. Perhaps a different colored box around the sidebars would make it easier to see what portion of the text pertains to the sidebar and what is the chapter material.

The portraits were great, detailed and added to the text. However, I too agree that maps would have made the book so much better. Yes, much of the information is dark and rather gruesome at times. But it was also quite an accurate retelling of the time period.

I did find some of the chapters to be disorganized and a bit difficult to follow. The conclusion seems rather incomplete as others have mentioned. But beyond that it was quite interesting and informative. It will make a great addition to my personal history library.

She seemed off her game for most of the book and not the badass she usually comes across as being. I hope she rebounds and comes back ready to take names and kick ass.

Seems like if you can make a power nullifying room , you could make a better prison or power nullifying exploding collar for prisoners. title: Good.
text: I really enjoyed this book. It kept me intrigued although I think the ending could have been much better. I don't want to elaborate too much and spoil the story but anyone who's read it knows what I mean. It's all about closure. I will definitely read more from this author.

title: Will it ever end?
text:
I am usually do enthralled with Gregory's book that I'm always surprised when they end. Sadly this was not one of them. I knew about Queen Jane but I didn't realize how deep QE1's resentment went with Kathryn. I was frankly bored though before we even got to Mary. By that time I just wondered when the rambling ends.
This might be one of the Tudor books you can skip.

title: Abrupt ending, felt like it needed more
text: As Mercy Watson lovers familiar with all of the original and Deckawoo Drive books, my kids and I were excited to read this book. The book is beautiful. It’s large with thick, colorful pages and the illustrations are wonderful. The pictures are very large, which allowed my 3 year old to enjoy it more, but my 6 and 7 year old loved them too. The story itself was just alright. It started great. Stella is one of our favorite characters and we love that she was the main one in this story. But the first time we read this, after I read the last page of the book, I turned it, expecting to see another page, but there was none. I hate that feeling. Like you don’t feel the story is perfectly wrapped up. Or maybe you just want more and you are disappointed it’s over. Either way, the end was a bit of a let down. The majority of the book is Stella trying to get people to carol with her, and then right at the very end, they show up and carol and that’s it. The end.

title: Content seems good but I was hoping for more classic books
text: The content for the few books I own is good, but this book primarily covers children’s books published in 2015 or later. I was hoping it would have more of the popular/classic titles I own, and since it doesn’t, its use is limited.

title: Good story with okay writing style
text:
I enjoyed the story about the relationships the main character forms. What I did not love was the writing style. It's mostly written as the young boy's stream of conscious. I found the repeated run on sentences annoying, and it just seemed like rambling to me. Then you have pages of dialogue that reads like a script with the characters name, a colon, then their dialogue with nothing in between.
It just wasn't my favorite writing style, but again, the story was good.
Also Walk Two Moons was my favorite book growing up, and this book was compared to that in the description. In my opinion, Walk Two Moons deserves five stars and this one just doesn't quite compare.

title: Ok
text:
The story was alright; the writing was alright too. It did seem pretty juvenile, which I think was the point because the queen was 18, but Victoria was immature and often playing with her dog, both of which caused some boring parts. I think Goodwins writing style was decent- not a masterpiece but no odd grammar or annoying use of dialogue or over explanation. It wasn't a page turner, but it was interesting enough that I wanted to read a little each day for a couple weeks.
If you read a lot of books and are looking for another, I'd try this. If you only have time to read one great book every couple months, I'd personally find a different one.

title: Somewhat confusing with overwhleming detail

I think it hurt my brain a little; and I can only guess the next books will get even more confusing to wrap my mind around. Maybe it's just me, but I don't typically want to work so hard to understand a novel... especially not a young adult one!

title: Beauty Queen Bound in Boulder Basement
text: Mournful devastation and deep pockets are capable of buying immunity from criminal convictions, even when deviant minds deserve harshly necessary AND severe punishments. As the sheltered elite go on living their lives, unsolved murders often become cold cases. This story is not for the faint of heart. It involves murder, drug use, animal torture, and repeated molestation of a minor. There are also repeated mentions of fractured families, deep-seated resentment, vindictive pranks, property damage, perversion, pornography, pedophilia, and incest. I did come across a few typos, and the overall flow seemed a bit choppy throughout. Betsy’s character was accidentally referred to as Patsy on numerous occasions, and the final message of the book seemed to be a forewarning to parents to keep a close eye on their kids. I read the entire book in less than an hour, but I honestly found it to be more disturbing than entertaining. Potential readers should proceed with well-informed caution.

title: Very good "grandma" advice, but horrible narrator in the audiobook version.
text:
My father had recommended me this book. I admit it took me a while to get to it, but I'm glad it did. It introduced me to the nutritarian lifestyle, which is pretty much just "eat veggies, mushrooms, fruits, and grains; cut out bad meat and bread." Pretty much it in a nutshell, but it's pretty hard to change a lifestyle I've been accustomed to for over three decades. But I'm glad I did. It's been a slow process; I started this audiobook about a year ago, and I'm still trying to change everything, but my diets are slowly becoming exclusively greens and grains. Sure, I'll have some unnecessary sugars and meats here and there (especially around the holidays), but I go back to my lifestyle almost immediately.

The audiobook version starts with the author in the introduction chapter, then switches to a professional narrator for the remainder of the book (excpet for the epilogue). The narrator is *awful*. His voice was not pleasing to listen to, and I felt that some of the information wasn't processed correctly because the narrator's voice wasn't really in the book. He sounded very much like a late-night hotline announcer, and that's what you hear for the entirety of the book save for those two aforementioned chapters. I wish the author read the whole book.

title: A whole lotta nothing, but still engaging.
text:
It's been well over two decades since last I read this book, and suddenly I felt compelled to reread this series. I think I stopped about halfway through, and jumped to the final book when it was released, just to find out the ending.
So after rereading it, I kept waiting for something more substantial to happen than what was happening in the book. Before I knew it, I was at the penultimate chapter and I still didn't feel like much had really happened. But after all was said and done, I recalled everything that happened in the book. The dialogue, while a bit dated, is memorable, but the plot overall was structure fairly weakly, leading up to nothing which advanced the teenagers' mission.

title: A bit dated, but enjoyable overall.
text:
Being written in the early 2000s, Scott Pilgrim was critical in exploding the nerdy pop culture we see in many webcomics that came after. Having grown up in the 90s, I related to a lot of the references. The name of the band? Easy. The X-Men patch? Easier.
This was during a time when it was too early to be nostalgic, but many years later we find the same sort of references and nostalgia-ridden humor in lots of other comics.

Plot-wise, it's okay. There's not much going on until closer to the end. It's the life of a twenty-something (not really millennial this early on) living a mediocre life in Canada. The illustrations are bright and lively, which help fill the void of the "mundane."
Of course, the really fun stuff starts toward the end, and it wasn't until then that I really felt engaged.

title: Fine listen, but really lets you know how much Zahn loves to use the word "sardonically."
text:
I listened to Zahn's first installment in the "Thrawn trilogy" with the audiobook. I tried reading the book but just couldn't get into it. I found it a bit dry. After recently getting into audiobooks, I saw this in my recommendations and decided to give it a try a second time, but in a new format. Took me a while to finish, but I finally got through it. The narrator does a fantastic job in general, but I feel he could work on his female voices. To be fair, they don't really have strong dialogues in the book.

The novel is fine. It's a great story following the events of the first three Star Wars films. Now, I write this in 2018. I have the prequels, The Clone Wars, the Disney acquisition, The Force Awakens, etc. Going back to these books for the first time with all this knowledge wasn't as jarring as I anticipated. I just have to remember there's nothing preceding these stories save for the original films, and the character of Thrawn is enough to keep me engaged.

That said, there's a lot of dry moments in this story. The story is more so political than the first three films; it's more reminiscent of the prequels, but at the same time these are novels, so there are more time and space to fill out the plots and backgrounds. I did feel that the female characters weren't as developed either but going from the previous material that's not saying much. Still, the female characters had the weakest dialogue, I feel.

The story was fine. What really drove it was Thrawn and Luke.

title: Illustrations are fantastic, but text is confusing, especially for newbs.

While the illustrations are pleasant, the text didn't help at all. Perhaps I was the wrong crowd for the text, but I'll keep it around for picture analysis.

title: Good for Starters, Which Is, I Suppose, Its Target Audience
text:
As the title states, this is a great book for the youngsters in your life. I reviewed many sections of the book, from anatomy to dinosaurs, and I was very entertained by its brief, though informative, sections, but was left bereft by its choppy sections (i.e., the overall structure of the book, moving from subject to subject, was well done) and wondered which topics to cover. For instance, when informing about the digestive system, it had random inserts on food (it makes sense, but the captions were obscurely chosen).

It's a great starter book on various things of this world for youngsters, but I'm sure they'll be getting their hands on more information after reading it.

When it came to her Hollywood life, she is an actress, writer and more, I found I wasn't as interested. I found she did a lot of name dropping, she spent a horrible amount of money on what only rich people do, and for some reason the Hollywood elite think the regular folks can't wait to read about them. title: Not bad
text:
I do not normally read horror, ghost, spirit type books and had never read anything in the stream of consciousness style. However, this one seemed to have an interesting premise, so I picked it up. I will say that I appreciate the author giving a heads up about the style right up front. Had she not done that, this book would be getting a one star. Once I read her explanation at the beginning I was able to let go of the errors and just read the story with an open mind.

The story takes place almost entirely in an old abandoned house. The single character had grown up next to the house and was familiar with the area and some of the back story on the dwelling. He moves in to help a friend and it all gets odd from there.

I liked the device the author used to convey the story through only one point of view. However, the character has a degree in Philosophy, but has no common sense at all, making him not very compelling. However, there is mention of something in his recent past that could have caused him to have less than critical thinking skills, so again I was able to overlook this flaw. The "writing in my diary" style was interesting. My attention was kept firmly in that first person narrow viewpoint and it tied all the events together in a way that got me in the character's head.

The book could use a good proofreading and editing. If leaving the manuscript completely as is with no revisions is how "stream of consciousness" is done, then I will likely not read this type of book again. The warning at the beginning of the book helped, but some of the misspellings, completely missed words and an odd capital letter in the middle of a word were just things that could have been fixed easily with a single read through. Had those been cleaned up a bit, they would not have been as distracting as I read the story.

My final disappointment with the book was the ending. I've never liked the kind of ending that leaves you hanging without really knowing what happened and this book did not change my mind on that. There were so many tantalizing little tidbits and hints that I eagerly kept reading to find out more about them, alas I was disappointed.

text: This novel was more about Thomas Moore, a long time officer still grieving the loss of his loving wife. The book introduces Jane Rizzoli who is nothing but vindictive toward her fellow male police officers and is not at all sympathetic toward victims.  In fact, she is an incredibly unlikable character.  And, Maura Isles never makes an appearance in the book.  To suggest this is a Rizzoli and Isles novel is misleading.  I have read and enjoyed later books in the Rizzoli and Isles series and don't recall Rizzoli being such a negative individual.  Other than this, the book is predictable and reads more like a script for a tv mini series than a literary work.  Actually, the Moore character was far more interesting and would have preferred seeing both sequels and prequels about him.

title: Unique for the Genre
text: This one started out as a love story and developed into a mystery.  Amy and Nick had a story book relationship until Nick loses his job at a magazine (the result of the preference of the Internet over the written word) and then Amy loses her job (although she has a substantial trust fund to fall back on).  With an ailing mother and father, Nick decides to return from NYC to his hometown in Missouri.  The relationship begins to falter in NYC but worsens in Missouri where Amy feels not only out of her element but feels to be the victim of the widening gulf in their relationship.  The story is told in first person by Nick and via diary entries by Amy through the first part of the book.  Part Two of the book takes a turn (I have to say I kind of saw the unexpected twist coming).  The biggest issue I had with this book was that although both characters seemed to be the kind of people everyone would like, ultimately neither had the kind of personalities that would endear them to anyone.  As a result, I stopped caring as to what would happen to either of them as much as I was curious to see where the book would lead.  The only character that I actually started to care about was Margo (Nick's twin sister) who helplessly looked on while trying to support her brother as the mystery unfolded.  I have to think the author wanted to create two characters that were so real that they had the flaws that were depicted.  The ending (some say it was unexpected) was somewhat unfullfilling but it leaves open a possible sequel to see what the future might be.

title: A Long and Winding Road (did I mention long?)
text: (This is a review of the unabridged Audible version) I was a big Creedence fan back in the day. Even as a kid in high school, it was obvious to us that CCR was mostly John C Fogerty. This was never more painfully apparent than when I first put their swan song effort “Mardi Gras” on my turntable. John was the singer, the songwriter, the arranger/producer and the main musician (guitar, sax, harmonica, keys, etc.) While he admits himself that he’s not a great player, he doesn’t need to be - his skills are mostly adequate and his voice was/is one of the most identifiable in rock and roll. His songs are crafted with skill and care and are some of the best in the genre. There’s no argument that he’s one of the most successful songwriters and artists of his era, and deservedly so. That having been said, I don’t think the book stands up to his usual quality standards. It’s long - marathon long, rambling and meandering in places, and probably would have benefitted from a bit more editing. Obviously, a lot is made of the bad blood between Fogerty and his former band mates and record label. We certainly get a clear explanation of Fogerty’s position, but it leaves me wondering what the other side(s) of the story might be. Sadly, the “songwriter/musician gets screwed over by manager/lawyer/promoter/label” story is not an unusual one. Fogerty makes it very clear that he has no respect for former US president Richard Nixon but has no problem with supporting (also) former US president Bill Clinton, whose antics arguably make Nixon’s look like a Boy Scout Jamboree in comparison. We also hear about his views on gun control (pro) and hunting (also pro) but most of the rest of the book thankfully eschews politics and sticks to music. Fogerty reads the book himself, (with later chapters read by his wife Julie) and it *sounds* like they’re reading it most of the time. It’s mostly a pretty stilted performance. All in all though, if you grew up listening to CCR in the late 60’s and early 70’s, it’s probably still worth sitting through the 15+ hours to better understand the story behind the man and his music.

title: Good as a Starting Point
text:
Retirement isn’t very far away for me and as a result, I have been reading more books on the subject than ever before. One that I just completed is The Ultimate Financial Guide to Retirement Planning.

This book serves as a good overview of the things important to retirement planning. Topics like budgeting, the differences between Roth IRA and traditional IRA, 401k plans, Social Security, real estate, and more are covered with insights on what you can expect from each. There is even a section on taxes, estate planning, and taking care of your health during your golden years.

The financial advice presented in this book is rather brief and it doesn’t cover topics to the extent that it should. In some instances, it even makes statements that are a little misleading. For example, there is one point in the book where it says, if you are spending $40k per year, you will need $1 million to retire comfortably for 25 years. Yes, that would be true IF you plan on letting your money sit in a non- interest bearing checking account and spending it until it’s complete depleted. But most people know they can get at least a small, safe investment return on their funds and when you take that into account, you don’t need $1 million to cover $40k of annual spending for 5 years.

One point that this book drives home again and again is that Social Security is not intended as a means to a full, enjoyable, retirement. It is intended as a supplement- it is up to you to cover the rest through retirement accounts, pensions, and other investments. I like that the book drives this point home so many times because many people lose sight of this. And I also like that it takes time to talk about education savings for your kids, life insurance, and other important matters.

Retirement is a subject to take seriously. The Ultimate Financial Guide to Retirement Planning is hardly the ultimate guide. It doesn’t cover things to the extent that it should and it could use additional editing to make the sentences more grammatically correct. But does serve as a good starting point to better understand this new chapter of your life and what you need to do so that your retirement years are the best they can be.

title: Is Your Job Important?
text:
Does your job seem fulfilling? Or, to put it more clearly, do you feel your job has a net positive value to society as opposed to just a way to make money? If your answer is no, or if you think a larger percentage of the world’s jobs fall under the low- value umbrella, then you might like this book

What this book proposes is that far too many jobs are of this variety. The individual working the job could quit tomorrow and nothing significantly negative would happen to the company he/she works for, or society at large. Far too many people are engaged in pointless employment, or so this book suggests, which raises the important question: Why is this happening in a capitalistic society, one that is supposed to strive toward efficiency with very few exceptions? The book attempts to answer that question, and others related to it, as it rambles on for nearly 300 pages.

As I read this book, I started to think about jobs I have held and others have held that fit the definition of this type of job. I can think one job of my own, from the past, that came close, but it still wouldn’t qualify. However, I can think of positions others have held that do, indeed, fit the definition. And it does make me wonder why the folks in charge allowed such a situation to occur.

This book does raise some interesting questions and it does get you thinking about the usefulness of employment. It makes you wonder why the workweek hasn’t been shortened and remains at 40 hours, at least here in the United States. It makes you wonder about the push for job creation by politicians of most every stripe and whether or not this push has, in some way, encouraged the proliferation of so many useless job positions. And it makes you wonder why someone with a do- nothing job wouldn’t enjoy it at least for the easy money, since we are so often told that most anyone will slack if given the opportunity.

I like any book that brings up thought- provoking questions and this book accomplishes exactly that. But it is not without its flaws, chief among them the fact that the book presents an idea without any formal research. It’s an idea that, while intriguing, has no official research to back it up. Another issue I have is the books repetition. It continues to repeat similar thoughts over and over. The book could have been reduced about one hundred pages and easily gotten its message across. And then, there are the estimations that book makes about b.s. jobs and their occurrence. I find it hard to believe that roughly one- third of all jobs qualify as useless. I can agree that most any job has its moments of uselessness and that most of us could finish our necessary tasks in fewer hours at work each day. But based on my own observation, I cannot see how so many jobs fall under the b.s designation.

Our free- market economy thrives on competition and the efficiency that is supposed to result. Capitalism is still the best system around for wealth creation and opportunity, but it is not without its flaws, and the same could be said for any other economic system. There are certainly useless jobs all around the world, and this book is a good way to at least get you thinking about these jobs, why they exist, and what it means for society. I have issues with this book, but it is still an interesting enough read to recommend.

title: Why Relativism and Constructivism are Wrong
text:
Is there such a thing as objective facts? Most would say yes, but there are those who take a different view and who think what we perceive as facts and how we construct knowledge has everything to do with culture and other conditions. There is no doubt that our culture influences what we think and believe, but does it mean that plain, evident, in- your- face truth is still relevant to the individual and his/her circumstances? A book that is ready to challenge this notion is Fear of Knowledge.

Short in length, this philosophical guide presents some of the common arguments in favor of relativism and constructivism and shows why they are not true. For someone like me, who is already against these two schools of thought, this book was a classic example of preaching to the choir. However, I did like some of the refutations it offers, and it did provide me some ammunition to use whenever someone tries to spout off in favor of these constructs.

This philosophical book will make the most sense to students of philosophy and others who already have a basic understanding of relativism and constructivism. If you do not, it might be good to consult a reputable online source and gain an understanding before you start to read. In fact, the book could have been improved by explaining and defining relativism and constructivism better than it does. I did like some of the examples it suggests, to help readers put things into perspective. But given the increased use of relativism and constructivism over the past few years, I can think of many better, real- world examples it could have used. In addition to explaining these concepts better, I also felt the book would have been improved if it spent more time showing why objectivism is correct. It instead devotes most of its space to explaining why the other side is wrong.

With the writing, Fear of Knowledge is good and generally free from errors, but it isn’t a book for light, easy reading. I found myself re- reading the text more than once, just to make sure I had a full grasp of what they author was trying to convey. It can get a little rough at times, but the same can be said of many philosophical books. Just be patient as you read and you shouldn’t have any trouble picking up on what the book is trying to say.

Relativism and constructivism are all around us. These concepts do not have much to support them philosophically, but there are diehards who still think we live in a relativistic world and that no objective truth exists. Fear of Knowledge is out to change all of that. It may not succeed at converting the full- fledged relativists among us, but it does make for some good, intellectual reading for those who want to better understand this area of philosophy and who need some tools to use to strike down those who follow it.

title: One Small Action, One Massive Response
text:
America’s National Anthem, the Star-Spangled Banner, is often the subject of controversy and has been for quite some time. The fact that the anthem was written about a battle bothers some people. Still others find its additional verses- the ones most people do not even know exist- to be exceptionally offensive. But the song remains our National Anthem and people view it as an extreme representation of American patriotism. That is why so many people blew a fuse when NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick decided to take place his knee on the ground while it was played and his actions, and those he inspired, are the subject of this book, The Kaepernick Effect.

What you get with this book is a collection of quotes and experiences from different individuals, from high school through professional sports, who were inspired in some way by Colin Kaepernick and decided to follow his lead. These individuals were not always aware of the risks they were taking, but they felt the need for social and racial justice was worth it. They were usually, but not always supported by teammates and coaches, but they went ahead and refused to stand during the National Anthem regardless, often leading to harassment, bullying, and even death threats from the public.

Most everyone is aware of Colin Kaepernick’s actions on the football field and the controversy that followed. Few, however, are aware of the ripple effect that he inspired. I knew things like this were going on, but I didn’t realize the degree to which Colin Kaepernick influenced other athletes to take a stand against injustice. The experiences of these individuals are outlined in this book and some of the backlash is downright shocking. People who claim to support freedom and the American way do not see a peaceful protest like this as an extension of freedom. They don’t want anyone to step out of line and are ready to attack and fight back against these knee- takers and others like them who dare to challenge the status quo.

I like the message of this book and I like that it includes so many real- life examples from around the United States, letting the reader know on a personal level what people had to go through for standing up to a system of injustice by refusing to stand during the National Anthem. However, I felt the book should have gone further with backing itself up with history and official statistics. The message of the book would have been stronger if it included, for example, actual statistics on the instances of police brutality; the history of American race relations and the fight for justice; and even a little more background on the National Anthem and the possible reasons why people get so extremely worked up when athletes refuse to stand. But there is nothing like that in this book.

Another thing I wish was different was the book’s organization. It contains only three chapters, which focus on athletes at each level of educational play: High School, College, and Pro. This makes for some lengthy chapters. I would prefer to have the chapters further broken down, to make it easier to find stopping points as you read.

Still, no matter what approach it takes, this book is certainly deserving of a read. The decision Colin Kaepernick made to take a knee during the National Anthem was one with far- reaching effects that no one foresaw. It has led to more athletes doing the same and, hopefully, will result in changes to the system and a gradual move toward racial and social justice and equality. There is much to learn about the motives of the individuals who decided to follow Colin Kaepernick’s lead, and this book is a good way to get acquainted with these brave individuals who risked their reputations and livelihoods to stand up to oppression and fight for justice and freedom.

title: Some Memorable Moments but Lacks Suspense
text:
Few people in the world can forget the infamous Chile mine incident back in 2010. Thirty- three men were trapped in the depths of the earth and remained there for nearly ten weeks until they were each plucked from the mine, one by one, the culmination of an extensive rescue effort that took weeks to complete. Their story is told in this book, Deep Down Dark.

This book tells the story of the mine collapse from the beginning to the end, when the men were finally rescued thanks to a multi- national effort. It introduces each of the men and includes background on their personal lives, children, wives, etc. It also details what they did after the fact and how the situation has impacted them as they attempt to return to normal living. The book details the struggles the men faced, their interactions with each other, and their ultimate return to civilization.

The story of humans trapped in a mine and the fact that all survived is certain a story worth sharing. Deep Down Dark, however, doesn’t really present the story in the most compelling way. Starting with the first few chapters, I was thrown off a little by the use of present tense to tell the story. I assume this was to make the reader feel like they are right there, in the moment, but it doesn’t work for me. But probably my greatest issue with this book is its lack of suspense. We know the men survive in the end, but a story told the right way can still keep readers on the edge of their seat. I can think of several other nonfiction books like this. Deep Down Dark isn’t one of them. It isn’t the page- turner I was hoping for.

Another addition that could have helped this book is more illustrations, like a quick diagram of the mine so that readers would have a visual representation of the different levels and the various places that the miners convened, slept, etc. The book does have small photos of each of the thirty- three men, which is good, but it doesn’t have anything else. Pics of the actual mine, the surrounding areas, the family members that get lots of mention, these all would have helped make the book better and more interesting.

Still, this is not a book to dismiss outright. It still has its moments, and it does get you thinking about what it would be like if something like this happened to you. Some of the tensions felt between the men as they struggled to survive might seem a little bizarre when you read about them. But I refrain from passing judgement because, unless and until I have been through something similar, I cannot really comment. I might act equally odd or irrational. There is no way to know, and I hope I never find out.

Being trapped underground in a working mine would certainly be a scary experience. The lack of food, the total uncertainty about your own life and chances for survival, the rescue effort, the worry that the mine could collapse further at any moment- these things and other factors would be enough to put a person over the edge and it would lead to behavior one would never expect. Deep Down Dark attempts to tell the story, but it has its share of hits and misses. I’m going to give it a middle rating and partial recommendation, because it does have some value, but it does frustrate me that the story wasn’t told in a more engaging and suspenseful way.

title: Are You Prepared for Retirement?
text:
Have you prepared properly for retirement? I would like to say I have but I know better. I haven’t reached retirement age yet, but I’m not that far away and because of this, I have found myself reaching for books on the subject more than usual. My sudden interest in all things golden- years related led me to read The Baby Boomer’s Guide to Surviving Retirement.

I’m not a baby boomer, but I am a gen x-er and thus my years of retirement are drawing near. I often wonder how best to prepare for retirement and what I will do in retirement. Therefore, I like to seek out guides such as this. I like retirement guides that don’t focus solely on the financial side of things because, while money is important, there are other things that matter, too, like finding ways to spend your spare time, keeping relationships strong, etc.

With this book, the reader does get a little bit of both financial and non- financial advice. I liked the sections on how to keep your relationships strong and I liked the advice on things a retiree can do to occupy his/her time. The financial advice the book presents, however, is a little lacking. The quotes and statistics offered, from official studies, are helpful, but there needs to be much more. Perhaps some added calculations that detail savings goals and how to achieve them would help. A budget worksheet would also be a nice addition.

Another problem I had with this book is the writing. It reads like it was rushed and wasn’t edited. There aren’t typos or anything glaring like that, which is good. But there are countless instances of awkward sentences; excessive and unnecessary prepositional phrases; sentences ending in prepositions; etc. Assigning an editor to re- write and clean up these problems would have made this a better read.

Retirement is a concern. Whether you are a baby boomer who is already retired or a member of another generation and are close to retirement, it is important to think about these years; how to prepare for them and how to maximize them to the fullest. The Baby Boomer’s Guide to Surviving Retirement is a good starting point to get you thinking more about retirement and what it involves. It has a conversationalist style and while not the greatest book on the topic, it does make some important points we all need to consider.

title: Government Intervention is Not Always the Way to Go
text:
What caused the financial meltdown that started in late 2007, early 2008 and had the United States teetering on the edge of an economic depression? Many explanations have been presented and many books have been written, most of which are biased in some way, politically or otherwise. A book that attempts to cover some ground and explain different causes in a short amount of space is this, Gambling with Other People’s Money.

This book talks about the circumstances that led to the financial crisis and while it does place blame on different factors, the position it aligns most strongly with is that of government bailouts and crony capitalism. Most businesses are extremely careful in the way they invest because they know the consequences of bad financial decisions. With financial institutions, however, there is a greater tendency for carelessness and the reason is because they are perceived as too important to lose, and thus more likely to receive government aid. Other businesses have been the recipient of public rescues also, but this is more likely with financial institutions. This, and the often-cozy relationships between the leaders of such businesses and government officials, is what the book claims were the main culprits in the crisis.

As I said previously, there have been many books written and many positions taken on the financial meltdown. Some take the position that the lack of government oversight and the rollback on regulations led to the situation. Others think that there was too much regulation and a more unfettered capitalistic approach would have been best. I can remember the crisis well and I remember the different causes and solutions offered by politicians, businesspeople, political pundits, and others. This book doesn’t delve too deeply into other causes, like the accusation that banks were practicing predatory lending and that bank officers were only looking for a quick commission. These possible causes are not examined, but the book does offer the sweeping generalization that, knowing your bad decisions can and will likely be covered by government aid, bank leadership is more likely to behave recklessly.

I think everyone would agree that crony capitalism was a major contributor to the crisis. I think many would also agree with one of the book’s key points that home ownership isn’t the end- all, American dream enabler that it is often promoted to be. I certainly agree also that the high probability of receiving government bailout money would have an impact on decision making, too, and often in a negative way. My main issue with the book is that it’s a little too short and thus doesn’t examine certain aspects of the financial crisis the way it should. There are not enough pages to thoroughly cover what went wrong, so don’t be surprised if you find yourself looking for more insight online or from other books.

It has been more than a decade since the financial crisis but much of the problems, like bailouts and the close relationships between businesses and politicians, are still with us today. Whether or not we have learned anything from this past experience remains to be seen and Gambling With Other People’s Money is a good way to learn more about this difficult time in U.S. financial history and what needs to be changed to lessen the chances it will happen again. It doesn’t provide the detail I would like, but it’s a good primer on the crisis and its potential causes.

title: Espionage in an Iowa Corn Field
text:
Spying is an age- old practice but in the modern world of high tech, it has taken on a whole new meaning and direction. One of the concerns we face today is industrial espionage and just a short time ago, there was one such case involving an attempt by a Chinese spy to steal agriculture- related intellectual property. That story is summarized in the page of this book, The Scientist and the Spy.

This book starts out by introducing some of the individuals who were involved in one way or another with this attempted theft. I liked these introductory chapters because they helped to explain the people and the events. The reader is prepped in a satisfactory way for the reading that follows, at least to the extent that you understand the situation and the people involved.

Where this book loses me is in its inability to thoroughly develop its focus on any one topic. For example, the book introduces the subject of industrial spying, but it doesn’t spend much time informing the reader or developing a strong position on this topic; what it entails, the repercussions, etc. You are left with unanswered questions at every turn. Also, I found the story itself is just not that compelling. I have read many non- fiction books about similar topics that held me in their grip from start to finish. I didn’t get that feeling with this read. It isn’t the page- turner that some promised it would be.

Another thing some readers may take issue with is the book’s bias. It isn’t a straight- forward retelling of the story; the type of book that sticks with the facts, steps back, and lets the reader form his/her own opinions. This book instead takes a more sympathetic tone toward the accused.

The chapters of this book are short and are laid out in chronological fashion. Rather than use chapter titles, the book uses the time span covered as the chapter names. This is less creative than expected. The short chapters do make it easy to find a good stopping point, so they at least serve that purpose. But again, the short chapters are, in many instances, too short. Just when you think the book is going to explain something thoroughly, the chapter ends.

Industrial spying is a crime of our modern times and as the world economy continues to develop, there will likely be more cases. The Scientist and the Spy is an average book on the topic and while it does bring some important issues to light and is well- written, it is far from the page- turning thriller I was hoping for.

title: What is the Best Way to Give?
text:
Giving back is important. In a world fraught with inequalities, injustice, unethical leadership, etc, we need to make up the shortfall through charitable giving. I give regularly to different organizations and my interest in the subject convinced me to read The Most Good You Can Do: How Effective Altruism Is Changing Ideas About Living Ethically.

This book’s premise can be summarized as follows: Giving matters, but what matters most is giving to organizations that work directly toward saving lives. Therefore, while you might have a genuine interest in the arts, in fitness, in education, and in other areas, you should refrain from giving to art museums, outdoor playgrounds, and private school foundations. You should instead focus your efforts on world hunger, disease prevention, and the like. This will help save the most lives and, until the world has significantly reduced the number of premature deaths, these live- saving charities represent the most good we can do and they should rank at the top of our charitable giving list.

Digesting what this book is all about left me with mixed feelings. I get what the book is trying to say and I must admit, I did learn about several unknown charities and charitable advisory services that do, indeed, work to save thousands of lives each year- organizations that, until I read this book, I didn’t know existed. But I have a hard time necessarily accepting this narrowed focus on giving. One could easily raise the argument, for example, that investing in education will lead to a better life for all in the long run. I do agree that there are some causes that are more about making us feel good than anything and certainly should rank lower on the list. But I’m not willing to rearrange my charitable giving to include only those non- profits that are involved in immediate saving of lives.

There were other, more specific aspects of this book that stand out in my memory. At the top of the list are the examples the book provides of certain individuals who are truly dedicated to the charitable giving cause. Some of the individuals and couples mentioned in the book give 30, 40, even 50 percent or more of their money to charities. This level of giving is, of course, unrealistic for most people. But it is inspiring to know that there are people out there who are this committed to giving back. I was also intrigued by the book’s last chapter, where the topic of human extinction is discussed. This took me by surprise but it makes sense that this topic get included since there is always that chance, however small, that humans could be destroyed by nuclear war, a massive asteroid, etc and that we should consider investing time and research to prevent some of these things from happening, whenever practical.

I have been giving to charitable causes for a long time and will always include giving as part of my monthly financial outlay. The Most Good You Can Do is a good enough book overall and worthy of a look if you’re interested in hearing about giving from a different perspective. I don’t necessarily think the book’s premise is the best, but I found enough good reading and good ideas overall to give this book a small recommendation.

title: Here's to a Healthy Heart
text:
Cooking is great for creative types. There is no end to the possibilities and there are many directions one can go when crafting and perfecting a recipe. Making up something can be fun, but it is also nice when someone else has already done the work for you, especially when you have a specific dietary need. And a good cookbook for a specific need is the 30 Minute Heart Healthy Cookbook.

I received a copy of this book from the publisher and I like how the book presents some background information before it launches into the recipes. The cookbook is, after all, dedicated to heart health so it makes sense to discuss exactly what it means for a recipe to be heart healthy. The book does exactly that when it discusses popular heart- healthy eating patterns, the principles of heart healthy eating, etc. Some of the advice in this section is debatable, but the bulk of it is good and can help those who are looking to improve heart health through better eating.

Moving to the recipes, this cookbook is divided into sections for breakfast and smoothies; salads, starters, and side dishes; vegetarian and vegan; seafood; poultry; meat; snacks and sweet treats; and staples. I like that the cookbook includes a variety and I know that those of the vegetarian/vegan persuasion will like that the cookbook has a separate section for those types of foods.

Each of the recipes in this book includes a description, ingredients, step by step instructions, nutritional facts; and sometimes tips on flavor boosting, ingredients, and substitutions. I have tried a few of the smoothies- I always seem to start with smoothies when I get a cookbook- and I have liked the results. The instructions are good, too, as they step you through the process.

One area where this cookbook lacks is illustrations. There is a single illustration at the beginning of each chapter for one of the recipes, and that is it. I like the visual appeal of illustrations- they go far in convincing me to give something a try. This cookbook is not a good option if you like to see the end result before you decide to pursue making the food or drink.

Eating heart- healthy foods is a good idea for everyone. I don’t have any heart issues, but I’m not going to wait for problems to develop- I’m taking steps now to reduce sodium and eat better foods to prolong heart healthiness. The 30 Minute Heart Healthy Cookbook is good for finding heart- friendly recipes and for crafting food dishes that don’t take long to make. I would like more illustrations and, as I said before, there is some debatable info in the front of the book. But this is still a good cookbook overall and perfect for those who want to reduce unhealthy fats and improve heart health.

title: Decent Guide for Kids, but There are Some Issues
text:
Learning a second language is smart for anyone and the best way to take those early steps down the bilingual path is by starting young. The majority of books on foreign language skills are too advanced for young people, but one book made specially for the little ones is My First Book of Spanish Words, a foreign language beginner’s guide.

My First Book of Spanish Words is a 32- page book about the Spanish language. Each set of pages contains pictures of common items to a specific place or idea, with a rectangular, white square pointing to specific objects/people/animals on the page. Within the white square is the English word, the Spanish word underneath, and a pronunciation aid in parentheses under that.

Some of the 13 sections include Family, Clothes, Bedroom, Farm, and Classroom. There are anywhere from two to eight words per page, with a grand total of exactly 10 words defined for each section. The book ends with a listing of the English and Spanish translation for the numbers 1 through 10, a list of common phrases, a short list of additional books to read, and an internet site to reference for more.

My First Book of Spanish Words is a simple book aimed at young kids age 5 and up and it serves as a good first- time book for children to get a grip on some of the more common words in the Spanish language. The reason this book works well for youngsters is because of its added pictures. They are actual pics, not cartoons or drawings. It is a like a short dictionary with added illustrations and kids will find it very useful to learn to associate an actual object with a specific word.

I like that this book helps kids learn to pronounce words as well as translate words because, as we know, Spanish letters do not all sound like the identical letter in English. There is one small issue that I noticed, however, and that is with words that use the letter v. As any student or speaker of Spanish knows, the letter v in Spanish is pronounced like a soft b, not a v. In this book, the pronunciations of words with the letter v are treated like they sound the same as the English v, which is not quite right. For instance, the Spanish word for sheep is la oveja. The pronunciation aid in the book tells kids to pronounce this as oh-VAY-hah.

My First Book of Spanish Words is a good first guide to Spanish. With 130 different, common words translated, along with some common phrases, kids can learn a few basics of the language. The issue with the letter v described above is not one I can easily overlook, but other than that, this is still a useful guide for the target age group.

title: Global Beer Tour Circumnavigates the Globe, but Visits too Few Breweries
text:
Beer tourism is growing in popularity. As a beer writer myself, I have noticed a strong increase in the topic of beer travel and I often see brewery visits listed among the things to do when I visit most any destination. Lonely Planet’s Global Beer Tour is a book dedicated to this new face of tourism, guiding the reader on a tour of the world, one brewery at a time.

Global Beer Tour is like a combination reference guide and reading volume, but it leans a little more toward the reference end. The book is organized by continent, and then alphabetical by country. Within each country, it lists some of the most popular, unique, or otherwise interesting breweries for tourists. It could be a brewery with critically- acclaimed beer, a brewery steeped in history, or a brewery with some sort of unique feature. The book includes many of the world’s greatest breweries, complete with a summary of the brewery’s offerings, a short bio, and a recommend list of things to do nearby.

One of this book’s strongest points is the illustrations and I like that the guide contains at least one picture for every featured brewery. It’s always helpful to see what things are like and the pictures do make a difference. The organization is useful, too, because it sorts first by continent, then by country. The foreign travel section is nice because travelers can quickly turn to the part of the globe in which they are visiting and lookup breweries to visit. The sorting of the United States breweries, which are listed alpha by city, would have been better had it been sorted first by region, and then by city, but it’s still useful like it is. Oh, and the things to do nearby is a good idea because it helps lead tourists to other places of interest that are not focused on beer, but are certainly worth seeing.

Where Global Beer Tour falters a bit is with the actual entries themselves. The amount of information on each brewery is far too brief- only a couple short paragraphs, in some instances. This isn’t enough to really get to know a brewery on a personal level and to entice me to want to visit. But I think the greatest problem I have with Global Beer Tour is the lack of breweries covered and nowhere is this clearer then with the United States. The book highlights some of the best- known breweries in America’s most popular beer cities, but far too many are overlooked. Yes, they covered the super heavyweights like San Diego, Denver, and Portland, Oregon. But cities like Philadelphia, Milwaukee, and others receive no mention at all. And when you consider the thousands of operating breweries in the United States, the fact that only about thirty- six are highlighted in this book, well, it just leaves you yearning for more.

Overall, however, I cannot say that Global Beer Tour is bad book because it isn’t. There is still some useful information here and the pictures are helpful. The writing is good as well and I like that the guide tries its best to cover a diverse set of breweries in different sections of the world. The low number of breweries receiving coverage and the scant amount of information on some of them makes the book less appealing than it would otherwise be, but there is enough good to give this book a middle rating and small recommendation.

title: A Mouse, a Cat, and a Cookie
text:
An ordinary book in most ways, Mouse’s Christmas book is a simple story about a cat, mouse, and a Christmas present that happens to be a cookie. The pages of the book feature cute, colorful, cartoon- style images and a basic story fit for the younger- age crowd, preschool to perhaps kindergarten.

Mouse’s Christmas Cookie is a very simple book with almost no dialogue, which makes it an okay choice of reading material for the target age group. Kids will be fixated mostly on the images, as the words on most pages are ‘stop mouse’, with only a handful of other words on the other pages. There is little actual reading to do, so some youngsters will find it to their liking.

With so little dialogue and a simple message, there really isn’t much to this book at all and while I realize it was intended for young children, it could prove too boring even for kids in the target group. The recommendation is three to six years, but I would stick to the lower end of this range. My young ones found it far too simple- even silly- and they told me the only redeeming quality was the cartoon pictures. I suppose it is good enough to recommend, but I do so with reservations, as it is a very ordinary book overall.

title: How to Save Money and Get More from Your Next Cruise
text:
Cruises are great fun but they can also be rather costly. Cruise ships have a seemingly endless number of services ready for purchase and if consumers aren't careful, they can easily double the original cost of a cabin when overall costs are added together. Fortunately, there are ways to get more for less and Cruise Power is here to help, with simple advice that can help cruisers get more than they expected from a cruise while still keeping costs under control.

Cruise Power's author has years and years of experience on cruise ships and he shares some of his price- cutting and other wisdom on each page. The book talks about cabin selection, upgrades, shore excursions, frequent cruiser programs, and other things that can help consumers get more for less. It even comes with a smaller guidebook that offers tips aimed at helping you get invited to dine with the ship's captain. The advice is straight forward, the reading is simple, and cruise vacationers have much to gain by following what the book recommends.

I have taken a cruise or two in my day and some of the advice offered here is common sense, but other tidbits are not and new cruisers, in particular, stand the most to gain. How many are aware of the high cost of shore excursions and the better offers available for purchase off of the ship? How many realize that paying up- front for a cruise is a bad idea and that placing a deposit today with payment later is really the best way to go? I found a few useful facts and advice myself and I really like the cruise website recommendations. I had not heard of several of them and now that I have logged in and checked, they appear to be very useful.

Cruise Power is a good book for saving money on a cruise and discovering hidden perks, but one problem I have with the book is the briefness of its coverage and advice. The book is short and doesn't really have enough space to cover everything. Some money- saving topics are barely touched and others could use a little more thoroughness. Additional appendices could also make a difference. Still, if you need some basic tips on ways to cut costs and get more from your next cruise, this book can serve as a useful resource. It is short, but there is some good wisdom within and cruise vacationers will come out ahead if they follow the book's advice.

title: Good Fairy Tale Story for Younger Crowd
text:
Thrice Upon a Marigold is a story about kidnapping- in this instance, the kidnapping of a baby princess. The story moves rather quickly and the book contains a decent supporting cast of characters, making it a good choice for older elementary school age children who like a good fantasy read.

The story line in this book develops rather quickly and the outcome is about what one would expect, with just a few surprises along the way. The different characters are likeable enough, even though no one character really stands out as exceptionally appealing. The children of the bad characters are probably the most memorable and many young readers will take to them right away. Their characters and relationship do manage to develop rather nicely as the story moves along and they are relatable to the target audience of the book, which is third to fifth graders.

This book seemed like an average one to me, but I can see how young readers will find it intriguing and memorable. There are other books in this series, but reading them is not necessary to make sense out of this book. Offer it to the younger reader in your house and see what happens. I predict most fiction- loving elementary school age kids will find the book a good one.

title: Can American Schools Improve?
text:
Mission Possible is a book dedicated to changing the American education system and improving student performance and interest in learning. The book is based on a successful charter school in New York that has achieved positive results with its education strategy and the authors want to share their secrets for success with other concerned parents and educators and, hopefully, change the education system for the better.

Most would agree that public education in the United States is well below where it should be. Statistics and official studies show that the U.S. is lagging behind other developed nations and continues to lose ground. Success Academy Charter Schools have over- achieved by most measures and the founder and CEO of the program wrote this book to show everyone that better education is achievable. The book talks about the secret for the Success Academy's success, offering some of its ideas for making the education process better, getting parents more involved, and creating an atmosphere where kids are anxious to get to school each day and actively participate in the learning process.

I can certainly agree that public schools are in poor shape as a whole and I agree completely that they tend to be far too easy and tend to lower standards so that no one feels left out. I like what these people have done in New York and Success Academy Charter Schools seem to have a winning formula. But what bothers me a little about this book is that it makes the process of success seem a little too simple. The book is very enthusiastic with its plan of action, but would these methods necessarily work in a majority of schools? What if parents are just not that involved or what if principals cannot convey the formula to their teachers? And what if the best people simply do not want to teach? Teacher pay is not that high and this fact alone keeps many of the best and brightest out of the teaching field as a career. What plan could this charter school offer to address this and other issues?

Mission Possible is an optimistic book and I applaud its ambition and determination to make American schools better than before. It might be better with a laid out, step by step plan of action in an accompanying workbook and I would like to see its formula adopted in other schools to better assess its effectiveness. Until then, this book is an average one overall. It ideas, while certainly nice on paper, have not been tried and tested enough to verify their effectiveness.

title: Student's Advantage is Here to Help You
text:
The Student's Advantage is a motivational guide for students; a guide designed to help high school students find their way and set themselves on the path toward career success. It is a book that stresses selection of a career, attending either college or a trade school, setting goals, and then taking the necessary actions to make those goals a reality.

This book is all about a student's future and the writing is written in a way that is obviously aimed at the high school junior or senior who perhaps has not thought much about post- graduation education or job training and could use some direction. Some young people already have a career path in place and know what they need to do. Others haven't a clue. They do not know what to do or where to begin and they lack the necessary discipline to make things happen. The Student's Advantage is a book ready to help the distraught high school student figure out where to go and how to get there.

The Student's Advantage is loaded with anecdotes and simple advice and it is written to students. It may seem a little blunt at times, but it is also very encouraging. The author seems genuinely interested in helping kids succeed and he wrote the book with success in mind. He points out over and over again the importance of education and he strongly encourages kids to either go to college or learn a trade in order to live a more fulfilling, prosperous life.

This book is a good starting point for the student in need of some direction, but one thing I am not too crazy about is the lack of sufficient coverage of so many different topics. The book contains fewer than 200 pages and some of the pages contain blank space or worksheets, making the actual book length even shorter still. The book seems like a nice warm- up to a longer, more thorough guide. It can't really stand alone as a book for career options and choices, but it does offer a nice starting point.

High school kids are often undecided when it comes to future careers and this book is a good guide for motivation and encouragement. The book shows kids what they need to do beyond high school to achieve their goals and live a satisfying life and while it may only scratch the surface in many ways, it is still a good motivational book and it can help the high school student in need of some direction.

title: Goldilicious is Plotless and Directionless, but it is Fantasy
text:
Goldilicious is a fantasy book about a girl, a unicorn, and the many adventures they share. It is written by one of the same individuals responsible for the Pinkalicious book, which was the first of its kind in the series. Goldilicious continues this colourful theme and is one of the latest in this line of books.

Goldilicious is focused on make- believe and it is a little different from other children's books. It is common for literature aimed at kids to include some type of message or life lesson, but this book isn't like that. It doesn't contain anything educational either. Rather, it relies on stimulation of the imagination to carry it through and it will strike a chord with children who have vivid imaginations. The book jumps around from one scene to the next, with the unicorn character doing one thing and then another, including flying, disappearing, and then reappearing at the end of the book next to her friend Pinkalicious, ready to say goodnight to her friend before going to bed.

Goldilicious doesn't really have any core message and it doesn't really follow any specific plot. For these reasons, many parents will not appreciate this book or see any value in adding it to their kid's libraries. The lack of a plot or any sense of direction does bother me a little, but on the other hand, the book is about fantasy and imagination so it makes some sense that the book would stress using imagination on the part of the reader and what better way to do that than to keep readers guessing and not knowing what to expect next.

Goldilicious has some good illustrations and offers some nice colors and it has more actual words than many other children's books. The extra words mean that younger kids will likely not be able to read it themselves. They will need some help from an adult, but those at the age of, say, six or older should have no trouble reading it solo.

All and all, I find Goldilicious an average children's book with its share of both good and bad points. I would prefer that the story line be stronger and more coherent rather than so loose and directionless, but I can agree that Goldilicious is a decent story book for children in the three to seven age group. There is no message here, except that using the imagination is a good thing and something kids should practice every day. And that should be enough to convince most kids- and parents- to like Pinkalicious and her fantasy unicorn friend.

title: Time for Some Basic Financial Training
text:
Personal finance is an important topic that affects everyone, yet it hasn't received the level of coverage that it deserves for most of the past few decades. The financial meltdown of the past few years has, thankfully, resulted in a newfound emphasis on personal finance and hundreds or perhaps even thousands of books have been published in response. Dollars and Uncommon Sense is one of those books. It is a book about financial responsibility and it emphasizes how we could all be a little better off financially with some simple basic training.

I'm a financial person myself and I have spent the past twenty- plus years advising people on financial matters, lecturing college classrooms about personal and corporate finance, and writing about financial topics. Thus, I am always ready to read another book on the topic, just to see if it presents any new ideas or advice on ways to manage money, reduce debt, invest wisely, etc. Dollars and Uncommon Sense covers most of the basics of personal finance, complete with tables, instructions, and other tips to help you get your financial house in order.

One thing I like about Dollars and Uncommon Sense is that the author has already been through a financial crisis of his own. He talks in the book about his own stint with debt and how he used to rack up credit card bills like there was no tomorrow. Because of this, he is able to relate to the reader who may be faced with a similar situation. He isn't just talking about what should work based on research- he is speaking from experience and he seems genuinely interested in helping others achieve their financial goals.

Dollars and Uncommon Sense starts off talking about attitude and how our personal perceptions and relationships with money are critical because they will determine whether or not we succeed financially. The book then proceeds to talk about three general areas of personal financial management: Spending, debt, and saving/investing. These are three very broad areas and there is very little space available in this book to cover all that needs to be covered. It discusses what its limited pages permit, but financial people in particular will quickly realize that many important topics such as insurance and education savings plans are not covered at all.

I generally like what this book offers, but one area of disagreement I have is with the basic plan for financial improvement. Specifically, I do not agree that people should give ten percent of their income to charity before they even touch any of their other responsibilities, like paying debt, investing, saving, etc. I am certainly a firm believer in charitable giving and I donate money on a monthly basis. However, I don't agree with this as a matter of priority for several reasons. First, many people cannot afford to give up ten percent of their earnings- they wouldn't have enough money left to survive. Second, even if all the important bills were paid and food was on the table, it would still make more sense to divide up the ten percent among accelerated debt payments, investments, and charity. Now, if you can actually afford to give up ten percent to charity, then by all means go ahead and give. But this should not be your top priority and I disagree with the book's advice that we move into a smaller home and downsize our lifestyle just so we can have enough cash to give away ten percent of it to non- profit organizations.

Other than my strong opposition to the book's spending allocation plan, Dollars and Uncommon Sense does offer some good, basic financial advice in many respects. Financial literacy is sorely lacking among most individuals and this book does offer at least some good, general basic training on personal finance.

title: Thomas, Erin, and Grandad have a Fun Outing at the Zoo
text:
Thomas and Erin with Granddad is a new adventure series that follows two young kids as they enjoy time with their grandpa. This particular adventure is the second in the series and it follows the two youngsters on an outing at the zoo. They get some close- up views of monkeys, tigers, giraffes, elephants, and other animals as they walk from one exhibit to the next.
