text: The patterns are beautiful, but the instructions are really confusing.  I am not a newbie crocheter, and often work in 30 or 40 cotton, making lace, very complicated patterns.  I thought this book would combine that sort of work with yarn that was a bit thicker and give me some fun, quick stuff to make.  It does use thicker yarn than what I'm used to, which is kind of nice, but I'm left struggling with what the woman is trying to say.  The book definitely needs more charting and less writing.

title: A bit disappointing
text: I've been a SE reader for years, and was delighted when I saw out they were coming out with this book.  I pre-ordered as soon as it became available.  On the website, it really sounded like there would be a lot more recipes than actually made the book.  Instead it seems to mostly be made up of an endless series of Best Of lists.  If you read SE there is absolutely no reason to buy the book, unless you simply want to support the site.  If you don't visit the SE site, you will probably find the book quite entertaining for its voice, but don't think for a second you will find any cooking treasures in there, because you won't.

title: Its just ok
text: Just was not as happy with this book as I though I'd be

title: where is the sunflowers
text: no sunflowers disappointing since sunflower represent fall

title: I dislike the little mini pics in the front of the book
text: Some of these books are cute but they have several annoying mini pages in the front that to me is a waste of paper Id love to see a few extra whole images instead of those...they really have no use to me...

title: Could be better
text: I love the images but there is one problem its not single sided and I like to use alcohol markers so disappointed

title: cute book but
text: one of the pages had its writing backwards but I love the images

title: This book is actually two books pulled togeter as one
text: I did not know that when I purchased it but it contains two different books one I already have I did not grab this one amazon  but I gave it three stars because of it being a republish double book and does not explain that but it clearly has the two authors on the book so I matched the images from my other books to this one  Going threw My creative haven books I have found two other done the same way..

title: Boring but factual
text: I found most of this pretty boring, with the author immersed in his own ego much of the time... however, the historical facts are pertinent and quite informative.  If another style of writing were used, this would be a great read.

title: A Very Dark Tale
text: This was dark, very, seriously dark. My introduction to Swanwick as well as Darger & Surplus came in several volumes of short stories. While those had a dark flavor there was usually one villain whom the pair of grifters would readily outfox and be on their way to their next con. Granted they did leave Buckingham Palace in flames when they fled London. But this novel had the room the short stories didn't have to reall dig into the darkness that is the postutopian world Darger & Surplus inhabit. Attempting to reach Moscow to pull some ambitious scam the pair happen upon a caravan also heading there to bring the Duke of Muscovy a group of genetically enhanced brides. They come across signs of the Utopian age when man and his marvelous AI made war upon each other and brought both groups low. Technology, even things as simple as radio are outlawed, detested and destroyed. Meanwhile monstrous beings with multiple minds/brains are bred in vats to be the thinking and processing power of the new postutopian world. Languages are learned with a pill. Drugs giving supernatural strength and the feeling of having encountered God are passed about like candy. Machines plot the death of every living thing down to bugs and grass. Humans are surgically altered to be slave beings. And through this Darger & Surplus stumble quite possibly bringing ruin to mother Russia. It was a good read, well put together but a little too dark for my mindset these days.

title: A Little Too Easy. . .
text:
A new Charlaine Harris book often feels like slipping on an old, well worn, pair of shoes. She's stumbled before but the Gunnie Rose books have been enjoyable. I really like alternate America in the early and middle years. The Alvin Maker series by Orson Card come to mind. This series (with no relationship to Card's work) happens sometime later, perhaps the late 1910s or 1920s. Rose and others are armed with model 1911 automatic pistols. I had erroneously thought because of the dialog and settings we were talking revolvers but it appears not.
Although sliding back into Gunnie Rose's world was pretty easy and comfortable. . . the story was too. Too easy. Too comfortable. Like it was on rails going around the track. I enjoyed it but there wasn't any true adversity. Everything just worked out. Towards the end the narrative started pushing out false foreshadowing. I hit one, then another and I literally stopped reading for the rest of that day because I was expecting something horrible to happen.
I don't know if this is the end of the series. I think this is a rich world for Rose and Eli to explore and have adventures in. I wouldn't mind reading more, I like these characters. But if this is The End, then it ended well.
A copy of this book was supplied by the publisher.

p.s. there are currently 666 reviews here on Amazon, I had to change that ;)

title: Less Than Impressive
text: Hints, tips, no Earth shaking revelations. I'm a fair amateur photographer and have been using multiple cameras since I was sixteen and was shooting on film with my Canon A-E1. I was fairly bored with this book. Perhaps if you were just starting out and wanted to learn about composition, rules of 3 or basic lighting needs this might be a good starting point. If, however, you've been taking pictures a while you probably won't get much use out of this.

title: Retold Tales
text: This is an illustrated collection of nine retellings of fairy tales from around the world. The artwork ranges from good, 'Jack and the Beanstalk' to mediocre, the title story 'The Nixie of the Millpond'. Some of the dialog doesn't really. . . it doesn't sing. 'Jack and the Beanstalk' for having really good artwork reads like a badly translated anime. 'Hamlin's Piper' has no dialog at all, it's told only through the art. I liked to a greater or lesser degree all the stories herein. I really don't know if it's for kids, maybe older teens.

title: Not As Good As The First
text: I read the first book, then shared it with everyone I could. It was hysterical and well done. This 3rd edition, I missed the 2nd,  reads like it was put together by someone dealing with a new child soon after having their 1st. But it lacks the prose and polish I had so enjoyed. Maybe a sub par entry was part of the joke. To me it was just an attempt to cash in while the brand was still hot. Not great.

title: Good Art, So So Story
text: I liked the artwork. Really well drawn. The story though was a bit anemic. I know I'm definitely not the target audience but while I do enjoy light YA reading, this was a little too light and unrealistic.

title: Confusing
text: Art was good. Found the story a little hard to follow. Guess I'm getting old or something.

title: More Future to Fear
text:
Thanks to NetGallery for a copy of this novel to review -
Much like Cory Doctorow this book paints a bleak near future I dread entering. Social media as social justice. The Hive was created to cut back on cyber bullying by allowing others, even those completely unaffected, to vote to 'condemn' a user for their activities. But it's still the same cowards hiding behind their phones and screens lashing out from the protection of their anonymity. When Cassie's crude joke goes spiraling down the rabbit hole we see, in a realistic, stomach churning way, how a corrupt system can get even a teenager sentenced to death by the votes of her peers. The conversations about Cassie, how they want to hurt and kill and worse, you can see that every day on the internet now. Anonymous bloodlust, no consequences for thought or so we thought.
My problem is in one chapter Cassie is a genius outhacking some of the best but then immediately doing the stupidest things. And in the end she faces no consequences, not for her joke. That was a terror inducing idea I hope never becomes a reality but Cassie faces no internal consequences for getting numerous people arrested, hurt and dear Cassie, people died because of your actions and that really didn't seem to affect you much.
I found it hard to like Cassie all that much.

title: Not the Ending I Wanted
text:
This took a while first because it was the first print book I've read in nearly nine years. Strange indeed. The print was small and strained the eyes some. But most of all I didn't want it to end. I've known of the existence of this book for a decade and a half but no library had a copy. Interlibrary loan requests came up empty. I even tried contacting the author to try and beg that these stories be released digitally. I finally found an "affordable" copy and I knew herein Felimid's tale truly ends and I didn't want to rush to that ending. . .
Now the book. We pick up not long after the events in the previous book. Felimid still grieving terribly over the loss of his love finally reaches the shores of his beloved Ireland only to find trouble at every turn. Bards walk about claiming and taking at a whim with none to stop them. The cross worshippers are making strong footholds in his once pagan land driving out the magic of the world. Worse a vile pretender to the rank of chief bard, held by Fergus, Felimid's grandfather has coveted the two ancient treasures of Ireland that Felimid carries and he will stop at nothing to obtain them.
The writing was good though it seemed to lack the luster the previous volumes had. The action moves well and we're kept on the edge wondering how this will end. And then it ends. The evil bard is overcome (no spoiler there, that was expected) but it happens fast, too easy. No quest or talisman, it just ends but it doesn't. The followers of the evil one pick up and continue the enmity their leader caused. Felimid's story. . . stops. We're treated to a brief history of the land and that's that. a somewhat disappointing end for a long lusty tale.

title: Nothing New Here
text: A very short collection of short stories. Quick and interesting read for new fans of Wilson and his Secret Histories. Long time fans will be sad to find nothing new between the covers of this collection. Some tales are more obscure but in the decades I've been a fan I've read everything here in other places. I was hoping for at least on 'never before released' story but, alas it was not to be. Don't get me wrong, these stories are good, well worth reading and it's been years since I encountered some but I really hoped for new words and he did introduce and briefly discuss each short story, so there's that.

title: Okay, Slow, Too Easy
text:
The majority of this book is told in two alternating viewpoints, one, the walkers, a growing group of people experiencing amazing metaphysical psychic powers to heal, to understand, to evolve. The other story arc is that of a murderous psychopath crisscrossing the United States slaughtering women at random.
The first half, maybe more, of the book was interesting if a little slow and meandering. And while I'm not a major fan of multiple story arcs in a single novel as I get comfortable and interested in how things are going in one place and all of a sudden you're somewhere else experiencing something else.
I liked this portion of the book. I even got the metaphysical goings on and could believe them right up until the author tried, repeatedly throughout the rest of the book, that if you decide to kill someone it's because that person wants to die. . . wait, what? Yes, anyone killed, murdered, hit by a meteorite, etc. has decided to die and picked you or that meteor as their method of death. No, I get interconnected consciousness. I get healing and taking away and casting away pain. I get spirit walking and vision quests but that? You were murdered because somewhere inside you decided to BE murdered or hit by a bus, whatever? Nope. Not buying it. Breaks the suspension of disbelief like a sledgehammer on an chicken egg.
Then in the latter portion of the book the murderer meets the walkers and. . . not going to spoil it but it didn't happen as I expected or wanted or was willing to accept. I didn't care for how it went but I'm not an evolved being like those members of the walkers.
The ending of the book was also a little too easy, too quick. Can humans overcome ego and the need for not possessions but recognition entirely? Not even in a generation but a few months? Is enlightenment that easy? I mean, yeah, I'd love to regrow all the teeth I've lost but could I shed my cell, tablet, Kindle (this book does take place before the technological gods have awoke), even my camera? Can I just walk (something I can barely do!) away and become a better person?
I just don't know. . .

title: Not Much Excitement
text: A somewhat slow paced first contact, end of a multiplanetary human race story. It doesn't plod, more so it meanders like a slow river on a summer day. Even the few action scenes are less than exciting. The characters are fleshed out enough to really get a feel for them. The aliens though don't feel really alien they're more like humans with different descriptions. I had to check for an original publication date when I saw the 2018 release date for this novel. It honestly has an early works feel to it and I thought it was a rerelease. Not a bad story just a little slow and I'm disbelieving the ending. The numbers, they're too large in the face of a pandemic than spanned planet systems. I'm just not buying the numbers.

title: Happy and Sad There's a New Black Company Book
text: I can only give it three stars. Throughout the first third of this book which happens early in the career of the Black Company but is never mentioned at in novels that span decades past this point in history. I was suspicious and then it's revealed why. Worse we get to a point in the story which is told in two parts (not a favorite type of storytelling) of the 'present' day Company and past time dominator era. This wind up and down, the main arc of the story gets set to the side for another mingling of past and present and then nothing! Ugh. I love the Black Company, I have read the series numerous times. I try to get all my friends who read fantasy to read Glen Cook but this novel drove me nuts. I loved seeing old friends, the Captain still being around and the old crew still kicking but it just got warped and weird towards the end. It's worth reading, don't get me wrong, just don't expect it to expand the Black Company story it's more of a sidetrack that goes nowhere and was never meant to. I still want the Company to move on from where we left it. Things were left up in the air.

title: Good But A Litttle Complex
text: Some of the art was a little complex for the beginner at coloring but for the most part it was an enjoyable coloring book.

title: Something of a Letdown
text:
I had high hopes for this book. The employees are all working at an Ikea knock-off store down to the silly Scandinavian names for everything they sell. The cast is diverse and each character is fairly well developed. There's some decent humor at the beginning of the book. Then two off the clock amateur ghost hunters convince everyone, except for the manager who's conveniently off on a task of his own, to take part in a seance in a building built over ground an intelligent person would never attempt such a task with no safety measures in place.
From this point on, up until a surprisingly twisted ending, it becomes low budget schlock, b-movie style horror.
[Slight Spoiler] You open a fake cabinet mounted where you KNOW it can go nowhere. All of a sudden there's a long, fetid, horrible smelling corridor. You're not a ghost hunter Do you:
A: Close the door and make a run for it?
B: Ignore the fact the corridor cannot possibly exist and go exploring?
So I've already told you this has switched from humorous and a little spooky to bad B-movie horror fare. You know the protagonists are going to make and keep making the worst decisions possible. The end comes as a surprise and quite possibly signals there may be a sequel in the works. I hope not. I think the ending was done right.

title: Not Great But Not Horrible
text: Very few scares very little spookiness the writing wasn't as good as the other stories I've read by this author. While I know it's a small thing it's bits like an author telling how her character is climbing a rocky, vine covered, trail and had to stop several times to remove leeches from her legs. Leeches live in water not on mountains. It's things like that which can tear you right out of the story saying "what the heck is she talking about?!" Ticks would have made sense. Leeches just shows a lack of rese or knowledge. The ending had a bit of a twist and was better than the full first half of the book. I've read better but at least I was able to finish this. As a time killer it's not bad. As a horror story it falls short.

title: Good But a Little Slow Paced
text: A decent read although the solution slaps the reader and protagonist in the face from very near the beginning of the book. From the moment we were shown the scene I kept saying your answer is there. You'll find light THERE but our protagonist was somewhat slow as was the story. The build up of tension and suspense wasn't badly written but it took a little too long and the end I found dissatisfying. First there should always be some sort of horrible loss and second it shouldn't be so easy for the characters to get out alive. The was a couple tense moments but they didn't last. The story kept me reading though it could have been better. It wasn't horrible but neither was it great. I will keep an eye out for this author in the future.

title: Starts off Like a Dragster. . . Crashes into the Wall In the Last Fifty Feet and Bursts Into Flames
text: No! No! No! The story should not have ended like this! I enjoyed this SO much. It was bizarre at every turn. Every inch of Anomaly Flats wants to kill you, change you or ruin your day. But it's also got a subtle charm and as one of the characters says, it's fascinating. I wanted to learn more about the weirdness that packs every corner of the town and the people who live there. I did NOT expect to come to despise, beyond belief, the main protagonist, Mallory, like I did. I knew she wasn't that nice of an person even before it was revealed why she was making a run for Canada but not only did I come to hate her the end of the story ticked me off like you wouldn't believe. It's like the author couldn't come up with a really good ending which was staring him in the face but either he or someone reading the book as he wrote it whispered in his ear "No, it's been really weird it's got to end weird instead of satisfying!" Maybe he had a couple drinks in him. Maybe he wanted to aggravate the reader. Maybe he wanted room for another stupid sequel. I don't know what he was thinking but he took a book that was fun and weird and strange and scary and ruined it. The first three quarters of the book were great, amazing, a blast to read. And then, if it weren't on my Kindle, I would have tossed the book across the room. I can't believe how much I hated the ending.

title: Overpriced Coloring Book, Sequel is Much Better
text: My mother loved Gladys Scanlon's other coloring book [[ASIN:142593482X Another Grown-Up's Coloring Book]] the second book had far better images to color they were detailed but less complex than those in this book. My mother's happy with this even though the second book was far better this books is worth coloring but not really worth the price we paid for it. It was far more than it was worth.

title: Not Quite What We Expected
text: Appeared in a search for adult coloring books. Most images would appeal more towards children as they're very simple and have limited complexity and no backgrounds. Still there's some chances to work on shading and can be a break from the more complex real adult style coloring book. It'll get used.

title: Not As Good As The Previous Novel
text: A little slower read than the second novel. About half the action of book two and half the bad romance from book one. A bit too much chatter. Too many coincidences. Better than the first book by far but nowhere near as good as the second book. Not a bad read until the ending. Sorry, no spoilers. I can't tell if the author just hit a wall of writers block and quit or she's looking to extend the series. Either way I was seriously disappointed in how the book ended. Still, if you've made it through the first two this is worth reading.

title: Well Written But Confusing
text:
I'm still confused. It's a horror story but it's not. It's a ghost story but it's not. JP's parents can't decide if he's getting better or worse. His mother's realized some but oh so far from the real truth while his father lives in a complete delusion where he believes it's just going to take a good talking to and maybe a shake or two and his boy will be just fine.
We come across a housekeeper at a local church who says that she can help the boy. I almost wish the author had let that story line play out. It would have changed things, extended the drama. Perhaps even brought the disbelievers, the priest and the father (who seemed to begin to understand something right at the end) deeper into the story. It felt a little rushed but also dragged in places. A better editing would help. I must say, even though there were a few breadcrumbs of hints the twist at the very end caught me pretty much by surprise. I also liked that it ended right there. Leave us guessing, let us wonder. And whatever you do NO sequels! Let the story stand on it's own. It shouldn't, it doesn't need to, continue. It's over. Let it rest.

title: Not The Author's Best Or Worst, Worth Reading
text: This one took a while to get through. There were quite a few times I put the Kindle down and thought about finding something else to read but there were some laugh out loud moments and moments of real, raw, humanity that kept me going. The gift and letter from father to son towards the end for me (someone who watched his father die quickly once the cancer got it's hooks into him) was an absolute tear jerker. It wasn't a great book but it was definitely readable. It had it's moments where I think we'll all see ourselves in the story. You may or may not like this. I'll probably not read it again but I made it all the way through.

title: A Fairly Decent Read
text:
A struggling but somewhat successful artists begins painting portraits of girls he's been dreaming of for months. A major gallery sees his art and decides to give him a show at their newest gallery, conveniently just a short ways from his home. Suddenly he's under investigation because the police have matched two of the three girls to girls who are presumed missing, run-away or worse. Also involved are demons and angels attached to each major person in the story but oddly we're not made aware of everyone's companion(s) (apparently we all have our own devil and angel with us using what minimal and sometimes stronger influence upon our persons). Though the book isn't preachy each chapter does end with a quote from a saint or famous person from biblical times. I truly was glad even though the guardian angels make a large part of the story religion wasn't specifically forced on the reader. All in all it wasn't a bad debut novel. It was a quick paced, action packed (slightly over the top, the Russian gangsters were somewhat unbelievable) novel that kept me guessing right up until the twist at the end that was completely unexpected. I enjoyed the book and would read more from this author.
I received a copy of this novel in exchange for my review.

title: Mostly Just A Coloring Book
text:
This book starts off with twelve pages of text, starting with an introduction to coloring and working up to some ideas; crosshatching, pointillism (coloring with dots instead of solid colors). This lasts as mentioned, just twelve pages.The rest of the book is (I didn't count, I'm going by the book's text) more than 100 images to color. Many of the images are quite complex and far from what you'd expect to find in a 'for dummies' book. also, with so many images the book becomes quite thick, even breaking the binding we've found it almost impossible to get the book to lay flat to color. We've taken to using a razor blade and carefully remove each page we wish to color. One od the good things about this book is the pictures are all printed single sided. There is no image backing the one you're coloring so if you're using a medium such as markers or watercolors, you don't have to worry about it bleeding through to the next image. Though if you're not removing the pages from the book as we are I highly recommend using several thick sheets of paper of as we do a back cover from an old coloring book to completely prevent any bleeding through to the next page (which is possible if you get the picture you're coloring wet enough.
Basically this is a middle to middle-advanced level coloring book with a few pages of suggestions and tips tacked onto the beginning. I honestly expected this to at least start of with a section for the beginner, then a more advanced section of images to color and so on but from the get go the majority of the images are fairly complex. Not really what we expected. There are some mixed in with the rest that are fairly quick and easy but not many. For the current price you get quite a fair number of pages to color but I had hoped for more information on blending and color theory, mixing mediums, etc. twelve pages is a bit light on the introduction to coloring for adults but they do provide quite a lot of colorable images,
I was torn between three and four stars but the limited text, hard to break binding and complex images from the start left me no choice to give it three stars. It's a coloring book with a short chapter on coloring in the beginning,

title: I Found it Slow & Boring
text: Like 'Finders Keepers' before it I felt this book didn't really need to be written. 'Mr. Mercedes' was decent and the story should have stopped there. Super villains with amazing powers and almost endless resources against the good guys who are armed with a plastic slingshot and half a clue found left out in the gutter after a rain storm. It was predictable, very, easily predictable and formulaic. I was so bored at the 75% point I almost quit and deleted it. I only finished it because Stephen King's been a long time favorite author of mine. I wasn't impressed. I expected the prolog (no spoilers) and it made my sad because I knew not because of what happens. Stephen King has really been hit or miss since his accident but the fans will keep buying anything he produces.

title: Not That Good
text: I love Neil Gaiman's writing and I've been a big fan of Douglas Adams forever but I just couldn't get into this book. I expected to be intrigued and fascinated how The Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy came into being from radio show to books to what wasn't a very good movie (well, except for Zooey Deschanel)  and how Adam's career grew from there but I couldn't drag myself halfway through this without giving up. It was just so slow and plodding and the sheer number of names being dropped that I didn't know just bored me beyond belief. Sorry Neil, sorry Doug. I just couldn't finish this and didn't enjoy it at all.

title: Boring, Easy, Simple. Good For Young Children.
text: These were just a little too easy. In most cases you didn't even need to fill in the dots to see what the picture was going to be. For young kids or the elderly who may have trouble with more complex dot-to-dot books this might be good. For everyone else this book is just too easy and simple. I really just can't recommend this.

title: Unimpressive Coloring Book, Sorry
text:
Sorry, I can only give this three stars. This is picture for picture exactly the same as the previously release swear word coloring book the only difference being the pages around the images are black, adding nothing really to the coloring experience. Once you've colored one you've colored the other. The black surround makes no real difference in the coloring experience. The pictures offer no change, no difference and being on a black page honestly adds or changes nothing to the experience from the previous book. About the only real difference is you can color outside frame of the picture though the pencil marks will still be somewhat visible. I can't get excited about one coloring book with exactly the same images as another. Some people may like black background. Neither my mother or I (both of us color in these books) were impressed. We'd be a lot happier with something new and different.
I received a copy of this book in exchange for my review.

title: Depressing Possible Future? Say It Ain't So.  .  .
text: Cory Doctorow paints such a bleak portrait of the nearly here future that on top of being depressing it's also somewhat terrifying. I see his world coming to fruition; maybe not exactly as he describes but the rise and frequent collapse of the financial system. People living in shanty towns with no police or fire service protection. Many without power. I'm disabled and I don't see a place for myself in this coming future. Stairs I can't climb, low seating I can't get off of. Doctorow's world even though the story had some upbeat points towards the end the book but the majority of the people in the book live, as Thoreau is oft misquoted as saying, 'lives of quiet desperation'. I don't want this future.

title: Not The Greatest Coloring Book
text: Torn between three and four stars. The flower designs themselves are four star work all day long. They're well drawn, very pretty and complex enough to present a challenge. Then you come to the border that's added to each image. They seem to have been made deliberately complex. Far more so than the flower designs they surround. Those I feel deserve three stars, Deliberately done to confuse and humble the colorist. Not the best collection of work. One saving grace is they're single sided and with a provided spacer page you can use markers to color these images. All in all, worthy of three and a half stars.

title: Somewhat Boring
text: Kind of boring. There isn't a lot of detail in many of the pictures and what there is is often marred by a poor conversion from the original posters which were glossy, a technique very hard to reproduce with crayon or colored pencil. Still, it's something different to color so there's that. Nothing to be excited about but not worth tossing.

title: Meh...
text: When I first started reading Kaufman the absurdity and bizarre story telling was interesting and different. Unfortunately it's starting to feel forced, almost like he wrote the story and then went back to add in even more strangeness. He also seem to have a weird obsession with precise times and measurements that leaves me cold. I'm not as enamored of this as I was "All My Friends..." or "Born Weird."

title: Not Kaufman's Best
text: This story was darker and more convoluted than either of the other two books of Kaufman's that I've read. This story jumps around telling bits and pieces of several arcs which had always been one of my least favorite story telling styles. Just as I get invested in one part of the story we switch to a new viewpoint,  lather, rinse, repeat. There was also the attempt to create a language and a religion both of which felt... rushed. I read and liked the book but had I started with this one I probably would have passed on any of Kaufman's other writings which would hqve bee a shame as 'All My Friends are Superheros' and 'Born Weird' were both very good... and better than this book.

title: Too Short
text: Wait? It's over? Already? This was way too short. I blinked and it was over. The writing was good, perhaps some of Wil Wheaton's best but I'd really like to see him branch out into something that doesn't come off like a blog post for the week. Still, this solidly puts Wil Wheaton on my list of authors to look out for.

title: Could Have been Much Better
text:
We've had better coloring books. True we've also had worse. The designs in this book are too repetitive to truly be fun. You get a large group of the same butterfly on a page. Then the same butterflies blown up so there are fewer on the page. Next the same butterfly with a flower. After that the repeating starts over with another different butterfly.

We're just not happy with the way this coloring book was padded out and we would have liked more variety instead of repetitiveness. Still, they are fun to color so we'll color one and put it away for a bit while coloring something else and then come back to it later.

One note, while the designs are printed on the facing side of the pages only if you plan on using markers I highly recommend using a backing board. We use the thin cardboard from an old calendar. The pages are reasonably thick but not thick enough to prevent bleed through.

title: The Series is Getting Better
text:
Picking up where the first novel left off Alex and his fellow escapees are soon recaptured by the evil warden and his henchmen and whisked off to `Solitary' confinement. This was pretty much given away by the title and the fact that this is a trilogy, they were going to get away that easily.

`Solitary' is somewhat better than the previous novel `Lockdown'. The suspense and tension are ramped up much higher and done better but the dialog and character development still suffer from a lack of depth. There are plot holes and inconsistencies in the story but they're not glaring so much as merely noticeable. As an example; some of the physical feats (long runs, high climbs, extreme exertion) later in the story would certainly be impossible due to the physical condition the prisoners are in.

This novel is recommended for readers in grades 7 - 9 and I think that's a good fit though it would probably also hold the interest of older students and adults. `Solitary' and the rest of the trilogy probably won't win any literary awards but they're worth reading.

title: Tries Too Hard
text:
Gibson tries too hard to be funny, often holding the joke up in the reader's face and practically yelling; "This is funny, isn't it?!", instead of letting the humor work itself out in the book. It feels more like he's gone back over an earlier version and tried to shoehorn as much comedy into it as possible. The author has talent, don't get me wrong, and with some polish and some practice and maybe a little less heavy of a hand I think it's safe bet that he has a good chance to turn out some fine writing. Unfortunately 'Stuff of Legends' feels more like a parody OF fantasy novels than a novel on it's own. Sadly it's not an 'Airplane' quality parody but more a 'Scary Movie IV' quality. I blame Hollywood and their incessant and increasingly bad parody movies..

I honestly didn't like the majority of characters in 'Stuff of Legends'; Eliott is a twit, a fifteen year old who still plays with dolls and acts more like an 11 year old girl seeing her favorite boy band at the mall than someone growing up in the places and settings of this novel.
Kess is an immortal elf (why are elves immortal?) who is Eliott's baby sitter, this relationship is never fully or reasonably explained, who is also something of a twit giving magic far too powerful to a child who has no connection with reality.
Jordan the Red I somewhat liked. He's grumpy, retired and just wants to be left alone. Unfortunately too much of the "LOOK THIS IS THE FUNNY PART" bits revolve around his character.
The rest of the players in the book are just filler to get the story from point A to point B, unremarkable, two dimensional, forgettable.

The world it's written into is a mishmash of mythologies & geographies never quite saying it's 'Earth' but at the same time mentioning Egypt and other locations on our planet. Also, one of my biggest pet peeves, the book brings modern things into a fantasy setting. Using 'cool' from the 1950's, the dollar as a monetary unit and going as far as to mention CPR just feels weird in a setting with swords and dragons.

title: Strange Brew - Audio Book Review
text:
This was my first and probably my last foray into audio books. I've discovered that I don't drive long enough distances to make listening to an audio book a viable form of entertainment. Even the shortest of short stories took several weeks to listen to as I only get out and drive short distances a couple times per week. I've also found that there's few other places to take advantage of audio books. You can't watch TV and listen to a book. You can't read a book and listen to a book and, for me at least, sitting around the house staring at the walls while being read to was incredibly boring. No one has read to me since I was five years old.

Like most collections of short stories, especially these days when they seem to be on the increase, some are hits, more are misses and a few are just... there. Butcher's story was an amusing side story about his famous wizard Harry Dresden. Harris' story was ok but not something you couldn't live without ever hearing.

What I'd really like to address, as a first timer with audio books, is the packaging and presentation. The discs are numbered but not, for some unknown reason, labeled with their contents or who's doing the reading. There is no accompanying literature with the packaging. While you can fix the labeling problem with a marker I don't really see why you should have to. Putting the story title and narrator on the corresponding disc can't be that expensive, can it? Maybe this is the way a lot of audio book packages are sold, being my first I have no experience in the matter, but I just wasn't impressed with the package as a whole. I think I'll stick to paper from now on.

title: Bite me... *sigh*
text:
I had a hard time writing this review. I also had a hard time reading 'Bite Me: A Love Story' it felt more like a chore than a pleasure. This is the third book in Christopher Moore's vampire saga and the seconds best of the bunch. 'Bloodsucking Fiends: A Love Story', the first book, blew me away. It was dark, funny, laugh out loud writing with romantic twist. Then came 'You Suck: A Love Story'... Maybe it was the twelve years in between sequels but You Suck which I'd happily anticipated wasn't all that. It introduced the character Abby Normal. A character so obnoxious she alone quadrupled the time it took to read the second book just by being in the story and being so annoying.

Not only is Abby back in 'Bite Me: A Love Story' the books is FULL of Abby and she's like, annoying... horribly annoying. Pages and pages of 'net speak and Valley Girl style slang mixed with fake hip-hop/ghetto talk. It's all like, horrible. Abby, it appears, is blogging her adventures. If I never see the word 'Kayso in print again I'll be a happy reader.

'Kayso, the story here IS better than the story in You Suck. The characters (except for Abby) seem more rounded and fleshed out. The story moves well and the conclusion (you can almost see the question mark creepily fade in after 'The End' at the end of the book) was, for me, completely unexpected.

'Kayso, sadly Abby and Abby alone drops this from a four (plus) star book to a three star rating (really three and a half.).

And I'm all, "Seriously, Chris, what were you thinking?"

title: I Slept with Joey Ramone: A Review
text:
When I first finished this book I put it down and thought to myself 'That Joey Ramone was a real nasty guy to his friends and family.' Then I began to think about things and realize he wasn't around to refute the claims of shoddy treatment by his brother Mickey. To some people he was a saint to others he wasn't. In all honesty the truth is probably somewhere in the middle and will never come to light.

I enjoyed the beginning of the book, the family's early years and the photographs that went with them far more than the 'Woe is Mickey' travails that seem to fill the latter sections.

I enjoyed the Ramones as a band but was never a fanatic about them. To me the book was a bit boring and a hard read. Perhaps to hard-core fans of the band this would appeal more.

title: A 'Return Policy' Review
text:
I wanted to give this book two stars. There were that many things wrong with it. But I kept reading and wanted to finish it to find out what happens. For that and that alone I'm giving it three stars.

The book's written in the first person, a technique very few authors pull off well and to me is, more often than not, detrimental to the story. The narrative also jumps from viewpoint to viewpoint, chapter to chapter amongst the three main characters of the story. This device is becoming more popular and I've always found it annoying. As you settle in with what Character A is doing you then jump to someone else's viewpoint.

My biggest problem with the book is one of the main plot devices; Willy Finneran's arrest, trial and conviction were ludicrous. They heavily draw the three characters of the book together, two would never had met otherwise, and it could NOT, ever have happened as written. It's wholly, entirely unbelievable. It isn't even implausible it's impossible. As written the scene with Children's Services is also entirely impossible. Child Services will not show up at your door, hand you a kid and say "This is yours, bye!" it doesn't work that way. These utter impossibilities hurt the story badly for me.

As badly as it was hurt, and it took me a couple days to pick the novel back up after getting annoyed with the above twists. I DID finish reading it and I didn't hate the novel. A bit of research, a week of watching Law & Order re-runs even, could have smoothed out the implausible parts and made it a far better story.

title: Not very exciting...
text:
First I have to say I respect the courage and dedication it took to complete the task of rowing across the Atlantic Ocean. That being said I just wasn't impressed by the story. I recommend not looking at the end papers they give away the gist of the story. The writing was good but flat, the thrill, the sense of excitement and danger that should exist in such a tale just aren't conveyed well or at all. All in all the story is rather bland and a bit boring.
I also honestly have to say I didn't like the Roz Savage I met in this book. At an early age during a trip to California she became convinced that materialism was the solution to everything, she also became hooked on self-help and quick fix nonsense books. She carried on a year long affair while married and when the affair is exposed and her husband doesn't toss her out she's relieved. She then turns around and makes plans to run away and start a new life with her boyfriend. Those plans she almost immediately given up on as well. While preparing for the journey she take up with an employee of the boatyard outfitting her craft who's half her age. At her first job she makes a simple mistake, wasting all of an hour, and she "never recovered [her] confidence". I was also confused that all her inner voices, 'self-doubt', 'self-critical', 'competitive' and 'guilt' are all referred to as being male. She's having a mid life crisis and looking for anything to fill some void she has inside her. I just wasn't impressed with her as a person and that, more than anything, detracted from the story.

title: Lockdown: Escape From Furnace - Book One
text:
Framed for murder fourteen year old Alex Sawyer is sentenced to life without the chance of parole in Furnace, a maximum security penitentiary built a mile underground (much like [[ASIN:B00005O5B6 Fortress]]) specifically for youthful offenders. Watched over by vicious, uncaring, silver eyed guards who are backed up by super dog-creatures ([[ASIN:B0002VEUV2 The Chronicles of Riddick (Widescreen Unrated Director's Cut)]]) and a warden who embodies evil there seems to be little hope offered to the inmates until Alex and friends form a daring escape plot.

On the narrative... The book is written in the first person. I rarely like books written from this point of view, it's often too narrow leaving out parts that could add to the story because the narrator didn't experience them. Beyond that we have to assume the narrator wins, survives, gets rescued, etc. simply because the manuscript exists.

I found the story line somewhat unbelievable. Children in what has to be the worst prison environment since Andersonville? Fed rotting slop and used for hideous biological experiments? I just can't see it ever happening.

That being said it's not a BAD book. It's unfortunately also not a great book. But it did keep me engaged. I'll be willing to check out the sequel to find out what happens next.

title: Just a Step-by-Step Manual
text:
I went into this with a tiny bit of coding experience and an open mind as I really would like to learn Swift/Xcode. I thought this would be more geared toward the coding aspect, but barely any of the code was really explained.
This book was a tutorial on how to make apps, and it allowed you to use Xcode to do that. I was able to make a few apps with step by step instructions. However, for example, the author would say "type in this code and put it here" and give a super brief, 1 or 2 sentence explanation as to why he did that. As a beginner to IOS and Swift, I have really no idea what the code means or why it was put there.
Other things like the actions, outlets, etc were explained well, stuff you would normally find in Xcode I guess. I just wish that the actual code that was given was more thoroughly explained instead of having the reader build an app and having no idea why the code worked the way it did.

I guess my suggestion would be to not put so many tutorials in the book and instead focus and expand on a few different types.

title: Was discontinued by NIST in 2018, but has some nuggets of good information
text:
I was provided a copy of the book by the company for which I work. It had been already withdrawn by NIST when I received this book, and unknown to my employer it was available for free download directly from NIST. That said, it does contain some extremely useful and still relevant information about CPIC itself. For that reason I rated it higher than I usually would for a book that was so out of date.

The main information that I found useful is the section on legislative and regulatory environment. I also liked the succinct discussions on prioritization, business case requirements, and related materials that can be used for any capital planning scenario, as well as the investment control activities. In that respect, even if you are not specifically concerned about integrating CPIC into security, you can still learn a lot about CPIC itself from a practical level from this book.

For me the main reason why this book continues to remain on my book shelf is the examples it provides in imparting information. I have learned more about information display from its tables and diagrams than I have from its CPIC-specific content. A case in point, the discussion of enterprise-level prioritization can be effectively used as a framework for prioritizing portfolios of any type. It is a complex subject, but this book distills all of the salient points into a few pages that are reinforced by illustrations.

title: Good info wrapped in some fluff
text:
The company for which I work provided me with a copy of this book. I am one of the TBM (and CPIC) consulting managers, so I already had a background in the subject matter.

I'll get the negative out of the way: parts of this book read like an infomercial for TBM. It detracted from some excellent information that the book also imparted. And although I was familiar with the overall material, I did come away with some insights and ideas that I had not considered in the past. In that respect reading this book was not a waste of time.

Personally, the book seems to not have a truly targeted audience. Some of the material is obviously of more use to executives, and some seems more useful to folks in the trenches, The problem is large portions of the book will be of interest to one or the other of those audiences.

If I had to characterize this book I would have to say that it is more concept and selling the concept than concrete implementation details. Of course, it does not pretend to be an implementation guide, but I am sure prospective buyers will have some expectations that it will provide at least a roadmap. On the other hand, there are some thought-provoking nuggets of information that is wrapped into some ponderous reading.

title: Needed for ITIL implementation & exams
text:
This is a necessary resource for either implementing the ITIL, or for anyone who is preparing for the certification exam. The focus of this guide is on the infrastructure and operational aspects of IT, and how security relates to service support and service delivery.
Note that this guide does not provide guidance for an enterprise-wide security posture, nor does it cover security from the security officer's perspective. However, the guidance provided needs to be integrated into an overall security program, and associated policies and procedures. Another fact worth noting is this book is circa 1999. Given the general nature of the material, though, this does not diminish the value of the content.
Key ITIL areas that the material in this book does address include: problem management (from the ITIL Service Support process areas), and business continuity planning, financial management, and service level management (from the ITIL Service Delivery process areas).
While this book's main value is to organizations implementing ITIL, or individuals pursuing certification, there is one aspect that does stand out - the way security is linked to service level agreements is an outstanding approach that is often overlooked outside of ITIL shops, and is a practice that should be incorporated in SLAs and included in service level management plans.

title: ITIL-specific approach
text:
If you are an ITIL practitioner, or are studying for certification this book outlines the approach to risk, which is especially applicable to the Service Delivery process areas related to service continuity management and availability management, as well as security management. It also has wider applications within the ITIL processes, but those are three two where it is directly related.
The book covers basic principles, and defines a fairly standard risk management framework that includes identification, evaluation and countermeasures. The material stratifies risk management at the strategic, program and project, and operational levels. These are also consistent with the PRINCE2 approach.
In addition to the risk framework, processes and procedures, this book also provides a business case template, and outlines for business continuity, communications and contingency plans, plus policy and process examples.
Highly useful to ITIL practitioners who want complete alignment to the ITIL set of processes, but otherwise only marginally useful outside that domain.

title: Weakest of ITIL series
text:
This ITIL guide is the weakest of the series because the approach is outmoded with respect to contemporary development life cycles. The chapters address the following key areas and follow the older waterfall SDLC:
(1) Requirements
(2) Design
(3) Build
(4) Deploy
(5) Operate
(6) Optimize
The latter three milestones - deploy, operate and optimize - spill over into service management covered in the Service Delivery and Service Support guides in the series. In that respect this guide does provide a comprehensive picture of applications delivery, and service and support delivery.
If you are pursuing ITIL certification you will need this guide, despite the shortcomings I noted because the material will be part of the exams. However, if you are only exploring ITIL as a viable framework for your organization I would bypass this book unless/until you decided to actually implement ITIL and/or pursue certification.

title: A lot of in info in a pamphlet
text:
On my first pass through this book I concluded that it was filled with inaccurate information and was not a book that I'd recommend. However, after thinking about it and rereading it I came to the firm conclusion that this is one of the most valuable resources available to the new technical support professional.

Why the 180 degree change in opinion? There are two major reasons - (1) it covers the essentials, such as tiered support, escalation and service level management, and (2) it gives excellent advice about setting user expectations. In fact, it ties these two key elements together in a coherent manner.

What I did not like (at first) was some of the definitions, such as support tiers, that the author provided. I realized that unless one is well versed in the ITIL (IT Infrastructure Library) and iSMF (International Service Management Forum) approaches (both of which are collaborative and completely aligned to one another), definitions are not as relevant as the principles - and the principles are the most difficult to grasp. To that end this book shines because it is an easy read and demystifies some of the more complex principles of technical support, and does so with clear writing.

If you are new to technical support I recommend that you read this book first before tackling some of the more detailed books on the subject, such as "IT Problem Management" by Gary S. Walker and Harris Kern (ISBN 013030770X) or "IT Service Management: An Introduction" Jan Van Bon (ISBN 9080671347), both of which will build upon the foundation laid in this book.

title: Some excelllent, but obfuscated ideas
text:
This book is manages to both delight and disappoint. The delight comes from the interesting perspective the author brings to modeling, and his obvious deep understanding of UML and its strengths and weaknesses. It disappoints because the writing is marred by overly academic format (copious footnotes and stilted language), and some disorganization.
Highlights include incorporating business rules, modeling and viewpoints to develop a business model that integrates IT and business. While the author appears to be going in the right direction, especially by touching on what I consider to be the major critical success factors and techniques, he manages to weaken this book by putting a non-standard spin on the topics. For example, his view of business rules seems to be more in line with what he proposed in his earlier book titled "Business Specifications", instead of the more mainstream approach that is well documented in Tony Morgan's "Business Rules and Information Systems" and Barbara Von Halle's "Business Rules Applied". The modeling approach itself departs from standard UML, even though the author does make a good case for doing so. The problem is that by sticking with an established standard, regardless of shortcomings, you will be consistent with accepted practices that are understood throughout industry. Going with the author's approach means a learning curve for your own staff as well as consultants, and serious problems when attempting to use mainstream tools, such as Rational Rose, to instantiate the business models.
I recommend this book to advanced practitioners in business modeling who want to mine some excellent ideas that are interwoven throughout, but do not recommend it to anyone who wants to learn business modeling.

title: Out-of-date; useful in areas for non-ISO 9001 shops
text:
This book is a good step-by-step description of 1994 version of ISO 9001 as it relates to software.
Book strengths are: (1) Not bogged down with history, the politics of standards or doom and gloom if you do not employ ISO 9001 as a foundation of software quality, (2)you are taken through the key elements of ISO 9001 and shown how to develop a quality manual, project quality plans and process documentation and (3) the conformance checklist, which will greatly aid you in sorting out what needs to be addressed.
Book weaknesses: Out of date (published in 1995 and only addresses ISO 9001 circa 1994).
This is still a valuable book for organizations that want to implement a quality foundation, particularly with respect to document control and repeatability in procedures. If you do purchase this book to assist you in pursuing ISO 9001 registration for software and services I strongly recommend augmenting it with "ISO 9001:2000 Explained" by Cianfrani, Tsiakals and West. That book will bring the material up to the 2000 version of ISO 9001. Also consider "ISO 9000-3: A Tool for Software Product and Process Improvement" by Raymond Kehoe, et al, which is a more comprehensive treatment of the subject (note that this book also is out of date with respect to the 2000 version of ISO 9001).

title: Has potential to be great - lacks coherency & focus
text:
This could have been *the* definitive reference on operational support systems. The author's uneven treatment of the subject and tendency to frequently go off topic or emphasize peripheral systems while leaving large gaps in the main subject have reduced this book to merely mediocre.
The strong points: the chapter on customer care and billing processes is remarkable. Here is a list of things that caught my attention and make this chapter so valuable: (1) the customer care maturity model is well thought out and serves as an excellent benchmarking tool, (2) the customer analysis and acquisition is on the mark, and (3) the customer interface management process and associated diagram comprise an excellent model for OSS processes. I also thought the way the author covered the problem handling process represents best practices, as does the section on SLA management. This is the stuff OSS is made of and it's covered both well and contains ideas and models in which service providers will be interested. The chapter provisioning and order processing is also strong and filled with excellent information for those who are seeking OSS-specific knowledge.
Weaknesses: Not only does this book overemphasize the network operations, which is important, but not central, but the author manages to drop this information into unexpected areas throughout the book. An example: Section 4.4 is an engrossing piece on the sales process that is succinct and filled with information, including tables and a diagram that reinforce the excellent information the author is imparting. Right in the middle of all this is a diagram that shows the use of a DMZ to separate intranets and extranets - not something anyone interested in sales processes cares about and is a big distraction. This happens throughout the book. Also, I agree with the comments made by a previous reviewer about wasting page count on product-specific information. This information needs to be moved to a web site where it can be maintained in an up-to-date fashion. Ironically, the publisher does this for other books. Finally, there are some major gaps: (1) no mention of the TeleManagement Forum, which is a global non-profit organization that is devoted to OSS. This organization has a technology integration map and numerous OSS-related processes that are De Facto standards in the OSS world, yet no mention of the organization and no mention of the wealth of material available that is directly related to OSS. (2) Section 7.4, which addresses migration from an existing to new billing system, misses some key considerations, which could have been developed into a discussion of strengths and weaknesses. For example, how do you segment and migrate subscribers? By CSA? Bill cycle? Region? Price plan? As the industry consolidates this particular issue keeps cropping up and a more in-depth treatment here is warranted. (3) No mention of TL 9000, which is an encompassing quality standard for telecommunications service providers. A portion of this standard applies directly to OSS.
Overall, this book contains some of the best information about OSS that has been collected and compiled into a single book. In fact, it's the only book on the subject. What is needed to make it great is a strong editor who understands OSS and who is not reticent about removing large pieces of superfluous material from this book. More information about standards that are directly related to OSS should also be included. If you work with operational support systems you really have no choice but to buy this book - I just hope that the next edition addresses the weaknesses.

title: Good for small company LANs and desktop support pros
text: This book is an uneven collection of articles, tips and techniques that is more applicable to a PC-centric computing and desktop office automation.  It's a great resource for small companies or workgroup administrators, but is a bit too light for enterprise-wide security.  If you are the LAN administrator for a small company that uses consumer operating systems and applications, such as Microsoft's Windows family, you will find this book to be an invaluable source of information.  If you are responsible for security in a larger multi-platform enterprise, especially one that spans multiple locations and is dependent upon business-critical applications and e-commerce or ERP suites, you will probably find this book too lite and not slanted towards the issues that you need to address.  If you call into the latter group I strongly recommend CERT Guide to System and Network Security Practices by Julia Allen.

title: An old friend that has aged gracefully
text:
Although this book is showing its age it remains one of the very few available books on data center operations. The foundation is three timeless concepts: (1) data is a resource, (2) data processing (or in more contemporary terms, systems management) is a service function, and (3) data processing is a production business.
Despite the slant towards "Big Blue" platforms and operating systems and the non-automated processes provided in this book, there are still valuable practices that can be gleaned, given a modern facelift and incorporated into client/server and e-commerce operations. For example, Section Two contains a wealth of information on achieving stable production processes that are as applicable in a modern data center as they were when this book was written. The best piece in this section is on component failure analysis, which is one of the most cogent approaches to building a high-availability foundation that I've come across. I also like the emphasis on problem and change management. Although the processes are manual, they are well thought out and are a good model for a most up-to-date and automated solution.
The section on production controls is on the mark from the standpoint of process, but out of date with respect to examples. However, you can glean a lot of information and ideas from the basics and build upon them using today's technology. The fundamentals and concepts are sound.
Overall, this book is something of a paradox - on the one hand it is nearly quaint, and on the other it contains practices that I fear are being quickly lost, yet still sorely needed in order to effectively manage operations in a large enterprise. I bought my copy when it first came out in 1989 and still refer to it from time to time. Considering how many obsolete books that I've donated to local libraries while steadfastly refusing to give this one up. I'm strongly recommending it despite its age, but am giving it 3 stars because of its age.

title: Disappointing for testing pros - OK for managers & PMs
text:
This book does not contain any useful information for software test professionals. It is little more than a whitepaper that takes a ten-thousand foot view of web testing and why it should be done, with lightweight examples.
However, this book does highlight activities and milestones that are essential to deploying web-based solutuions. From this point of view it does have value for managers and PMs who are responsible for making a business case for web-based projects.
For professional testers I recommend either Testing Applications on the Web by Hung Quoc Nguyen or Client Server Testing on the Desktop and Web by Daniel J. Mosley.
For project sponsors and project managers this book would nicely augment Web Project Management: Delivering Successful Commercial Web Sites by Ashley Friedlein.

title: Not what I expected
text: I'm debating sending it back, this is kind of different than what I expected. I was hoping to get some large map sections and whats available on each exit. This is more of a phone book covering highways/exits and all, but it seems very confusing and not easy to read!? I'll ponder over it some more and see if it grows on me.

title: Average
text: An average mystery. The characters are average. The plot is average. The settings are average. In short, the book is totally unremarkable.

title: eh!
text: not really much to it. a very short diversion. I gave it a 3 because it was slightly amusing but i wouldn't buy it again.

title: The system here is a bit broken and we have the usual dungeon core flaw
text:
The usual dungeon core flaw is that the spirit that controls the dungeon core ends up being a heartless almost soulless entity that exists more as a part of the plot than a true character. And strangely that is exactly what I ended up feeling about Rick and his fellow hired cores Freja and Salter.

The idea here is wonderful. A MMO that is struggling to keep players decides to playtest a new variant where individual players will build and populate a dungeon, receiving experience for every delver they kill. Of course the company hires main character Rick as well as two others Freja and Salter to run the playtest dungeons.

And that is about all we learn about the characters themselves. They give a bit of backstory, but the never interact outside of messages in the game while they are running their individual dungeons or planning out upgrades/changes. Rick could have been a special AI, an intelligent monkey or an alien and the story would not really have changed much. His personality doesn't come out at all in this tale.

And the rules for dungeon formation and adding monsters was not well defined, and I'd argue poorly thought out. The "mana" values for everything appeared to be arbitrary and designed to generate problems to be solved without giving us a good view under the hood into the costs and balances of the system. It ended up feeling broken, but then again the way several of the delves went made it clear that it very much was broken.

Still, I enjoyed the read. The idea is not unique overall as the dungeon core genre has been around for a while, and once you get past the reason Rick became a core the mechanics are fairly standard overall. But there was a bit of imagination used and even a couple of good humor moments in a genre that rarely has any.

I give this a high 3 stars. I might not get a sequel should one come out, but its not bad and better than many dungeon core books I have encountered. I just wish it had managed to overcome the lack of character problem that is so common in the genre.

title: Typical Logan Jacobs tale.  The characters aren't dynamic
text:
My main complaint about Logan Jacobs tales is that the characters tend to be limited. And because of those limits I end up bored reading his tales. I don't dislike anything about them, but they just fail to keep me interested.

I think its partly based on the lack of depth to the world and the characters. The backstories for the characters exist, but largely just to be commented on. I rarely see a moment where the backstory results in a character acting a certain way. The world also isn't built out as well as it could be. The people occupying towns and buildings that the main character visits have little to no story attached, or if they do, its not weaved into the plot and instead is a temporary departure from the tale that doesn't add to the development of the main characters.

Logan is a talented writer, and he has a good editor so his stories read easily. I just don't find his stories compelling. They are readable, but I never love the characters or the plot.

This is another 3 star.

title: Bleh, the twists didn't work for me.
text:
This story has a number of plot twists. We do get to learn a bit more about the main character and about events that occured before book 1 in this series. This was impressive. The amount of backstory was something that I like to see. I always like when an author has put effort into developing his characters and giving them life.

Unfortunately while I like the main character and the backstory he has, the stories of his students did not engage with me. Worse, this entire tale is based on a great betrayal. The people involved and the excuses just did not work for me. I wanted to enjoy the story, but it felt like it broke down the characters in a less than impressive way.

The twists definitely changed my impression of the entire series. I want to give this a higher score, but sadly I can only give it 3 stars. Its well written, and there is a lot of effort into the plot. Unfortunately the plot just doesn't work for me.

title: No real sports, characters with no depth
text:
I've read many books and series written by Simon Archer. He is one of a small group of authors who specialize in quickly written harem tales that are clearly written for a rather specific audience. I'll admit that I'm not part of the core audience he writes for.

And I have some rather consistent complaints about his books. His plots tend to barely have any foundation and exist largely to allow the singular male character to meet and have sex with a number of plastic female characters who lack personality and agency. Honestly, the female characters in his stories tend to be less free to move than a lion in too small of a cage. Its frightening to think about just how limited his characters end up.

And this tale is just that. Supposedly its about some mathematical genius who uses money ball techniques to track football and baseball so that he wins fantasy sports leagues. he winds up in a new world where the women play a sport that is a variant of rugby, volleyball, basketball and red rover. This sport makes little to no sense even before the main character discovers that anyone playing will be good/expert at one position for 400 plays and then their skills shift. This is a major plot point, but this plot is thin and actually doesn't matter by the end of the book.

I won't read book 2. This is not a bad book, but as I seem to say often, this book was not for me. I want far more character and plot in my tales.

title: I like the idea, but it felt a bit empty
text:
My biggest complaint about dungeon core tales has always been how the power given to the dungeon core twists and warps the character development. This book Monster Girl Dungeon is in many ways an excellent example of how the power given to the main character and the form of the enemy he faces resulted in the majority of the characters just not really having any.

In many ways its disappointing because while the main character gets the core accidentally it is in a way that was plausible considering the universe the author is creating. Even the decisions he makes once he is bonded to the core are largely sensible. He's trying to survive in a situation where he's already broken so many established traditions and rules that he has to take risks and rush into things.

But after that, the plot ends up without a good anchor. Yes, there is a crime lord's son trying to get the core which means he has to kill the main character. yes, the local adventurer's guild has issues with the sudden development of a new dungeon within the boundaries of the city. But both issues felt contrived rather than organic to the story. I had a hard time establishing any emotional ties to the tale because of the lack of depth in the characters and the plot.

This is a fair first story. The characters are not completely two-dimensional, and there actually was more than a little imagination put into the development of the idea. But I do think that the plot needed more time to simmer and that some editing designed to push in some character development moments and to slow down the advancement of the plot to give it some foundation and depth were needed.

Call this a high 3 star tale.

title: Its rather "meh"
text:
The problem I have with this story was similar to the ones I've had with many of these isekai harem tales. The female characters just don't have enough depth to support the rather thin plot. The villain is a bit over the top, but the motives and personality of the villain are so heavily clouded that it was hard to get into that part of the tale.

Honestly, I was just not excited. There was a clear cliffhanger ending and I find it hard to imagine reading book 3. Its not a bad book, but its just a story that is told with little flair and characters that lack depth and personality. Sorry, but a female character who has one emotional mode outside of "horny and ready to get neek'd" is not interesting to me.

If you like the genre, this is a solid tale within the genre, but as seems to be normal, I consider it no better than a 3 star.

title: Harry is not my kind of hero
text:
I ran into someone who was shocked that I did not praise this series. It was clear they were a huge fan, and their enthusiasm convinced me to try the first book.

Now I can say I understand why some people enjoy this tale. Harry's character and monologues are definitely different from most other books you'll find, and the mix of magic and a relatively modern setting is not common with a male lead. (urban fantasy reverse harem tales seem to be the rule when its a modern setting and has magic.) But while the setting was different and Harry is not meant to be a poor or boring character, I found that I was no more than ambivalent about him.

I think the problem is that Harry keeps making bad decisions throughout this tale. Add in the White Council representative who is cliche, boring and blind to justice and acts as a plot device rather than a fleshed out character, and I felt more disappointment towards the plot than pleasure at the attempt to combine magic with a film-noir mystery setting. Harry just doesn't fit my image of the tarnished paladin that you find in many noir mysteries, and I felt his lack of stature in many ways.

This wasn't a bad book, but I just didn't fall into it the way I want to with any mystery. I can only give it 3 stars.

title: is there a formula for writing this kind of Isekai?  I've read this too many times.
text:
Man gets transported to another world and has to save a group of all female characters. Its become a very popular trope in a segment of the fantasy genre, and it seems I encounter a few books every month. Occasionally I risk my sanity and pick one up.

Monster Girl Safari is not a bad book. I did finish reading it. For the genre, it was perhaps a bit above average. I don't remember hating the main character, but he was nothing special. the harem he assembles was very average for the genre, with no character who really impressed me but none that had me completely shaking my head due to them seeming to be central casting rejects.

I wish I could give this more than three stars, but while it was definitely not a bad book, it also left me shrugging overall. It just did not impress me or excite me. I read it all the way through, but am not going to get book 2.

So, if you like the genre, this will almost definitely impress.

title: Someday I'll prevent myself from picking up a book from an author I have reservations about.
text:
This was one of two books I picked up from different authors that I've read before. Both authors write largely what I've started to call incel harem fantasy. The main characters are almost never impressive in any way and largely passive early on. The tales tend to be isekai (man pulled into another universe) and the females he runs into tend to have extremely bland personalities while at the same time having the morality of a lawyer dying of some terrible wasting disease.

The strangest thing was that the two books are so similar that I could almost copy and paste this review into that one, as both involve a youngish man who happens to have a job as a long-haul trucker driving through a portal into a new world, meeting a beautiful woman who attaches herself to him, receiving a ton of gemstones as a gift, and their starting a new trade of gems to a pawn shop in the US for items they can resell/use in the fantasy world that they are now able to enter and exit when the story calls for it.

Ok, that's oversimplified, but that's what it felt like. And as I already said, the main character in Monster Girl Trucker is horrible. When we first meet him he's worried about the fact that his father hates that he is a driver, although his deceased grandfather's stories were what convinced him to try. Worse while he's driving through Nevada he gets lost. (In Nevada, while on a long run? Nevada doesn't have the kind of highway network that you could unless you are dumber than your average rock.) He was not really unlikeable, but he was still not impressive and his antics regarding his truck kept me from suspending my disbelief.

Now I have to admit that his first harem participant had a reason to join him. The catgirl wanted out of the little truckstop she was stuck at so she trades repairs/upgrades on the truck in exchange for a ride. It might have worked, but once she's riding with him her personality just froze. Honestly she never seemed to bring much to the tale. And the dialogue was just bad, even when they met with a few more of the isekai world's inhabitants.

Lovers of this kind of fiction will enjoy this tale, but its definitely no better than average even for the genre. I can just barely give this 3 stars. I knew that I had been avoiding the author for a reason, but took a risk, and eventually regretted allowing Amazon to convince me that this book just might interest me.

title: A quick reminder to me of why I dislike this author
text:
This was one of two books I picked up from different authors that I've read before. Both authors write largely what I've started to call incel harem fantasy. The main characters are almost never impressive in any way and largely passive early on. The tales tend to be isekai (man pulled into another universe) and the females he runs into tend to have extremely bland personalities while at the same time having the morality of a lawyer dying of some terrible wasting disease.

The strangest thing was that the two books are so similar that I could almost copy and paste this review into that one, as both involve a youngish man who happens to have a job as a long-haul trucker driving through a portal into a new world, meeting a beautiful woman who attaches herself to him, receiving a ton of gemstones as a gift, and their starting a new trade of gems to a pawn shop in the US for items they can resell/use in the fantasy world that they are now able to enter and exit when the story calls for it.
