text:
In my opinion this series has really gone downhill from the first book. I think the problem is especially easy to spot here.

Ozma has the potential to be a great character, but she's become a bit too much of the "I need something to perform X action" problem solver. Need to find a person, no problem she can magic up a fishbowl complete with fish and you have a special compass that points to the person. Need disguises, she has special glasses. Need to survive a long fall, she has several tricks in her bag. It does keep the story moving, but... its just too overpowered for the world in my opinion.

Shelly the computer program that goes anywhere is another item that seems to be great in very small doses, but which quickly becomes a frustrating plot force.

And this tale once again became more about Hope investigating a problem than truly fighting evil, although in this story she ran into set piece fight after set piece fight. Honestly, this seemed to read like a proposed script for some strange Matrix ripoff rather than a tight superhero action adventure.

I'll admit that my feelings are biased by my tastes in stories and characters. I'm not a huge fan of Shelly or Ozma and I absolutely hate Kitsune, so this tale kept frustrating me. I ended up thinking that it was going the wrong direction, but I could also see what Marion was trying to do. I just think he once again proved that he needs to write the adventure parts and avoid trying to write investigation/mystery tales. Hope doesn't play well in that environment and the plot twists end up feeling obvious and predictable.

I think this could have been far better. I can only give it 3 stars. Its still a fun read, but I can't say I liked it or would ever recommend it.

title: Plots are repetitive enough to annoy me.
text:
I hate to write this review, but I feel I have to. R.J. Ross started out writing of an unusual and largely interesting world where heroes and villains worked together to put on a show for the rest of the world while they worked together to stop the true supervillains who endangered everyone.

She populated the world with some interesting characters and put all the teenagers in a special school that seemed to be wrong but at the same time perfect for what was needed.

As a formula, it worked well.

The problem I had with Super Villain Grandpa, is that in so many ways it felt like I was reading previous books in the series. The "grandpa" was not much different from the Super Villain Dad from book 1, (and there were plot points around that.).

The villains were also a problem. The main one is so obvious at times that I had to shake my head. I've read about terminally ill lemmings that had more sense of self preservation than a couple of these villains, and it hurt.

Honestly, I think R.J. needs to stop writing teenage origin stories, which is basically what all 14 of her books are. Each time she publishes one it introduces in depth one or two characters. Its usually one who recently was a minor player in the plot of the previous 2-3 books. However, with the exception of book 13 (which annoyed me for other reasons) each book seems to forget older characters in the endless "I want to introduce new characters" drive.

If you like the series and the style of the previous books, this is worth it, but its nothing you haven't read before with characters that had a different name and slightly different power.

I DON'T recommend this book. R.J.'s constant use of the same plot devices made this a disappointment. Only if you truly love the series would I get this book

title: Flat story that should/could have been a lot better.
text:
Ex-Heroes did the zombie v superhero tale much better, and this one only compounded the problem by trying to make it an elitest rich ruling class humans v exiled superheroes v zombies mystery with very little action.

The lack of action really was the main problem. The character is interesting, but with no action around him and his powers being way too flexible the story fell flat.

title: Am I supposed to care?
text:
Missy wrote an interesting tale. The main character is a powerless desk jockey who stumbles into a conspiracy group aiming to expose the heroes failings.

It's a great idea. Its a wonderful plot foundation.

It didn't really work.

Sadly, while the idea is great, I couldn't get into the characters and the whirlwind ending to this "book 1" was such a rollercoaster ride of insanity that I felt disappointed when I got to the ending not because it ended, but because it failed to make me want to see the ending. I just didn't care as much as I should have at the end.

I'm interested in where Missy Meyer takes this tale, but as a stand-alone novel I have to call this one a narrow miss.

title: Too much power, too little character and plot.
text:
One complaint I often find I have with any story about "superheroes" is what I call the "over the top" powerlevels. An author will seem to decide to hide problems developing plot or character by ramping up the powerlevels until my ability to suspend my disbelief is gone.

Sadly, that is what happened in this story. Not just in the powerlevels, but in the intrigue of the schemes. The villain here is almost (in my opinion) deliberately unreal. I'm sure part is due to the fact that from the start the city the story is based in makes the most lawless cities of today look like beacons of civic virtue led A.K. Sinquefield to decide to make the villain into the worst possible being to walk the Earth.

I can accept that. I can almost forgive it. If the characters developed and grew, but while the story does cover an interesting if very cliché origin story, the central conflict seems to be half sideline until the climax which was so convoluted and complicated that at one point I had to stop reading while I allowed my anger at the way the story was twisting to fade. It just was that over the top and forced.

Interesting idea, and the characters are likable if way to bland and indistinct. If you love superhero tales this might be one you like. Otherwise its really about a 2.6 star story and probably won't thrill most readers.

title: Strong start dissolves into just another story.
text:
I was offered a free copy in exchange for a review.

That said I'll get into the meat of the review.

This was a story that started out with a lot of potential. The basic premise was strong and Chris the narrative character was a solid "everyman" type character. The plot appeared to have lots of room for character growth.

Unfortunately as Casey added more plot twists and events the story began to sink under the weight of the plot. There were just too many little additions to the story that Casey tries to sneak in. It overwhelmed any character development.

And that was what I remember most when I reached the end. I wasn't happy to see the ending, or sad to think that my journey with the characters was done, but rather just tired of the story. I couldn't hate the various villains, who were too often faceless and invisible. Which was a problem in itself. If the villains are largely faceless and invisible they can become too unreal for any suspension of disbelief. That was a major factor here. The way the bad guys were presented eventually reached a point where I just didn't care because I wasn't immersed in the story. It was almost as if I was reading an old science or computer science textbook, although it wasn't meant to be that dry.

Casey is clearly a talented author. Chris started out appearing to be a strong and interesting character and the "voice" used by the author is compelling, but the story needs to both carry the characters as well as be carried by them. This story manages neither. The plot is too complex to lift characters that don't have strong foundations while at the same time the lack of focus on the characters meant they couldn't really carry the plot through the many twists.

This will be a good read for lovers of superhero fiction as its close to being a four star, but I do warn that the story fades badly in the last third

title: Good action book, but skips a bit on plot and character.
text:
I have to start out by saying that Mike noticed my reviews and challenged me to read this book and review it saying that it would prove to be better than some other books I read recently.

In that he was correct. This book despite a description that left me wondering what it was about proved to be a fun, light read.

Mike demonstrated skill at setting an environment and establishing the foundation for his characters. He knew who his characters were and what they were going to be doing. It made for a book that it was possible to get into quickly and made it so that I did want to find out what happened to the main character Lily.

However, I find that there are some flaws in the presentation that made me downgrade this story to 3 stars. They are not major, but I expect some readers will find them to be perplexing or even minor turnoffs.

First, while the characters clearly have strong backgrounds and foundations, this rarely came out in the book. Mike wrote as if you already knew these characters and would require very little exposition about them. This was especially noticeable with the villain who was clearly a psychopath, but the reasons and motivations for this were clouded until very late in the storyline.

Second, early on there are near constant references to recent movies and other elements of pop culture. It was vaguely amusing the first time, but this happened multiple times over a small section of the book and I found it a bit excessive. It's nice that Mike wanted to let me know what kind of books and movies he loves, but he didn't need to beat me over the head with that information and it felt like he had.

My final issue would have been just how slow the book started. I was 20% in before the action really got going and when it does you jump in like you are at the top of a rollercoaster and never going to reach the bottom of the first slope. The second half of the book especially is a wild adrenaline rush, and makes the story fascinating.

It's a solid effort and definitely entertaining, but I can't consider it a great book and its definitely not a classic a reader will bring out year after year. For lovers of action films and stories this will be a great addition to their book collection.

title: No depth and mostly action, makes for a dull book.
text:
I can just barely give this 3 stars, and that mostly because Tim does try to humanize a couple of his characters. Unfortunately I don't really think you can humanize psychopaths, but he does try and manages to a degree. It doesn't really make them likable or the story all that readable.

However when you combine that with Tim Nolen's kinetic writing style with hell breaking out every other chapter, you end up with a tale that some will love for the action, but which in the end doesn't really fill up a reader with a lot of interesting and fun story to read.

If you like Tim Nolen's Defiant tales, or if you love action novels, this will be enjoyable. If you want deep characters, look elsewhere because despite Tim putting a bit more time into character development there is little of that here.

title: Ends with no closure
text:
This story ended at a break in the narrative, but unlike the first two there is no real conclusion. Instead we are left in the middle of the villains scheme.

Worse, the character development seemed to step backwards. It was already rather light considering that just about every other chapter ends with some variant of "and then all hell broke loose." Or at least seems to. However, that's no excuse to throw away all the possible character development.

It's hard to say more without revealing a ton of spoilers. All of the characters you know and love are here, including Defiant, Fade, Veer, Boost, Search, and Spark. As Homefront they get to fight one set of badguys while the A-team of this universe stumble off in search of new problems.

Honestly, this story was a bit of a disappointment. The plot felt more than a little forced and I'm getting sick of a few of the character antics. I can understand the initial thrust of some of the storylines, but more than one is getting a bit old and really ruins the possibility of me getting fully into the tale.

I really enjoyed the first book, and the second one impressed me. This third book in the series disappointed me. I worry about the next one.

title: Good first tale, but issues drag down overall rating.
text:
whenever I read a tale like this I wonder a bit about the childhood of the author. The concept here is very good, but the main character here has so many issues that at times I wonder how he can get out of bed each morning.

It seems like Tom Reynolds had a great concept, but was terrified of having his main character be considered too powerful. To compensate he made the character neurotic to the point that he makes multiple basic mistakes.

the supporting characters aren't much better. The allies our character collects are about a friendly as a rabid wolverine, berating our hero and never explaining anything adequately. The villain is completely insane and in the end the final conflict ends up almost anti-climatic both because the victory is accomplished through a cheap trick, but not even completed by the hero.

It's a good foundation for a series, and the main character could grow into the role, but for now, its no where near the level of the top books in this genre

title: Teen Angst - Oh Joy.
text:
I am suddenly reminded of why I tend to avoid urban fantasy novels, especially when they are written for the young adult market.

Of course, this wasn't labeled urban fantasy, but rather as a "superhero" novel. Well, it's basically urban fantasy with a different plot. You have the female character with great powers, but who ends up needing help from the hunky guy.

Of course the hunky guy is a mystery in some ways, with the truth to be revealed in the future.

In this case add in boarding school, a sidekick who seems to have no emotion and a girl who finds her powers gone.

I liked the plot. I liked the characters for the most part. I even liked the writing style of having all the chapters be basically entries in the lead character's diary.

I could have done without all of the angst. The worries about the possible boyfriend. The worries about the new best friend. The worries about the school. Etc.... I read to escape, and while someone might smile reading this thinking "I have a better life than this idiot". This wasn't an escape for me.

Still fun and interesting though. Although none of the plot twists was a surprise. Too much pulled from the closest of endless clichés I think.

title: Great premise.  Solid characters, Plot ran thin.
text:
The basic idea here is one I haven't seen attempted quite this way since the movie Mystery Men used satire to point out that a hero who accepts merchandising contracts could become more concerned with image than performing heroic acts. Here this conflict isn't openly brought out, but it becomes a major plot thread, interweaved with the other schemes and plans being put forth by the various villains.

Overall, the story is solid and strong. I liked the main character and several of the other "B-list" heroes and the relationships they had felt strong.

Sadly, the plot didn't hold up throughout the story. Certain twists and turns in the plot resulted in the finale feeling rushed and extremely flat. I think Daniel Jung had an idea that his ending wasn't the best as his final sentences hint that even his heroes didn't exactly feel like they had won anything.

I do look forward to more work from this author. The ideas and writing here were strong. Perhaps keeping the narrative a bit simpiler would have improved the result, but this story is still good and will please most lovers of superhero fiction.

title: Seemed to lack something
text:
I guess after reading stories like Confessions of a D-list Supervillian and Wearing the Cape I have a slightly higher standard when it comes to superhero books than others. This is an interesting story with an imaginative plot, but it seemed to lack something.

I'll admit that the main character didn't really draw me in. He does grow quite a bit through the story and as she supposedly starts out as a 12 year old, some of his immaturity is understandable, but he also ends up just too weak a personality. I was intriqued by his story, but not gripped by his trials and perils.

The rest of the cast seemed to come out of comic-book central casting. Motives were almost mindlessly simple, something that more than one character noted in the later chapters. The backstory of the universe adn the previous generations of super-villians was left remarkably undiscussed. Many of the motives seemed more pro-forma than built out of some deep elaborate character personal involvement.

THis is a fast read and definitely interesting. A teenager or a lover of comic-books will find it increbily fun to read, but someone who expects a bit more from his stories will likely end up feeling like the story isn't finished. There is just too little depth to the characters and plot to allow me to give this book more than 3 stars.

title: Disappointing
text:
I like the overall premise.

And Keeley could have been a great character.

Unfortunately, this story just doesn't come together for me. I think part of the problem was the way P.S. Power seems to hate adult men. I don't think there was a single father in the story who comes across as even slightly sympathetic. Most were venal and evil men who were mere foils for the main character and her suddenly discovered older half-sister.

The rest of the cast also plays a bit towards the "faceless cilche character". Keeley is definitely fleshed out, but beyond her the story is mostly fluff. I had a hard time finding the main plot thread and the story meanders around at times. It was almost as if P.S. Power wasn't sure where she wanted to take the story. I never got a feeling that the events being described were for a specific reason and they just appeared to be occuring to move the story along.

This might be because this is the first book in a series and P.S. Power was attempting to set up future plot lines, which is what the story felt like. But if its going to be a setup piece, the characters have to be much more engaging. I found this story interesting, but not engaging, and I have yet to decide if I'll pick up book two. Currently I'm not looking at getting it anytime soon.

title: A Story dragged out a bit too far
text:
The first book in this series "Here be Dragons" was a fun read despite the fact that the plot was about as close to outlandish fantasy as any I have encountered. The main political conflict seemed over-the-top. I had remembered a similar basic plot in a book called Gryphon that I'd ready back in the early 1990's.

However, the characters made up for that.

Unfortunately, Against the Tide is the third book in the series and the plot is wearing very thin. By now the seemingly endless villians felt almsot impossible to beleive in. IN this story we finally get a glimpse into the mind of the "mastermind" who started the initial conflict that lead to the master computer shutting down all power. And the truth is that I found it nearly impossible to believe that he could have managed the near coup.

The transformational tech used on people also got to be a bit too much. By now the villians are using it on nearly everyone they capture and "breeding" mroe warriors, but the small band of free warriors are managing to win battle after battle despite being out-manned and unable to use any similar technology.

This is an interesting read, but I can't really recommand it to anyone who isn't in lose with the first two books and the basic subject matter. It seems to read mroe like a twisted way for a writer who loves military history to rewrite historical battle using orcs, goblins, wyverns, dragons and other cratures of fantasy.

It's fun to read, but nowhere near great

title: Fun, but fluffy
text:
Ah, this was a nice story, with lots of fluff.

Unfortunately, fluff in this case was empty characters, empty plot twists and in general a storyline that lacked gravitas and emotion, despite the main character living with plenty of angst.

The problem was that we never really get to know the characters. Everything is kept superficial. Jo is described, but her history is kept even more vague than most comicbook superhero biographies. At no point to we learn much about Jo. We discover that she had a few friends before developing powers, but that was about it. Her powers are also kept vague enoogh to allow a few moments of explosive power to intrude.

the plot itself is fun, if a bit silly. The villians are predictably over-the-top and at the same time friendly. There was a lot of "feel-good" sentiment hidden in the tale.

In the end, I liked the story, but definitely found it unsatisfying in many ways. It felt just a little too unfinished. Lovers of superhero tales will definitely find this entertaining, but it doesn't rise to the level of the best of the genre.

title: Light Read and fun
text:
This was the first story by Mike Sirota that I've read. Overall, I'd rate it an interesting read. The characters were fleshed out some, the plot was intersting and not overly cliche, and the writing was solid.

But it isn't an classic. I found many of the characters a bit underdeveloped, and in a couple of cases couldn't really see the motiviation for the character. There was a bit too much reliance on some rather common fantasy standards.

The conflicts also ended up rather understated. Instead of open fighting beteween the main character and his rivals, the story is centered on a burning need for revenge that the main character has, but he wants it to play out a specific way. The lack of open conflict diminishes the impact of the conflict. It's there, but it never drew me in.

Still, it is a fun story, and far batter than some of the other stories I've struggled through. I recommend this to thsoe who love mideval style fantasy worlds.

title: Solid enjoyable read, but nothing special
text:
This book is interesting in that it follows one main character over a period of more than two decades as they take up a quest for a god and pursue their duties with patient diligence.

The characters were interesting, but a little flat. Most seemed more like ideas that were never fleshed out and more than a few characters appeared to have no motivation for their actions. I could almost picture an actor asked to play some of the parts reading the script and then saying "I don't understand my character. What's my motivation?"

Overall the story reads smoothly and quick. The heroine is interesting and the challenges aren't too outlandish.

For lovers of stories of intrigue this plays out well. The plot involves protecting somehting while also helping a number of people solve problems, some of which they don't even realize they have. However, there is almost no action, and the final climax is sedate compared to most fantasy tales.

I cannot really recommend this book. It's good and I did end up pushing through to the end of the story rather than waiting for my next lunchtime reading session, but it's not one I can ever see myself reading again. There just wasn't enough emotion in the story.

title: Middle book that wasn't as good as the others
text:
I enjoyed book one in this series "Mutineer's Moon". I enjoyed book 3 "Heirs to Empire". I found this book tolerable, but hardly outstanding.

This book has many of the same flaws recent David Weber books have. The battles are epic, but end up being frighteningly quick due to technological tricks and plans. Instead of a slowly building battle where we get to see how the characters react, we get fights that run for just a few pages before we move on to the aftermatch.

Even the siege of Earth ends up feeling shortened. The length of time in the book is long, but descriptions of individual battles are simplified and few characters get much face time as a faceless enemy attacks Earth again and again.

The final battles were even less compelling as the reader gets to see them from a distance as mostly automatic weapons fight it out with a still faceless enemy in a star system some distance from Earth.

In all, this book lacked the characters that made the first and third interesting, and lost any focus as the battles were too big for the rest of hte story.

If any earlier book as prophetic about how David Weber would lose his way in his later novels and get lost writing epic scenes without any focus on characters, this book was it.

Readable, but nowhere near the best of Weber and not necessary to completely understand book 3, read it if you like to complete series, or if you lose epic space opera, others should find a less ambitious story to read.

title: Interesting compendium of short stories
text:
This is a collection of stories Mercedes has written over the years. Some good, some just ok. None that really qualify as horrible, but also none that I considered great.

Did have one that was later expandied into Bardic Voices Book 1 "Lark and Wren". Much of the story was translated almost word for word. For a writer it might be interesting to see just how little she changed, and yet she took a short story and turned it into a decent novel.

If you love Mercedes work, this book will definitely interest you. Lovers of fantasy will also likely find at least one story to enjoy, there are several good ones and the bredth of topics should mean there is at least one story a reader will enjoy.

title: Sequel that suffered from poor characters
text:
The first book in this series "Rising Tide" was strong. The characters seemed to be multi-dimensional and had lives that intertwined with the plot, bringing a depth to the tale you don't often find.

Sadly, the sequel failed to build on the same foundation. We do see several characters return, but their development and growth was stunted by a fragmented plot. Worse, multiple new characters are named and described, but receive almost no attention except as scene filler. New heroes participate in battles and intrigues, but I never felt they got enough "screen time" to really develop.

This and the fact that the main plot felt forced brought the book down quite a bit. I read straight through this, and do hope to see more in the future, but in the end I felt cheated by the ending and the fact that I never really saw heroes I could cheer for like I did in the first book. Even the returning ones lost a lot of their appeal during this tale.

It's clear that this husband and wife team of writers are still finding their voice. They have created an interesting world, and there is definitely a lot of potential in several of their characters. I hope they write more.

If you like West Pacific Supers: Rising Tide, you'll most likely enjoy this story. Just don't expect it to be as good. The plot is not as strong, and the lack of character development brings this down so that i can only give it 3 stars.

title: Fun yet flawed
text:
I like much of Mercedes Lackey's early work. I have copies of some of her Valdemar tales that are 20 years old and showing signs of multiple readings.

The free and flowing writing style that so enthralls me in many of those earlier books doesn't come out in this one. The initial storyline of a young ballet dancer fired from the Paris Ballet when she gets too good of a review and a star feels threatened who then has a talking cat take over and lead her to a new dancing opportunity in Blackpool is a wonderful semi-modernization of the old Puss in Boots fairy tale.

If it had remained on that vein and concentrated on the girl and her mysterious and wonderful cat it might have turned into a great story, and the elements surrounding the girl Ninette and her trials in joining a new dance company are definitely the highlight of the rest of the book. The cat Thomas is well written, embodying the essense of being a cat while having a paternalistic interest in protecting Ninette.

Sadly, Mercedes decided she needed more. She adds a horrible romance with Johnathan, who is barely fleshed out, and described so negatively by most of the other characters that I wondered why anyone would like him. I know girls seem to go for the mysterious and dangerous, after all why else would half of all urban fantasy stories have the girl swooning over some dead 200 years vampire, but it helps if the romance seems to grow naturally. And the "troll" made less sense. Worse, she was boring. There are 2 passages late in the book that I pretty much skipped because they added nothing to the story. More than 30 pages of the book were tied into this fluff.

If you love Mercedes Lackey this will most likely disappoint. It has its high points, but the lack of consistency and the overwriting of the villain drag it down to no better than average.

title: Good writing spoiled a bit by questionable plotting
text:
Compared to book 2 at least this story ties into events from book 1, and brings back some of the characters from that story. It still could almost stand alone, but the nature of the main magical villain falls a bit flat even with the extensive flashbacks by Moiron during her pursuit of him.

Sadly, the appearance of the now near endless plot twists that are pushed in one direction or another by Moiron consulting with her god soul, or by the appearance of her former lover seem legion. Moiron never enjoys a conference with her friends where tehy talk about a situation. Everything is directed from outside and she's almost along for the ride as the plot takes her through the world.

The character development is equally weak. Only the writing quality and the ability of Jacqueline to draw pictures with words keeps this story together. Her talent makes it worth reading, but it feels like it was rushed to reach a deadline rather than a well thought out and planned novel. Definitely a disappointment.

title: Second book in a Trilogy.
text:
This is the second book in a trilogy and sadly it shows. For all of the movement of the characters as Moiron and Bao travel from the world's China, to Mongolia, to Russia and finally to India there is little actual movement of the plot. Characters introduced in this story are there only for a few scenes and then vanish, never to be seen again. Many aren't even mentioned after that and some plot threads are left to twist in the wind forever.

And as others have noted while Jacqueline spins beautiful and sometimes exciting pictures with words in this story she struggles to provide any motivation that doesn't have some element of "deus ex machina" about it. Enemies just happen to be in the perfect place to stage a kidnapping of Moiron and they even have special chains designed to block her magic, which work despite the maker not knowing about how her magic works. Bao just happens to believe a man who had no reason to tell him the truth about where Moiron was and travels miles in the wrong direction and ends up captivated by another woman and her magic. Even when the couple is reunited its helped because Moiron happened to befriend a widow who is immune to the desire magic and is able to break the spell on others.

It's still a fun book and I like the characters but you could get away with only reading this book in the trilogy because it doesn't really tie in directly into the others. You'd miss a lot of the backstory, but it has little effect on the plot here.

title: Lots of words, little action
text:
So much happens in this story. Or at least someone looking at the number of pages to this book would believe that.

The truth is that despite the huge number of pages this volume 2 of what is supposedly a 5 book epic series doesn't appear to move the plot much at all.

The characters have all been seperates, and remain seperated. With very few exceptions none of the 4 main heroes meet during this entire book, and in many cases they are moving away from each other, rather than toward each other.

There are still possibilites in the plot. J.V. Jones has created an interesting main enemy and populated her world with many venal and cowardly men who will happily aid the darkness hoping to be rewarded.

But the story is disjointed. Half of this volume felt like filler rather than a solid attempt to move the story forward. One can only hope that the future books tighten the storyline and reduce the number of characters J.V. Jones feels impelled to follow. Right now this story barely rates 3 stas, and that only for the quality of the original idea. Its fallen prey to the same flaws most epic fantasy stories seem to embrace. Too many characters, too many characters the author wants to follow, no focus.

J.R.R. Tolkien got away with having multiple storylines during "The Two Towers" portion of the Fellowship of the RIngs. Since then it seems that almost every author that tries to write a fantasy epic attempts to emulate the master by spreading out the characters and following each one for a chapter before jumping to the next. Few succeed in making the story engaging through this. This Epic definitely is one of the failures.

title: Long and winding start to a story
text:
Epic fantasy appears to be a new rage after the phenomenal financial success found by George R.R. Martin with his series. In this first book of a new Epic, J. V. Jones demonstrates the joy that is epic fantasy at the same time she falls in to many of hte same pitfalls.

I liked this story enough to hunt down books 2 and 3 at the local library so I could read more. However, I already can see that this story is likely to be hundreds of pages longer than the plot really supports. J.V. changes the POV character with every chapter and not only gives us a good idea of what the main characters are doing. all 4 or 5 she develops in this first book.), But she tires to tease the reader with short chapters spent looking over the shoulder of some of hte villians she cultivates.

It makes the story move very slowly because instead of sticking with a single point of view and developing the plot. J.V. jumps aorund, allowing her to slow the progress of the story.

Its maddening, and frustating. If the story was not very good, I'd be tempted to grade this story even lower, but it was interesting and the world J.V. Jones has created is solid and detailed.

If you love epic fantasy this is worth a shot, otherwise, it will likely frustrate a reader due to its long dry passages and lack of a clear plot line.

title: Interesting, but tangled tale.
text:
I had never before read a book by Jacqueline Carey. However, the cover art and descriptions intrigued me and when I had the opportunity to read the first book of one of her trilogies I took a chance.

This story was not what I expected. Although I'd be hard pressed to explain what I expected. Jacqueline does a good job creating characters and giving them some complex motivations. The story is woven with borrowed myths and legends, retouched and modified to fit the peculiar world.

It makes this story intersting and even fun to read. However, while I enjoyed reading this story and will look to read the rest of the series. I can't see putting this on my list of best novels I have read.

The problem is in the way the story meanders all over. The intro is long and while parts are definitely necessary the depth of the descriptions was wasted when the author has heroine travel far from home and leave all she knew behind. This takes her to a new place and introduces new characters, who dominate the middle part of this book, only to be left behind again as the heroine travels once more, although this time she is with a few friends.

Even the political manueverings are predictable and ponderous, lacking the verve I expected.

For those who love a romantic tale and don't ask for much action, this story works well, I just like a bit lighter touch and think this story would have been fine at 200-300 fewer pages.

title: You're going to need a bigger hammer
text:
I really enjoy John Ringo's work. He weaves tales that combine sci-fi with good action and usually ties in some strong character development. Unfortunately, this story clearly got away from him at some point and what plot there was in this story quickly gets lost in side stories about cultures and politics.

Worse, the final battle scene is one of the worst developed I've encountered in some time. I got tired of David Weber's system of have one side throw 1 million missiles into space and get enough hits to wipe out the other side. This story actually takes that and tries to outdo it. I can see no reason that the alien race the RAngora would attempt a third attack against the humans with less forces than the minimum advised by their analysts, but not only do they, but they throw just about every ship they have into the fray.

This didn't read like the final book in a trilogy. But at the same time there was little done to move any part of hte plot forward or to develop characters. Sadly, this read like an attempt to fill a bank account. It's fun to read, but not very satisfying and I much prefer other works by this author to this one.

title: Fun historical fiction.
text:
I've had this book for a long time. Its interesting, especially for the detail about life in Rome in the time after Nero was emperor.

The story itself isn't very deep though. The kidnapping of Tertullia which starts the search which gives the book its title ends up being an attempt to generate a red herring allowing a corrupt politican to eliminate an accountant who would have revealed the extent of his corruption and embezellment.

Still its a godo story and worth reading for the amount of historical detail.

title: Good, but not outstanding story of a new world
text:
I remember when this book first came out and I recognized it as an expansion of the short story "Thorns of Barevi", which had appeared in the collection "Get Off the Unicorn" about a decade before this novel came out. This novel proved to be a good expansion of the original story and did a solid job of establishing the character of Kris Bjornsen, the main character.

However, I've picked this book up to re-read recently and have noticed that while its a good story, its not noteworthy either. Beyond Kris and to a lesser extent the Catteni Zainal, none of the other characters gets developed much. Many characters are used for a few scenes and then rotated out of the main plot thread. This did allow Anne McCaffrey to keep the focus on her two main characters, but it seemed to leave a lot of the emotional impact of the characters all being stuck on a new planet out of the plot.

For people who love lighter science fiction with some character development and an easy to read writing style. This book as with almost all Anne McCaffrey books is an excellent choice. If you are looking for something that pushes the plot into new paths and expands on the charactesr, this story will prove to be rather inadequate.

Not bad, but could have been better.

title: Not wonderful, but not a bad read either
text:
Let's see if I can expand on this manga without revealing too much

Pretty girls - Check
Young man with past - Check
Girls have magical power - check
Man has the ability to increase girls power - check
Man can do this wtih more than one girl - check
Girls don't like each other - check
Monsters attacking school - check

Fights tend to destroy parts of the campus - check

Simple, cliche, standard. That's a way to describe My-HIME.

The girls are well drawn and each has her own personality even if not much about them is revealed in the short chapters. The two main girls fight of the main character. Parly because he can increase their power, but there seemed to be some animosity from before that was never quite explained.

The artwork is well drawn, although sometimes a panel gets busy with all the detail. There is fanservice, but its mostly mild with quick shofts of panties under a short skirt. I don't see it as offensive, but some will.

Fun series through the first volume, but so far limited in imagination and score.

title: Fascinating if Impossible world created by a skilled writer
text:
I usually find Wen Spencer's work to be easy to read. The stories tend to flow smoothly and there are rarely any obvious continuity errors or characters lacking development. This book is a wonderful example of that as despite my concerns about the world and some of hte plot twists, the story itself is one I've taken the time to re-read for enjoyment.

That said, the story does have a few points that will probably raise a few eyebrows. The world in this book is one where 90% or more of all children born are girls, and Wen took advantage of this twist to explore some possible gender roles if men were a scarce resource. She does make this a more pointed issue by having sexually transmitted diseases be a major concern in a pre-industrial world that doesn't have the knowledge necessary to treat the diseases, and often can't even detect the diseases ahead of time.

But Wen tries to cover for most of the major reasons the social structures from this world wouldn't work. The world is pre-industrial, but not pre-gunpowder, allowing her to argue that the greater physical strength of men is less of a concern when 5-8 women are willing to throw themselves on a man, and can shoot other women who might interfere. The story mentions "husband raids" more than once and in fact the Brother of the story gets kidnapped at one point by a family of "sisters" looking for a certain type of man to be their husband.

None of this takes away from the story for what it is. Its a fun fantasy with good characters and an imaginative situation. Avoid becoming too concerned with the social philosophies being thrown around and its a good read. Just be prepared to shake your head at times at the silly premises.

title: Dimensions and Ease of Use
text:
Dimensions: 7" X 41/4" X 1 5/16". The one and five-sixteenth of an inch is the width of the spine; you'll have to hold the pages tightly to get that reading, especially if you've used the dictionary a few times, since pages tend to fan out. I don't have a reliable scale on hand, but it does weigh more than a pound can of Libby's string beans, perhaps one and a half pounds. I have a few dictionaries that fit in my back jeans' pocket, this isn't one of them.

As for the ease of use, the print is so close to the binding that you may need to spread the pages apart to see the print near the inside margin because it has a clearance of approximately 1/4" or less in some areas. That's the main reason I gave it a three star rating. For $6.95 and 135,000 words, however, it's an excellent buy. The target words are written in bold print, which is about font size 10.

I bought this Italian-English dictionary to replace my combersome Webster and the ancient Mondadori, which is apparently no longer in print. I liked the Mondadori and neither the Webster or the Larousse compare in functionality and weight, but they'll do until something better comes along.

title: Should have been more succint.
text:
Good ideas in the book and examples/case studies. However, the book should have been more succint. It takes far too many pages to make the point about dexterity, etc. The organization of the book could benefit from a restructure.
Additionally, the examples tend to be the typical Amazon, Kodak, Fuji, Netflix examples we all have heard about before. I desire a book that addresses small businesses and their growth, not just these enormous monster companies. Surely, there must be successes in businesses that are more applicable to the rest of us in local or even global "small businesses"? And can we find examples of business dexterity on a smaller, more specific scale? It is hard to apply these principles to every day business when the examples are always of enormous, well-known companies.
Read this book for a grad class. Would not recommend otherwise. An abbreviated version would have sufficed. Nothing new here. The same business ideas of environmental scanning, strategy, and visioning just packaged in a different book.

title: Board game
text:
Recent Grisham story-writing formula:
1. Great story for 95% of book
2. Unrealistic, unsatisfying ending in last chapter

Formula for this one:
1. Great story for 45% of book
2. Jump shark
3. Write about small Caribbean countries
4. Implausible wrap up in last few chapters.

A lawyer stupid enough to get sent to jail for money-laundering breaks the trust of a fellow inmate, and fingers him for the murder of a prominent legal luminary. Of course he wants a "Get out of jail free" card and his lump sum for passing "Go", and he convinces the Feds to play along.

Naturally, he has a bigger game plan, and runs circles around the Feds while he plays an elaborate chess game with several pawns. Somewhere along the line it becomes checkers as he hops around sacrificing game pieces while racing to get to his goal.

Although there's enough to keep the pages turning, the characters are unlikeable and the plot implausible, and this turns a story of theft, greed and manipulation into something that makes the reader feel a little dirty by the last chapter.

Amanda Richards, October 27, 2012

title: Rice without rhythm
text:
This is a fanciful tale of a grain of Patna rice that accidentally winds up on board a ship bound for the New World. He escapes the fate of his fellow grains in the hold of the ship when a sailor steps on him and he gets stuck to the bottom of the sailor's shoe.

Along the way, he makes friends with a Myna bird named Trupti, who patiently explains that it's highly unlikely that he's ever going to see India again. Having debated that issue, they are then set upon by the ship's dog, who certainly doesn't like sharing his domain with talking birds and rice grains.

The illustrations are in color and are certainly kid-friendly, but there are two things that I didn't like about this book. First of all, the layout uses several different fonts, in varying colors and sizes, and it is sometimes difficult to follow the story in sequence. Secondly, the intention is to tell the tale in rhyme, but the meter is totally off and many of the words don't even come close to rhyming. This makes it hard to read out loud to young children. This would be a much better book with some editing and catchy rhymes.

Amanda Richards, April 1, 2012

title: Limited in usefulness
text:
Essentially a collection of 500 portraits, this book contains a lot of photographs of women, divided into the following sections of poses:

Head and shoulders
Waist up
¾ length reclining
¾ length seated
¾ length standing
Full length reclining
Full length seated
Full length standing

Each photograph gives credit to the photographer, but no other information.
There's also a short section on posing basics and a long section about the contributing photographers.

I didn't find it as useful as it could have been, as many of the poses were duplicated except for the model and the background, and I would have preferred if it were divided into casual, traditional, glamour, fashion and environmental sections. That way, if I'm shooting outdoors in a casual setting, I can go straight to that section and see all the illustrated poses for that type of photo shoot.

It would also have been helpful if some footnotes were used for each portrait, emphasizing a few significant elements of its composition and lighting. (eg - 3/4 view, natural lighting with fill flash, note the tilt of the head and curve of the wrist)

Some of the "poses" were nothing special, the beauty of the photograph being due to other elements such as the background architecture and props, and some photographs looked like amateur point and shoot quality.

The posing basics section was informative, and some of the portraits are inspiring, but as a "visual sourcebook" it's rather limited.

Amanda Richards, January 17, 2012

title: Foot fetishists
text:
An unlikely group of characters interact in a twisted ballet involving blood, body parts, bio-tech and, as the title of this review suggests, a foot. Said foot is in fact the lynchpin around which the story revolves, despite being severed from the leg of its now-deceased owner.

A rookie paramedic turns up at an accident scene and is unable to save the life of a young woman whose foot has been severed, and strangely enough, said appendage has disappeared. Unable to forget the young woman, finding the foot becomes an obsession with him, leading him to check up on ....

.... A Goth albino pseudo-vampire with a habit of keeping other people's body parts on ice, a pastime that makes him heavily indebted to some nasty body part dealers. To get out of his financial hole, he discovers ....

.... A research student with the rarest type of exotic blood, a couple of pints of which would greatly assist with cash flow.

The strongest part of the novel evolves around the paramedic, the most realistic of the characters, and it provides a rare look into a world where body parts are big business, and blood is worth its weight in gold.

The rest of the story develops the characters, flaws and all, but gets too caught up in their respective lives and backgrounds, which don't add anything to the flow of the story. Ultimately, the far-fetched plot and unlikely characters don't mesh into a cohesive story, and unfortunately the novel doesn't quite live up to the promise of the back cover blurb.

Amanda Richards, December 2, 2011

title: The Longer Road
text:
This is a post-apocalyptic novel in the vein of "The Road", except much longer and with a lot more characters.

The Good:
Extremely imaginative story-line with a cast of:
- One messianic leader with a dark secret, gathering sheep for his flock of survivors, who picks up ...
- A Marine traveling with a young cadet, joined telepathically and otherwise to ...
- A doctor who is also a witch, with a complicated past, searching for her abducted son, who calls for help from ...
- Another Marine, who's been crazy-mad in love with her for fifteen years.
Plus,
- A weather-predicting storm-tracker captured after her helicopter crashes
- A doctor and his wife
- A TV star survivor of a cruise ship wreck
- A supporting cast of survivors, guerillas, slavers, wild animals, deranged birds et al.

The Bad:
- The story is so heavy with main characters that it goes on too long, and this is only the first book of a trilogy. Some plot points are just barely introduced in this installment, and from the prologue, we still don't know jack about the characters.
- The ending isn't there - it just stops. To be picked up in the second installment)

The Ugly:
- The grammatical errors are just too many to ignore.
- The jumping from first person to third person and back, and the switching between past, present and future can make you dizzy.

The plot is enough to keep you reading despite the flaws, and you can see and appreciate the images that the author is trying to create. Unfortunately, these images aren't coming through clearly enough.

In summary, this is a good story hidden in dense verbiage, bad grammar and implausible scenarios, which would be a zillion times better with some professional editing.

Amanda Richards, October 15, 2011

title: Much ado about nothing much
text:
Short Attention Span Summary:

1. Main character is a level-headed, kind-hearted Bavarian hangman who also functions as a torturer, street cleaner and medicinal herbalist.
2. Other leading characters are a half-trained doctor, a village big-wig and a villain with a white bony hand.
3. Title character is of limited importance to plot, except during scanty romantic scenes with a leading character, and as a plot device towards the end.
4. Story begins nicely with murdered orphans, a midwife accused of witchcraft, the devil running around the place, and a lot of huffing and puffing by village big-wigs.
5. Story progresses well with hangman investigating murders to save midwife's life, plus a major fire and destruction of property.
6. Story begins to drag repetitively
7. and drag repetitively
8. and drag
9. ad nauseum
10. Ending is nothing exceptionally memorable after waiting so long to get to it.

If only the first third of the book had carried over to completion, this would have been a heckuva good book. As it stands, it goes on a few hundred pages too long, and draws out some of the "action" scenes until boredom sets in.

It has a good heart, but far too much body.

Amanda Richards, October 11, 2011

title: Roses are red, Kindles are pink?
text:
Even for someone not inclined towards new-fangled gadgets, Wesley should have known that something was wrong when his brand new Kindle arrived -in a fetching shade of pink. Kindles you see, come in color choices ranging between black or white, and black (and certainly not pink) is the new white.

As an English instructor, warning bells should have been ringing when previously unknown works of literature began popping up, and even more so when he continued exploring his new toy and found the news features which were certainly new to Kindle.

An amusing short story about Amazon's popular e-reader bending the space-time continuum, but with an anti-climactic ending that's not up to the build-up. Mostly a good Stephen King short story, but falls quite a bit short of great in any Ur.

Amanda Richards, September 11, 2011

title: Consequences
text:
When the sun and the moon get into a silly quarrel, they retreat into their respective corners and forget about the jobs they are supposed to be doing. As a result, the earth is severely affected until the combatants realize the consequences of their actions.

Beautiful color illustrations and a timely message are the high points of this book, which could have been vastly improved if the rhymes flowed a bit better and the language made a whole lot simpler. I also wish that the author had laid out the poem in the normal way, with the rhyming words at the end of the lines.

As it is, the rhythm of the poem is lost, and the "interruption" in the middle of the story totally unnecessary in that particular placement. A good idea, but spoiled by some of the content which is above the level of the intended age group.

Amanda Richards, August 2, 2010

title: The raindrop's circle
text:
"I want to know, have you ever seen the rain
comin' down on a sunny day?"

This is a cute little children's story with two main themes. Firstly, it tells a simplified version of the water cycle from the point of view of a raindrop, and secondly, it teaches that everybody and everything has a purpose on this earth, regardless of size or status.

The book is just the right size for a children's story book, not too small and not too thick, and the full color illustrations are eye-catching. The one fault in my opinion is that the rhymes are inconsistent throughout the story, sometimes rhyming, as in:

"Within seconds the Raindrop flew out of the hose,
It was covered in light from its head to its toes.
It happened so fast, in the blink of an eye,
That the raindrop had no time, to laugh or to cry."

... and sometimes (most times) not at all.

Also, even though it is intended to be a story in verse, the text is laid out like a regular (non-rhyming) story, making it rather confusing for reading out loud.

A wonderful concept, but the writing could have used a little tweaking.

"'Til forever on it goes through the circle fast and slow,
I know, and it can't stop, I wonder."

(Lyrics by Creedence Clearwater Revival)

Amanda Richards, July 25, 2010

title: Bare bones
text:
According to the author, you have too much stuff in your house.

Readers of this book should keep in mind that the items are recommended by a single empty-nester, so not everything would be practical for other types of households. There are some useful ideas and recommendations in here, and some interesting trivia about the history of appliances and whatnot, but in the present format it's hard to get enthusiastic about it.

The book is fairly small, and everything inside's in black and white. On this book

title: The giants are revolting (yes, they certainly are)
text:
Down in the Florida swamps lies a giant problem. No, make that several giant problems. The fire-breathing giants are beginning to wake up, and only people with "the sight" can see them.

When the giants lay waste to an entire housing development project, it's high time for the giant slaying team to do something about it.

Unfortunately, the giant slaying team is made up of an old blind man, a chubby youth named Nick, his stepsister Laurie, his older brother Jules, and Jules' girlfriend Cindy.

Continuing the adventure from book one, The Nixie's Song, this episode pushes the envelope trying to cram too many things into one little book. You also get the impression that the author was in a bit of a hurry, as there are loose ends, continuity problems and far too many coincidences.

A quick read, and as usual, beautifully illustrated, but certainly not in the league of the original Spiderwick Chronicles. On the bright side, the ending of the book indicates that there's lots of excitement to come. Get this if you've already read The Nixie's Song, and hope that the next one will be better.

Amanda Richards, October 4, 2008

title: L.A. Law and Disorder
text:
Having read this novel, my Wambaugh total is now up to - well - one, to be exact. It's about LA Cops and LA people, and provides a little peek into the sordid underbelly (apologies, but I always wanted to get an opportunity to say that) of life on the Hollywood streets.

The story isn't about the famous sign or the stars on the pavement, and it's not about black birds or old women, and to be quite honest, the plot isn't really that good in the first place, but the black humor and the low morality level is what keeps the reader turning the pages.

On the side of law and order (chung-chung!) we meet Matthew McConaughey-type surfer cops Flotsam and Jetsam, who have a knack for finding trouble and a lot of true grit (from the beach). There's veteran Bix Ramstead, a loving family man coasting towards retirement, and then there's potentially famous actor Nate Weiss biding his time before being discovered. There's a trio of strong female officers named Cat, Ronnie and Gert, and a few others including the officious and clueless Sergeant Treakle, but you can read about them for yourself.

On the civilian side, there's a weaselly little cokehead named Leonard, a strip club owner named Ali Aziz, his ravishingly beautiful wife (and ex-employee) Margot, and a Mexican pharmacist who's willing to turn the other cheek for a treat and a trick. You'll also find out what goes on behind the scenes with Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman and all the other characters on the strip.

Naturally, some of them come into contact while Wambaugh turns his all-too-human characters into the terribly obvious story-line, and although he blows most of the suspense by straight-out telling you most of the details, there are one or two little twists he keeps until the right time. He also hits pretty hard at police procedure and bureaucracy in the light of the need to maintain an untarnished image after the Rampart affair.

I'm gathering that he's written better books, and although I don't think this is one of them, it has enough juicy stuff to make you look.

Amanda Richards, July 22, 2008

title: You get what you pay for
text:
In the heat of the day
With the breeze of a fan
When your child wants to draw
And you say that he can
And he wants to draw faces

So you take out this book
(Which costs so little money)

With cartoony sketches
In various stages
Then his little brow furrows
With pencil in hand
As he tries to find faces
Not ugly or bland

"Mummy," says he,
"These are all rather cheesy
Some are quite hard
And some are too easy
The clown is too sad
And the vampire sucks
I think that I'd rather
Go draw me some [[ASIN:0486281140 Trucks]]"

I looked at the book
And I saw what he meant
Although younger children
Might well be content
I'd hoped it would show
Faces happy and sad
Or laughing or yelling
Or angry or mad

It lacks inspiration
The drawings aren't nice
You get what you pay for
At such a low price

Amanda Richards, July 10, 2008

title: Capitalist vices
text:
Diana: Some things are not for sale.
John: Such as?
Diana: Well you can't buy people.
(Quotation from the movie "Indecent Proposal")

This book pulls a switcheroo on the "Indecent Proposal" plotline, where a wealthy man offers a cash-strapped couple one million dollars in exchange for certain favors.

Short Attention Span Summary (SASS):

1. Ex-quarterback Griff Burkett has just been released from prison
2. He's admitted to receiving a payout for influencing the outcome of a game to facilitate some unsavory characters
3. He may also have murdered somebody
4. He's definitely not a nice guy
5. A wealthy businessman is desperately seeking an heir
6. He's confined to a wheelchair
7. His young wife is prepared to go to any length to fulfill his wish
8. The businessman makes Griff an indecent proposal in exchange for a decent cash payment and his silence.
9. Apparently, some people CAN be bought
10. Griff has a dangerous and ruthless enemy who enjoys seeing him suffer
11. Griff suffers
12. Intriguing premise turns absurd, and despite some page-turning action, the ending is rather preposterous

If you can get past the fact that all the major characters in the book are unlikeable, the beginning and middle sections of the book are entertaining, albeit unbelievable and unlikely, but when you get down to the ending, the story unravels untidily while attempting to tie off the loose ends.

Amanda Richards, May 30, 2008

title: A whole lotta latte going on
text:
I'd heard about this series from friends, but this is the first one I've actually read. Chopping Spree is book eleven of the series, which now has fourteen books.

1. Catering to Nobody
2. Dying for Chocolate
3. The Cereal Murders
4. The Last Suppers
5. Killer Pancake
6. The Main Corpse
7. The Grilling Season
8. Prime Cut
9. Tough Cookie
10. Sticks and Scones
11. Chopping Spree
12. Double Shot
13. Dark Tort
14. Sweet Revenge

The series features Gertrude "Goldy" Schulz, a Colorado caterer who solves murder mysteries between courses. What's different about these books is that each book includes a set of recipes for dishes being served up by Goldilock's Catering.

Everybody who knows me knows that I'm no cook, but I do enjoy good food and a murder mystery. Unfortunately, something seemed missing from this book, and I didn't enjoy it as much as I thought I would have.

Short Attention Span Summary (SASS):

Goldy is hired to cater a party at a shopping mall for a group of "Elite Shoppers".
Goldy consumes a lot of espresso and chocolate
Someone tries to run a truck over Goldy and friends just before the event starts.
Someone succeeds in killing somebody else, with a knife, in the shopping mall.
The clues point towards Goldilock's Catering.
Goldy downs more caffeine.
Goldy hunts down the killer, keeps her hubby happy, tolerates her bratty son, chops and dices, snoops and spies, deals with personal problems of her assistants, and yes, drinks enough coffee to cause a worldwide bean shortage.

Recipes in this book:
1. Spice of Life Cookies
2. Shoppers' Chocolate Truffles
3. Sweethearts' Swedish Meatballs in Burgundy Sauce
4. Diamond Lovers' Hot Crab Dip
5. Quiche Me Quick
6. Today-Only Avocado-Shrimp Boats
7. Super spenders' Strawberry-Rhubarb Cobbler
8. Ad Guys' Roast Beef and Gravy
9. Wild Girls' Grilled Mushroom Salad
10. Chopping Spree salad

This one is marred by a slightly ridiculous plot and some puzzling situations, but would be fine for those times when your brain cells won't tolerate literary abuse. Also recommended for those who aren't challenged when it comes to culinary matters.

Amanda Richards, December 15, 2007

title: Sempra fugits
text:
This book has some similarities to the novel "Eragon", in that both authors are young, big fans of fantasy books and movies, and crazy for dragons. One of the characters in this book is even named Paolin, which is pretty close to Paolini, the author of the aforementioned Eragon and the sequel, Eldest.

Anyway, back to Amentha's War, the story is about two young people who accidentally find themselves transported to a strange land, which is inhabited by dragons, elves, dwarves and trolls, and where the forces of good and evil are constantly at war.

It seems that the girl, Ginny, has a special link to the land of Sempra, and nobody's about to tell her what it is. With the help of some friendly folk, she learns a bit of the language, a little touch of magic, and even how to wield a mean sword in battle.

Predictably, there are factions who want to seize control of Sempra from the current rulers, and the bad guys are prepared to do anything to get their own way. Kidnapping and treachery prepare the way for the great battle that always ends such tales.

Of reasonable length for short attention spans, rich in description and full of interesting characters, the bottom line is that a gripping young adult novel is marred by poor editing and atrocious spelling, which both detracts from the plot and distracts the reader.

In summary, this is a promising first effort from a young writer with great imagination, but this edition is sorely in need of an editor and a thorough run through the spell checker.

Amanda Richards, October 13, 2007

title: Design flaw
text:
This is definitely not the best book I've read this year, but it's also not the worst. If you read it as a thriller, and treat the religious and scientific "conclusions" as plot devices, you are left with the opening narrative hook, a treasure hunt, the requisite stock characters such as villains and dumb henchmen (it even includes a one-eyed man), some sexual tension, and an anti-climatic ending.

Apparently Albert Einstein and his friend Bhartiya Bharti once made a significant discovery about the big bang, which they chose to hide from the world for the good of mankind. The secret was then to be passed on to Bharti's granddaughter, through a series of clues, so that the decision to disclose would be in her hands.

Kammy Bharti had already made some bible-toting enemies through the publication of one of her allegedly blasphemous articles, and barely escaped death at the hands of the henchmen. When the Klan and the Fundamentalist Christians learn that she intends to tell all to National Geographic, they decide to silence her, as well as her group of friends. Eventually, it all boils down to a lot of ado over nothing much.

Somewhere under all the scientific and religious mumbo jumbo, spelling errors and grammatical lapses, there lies an innovative little story that's just waiting to be edited out of hiding.

Rated: 2.5 stars, and a possible 3 after editing.

Amanda Richards, September 22, 2007

title: Let's start at the very beginning....
text:
...a very good place to start - except that I've already read two others in the series, namely [[ASIN:0425210278 Predator]] and [[ASIN:0425204693 From Potter's Field]].

The series so far:

Postmortem (1990)
Body of Evidence (1991)
All That Remains (1992)
Cruel and Unusual (1993)
The Body Farm (1994)
From Potter's Field (1995)
Cause of Death (1996)
Unnatural Exposure (1996)
Point of Origin (1998)
Black Notice (1999)
The Last Precinct (2000)
Blow Fly (2003)
Trace (2004)
Predator (2005)

(Book of the Dead is scheduled for Oct 2007.)

Fortunately, there's no need to read them in order, and the reading experience was actually better given that I already knew how some of the characters would be developed in the future.

On its own the book isn't bad for a debut novel, except that it tends to get bogged down in places, the characters don't really come to life until later down the series, and the technology is understandably dated, given the techniques now available. (Naturally, it may have been cutting edge stuff when the book was written, which I took into consideration when reading it)

There's a little more CSI involved than in the ones I've read before (it gets less and less in later books) and the story revolves around a serial killer who eventually gets around to the Chief Medical Examiner. The modus operandi of the killer is suitably gruesome, but for the majority of the book Scarpetta seems to the weakest link as she struggles to hold her own in a world of men.

About the same as "From Potter's Field", but better than "Predator".

Rated: 3.5 stars

Amanda Richards, September 15, 2007

title: Wuf! So long, and thanks for all the frogs
text:
This book is classic Tom Robbins in the sense that almost every page has some hilariously humorous play on words, or unreal observation about real events, including a lot of incisive commentary on the subject of Washington's allegedly wooden teeth. (I kept wondering if he got knot holes instead of cavities, and whether he used Terminix for dental services*)

That said, this is not one of his best books by a long shot. It starts slowly, works up to a purple passion and then lands flat on its squatty Buddha-esque rear end. The tortuous tale twists around a feckless female Filipino stock broker, facing the fall of the fickle stock market over the Good Friday weekend, frantically forming far-fetched formulae to foil her forthcoming firing. Her acquaintances include a traditionally built psychic, whose fall-back occupation is watching home movies of the lonely and attention-deficient, a philanthropic Lutheran real estate broker who desperately wants to marry her, and last of all, a born again Barbary ape with a yen for banana popsicles and larceny.

While living through the worst days of her lives, she meets a tattooed ex-broker recently back from Timbuktu, and tracks him to his den of decadence beneath a bowling alley. Through this earth shaking incident, not all of which could be blamed on the rise and fall of the bowling pins, she has an Alice in Wonderland experience involving a distant planet, a toothy Japanese doctor who is said to have found a cure for cancer, an inscrutable Indian and a whole lot of amphibians.

Highly pseudo-philosophic, with unlikeable characters and flimsy plot, the main thing this has going for it is the dry humor of the word play, and all the rain in Seattle can't wash that away.

Amanda Richards, May 26, 2007

*Not a Tom Robbins quote, but it might have been if I didn't write it first

title: Not TSA approved
text:
I recently picked up this book for four reasons:

1. It was on sale

2. I'd just finished reading "The Husband"

3. I needed light entertainment for a long flight

4. I was in a hurry and it was conveniently stacked near to the register

It was only during the boarding process that I glanced at the back cover, and discovered my faux pas, which did not escape the notice of a literate cabin attendant who gave me "the look".

Okay, maybe a novel about a plane crash is not ideal for a five hour flight, but I'm not superstitious that way (knock wood). Unfortunately, this is a typical Dean Koontz book - it starts off smoothly, gains momentum, takes off and gets moving at high speed, and just when you're enjoying the flight, it suddenly goes crazily off course, crashes and burns.

A crime reporter loses his wife and two daughters in a bizarre plane crash that kills everybody on board. A year later he's still in depression, but then he meets a woman who apparently survived the crash. He starts tracking her down, and relatives of the other victims suddenly start committing suicide under very strange circumstances. When he eventually finds her, things get even weirder, and we're back to secret labs, mad scientists and illegal experiments, mixed with cults, conspiracies and magic pictures.

Enjoy the ride while it lasts, but beware of the sudden stop.

Rated: 3.5 stars

Amanda Richards, August 30, 2006

title: Missing something
text:
Alex Brennan moves to the UK to read for a Masters degree in English, because firstly, she's bored in New York and secondly, she decides to defy an ex-boyfriend who said she couldn't do it. She can't get into Oxford, so she takes a loan from her father and sets off for another university, where she proceeds to drink and smoke herself into oblivion.

This novel is about that year of excess, and while it is entertaining in parts, and so very British in humor, you never get deep inside any of the unlikable characters, so you don't get a sense of why they're doing the things they do. Alex herself seems extremely immature for a 26 year old woman with prior work experience, and how she survived the year is anybody's guess.

This novel is about alcohol, nicotine, caffeine, casual relationships, stalkers, nutcases and immature behavior, and while it's easy to read, alcoholism in the UK seems to be the central theme.

Funny in places, but mostly shallow and bitter.

Amanda Richards, December 27, 2005

title: So what's your ring tone?
text:
Imagine, a whole album that sounds like your worst cell phone nightmare! Listening to this album in its entirety is like being trapped in a crowded room with everybody's cell phone going off, one at a time, for eternity, while having bamboo sticks pushed up under your fingernails.

As a gimmick album it's great fun, and some of the songs have hooks that will stick in your brain and have you humming them at inopportune moments. Be warned however, that only the brave or foolhardy will attempt to listen to the whole thing in one sitting.

The best track is the Brit-hit "Axel F", a totally loveable adaptation of the Harold Faltermeyer `80s instrumental classic, and the main reason for buying this album. Fortunately, you can also find it on Now Music 61, and get a much better package to go with it.

Other tracks that will stick in your earwax are perennial favorite "Popcorn"; dance number "Pump Up the Jam" (when last have you heard that one?); the perky "Pinocchio"; the "Dallas" theme; and of course the theme from "The Pink Panther".

Listen to it in bits when you're feeling down, and be prepared to either bounce madly around or throw your cell phone out of the window.

Amanda Richards, September 10, 2005

title: Some good ideas, but...
text:
I was a little disappointed in this book. It has a nice cover and all that, but the pages inside were a little low budget in appearance, and that psychologically made the recipes less exciting than they really are.

Cooking definitely isn't a passion of mine, so the quickest and easiest recipes are the ones that appeal to me most. However, without pictures of the finished product, I found it hard to choose recipes, because firstly, I want to see what I'm getting, and secondly, I really like seeing if my creation kinda looks similar to the professional one.

One of my problems was getting some of the basic ingredients - there are a lot of capers and anchovies required - but people living in the USA shouldn't have a problem. A lack of the various deli items and cheeses as well as the specialty bottled sauces made half the recipes impossible without substitution, but again, if you have these things close at hand you should do fine.

The recipes are easy to follow, even though I noticed that one of them omitted to tell you when to put in a certain key ingredient, and they have cute names - nothing highbrow here. I don't need step by step pictures, but some finished food shots would have made all the difference for me.

Okay for experienced cooks looking for some quick recipes, but a bit underwhelming for beginners.

Amanda Richards, June 12, 2005

title: Brutal editing may have kept me awake.
text:
This book took me much longer than 24 hours to read, and sent me into a dead sleep many times. The premise is an excellently creepy one, but the book suffers from the "when it's good, it's very, very, good" syndrome.

This is an erotically charged story of possession, murder and deception, in which oil man John Waters bites off much more than he can chew when he falls for the mysterious stranger who somehow knows all his darkest secrets.

Teetering helplessly on the brink of self destruction, he finds himself in a situation where he could lose his family, his best friend and his lifestyle, and he can't trust anybody, not even himself.

The fault with the book is that it rambles and rambles sometimes, covering "key" points over and over, overemphasizing things and explaining far too much. In a nutshell, the liposuction of about 100 pages would have kept the story taut and edge-of-the-seat gripping, despite the fact that all of the main characters are extremely unlikable.

Gripping sometimes, yes - but a bit of a drag in places.

Amanda Richards, April 19, 2005

(Note: For an excellent book dealing with similar subject matter, but in a sportier context, you may want to check out "Walk-On" by D. Mikels.)

title: Could have saved a few trees
text:
Maybe I should have read "Light in Shadow" first, or maybe I shouldn't have read the flyleaf, because this bestselling novel did not deliver the suspense, intriguing subplots and romantic twist that were luridly promised.

Many of the supporting characters are two dimensional for most of the book, and then suddenly beefed up in a few paragraphs at a suitable time to enhance whichever tangent the writer was angling for at the time.

The main characters all have dark or unhappy pasts, which they bear either stoically (most of the men) or hysterically (most of the women), and even though there are some good parts peeking through the cobwebs, it rambles around all sorts of other space-filling things, and when you get to the ending, everything wraps up at warp speed, not even pausing for a coherent thought.

As a romance it fails miserably, because there's nothing even vaguely rapturous or tempestuous in there. As a suspense novel, it does a little better, but the ending drags it down considerably. The jury is still out on the intriguing subplots, because I seemed to have missed them completely.

If you have enjoyed other books by this author, and are having a slow afternoon, maybe this book will serve to pass a few hours, but wouldn't be the best choice if you've got other stuff on your to-read list. It's a 2.5 star effort at best.

Amanda Richards, February 5, 2005

title: Overbrimming with adventure
text:
This is a reasonable first effort, showing promise for subsequent adventures. It is however difficult to guess what other new adventures could sequentially follow, as this one seems to have thrown every possible fantasy genre plot into the pot, shaken as opposed to stirred.

It contains almost every fictional or mythical creature ever to appear in a fantasy book - centaurs, satyrs, dryads, witches, dwarves, goblins, griffins, wolves, bears, ettins, dragons, even a phoenix, among others.

From the beginning, readers would find it easier going if they made little notes on the characters, because the author introduces them faster than a speeding griffin, often with the depth of a trickling brook.

It is extremely fast paced, and written in simple style for young readers, a style which may not appeal to older folk. Young fans of fantasy should however have fun reading this book, which as mentioned before has more action than should physically be able to fit between the pages.

Careful reading will reveal a little mistake that slipped by the editors. If any young reader can pick it up, just e-mail me and I'll petition the author to send you a badge with the Silverlance logo.
