Amanda Richards October 24, 2004

title: Maybe it's just me...
text:
Maybe it's just the order I'm reading the books, but after "Still Life With Woodpecker" and "Jitterbug Perfume", this one came up a bit short.

Maybe he just got better with age, like fine wine and aged cheese.

Maybe I just haven't read enough of Tom Robbins' books, and so haven't acquired a complete appreciation for the clever wordplay, but this one seems to be far too wordy at the expense of content and story. There are at least two chapters that unapologetically say absolutely nothing, and do not advance the story in any way.

Maybe I was just too impatient to get to the "meat" of the story, and got frustrated with the rambling.

As I said, maybe it's just me.

The characters are very Tom Robbins, especially Sissy Hanshaw, the super-sized digited ugly duckling who grew up to be a hitchhiker, model and cowgirl, the delightfully named Bonanza Jellybean, ranch boss and all cowgirl, the hygienically challenged Countess with castanets for teeth, Delores del Ruby, whip maestro and forewoman, and the Chink, pecker waving yam lover.

Parts of the story are very similar to "Jitterbug Perfume", especially if you consider the Chink as an oriental Pan, all musky and ready to rut, and compare the Clockworks tribe to the Bandaloop, both of whom possess the wisdom of the ages and are more finely attuned to nature than the rest of us.

Readers of "Still Life" will note that "O O Spaghetti O" makes about as much sense as "Ha ha ho ho and hee hee"

There's a wonderful storyline here, with our thumb-tied heroine struggling to find herself, the all cowgirl ranch, and the interrupted migration of the protected whooping cranes, but alas, it was hidden amongst the rambling passages, and I almost couldn't see the story for the words.

In my opinion, not a good beginner's guide to Tom Robbins - there are better - but still a clever concept teeming with physical and spiritual love, nature and magic, cultural differences, freedom, overcoming handicaps and of course, hitchhiking. It's a three thumbs up, but could have been a five.

Ha ha ho ho and hee hee

Amanda Richards, edited August 30, 2004

title: Beautifully presented, but not very detailed
text:
This is a very nicely presented book. It is a conveniently sized hardcover with attractive dust cover, and has excellent pictures. It can even be used as a coffee table book.
With regard to the content, there are some very good ideas, but firstly, some of the items required are not easy to get, and secondly, the more complicated projects do not have enough detail in the instructions.
I also found that some of the projects don't look that good if you take away the fancy settings and lighting effects used for the photographs.
Not a bad book, but it's more for show than function

title: not necessary
text: Unless you have the energy to walk more than you will do already in Paris, this book is just something else to carry.

title: Helped me
text:
A fair amount of what's written in this book doesn't seem to relate to teaching a running technique. And to me, some of it seems kind of odd and out of place. The book did however, help me learn how to run and I still remember and use some of the concepts the book teaches.

The real breakthrough for me came from seeing someone actually running using (what I think was) the Chi Running approach.

There may be many running books more helpful than this one, however, this was the right book at the right time for me.

title: Confessions by Thomas De Quincey
text: An unusual but interesting read

title: Easy and useful and informative
text:
All the tips for your Shih Tzu dog right here in this book. Easy useful book with pictures and questions you need answered.
I bought it for my mother for Christmas, but any time will do.

title: Nice book to figure out your dog
text: Nice tips and suggestions for your Shih Tzu. Grooming, attitude, and everything else.  I got this for a friend for Christmas and was a great reference point for her dog.

title: Average
text: Avrrage

title: Too long & repetitive
text: It seemed the author was dragging out the story. It became predictable after awhile. It went on too long but by the time her father was involved, I just wanted It to end.

title: The relationships are drawn out.
text: The book began suspenseful enough, but it grew confusing & tiresome after awhile.

title: Confusing
text: I kept waiting for this book to become suspenseful, but it was filled with confusing shifts of scenery. I understand that they were sick characters, but their self-absorption became tiresome.

title: Gets confusing at times
text: I read the paperback, but lost interest at times.

title: Will the future really be this bleak?
text: Although this was a very informative book, I think that most people would prefer to shut their eyes to what's around them. It seems that we have enough of our own problems without worrying about fresh water supply,  killer viruses, 3rd. world countries, environmental hazards, etc. The  writing is quite matter-of-fact, and sometimes dry. However, his discussion  on over-population really is the reason for many problems. I live in  Chicago, and our utility company can't seem to keep up with the demands for  electricity. It's an old system, needing repairs, but falling behind in the  constant demand for more service. I think over-population, especially by  those who are not fit to be parents, who can least afford to have them, or  are far too young will be the root cause of The Quickening.

title: Thought she would enjoy reading it
text: This book but has small print , it was written in 1938. ( and not updated) I bought this book for an elderly friend who knits avidly. Thought she would enjoy reading it.

title: Three Stars
text: Just too difficult to follow for me

title: You'll enjoy this one!
text: This spiral bound book has recipes that you need more than cake mix, fruit and butter to bake a cake. Good for beginner  baker because recipes are easy and look like you've been baking all day. I bought this book as a gift for a friend who likes to bake.

title: A book to read!
text: People, I picked this book up on a whim, I'm not an erotica reader - but all the other things going on, made erotica a smaller part of the book. It's a good read, think of Fifty Shades - but more for everyone! I gave 3 stars, cause of the overall effect it has on me.

title: Kidnapped kids!
text: Henrik is a well developed character but the story lacks information about title.  I thought there would be much more to the story behind and about the pastel orphans.  Other than the small section about where some may be and Henrik looking at those few locations there was very little told.  The story seems more about a boy turning into a man on a journey to locate his kidnapped sister.

title: Enjoyable, was a little turned off by the end
text: I really enjoyed this read, for a quick mystery, but had not anticipated how sci-fy it would become. Still fun though.

title: Subterranean's Maze
text: It is quite apparent that James Rollins is an excellent storyteller.  His descriptions are excellent.  I read the book in two sittings.  My frustration is that the time lapses felt unrealistic.  As well, the group of experts would have been carefully researched before such a mission. The real Khalid's family would have surely known something bad had happened--or was this a family coverup?  Major faux pas. The Major's brother just happens to be the only survivor of the previous mission-- too convenient. Rollins maneuvered the story a bit too much for me.  Still a fun read.

title: Not really for beginners
text:
I'm actually disappointed with this book. There are some pretty parks represented by the patterns, but the two parks I was interested in aren't included. Big Bend National Park and the Petrified Forest National Park aren't included.

The only way I can see to make these patterns easy to work with is to photograph one, enlarge it and print a copy. That's a lot of aggravation for me - the code isn't easy to see otherwise. I think I'll just stick to regular, stamped cross stitch kits.

title: Plot is interesting
text: I can't quite put my finger on what exactly was wrong with book for me. I think the story/plot was interesting and I was excited to read it. Unfortunately, it sort of fell apart midway through for me. The writing was fine, but there was a point where I just lost interest.

title: Light zombie fare
text:
I actually liked this book more than other folks apparently. But I didn't love it. The base story is solid and interesting for sure. The Audible narrator is pretty good and her inflections were dead on.

Unfortunately, the lead character feels cold and irrational to me. Her grief at losing loved ones was miniscule and fleeting. They made foolish choices and got lucky throughout the book. Nonetheless, I still enjoyed it and the external world building around the pandemic.

title: Talented wordsmithing
text: We spent two weeks in Cambodia a couple of years ago and the effects of the Khmer Rouge holocaust are still evident if you pay attention beyond the Killing Fields and Angkor Wat. Of course, these amazing people have overcome so much of the horror of just a generation ago and are rebuilding a strong and independent nation and recovering their cultural identity. I wasn't sure if I would like a fictional story drawn from that terrible recent past. I think the book itself is well written and the tale well woven overall. In the end,  the book never set well with me. It felt like reducing a genocide to nothing more than a reach for potential movie rights offers. My husband disagreed and thought this was a decent book and with respect for the history. You'll have to make up your own mind.

title: Interesting ideas, but didn't grab my attention
text: I admit,  it took me three tries to read this book over a period of two months.  The first third just seemed to drag and dump information rather than read like a character driven tale. The premise is interesting and the ideas put forth regarding our interactions with AI in daily life in the near future.  I don't dislike this book, but I expected something different  - more along the line of Minority Report I guess.

title: Not as funny or natural as her older books
text:
I'm a fan of Jen and I pre-order each book on Audible, so I am obviously comfortable with her style in general. She's quite relatable to us Gen X women who have little patience for nonsense, but endless time for animals.

Unfortunately, Stories I'll Tell In Bars felt forced and like it was reaching and not quite getting there. The Italy trip story dragged and there were hints of the earlier bitey humor, but in a weird, obligatory way. Like trying to be funny vs natural flow creating raucous silliness.

I'm not giving up on Lancaster at all, Fletch and the dogs are far more interesting than most junk on TV. Let's just hope Jen finds her groove again

title: Author never explains why important things happen
text:
I was really looking forward to this book and even skipped two others to read this one first. Unfortunately, it doesn't live up to the back cover blurb. It's a decent sci- fi story overall, the mechanics of space travel and functioning long term in space was well done.

My issue is the bottom line premise that women have been returned to the kitchen in bare feet and forbidden from holding positions of importance. The author sets up the entire book on this foundation. Yet she never bothers to flesh it out or actually explain why and how it happens. That drove me nuts and left me unable to commit to the characters or their motivations. My take on the book is...meh.

title: Interesting cause for the end of the world.  Lots of unnecessary drama
text:
I want to love this book and there are several things here that are very good, but it wasn't entirely put together. I have Audible audio version and the two narrators did a great job - love Ms Whelan. The overall plot is gripping and the disappearance of all the living creatures on Earth was handled in a new way. Not your typical plague, zombies or alien attack.

My issue is unnecessary and repetitive critical mistakes and manufactured drama as the story progresses. It felt like the author was trying to stretch book one to justify a trilogy. There are a few plot holes that can be ignored for the most part and I'm willing to use a credit on book two. I want to see where things go, but I hope the second part is more put together.

title: Very basic. Intended for first timers
text: This is a cute book that has its place. It's very simple and covers an outline of the basics for first time campers. It is not in depth or detailed on any subject or skill set you may be needing. However,  if you just want to load the family up for first time weekend in the tent and very light hiking, this is going to get you started. It does offer some tips on map reading, packing and how to build a fire if you're allowed to. One tip I have is NEVER rely on a cellphone anywhere in our National Park system  - always have a current,  physical map and a real flashlight on your person if you're hiking.

title: Bad ending
text:
I'm a huge Dr Who fan, though I think David Tennant was the best Doctor and neither of the two subsequent actors have come close to him. I want to get my nieces started with Dr Who and this book is a neat way to do that. The illustrations are vibrant and draw the eye on every page. It's a simple and cute story, but the end is problematic.

The girls were very concerned about the little stowaway never seeing its family again because the girl kidnapped him. Frankly, I'm bothered by that too. Since when does Dr Who make pets out of other sentient beings??

title: Too dark and violent for me
text: I don't think I have the stomach for the violence in this book. It reminded me of that movie, 8MM...dark and awful and creepy. I think the writing is fine and I would try another tale by this author. I just could not get through this one.

title: Just not quite what the cover suggests
text: I love a thriller, and I love a chase story. But I don't love this book. It just fell flat and felt very predictable. The lure of humor never came to fruition for me. The characters didn't encourage me to root for any of them - most felt one dimensional... good, bad or evil. This isn't terrible,  but it's not one I would read again.

title: The usual tips on focusing on the here rather than tech etc while traveling
text:
My gut instinct after reading this book is basically... Meh. I've been fortunate to travel the world and see lots of places out of the way and off the beaten path as well as the big tourist attractions. I've gone to Greece, South America and Asia alone and later with my husband. We've seen Thailand, Cambodia, United Emirates and all of Central America and Europe. We're in the prep stages for driving across the US for a year. My point is that I fully grasp the mental, emotional and spiritual requirements, tolls and rewards that travel brings.

I don't know exactly what I expected from this book to be honest. Maybe more than bullet points and meditation tips. This has all the usual suggestions to turn off your phone, look around with real attention to the current moments rather than just the camera lens, try new things and take time to be internally still. None of that is new ground and has been shared by tons of other books. This one isn't terrible by any means, but for me, it just didn't resonate as special.

title: More fluff than nuts and bolts
text:
I thought this was going to be a guide to designing an escape vehicle via van or rv. I mean, that's exactly what the title implies. It is not that. This is a beautifully produced book with lots of photos of various folks in their mobile homes. It talks a lot about who they are, why they have chosen to go nomadic, and a look at their vehicles of choice.

What it does not do is explain how to get started, what efforts are required to actually live in a hygienic and comfortable manner if you're building out a vehicle or renovating an old rv. This is sort of a glamorous look at the finished product without any behind the scenes info. Sort of like those instagram jokes who never admit that van life means no real toilets and using public showers. As a fluff piece, this is a nice coffee table book.

title: Immature voice and style. Ok, but not a great read
text:
First a warning....there are dogs who die in this book and if that upsets you, you need to know. I, for one, fully understand the agony of losing a beloved dog and I try to avoid it in books and movies. Weak? Perhaps, but I don't need that sadness.

I really wanted to love this book and looked forward to reading it. Unfortunately, the writing is not great and there's more about the author's emotional life than the dogs. Now having said that, there's no question in my mind that this woman absolutely loves her dogs and is deeply connected to them. That was the story I thought I was getting, but in some ways the dogs are secondary.

There's an awful lot here that a better editor could have corrected or smoothed out. Choosing better photos and more of them would have brought the story into sharper focus. Eliminating most of the baby talk comments from Max would add maturity to the writing. Instead, it feels childish and creepy. The overall book is by no means awful, it's just ok. I never felt compelled to read page after page in a binge.

title: Tends to be dry and slow
text: I have to say that this book wasn't quite what I was expecting. It's reasonably well written, but trends toward being dry and feeling like a text book. The author has done a lot of research and included just tons of historic facts and information about past close calls with Toba and the Cuban Missile crisis etc. That's fine, but again, reads like a text book. I was looking for more of a "what if and what to expect" book instead of a "this almost happened and might yet happen" book.

title: Lead is arrogant
text:
I've never heard of this author before, so I was able to read this book without any preconceptions. It's not a bad story, but something here just never clicked for me. I didn't actually like Gabriella much. She felt so self righteous and arrogant to me from the first few pages and that never changed. She treats Eli like he's beneath her even when the poor guy is going above and beyond to help her.

The simple fact that this girl takes off to find/protect/save her brother bothered me. It's an immature and reckless move for a ton of reasons. Nonetheless, without this first foolish choice, there couldn't be a story at all. The book isn't bad, but it just wasn't for me....I found myself drifting off to read other things in the middle of this.

title: Lead is whiny and spoiled and grating
text:
I don't remember Emma actually, so I came to this book with a relatively blank slate and no expectations. I love fiction set in India - movies, tv shows and books. There's something both foreign and familiar in the cultural differences between Texas and India.

This isn't a bad book, but it's not a great book either. The humor feels forced when it appears and sometimes even a little mean spirited. I just never felt anything for the lead, Ania, except disdain and aggravation. She is spoiled, entitled and whiny. She grated on my nerves from the first page and I never warmed to her.

title: Great race descriptions soured by self indulgent nonsense
text:
As a woman who has spent my life riding, showing and training horses in multiple disciplines, I can absolutely relate to love of horses and the desire for an adventure on horseback. Sort of that foggy romanticized vision of horses equalling freedom of spirit. So I was excited to read this story of a young woman's daring acceptance of the Mongolian Derby challenge.

Unfortunately, what I got was the ramblings and navel gazing of a child who was far more reckless, immature and sloppy than daring or admirable. I really didn't care for her at all and frankly, found everything about her slightly....off. At first I thought she was just ditzy and truly in over her head without being savvy enough to recognize it. However, by the end of the book, I find myself suspecting the author has shined us on with a fake persona to generate extra attention. In the end, it feels like she harbors disdain for the other riders, the local culture and customs of the Mongolians and even a few of the ponies she rode.

The race itself and descriptions of the horses and their personalities was fascinating and very well done. The hardships of the bad weather, wild endless spaces, loneliness and physical strain were just as vivid and compellingly written. I think this would be a five star book if there had been better editing and photos included. The smooth action of the actual race is ruined in every chapter by random daydreams, descriptions of her sleeping dreams and just stream of consciousness ramblings. It's disjointed and jarring. Eliminate most of that and distill this down to the purity of the race experience and this is a book worth reading and enjoying.

title: Only a page or two for most parks. Very basic
text:
I have been teaching my nieces about Texas History and the National Parks through out the country. Our family spends time at Big Bend National Park annually and we've been to almost every other park in the 48 states and Alaska - we're park people.

I wanted to use this book to get the girls talking about the different parks and the climate differences between our beloved Big Bend and say Glacier Park. The book is pretty basic. There are just a couple of pages for each park with the bare minimum information on each. There are lots of lovely photos and it's not a bad beginning step for our project.

title: Sort of creepy.
text: I'm not sure what I just read. It's supposed to be a funny look at life from the opposite perspective - human as pet in a world run by cats. For me, this was more creepy and weird than anything else. Maybe I was expecting something more along the lines of the timeless Gary Larsen sort of humor - this is nothing at all like the magnificent Far Side.

title: Slow in places. Less dystopian version of The Handmaid's Tale
text: I think I expected too much from this book and found it lacking in some vague, undefinable way. The storyline is very much inspired by The Handmaid's Tale. The differences are minor - Jane is being paid for renting her womb rather than being compelled under threat of death. The underlying messages are the same - the Have vs Have Nots, power, and desperation. I might have enjoyed this book more if it moved more quickly. It's definitely a character study and crawls along in spots. It wasn't bad by any means, but it just didn't enthrall me. Where as The Handmaid's Tale was compelling and hypnotically well written.

title: A little funny, a little mean and a lot of cringe
text:
I had such high hopes for this book. It's fresh and unique and that's difficult today, so I definitely respect the idea here. The execution.... well that's hit and miss throughout. The author engages strangers with absurd and stupid help wanted ads. Pretty simple scheme, but some of her *gigs" are just too far over the top and I honestly have a hard time believing anyone replied, much less wanted to reenact a bad dream or be a human pinata.

The correspondence between the author and marks range from funny to cringe worthy. I think she carries things way too far multiple times and what starts out as cute or funny quickly devolves into the absurd. There's a definite sense of self superiority by the author in the tone of several prank ads and conversations. This is not awful, but really needed a better editor to curate the gags more carefully.

title: Drags in parts. Good story, but slow
text: I loved Dan Wells book Zero G and jumped into the Partials immediately. I was a little disappointed though - Partials isn't a bad story at all. However, it drafs in places with extra, unnecessary details about tiny things. Compared to Zero G, this book plods along and getting to the point where some key information is imparted takes forever. All that being said, I can actually see this becoming a movie.

title: Lead character is bedbug crazy. Story is slow
text:
Elizabeth/Juliette is just creepy and out of her mind. It's like watching a trainwreck in slow motion. She is just cold and soul dead with no sympathic qualities. Even with disturbed, vicious main characters, they need to be engaging and have some redeeming quality to make me care about their point of view in the story. I never found Elizabeth anything other than awful.

The book opens with a very bad thing that, I guess, was supposed to establish the groundwork for why she is a sociopath. It does explain some of her crazy, but I'm not a fan of the flashback info dump technique and this book does it often. It just takes you out of any building tension in the plot.

This book is not bad by any means, but it just never felt smooth and moved slowly for me. I never found a reason to care about Elizabeth or feel anything other than pity for Nathan. I actually stopped halfway through and read an entire second novel before wanting to return to The Perfect Girlfriend. I'm sure other folks will love this, but it just wasn't for me.

title: Cute idea that was done by Ty Foster a year earlier
text: This is a cute idea, photos of fun dogs mid-lick, making silly faces. However, it's a total copy cat book of Lick by Ty Foster that was published a year before this one. The layout is almost the same and the photos in both books are set up almost identically. I find this a little odd because this project could have been done just as well with some original ideas. These photos are fun and taken professionally. However, I just find the recreation of someone else's idea feels creepy.

title: Tiny spoiler at end of review.
text:
This is a review of the Audible version. wanted to love this, but in the end I am not going to continue the series. The narrator was very good and I would listen to another book narrated by Barnaby Edwards. He managed to distinguish each character and keep them easily identifiable by the listener.

The world building here is somewhat unique, but Dr Who has done the mobile super cities in a couple of episodes dating way back and relatively recently. That's fine, but the tv show versions were easier to grasp the concept of and the reasons why they exist. The plot here is pretty simple and easy to get ahead of. I just never connected with the characters and killing a dog is a deal breaker for me. I liked this book, but that's all.

title: Tiny print maps, very few photos and not enough info about the crime
text:
I'm a devoted user of the Fodor guides for trip planning and education about laces we're going for the first time. However, this one on Rio is lacking some key things. First, very few photos and the maps are really small print. Carrying this with you while on the go would be problematic because Rio is crowded and fast moving and dangerous for tourists who look helpless or lost - not a great idea to be lurking on the street trying to read these maps.

My second issue is simply the lack of realistic, detailed info about the crime issues and risks. They do mention pick pockets and the driving risk, but only as it refers to other drivers running red lights as they flee carjackers. The crime problem against tourists is a very serious and high risk issue and the truth is it needs to be fully addressed. In comparison to a For or guide for Cambodia from several years ago, this one just falls short.

title: Slow enough to detract from the mystery
text: The narrator for the audio book is good with a soft Irish lilt and a voice that's easy to follow. The story though is a little slow and repetitive in spots. The mystery itself was a pretty good one, well two mysteries that end up in the same place. If you're looking for action of any kind, this isn't your book. It is mostly step by step police procedures and interminable conversations between all the characters.

title: Has some gruesome scenes, some humor and a crazy lead character. But I didn't love it
text:
I had high hopes for this book - a slasher in the midst of the high fashion narcissists...yes, please. The main character, Anya, is a nut job in every respect and that's definitely interesting. The pressure of never being good enough and being treated badly by the too thin, too vain and too haughty is her rationalization for her murderous proclivities.

The story moves quickly along and sort of reminded of both American Psycho and Dexter. The problem for me is that unlike both those shows, Anya just wasn't compelling or fun. There's definitely humor in this book, but a lot of the snide jokes wore thin halfway through. In the end, I just felt like my mind was drifting to other things. This is not a bad book at all, it just isn't one that I ever got excited to read.

title: Nice setting and mystery. Main character was just totally unlikeable and smug
text:
I love the idea of a farrier as the lead character and this was handled well. The author clearly knows horses and about the basics of hoof care - she was able to weave the horse shoe business into the story and mystery smoothly. The mystery itself is well done and interesting - the story flows quickly and is a fun read for the most part.

However, I just absolutely hated the main character, Rainey. Every interaction with her was grating and over the top with the bitterness and overt hostility toward the world. I get that her background was pretty awful and she's carrying scars, but Rainy was just so snide and passive aggressive toward her boyfriend that I was totally turned off. I couldn't understand why or believe that Guy would send five minutes with Rainy, nevermind living with her a year. I couldn't root for either of them and that turned a good book to just an ok book for me.

title: Loved the first Tom Stranger. Manatees just got lost and feels a bit forced
text: I'm disappointed with Manatees. I absolutely LOVED the first Tom Stranger story and have listened to it multiple times. It was literally laugh out loud, rewind and laugh some more good. However, this one just lost me. I would have loved more Tom Stranger and way less of the slacker intern. Adam Baldwin is once again a great narrator and brings a genuine excitement, wry amusement and variety of accents to the characters. Some of the brilliant irreverent humor and originality of the first book is lost here.

title: Early plotholes left me unenthusiastic for the rest of the book
text:
I really wanted to love this book - dystopian near future and plucky young people making things better... Yes please. However, it just never quite gelled for me and I can't quite put my finger on exactly why. The idea here is definitely interesting. Trying to lie proof the politicians and the press alone is a fascinating premise. Add in all the subsequent complications of that and you have a pretty good storyline started.

I started to have an issue with the character names immediately. I just couldn't hear "Rebe or Boob" in my head - I kept getting "Reba and Bob" instead. That's on me, but it aggravated me through the entire book. Secondly, I never did believe or accept the explanation of how these high school kids had extremely advanced, expensive and very large piece of medical equipment in the garage in the first place. If the culture was such that a jailable curfew and corrupt police force ruled a desperately poor society with an iron fist, how did these teens sneak an MRI machine home?

I think this book will appeal to a lot of folks and the technical storytelling here is done well. It just didn't work for me from the opening chapters and I was never able to just give myself over to the rest of the book.

title: Designed more for the first time dog trekker
text:
This is a pocket book style with extremely tiny print. It's really geared toward the person who has never traveled with a dog before and literally has no clue where to start. That's fine and it covers some important things and drops the ball in other respects.

I wasn't impressed with the list of items for your travel first aid kit at all. The author left out some critical stuff - wound wash with lidocaine, Benadryl for allergic reactions, kwikstop blood stop powder, canine aspirin, burn gel, vet wrap bandages, snake bite kit and treats! I've traveled cross country multiple times with multiple dogs over the year and at one point or another, I've needed everything on my list.

Dog travel requires pre-planning, common sense, serious organization and schedules as similar to home as possible. I roadtrip with two to four large hound dogs (Ridgebacks and a Plott Hound and a Swiss Mountain Dog) and my guys all wear harnesses and have designated seats in the truck to prevent chaos. We carry an extra three days of food on the road just in case there's a delay getting home and we stop and feed dogs at their normal time no matter what....never ever feed a new food or restaurant scraps on the road or risk upset digestive systems. Always take your own dog beds from home and crates so your dogs are feeling comfortable with their own stuff in a new hotel or cabin. I also discourage multiple strangers from trying to pet my dogs in transit - it's easy to overstimulate a dog traveling and they need a break sometimes. Our dogs love to travel and we have had more fun with them on the road - totally worth the pre trip efforts.

title: Takes ideas from classic novels from page one. Predictable, but a quick read
text:
I'm a little torn between giving Grace and Fury 3 or 4 stars. On the one hand, superficially, this is a fun, fast moving story that I did enjoy reading. It's good beach book material for sure. However, a few things bothered me from page one and have continued to bother me after finishing the book.

The very first pages just scream Hunger Games to me - the choosing of representatives from various districts for the ruler's nefarious purposes...Catniss much? Further along you learn that the "Graces" are just concubines for the ruler and expected to produce heirs. So now we see shades of Margaret Atwood's "Handmaid's Tale". Then we see the prison island for Serina and all I could think was devaju to "Lord of the Flies" - fighting for food, violence and tribes.

It just felt like there wasn't an original idea anywhere here. Lots of other, classic themes that are so close to the originals it makes you compare this book to the others without necessarily wanting to. The story itself is predictable and there really aren't any surpises here. In the end, this is a three star book for me.

title: More about vanity in a certain type of woman than real life.
text:
As a woman in my mid 40s, I can certainly relate to some of the bullet points the author included in this book. The comparison ended pretty quickly though. Mrs Druckerman is very, very concerned with her looks and the appearances of her friends. And their wardrobes. Almost obsessively. A lot of the book references how people look older and that wrinkles are something to be sad about both for yourself and others. Let me be clear, I'm not allowing grey hair to take over or forgoing my face cream and moisturizer, but I do not judge other women for ignoring these things - especially not my friends. Being 40 something means (to me) you live and let live - especially with people you love. I just never got that feeling from this book.

The pre chapter quips on how you know you're in your 40s are clever and cute and many are true - but some just screamed materialistic vanity to me. Telling men to "invest in hand stitched brogues"... seriously? Yes, every grown man should have great quality shoes, but that's not an existential aging lesson.

My lessons from my 40s? Accept joy anywhere you find it.
Kick off your shoes and play on the lawn with a puppy.
Welcome new friends in your circle with an open mind and full cappuccino for everyone.
Answer that 2am phone call with grace and calm - bad news is never made better with panic.
Never waste another minute listening to music you dislike or reading bad books.

title: Ruth is immature and drove me nuts. Beach reading at best
text:
This is one of those books you read by the pool or beach with half your attention on other things or just drifting. Pick up a chapter here and there and you're not really missing the story when you put it down for an hour or a day. That's ok, we need books like this.

Unfortunately, for me, the lead, Ruthie was so shallow that I couldn't care one whit about her or her life. She's focused on keeping up with the Jones and living way beyond her means financially and socially. For years renting her family's home out every summer so they can barely afford to live there the rest of the year. Her husband and daughter hate it and frankly, I agreed with them....the whole situation felt selfish and cruel to me. Just relocate to a place you can afford and relax in and have a healthier life for all.

That same blatant social climbing and materialistic inclinations spoil the rest of Ruth's life as well. She is wronged and seeks revenge like a teen girl. She sinks to throwing things on people's porches and illegal acts. I just felt like I couldn't empathize with this immature, greedy character. All that said, I think the writing here is good and the story moves forward at a reasonable pace. It just wasn't a story that I ended up caring about.

title: Unlikeable characters that never improve. That ruined the story for me
text:
I'm a big fan of the Suburban Mystery/Thriller genre and looked forward to this book. A missing college girl with a sordid secret life and the various characters orbiting her disappearance sounds compelling. The mystery and basic story outline are good here and the writing is pretty good as well.

However, I literally detested every single character in the book. None of the adults had any redeeming qualities and even the kids were obnoxious. Leah is a sloppy drunk who is so focused on whining that she neglects her family and becomes a trespasser and thief. Clay is less sloppy, but still a daily drunk, blaming his weakness on his brewery business. He is a liar and more than a little creepy - everything about these people is sketchy. Actually, in hindsight, they are a couple that deserves each other. The next door neighbors are equally distasteful for different reasons. None of these people are worth caring about or rooting for. I just wanted everyone to die in a massive booze caused house fire by page 200. It was, honestly, difficult to finish the book.

title: Over the top lead character who irritated me page after page
text:
I'm a fan of strong female lead characters, but I also require them to be believable and smart. Harley just isn't believable. She's too much of...well, everything. Too tough, too jaded and her over the top obsession with the "Rubies" shelter feels like nobless oblige rather than honest concern.

She's wrapped up in a non-stop self congratulatory inner dialogue that crosses with an obsessive adoration of her dead mother. I just really didn't like Harley and that tainted every page. The undertone throughout the book is that men are bad, and all women are weak except for Harley because she's "special". There's lots of violence and gore and yet it never really gelled as a thriller to me.

title: The cute gimmick loses it's charm with uninspiring main characters
text:
I liked the idea of this book - a cat who creates an introduction between her human and a cute guy next door. The author definitely seems to understand cat behavior and the cat was fun and written with heart. The main character, Jamie, seemed like a strong young woman out to change her life from the ground up.

However, the cuteness was overplayed early on and got old fast. There were a lot of random quirky characters with behavior that felt slightly off. The actual writing also felt off to me - in some places the book reads like it's written for pre-teens. It's a cute premise that just lost me about half way through.

title: Fun story, very, VERY similar to The Maze Runner in plot, characters and world
text:
I love a good dystopian plot and The Initiation delivers for the most part. The world building is fairly well done with just a few plot holes, but it's easy to picture as you read. The bleak, hungry, grey world is stark and offers numerous questions about why and how it became that way. The answers are provided and they are a reasonably believable. The characters are annoying, even whiny for the first quarter of the book, but they definitely develop more as the actual Initiation tests begin. Once you cross the halfway mark, the book sort of takes off with lots of action, very interesting puzzles and it doesn't slow down until the last few pages.

I have two complaints - this is a set up for yet another multi-book series instead of a fully fleshed out stand alone story. I'm really tired of being milked for as much money as possible by every author in a bookstore. However, my main reason for the star deduction is because this entire story just screams "Maze Runner" to me from the first chapters through the end. A group of mismatched teens, an obstacle course of dangerous trials, big government conspiracy, special covert operation for the surviving kids, all set in a dystopian future. The Initiation is so close to Maze Runner that I'm surprised the publisher allowed it.

title: Loses momentum very quickly with very slow pace. Drifts back and forth past to present
text:
This isn't a bad book, but it's just not the story that I was expecting and excited to read. The disappearance of a young man in Nigeria and the mystery around his disappearance with all the associated drama is what I thought I was getting.

The story drifts in a very slow current from the present to the past and loses it's way in family stories and random minutiae. Almost as if the mystery of the wayward son was an afterthought. The author has a nice writing style and I found the descriptions of daily life in Nigeria fascinating. Unfortunately, I just lost interest and felt no compulsion to keep reading a little more than halfway through. The plot was slow and the pacing was slow and I had to move on to something else.

title: Moves a little slow, left me feeling melancholy.
text:
There's an old saying "You can never go home again" and this story brought that to mind for me. The idea of being haunted by old tragedy and building a new life elsewhere can be very appealing. Yet the ties to home can never really be severed.

Nate is a broody guy with sad overtones and plenty of reasons for it. I actually found this book to be depressing rather than fun. It's an interesting tale and a decent mystery, but I just felt melancholy from start to finish. The writing is solid and the location is very interesting - I looked it up and was surprised to learn that hurricanes can reach the Adirondacks. I liked this book, but I didn't love it.

title: Characters feel flat and rushed. Interesting format though.
text:
I had never heard of Bookshots before this book and I can see the appeal. It's under 100 pages and can be finished on a long car trip or flight or in a waiting room. There's not enough to the story to get invested in and you can read and toss out or leave for someone else.

Unfortunately, this particular one was a total cliche and I just had no feelings towards the two main characters at all. I think that this needed more time for Tanner and Madeline to get to know each other, despite the short story format. Their "love" was really just infatuation and felt false to me.

title: Interesting premise, but I found the lead mostly unlikeable
text:
I wanted to really like this book, but it just never resonated with me. I think the idea of a murder mystery that behaves differently from the usual tropes is good. You have a cub reporter in a new city trying to make a name for herself and stumbling into a mystery. Her inexperience in a city of endless stories should have been gripping.

There was just something about Copper that I didn't like. She struck me as vain and arrogant when she hadn't earned the right yet. The writing is fine and the story moves along reasonably well. However, in the end I never felt compelled to read this book - it was very easy to do other stuff first. It just wasn't for me.

title: Stilted dialogue and too many unnecessary details of office life
text:
The book cover blurb compared Noble Chase to Grisham and Iles. That's just disappointing because the only comparison is the main characters are lawyers. This is not a legal thriller of that caliber. It's an ok book that could have been lots of fun if the author had gotten out of his own way.

Lots of stilted dialogue between characters that just never sounds or feels natural. The sailing portions are really good and I immediately felt the author was comfortable and at home with the topic. Whereas in the sleuthing portions of the story, things often felt forced. I just got bored at some spots due to the extra details and unnecessary conversations with minor players that had nothing to do with moving the plot forward. This book is an ok poolside casual read.

title: Lots of repetition from the first two books - similar actions, similar conversations, and the usual cliffhanger
text:
This is a review of the Audible audio book version. Fortunately, they kept R.C. Bray as the narrator and he's very good. He has the Skippy and Colonel Joe voices, personalities and the snide humor down pat.

I loved the first two books in this series, but this one has some problems. I was glad to return to Pardise and reconnect with the humans stranded there - apparently, we're supposed to just forget them now and move on. That really bothers me on several levels because we don't leave our own behind with the enemies.

Paradise has a lot of repetitive sections and scenes that we've experienced in both the first two books. I'm pretty sure that Skippy and Joe have had the same conversation at least three times in each book. Skippy is appalled because Joe has a good idea, they trick the lizards and save the (insert planet name here) and Skippy casually manipulates wormholes...basically, the plot for all three books is the same. At this point, I am still going to read book four, but if we don't get some new dialogue and perhaps a dose of the Elders, I'll be done with this series.

title: Cute, small book with some interesting photos. Several are repeated through the book though
text:
I like the idea of snow, but as a native West Texan, I have zero interest in actually being in snow. So this little book caught my eye as a way to see the beauty of a snowy landscape without having to actually be cold and miserable.

There are some really lovely photos on these pages and some mediocre pictures. I do love the laundry list of New York City architecture and many of the photos highlight some very interesting architectural styles. It's a shame this is a physically small book rather than a true coffee table book because there are several pictures that would have been better served by being larger so we could really see the details. My primary reason for the one star deduction is for the repetition of many of the same photos - they are repeated several pages later in a different size. I can't believe that the photographer and editor couldn't come up with enough unique photos of the busiest city in America to fill one small book.

title: Fascinating story, but the book is dry with big info dumps, very little human connection
text:
I was excited to read this book because I have been told some of this story by a historian friend, who has traveled through parts of Russia and could really explain the horror of a Siberian winter. It's sort of a forgotten history here.

Unfortunately, this book just didn't bring the emotional impact that my friend's story did. The hardships are explained, described, but as a reader, I just never felt emotionally connected to the men or their struggles. The book feels dry and very text book like. There are huge blocks of information that become repetitive in several spots. (More paragraph breaks would definitely be easier on the eyes). Another author with fiction experience might have been helpful with regard to drawing out the humanity of the trekkers.

title: Feel like a snide, slightly hostile gossip rag. Does explain the freak show though
text:
This book has certainly reinforced my original opinion of these people - trashy gold diggers, one and all. According to this, Kris started gold digging as a teenager and flitted from man to man until she found one with deep enough pockets. Such sleazy behavior would explain the future pimping out of her daughters for money and attention.

It's such a shame that these are the people influencing an entire generation of teen girls. Greed, selfishness, materialism in extreme measures, and publicly lewd behavior are not values to be rewarded. However, my three star rating isn't about the actual subject matter. I just found the entire book carried a tone of disdain - as if the author was describing something truly offensive. The constant snide commentary dotted with his personal feelings became distracting pretty quickly. Make no mistake, I have no use for these people either, but I do give them credit for being wiley enough to manipulate the media daily for their own financial gain. Because the author has such a dislike for them, I have to take the entire book with several grains of salt.

title: Interesting ideas and plenty of humor. Could have been shorter without suffering
text:
I was excited to read this book - the idea here is creatively great - of the Afterlife being an immortality in exchange for full amnesia of one's Beforelife (prior to death). The world building is pretty solid and most of the "whys and hows" are addressed well.

I just never really cared for the primary characters, never connected with them, not even Ian. I fully understand why Ian wants to hold onto his memory and reconnect with his wife. However, I just didn't understand why he refused to slow down and really learn about the Afterlife rules, political hierarchy and laws before traipsing around roughshod. This is not a bad book, the writing is solid and there's lots of humor throughout. In some ways, this felt very much like a series of Monty Python skits with the giant foot stomping out of a cloud. I just found it not to my taste.

title: Bogs down in extraneous details, tries to tell three stories at once
text:
I'm a big fan of historic biographies and in depth looks at how the world worked in the past. Additionally, I have a large interest in the African and Indian colonial period. So this book should have been right up my alley.

It's a mix of the author's personal travel history, the story of his long lost great, great uncle in India, and background information on the history of British colonialism in India. These are all interesting, in and of themselves, but all together in one book is too much. The story of the Uncle and the history of the when and where of his life is hard to follow. It's a bouncy narration and a tremendous amount of unnecessary, extra details about minutiae that really have little bearing on the overall story. I finally lost interest two thirds of the way through. It just wasn't for me in the long run.

title: Very fast read, writing talent is here. She never addressed the big warning signs she ignored early on
text:
From a story telling point of view, this reads like a novel in the vein of Gone Girl - the flashing between the past and present. It flows along and is compelling for the most part. Waite is certainly capable of crafting a very readable tale. You can definitely feel her heart break and anguish in each page.

My issue is the recurring theme of the entire situation being her husband's fault - the idea that she was manipulated into the relationship and subsequent nasty divorce with a truly innocent baby in the middle of this mess. No doubt, her husband was a class A cad, philanderer, and sleaze ball who will probably never change. But....Ms. Waite was perfectly willing to ignore the giant red flags from day one.

This guy was moving very, very fast from their first meeting. He was far too complimentary and obsessive about being with her from the beginning. They were both seeing other people when they first became intimate. He had a known history of fathering a child with a woman he didn't marry and treating the son as an afterthought. He was an admitted criminal, having stayed and worked in the U.S. illegally for twelve years. He happily took tens of thousands of dollars from her for a half baked idea and she blithely gave it to him with no legal advice or conditions. These were all giant warning signs to the author long before she got pregnant or even married this guy. Yes, she loved him and he treated her poorly, treated his children terribly, but she definitely has culpability here as well. I just felt like that was never addressed in the book. I'm happy she's moved on, having well to do family that's able and willing to support her for months on end was a huge blessing. As a woman, I just don't see this story as exceptional.

title: The women are still weak, the overwrought inner dialogues are all consuming. This could have been a single thick book, not three
text:
This is a review of the Audible audio book version. The narrator is Bronson Pinchot returning from the first two books in the series and while I like Pinchot in a other audio books, his intonations seem overly drawn out and actually reflect surprise in weird places. Though...that may be the mediocre dialogue he's reading.

As with both books one and two, I find the overall treatment of the female characters here to be, at times, condescending. Kate is supposed to be this medical research genius and Meg is a former firefighter and yet...they whine and cower and are applauded for any tiny act of courage they can scrape up when the men aren't around. Kate is so focused on her worry,fear, and love for Beckham that she loses her train of thought during scientific work often. Or she's so wrapped up in the kids that she gets all weepy and remorseful for her virus that created the variants. Meg, bless her, started out in book two as a strong, sensible character and by the end of book three, she's a sweaty, nervous wreck half in love with a member of Ghost Team just days after being rescued. Not one of the military leaders or even Ghost team bothers to ask her for intelligence & information on her experiences in the tunnels at the hands of the variants.

My other issue is the long, drawn out, overly emotional inner dialogues at critical moments in the action. Beckham, Horn, Riley... this constant overwrought, repetitive, over explanation of every potentially controversial decision is driving me crazy. The one saving grace here are Finn and the dog, Apollo. I keep wondering though, why on earth these guys don't carry some grenades or RPGs? Seriously. They seem to have an endless supply of gun ammo, yet I wonder if some grenades wouldn't have been helpful during the beach battle. I might continue this serious, but I honestly have had all the weak women, crying kids and miraculous escapes by Beckham at the last possible second that I can handle. I'm done.

title: Not truly funny, lacks heart. The overall writing is decent & the story moves right along
text:
You know that feeling of cringing at a live show when the star is just bombing? That's sort of the feeling that I had reading parts of this book. It's a reworking of the classic Agatha Christie murder weekend, but it just doesn't live up to expectations.

The various comedians are mash ups of real life performers, but none felt real or fleshed out. For example the "Redneck" is clearly based on Larry the Cable Guy and TJ Martinez sort of felt like Jay Leno, but off in little ways. The author has included pieces of the ten comedians' acts before certain chapters, yet none of it was particularly funny.

All that aside, the actual writing, when not attempting to force faux comedic rants, is pretty good. The story moves pretty quickly and flows easily. I suspect that the author might do a great job writing a story of his own without leaning on an idea from a novel by someone else.

title: Ending is rushed and the explanation of the full motivation of the guilty party isn't satisfying
text:
The story idea is good if you can ignore some plot holes and the extra dialogue throughout. Unfortunately, the author gets in her own way with unnecessary, repetitive conversations and thought trains in Anna's head.

Anna makes enemies she can ill afford simply by being self absorbed and arrogant. There were several moments when I almost stopped reading entirely because of this. The plot twist is easy to figure out if you're paying attention, but the reason for it seemed rushed. The end was also rushed and felt unsatisfactory.

title: Not bad, but not quite what I expected. Lots of period heavy dialogue
text:
I don't really read many romances, but I do like a Highland romance now and then. This book just didn't do much for me. It felt more like a history lesson in places and I didn't get the impression that were real feelings or passion between Adham and Fiona.

The constant influx of period dialogue made some sections almost incomprehensible rather than adding a dash of realism. It was distracting to have to flip to the glossary to figure out what was being said. I will say that the overall writing is good, but this just wasn't the type of Scottish romance that I expected.

title: Ok audio book for a quick romance, but not a great story. More violence than expected
text:
This is a review of the Audible audio book version. First - the narrator was quite good and her attempt at a Scottish accent was decent enough to pull me in. This is an ok book. Not bad, but nothing special either. There really hasn't been a truly great Highland romance (for me) since the end of the Highlander series by Karen Marie Moning.

I was surprised by how self absorbed Melanie was. She seemed very dislikable from chapter one. She did more than her fair share of whining and complaining throughout the first two thirds of the book, but grew up a bit before the end. Darcy was a decent guy who kept my interest and had a sense of humor and I liked the plot switch of him being inexperienced in the boudoir rather than the tired old "virgin damsel" trope. There is more violence and an unexpected, unpleasant animal death that was more graphic and felt absolutely unnecessary for a romance novel.

title: Lead character isn't a woman I would travel with. Forgettable fluff
text:
I normally enjoy a bit of a fluffy read now and then. Wild Woman's Guide is definitely fluffy and utterly forgettable - I put it down on chapter 4 and forgot to pick it up again for almost a week while I read a different book.

When I tried again to finish it, I realized that the heroine, Sophie, is just ridiculous and self absorbed. I wasn't a big fan of Carson either and frankly, I never figured out why a woman like Sophie would ever consider a long term relationship with him. The story has a cute premise and average writing, but I just lost interest halfway through. It wasn't terrible, but it wasn't for me.

title: Spoiler Free.... sufficient end to the trilogy. Self indulgent, maudlin and slow beginning. Picks up the pace halfway through
text:
This is a review of the Audible audio book. The narration has been excellent throughout the three books, Tim Gerard Reynolds does a fantastic job with each character and the various moods.

I have to admit that the first quarter of this book was a slog. Every chapter was a lesson in how much maudlin whining Darrow could do. He was selfish, arrogant and wallowing in self pity. He actually became a liability for his own cause at one point. Things do pick up and we see a distinct change in Darrow as the mid point of the book begins, but to be honest, it almost wasn't worth it to get there.

The second guessing and self doubt clouds Darrow's mind throughout the entire book. He repeatedly makes foolish emotional choices that cause heartache and damage to almost everyone around him unnecessarily. This drove me nuts, but the plot was moving very quickly at least. The end is a reasonable solution to the series - a little too trite in some respects perhaps. I'm pleased with the entire trilogy as whole and I think the world building was outstanding.

title: Starts out interesting and drifts to a slow, disjointed, pointless end.
text:
Wibbly-Wobbly timeline messiness. The idea here is actually quite good and the first half of this story is very interesting and fun. Two points of view with four main characters whose timelines and actions will presumably cross/intersect and something important will happen or be revealed as a result. Awesome.

Except that isn't quite what you get with the second half of the book. It begins to just slowly fall apart and drift into confusion. The characters aren't kept straight or clear and the motivations behind the protagonist's actions aren't any less muddy than they were on page one. Heck, the results of her actions are just as vague and pointless at the end of the book. I had a hard time finishing it without skimming pages. There were so many missed opportunities to make this a really good sci-fi adventure and the author has the writing skill, so I am coming away disappointed.

title: Not like Black Beauty at all. Fast moving story about obsession and greed.
text:
Dark Horses is in no way similar to Anna Sewell's elegant, timeless,l literary masterpiece Black Beauty. The only possible similarity is the fact that half of this book is told from the horse's perspective and his own voice. Dark Horses is a story about teenage angst, drug & alcohol abuse, and obsession from several parties.

Once I realized that cover blurbs weren't quite accurate and the plot had to be taken at face value, I actually enjoyed the story and the book moves very quickly for the most part. This is clearly written with a specific audience in mind - teen girls with drama and show jumping fantasies. (The current references to tv shows and phone apps may not age well) The characters are driven by different types of greed - money, popularity, freedom from parental responsibility, constant time with one person - and there are some things that definitely seem farfetched. Of course, if you accept the premise of a narration by horse, then some of the sillier plot machinations won't phase you much. I do appreciate that the author has a real, perhaps working knowledge of horses, show jumping and the routine & stress of being on the national circuit. At best, I would classify this as a rainy weekend type of book for horse crazy girls.

title: Most of the ideas are taken right out of popular sci-fi t.v. shows & books.
text:
Ninth City Burning is a collection of fun new characters woven into a series of borrowed ideas from previous sci-fi classics and presented in a creatively told, very detailed story. I think the author has a good story here and I very much enjoyed it, but it's not entirely original.

I found myself stopping time after time to think about why I was having a sense of deja-vu as I read this book. For example - the entire concept of the Thelemity is just a restructuring of the Force from Star Wars. The "Equui" armored vehicles could have come from Transformers. The big modern cities juxtaposed against the settlements scrounging in poverty and conscripted military service felt very much like Hunger Games. The self contained flying city bouncing into a new "realm", ummm Stargate Atlantis anyone? Heck, even the Fontani dream state with entire fantasy worlds of benign life activities screamed Justin Cronin's "City of Mirrors" and the passing of time/dream state for Amy while imprisoned.

If you can accept the use of other's ideas for the underlying foundation of this tale, then settle in because the tale of Earth being bombarded by unknown, evil aliens in a centuries old war is a pretty solid book. There are parts with way too many unnecessary details that slow the pace and serve no real purpose. Better editing could have eliminated 100 pages and lost none of the important things. This book does stand alone at the end, but clearly could become a series. For me though, the fact that I could identify so much of the book in so many previous television shows or books was a serious distraction and it means that I won't be back for any further installments.

title: How does a marriage destroy everyone around it? Loose, incomplete ending.
text:
First thing - Mercury is not a book about a horse, if you're looking for a horse story, this isn't one. What Mercury actually is is a tale about what happens when two self absorbed people marry and forget about the Partnership part of marriage and focus instead on themselves & their personal desires & needs.

You have Viv, the wife, who has been a mediocre wife, a mediocre mother, a mediocre mid-level employee, and a failure at everything else. Instead of learning from failure, she's always just run away - as a Big Sister in college and as a competitive equestrian. Suddenly this horse with tremendous potential enters the picture and she obessess on reclaiming a former fantasy of greatness in the show ring. At the expense of her husband, children, business partner and what little integrity she might ever have possessed.

Donald, the husband, is no prize either. He's always been a coward and a follower, requiring the slightest push to bend to someone else's will. He pretends to care about right from wrong, but he's so busy wallowing in depression and bitterness that he can't be bothered to actually DO the right things. This apathy/selfish indulgence snowballs of course.

Marriage is about two people sharing the weights together. When one goes off the deep end, the other must "cowboy up" and rein them back in before irreparable harm is done. Sometimes it means saying the hard truths and sometimes it means hearing those truths. Neither of these characters cared enough about each other or anyone else to notice the runaway train until it hit them all.

This is actually a pretty good story and I only have two complaints. There was way too much rambling detail about Donald's childhood and his friend, Robert was just unnecessary. This guy popping up as an adult felt like filler and served no real purpose. Donald could have answered that question by talking to his dead father just as simply. Secondly, the ending! Terrible, terrible, loose unfinished ending. It's as if the author just gave up or forgot to include the actual last chapter.

title: Moments of funny shine through under loads of Text Speak & name dropping
text:
Odd Mom Out is one my regular DVR recordings and a guilty late night pleasure. I don't have kids and don't live in NYC, but I fully appreciate the snarky humor and not so subtle jabs at the more ridiculous aspects of trendy nonsense. It's not the best show on t.v., but it's definitely got its moments. Until I began watching the show, I had never heard of Jill Kargman. This book was a first look at her writing for me.

Glitter has some very funny passages and some similar themes as the show - calling out the absurdities of the super rich when it comes to having staff raising their children, their over the top dietary restrictions based on momentary fads, the competition to get in to the "right" preschool, the one upmanship games of leasing vs owning a private jet or Hampton house etc.

Unfortunately, Jill's immature vocabulary gets in the way and becomes an enormous distraction time after time, page after page. She uses cutesy phrases like "BTDubs", ""totes magotes", "whateves" or changes locations such as South Africa to "SoAfs" and Hamptons to "Cramptons" .... The first few times this is ok and gives the impression that she's making a specific point. Halfway through the book, you realize she's just trying way too hard to be trendy and appeal to someone out in the Twitterverse - Tedious much?

The other issue here is all the unnecessary name dropping. Do we need to know that John Kerry (Secretary of State) vouched for her family so they could get into a fancier cemetery? That whole thing struck me as the exact sort of thing she rails against in her show and other segments of the book. This isn't a bad book, it just isn't great. It has it's moments and if it had been nothing but a collection of her one line lists of things that are bizarre, unnecessary or ridiculous, I probably would have loved it.

title: More angst, ennui and self doubt than humor. Lovely dogs, loses its way in the end
text:
With so much ennui and existential angst on almost every page, you might be hard pressed to find the humor in Jonathon Unleashed. I loved the dogs, Sissy and Dante, a great deal and they felt like dogs I know. The story moves along at a glacial pace which is fitting for the inertia of Jonathan's life in general. He hates his mindless cube farm job, his dull long time girlfriend is easier to keep than replace or understand, and the only truly good thing in his meaningless world are the dogs that don't actually belong to him.

There are truly funny spots scattered throughout and bright spots of insight about the beauty of allowing a dog to show us the path - literally and metaphorically. My problem is that the book meanders too much and becomes ridiculous in the last third. No longer a cute look at a young man finding himself and a new life that is about more than selfish materialism, but a complete farce that loses its heart. Borrow from the library, but not purchase worthy.

title: Depressing from page one. Lead character is another weak woman unable to move on from the Ex-boyfriend
text:
This not really a mystery, not exactly a thriller and not a nail biter of a puzzle by any stretch - I actually find the comparisons to Girl on the Train to be misleading. The only similarities between the two are England and alcoholism. I'll be honest, I am utterly over the latest obsession with adult female leads in books who are extremely self destructive, emotionally incapable of forward growth, financially and sexually irresponsible and barely functioning in society despite themselves. Alex Dale is not sympathetic and the constant self pity she wallows in as an excuse to continue drinking herself into a daily stupor was tedious after the first interaction with her police detective ex. Without his pity for her pushing him to help her and giving her the clues, Alex would have accomplished nothing in this book.

The victim's story was told in flash backs and spotty stream of consciousness thoughts from behind her silent mind as she lies in a vegetative state. She seems to comprehend some of the interaction with Alex and other characters, but we feel the vague, fugue state Amy exists in. The author actually pulled this off rather well. There was no satisfactory end for Amy. Honestly, I am glad to finish this book and can't wait to read something else - anything else with characters that I can feel happy about.

title: Heroine is witless, big plot holes. Reasonable romance, bad thriller
text:
I don't read a lot of romance as a rule and I've never heard of this author before, but the blurb sounded interesting. The guys of this group, Ares Security, are interesting and I was drawn into them and their back story immediately. The interactions between Rafe & Teagan felt like those of some men I know. I also found the overall mystery of the serial killer history connection to the leading lady a nice change from the typical romance plot. Unfortunately, I just didn't buy the whole visions thing with Annie - the set up with the men is based on harsh reality and then this weird, random hocus-pocus is A-OK with Rafe? Seems unlikely.

Additionally, there are just enormous plot holes throughout the book that drove me crazy. How does a man get murdered in police custody and there's no further investigation? Copy cat serial killings happen again in the same tiny, rural community and there's no federal investigation? No swarm of national press everywhere? Annie just agrees to stay in a strange man's home without doing any background checks on him first? I liked the connection between the characters actually and if this was just a romance, I would rate it higher. As a mystery...it's not a good book.

title: Not exactly strangers. This was better as short magazine stories for me.
text:
I love the idea of this couple and their story. However, it turns out that I don't actually love the book. The hype was that these two are strangers and they bound off on a whim & a prayer for three weeks, but that's not exactly right. Turns out they had known one another and dated for several weeks prior to this fanciful excursion. Granted, that isn't a long time, but still they had a very intimate relationship and connection before they got on the flight to Turkey. Day trips, weekends and jaunts around Texas - so the premise of "strangers meeting on the internet and having a three week date" isn't exactly what the book is.

I found Jeff to be a bundle of nervous chaotic energy. To travel well with a man like that, you need to be self assured, strong and free wheeling. Clara struck me as floating between those traits and being led around like a child at times. Maybe this is the relationship dynamic that makes them happy - if so, good for them. But it bothered me throughout the entire book. Repeatedly I wanted to scream "Clara! Tell him to get a grip. Get a backbone girl, don't allow him to dictate every step to you." I wish them well in the future, but I will pass on future books - this tale is better served as a magazine story.

title: Slow and lost it's way with the modern day storyline.
text: If this book had simply been the story of the Duchess of Marlborough ( Gladys Spencer-Churchill), I probably would have loved it. The secondary story line with Annie and her mother, Laurel, just dragged and felt entirely irrelevant to me. Neither of those women were of any interest to me. They were in the way of the really interesting character and story - The Duchess. I found myself just skipping pages because I wasn't invested in the book and actually choosing to read other things first. The writing here isn't bad, it just wasn't a tale I could get lost in.

title: Hooked me in the first few pages, but the last half just dragged. Even paradise can't hide your true self.
text:
The first half of this book really drew me in and I was invested in Ann & Richard. Their lives were wrapped around all the modern amenities we can all relate to - constant connection, work pressure, financial riddles, untrustworthy friends, questions about how to start a family, and the usual marital ups and downs. Like a lightening bolt they are flipped over and need to skip town for a bit and figure out how to fix the mess they find themselves in.

The rest of the book just sort of coasts to a meandering, navel gazing bit of drudgery. Once Ann and Richard settle onto the island, we discover that they and every one else there, are just as shallow, dishonest and self absorbed as they were at home. The characters are drawn out nicely and I felt like I knew each of them - to my regret in the case of Wende and Cooked. Paradise is a fantasy ruined by alcohol binges and passive aggressive behavior because you can't hide from yourself.

title: Disjointed and many unanswered questions. Author should have kept a journal to write the book with
text:
I wanted to love this book - I love the idea behind it. A woman striking out to explore some of the most fascinating areas of the world, on her own, on foot and without the typical tourist luxuries. Almost immediately, I realized that I don't like Sarah Marquis much - as a writer, as a person or as another woman. That's a shame because this book is all about her and it is her story, so finding her bothersome tainted every word. As a woman who has traveled some difficult locales alone, I fully respect and understand the urge to go and see and experience the planet. My problem with Ms Marquis is her hubris and her selfishness while she followed this same urge. Ms Marquis repeatedly seems disdainful of the local people she has contact with throughout her journey in Mongolia and China.

The book is written in a manner that feels more like a jumble of memories tossed together with a stream of consciousness instead of from notes or journals kept during the adventure. Events happen and are never resolved, questions are never answered - why did Mongolian men urinate on or near her repeatedly? Did she ever actually see wolves, or just dream about it? Why did she schedule this adventure knowing her beloved dog was elderly and likely wouldn't live until her return? Why not wait? Why didn't she bother to educate herself about basic culture and customs before traipsing through China? She states that she was glad she didn't fill her mind with this extra information, but that struck me as arrogant and dangerous. Maybe if she had, she could have avoided putting herself in multiple dangerous positions. Many of the problems she had throughout the book were self inflicted. I don't hate this book, but I don't like it enough to recommend it to my friends - all of whom would ask the same questions.

title: Left me feeling like I was witnessing ugly gossip mongering.
text:
I love stories of Old Hollywood and of course, the classic movies from that era - the 1930s through the 1950s. All the glitz and glamour and no overt vulgarity and muted violence. The scandalous real life behavior behind-the-scenes remained where it belonged - behind closed doors and in private rather than splashed on every front page for profit. I was expecting more of a biographical book with All The Stars in the Heavens and it's like a cross between a fiction novel and a tabloid.

I have never read anything else by Adriana Trigiani and to be honest, I don't care for her style as evidenced by this novel. The dialogue in many places is difficult to follow and can run on long enough to lose track of who is saying what. There are some characters and scenes that feel very one dimensional and flat when the circumstances should be very emotional and involved. The book would have been much better if it had been trimmed significantly - maybe 100 pages shorter. As with any fictionalized account of real people's stories, there is certainly some speculation and guess work by the author as to what may or may not have happened, been said, been felt or thought by Ms. Young, Mr Gable, Mr Tracy or any of the other people in Loretta Young's world. Take what you read with a grain of salt. I just came away from this book feeling slightly sleazy - like I had eavesdropped on tacky mean girl gossip.

title: Great story, but falls short of the first book in the set
text:
You absolutely need to read The Living first and then read this book. Essentially the two books are just one really long novel cut in half, missing the first one will leave you lost from page one of The Hunted. The Hunted moves as quickly as The Living did and that's a good thing because it's got a lot of ground to cover.

This is an excellent plot and storyline. There's a bit of a young love angle, a rediscovered family connection when all seems lost, hardship and determination, bad guys, good guys and plenty of action.
