It's very refreshing to find young adult Latino characters in any book, especially a strong young woman like Carmen. I wanted to love this book. I really liked The Living and gave it four stars. But....The Hunted fell short. It felt very predictable and the main characters repeatedly made stupid choices that should have gotten them killed in the first couple of chapters. This happens time after time (I would list examples, but that would involve spoilers). The dialogue that felt real in the first book seemed to deteriorate and become repetitive in places and lost it's freshness. I am glad I found this author and I'm going to check out more of his work.

title: Terrible narrator for audible version, lead character is no Kate Daniels
text:
This is a review of the Audible audio book version of Clean Sweep. I love the writing team that is Ilona Andrews and their Magic series. Kate is a strong, smart female lead who is also balanced with humor and softness. I expected something similar coming into Clean Sweep. The idea is a good one - a magical inn and innkeeper who is supposed to maintain neutrality amidst the magical goings-on outside her property's boundaries.

I just never felt invested in this story or any of the characters. Dina is in no way equal to Kate (from the Magic series) - this character is markedly weaker and wishy-washy with none of the sarcastic humor from either the Magic or Edge books. Additionally, the narrator was verging on ridiculous and obnoxious constantly which definitely took me out of the story. She has an overly fake sweet tone that grates and then she over accentuates the Southern accent to the point of parody - almost as if she were trying to be offensive. I found myself just not wanting to finish the book at all as a result. I may try again later.

title: Lovely descriptive writing marred by stilted, forced dialogue
text: The descriptions of Greece and the food and the people and the old traditions in this novel were deftly done and fascinating. The author clearly knows from whence she speaks. I found myself craving a plate of baked feta and olives more than once. The overall story of coming back to your roots, finding your way home in spirit and heart after being away too long appeals to me for many reasons. I loved the grandmother in When the Cypress Whispers and the character of Greece itself, but I found Daphne weak and Popi grating. I think my issue with this book is the dialogue actually. Every conversation struck me as stilted, forced and never felt like real people.... I just couldn't "hear" actual people speaking to each other, it took me out of the story entirely unfortunately, because I very much wanted to sit on a terrace in Greece under olive trees, smelling fresh basil and watching the sun glint off the water in the distance.

title: Not a story of horses.
text: This is a fascinating look at Spain and the history of the Moors and the early Christian/Muslim territory battles for the Andlusian plains. It is also a fascinating look at a variety of lives in a variety of situations of the times - royalty, slaves, women in harems, warriors, conscripted soldiers, monks, rogues, knights, and our hero, Diego who very much wants to be a horse healer and save his sisters, stolen and forced into the slavery of a harem. Yet, like another reviewer, the Horse Healer was not the story I thought it was going to be. I expected and was wanting to read about a young man learning the trade of horse healing, working with horses... I wanted a story of the great horses and their roles in the history of Spain. That is is not this book. So I was disappointed and the story it actually is, is fine, but not gripping and in places struck me as meandering and a bit lost with stilted dialogue and clumsy transitions of points of view.

title: Moves quickly, chick lit playing dress up
text:
I'll be honest, I read the Great Gatsby, but I barely remember a word of it....it was 25 years ago and I didn't like it or I would have have come back to it as an adult. However, I gave this book a try hoping a more modern take on the story would be more palatable. Great was...at best...a middle of the road, beach read to be forgotten and tossed aside upon completion. At worst, it can be described as chick lit trying to skate on the coat tails of an established classic.

The characters felt very much like cliches from pop culture television shows and the dialogue, actions and conversations they had reflected this as well. Constant references to Clueless, Twitter, Facebook, Legally Blonde, Martha Stewart,, various designers, etc Some of these will survive the test of time, obviously, but the book is destined to be dated by next summer. So much modern, entitled spoiled brat behavior that felt like I was reading an episode of the Kardashian clan or something similar in places. I am not sure who I dislike more - Naomi for her spineless self pity, Delilah for her vapid drug use, Teddy for his selfish arrogance, or Jacinta for her stupidity all around...or all of them for pretending they are entitled to and deserve the lives they live and are destined to grow into.

I didn't care for this book much and I waffled between two and three stars. I went with three because it's is actually well written, moved along quickly and I would consider reading an original idea from this author in the future.

title: Not for me - weak & overwrought females, feels derivative of other similar books
text:
I am new to Harry Hunsicker and The Contractors was not the best introduction to his work. Make no mistake, I LOVE a good shoot 'em up story and I really love a good chase story - especially when it rolls through West Texas, so I was excited to pick this book up and looked forward to settling in for weekend immersed in a thriller I could not put down. It was not to be. This book is about 200 pages too long with ten characters too many and frankly I kept stopping to do other things and finding myself not caring if I picked it back up or not.

The good things were very good - the author knows Texas fairly well and has clearly read a map and traveled some of our back roads, so kudos there. The action scenes, when they finally showed up, were tight and pretty well done and the weapon descriptions and use by the various actors was correct and plausible. My interest began to wane significantly very early though with the introduction of Piper, our hero Jon Cantrell's lover and partner. This woman was so weak, so over burdened by emotional baggage and thus rendered unstable and irrational that she would never be suitable or even reasonably considered for a position as federal contractor, much less a working partner to a guy we're supposed to believe is a good agent/contractor former cop. I just could not suspend belief long enough to accept that Cantrell didn't want to kill Piper himself as much as I did.

It was about the three quarter mark that I realized I was having a faint dejavu moment and why with this entire book. It totally reminded me of both In the Electric Mist and No Country For Old Men! Both of which were done years earlier and worth five stars all day long for so many reasons.

title: Couldn't decide what story it wanted to be - mystery, romance, mid-life angst....not great
text: Wait? What happened??? The Stories We Tell started out as a story I really wanted to be told and then it was as if the author lost her place and forgot what story she wanted to tell. Was it about the inner turmoil of a marriage losing it's way and a couple forgetting how to be a couple, a team, a pair united into a family by their own choices? Or was it a mystery involving a suspicious car crash with the husband and his wife's sister (with whom he should never have been driving around late at night anyway)? Or was this going to be a tale of random middle class, mid-life angst and narcissism gone overboard? Sadly, this book tries to be all three AND a half hearted romance at the last second and it just flailed about and ultimately drowned in a tepid, too easy ending. Sorry, but no husband who is that arrogant and that desperate is going to simply shrug off the loss of his wife, only child, income, social status and how on Earth did Eve afford to support herself, her kid, her sister, an employee, an apartment and an entire building for her small business with no further financial stress after all the previous drama just two months earlier? There are far better books out there and I am off to find one now.

title: Mindless happily ever after escapism based on every Hallmark channel movie plot ever made
text: If you take every Lifetime and Hallmark channel Christmas tv movie plot, then you have Love Is Pink. Obnoxious, self absorbed, whiney, single girl...Check. Gorgeous, hunky, loveable guy with heart of gold and secret fortune....Check. Precocious, tow-headed, irresistible 5-year girl....Check. Big dog in need of rescue....Check. Throw in a bit of suspended disbelief for ridiculous circumstance and an overabundance of arrogance from leading lady, way more patience than any real man would have from our hero and so much sweet cuteness that I wondered if the kid was secretly being tranquilized and maybe that would be a sub-plot. The dialogue was stilted at times, but I chalked it up to being a translation issue and didn't let it bother me. Overall, this was a mindless, happily-ever-after story to kill a few hours in various waiting rooms at doctor visits. A cute little book that served it's purpose, but not one I am likely to remember much about a month from now.

title: Writing style distracts from a disjointed collection of stories
text: Good grief. I tried so hard. I wanted to enjoy this book, I wanted to laugh out at suicidal chickens and modern literary wit with an intellectual bent. Instead I was aggravated and felt like my eyes were being assaulted page after exasperating page. The book couldn't decide if it was a novel or a disjointed collection of rants and stories strung together by seemingly endless run on sentences. The humor would peek through here and there and my interest would gasp back to life, only to drown in the author's disdain for his subject matter and the reader's sanity. I literally threw "Against The Country"  against the wall in a fit of pique upon reading the 105 word sentence on page 94. 105 WORDS and seven commas in one sentence. Cormac McCarthy can get away with some of that, but even the great man himself knows where to draw the line. Mr. McCarthy's tales are hypnotic, this was not.

title: Excellent writing hampered by a mediocre story
text:
I found this book to be both at once a refreshing step back in time and a depressing study of vapid girls trapped in a story that had no place to go. The writing was at times lovely and captivating - primarily when the author was setting the scene and taking us into 1955 Manhattan. Yet that spell waned as the plot needed to move forward and our characters had to find and act on their various motivations.

The author clearly stated his motivation for the novel was the long and fabled history of the Barbizon Hotel and the Barbizon Girls who resided there through the decades. Painting that picture for the reader is where this book shines and was outstanding....The research was dead on from the fashion and moral sensibilities to the simple discomfort of the relative rarity of central air conditioning. Had "Searching for Grace Kelly" been a biography of the Barbizon and it's real life occupants, it could truly have been special. As a fiction novel? It's just another average story about three girls looking for Mr. Right who happen to live in a neat place.

title: Well done mystery & characters - bad ending
text:
First the good stuff - the narration on the Audible version is excellent! You can really feel the tension & anxiety and even arrogance in each character as the story moves along. I listened to this book on a round trip to & from New Orleans and was completely hooked. The characters are intensely developed and the plot is very tightly woven and tied together smoothly as the point of view slips from the husband to the wife and back again. None of the characters in this book are likeable and to be honest, I wanted bad things to happen to all of them - that is normally a deal breaker for me with a book. But Gone Girl was so well written and captivating that I could not put it down.

The bad stuff and the reason for a two star deduction - The opening pages were tedious and overly descriptive. Almost as if the author was showing off for future magazine reviewers. There is a very snide, derisive tone toward regular people through the entire book. At first I thought maybe that was deliberate and a trait specific to Amy, but by the end, I realized that haughtiness was shown in every character - Amy, Nick, Amy's parents, Nick's sister, their friends, etc. But the main problem is the ending. The rest of the novel was precise and tense and obviously very well thought out, but the ending felt rushed and unfinished. Almost as if, after all that meticulous plot arranging, the author just had no idea what to do with the characters. What a shame... real closure would have made Gone Girl a five star book!

title: Tiny print, some good info, lacking in some areas
text:
I've been lucky over the years and have traveled in & around almost every state in the US and I take travel guides seriously. Normally, I normally like the Lonely Planet books for a number of reasons, but this one is distinctly lacking. I realze that attempting to cover the whole of the United States in a single book means a ton of stuff has to be left out and that's ok - you get the highlights only. What aggravated me was the portion on Texas.... The biggest state in the continental US, home to NASA & the 4th largest city in the nation, an enormous National Park & some other smaller ones, and oh yeah, a state with four distinct eco systems, yet this book has all of three pages talking about only two cities. Really? Admittedly, my irritation may be prejudiced by the fact that I am a Texan. But it makes me wonder what staples have been left out of other states or cities.

My other issue with this book is the fact that the print is extremely tiny! If you have any sort of vision issues you'll need more than reading glasses to see the words here - plan on using a magnifying glass. I can tell you this - I for one, don't care to be seen on a plane with a magnifying glass in my hand while I try to sort out key info from a travel guide! Having said all that, there is still some good info for first time visitors to the United States. The entire book seems to be geared toward folks who have just a day or two in any one location. So it gets three stars overall - 1 deducted for the tiny print & 1 deducted for scarcity of info.

title: Not up to the previous books' quality
text: I LOVE LOVE LOVE Sookie and this entire series. It's one of the few books that I pre-order without hesitation. Sadly, this 11th book in the set is a disappointment. With the large print and very thin story line, this entire book should really have just been 10 additional chapters at the end of book 10. No way was this a full Sookie adventure on par with the previous books and it could easily have been condensed & added to the other book. There are continuity problems and it almost seems as if the author is throwing away some of the main characters for reasons that just make no sense. Honestly, at this point I think the HBO show "True Blood" is a better story even with the changes HBO has made. I will finish this series, but I think I'll wait and buy the next book used a few weeks after it's released.

title: Would have been EXCELLENT with 100 less pages
text:
The negative first.... At 386 pages in length, I expected tremendous detail about the disease and the it's effects on the society of this family's town as a whole. I expected this story to tell us more about their world as a whole - their neighborhood, their extended family, their town, their actual survival as the weeks progressed, how they ACTUALLY got through. Instead we got tedious daily word for word conversation after conversation page after page after page. Every thought that ran through each character's head was shared with the reader no matter how trivial or mundane or ridiculous. Every single argument the two preteen daughters had was drawn out in detail for the reader. The result was a loss of momentum for the real story. The simple fact that the actual world was falling apart outside their front door and people were literally dropping dead, no help was going to be coming from the government, food was becoming scarce, freezing to death was a real possiblity, theft of their meager supplies was a real possibility, the adults in this story were woefully unprepared physically and emotionally for dealing with these things and yet the author wasted pages and PAGES on melodramatic and completely unecessary dialogue that at times utterly ruined the flow and destroyed the very feeling she had just spent pages trying to build. It drove me crazy. My second major irk with this book was the Mother "Ann". More times than I cared to count I wanted to smack this woman. In real life, she would be someone I would grab by the shoulders and say "Cowboy Up already!" When things go to Hell in a Handbasket, you have to toughen up fast, you must adapt, change your thought patterns, make the very hard choices and take risks and MOVE ON. Holding on to the past, allowing herself to be emotionally crippled and cowering until the last possible second like this character was doing would have gotten her children killed. (Ask anyone who made it through Hurricanes Katrina or Rita or Ike.)

Now the Positives... Despite the lags brought on by the mewling extraneous conversations, this book did in fact flow pretty well throughout. The pandemic was well thought out and realistic as heck. The sense of isolation was compounded by the distrust of all people and fear of infection through simple contact of any kind. Making the transition from our electronic based daily life to something totally opposite is a shock to the system that we never think about - the author nailed that! Those little details like the cold water from hand washing dishes by candle light to washing your hair with a cup of cold water poured over it in the dark bathtub by hand longing for the days of a simple hot shower or even the simplicity of turning on the garage light to find your way in the dark. The author also took into account the street crime issue and price gouging at the stores that might still have supplies available for purchase weeks into the crisis, bartering in a situation such as a contagious disease would not be an option. A strong lesson to be learned from this book and others in the genre - keep a fully stocked and fresh first aid kit on hand in your car and home at ALL TIMES. I also think the author toward the last third of the book found more strength of voice - Bravo. I did find myself reading this book very quickly and the story was compelling over all - I would recommend it though I would caution to skip over some of the conversational parts, you won't miss anything by the end of the book. I would read another book by this author.

title: Starts well, ground to a halt for me.
text:
I really have had a very difficult time with this book for a number of reasons. The opening chapters really gripped me and had me turning page after page. It opened deep inside the mind of a serial killer - a chilling look into the way he thought, the way he worked, the way he found and lured each new victim and justified his actions. An indepth glimpse of how an anorexic mind misfires from normal relations with food and health as it descends into the insanity that allows a person to starve themselves literally to death despite the pleas of their loved ones. Then the look into the small town mentality and how each person brushes against the next one without realizing the effect they can have on each other's lives. I am not sure where I lost interest in this novel or where the novel and the characters in it lost me to be honest, it just sort of happened along the way.

Hayley Jo gradually disappeared from my radar as someone I cared about and maybe that was sort of the author's point? To show that we slip in and out of other's lives in a ripple effect without being aware of it and in the end we really don't matter all that much? I don't know. What I do know is that after several weeks of waffling about what review I would write and what rating to give "Twisted Tree", I'm still not sure. I do know that I came away from the book with a bitter after taste and honestly wish I just had not read it at all. I can say it left me thinking and for that alone I am giving it 3 stars instead of just 1 star - it's pretty rare that a book I did NOT LIKE can make me think and feel something weeks later.

title: Depressing
text:
While the opening chapters of this book were quite funny and made me want to read on and learn more.... the rest just became more and more sordid and sad and depressing as the pages turned. I came away feeling down in the dumps and just overall listless, wishing I had not bothered with this book at all.

On the plus side of things though - the author writes in a way that flows and keeps things moving along and I would be interested in reading more by him in the future.

title: Sort of Funny in a disjointed drunken fashion
text:
I'm torn really with this book and this author. It started out funny and light hearted and I really wanted to like the book. Going in, her voice felt slightly "off" to me, but I thought I would warm to her and she would find her pace as the pages passed. Instead what I found were the stories of her life repeatedly seemed a little sordid and seedy. Rather than the humor flowing naturally and being self evident, it was force fed in many instances as if the author was struggling to make sure the reader KNEW SOMETHING FUNNY was hidden down there in the ickyiness of freebasing cocaine, random other drug use, daily alcohol consumption, rampant low level job hopping, and failure to pay attention to the world around her.

While I did find some of her trials and tribulations funny and I appreciate that she grew through and past them and has become a successful adult, this particular book just wasn't my cup of tea. I much prefer the tone and voice of Jen Lancaster's books in the same genre - she's smoother and her delivery is just honestly funnier.

title: Lost me in the middle - too slow and plodding
text: I wanted so much to love this book - my husband did and we usually have similar tastes in books and authors. However, I had a hard time caring about any of the characters and the middle just sort of plodded along with excessive descriptions of visuals that took away from the action and suspense. I could not finish this book and that is rare, normally I try to slog through slow or bad parts to the end. I just could not do it. I am giving this book 3 stars - I hated it, but my husband loved it, so this one lands in the middle between great and awful.

title: Just too corny for me
text: I had high hopes for this book actually and it was just toooooo corny and silly for me all the way around. Some of the early sex scenes were really hot, but then we had to go to the gay male sex scene and afterward the men all had emotional issues laying around that dragged the rest of the story down. I wound up not able to finish the book - think I got 2/3 of the way through it before I gave up.

title: Not as good as the first book in this series
text: The first book was good enough to make me want to read the next one immediately. A bit of a let down - I thought the Atlantis Rising was far better than Atlantis Awakening. For one thing the same "dead" villians have returned for the second book. I found that lazy on the author's part - the conclusion of the first book was a triumph over the bad guys etc etc etc. Was it that hard to find new villians for a romance novel? I'm not going to buy the third book in this series, if someone gave it to me, I would read it, but I won't be spending my money on it.

title: Good idea. Would be better at half the length.
text: This book is based on an excellent idea that is mostly followed through on. However, it's difficult to like any of the characters. Their mental stability, social standings and interactions and sex lives are studied tediously over and over. Without some of the nonsense this could have been a thoroughly enjoyable book of half the length and I would not have had to skip pages and pages to finish it. By the way - the skipping of long detailed explanations of individual views of the society did not cause a rift in the story.

title: Cute book, not a travel guide
text: This has basic information for the majority of Texas towns on main roads and such. If you're looking for real history or a real travel book, then  keep looking. This book basically is a collection of trivia and odds & ends. It is not a real travel guide nor is it a history of Texas by any stretch fo the imagination.

title: Fascinating Story, Bad Writing
text: The story here is pretty amazing, the author though should have gotten real help with a co-author or ghost writer even. It's written on a 7th grade level at best and some of the early chapters are written for a 5th grade level. The hardships placed on these women in general by their religion are outrageous in the eyes of the rest of the world and why on Earth states like Utah, Idaho and Arizona haven't cracked down on these cults is beyond my comprehension. Freedom of religion is one thing, being born into slavery and neglect under the guise of religion is what really goes on inside these groups.

title: Needs color photos and better tricks.
text: Overall this is an adequate little trick book. Needs color photos and better tricks however. I'm sorry I paid full price for this one.

title: Reminiscent of a Research Paper
text:
This book is not what I expected. There is nothing wrong with it, other than it's just not my style of reading. This book reminds me more of like a research paper. There are a lot of quotes from various resources in the book, which is fine, but I would have rather read more about what the author's views were on each of these resources with the resources credited in the footnotes.

Overall, the book is Biblically based, and thoroughly researched. Just not the type of book I enjoy reading.

title: For those who love both science and art
text:
This is a book all about science and art, just as the title reveals.

Mary Kirsch Boehm says "At first, I have to admit, I viewed the two [science and art] as separate and never considered the possibility of connections between them. But gradually I learned that they did not exist in a vacuum and were indeed related and in many ways. For me, this was a different and very interesting approach, and it was one that added to my understanding and appreciation of science and art."

The writing is a little bland at times, I didn't get a sense of the author's excitement about the subject she is writing about. But I did find it interesting to learn about people in science and some artwork that I was unfamiliar with before I read the book. The book peaked my curiosity and I ended up looking up some things for even greater information. So at the end of the day, I learned some new things which is always a good thing.

I think to enjoy this book you really need to be into both science AND art.

title: Cute
text: This is a cute little book.  If you like cats and like to draw, this might be something you would enjoy.  The cats in this book are all cartoonish.  (nothing wrong with that, they are cute, but if you are looking to draw realistic cats, this book is not for you).  I did like the beginning of the book much better than the end of the book.  The end of the book included how to draw cats that looked like, or were incorporated into food and other non living items, like plants, etc.  So there is a cat stapler, and a cat cactus, and a cat mushroom.  This just seemed odd to me.  Overall, a cute book.

title: Good book
text: I will start by saying that I was comparing this book to Scarlet's book "Afraid of All the Things" from the first word of this book.  In my opinion "You're the Worst Person in the World" is not quite as good.  I think this is just because I related to that first book better.  However, with that said, this is worth the read.  And Scarlet's humor is pretty fantastic and I thoroughly enjoyed that as well as the personal stories she relates to bigger meaning.  Overall, a good book and one I would not hesitate to recommend to others.

title: Great Book for Papercraft Ideas
text:
This is a very detailed book about all things papercraft.  You will learn a lot about the history of paper crafting as well as the tools needed to make your own paper crafts.  As a newbie card maker, I did enjoy this section of the book and came up with some ideas for cards.  I also gleaned some tips on how to do things more efficiently.  There is also another section on actual paper crafts.  And this section is huge.  With LOTS of projects with step by step instructions on how to do this yourself.  This part was not as interesting to me as the other section on the history and tools of the trade.  However, there were also some ideas in there I will likely incorporate some way into my cards.  I especially loved the project on including seeds in your homemade paper.  I also enjoyed learning about the actual artists that were featured in the book.  Such talented people.  

All in all, this would be an enjoyable book for anyone looking for some ideas about working with paper.  And also a great read for people who are just interested in art and art history in general...even if you don't ever intend to make any papercrafts/art.

title: Food Triggers really says it all
text: Food Triggers offers a great perspective of food.  Amber Lia covers all the triggers that cause us to eat unnecessarily.  She brings research and faith into the conversation to round out some positive and right thinking about food.

title: Cute book for the discouraged
text: You Are Essential is a cute little gift book for those who feel discouraged about their life.  Each day there is a small one-page uplifting story that will give some encouragement to whoever reads it.  And in all honesty, this book could be given to just about anyone to just brighten their day.  Even people who do not like to read can definitely handle this book.

title: Networking as an Introvert Made Easier
text:
This book is exactly what the title implies. It’s a book about networking as an introvert and how to make it work for you. And I would think this book would be perfect for introvert people who want to be able to network better. There are many good things to take away from this book.

Matthew Pollard first guides you in coming up with your “story” to use when networking and then explains how to work that story into the networking arena. The ideas presented in the book are pretty good ideas for those networking. I personally will be working in a few of the suggestions into my own life, and even in areas not related to networking. I liked Pollard's view on the various types of people networking; the "givers, takers, and balance sheet makers" and also how Pollard works a room when networking.

Since I used this book kind of like a workbook, where I read a chapter and then worked through the concepts presented, this book was a slow read for me.

Overall, a useful book for introverted people who are networking or who want to learn to network.

title: In search of a creative spark?
text:
I was excited at the potential this book held. But it turned out to be just average. As I started reading this book, about sharing yourself with others and letting them share themselves with you, I was totally into the book. Once I had read approximately 10% of the book, I was excited. By 25% in my excitement was waning. Then by the end of the book, I was slightly disappointed.

The book is laid out by posing one question per chapter, Laura Tremaine then answers that question by giving examples from her own life, and then throws the ball into your court asking you to answer that same question in a journal privately or verbally with another person.

This book offers many thought provoking questions. And if you are a writer, you might even be able to use this book to get some writing ideas or just for writing inspiration, or to fuel your writing creativity. If you use this book that way, this book would be most helpful if read one chapter at a time with time in between to reflect and write. This is not the kind of book I thought this was going to be.

Laura Tremaine opens herself up with her own personal stories, hence the “I’ll Go First” in the title. And these stories are interesting, but also within each chapter are almost bunched together so you don’t realize she is moving to a new story. (This may have been because I read this on a kindle…maybe the formatting was off).

After Laura gives her own examples, the question is posed, “your turn.” This is where Laura gives the reader some follow up questions to get thoughts moving in a creative way to answer this question. However, this part gets less and less helpful as the book progresses, especially in chapters 8 and 9; which also happen to be the two hardest questions to answer. (At least for me.) I felt the guide part this book promised was lacking.

At the end of each chapter is a top ten-like list of things like, 10 things I learned from my sister, or 10 pieces of unsolicited advice. Again, these might be great for the creative writer, but not really what I look for in a book.
And just a word to those who are more conservative in their religious beliefs, there are a couple swear words, and the author has a more liberal definition of god.

So, if you are a writer in search of a creative spark or if you are just looking for an easy read, this book might be for you. But if you are just looking for a memoir or even a guide book, this might not be the book you are looking for.

title: For Musicians or Poets
text:
I will be honest. This book is not for me. It was not written in a logical way, probably due to the author’s artistic bend. I just could not wrap my head around the way this book progressed. And a lot of the people he talked about in the book, I had no idea who they were. (I assume most were in the music industry).

There were a few things I did pull from the book which I thought were interesting. Such as Bach writing “Jesu Juva” at the top of all his manuscripts. And I liked the Afterword “Nuts and Bolts” section. This basically summed up the entire book in a few pages.

Overall, I think this book was written with a different audience than me; such as a musician or a poet.

title: IT'S HUGE!
text: This is not your typical sized journal...it's bigger.  The pages are on the thin side, it reminds me of a coloring book.

title: Cute and Uplifting
text: Walking with Henry is a very interesting story line.  I like the way the author tells her stories and ties in her experiences with donkeys to Biblical themes.  I am only giving this 3 stars because I am a little concerned about a few passages from the book and how that might affect the reader.  For example, the author uses "the KonMari method of spiritual housekeeping".  How can you pick and choose what to believe about God's own words, this is concerning.  I also am concerned about some of the resources she recommends in the book.  But over all, this book is a fun read with a very uplifting message.

title: A funny uplifting, yet truthful and realistic, book on Crohn's
text: This book is okay.  A lot of things throughout the book are repeated over and over again.  However, it was interesting to hear another's prospective on having Crohn's disease.  I also disagreed with some of the "advice" given, but maybe things here in the USA are different than they are in UK.  Overall, the book was funny and the message of not letting your disease keep you from living your life is an excellent one.  And honestly, I do believe that anyone with Crohn's or Colitis could benefit from reading this book.

title: Disappointed
text: This is NOT a large print book

title: Like these Better as a Kid
text: I liked these better as kid, but they're still a good read especially if you're trying to find good clean books for younger children to read.

title: Just Okay
text: I loved these when I was younger, but they don't seem to have the same appeal as they did then.  If you're a kid, they're still great, but if you're trying to reread them as an adult, they're only okay.

title: Did not like the format and returned it
text: Love the Katie Daisy product much more

title: Okay book in comparison...
text: I own the Secret & Secret Daily Teachings which are great books. I purchased this one for my daughter. For some reason I was expecting more or a clearer message for kids, but it could just be that I'm reading it as an adult.

title: ITTY BITTY BOOK!!
text:
The ONE TIME I don't read the reviews, I got hoodwinked.
This book is a tiny booklet that fits in the palm of your hand!

I did not see miniature listed when I bought it, and didn't think a hardcover book would be palm size. So, the joke is on me. Ridiculously small. Disappointed. My rating is based on the size, not the content. Ugh.

title: Be careful... her artificial sweetener info is NOT correct.
text:
ok, folks have to understand that mainly, her description of the artificial sweeteners is WAY off!!
Everyone has their own opinions about shakes, but I have to clarify/correct her brand name artificial sweetener labels.

Splenda:
this is made of SUCRALOSE, and well-tolerated by most people.

Sweet-n-Low:
this is made from SACCHARINE, not aspartame, as she claims in her book. It is considered safe to eat.
The big hubbub back in the 1970's over it causing cancer was a manipulated testing. Lab rats were fed the equivalent of 600 diet sodas a day, something normal people come nowhere close to, no matter how much you love sodas. The "study" just "happened to" coincide with the big release of Nutrasweet, the newest lab sweetener on the block. Every household in the country got a strip of five gumballs sweetened with this new miracle sweetener, while saccharine was vilified. Note that saccharine has subsequently been cleared as no more harmful than any other sweetener, but the P/R damage was already done. Of more concern are later studies which seem to suggest that saccharine, while cleared as a carcinogen, seems to metabolize in your body similar to sugar. In other words, if you deal with high blood sugar, Sweet-n-Low will be viewed by your body about the same way regular table sugar would. It might make blood sugar stabilization harder. If you are only seeking reduced calorie amounts, then this is still a decent option.

Equal:
The old blue packets are a mix of aspartame, dextrose, maltodextrin and acesulfame potasium.
Enough said. Note that Equal didn't want to lose any of the revenue from those using artificial sweeteners of any kind, and are making other sweeteners under the Equal brand name, including saccharine-only, sucralose-only and their latest one, Equal Next, a blend of aspartame and saccharine. Yikes.

NutraSweet:
This is the cutsie name given to the creation of aspartame. Folks, this is just my opinion, but aspartame is something I recommend people avoid like the plague! The physical interaction list is long, and range from just feeling bad to headaches, rashes, etc. In just our family, it gives my husband migraine headaches, and makes my tongue and lips swell up in an allergic reaction. Everyone can do better.

Of course now there are other less volatile options available, such as well-received stevia (although too much tastes bitter instead of sweet), and several types of sugar alcohols, such as mannitol, erythritol and xylitol, the latter of which also seems to offer some dental benefits. Sugar alcohols (also often called polyols) need to be consumed in moderation, because they can have a laxative effect when used too much. They do work well in recipes though, and there are a lot of cookbooks for low-carbers that use the polyols as the sweetener.

Over all, this book might offer a variety of recipes that beats just water and a scoop of powder in your blender, but her misinformation about artificial sweeteners has me questioning what else she's stated as facts that are incorrect. Going to pass on this one!

title: Meh.  Nothing super secret, nothing spectacular
text:
Well, I bought this one for a Christmas gift for one of my two chefs in the house.
It didn't really make a good impression! There were a couple things that have been flagged to try, but nothing that was "wow, I have to try this!". Overall, somewhat disappointing, and I can't recommend it.

title: Disappointing, to be honest
text:
Well, I have to say that I admire almost all artists, and Ms. Bucklew
is no exception. I loved the look of her quilts, and wanted to learn more about the process
of doing portrait quilts.

When I got the book, I thought at first it was a mistake. It was SO THIN!!
The book is extremely skinny. I thought it would be average size,
chock-full of photos of completed quilts, quilts in process, etc etc.
I suppose shame on me for assuming what the book might be. There was no page count information
in the description at the time I purchased it. It is only 43 pages long,
and 7 of those are for a copy of a kitten pattern of hers, so minus that and the one-page
introduction, there are only 35 pages of actual instruction. The font used is pretty large as
well. My old eyes appreciated that, but it stretched out that little bit of information farther
simply by the formatting. In the end, there's just not much book for the price tag!

While it does indeed explain how to break a photo down to get
realistic portrait effects for quilting, the book assumes that you are already a quilter.
It is mainly explaining how to use various computer programs to get a value (color value) breakdown
of your photo for easier layering for portrait effects. The author is very detailed and goes step-by-step
on three different computer graphics programs as to how to achieve layers in a graphic
and how to tweak photos.

That is all well and good, but as someone who already knew how to use Photoshop Elements and how
to tweak photos, I was looking for more quilting information.
I might be alone out here, but I was NOT happy with the book.
The price alone was quite high, at least for me. I don't have a lot of extra money, and what I
do get, I like to spend on fabrics. I "invested" in this book to learn more about how to properly
quilt a portrait quilt, but instead got lessons on how to use Photoshop Elements or GIMP. I didn't
need that.

At this point, I am contemplating sending it back, but not sure. In the future, I am sure I can glean
something I don't already know from the book, but I haven't even opened it since the first read-through
the day it arrived. I didn't see a thing I didn't already know being explained. I do realize that is not the
case for everyone, so someone with no experience with a graphics program will find her instructions helpful.
If you are not comfortable with computers or software, then this book could indeed help you. However, if you
scan your photos or upload them to your computer digitally, and already crop and adjust the color/brightness,
you won't learn much from this book.

Very thin book, very limited explanation of how to actually do the quilting.
For example, I like the multiple borders around the quilts in many of the photos, and would have liked to
know how to do those - I don't know how and still don't. It wasn't addressed in the book, despite being in
some of the photographed quilts.

So in the end,I felt a bit ripped off. Just be aware that the previews tell you about all you'll get from this book.
If you have the extra money to spend on a 43-page book (several pages of which are HER patterns, which is fine if you
want to copy someone else - I want to do my own), and have no computer experience, then okay.
Otherwise, your money is better spent elsewhere to actually learn art quilting technique.

title: Some decent recipes, but Kindle edition is not great ...
text:
I collect cookbooks, and I'm sometimes faced with the prospect of cooking in a kitchen that doesn't "measure up" in terms of size, storage, layout, etc. It's nice to have recipes intended to work in that kind of environment -- even recipes that date from 40 yrs ago (the original hardcover book was published in 1979).

This book is ... OK ... for that purpose. There are some good tips in the introductory material for outfitting a small kitchen, how to maximize minimal spaces, the bare minimum in pans and utensils that will save on storage, etc. The recipes themselves are not bad, although there are more than a few that I know I'll never prepare.

So let's get right to the recipes. My usual practice is to prepare 3 recipes from any cookbook I review, and I followed that protocol here.

1. South African Style Lamb and Black-Eyed Peas
Made with lamb shoulder, onion, green chilis, lemon juice, curry powder, garlic, and black-eyed peas.
A nice flavorful lamb casserole, rich and fragrant. However, instructions need editing: the ingredient list calls for “2 pounds lamb shoulder, cut into 1-inch cubes,” while the recipe says “ … return to oven until meat is nearly falling off the bones.” Uh … which bones? In order to cut it into 1-inch cubes, I had to take the meat off the bone, so there’s no bone for the meat to fall off of. The dish was tasty and I'll make it again. I served it with a fairly plain green salad (romaine and butter lettuce with jicama slivers) with a pomegranate vinaigrette.

2. Flank Steak with Whole-Pepper Marinade
I used a 1 lb flank steak and cut the recipe in half. The marinade is made from cracked black peppercorns, onion, garlic, bay leaf, red wine, olive oil, and cognac. I marinated it for 24 hrs and grilled it on my outdoor gas grill. Easy, no-fuss, and good results. I served it with the accompanying “suggested” side dish: Orange-Glazed Carrot Ribbons — another really easy stove-top dish, using carrots cut into thin ribbons via a vegetable peeler, then sautéd in butter and finished with orange juice cooked down to a syrupy glaze.

3. Caribbean Fudge Pie
Chocolate, rum, coffee, walnuts — what’s not to like? This was easier than it sounds — basically, a chocolate pie that comes together easily by mixing butter, melted chocolate, rum, brown sugar, instant coffee, eggs, chopped walnuts and a little flour, baked in a 9-inch pie shell (I used a frozen deep-dish pie shell). Nothing tricky at all — served it with whipped cream. It’s rich, decadent, and worth the calories.

My biggest beef with this book, however, is the Kindle formatting. There's a broad table of contents organized by category but no way to select an individual recipe. Also, the categories don't make a lot of sense. For example, there's no chapter for meat/poultry/fish. You get "One-Pot Dinners," "Skillet Cooking," and "Dinners for Two" (or "Four") along with "Desserts," "Soups," "Pasta," "Salads and Raw Foods." So where can I find a recipe for chicken? Let's try the Index. Yes, there's an Index, but it's totally unusable as there are NO links back to the referenced recipe or ingredient and no page numbers. So if I find, say, "Chicken, and asparagus in black bean sauce" in the Index, I have no idea where to begin to look for the recipe. Is it in "One-Pot Dinners"? "Dinners for Four"? or somewhere else? No clue. No, I have to use Kindle's "Search" feature (I used the search term "Asparagus" and got 47 matches) in order to find the recipe. I've had this gripe before with Kindle "translations" of cookbooks, but this Kindle edition was just released in 2018 -- you'd think the publisher would have it figured out how to do this properly.

Overall, I can't really give this more than 3 stars. While some of the recipes look interesting (and the 3 I tried were more or less OK), I'm not patient enough to try to slog through the limited table of contents and non-functioning Index to discover something new and creative to prepare. If you're really interested in adding this book to your collection, I'd recommend getting the hardcover edition -- it's cheaper than the Kindle edition and will be easier to use.

title: Hoping for more ... great if you like making oversized crepe-paper flowers ...
text:
I have very mixed feeling about this book. On the one hand, it's beautifully produced, typical of other Dorling Kindersley (DK) publishers. The photos are clear, the construction is first-rate (the cover especially). It has a substantial feel about it.

However, the content is another matter. I do papercrafts -- mostly hand-crafted greeting cards, some quilling, 3D decoupage, and a smattering of origami. This book contains examples of most of those (no decoupage), but with very limited projects. You would think from looking at the cover (and seeing all the "Sponsored products related to this item" that Amazon so conveniently exposes on the product page) that quilling would be somewhat featured in the book. Not so. Only a few pages are devoted to quilling and the primary project featured is a pair of earrings which although nice aren't that useful, really.

My primary craft, card making, is also covered only minimally, and what's there isn't again very useful or unique.

Where the book shines, however, is the section on making large over-sized flowers out of sheets of crepe paper. Almost 1/3 of the book is devoted to this, and the results are stunning. Useful? maybe, maybe not. You'd expect with the number of pages and projects illustrating this craft that there would be some sponsored product ads related to the supplies needed to produce these (crepe paper sheets or rolls, etc.), but no.

So if you're looking for some sort of introductory book that illustrates a variety of paper crafts in enough depth to actually produce something useful, you might be disappointed. If you're looking for a book that is primarily about making large (albeit beautiful) crepe paper flowers, with a smattering of info about some other paper crafts, this might be just the book for you. I can give it no more than 3 stars (it's OK).

title: Decent specific guide but leaves out too much territory ...
text:
If you're interested only in the east side of south Florida, the Everglades, and the Keys, this book will work nicely for you. But if you're interested in the WEST side of south Florida, you'll be disappointed.

I got this specifically because I'll be visiting Florida in October of next year at the end of a Panama Canal cruise that docks in Miami. My plan is to take 7-10 days exploring south Florida by rental car, and then fly home to the Pacific NW.

Unfortunately, I'll definitely need another guide to check out Naples, Marco Island, Fort Myers, Sanibel Island -- basically, anything on the Gulf side of the southern part of Florida, since these aren't covered at all other than brief references to things like catching a ferry to the Keys or a place to eat if you're visiting the Everglades.

The good news is that Miami, Ft. Lauderdale, Boca Raton, Palm Beach, the Keys, and the Everglades are nicely covered with a lot of good current info. I've been to Miami several times, so I'm already somewhat familiar with that area, but I'm definitely looking forward to visiting the Keys as well as the Everglades. Lots of good guidance, including some recommendations for "off the beaten path" attractions.

You'll also need to get a good map. The only maps provided in the book are for Miami city and Orlando -- which is in the north part of the state, not the focus of this guide. I really don't understand including it at all!

Others have mentioned the printing, and I, too, found it difficult to read. My plan now is to use this along with at least one or two other guides plus various websites to plan my road trip itinerary and take notes, then leave the book home.

If your need for a guide to south Florida is very specific to just the few south Florida places that are covered here, and your eyesight is much better than mine, you will probably find this book a reasonable source of info. But the lack of a good comprehensive map and its lack of coverage of the west side of south Florida makes it probably not the best choice. Three stars is the max I can give it.

title: Not for the faint of heart -- recipes that should be attempted primarily by experienced cooks with plenty of time ...
text:
I’m not a regular listener of the “The Splendid Table” radio program although I’ve heard of it and have one other Splendid Table cookbook, but I am a cookbook junky. So I was curious to see what the authors’ take on “weekend cooking” might be.

The recipes are interspersed with essays and commentary about the authors’ creative process, histories of some of the dishes, specifics about various ethnic cuisines and ingredients. I enjoyed this aspect a lot — I’m always interested in how and why cooks develop their recipes and menus. There’s a lot of good info here. But the bulk of the book focuses on recipes.

The first thing you need to know about the recipes in this cookbook is that they are NOT quick-fix easy dishes for those times when you have to get dinner on the table fast. No, these are recipes meant to be pampered, cared for, and nurtured over some hours — lots of hours in some cases. From the introduction:
“What is eating weekends? We think of it as the luxury and the pleasure of taking the time to make things from scratch because they taste better than anything found on a supermarket shelf. It’s about spending a lazy afternoon in a new neighborhood where maybe we don’t speak the language, but can find new markets and restaurants. It’s about the excitement of weaving ourselves into other cultures, and bringing them to our tables with our own hands.”

So if you’re looking for quick and easy dishes, you’ll likely be disappointed in this book.

However, if you’re looking for recipes that require some time and care and you really really love to cook, this might work for you.

I’m somewhere in the middle. I like to cook, but I’m single and don’t usually want to take that much time and effort on a meal just for myself. I did make several of the recipes just to test them out. Here are the results:

1. Moroccan Harira Red Lentil Soup
One of the less-complicated recipes, this one uses fairly basic supermarket ingredients and readily available spices: onion, carrot, parsley, cilantro, garlic, ginger, turmeric, cinnamon, red lentils, paprika, canned tomatoes, and vegetable broth.
I make this recipe as written — no substitutions — and it had good flavor and was easy to prepare. There are a number of “accompaniments” that are listed for serving — dried fruits, phyllo pastries, lemon wedges — that I chose to forego since I was cooking just for myself. But their addition might add a degree of festivity to what is a fairly basic (but tasty) soup. I froze the leftover for later, and it does freeze nicely (defrosted and heated up one serving so far, and it was fine — no loss of flavor or texture). I’ll make this again, and I may use it as a base for adding chicken or lamb to make a more nutritionally robust soup.

2. Charred Lamb with Smoked Romesco
Another dish that’s not quite so complicated, but still packs a flavor punch. I followed the recipe as written. The lamb preparation is fairly simple: leg of lamb cut into chunks and tossed with oil, salt, pepper and a little dark brown sugar, then grilled or roasted (I chose the oven roasting method). The sauce is one I think I’ll use again for grilled chicken: oil, bread, almonds, garlic, red pepper, smoked Spanish paprika, tomatoes, sweet red pepper (roasted), and sherry vinegar, all put through a blender to make a smooth sauce.
Yes, some of these ingredients might a bit tricky to find — we have one local supermarket that seems to specialize in more international ingredients (especially spices), so I was able to get what I needed at one store. The preparation isn’t tricky at all, and the results are quite good. I had leftovers and they were still good the next day (reheated the lamb; the sauce is served at room temperature).

3. Farmer’s Market Pasta
My CSA (consumer supported agriculture) delivery included a couple of zucchini and a fresh Italian chile pepper, so doing this recipe seemed like a no-brainer.
Not tricky at all — I did cut it in half since that’s all the zucchini I had, but it still turned out just fine. I used fettuccine as the pasta, and I had fresh basil on hand (probably the last of my home-grown basil crop - I think it’s about finished for the season). The sauce is garlic, onion, lemon juice, the chile, and a little salt (and optional anchovy fillets — not a fan of anchovies). You make the sauce, cook the pasta and add the zucchini to the pot of pasta when there are 4 minutes left for the pasta to cook. You mix some of the pasta water along with fresh herbs and oil into the sauce, then toss everything together.
This was good — really good — and could be made with just about any vegetable besides zucchini (butternut squash, broccoli, parsnips, carrots, asparagus, etc.). Will make this one again.

So there it is. All the recipes that I tried produced good results with not *too* much effort. But here’s the thing: MOST of the other recipes take a lot of time and energy to produce, with long complex ingredient lists, multiple steps, and hours — even days — of prep and cooking time. And there are very few pictures, so if you're a cook that depends on photos to tell you how a dish should look or how it should be plated, you'll be disappointed. Only you can say whether the ends justify the means. I’ll probably use a few of the more complex recipes for very VERY special occasions for family/friends. Otherwise, this is a book that will likely remain in my “overflow” bookcase of books I seldom reference.

Can’t really justify more than 3 stars for this one, I’m afraid. It’s OK — I don’t dislike it, but I won’t be using it enough to warrant a 4-star “I like it” rating.

title: I wanted to like this more than I did ...
text:
There's a lot to digest in this book, and the twelve basic concepts are fairly simple, really. But the author spends so much time circling some of the focal points that I found myself losing track of what, precisely, he was trying to say.

A little background: I was raised in a predominantly Methodist household, "dropped out" of all things religious for many years, and got back into it fairly late in life. After I retired in 2003, I returned to college at a small Wesleyan university to major in music and ended up minoring in theology. I was also a church musician for over 20 years, in both United Methodist as well as Episcopal churches. So I have very strong "Wesleyan" roots, and it is from that perspective that I approached this book.

The biggest problem I have is the use of overly complicated explanations to illustrate the points the author is trying to make.

The first chapter is a good example. "Worship, not Performance: How We Love God". This chapter seems to be encouraging us to avoid the appearance of acting like a "proper" Christian, "performing" the role, and instead to engage in unselfconscious enthusiastic worship. How it gets there is a long winding road.

The opening example is a description of how the author's children naturally responded to praise band music by dancing in the aisles to illustrate "uninhibited worship." From the first part of the chapter: "That is worship. That's what human existence is supposed to be. God is the DJ of the dance party that is our world. Like every good DJ, God's goal is to make us dance with abandon and wonder. Without an agenda. Without worrying what other people think."

We then journey through Adam and Eve's loss of innocence and the birth of self-consciousness that resulted from eating the fruit; through the forest of self-justification and it's relationship to hypocrisy (using examples from the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:2-6, 16-18). Per the author: "Religion has always been filled with divas trying to outperform each other. If you're really good at being right, it's to your advantage to make worshiping God into an übercompetitive performance of posturing with all the right pieties. This is how Christians turn the worship that is supposed to cultivate innocent delight in God into a masquerade ball of parroted right answers and exhibitionist false humility."

OK, I get it, I think. But the author also seems to imply that unless we dance in the aisles, we're not doing "authentic worship," that the only legitimate response to casting off the yoke of self-justification / pious "performance" is to adopt the child's response born out of innocence -- "Faith isn't the performance that passes God's test to earn us a ticket to heaven; it's the abolition of performance that liberates us from the hell of self-justification and restores us to a life of authentic worship." I would counter: cannot "authentic worship" include allowing a hymn (old or new) to transport us to a quiet but intense understanding of God's presence? "Letting oneself go" in the presence of God doesn't necessarily have to involve the same actions/behaviors for every person, does it?

I think the underlying concepts here are good ones and clearly belie a comforting Wesleyan "slant." Blind adherence to a particular interpretation of "rules" in an attempt to "earn" one's salvation, with no attempt to consider other alternate interpretations, leads to some pretty ugly behaviors among folks who consider themselves "Christians." Love conquers hate. But I feel they're often overly complicated with a lot of extraneous "stuff." Sometimes, this "scenic route" approach to making the point works (Chapter 5: Honor, Not Terror: How We Live By Truth" is especially good); sometimes, not so much.

Overall, then, there are some good bits here, but it requires a lot of digging sometimes to get there. And some of the side trips around various anecdotes and literature references don't seem to fit the concept very comfortably. Solid 3 stars ("It's OK").

title: Nice vintage thread crochet patterns, but the Kindle edition is difficult to use ...
text:
This review is for the KINDLE edition of this book. I have both the paperback as well as the Kindle versions. The paperback version rates 5 stars. However, the Kindle version has some serious formatting issues that really interfere with its usability.

The patterns here are reprinted from old crochet pattern leaflets, and the instructions are reasonably clear and easy enough to follow for intermediate- to advance-level crocheters. And there is a black-and-white photo of each project, including many "close-up" views of the individual motifs.

The problem arises when the photo(s) of a project are separated from the instructions. For example, you see a photo of "Hospitality Tablecloth" - looks wonderful! I want to do this one! Under the photo: "Directions on page 72" -- uh, OK. Where is page 72? There aren't any page numbers in the Kindle edition. So you have to flip through page after page of other photos and instructions until you find the set of instructions under a DIFFERENT photo for another tablecloth (whose directions are somewhere else) that are labeled for the photo of the item you wish to make -- in this case, ** 20 ** pages after the photo. How difficult would it have been for someone to either include clickable links to the instruction page or actually move things around so that the photos are followed immediately by the directions?

I love Dover's needlecraft series, and they've done a lot to make these vintage patterns available for a reasonable price. But if you're going to do a Kindle edition of something, I believe that a little care should be taken to reformat to fit the idiosyncrasies of that device (i.e. "locations" rather than "page numbers").

The patterns are still useful, the photos are still relatively clear, but finding what you're looking for is frankly a royal pain. I'm giving this 3 stars -- it's OK. I don't hate it, but it's more difficult to use than it should be.

title: Hit or miss -- a real mixed bag ...
text:
I've used the Lonely Planet guides for years, and they're usually quite good. And I LOVE taking road trips, so anything that helps with planning is a good thing.

This new release from LP is quite good in certain areas, and not so good in others. It's clear there were multiple authors with very different approaches/insights. Some chapters are filled with towns and attractions that are "off the beaten path," or less obvious; others contain the same old tired tourist traps, with no real new and exciting places to go and things to see.

I decided to check out the treatment of places I'm most familiar with: Pacific NW (specifically WA state), California (specifically northern CA), and the Great Plains. I grew up in the midwest, live in CA for 28 yrs, and now call the Pacific NW home.

The good stuff: the Pacific NW section is good, as far as it goes. It doesn't include a lot of "trips," but the included trips are detailed enough, and include enough esoteric info to make them standouts. The Cascade Drive and the Olympic Peninsula Loop are filled with enough detail to keep one occupied for 4 or 5 days (and I've done both of these trips).

The Great Plains trips are likewise detailed enough to spark interest. Again, there aren't very many trips, and nothing, really, in Iowa (where I can personally recommend a day or two in the Amana Colonies), but the ones that are presented are quite good.

The California section was a definite let-down. On the Pacific Coast Highways trip, for example, virtually every "highlight" is a well-known tourist mecca (Golden Gate Park? Hearst Castle? Monterey Bay Aquarium? really? Nothing new here ...). Even the more detailed San Francisco, Marin and Napa Loop contains very little that you couldn't find on the AAA website. I really wanted to see more "discoveries," not the same old stuff that's been written about in popular travel guides.

For the serious road tripper, I would invest instead in more localized guides at the regional, state, or city level. I can definitely vouch for the Lonely Planet guides [[ASIN:1742203019 Lonely Planet Washington, Oregon & the Pacific Northwest (Travel Guide)]], [[ASIN:1741794064 Lonely Planet Yosemite, Sequoia & Kings Canyon National Parks (Travel Guide)]], and [[ASIN:1742207456 Lonely Planet British Columbia & the Canadian Rockies (Travel Guide)]], as I've used all three of these to plan trips. FIgure out where you want to go, and get the local or regional Lonely Planet guide for that area, and I think you'll be happier.

This book works as an overview; not as a detailed trip planner.

title: An odd little book ...
text:
I rather enjoyed reading parts of this book, but I'm not sure what purpose it actually serves. Tips? A few, yes. But the alphabetical organization and spotty coverage of topics, combined with the fact that many "tips" are VERY lengthy "articles" on the history and/or usage of an item make it somewhat difficult to discover anything that can be put to use in the kitchen NOW.

This might be the perfect "bathroom reading" book -- something to digest piecemeal in short reading sessions. But I didn't find it particularly useful as a reference, and the mixture of articles, "tips," and recipes makes it difficult to pin down.

An odd, if somewhat interesting, little book, indeed.

title: So much potential to be a masterpiece but falling short
text: This book had the potential to be so great. I enjoyed it in the beginning but as the book continued, the main character became less likable and her behavior increasingly unbelievable by making many rash decisions that put others in danger. Many events did not seem to fit together. For example- keeping up the appearances of dinner parties and church. Both of these happened once in the beginning but there is no further mention of any further church appearances or parties. It also did not make sense that Anna & the Kommandant would be keeping their relationship a secret but yet they would be having dinner and going to the symphony regularly. Since he was such an eligible bachelor and given his position, if they were on the social scene in public even a few times, the secret would have been impossible to keep.  Anna's anger at the Kommandant for his wife's death was nonsensical. The book indicates he could not save his father in law without putting his wife's life in danger. It seemed like Anna would have understood that and had been drawn closer to him as opposed to farther away. It was a disappointing ending. I do not believe the Kommandant would have shot her, as she & Marta day would have happened. It is much more believable that he would have shot himself when he found out that Anna was Jewish; or, he may have run away with her when he found out the truth. Finally, Anna's “attachment” to her husband did not seem sincere. His attachment to her I also question, with him being so close to her so often and not being able to even give her a little more contact. The book seemed half-baked. It would benefit greatly from being edited and reworked to be a masterpiece, which it has the potential to be.

title: I guess I'm the only one that didn't like it...
text: I don't want to be the negative one here, but I was disappointed. There didn't seem to be anything novel. It came across as just some big ideas that may or may not work. The authors themselves mention that they're still learning about the subject, which is understandable of course, as we are all lifelong learners, but I felt like they should have been a little further along in the learning process before writing a book. The layout of the book is like a "Diary of a Wimpy Kid" for adults. Half the book is black pages with a small quote on it, and the rest of the pages are half text and half useless drawings that do nothing to further explain what you just read. You could read it in a few hours, which is probably why there's not much to take out of it. Wow. I kind of sound like a jerk. There were a few tidbits I was able to pull out, such as, "What am I deciding for my students that they could be deciding for themselves?" Anyways. That's my two cents. Hopefully it helps.

title: A reasonable System C text, not perfect though
text:
The editorial reviews and title for "A SystemC Primer" seem reasonably accurate. It's definitely a primer level of text, and there are numerous examples throughout. Some I would consider a bit basic, but then I've done a LOT of hardware design, and for someone in school or starting out, I would think basic is good. I should note for completeness, that there is also a SystemC IEEE standard in process, and that would be a good adjunct to this book, as it gets into more depth and detail on the language. Overall though, the Primer gets the job done as a Primer. I do have some negatives, unfortunately:

(1) The price (currently $80+ at time of writing) is a little outrageous (granted, a trend in college level texts, not unexpected, but really still a bit expensive for what you're getting here),

(2) the Primer is a bit weak in the high-level aspects of SystemC and using C++ (which is where some of the power is, high or architectural level descriptions as versus lower level languages, using SystemC for gate level stuff is going to be occasionally necessary but mostly inappropriate), and

(3)"SystemC from the Ground Up" might be the better first purchase (a little less expensive and a bit more breadth, but less an entry level primer)

title: Collection of essays for those considering rehabilitation, NOT a how-to or reference text for experienced rehabilitators.
text:
A useful text, but to be clear this is NOT meant to be a comprehensive reference book about wildlife rehabilitation. This publication (its a 3 ring binder with inserts) is better described as a collection of editorials about topics in wildlife, and the actual reference material is minimal, though useful where it does appear. This book isn't meant to be a guide for situations where the rehabber finds him or herself dealing with an emergency or species to which they're not accustomed, or a collection of scientific, veterinary, or taxonomic information (which is what I was hoping for). This is more for "getting your feet wet" and seems to be geared towards someone *considering* entering wildlife rehabilitation than towards the experienced rehabilitator (or animal professional) who needs a text to reference to fill in holes in their experience or to double check their knowledge.

Because it's basically a collection of essays, it can be very difficult to locate the information you need-- or to even tell if it's in the book at all-- within the text. A given essay on a topic may or may not touch on the info you're looking for, and typically doesn't go into sufficient depth for practical application.

It does offer a lot of good tips for legally establishing yourself as a rehabilitator and opening a center/fundraising etc along those lines, but most topics on actual rehabilitation of wildlife are remedial at best. Typically the reader is advised to just take the animal to the vet, to another rehabilitator, or to euthanize it (or rather, have a vet do so). However in the real world those options aren't always available, especially in emergency situations. This text will unfortunately be of little additional help if a rehabilitator needs a quick run-down on how to handle a less-than-ideal situation. Most experienced rehabilitators will find this text of only minimal value, at best.

I completely understand why the NWRA doesn't want to enable lay people without the proper experience or supervision to start billing themselves as rehabilitators or to think they're capable or rehabilitation simply because they purchased a book, and that's definitely the perspective from which the text is written. However, as an experienced rehabilitator and a professional in an animal husbandry industry, I feel there's great need for the kind of reference that this text misleadingly bills itself as. As it stands I've gotten very little use out of this purchase and was overall very disappointed with the depth of material.

title: Great book for the beginner, but otherwise don't bother
text:
It is a well known fact that James Wofford is one of the best instructors of our time and a superior rider. That being said, don't expect an advanced treatise on Eventing from "101 Eventing Tips". The majority of the tips are basic at best, often downright obvious (eg: "Follow the Rules"). That is not to say this book doesn't have its place or wouldn't be valuable to many riders, but with most tips only a couple paragraphs in length, there is little depth to the material.

I have never read anything from the "101 Tips" series, and was hoping to find some technical advise on difficult Eventing "questions" (especially in Cross Country, the discipline unique to Eventing), or suggestions for improving my show-day performance which can only be learned after years of experience. While there were some very helpful tips, I would say by and large most of the information is fairly obvious to anyone who has Evented before, or perhaps even just shown before.

I do believe that this book would be valuable to the right rider: a beginner to horses who is thinking about taking up Eventing might find these tips invaluable. However, for the experienced (even mildly so) rider, I would recommend you take your money elsewhere (for example, Mr. Wofford also has an EXCELLENT book on gymnastic exercises).

I was also surprised to discover this book is undersized (I had envisioned a large book from the picture, but it is actually only about 4 or 5 inches long at the spine), and has no color pictures. I was able to read it in less than 2 hours (it may have been even quicker than that, as I was reading it while doing other things). To summarize, this book would be helpful for the beginner interested in Eventing, but don't expect anything truly life-altering. If you have been Eventing before, this book will probably not give you "that edge" that you're looking for. For the intermediate to advanced rider, you will get only paltry value from this book and may be better served looking elsewhere.

Btw, these are recipes that had been jotted down and not all have been tested by author. I can now say that I have a good Racoon Roast recipe now, LOL. (blegh).

Some notes, trivia and old time advertisement fodder aren't as precious, entertaining, or informative as I would like. Tiny print. Would much prefer some functional notes. But this was printed in the late 80s, and I am sure this was more for (kind of) learning about the era rather than having a need for return to that era--which we have now. Hello 2020's. I imagine there will be a surge of people buying up books like this for at home library. Choose wisely. This isn't useless, but it may fall very short.
