text:
I cannot express how dreadful this book is. Is it a biography? History? Fiction? Book for Dummies? The only nice thing is the glossy colorful hardcover, no jacket required. The inside pages are printed on rough white paper that does nothing for photos. The book is nearly 300 pages and what is suprising is all the subheadings within the stories. The writer is an entertainment journalist.

Good lord, the photos! There are over 200 black and white photos sprinkled throughout. The photos are grainy, too light, too small, too large, and excessive. Clearly, many are unimportant and/or insignificant. Moreso, on the insignificant. Often, with 6 people squeezing into a photo frame, we, the reader can see nothing but six blurs.

And what is with the some newer bios lately, dumping the photos all over the pages. What happened to the books where the middle section that contained all the photos in one spot.

Generally, a biography begins with a shocking story, something we can grab on to continue reading. So, the shocking news was during a 2005 Riverpark concert in Tennessee, they came across pretty bad, most likely the audience didn't notice or care. The story covers their days when they were called the Tennessee River Boys, and includes a bio on each member. Remember, there are SIX members, six stories that get muddled throughout, and their trials and tribulations. The problem with trying to give us the life stories of six band members, is that each person takes up space, interesting or not, and focus point on the Band gets lost.

Then, it ends with where they are now, including family news, more pics. The last few pages include acknowledgements and a list of major awards and nominations.

If you are not a hardcore fan, this book doesn't do any justice. The stories are not interesting, nothing touching, nothing surprising, nothing new, no dirt, etc. etc. It is too all over the place. And, to sum it up, there were just too many irrelevant photos that are, clearly, not visible. I enjoyed the early days of Diamond Rio, but don't listen to much of later stuff. I think we could have done without this book .......Rizzo

title: Don’t waste your money
text:
I ordered this book thinking that the answers had rationales for the right/wrong answers in the answer section. Basically, the “rationale” is a repeat of the answer and nothing else. For example, if the question is “A baby is born with trisomy 21. What is most likely associated with this syndrome?” A. Coarc
B. Duodenal Atresia or C. Tetralogy of Fellot.
The answer is B because Duodenal Atresia is associated with Trisomy 21. The other books I have go into what the other wrong answers are associated with or what they are, and what the right answer means and what it is. And the questions do not seem to have a difficulty level of the other books I have.

title: Everything But the Kitchen Sink
text:
One of the differences between THE ANDROMEDA STRAIN the film and THE ANDROMEDA STRAIN the book was in the film they actually kill the virus at the end; in the book it mutates into a non-infectious form and they let it be. That decision comes back to bite them in the butt in this recent sequel to the classic novel: something dark and sinister is starting to grow in the midst of the Amazon rain forest at the equator. And nothing seems to stop its progress. Luckily Project Eternal Vigilance has never forgotten Andromeda, and when word comes, a new Project Wildfire team is assembled to investigate the Amazon growth: an Indian doctor, an African scientist, a Chinese pathologist, an American astronaut/scientist monitoring the situation from the International Space Station, and a last minute replacement, the son of one of the original Project Wildfire scientists, James Stone, son of Jeremy Stone.

The original novel was a taut, quiet thriller taking place in a laboratory. This story is what happens when you take the original story and graft on a half-dozen other Crichton ideas, including SPHERE and JURASSIC PARK, add duplicitous military men, an Amazon native tribe, a "space elevator," and a woman who has a genius mind but whose physical problems really should have a deterrent to her being assigned to the Space Station in the first place. Elements of horror films creep in everywhere, whether in the jungle, in the installation in the midst of said jungle, and up on the space station. People get swallowed up, native Amazonians get massacred, and the space station sequences have elements of ALIEN and DOCTOR WHO's "The Ark in Space." The result is a mess, and the only reason I kept reading was because I wanted to see what happened to James Stone. The most interesting thing in the story is the one other link it has to the original novel, which made did make me smile.

title: Not Worth the Wait...
text:
Penelope Thornton-McClure recommends a spicy new potboiler to a woman who walks into her aunt's small bookshop, only to have the women see a photo of the author and claim it's a photo of her! She then runs out of the shop, with the book unpaid for, furious. And when Pen ferrets out who she is and where she lives, and visits to get her money or the book back, she finds the woman dead after falling off a balcony. The bonehead chief of police thinks it's a suicide; Jack Shepard, the 1940s-era ghost who haunts Aunt Sadie's bookshop thinks it's murder. And then things get really strange: can Pen's old classmate, bookish J. Brainerd Parker, have anything to do with the racy bestseller? And what is Pen to do about the girl her eleven-year-old son ran away from school with, so the grieving child could attend her father's funeral?

I have a love-hate relationship with this series of books, originally written under the pen name "Alice Kimberly." Although it takes place in Rhode Island, my home state, the author doesn't seem to know a damn thing about RI, and populates her fictional Quindicott village with a bunch of eccentric Yankees straight out of Cabot Cove on TV, when RI is primarily made up of people of Italian, Portuguese, Vietnamese, and Hispanic heritage. Nobody in Quindicott ever goes to Dunkin Donuts, eats clam cakes at Aunt Carrie's, buys doughboys at Oakland Beach, attends Catholic church feasts in the summer, and mourns the loss of traditional stores like Benny's and the Outlet Company. Instead they patronize the various quaint little shops with goofy pun names that populate every single cozy mystery small town. I was frankly astonished that in this book they actually use a specific "only in RI item" as a clue and actually included a person with the surname "Silva." Wow. Maybe this is progress?

The last one of this series was written in 2009, and, besides the usual gaffs mentioned above, I'm wondering what in holy hell happened with the characters in the past eleven years. Except for the murder angle, the story seems written more as a comedy than a mystery. Seymour Tarnish the postman babbles on with his supposedly fannish dialog and old media references, more annoying than ever. After seeing the mysterious woman's dead body, Penelope starts brooding about the suicide of her husband and wondering if she failed him, when in the previous books he was a creepy spoiled scion of a wealthy family who pretty much killed himself to spite her, and his equally creepy family kept trying to take her son Spencer away from her and bring him up as "an Aryan from Darien," to quote Auntie Mame. Police chief Ciders, who reminds me of the hidebound and useless police detective on FATHER BROWN seems to have gotten stupider in the interim. And what the dickens is with Jack? In the previous books he was impatient but also wise, and even sort of romantic, a cynic with a heart of gold and a soft spot for Penelope, both emotionally and sexually. In this book he just nags and nags and nags with his 1940s slang growing deeper and deeper with every page. You would think what with being a ghost stuck the 21st century he would modernize his vocabulary a little (I mean, in one part of the book he even plays and masters one of Spencer's video games, so he can learn)! If he nagged me as much as he nagged Penelope in this book, I would take the nickel that links Jack's ghost to the store, drive out to Newport, and go toss it out in the ocean at Brenton Point!

title: He Really, Really Wanted to Like It
text:
Fair notice: I ordered this for my husband, who was in Naval aviation (aerographer). He has more military aircraft reference books than you can possibly count, and he's been researching this stuff since he was a small boy (he's now 62). He's a big fan of all aviation movies, even if the best thing about a film is the shots of the aircraft, and he loves TOP GUN the film (except, as he says, for the romantic stuff).

His Pros: There are some very good photographs in this volume. Interesting information was given about the original movie, but just a few hints of the upcoming sequel. Maverick's F-18 is referenced, but no photos are shown. Some of the history stated was okay.

His Cons: Photographic captions are incorrect in many cases; example, there are two photos saying the aircraft is "F-18 Tomcat." One of them is the opening photo for chapter 1! The F-14 is a Tomcat, not an F-18. Another photo is purportedly a photo of Canadian ace Alfred Ball sitting in the cockpit of his SE5A. There is no airplane in the picture. Plus there are no photographs whatsoever of the F6F "Hellcat" and F4U "Corsair," which were famous for their exploits in World War II. How can you do a history of fighter pilots without showing these two aircraft?

The narrative is disjointed. The first chapter is about the original movie and then the next about the founding of the real life school "Topgun" (always one word for the school; TOP GUN, two words, is the movie), then they skip to a "history" of Naval aviation films, not mentioning some significant ones (FLIGHT OF THE INTRUDER, THUNDERBOLT, MEN OF THE FIGHTING LADY, for example), but also talking about KING KONG (which is not an aviation film by any stretch of the imagination). There is also a photograph of Grace Kelly and another of Charles Lindbergh in the movie section, with no text indicating what they have to do with aviation films. Then they go into different time periods that used fighter aircraft and jump back and forth from the modern era to WWI, WWII, Korea, Vietnam, with no rhyme nor reason.

Plus there is a chapter about fighter pilots in pulp magazines and comic strips, with no mention of the three most famous comic strips concerning pilots: TERRY AND THE PIRATES, BUZ SAWYER, and STEVE CANYON!

There is also a chapter about training a fighter pilot with no photos of the Navy's standard jet trainer. Most of the chapter is, in fact, taken over by the story of an Air Force mechanic who "stole" an F-86 fighter in 1956, without ever going into what fighter pilot training is like. There was also what he thought was an irrelevant sidebar about Chuck Yeager.

Husband suggests this book needs an editor who has a better knowledge of aviation, aircraft, and aviation film history. If you ARE interested in aviation on film, he suggests the books CELLULOID WINGS and FLYING ON FILM.

title: A Science Lesson Dressed Up as a Narrative
text:
When I saw the comparison of this book to A WRINKLE IN TIME, I was very intrigued. I read WRINKLE in seventh grade and loved it. And I'm sorry, there is no comparison.

Yes, I am a lot older than seventh grade now, and you may think that has colored my review of this book. But I remember what I was reading at age "10 and up," which is what is the age range for this book is: Albert Payson Terhune and JOHNNY TREMAIN and THE GREEN POODLES and THE GOOD MASTER and its sequel, and NATIONAL VELVET. And compared to any of those, especially A WRINKLE IN TIME, this book is terribly shallow. There is a stereotypical unusual kid, who despite being a child genius is having a conflict with an older sibling, she's got nice parents who overprotect her because she's bullied because of her genius--everything by the numbers. You don't get any deeper into the characters than that--they're all very superficial. By the end of A WRINKLE IN TIME I feel I know each of the Murry family members (even Sandy and Dennys, who only have a small role); in this book the characters are like paper. Plus Lily is being a brat and her parents just shrug it off as her "just being a teenager" and having hormones. Since when does that excuse her from being a brat?

The scientific principles are presented in a very understandable manner for "10 and up," and Maisie's unique solution to the problem is neat, but it doesn't make up for the 2D characters accompanying them.

title: Disappointed Once Again
text:
I should have been suspicious when I noted on the title page that it was an expansion of the ANNE OF GREEN GABLES COOKBOOK from 1985, which came out after the Kevin Sullivan version of the story. I remember seeing that one and remembering how few recipes it had in it. This is just that version "prettied up" with some pleasant flowery artwork and a few more recipes in it. I was hoping against hope it was more like the LITTLE HOUSE COOKBOOK, which includes historical food information and the science of why the recipes work, and why and how Ma Ingalls would have used that particular recipe (for instance, she would have used sourdough starter for her bread on the prairie because they had no yeast). It could have at least been expanded to show the type of food Anne might have made for her children, and the meatless, wheatless menu the Blythes might have eaten during the World War I timeframe of RILLA OF INGLESIDE.

Nice enough if you want a few recipes from the Anne novels and a pretty volume on your cookbook shelf. Otherwise pretty sad.

title: Unsatisfying Postwar Mystery
text:
It's Christmas at Foxwood Manor, the first after the Great War, and the Renshaw family is hosting guests to help them celebrate the holidays, including Lord Allerton, soon to be engaged to the eldest of the Renshaw daughters, Julia. But on Christmas night, Phoebe, the progressive and curious middle daughter, comes downstairs to find Henry, Lord Allerton, and her sister Julia arguing, each apparently knowing a terrible secret about the other. Next morning, Lord Allerton doesn't show up for breakfast, but no one except his mother seems very alarmed—until Boxing Day gifts sent to the servants' families contain unpleasant gifts relating to the young lord. Phoebe is determined to find out what's happened, as is one of the lady's maids in the household, Eva Huntford.

This belongs to the breed of modern country house mystery stories in which much or all of the family is kind to the servants, and a degree of progressiveism in class relations is portrayed, sort of DOWNTON ABBEY Lite with a mystery attached. Sometimes the PC is maddening, as when Phoebe describes the forbidden-by-Grandma American novel her grandfather is secretly reading as "the one about the boy...and his African friend." As if a Brit in that day and age wouldn't have used what is now a more offensive term as a commonplace thing; it seems so evidently stuck in there to show the family (or at least Phoebe) is progressive. The only Renshaw son is snarky in a manner that I think no British boy would allowed to be back then, and there are continued references to him going to "Eaton," as if he's shopping in a Canadian department store rather than going to one of the most famous boys' public schools in England, Eton.

Frankly this isn't much different from a half-dozen other recreations of the past done in the last ten or twenty years, with an ingenuous young heroine (sometimes hero) ahead of her time and her egalitarian ways with those who are supposed to be her social inferiors. Phoebe and Eva are both nice young woman, but there's nothing really special about them, the mystery breaks no new ground, and everything has the polish of veneer and plastic rather than old wood and porcelain.

title: Good Grief...Where Do I Start?
text:
(SPOILERS--but not to "whodunnit.")

By the time I was about a third through with this book, I had to go back and check to see if the author was indeed a guy. Otherwise I would have wondered if our heroine's name was Mary SUE Handley.

I picked this up as a Vine book because I read many Victorian/Edwardian/early 20th century mysteries (Sarah Brandt, Maisie Dobbs, Molly Murphy, Anne Perry's books, etc.). A young woman setting herself up as a "consulting detective" (like her hero, Sherlock Holmes) in 1890 New York sounded like just the ticket. I hadn't read the first book in the series, SECOND STREET STATION, but the characters seemed pretty self-explanatory. Mary is from a middle class Irish family; she has a policeman brother who she can outwit at chess; her mother complains about her not being married; she's blonde, blue eyed and pretty and basically has educated herself via her brother's encyclopedia and reading voraciously (thus some reviews reference Maisie Dobbs—trust me, this is no Maisie Dobbs-type novel); and in the previous book she solved something called the Goodrich mystery and now all of New York knows who she is. But it's been quite some time since the Goodrich case and she's relieved when a woman named Emily Worsham appears asking her to find out if her deceased uncle might have been murdered.

In a trice, Mary is catapulted into a mystery involving—although she doesn't know it at first—the real-life fight between New York and Brooklyn (Brooklyn wishes to remain its own city; New York wishes to annex it) which includes dirty politicians (of course), a few New York millionaires (Levy involves just about every famous name in his story: the Vanderbilts, the Carnegies, the Rockefellers, Leland Stanford, etc.), an elderly woman who chats with her cats, a flipped-out method actress and her adoring friend, a supposedly dead husband, an OCD lawyer—and, if all these characters were too tame for you, a character who seems to come from another book entirely, one of those LAW & ORDER: SVU creepoids by way of a noir mystery, a hired killer who gets sexually aroused by murder and fire. (And yes, it's described in detail. Ew.)

Our Mary forges on, especially when she discovers the coffin of the "dead uncle" is filled with rocks. She follows clue after clue, fends attackers off with ju jitsu which she learned from a Chinese instructor (and then later in the book it's revealed she also knows "the French art of kickboxing known as savatte"), is so plucky that most people have no problem with the fact that it's 1890—a time where a woman can't walk down the street un-escorted without being looked at askance—and she's a "lady detective," and is so brave and forthright that George Vanderbilt falls madly in love with her and at one point is willing to give up building his dream home, Biltmore House, for her. Or that in another chapter Mary is shot in the back and the bullet hits nothing vital and the blood transfusion she gets from George works even though doctors back then didn't know about blood typing and there's a 50 percent chance she might have died. (Incidentally the guy who shot her runs away into the woods and gets killed by a bear...honest.)

Let's not leave out the fact that Levy peppers his text with myriad little facts about the era or quotes from writers as if he couldn't bear to leave any of his research behind (in one chapter, Mary and George go to Richmond, Virginia, where Mary brightly observes that Richmond has electric trolleys, the first ones in the United States, and Manhattan is so behind the times). Or that no matter how much research he did, modern verbiage pops up to kick you out of the story (like the gay character who refers to himself as gay when that wouldn't be a term until 80 years later).

In the end I'm giving this book two stars, one because Mary was kind of a neat character who needed a much different author (even Carolyn Keene would have done, since I kept thinking of Nancy Drew), and the other star for the laughs it provided to my husband and I at bedtime last night as I was discussing the story with him.

title: Missing Jewel, Halfhearted Story
text:
It's Three Kings Day at the Montoya family rancho, and they've welcomed guests, included Don Javier, an old beau of Tia Dolores, who is now Josefina's stepmother. He has brought Tia Dolores a beautiful ruby ring which is an inheritance from her aunt. Also visiting is Senor Fernando, a man who is considering buying a horse from Josefina's father. During the festivities, the ruby ring disappears. Could Don Javier be the culprit? Senor Fernando? Or is it the strange man Josefina has seen hanging around near their hacienda? And why does Tia Dolores seem so dispirited? Can it be she regrets coming to the rancho and marrying Mr. Montoya?

I can't believe Valerie Tripp wrote this. It's so very obvious who the culprit is (think the LOST IN SPACE episode "The Golden Man") and what happened to the ruby. And, maybe it's because I'm an adult, I also figured out why Tia Dolores was so unhappy from page 20. Just because the readers are kids doesn't mean you need to give them a storyline with cliched aspects. Disappointing.

title: The Complaint Department
text:
I was about to buy Bryson's newest, THE ROAD TO LITTLE DRIBBLING, having enjoyed his earlier NOTES FROM A SMALL ISLAND, MOTHER TONGUE, MADE IN AMERICA, etc., but the reviews about bitter humor gave me pause. Did I actually want to spend the money to buy this in hardback? Why not instead read one of the three Bryson books I still had in my "to be read" pile? So I picked up this one. The premise: Bryson, after years of living in England, comes home to the midwest (Iowa) in 1988 and drives around most of the country in a little Chevette (one of which I had once), commenting about the odd and the unusual.

Well, there's some of that, some nice descriptions of a couple of national parks, and some nostalgia about family vacation trips when he was a kid. The rest is an endless kvetch, kvetch, kvetch about everything: the bad food, the ugly homes, the tourists—Bill, Bill, Bill, you go to national parks and tourist areas and then complain about how crowded they are; should they be empty, just for your pleasure?—looking for some Shangri-La of a small town. The funny part is that he travels through the Midwest and the South—badmouthing everyone in the latter as if it were still 1955; he is astonished, apparently, that in 1988, black people and white people actually EAT together in the South!—and can't find the ideal small town, then when he gets into New England and finds some picture-perfect ones, heavens, they're TOO perfect.

Okay, I know he's supposed to be commenting wryly on the American scene, and his observations on tourist traps are spot on, but really, after pages and pages of this stuff, can you blame the reader if he or she is the one who wants to kvetch, kvetch, kvetch right back? Along the way he trashes country music, Mexican music, farmers, hillbillies...and heaven forbid that you are female and overweight! It seems every few pages or so he goes into a diatribe about obese women, which is rich considering he describes himself as overweight several times. Plus, as far as I can tell, the only things he liked that he saw were a few scenic spots, Cooperstown, and the Henry Ford Museum/Greenfield Village. He writes off Williamsburg because, you know, some of the buildings are reconstructed; doesn't like that all the treasures of the Smithsonian are now in separate buildings instead of piled higgledy-piggledy in the Castle to discover in a corner; and is sour because most places don't look like the pictures.

Unless you like endless jokes about fat women, motor homes, and stereotypical waitresses, borrow this from the library, okay?

title: Atmospheric, But Lacking, and Violence Toward Women Troubling
text:
Having sampled Shepherd's THE SOLITARY HOUSE and found it a fairly interesting mystery despite not having read the Dickens' novel that was its inspiration (BLEAK HOUSE), I thought I would give this newest effort a try. I'm sorry to say I found it a less-than-stellar knockoff of DRACULA. Victorian investigator Charles Maddox visits Baron Von Reisenberg in Austria to see if a donation promised to Oxford University by the Baron is legitimate. Instead he finds Von Reisenberg's name strikes terror in those whose homes surround his castle and the homestead itself is a place of horror. He escapes only by being confined to a hospital with a fever. But once back in London, he discovers the Baron has arrived there as well.

Shepherd's description, especially in the first third of the book where Maddox is in Austria, is haunting and atmospheric. You feel the penetrating cold, witness extraordinary and terrifying sights, shudder at the atmosphere of evil which permeates the surroundings. The problem is that the story itself doesn't live up to the descriptive language, and frankly Maddox isn't a very appealing protagonist. I was also bothered by the fact that this is the second novel of Shepherd's that I've read that features terrifyingly brutal things happening to women; some of the narrative is extremely hard to endure. Since I haven't sampled her first novel or the one that preceded THE PIERCED HEART, I'm not sure if this is a regular feature of her mysteries, but for myself twice is enough. I won't be ordering another one of her books again.

title: Conquered
text: My favorite science in school was "earth science" and I was excited upon seeing this book as it looked as if it were an interesting geological history of the planet. I never like to admit that I didn't finish a book, especially one that I had sent for that looked so promising, and don't like to submit a review of a book I didn't finish, but I must be honest...I never have finished this book. Maybe it improved in the last half. I still have it and perhaps my tastes will have changed in the future and I will tackle it again.

title: Misleading Title
text:
This volume had a misleading title. When I saw "two novellas" I thought someone might have rediscovered a couple of stories Hammett did for the pulp magazines (whether published or nonpublished) based on THE THIN MAN (perhaps even using the original elements of the book rather than the movie--in the book, for instance, Asta is a Schnauzer, not a wire-haired fox terrier and is also female). I was therefore dismayed to discover that they were just outlines for the next two THIN MAN films. I pretty much found these plodding and dull to read.

Richard Layman's introduction, as well as the additional material by Julie Rivett, which tells of the relationship between Hammett and the studio and how the sequel films were made are excellent; for die-hard fans of the films you might want to buy the book just for this alone. But if you are looking for "novellas," they aren't here. You may feel comfortable reading script summaries and gain some enlightenment from them, but I was simply bored. Your mileage, as they say, may vary. My apologies for a lackluster review, but this was a lackluster volume.

title: A Pale Version of the Original
text:
I became friends with Rebecca Rowena Randall via a Whitman hardback, way back when I was eight years old, admiring her grit, her creativity, and her blossoming from feckless young girl to poised young woman, rejoicing in her successes and commiserating in her defeats. I was delighted later to find a second book of her adventures that added more childhood events and even stories about her friends.

Eric Wiggin isn't related to Kate Douglas Wiggin, although some of his biographies have stated so. He took two classics, REBECCA OF SUNNYBROOK FARM and NEW CHRONICLES OF REBECCA, simplified all of Kate Wiggin's lovely poetic Edwardian language, and blended them into one narrative spanning two books, then produced this novel, a sequel to both, layering on a thick smear of overt Christianity to what was already a Christian-themed book. Not only does this heavy-handed moralizing reduce poor Rebecca to boring adulthood, but Wiggin also saddles every country character (like Rebecca's mother) with cheap rural accents (Aunt Jane suddenly has one, too). Kate Wiggin says John Randall went to medical school; in this John stays around to do farm chores. Where Eric Wiggin might have expanded on the characters of Rebecca's siblings Mark, Fanny, and Jenny, instead they are reduced to the background, while we listen to Adam Ladd repeat what improvements the railroad will make to Sunnybrook and the surrounding countryside ad infinitum. (Just how many times can you comment about the difference a standard-gauge railway instead of a narrow-gauge one will make?) (I also noticed Mr. Wiggin lowers "Mr. Aladdin's" age so hopefully people will forget Rebecca's being courted by a man twenty years older than she is.) Oh, and Harriet Beecher Stowe makes an appearance, despite the fact that Rebecca was written in 1904 and in this book everyone is getting a telephone, and Stowe died in 1896.

Add to the fact that Mr. Wiggin kills off a regular character and then spends his time indiscriminately matching up adult characters in holy wedlock...well, the book ends up being a disservice to Kate Wiggin, but most of all to the wonderful spirit of Rebecca Randall. Phooey.

title: Chicka Chicka Boom Boom with a new title, very annoyed
text: Quality book, but this is not a NEW or DIFFERENT book....it’s almost exactly the same as Chicka Chicka Boom Boom with only very minor changes. Don’t waste your money on this one and buy the original.

title: Dean Koontz Dissapoints Again
text:
I've been a lifelong fan of SOME of Dean Koontz's work. His books are very hit or miss for me. I have loved some of his books and I have loathed others. This one was not the worst but it was definitely a disappointment.

Koontz spends pages developing a character who dies suddently and unceremoniously half way through the book, but barely explains the background of characters who are integral parts of the story! It seems almost elementary - he inserts such great care and detail into the beginning of the book (with some of his fantastic descriptive writing I have come to love), but the end just seems slapped together. The entire confrontation with the "bad guys" only lasts about a page and then it's over in a very abrupt and cheesy manner (I love fantasy/sci fi, but come on!).

The whole book is a big chaotic and hard to follow in general. If you want to read Koontz, take a look at Life Expectancy or the Odd Thomas series. I highly advise steering clear of this one!

title: Good but not what I though
text: I thought this was going to give me a couple of things history put on paper a little an entirely different way.  Lots of just black and whit on a page with some inked pages of drawings.  I had a coule other books to try to get me to the cutting edge stuff which is what I was needing at the time and it still sits on my shelf opened one time...look into its contents before buying I thought a different outcome from the title.

title: Slow, Banal, and Boring
text: As a sci fi fan who cut his teeth on the flood of nuclear armageddon stories that flooded the sci fi world in the 1950s, I was very much looking forward to this book. Having read, watched, and listened to more end of the world tales than I can count, a new take on the apocalypse is always welcome. Sadly, Last Day was a total disappointment for me. One quarter of the way into the book, all I've encountered are damaged characters ranging from the unlikable to the forgettable, each of them as boring as their lives are. Nothing in the narrative drew me into the story or gave me any reason to keep reading. Instead, I was forcing myself to continue for the sake of this review. When I got to the part about a rich guy floating bubbles of mouse pee in a weightless space station because he had so much money he could get away with it, I threw in the towel. Perhaps this book eventually does something interesting with these folks. Personally I don't care enough about any of them to stick around any longer to see. Peace out.

title: Third Grade Reading Level
text: The characters are one-dimensional cardboard figures cut out from some big book of stereotypes. The plot is obvious and predictable. The writing is at the third grade reading level but any smart third grader will see it for what it is - trite, trashy story telling.

title: The Story Is A Confusing Mess
text:
You won't see "verified purchaser" attached to this review because I read a library copy. Having just finished the book I'm very glad I didn't buy it. The author is playing with memories, illusion, and reality, with her story revolving around the question of how you tell them apart. That's all well and good but she goes on to spin the reader into the same confusion the heroine is experiencing. That approach takes a lot of skill to pull off and for me Harrison misses the mark by a mile. Repeatedly throughout the book I found myself wondering what the heck was going on. There is so much unexplained and/or missing back story that half way through I went online to see if this book was the latter part of a series. Nope, it's the beginning of the series and a very muddled beginning.

Then the plot, with it's repeated double and triple crosses and it's escape/recapture/escape pattern started getting tedious. I understand those plot twists were necessary to illustrate the problems the heroine was encountering. Unfortunately the twists were not handled well enough to keep my interest.

Beyond all that I simply didn't care for any of the characters in the book. I found myself repeatedly cussing out loud "How can you be so #@*% stupid!" Their behavior just irritated me and that's not a good basis on which to care about them. Harrison is a good writer and I've liked other books of hers. This series I'll just pass on though.

title: Great for putting you to sleep
text: I love Jo Goodman, but this book just slugged along and I found myself skimming over pages. There was nothing about the book that caught my interest as it was slow building. Mitch was a good character, and Thea was ok, just couldn't understand how anyone could want a personal relationship with her. She comes across as being cold and aloof - how many people would give her chance after chance and still want to keep trying? The book bored me and I could barely finish. Love her historicals, didn't mind this was a contemporary, but seriously, the book should have been a lot shorter - 407 pages of pure sludge.

title: YAWN!!
text: First off, let me state that I love LLM and her books are on my auto-buy list. This book, however, is so boring I had to force myself to finish it. There was basically no storyline worth almost 400 pages - this should have been a novella. The story dragged on and on with immaterial, daily life stuff and conversations and redundant secret thoughts and feelings by the characters. It had no sexual tension and very little emotional angst - by the middle of the book I didn't care about either H/h and just wanted it to end.  I doubt if I will buy the other two in the series when they come out.

title: I really should have enjoyed it, but I didn’t.
text:
I really should have enjoyed Lisa Jackson’s “Liar Liar”. It had everything that should have made it a fascinating read - murders, bad guys and complicated twists/turns, but something was missing and I ended up just working through it, not really enjoying the story.

The Plot: Didi Storm wanted to be a star, but as luck would have it, she was a single mother of three and a second-rate Marilyn Monroe impersonator. She was always hoping for a big pay day, even if it meant selling one of her twins. Remmi, Didi’s teenage daughter, is tasked with keeping her mom’s secrets (among them that she didn’t have just one baby but two) she just didn’t know what exactly that would mean. So one night, Remmi (accidentally) stows away in the hidden compartment of her mother’s car and finds herself in the desert with Didi, who is up to no good. Unfortunately, she witnesses something that would haunt her for her remaining days – the supposed death of her baby sister, who was dressed like her baby brother. Never admitting that she was there, Remmi returns home wondering how her mother will explain it all. Instead of explaining, her mother disappears without a trace and so does everyone else who she holds near and dear. Skip ahead a few years later, a book has been released surrounding her mother’s disappearance, and Remmi witnesses her mother’s look-alike jump to her death. What in the world does this suicide (or is it murder) have to do with her mother’s disappearance? She doesn’t know, but intends to find out with the help of her childhood friend (Noah) who is intrinsically intertwined with the mystery from years ago. Just who is behind the disappearance of Didi, her twins (Ariel and Adam) and their trusted nanny (Seneca)? Just what is going on? As the story unravels we find a murderous killer who is determined to cover his steps by any means necessary and a plot that fell a little short.

I had a lot of hope for this story and really anticipated being riveted. Unfortunately, I wasn’t. And a story that should have held my attention, seemed to drag on and on. There was a lot that I would have cut out, to streamline the story and keep the plot moving. I also wasn’t really invested in the characters. Again, there was something that was missing from the story, but I don’t know exactly what. And perhaps more disappointing was the fact that after powering through the story, the ending and the reason behind the whole story, was lack-luster and bland. Ironically, this was not my first Lisa Jackson novel, but it was amongst my least favorite. I found myself just getting through the story and not really enjoying it although the ending was somewhat entertaining. I wouldn’t recommend this one and would give it 2 stars.

title: Tons of potential but I was disappointed.
text:
People who know me, really know me, can tell you several things about me. (1) I have a passion for reading. (2) While I will read anything, I don’t gravitate toward biographies (although a few have caught my interest) or historical/period pieces. They aren’t exactly my thing or cup of tea. [Not, I’m not saying that this is a biography, just stating a fact.] (3) I tend to lean towards crime, mystery/suspense or supernatural novels. After all, who doesn’t love a good zombie, werewolf, vampire or shapeshifter. And (4) once I start a book, even if I know that I’m not enjoying it, I will finish it although there have been a few exceptions (this being one among them). I hate to admit it but while I really wanted to enjoy “Don’t Believe It” by Charlie Donlea, I struggled to read it and I don’t even know why. It was a struggle for me even though it had everything that should have made it a riveting read. I mean there is deception, murder, red herrings and the exotic location of St. Lucia, but it just wasn’t enough. While I shouldn’t have been able to put this book down, I could and did, constantly.

Now a brief synopsis. We have all heard or read stories about an “innocent” person being exonerated thru an innocence project (DNA), some newly discovered information or just someone honestly seeking the truth. Donlea’s “Don’t Believe It” explores this very issue. Grace Sebold has been jailed for several years following her arrest and conviction for the brutal death of her boyfriend, Julien. As she sees it, her last hope of uncovering the truth is filmmaker, Sidney Ryan. Grace hopes that Sidney’s ambition and thirst for a good story will lead to new clues in the case and unveil the real killer once and for all. The question becomes, can Sidney uncover the truth within the allotted time before the end of production?

In the end the problem for me was the fact that not even the cute little style changes (the letters, flashbacks, etc) could make up for the slow, monotonous story that unfortunately fell a little flat to me. I kind of chugged through a few hundred pages and then gave up. To be honest, I just didn’t feel invested in the story, or the characters enough to care how it all ended. With that being said, I will try to revisit the book and update my review if I am ever able to finish it. Sorry. 2 stars.

title: I just didn't get it.
text:
“Half Moon Bay” was my first attempt at reading a novel by Alice LaPlante and oddly enough, I just couldn’t finish reading (or really get into) it. To be honest, I’m not sure what the problem was- meaning was it the storyline or the writing style. Regardless, I found it all to be a bit confusing. When I read, it is for enjoyment and as an escape, but if you make it too difficult (this one was filled with lyrical prose and complicated symbolisms) or the plot too hard to follow, I end up losing interest and will put it down. This happened several times while I was reading this story, until I finally didn’t care enough to even know how it ended.

Initially, I thought that I would be able to get into the story (based on the book description). The main character, Jane, has a tragic past that involves the death of her child. In an effort to heal, she decides she needs a fresh start and moves to a new town, Half Moon Bay. Here she finds herself in the middle of a nightmare, that hits a little too close to home. Children are mysteriously disappearing, and while she is trying to rebuild her life (which includes a new love interest, Edward), she is moved to figure out who is responsible for taking the children and why. Ironically, this is where I lost interest. What should have been a pretty easy read (it is broken down into three parts: Losses, Trespasses and Love), proved instead to be a meandering tale told in the 3rd person, that left me of dazed and confused. Literally. There was so much symbolism and complicated (and at times) meaningless dialog that I just didn’t get. I eventually gave up on this story. It just wasn’t my cup of tea.

title: Should have loved it, but didn’t. 2.5
text:
Beautiful/independent Honor Brown has purchased her first home, ok, it’s a real fixer upper, but it’s all hers. So when she and her best-friend, Lexi, make a real entrance by running into a trashcan with a moving van- they find themselves the object of her neighbor’s attention. Witnessing her embarrassment is the very sexy handman/neighbor (Jason), his brooding brother (Hogan) and his adorable nephew (Colt). But accepting help does not come easy for Honor, so she sets out trying to do the rehab on the house and her life on her own.

I have read other Lori Foster books that I liked better than “Don’t tempt me”. I think the problem for me was that Foster was trying to do too much, perhaps setting the stage or the basis for her new series, that will undoubtedly revolve around the Guthrie brothers. #1: There was the introduction of a ton of characters. There’s Honor, Lexie, Colt, Hogan, Jacob, a sexy Sheriff (Nathan), a martial arts teacher (Sullivan Dean) and the sultry red-head (Violet). In other words, too many partial back stories told, but not enough to really get invested in any of the characters. #2: While the main character, Honor, should have been endearing, she came off as irritating. I mean in the beginning she was cloaked in mystery, only to end up NOT being so mysterious and instead a little silly and insecure. And when her eventual secrets were revealed they fell a little flat to me. And Jacob was ok, the typical rescuer. #3: For this to be a romance novel, the sex scenes were mediocre and sparse. Again maybe that was because of the efforts of Foster to build a series. #4: Too many plots. There was some romance, some random burglaries, some heartbreak, and some mud volleyball and one over-arching storyline (Honor’s), but all of them were lackluster.

In conclusion, this review was perhaps one of the hardest for me to write because I really should have liked this book. But it fell a little flat and while I can name a few of the reasons, others elude me. So while I usually enjoy Lori Foster books, if this had been my first, it probably would be my last.

title: Torn. I should have loved it.
text:
I should have loved this story. It had everything that should have made this a riveting read. There was a mystery, interesting characters and a twist. I shouldn’t have been able to put this book down, but I found that I did over and over again, and had to force myself to pick it up. So in an effort to be fair to the author, who I am sure put her heart and soul into this story, I will explain my rating by dividing this review into two portions: what I like and what I didn’t.

What I liked:
*Plot potential. Basically Solemn is a young girl, living in a trailer park, who sees something she shouldn’t. She is a keeper of several secrets.
*Tons of imagery. Even the trailer park itself is symbolic of a sense of despair and isolation.
*Interesting characters. The story is told from various point of views. Among them the young girl, a police officer and a mother. You see the events through their eyes. Their perception of the events vary depending on their perspective and interests.
*There were undertones of various social issues (i.e., education, poverty, race, domestic violence, alcoholism and drug use) woven throughout the story.

What I didn’t like (which explains my low rating):
*The story was hard to follow, and hard to read. It almost seemed like a collaboration between Toni Morrison, Alice Walker and Sapphire, with a little Octavia Butler thrown in for good measure. What should have worked in theory didn’t. Instead it seemed a little all over the place. Unfort
unately, instead of one cohesive story or collaboration, it meandered and skipped around. There were times that the writing was so wordy, that I got a little lost and confused in the story. I found myself skipping sections or re-reading sections which isn’t a good sign. Perhaps in the next few weeks, I will re-read this book and revisit my review. Otherwise, I give this story 2 stars.

title: A little much. 2 - 2.5 stars
text:
The book “Confessions of a Wild Child” offers a glimpse into the background (i.e., childhood) of Lucky “Saint” Santangelo. Initially I thought this was going to be a great read, but it actually turned out to be ……exhausting. “Lucky” is definitely a handful and gets into more trouble before she was even 16 years old than the average teen. With the exception of knowing that she discovered her murdered mother’s body in the pool and loves her brother, I didn’t remember much about Jackie Collins’ Lucky (it’s been a few years). Confessions chronicles Lucky’s misspent youth. We see her: escaping from various boarding schools; trying to get her father (Gino the Ram) to realize she should take over the business even though she is a girl; exploring her sexuality (i.e., going “almost” all the way with boys); places herself into dangerous situations; fleeing the country with no money and surviving in Paris; protecting her gay brother (Dario); and proclaiming her unrequited love for Marco (her father’s close associate). The story ends with Gino arranging Lucky’s marriage to Craven Richmond, the awkward son of a Senator.

Personally, I was a little disappointed…although I know the story is dated….Lucky was involved in some very risky behavior (i.e., riding with strangers, taking up for a puppy that is being beaten by two losers). I know the story took place in the late 80’s (hence the fashion and cocaine references), but marrying off your 16 year-old daughter (the same week of her 16th birthday) to a 21 year old is in poor taste. While the backdrop of a story in Vegas should be exciting, I found the whole storyline to be a tad forced. Still, I plan to re-read “Lucky” because I don’t remember it, and hopefully it will be better than this one and make sense.

title: Just ok.....2-2.5 stars
text:
Having recently gone thru a divorce (from her movie star husband) and having recently retired from her career as a soap opera star, Abby Langford believes that returning to her hometown (with her young daughter) and writing a mystery novel may be just what the doctor ordered. But while cleaning her home, she stumbles across an old knife, covered in what looks like blood, and sets out to solve a mystery. The only problem is, when you she reports it to the police, the Chief (Josh Kincaid) thinks she might just be looking for publicity. What she doesn't understand is that Josh is skeptical because of his past relationship that involves his ex-wife who just had a baby with his ex-best friend. And what he doesn't know is that she wasn't the problem in her past relationship, that it was her cheating ex-husband. While the two initially dislike for each other, they can't fight their growing attraction for each other. They find that they have more in common than they initially thought.
As threats against Abby increase, they must determine if the threats are related to her character on the soap Private Affairs, or something else. So when she is killed off of the soap, and the threats continue, Josh isn't so sure about anymore.

This wasn't the worst book that I have read, but it wasn't even close to the best. To me, Josh and Abby were kind of annoying. They were a little one dimensional.....Josh was the huge, larger than life Sheriff who was self-righteous but sleeping with a 20-year-old because he didn't want attachments.....Abby believes she might be psychic, but regardless is so self-sacrificing that she would let her husband spread untrue rumors (in the media) about her just to keep him from.....ok, I was never sure what.....because it was easier?

In conclusion, I couldn't give this book over a 2.5 to 3. Why? Because the plot was predictable; the characters (both main and supporting) were annoying 75-80% of the time and lacked any real depth; the ending was predictable (you'll guess it, 75% thru the book), and the writing was lack-luster. It was missing something and I can't put my finger on it. Regardless, I wouldn't recommend "Dangerous Affairs" to a real suspense/romance lover.

title: (Sigh) I should have loved it. 2-2.5 stars
text:
I personally enjoy reading supernatural or paranormal stories. If there is a witch, ghost, vampire, werewolf or fae, in the story, I'm game to read it. And while I really should have loved this story, I thought it was just ok. There was everything that should have made this story great.....vampires, hunters, Nazi experiments, some romance and a hunt , but it just never came together for me. I mean really come together in that way that made me think....I want to read the sequel. Instead, it just fell a little flat and in the end I just kind of closed it and picked up another book to read. I didn't stop and ponder, nor did I see when the next one would be released or look to see what other books were available by the author.

The plot was ok, although not too original. Claire, a reporter is trying to determine what is behind her sister, Amanda's, most recent mental breakdown. Amanda is in a hospital and believes (telling everyone she encounters) that a vampire has been feeding from her. Of course no one believes her, especially her sister until she sees some very curious things. Meanwhile she encounters a number of people who not only believe Amanda, but seem to have some ideas on the subject themselves. Enters, George, who not only knows that vampires exist, but may be the very hybrid that vampire hunters, possibly dispatched by the Vatican or some other clandestine organization, have been searching for. So when Claire and George go on the run, they attempt to outrun those meaning to capture them. And while Claire doesn't entirely trust George or his motives, he is able to fill in holes in the information that she has been given thus far. It seems George has a story that he doesn't mind sharing and she is willing to listen, especially if it will help her understand what is happening to her sister. As they learn more about each other, they must also elude those (Whitman & Bishop) who are trying to capture or even kill them. And sandwiched between the hunt and the chase, is a little romance between George and Claire (yes, that too seemed a little forced...I guess we are to assume that every vampire is so irresistible that even when you are trying to stay alive, and prevent yourself from being killed, you have time to get busy....).

There were a few things that left me scratching my head......I didn't really understand Amanda's supposed hatred for Claire, nor did I understand George's feelings for Claire at the end. Some of the stuff just never came together. And while this could have been a great novel, it was just ok. However, I did love the short, easy to read chapters that usually ended with a cliffhanger. And while this did distract from the story at times, because it seemed a little forced, I tried to ignore it in case it was the result of being translated from another language. To me, ending each chapter in a "tad a" moment, took away from the final cliffhanger, that just kind of hung there....especially since I was never really invested in any of the characters (I was indifferent), and wasn't sure if I would want to read a sequel even if it was available. With that being said, I am sure that this is a story that some will enjoy, but it wasn't my cup of tea. I give it 2 to 2.5 stars.

title: Not really my cup of tea!
text:
Kimberly "Kiki Mimi" Kind should have it all. She's a successful attorney who is working as an Assistant District Attorney in New York City. She's got looks and she's smart, BUT she's a mess...literally. For starters, Kimberly seems to have a substance abuse problem. She drinks Jameson like she's drinking water and she's popping pain pills like they are candy. The main witness in her high profile case was murdered while she was suppose to be protecting him; her best friend/roommate is now dating her boyfriend; she ended a recent affair with her boss, the DA; she's still experiencing pain as a result of injuries she suffered in an accident with her best friend; and her antics are likely to cost her her job. And to complicate matters, she just started an affair with her complete opposite, a white tough guy named Rig "King" McDonnell, who may very well turn out to be someone far different than she initially thought. And woven throughout all of this is drama is her personal life (i.e., story) that involves an alcoholic father, a sex-addicted twin brother, and a crack-addicted mother. So I guess there's no wonder that she is a mess.

Personally, I had high hopes for "Hold Me in Contempt". If for no other reason, I thought Wendy Williams would weave a pretty entertaining tale. Anyone who watches her day-time talk-show knows she can tell a story like no one else. HOWEVER, in my humble opinion, she fell short in this story and there really wasn't any excuse for her missing the mark. There was everything present that should have made this a riveting read: danger, suspense and sex, all peppered with a ton of secrets. But to me, none of these things came together into a cohesive and enjoyable read. And there were even portions that seemed forced. And I am not sure which was worse, the erotica, the constant urban lingo (and I really hated her nickname....Kiki MiMi) or the attempt at the end to bring some kind of closure. So read this book with no expectations and at your own risk. That way you won't be disappointed or surprised. 2 stars

title: Disappointing!
text:
This was my first Lori Foster novel, and I fear my last. What started out as an interesting premise (human trafficking), ended up falling a little flat for me. I didn't even find the characters to be endearing or likable, with the exception of Rowdy, who could at times be a little irritating. In the end, what I expected to be a suspense novel filled with a little romance, turned out to be a story that at times seemed forced and silly.

Alice Appleton is Detective Reese Bareden's neighbor, and when a group of thugs enter his home and hold him hostage (along with some of his co-workers), she doesn't flinch and comes to the rescue. Reese is grateful, but begins to wonder who his neighbor really is and what secret(s) is she hiding? It's obvious that she has a past, and one that she isn't too anxious to share. Wanting to discover the truth, and possibly get in her pants, Reese sets out know, protect and love Alice, even if he has to use her love for his sweet dog (Cash) to do it. So while they navigate their budding romance, each learning to trust the other, they must determine who is behind the sale of women in their city.

As I write this review, I try to determine what was in about this novel that I didn't like. Was it that Reese was supposedly the only person who could see the "real" Alice, even before the makeover (done by Pepper)? Was it the corny part in the story when Alice, armed with a stun gun and a kick butt attitude, takes matters into her own hands and rescues one of the tattooed women? Or was it the whole concept behind Reese? While he should have been the whole package (sexy, hot, loyal and zealous), he was just typical and kind of irritating with all of the macho talk and over-protectiveness. Or was it the irritating things that he did like walking the dog without his shirt? Or it could have been the ridiculous dialog and conversations between the characters (Rowdy, Pepper, Logan) that seemed childish? At times it seemed so forced and juvenile, that it made reading this book a chore. Ironically, even the human trafficking storyline didn't help move this story along, probably because there was so much emphasis placed on Alice's past and her insecurities about her relationship with Reese, that it faded in the background. Anyway, a book that normally shouldn't have taken a few days to read took over a week. It was really difficult for me to get through. I give it 2 stars.

title: I should have loved it, but it was just so so..... 2/2.5
text: I usually enjoy paranormal reads, but this one was just ok. You have some romance (ok, a love triangle), some danger (at every turn), a quest for psychically charged relics and a little mystery (who could be behind it all). But "Guardians of Stone, A Relic Seekers Novel" ended up being mediocre. Kendall Morgan, a beautiful archeologist with paranormal powers/a sixth sense, is working for Nathan Larraby (, a mysterious billionaire). Larraby is searching for several relics, among them possibly a box that might contain the spear believed to have pierced Jesus' side while he hung on the cross. Regardless, Larraby has hired the "rough around the edges" mercenary Jake Stone (who doesn't believe in psychics or the paranormal, has a secret...and seems to be tortured by something in his past) to protect her while she is on this quest. And while Stone himself does not believe in the paranormal, he must save Kendall from herself (she has a tendency to go out on her own, even if every time she does there are deadly consequences) and from those trying to get the very same objects that they are searching for. They kiss; encounter ghosts and various shady characters; find several dead bodies; they visit castles and catacombs; are locked in a tower and almost killed in an explosion. All while constantly fighting their attraction to each other and denying their chemistry to each other and to themselves. Did I mention, Larraby also seems to have a thing for the "beguiling" Kendall? Makes you wonder how their working relationship will be affected by their growing infatuation for the same lady? From that description, you would think that I loved it. But instead, I found it to be a little hard to read and slow. Don't get me wrong, the writing itself was simple enough, but the plot was a little thin and boring. I found myself skipping parts, and even putting the book down for a couple of days. The action was lack luster and some of the conversations seemed forced and contrite. I kind of liked the characters, but because of the lack of creativity or slow moving story, I never really became invested. Perhaps, future stories in the series will be more appealing, but for now, I will give this book a 2/2.5.

title: The Hunter & His Prey. 2 - 2.5 stars
text:
Alex Cross is involved in some of the most intriguing murder investigations to hit DC in a while. So in between planning his wedding (to Detective Bree Stone), and parenting his kids, Alex must also juggle several complicated investigations. One deals with a pair of snipers (who are killing influential people believed to have been involved in corruption); while the other involves a killer who is leaving complicated mathematical equations on his victim's bodies. Oh yeah, and by the way, did I mention the fact that his nemesis (Kyle Craig) has reemerged (having escaped prison) and is bent on revenge. Kyle has even gone so far as to change his face (to that of undercover FBI Agent Max Siegel), just so that he can insert himself into the investigation. As the investigation progress, Max (AKA Kyle) wants nothing more than to goad Alex at every turn, even adding to the confusion with some copy cat murders.

To me, this was a typical Alex Cross novel. There were one or two small surprises, but otherwise it lived up to my expectation (which wasn't much). Regardless, as the book comes to a semi-anticlimactic end, you wonder is it all over (and those who know the series will know what I mean) or has Patterson once again given us a red herring. What I am sure of is that we haven't seen the last of Alex or his grisly investigations.

title: Not as much fun to read as I thought it would be. 2 to 2.5 stars
text:
Television Reporter Laura Stark is afraid that her ex-husband (Max Stark) is stalking her...AGAIN, or at least indicating (thru various signs) that he is back in her life. Fearing that she has alienated the police (because of a past news story that she investigated which destroyed the career of a potential Police Chief and eventually led to his suicide), she turns to the private sector for help. After all she's worried, if it's not her Clown/Carnival performing husband, it might have something to do with her recent interview of reputed "bad guy" Ray "The Machete" Marchetti. Regardless, she needs help and Former NYPD Detectives turned Private Investigators Paul Chang and Nelson Rodgers seem to fit the bill. They seem to at least be taking her concerns seriously and are willing to dig deep to discover the truth.

I don't know, for me this was a pretty difficult (or rough) read. While the chapters were short and outlined with titles, the writing seemed to skip about, making it a tad bit convoluted. It could be that there seemed to be a little too much going on in the story for me to appreciate the subtle innuendos and nuances that I am sure J. Gregory Smith intended. I have to admit, I have never read any of the previous Detective Chang mysteries, or any of Smith's other works, which may account for my lack of appreciation. If you are already invested in the characters (Chang & Rodgers) you would probably appreciate this story, but because I was an "outsider" so to speak, I didn't think that this was a good stand alone book. BUT don't get me wrong, Chang and Rodgers were definitely interesting characters. Each came with their own set of baggage: Chang had his mother (who died at the beginning of the story) and ex-wife Colleen (who always seems to be there for him regardless of the current state of their relationship), and Rodgers has his eccentric habits, bizarre (slightly off-kilter) personality and scars (literally & figuratively). They definitely seem to work well, and or play off of each other, which made for some pretty interesting scenes and witty dialog. It was the story that seemed to be a little all over the place. There was everything that should have made this a riveting read. There was danger and suspense woven throughout a rather long and wordy tale of: bombs, Russians, extortionist, blackmailers, crooked cops and politicians, circus acts, and a myriad of other happenings. Unfortunately, I found myself stopping, putting the book down, reading something else, or simply staring into space trying to digest it all. In the end, this was a slightly confusing tale that just seemed to circle around and around, into a pretty predictable ending....leaving me unsatisfied and puzzled for some reason. So, I probably would not recommend this book to someone unfamiliar with the writing style or the series. I give it 2 - 2.5 stars

title: A complicated tale of secrets, desire and betrayal. (2-2.5 stars)
text:
I really, really wanted to like this book, and from the description, I had high hopes. But the truth is, "Mystery Girl" was a great disappointment. To me the story was complicated and at times down right convoluted.

The story had everything that should have made it a great read. There was a mystery surrounding a girl who starred in D rated movies (porn involving demons & succubi); a mysterious director with issues; mental patients; and a zany cast of characters that include: a defunct writer going thru a separation; his lesbian friend; the owner of a used bookstore who loves old obscure films; and an overweight detective). However, in the end, what I found to be missing was that feeling of satisfaction that you get when you finish a book and understand all. Simply stated, the potential of the story was so deeply buried in heavy words and themes that I ended up struggling to just get thru it.

Sam Kornberg is at a crossroads. His wife (Lala) wants a trial separation; he hasn't worked since god knows when; and he's having trouble writing a novel that he believes he must write. Wanting to at least show his wife that he hears her concerns, he seeks employment and is hired to be the assistant to an over-weight Detective Lonsky (a recluse suffering from agoraphobia (the fear of going outside). Lonsky wants Sam to follow Mona Naught and report her every move back to him. Soon Sam finds himself involved in a rather complicated tale of desire, secrets and betrayals.

In conclusion, it is my opinion (and yeah, I know everyone has one), that this book was simply difficult to read. The writing was heavy, at times preachy (about books and movies), and slow. I found myself re-reading portions just to make sure I didn't miss something and skimmed some others (when he rattles off the names of writers, movies or works that he cared about). I was even able to sit this book aside and read something else. Why then the 2-2.5 rating....the concept and ending were brilliant, I just didn't necessarily enjoy the journey getting there. David Gordon's "Mystery Girl" just wasn't for me.

title: Disappointing.
text:
Wendy Gould has made a mistake that will haunt her for the rest of her life. Essentially making a decision that will have far reaching consequences and send her running for her life. Following an argument with her husband of 10 years, Wendy goes to meet a friend for a drink when she is tempted to cheat with a reporter/musician. Things go from bad to worse when she witnesses his murder. Confronted by the murderers, she kills one in self-defense and goes on the run from the other. She soon learns that everything is not what it seems when she learns of the killer's identities. Wendy must use everything at her disposal to determine who is trying to set her up and why. After all, she has tons to lose, beginning with her freedom if she can't prove her innocence.  

Meanwhile, Lauritzia Velez, thinks that she has escaped her past, and is enjoying her new life as a student and nanny. But when someone tries to kill her while she is at the mall with two kids, she knows that her past has come to haunt her.  She will have to depend on the help of others and her wits to stay alive. 

What I didn't necessarily like about this story.....there is an awful lot of stuff going on in the story....there are Mexican drug lords; a ruthless Cartel leader "El Pirate" (Eduardo Cano); crooked DEA/HSA/FBI agents; illegal gun sales; some gang stuff (Los Zetas); the murders of 3 college students and 2 agents (that seem to be the catalyst of all this); and various other government coverups and conspiracies. I hate to admit it, but that is what I didn't enjoy about this book. There was a little too much going on and at times it became confusing. I also thought that Gross could have done a better job tying the plots together, to make it a more enjoyable read. It seemed to be all over the place at one point. There was foreshadowing and hints of things to come, but some of them never did. I also didn't even care, one way or another, about the main character Wendy. And I know for a fact that if I am ambivalent about the main character, I usually don't invest in the story. In conclusion, I really wanted to like this story, but just couldn't. It was a little disjointed for me, and some of the stuff that happened was unrealistic and illogical. I was very disappointed in "No Way Back".

title: Sizzle, Burn and Fizzle.
text:
Jayne Ann Krantz's "Copper Beach" is a paranormal tale of a hunt for a psy-infused book. Abby Radwell has been shunned and alienated by her family for years because of her belief that she has some psychic abilities/talents. Deemed "crazy" and sent to live in a home for troubled teens, she had spent most of her life hiding her talents, vowing to only dealing with those referred to her as clients. So when someone starts blackmailing her she decides to hire Sam Coppersmith, a PI. Her blackmailers wants her to locate a book that can only be opened using her special ability to unlock encrypted texts/books. Sam proves quite the partner, especially when she learns that he has just as much to lose if the book falls into the wrong hands. His goal is to locate the book (for his family), protect Abby and discovery the truth. What she wasn't prepared for or expected was the irresistible pull that she feels between them, which results in an increase or heightening in both of their powers. As the body count rises, so too does the realization that they have to learn to trust each other.

To me, this is a typical Krantz novel. There was nothing new or original...you have some paranormal happenings, a mystical object, a dysfunctional family, a romance (love or sex at first sight), some unusual deaths (paranormally caused) and an "ok" mystery. For those who enjoy Krantz, they will probably enjoy it.

title: Forget blinking, perhaps turn your head. 2.5 stars
text:
Citizen Reporter Nick Daniels has been given the scope of a lifetime....the opportunity to interview an ex-Yankee pitcher turned recluse, who apparently betrayed all of New York for drugs and a gambling debt. However, it would appear that time has not changed Robinson and again he is late for the show. What Daniels never expected was to be an eyewitness to a mob hit, while he was waiting for Robinson, at the table right beside him. As Daniels delves into the mystery of the murder and follows the clues to the truth, he soon realizes that everything is more complicated than he initially thought.

As far as Patterson collaborations go, this one is average. This is a semi-decent thriller with an underlying love story (that is predictable). It is a quick and easy read. While I don't think reading this novel was a complete waste of time, I am not sure if I would recommend it.

title: Disappointed.
text:
I was looking forward to reading "Team Human" after reading the description...there are vamps, zombies, teen angst and romance. Unfortunately, after reading 300+ pages, I was disappointed. What should have been the formula for a fantastic young adult novel, fell a little flat for me!

PROS
-These days, young adult novelist are jumping on the vampire/zombie craze, that is all the rage. I, like most, love vampires, werewolves, witches and zombies, so of course a story about any of these or a combination of these supernatural entities would be extremely entertaining.
-The novel has nice short, easy to read chapters.

CONS
-The main character Mel, was so judgmental and overpowering that she drained the life out of me and in my opinion took away from the story. At first I thought her feelings about vampires, while I didn't agree with it, was at least a perspective of maybe a victim...but then, when it came out that she simply did not like them just because, or for "no real reason" except maybe something that happened to her friend, I didn't get it. And while her dislike of vampires, or anyone willing to live, associate or love vampires was her prerogative, her bigotry and negative attitude overshadowed everything else in the story and instead made her seem inflexible and unlikeable. She usually came off as harsh and mean¸ her rigidness making her unlikeable. Mel's issues with the undead usually overshadowed the primary story. How then can you build a storyline and book around an unlikeable character?
-Many of the characters that could have made Mel more redeemable were not developed well. I wished the authors would have given us more of Francis' and Cathy's story. Even the storyline between Principal Saunders and Anna could have been ferreted out a little more. Regardless, there were times that the storyline seemed fractured and disjointed.

In the end, I am not sure that I would recommend this story. While the storyline has tons of potential (Nancy Drew meets Buffy the Vampire Slayer visits the Walking Dead) there was a distinct disconnect between the main character and the reader. To me, a successful story has a likeable main character.

title: So disappointed. I kind of wish that I had not read it. 2
text:
For months, I have been struggling with my decision not to read the last book in the trilogy surrounding the life and times of forensic sculptor Eve Duncan. Having read some of Eve's stories in the past, I too was invested in discovering what happened to her beloved child (missing and presumed dead) Bonnie. Over the years I have witnessed Eve's painstaking efforts to bring her own child's remains home while helping other families find peace. However, after reading "Eve" and "Quinn", I wasn't sure I wanted or needed to know the truth, which is bad since I was supposedly invested in the characters and storyline.

First criticism: Why did it take three books to unravel the complicated but bizarre but obvious truth surrounding Bonnie's death? To me, this story could have been told in one well written and concise book. Iris Johansen stretched it (a bit thin at times) with tons of complicated relationships and red herrings. From the beginning (of the trilogy), I could see the complicated pattern of a mystery forming that was, in my opinion, pointless.

Second: The evolution of Eve. I really stopped feeling sorry for Eve half-way thru the trilogy. While I totally sympathize with the loss of her child, and celebrate her determination/dedication to bring other children home while searching for the answer to her own questions concerning Bonnie's disappearance, by the time I read this book, I didn't really like her anymore. To me she seemed at times selfish and whiny. No matter how much Bonnie told her that "it wasn't her time", or to "move beyond her death", Eve constantly tries to hasten the end of her life, regardless of her love for Joe or Jane (her adopted "artist" daughter, who is only mentioned briefly, almost like an after- thought, in this book). And yet everyone, and I mean everyone (Catherine, Gallo, Joe, etc.) is risking their lives to rescue Eve and give her the answers she needs.

Third: Character development. Catherine Ling, who while I do agree should feel some debt to Eve for bringing her kidnapped son home, is willing to risk everything - travel around the world (ok, Georgia in this book) - to give Eve some closure. She even leaves her beloved son, who was just returned to her with Eve's help, behind to follow clues in the Bonnie murder investigation. Meanwhile, she even fights her attraction to Gallo, Eve's old lover/Bonnie's father, if it will affect her relationship with Eve. Furthermore, she is ven willing to risk her career with the CIA (going rogue at times or off the reservation) to give Eve the answers she so desires. Then there is Joe, who is a promising detective in Atlanta but due to his love of Eve has taken a hiatus to assist in the investigation. And poor John Gallo, who has experienced every atrocity imaginable, from child abuse to being a prisoner of war, is so confused about his feelings about Eve, Catherine and Bonnie, that he seems to brood and be moody most of the time. But he too is driven to discover the elusive truth no matter the consequences. Not to mention he is constantly fighting his attraction to the lethal Catherine. Perhaps the biggest transformation was in Bonnie herself, who appeared to Eve, Joe, Catherine and John as a child (in her Bugs Bunny t-shirt), but had very adult conversations, sounding and acting far older than her 7 years.

Fourth: The Mystery itself. At the end of the book, when the events leading to Bonnie's death are revealed, I wasn't really surprised. Instead I felt cheated and somewhat saddened that that was all there was to it. I would have expected, with all of the red herrings throughout the series, for there to be just a little something more, but there wasn't. And while I know most crimes, especially murders, are that simple, why even go thru the whole espionage storyline. It just felt wrong.

Now let me focus on the good things about the story....

Well I think Johansen did a decent job with the paranormal (i.e., ghost or supernatural) aspect of the story. While it did seem forced at times (i.e., long talks with Bonnie....who no longer sounded like a child but a wise adult), at least provided some depth to the story. Bonnie's constant presence provided just the right amount of mystery. And while there were some times that I would scratch my head....because I was torn between Johansen wanting to remake "The Lovely Bones" or "What Dreams May Come", I at least appreciated her attempts to introduce another element into the story.

Overall, I probably would have been just as happy not knowing the truth BUT now I can at least say that I did read the entire trilogy. Would I read another Eve Duncan, forensic sculptor extraordinaire, book? Probably not for awhile.

title: Not a favorite.
text: I had great expectations....after all this story was marketed as a "bold, inventive and slyly witty" novel (chick-lit) about how the lives of several women intersect to form a cohesive and appealing story of heartache, friendship and love. You know from the first couple of stories to expect a little sadness (Laurie had reoccurring cancer) but also you expect something redeemable or beautiful to come out of the survival, especially since these women, who you should have formed some bond with, have redeeming qualities that include, in most cases, strength. However, there were some things that I just didn't get or understand....there wasn't the usual quirkiness that I had come to expect in a stories like Bridgett Jones Diary (Fielding), Sex in the City (Bushnell) or The Misadventures of Waverly Brinson (Murname), but instead I found the "Kissing List" to be a little dark, depressing and at times hard to enjoy. While I found the possibilities of the storyline to be limitless... quirky musings sandwiched between the stories of several women who were struggling to find and know themselves... what I found were a bunch of odd stories, linking characters, with oddly placed footnotes.
