This story was set in old school Italy, so maybe arranged marriages where the husband keeps the wife in the dark are perfectly permissible, but as far as I'm concerned leaving the good reader in the dark just makes your story drag.

Three, to pick up on the tail end of my complaint number two, the intrigue I this book was weak. I didn't care about it. At all. The Don leaves his bride on their wedding night. He has mysterious guests that no one can see. He has this strange power. No one speaks of. He's referred to in passing as having associations with a demon. He's got these brothers you never know if you can trust. He's got these neurotic women (cousins) living with him. He knows someone wants him dead,and yet can't resist marrying Niccola, and bringing her under risk. There was too much happening and not enough tidbits being shared. The characters reactions to the Grandfather...extreme. And yet her comes happy sunny Niccola befriending the grandfather, barely scratching the surface of everything else. It was just all too much.

And lastly, four, I never actually thought our hero/heroine were in love.

Oh and seriously, if I had to hear one more time about Niccola forgetting to F'in wear shoes I would have broken my kindle. This book annoyed me more than anything and I ordinarily loveeee this author!

title: 2 1/2 stars
text:
This is the story of Caroline and Thorn; a more contrived plot line there never was. The prologue sets us up for the happy ending that the author wants to seems impossible throughout the book. Caro and her twin brother are in London, trying to hide from some man's family in France, aside from the assumed last name and Caro's wig - there are no disguises, and they aren't exactly doing their best to blend in. Caro, to save her brother from a bad loss gambling, announces to everyone that the Duke of Penborne is her lover. The Duke of Penborne, Thorn, is a recluse after returning from the war scarred. He hears about this girl's claim, comes to London, meets her at a ball, and propositions her. She does it for the money and makes him believe she is a courtesan by trade. He offers her the position of mistress, she turns him down. Thorn is still trying to clarify some things from his time in France and while at the home of an acquaintance he attempts to stop a burglary. Imagine this...its Caro and her brother. Thorn is curious. 16 months later they just so happen to run into each other. She has yet another assumed name. He's curious and learns more about her and her son (his son). Her Brother goes off for a meeting and doesn't come back; she leaves her baby with the neighbor and chases after him. Thorn comes to visit and hears of this, so he chases after her. He encounters her posing as a prostitute/serving girl, trying to pull information from some random people at some random tavern. Thorn propositions the tavern owner for time with Caro. She hears, "a gentlemen wants to see you upstairs". Caro figures maybe this gentlemen will have connections to her brothers disappearance, so she goes - knowing the owner she just met will come running if she screams. Thorn and her become intimate in this room... Her Brother (who happened to make his own escape unbeknown to the reader until he miraculously shows up here), his friend, and the fancy lady neighbor who was watching the baby ALL find them in this room. I'm going to stop now...

Like another reviewer said, this plot was so contrived it was tough to get through. Its like the author wanted Caro to be on the run again, so the staid life she had needed uprooting. Ok, how about we put the fancy lady neighbor in the run-down tavern so she can see Caro with the Duke and then want to sever all ties? OK, done. Oh but now the man you thought you killed has family who is so much closer to tracking you down (after all they had your brother for 2 days!), so you've got to get going to the next name/town, but uh uh oh...first, lets pause to pack and sort through all the belongings in your home. Uh oh...they have too much to carry. I know! Lets have Thorn send a carriage, and not take no for an answer. So off they go to Thorn's home.

The relationship with Caro and Thorn, it was ok. I really did like Thorn and Caro, but I wish the author let us into their heads - let the reader know what they're thinking, though she did allow this with Thorn more than Caro. The author instead gave us one act after another with nothing more than a thin thread connecting them.

This book had an excellent premise, just seriously lacked in the execution.

title: Dragged.
text:
This book had a lot of promise. The characters were both very strong which made for some interesting dialogue. But the lulls in between just made this book drag on endlessly. I'm surprised I made it through. I like strong willed people, I can handle a heroine like Lydia, in fact I like her kind more - especially when up against someone like Vere. But the romance wasn't there, the last plot twist, I'm convinced happened because Chase had some page quota to achieve. Once the couple was married, this was a shock in itself, proposal, race and marriage all within maybe 10 pgs? Sorry I read this on my Kindle, so not sure how many pages were actually there. Anyways, once they were married, that's when it went from SOME lively dialogue to nothing but mind numbing boring. In fact I caught myself skimming towards the end more then anything else.

When Robbie's sisters just appear in the middle of the book, reading the Argus like it was their shrine, it just felt like they got planted in there with no apparent reason. And then some 80 pages later they're planted again. And then it becomes rather obvious, SPOILER, their running away was going to collide head first with Lydia's nemesis. So then Lydia saves them - yay! Although I stopped caring at that point and whooopss there's another 20 pgs to fill. Lets now go look at Lydia's past...whada'ya know here's another surprise twist to make the ending a little happier.

I'd rather the tension between Lydia and Vere played out more. It was like they'd get together, one would say something cutting and rather then resulting in some passion, they walk away from each other. But you never really knew what either was thinking.

Lots of promise, only to disappoint.

title: disjointed.
text:
This book is so disjointed I had to reread the first few pages to make the next make sense - and it only helped a little, I ended up just reading past what didn't make sense and got some clarification later. The rest of the story flows smoother, but is so disjointed its distracting. The hero of the story, Sebestian, leaves his wife for 6 years and no one knows why, he comes back reinvigorated with love for his wife Eleanor and she receives him happily. I was reading this on a Kindle and so don't have the usual sense of where in book I am, but it seemed like the first half this book was only content from the two main characters and the author realized there is nothing else going on besides this "oh-so mysterious" intrigue that all the sudden other characters popped up. Its intrigue was not intriguing. There was no mystery. The characters were likable enough, but lacked depth. If your husband leaves off and on for 3 years and then just gone for 3 years - would you ask questions? I guess Eleanor was so relieved to have him back and continue her "spy-work" that she just accepted his return. The entire thing was tedious to get through. And towards the end, well it sucked. Things just happened because you made it to a new page. The story had potential, but overall its disjointed and lacking.

It must be known that an author like Jillian Hunter can sell based on her name alone, but now I just feel taken advantage of - this book is not worth your money. With a disappointment like this...I'm not sure how she'll redeem herself.

title: Couldn't bring myself to finish it
text:
I only give this 2 star because ordanarily I LOVE Christina Dodd books and finish them in one sitting. But I just couldn't bring myself to finish reading this and I did try twice, but it was so disjointed I just couldn't do it. The other reviewers were right, their relationship between Rand and Sylvan was just terrible. Rand has nice moments and then because of his injury he's supposed to be forgiven for being a complete and utter ***. I didn't even make it to a part where he showed any remorse, if there was any. Sylvan had the makings of a strong character, but I just didn't like her. And for that matter I didn't like Rand. Another odd part to swallow was that it was so OK for them to be "together" I've rarely seen anything like it in a historical novel.

There was some mysterry, but a lot of it could be guessed and it just wasn't enough to keep me tuned in. One of the reviewers had it right, rather then experiencing the romance you were told it was a romance, but not well (at all!) and this really is not up to my preconceived Dodd standard.

Just an FYI, this was initially published in 1995 (pre-Dodd bestsellers??) and I haven't checked but I wonder what the reviews are on the original version.

title: Light on ethnic representation
text: I was underwhelmed by the drawings themselves, and disappointed that not a single man with African features is included in this how-to book. I picked this book up for my 8 year old son, as he has an interest in creating realistic drawings of people. My son is Black and Hispanic.The title should be "How to Draw Caucasian Female Faces." It does include an odd looking character with mutton chop facial hair, but skips over a basic prototype for a Black/ African man. The majority of the book is variations on Caucasian, predominately females. I believe there is a single Asian individual as well. I did not notice any clear Hispanic representation either, after quickly scanning through the book. Just not a lot of real variety here. If you want to draw Caucasian females, this book will get you started.

title: Extremely second-wave feminism
text: I was excited about this book, having seen so many positive reviews, but there just wasn’t much here for me. If you’ve never considered the extreme misogynistic bias of many foundational myths at all, the first portion of this book could be interesting. If you are still deeply invested in the second-wave idea that there would be no wars if women ran the world and find it near-miraculous and praiseworthy when men do bare-minimum parenting tasks you might find the second half appealing. I tried multiple times to get through this and just could not do it.

title: Average
text: The stories in this collection were well written, however I didn't find them scary and the overall blandness would keep me from recommending it to another horror fan.

title: Unlikable chatacters.
text: This had to be the messiest book I’ve read in a long time. I didn’t like the characters (I HATE whiny) and the only good thing was the premise. The story jumps all around and too many things are going on. Lexi has a split personality. One minute she’s a tough and confident business woman and the next she’s an indecisive and petulant child. This one didn’t deliver.  (I voluntarily reviewed an ARC).

title: Unless you have a specific interest in this topic (which we do) skip it.
text: Not that well written. Not compelling.

title: Where Did the Great Characters and Story Feel Disappear To? HUGE miss!
text: After thoroughly enjoying the first 2 books in this series, I was eager for this one. I actually reread both it’s predecessors so everything would be fresh in my mind. What a disappointment! In this volume, Cromwell lacked all the humanizing touches that had made his character so compelling and likable. Events no longer revealed the characters but came across more like dry facts included by the author for historical accuracy. I found it impossible to immerse myself into the lives and events; the characters I’d grown to know and care for in the previous 2 books had become strangers. I made it about 1/3 of the way through the book before setting it aside and moving on to other stories, although I continued to read a little nearly every day until I eventually made it to the end. I was glad when it was over and almost felt like I deserved a reward—-which is sad. Normally finishing a good book is reward enough in itself! And then there’s that regret that the author missed the opportunity to finish the series with the same qualities and excellence that were present in the preceding two books. Too bad we can’t get a do-over!

title: Wait For The Movie!
text: What an incredible disappointment after all the hype and stellar reviews! This book is boringgggg and never manages to develop even the tiniest bit of dramatic tension. Endless pages devoted to her daily routine of drinking wine to excess, abusing prescription drugs, and her daily internet activity— an agoraphobia support website and online chess:  again and again and again. Oh, and spying on her neighbors! That’s what leads to the big conflict in the book! Honestly? The plot seemed pretty lame and completely contrived. Sure, we get the requisite false trails per genre formula, but they really are difficult to buy, and the bad guy turned out to be exactly who I thought! I’m actually kinda looking forward to seeing this as a movie after a competent writer gets in there and eliminates a solid 35%, fleshes out the characters, and introduces a heaping dose of suspense! It still won’t be anything amazing or original, but it will at least hold its own. The only real suspense in the book came from wondering whether I was going to be able to persevere to the end! Just wait for the movie!

title: Substantial Pacing Problems/Shallow Plot
text: The author wastes no time in instantly (and a little too conveniently) plunging readers into the heart of the conflict, and characters are similarly divided onto opposing sides. The descriptions of the majority of the principal players is just plain weird; pretty much everyone is exceptionally good-looking, athletic, smart, and talented. The descriptions would be more appropriate in cheesy romance novels coming from a lovestruck adolescent girl instead of one’s 50 year old, same gender archeology professor. And virtually all of them are sappy superlative in the same way. As we are being introduced to these paragons of virtue or ultra-villains, we are simultaneously being rushed straight into the heart of the conflict. Relationships between characters begin and mature at warp speed and are—of course—extra strong and everlasting. It’s just plain hokey, unless the target audience is that outcast group of middle school losers with bad skin who engage in elaborate role playing games and fantasize about having superpowers that will 1) save the world and 2) allow them to exact revenge from the popular kids. Honestly, I would have had a very hard time believing that this book was written by an adult, except that the author manages to include a vast amount of world history—as crucial to understanding the nature of the main conflict, of course. Don’t expect to get confused by a bunch of meandering subplots or complex twists or quirks or character! We are on a singleminded quest. And then it is just as quickly done and just as predictably over. I wish I could say it was satisfying. As an adult reader who very frequently reads Young Adult fantasy/science fiction novels, I am left scratching my head. This book doesn’t really have the necessary attributes to appeal to fans of that genre, nor does it possess the sophistication and complexity to appeal to adult fantasy/sci fi fans. In any case, I won’t be impatiently waiting for the next novel, nor would I encourage others to waste their time with this one. There’s just way too many better plotted and more engaging novels in this genre out there. Skip it!

title: Premise interesting
text: Unfortunately characters' relationships not fully developed. Plot not nurtured or developed. Cop out ending. The devil did it.  I like psychic and magic and things that go bump in the night but this story p!aces them there without much effort to develop. Big letdown.

title: Condition was not accurate
text: Description said "good condition- clean and bright" but all the pages including the cover has gross yellow stain or tint that goes all the way around on all the outer edges of the page.

title: Just Not Inspiring Much At All For Me
text:
I want to start by saying I am well aware that everyone is not at the same level of creativity so what appeals to some might not to others. I do realize that. This review, however will be done from my point of view which is that of an artistic person who loves color, creativity, and art.

BOOK LAYOUT
The layout of the book is pretty nice. It is clearly marked and the sections are well defined. There are sections to explore materials, color, and then creativity sections too. There are helpful tips along the way to give you ideas in how to approach different techniques.

QUALITY OF PAGES AND PRINT
The print is light, but still readable. The photos are a little dull, but they still look okay. The pages are pretty thick and decent quality. They are not shiny or hard to read surface-wise.

CONTENT
That is where I have a disappointment in this book. I love color. I love art. I love being creative and exploring different techniques. Having said that, most of what I see in this book is either grade school or middle school level crafting, or it is so non-appealing that I am really not motivated to emulate it.

There are a few things in here which I am trying but not many. It just isn't really clear on the purpose of this book. I don't feel inspired to do more than thumb through it although I have tried at least a dozen times to get involved with this.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This book is good quality print and pages. The layout is nice, but the content is lacking for me. I just don't feel motivated to try much of anything in here, although I am trying a few things. I just think for the price of the book and printing that they could have done a much nicer job than this.

MY RATING
TWO STARS. This isn't for me. If you are into really pretty creative colorful artwork, it might not be for you either.

title: This Book Has Its Place, But It Was Not Our Taste- At All (Except for One Thing)
text:
When I review books, I realize that they are subject to the tastes of the reader. When I read this book through, I was so shocked at what I found inside that I had four other people take a look at it just to be sure that I was not over reacting.

WHAT IS THIS BOOK LIKE?
This book has great potential. It is a book that focuses on color, or so it says. The book itself is hard cover and it has color photos throughout the book. It is broken into sections for decorating ideas for rooms of the home such as Living Room, Bedroom, Kitchen, And Dining Room. There are furniture ideas and crafts featured to inspire decorating of your living space.

THE CRAFTS
Okay, I am trying really hard to be honest here without being unnecessarily biting. So, let me quote from some of the others (mixed genders) that I had read this:

"What is this? It looks like some of the kids I baby sit for made this in Kindergarten!"
"What a terrible sense of color!"
"Did she make this book out of ideas from nursery school craft classes?"
"I saw this in people's houses I worked at - their kids made it or they probably would not have kept them"
"I never understood this type of thinking when decorating a house. It looks junky"

Now, those are not what I said, that is what others I asked to react to this said.

The color in this book is nice quality. The combinations, well they really seem to be rinky dink. Don't get me wrong- I am an artist that happens to love bright colors. Bright colors and bold design are fun for me. I don't even mind things that have a twist of childhood in them. Some people are turned off by bright color or bold statements. I am not.

This on the other hand is more of a summer camp, nursery school, or grade school style of decorating. I don't know any other way to say it. I mean the type of thing you bring home to your mom that you made in school out of glue and bits of things.

FURNITURE
As for the furniture ideas, there was nothing in this book that appealed to any of us that made us want to emulate or seek out any of the furniture to sit on or to have in our home.

IS THERE ANYTHING WE LIKED?
Interestingly, there was one craft that everyone that looked at the book mentioned they liked- the use of temporary tattoos on hangers which were sealed to make them more durable. That was the only thing everyone said they liked or were attracted to at all.

WHO MIGHT LIKE THIS
--If you have kids or a kids type business like doctor's office, daycare, nursery school, or even classrooms that specialize in younger children, there are some great ideas in here.

--Those who find comfort and solace in juvenile style decorating might really enjoy this. Perhaps it would help embrace something you miss or never had growing up.

--Anyone who enjoys simple overstated crafty things

WHO MIGHT NOT LIKE THIS
--Anyone who does not like bright colors
--Someone who throws away little crafts their kids make because it won't go with their house
--Anyone who does not like childish or simple things
--Someone stuck in the current gray fad

THE BOTTOM LINE
If you want a simple way to decorate your home that might be reminiscent of childhood for one reason or another, this book may be for you. If you prefer more complex sophisticated designs or simplicity that looks austere but not childish, this book would probably not appeal to you.

MY RATING
Two stars- I really debated between this and one star, but because it has its place with businesses or homes that want a childlike focus, I left it at two stars. For us, it really was not our style. Not even the kids liked it.

title: Didn't Flow Well And Hard To Wade Through
text:
(This review is based upon an Advanced Copy of the Book which could have further revisions upon release)
(Review completely revised)

Every now and then I will review something and not be happy with the review I wrote. This book was such a case. Have you ever had someone you know casually walk by and you inquire about how they are, but instead of a quick "Fine" or simple answer, you get a rambling diatribe of all kinds of things- WAY more than you really wanted to know- and you are left wishing you never asked, or wanting to disappear quietly?

Perhaps you haven't. That, however is how I felt after reading this book. Alexander McQueen's designs are similar to the way I like to do things- and he got to take them to the Nth degree, which was fun to see on the occasions I was able to. I found some of his work fascinating and interesting. I was not as kindred to Galliano, but was willing to explore and learn about him too.

What I found the book to be was a mish-mash of writing that seemed to have a lot of verbal clutter involved. The story started out well, but it just got too bogged down in too many details and "he said/she said" type of things. I felt that the book really stopped flowing and became drudgery to finish.

Although I didn't like this book and found it a burden to read after a while, there are people who will enjoy it.

If you are avid fans of both of these designers and hungry for every lurid detail of their lives, then you will probably enjoy it more than I did. If you are in the fashion industry and this type of information is familiar to you and you can skim through without being bogged down with details you live with every day, perhaps you will love this too.

I was expecting more of a finely honed presentation, but what I felt like I got was much less organized bogged down over abundance of details that seemed to detract rather than to add to the flow of the book.

title: What a HUGE disappointment
text:
I was SO excited to get this book I could not WAIT. Fashion? Style? Unique? I am ALL about that. When I first thumbed through the book, I was like, "Are you KIDDING me?" Boring does not come close to what I was feeling about it. Frumpy? Um, blah. I don't know. I was expecting a little more pizazz the way everyone raved about the book.

PLEASE don't take this as criticism for those of you who love it- I am GLAD you do. Not everyone has the same style so I don't expect to like what everyone else does all of the time.

For me, however, this was rather unspectacular. I will take more time to read through before I decide if I will return it- as what is written might be worth the price of the book. But the styles and glances at what is in the book left me really feeling, well, like I got worked up for a huge disappointment and paid for the experience.

I love avant garde stuff. I love unique handmade things and I love weaving and knitting with all kinds of interesting things. This almost seemed like- Okay, don't waste fabric, just drape it on your shoulders and connect the sides. It is a bit more than that, but it all looks rather sack-like. This, however, just is not my style. I will look elsewhere for my inspiration, I guess.

EDIT-UPDATE 10-20-2014
I have had some time to read a good portion of the book. It has some good information in it about using a rigid heddle loom, including setting it up and creating some different cloth designs. For all of the information on basic usage, I am probably going to keep the book- will know more when I finish examining it in more detail. However, I still am not motivated to re-create any of the designs in this book as far as clothing pieces go. I have to determine if I can find the same information in another book that WILL motivate me. I realize books on rigid heddle weaving are not overly plentiful, which is why I am trying to determine if I want to keep it.

The author does say that she does not have experience with clothing design, cutting, fitting, etc (as in sewing), so her focus is merely not having to cut fabric and still be able to wear it.

She accomplished that. I just am not excited over the styles that she came up with by doing that, as I am experienced in sewing and clothing design. I am still not sure the book is worth the price for what I might gain from it overall, but I wanted to update for anyone who was interested in a bit more information.

title: I WISH that I had not purchased this book
text:
As an avid beader, I am always looking for inspirational books to prod my creativity along during dry spells. After reading all of the sterling reviews of this book SHAPED BEADWORK, I was really expecting some lovely eye candy and ideas to spin off of for my personal beadwork.

What I got instead was a HUGE disappointment. The book is rather stark in design. Everything looks almost utilitarian- extremely geometric and not exciting at all.

The book uses ONLY delica beads, mostly in metallic colors for the *metal* effect and there is very little variation of that. There are some geometric chains, and some sort of gothic looking things, but as a big fan of goth things, none of these thrilled me. The Delica beads are SO expensive that I found this book not inspiring at all. In fact, I found myself wanting to toss it aside and rarely look at it again.

I am motivated by color, movement, texture and interest when it comes to beadwork. This book is very boring in that department. Not only are the bead designs ho hum, but the layout of the book itself is a bit on the austere side for me. It is okay to look at, so I gave it two stars, but I really won't be looking at it much again after this. Only a few things mildly appealed to me, but it was not worth the price of the book.

If you are looking for lush creativity with color movement and delightful designs, this book is probably not for you. If you like very angular things with steel cold look to much of it and if you really are turned on by geometric figures and delicas, then this book might just be up your alley.

As for me, I really am not that thrilled with this book at all.

title: This is a BEDTIME story?
text:
My children have become very involved in my reviewing process of late. When a box arrives from Amazon, the customary question is, "Can I PLEASE open it?" If I know that I am receiving something appropriate for them to see, I will let them.

WHAT'S UNDER THE BED arrived one day and my nine year old daughter snatched the book and ran into her room to read it. Her expression when she came out was a bit puzzled. "Is this supposed to make kids feel better before they go to sleep?"

Then my son became equally interested and promptly grabbed the book before I could take a look and read the book. His response was, "What the.....Are you supposed to read this to a kid to make them not feel afraid? This is a very strange book."

Well, I could not wait to sit down and take a leisurely look at the book, which I have finally been able to do, and I must agree with my children. This book is an odd thing to read to a child before bed time.

The illustrations are kind of cute- at first. The main character is a little tiny bodied boy with a very large head and glasses. It is interesting to look at him.The colors are shades of gray, black and white with light blue on the boy's body.

In a few places there is a splash of color which is really fun. There are little things that the child is afraid of that are around the room, from his imagination, but then it crosses over into the obtuse.

As adults it is not common to be afraid of yucky looking monsters, but to a little child who is often irrationally afraid, to put a monster in such detail in a book about going to bed is counterproductive in my opinion.

I know that the author was attempting to be cute when they put the monster in the bed at the end making it afraid of the little boy who found his teddy bear under the bed, but I think it failed.

If the illustrations were made so the monster was a little less extreme and repulsive, it might have worked. As it is, I think this book is okay until the illustrations of the monsters start in. They are too frightening for a little kid who might already be afraid of things at night.

This book just did not hit it right for us.

As an aside, when my husband heard the hullabaloo about this book at the table, he took it and read it and his comment was ," Are you supposed to read this to a kid to make them feel BETTER at night? What is this?"

So, I guess it is unanimous here. Thumbs down on this book for little ones.

title: Is this for pressure cookers, canner or crock pot users?
text: I really struggled with this book.  I need to clarify that I am an owner of a Presto 16 qt stovetop pressure canner/cooker and an Cuisinart electric countertop pressure cooker.  I am not new to pressure cooking.  So, I tried to look at this book with an open mind as if I were a new user.  What I found out was that so much of the book doesn't really deal with actual pressure cooking.  There is a section in there that talks about slow cookers/crock pots, one for pressure canning and one for pressure cooking.  What it doesn't really deal with is adapting any of your current recipes to pressure cookers, so that was a big disappointment. I really wasn't looking for a crockpot book.  What's more is there is really not a whole lot of recipes either.  I own many other pressure cooker books and they are far better than this one.  Most of the other pressure cooker books out there have enough basics that a person that is new to pressure cooking can learn from them and they are loaded with recipes.  They are focused only on pressure cooking instead of all over the map like this one.  I would invest in these.  My two favorite books are Cooking Under Pressure and Pressure Perfect.  I would invest my money in these books instead.

title: A bit disappointed in this book...
text:
First, let me say that I have been decorating cakes for years and I am very familiar with fondant and sugar gum paste methods. So, I am able to look at all of these final pictures of the cakes and reproduce them without issue. However, if I was a person that was new to cake decorating, this book would be horrible. The cakes are cute and fun, but they aren't really much different than the pictures you can find for free online. So, when I looked at this book I was looking at it from a perspective of... could you make the cakes if you had never had any cake decorating training and could you make them with a child? I feel the answer to this is that it is highly unlikely.

The book sections are divided very strangely. It is kind of divided into three major sections, 1) Tools and Recipes 2) Projects 3) Techniques. I tried one of the cake recipes (Cereal Cupcakes) and the recipe was good, but not great.

RECIPE SECTION - There are only a total of six cookie/cake recipes and only four frosting recipes. What they refer to as sugar paste I would refer to as fondant and what they refer to as petal paste, I would refer to as gum paste. I found it interesting that they provided recipes for buttercream, maple frosting and a ganache, but they don't give you any recipes for the sugar gum paste and the fondant. They tell you to purchase these at the store. I would never purchase store bought fondant, as it tastes terrible. You can make very good fondant very easily with marshmallows and powdered sugar that tastes wonderful.

PROJECT SECTION - The second section is the project section. It gives you a whole lot of step text and very limited visuals/photos. The photos it does give you don't really seem to be all that helpful. Some are even a bit fuzzy. Extremely lacking in help if you have never decorated cakes before and a child certainly couldn't do it. I had my teenager help me that also knows how to decorate cakes and she said, "It doesn't even show you what to do."

TECHNIQUES SECTION - Some of these cakes are pretty technical. I wish all technical information would have just been put with the cake project we were working on. But instead, it is all in the back of the book in the last section. So, we went to the techniques section hoping to get more detail on how they wanted things done. Basically, there still wasn't detailed information. They showed the final piece done, but hardly any visuals on each step to get to the final. For example, there is a really cute cake in here with teddy bears having a picnic. It shows all of the pieces... two bears, cake grapes, chicken, etc that are part of the picnic. It shows the finished result and it shows the smaller completed pieces like a single bear, but no in between visuals. There is a beautiful winter swan cake that also has the same issues.

Overall, I have a lot of cake decorating books and this is by far my least favorite. If you are a visual learner, you probably will not like this book. However, if you are a person that prefers text and follows textual instructions better, then you might like this. For me, I wouldn't recommend it.

title: Todays rubber chicken award
text:
Hey, it's a funny old world....different strokes for different folks.
Some people get off watching naughty dvd's, others might peruse risque magazines.....it seems there must even be some who really (i mean !@!really!) enjoy stories depicting the graphic nuclear death of 20 million german civilians in an alternate ending WW2, even while they unsuccessfully plead for mercy via radio conversations with the bomb dropping aircrews........
I could find no info ref the author on the cover of the book, and frankly i'm not too surprised,- maybe he/she still writes in crayon....and surely this plotline would work much better in a "marvel" comic or abbreviated graphic novel than this p*sspoor attempt at a real book.

In my opinion, if one is going to write a passable alternate history novel, you must have at least these three things:-
1> The ability to write readable fiction without having to use almost one-third of your prose as 'out of plot line narrative' to explain what's going on.
2> A historical event fork that leads the reader to your imagined alternate timeline with some reasonable credulity.
3> A proofreader so that every poor sap who buys the book doesn't end up having to do the task themselves.
Having said that, Stuart Slade manages to miss requirements 1, 2 & 3 in their totality.
In my opinion, the author fails to write above high-school level, succeeds in padding out a tale of a nuclear bomber raid into Germany by adding in totally spurious and pointless sidebars about India/Thailand and the death of Ghandi, plus the sinking of a USN Carrier off the french coast.
(WTH was the point Mr. Slade? You never succeeded in bringing these elements together, - were you simply paid by the word?) Not to mention that a disproprtionately large piece of the text is utilised as a "when this occured, that happended, and so blah blah followed on" narrative.....the publisher couldn't even be bothered to use italics for these portions - it just gets old fast.
And try as i might, - and i tried....i just couldn't get behind the idea that a capitulating Britain would automatically catalyze instant warrior nation status in the USA, especially without Pearl Harbor...and no conflict in the pacific at all!
Plus as others have stated - the proofreading/spell & grammar checking on this text is nonexistent, the result is an infuriatingly difficult read.

Further, the protagonist is all so SO terribly 'might is right' unidimensional, with the USA winning almost every individual battle with a mix of stellar cunning, unmatched forward thinking, overly cutting edge technology (i'd say that having a female AI onboard a 1947-era bomber is pretty cutting edge!), and unassailable good fortune....while the Nazis fail at almost everything, - and it's somehow only republicans & conservatives within the US and it's Allies who are the good guys. Juvenile is perhaps too kind of a description.....i fear this was the result of 'vanity' or 'self publishing' - which means the author paid for the printing and distribution of his first work himself....then his readers pay for his vanity by being subject to his errors and ego.

SUCH A SHAME....as i've stated in other reviews I'm a big fan of AH novels and given the advertised storyline I really wanted to like this book, I thought it truly held some promise.

If you're an AH afficiando too, - and think you might enjoy the book despite it's shortcomings.....please accept my advice and find a copy as far below list price as you can.

PS - it can't possibly be this bad, can it?
Read it and weep.

title: So disappointed!
text: Couldn't decide between one or two stars... Thought I would error on the side of charity since I just finished Pulitzer prize winning author David McCoullough's John Adams, so I'm spoiled by his research and mature writing. Right out of the gate, had to quibble with the authors.  They are completely inaccurate on Jefferson according to McCoullough.  Authors rightly remark that New Englanders and Federalists were for a Navy, while Southerners and Republicans were not - this, while arguing that Jefferson was FOR the Navy. Makes no sense. Jefferson was a Southerner, a Republican and very much against a US Navy since he feared it would be used to make war on the French during the French revolution.  Certainly, he was against it before he was for it, which would have been an interesting insight to include. John Adams, on the other hand, was a New Englander and a Federalist. In fact, he is the recognized founder of the Navy. He was for the Navy 100% the whole time, though he recognized funding was a problem and agreed with Jefferson that stop gap measures might be in order until Congress authorized one.  It was Adam's lifelong quest to maintain a standing Navy, though he was against a standing Army.  Oddly, the authors continue to give George Washington credit for the Navy through the early 1800's until Jefferson is president, ignoring that George Washington was dead and that John Adams was president for those four years. In addition, George had actually helped dissolve the Navy thinking it would draw us into international conflict.  If you are going to simplify and generalize, at least get it right.  Sloppy and inaccurate!

There were too many strange, two-line paragraphs made up of nothing but sentence fragments, too many facial expressions depicted in terms of what people did with their eyebrows, overuse of gerunds and past perfect tense, way too much rambling dialog, and far too many sentences that began with the word "and" or "but."
I felt empty when I finished the book this morning. What a disappointment.

title: Uses outdated, confusing constellation lines
text:
Get H.A. Rey's "The Stars" in which he clearly lays out a very rational argument not to use the arcane and indecipherable constellation lines featured in this book. Instead, he presents far more intelligible shapes for the constellations that have been since antiquity. From ancient times, there has never been anything significant about the "lines" between the stars, but only the group of stars. Throughout history, people have used various lines to help themselves learn to recognize groups of stars, constellations (which obviously have no lines). The problem with this book is the lines given form confusing, unfamiliar and non-sensical shapes. They don't look like what they're called.

H.A. Rey also wrote a simpler book, "Find the Constellations." This one was unfortunately defaced by the publisher in a subsequent edition to remove Pluto, but otherwise it is a concise guide to learning the constellations.

I also highly recommend the Stellarium app which can be configured with H.A. Rey's lines under Sky & Viewing Options > Starlore.

title: the agenda
text:
I have mixed feelings about the purpose behind this book and the results. The 'sequence' this book outlines and the concept of the core knowledge sequence is a purposeful agenda to create a 'school culture' in America. This agenda is pervasive in US institutional education (public and private) and even many homeschoolers are accepting it (and buying this book). The core-knowledge sequence purportedly allows institutional educators to inculcate specific knowledge by following the guidelines of consensus. This book essentially outlines that consensus. There are practical advantages to this. For example, an institutionally educated child won't be introduced to "Charlotte's Web" in multiple grades, and a child progressing from one grade to another can be expected to have been exposed to certain topics. The important thing to understand is that this does not mean the child has attained a minimum "level" of education, which is what I fear parents and homeschoolers may believe.

Let me use an example to explain. Suppose a child is educated by a series of teachers following the consensus of the core knowledge sequence. The child is told something about Christopher Columbus and Abraham Lincoln in Kingergarten. Something is mentioned to them about ancient Egypt in first grade, and in second grade they're told about civilization along the Indus and Ganges rivers. I could teach my child about all of those things at age six, and suppose that my child is "ahead" of institutionally educated children. On the other hand, I might not teach history at all, or any math, but concentrate entirely on reading skills, literature, and creative writing. Would the child be "behind" in their education? They might be able to read in one afternoon everything the other child learned the previous three years.

So the "core knowledge sequence is not about gauging or pacing education to a standard. Ultimately it's about an agenda to set everyone in a cultural consensus. Ostensibly that cultural consensus is purported to create "fairness." It does so by inhibiting innovation (this book replaces free thought with lists). Besides effecting a shoddy crutch for educators, it permits the indoctrination of the children by those who set the 'consensus.'

If you think 'indoctrination' is going a bit far, consider this. Look at the list of biographies in the core knowledge sequence, and ask yourself why these were chosen and not others. Look at the lists of literature, and ask yourself if there was anything else written and why it wasn't included.

Are you willing to buy this consensus?

title: big profits
text:
I bought three level sets of these at Costco for a little less than Amazon. The books are thin with simple pencil-drawn illustrations. My 4 year old who likes to read took off with the level 2 set right away. He'll probably be done with the level 3 set by the end of the week and then the books will hold no further interest because they are totally boring texts with very poor illustrations. I mostly bought these for my 5 year old who would rather tell his own stories than read. I understood the stories are rather mechanical and not interesting. Think Dick and Jane rather than Cat in the Hat and Green Eggs and Ham. The texts are mostly at the pre-decodable level and advance up to early decodable sentences. As such, they're a tool we can use to get going, but only when used with inspiring read-alouds, well-illustrated stories, sight-word memorization, and decoding skill-builders.

If you understand that BOB books are not a complete reading instruction program, then you will want to compare them primarily with alternatives that serve a similar function. The SRA leveled readers are better. They're a lot more expensive, but hopefully available at your local library. I have about a dozen of the SRA books, and photocopies of about 60 more. The stories are more interesting. The illustrations are not wonderful but still much better than BOB. I also have some from Hooked on Phonics. I rate them closer to BOB.

Of course you really want to work past these pre-decodable type leveled readers and get into something fun like the aforementioned Suess, the Berenstein Bears, Curious George, Babar, and so on. This area is rich and I hope to have my children exploit it in reading as much as I have in read-aloud before we inevitably venture into the world of "chapter books" that is no doubt strewn with more boring tomes just like BOB Books.

For other components of a reading program, I suggest working on sightwords with flash cards, tiles, writing them on a board, writing them on paper etc. Lists can be found on the Internet without purchasing anything. For building decoding skills, there's some good workbooks. I've used pages from American Education Publishing, School Specialty, School Zone, Kumon, DK, BrainQuest, and so on. The specific skill here would be focused on in books like the "Explode the Code" series, or one of Sylvan's Language Arts super books.

For read-alouds and well-illustrated books, the library is full of them. In my mind this latter component is the thing most children miss out on. They're over-indulged in mostly senseless entertainment and while they are perfectly capable of understanding inspiring and intriguing stories, few capable of telling them are willing to take the time. Most television is designed only to be sufficiently entertaining to get people to watch the advertisments, and more serious efforts at story-telling are rarely undertaken unless there's a big merchandizing deal to make it worthwhile. Parents who grew up fed by MTV are often not fluent enough to read Mark Twain without stumbling. But don't imagine that I'm just lamenting TV or deriding under-educated parents. I'm all that myself (a dropout that enjoyed Beavis and Butthead of all things). So rather I am goading you to pick up something, Tom Sawyer, Old Yeller, Little House on the Prarie, and have a go at it. Soon you'll be reading Hawthorne, Melville and the King James Version. Beats the pants off Sponge Bob.

title: "Millennial Noir" is an interesting description but...
text:
You know you don't like a book when a review of it (the one from Frank Antix, the person before me) was better than the actual book lol.

Bottled, in a nutshell, is about unlikeable characters doing nothing to redeem themselves while doing horrible crap to other unlikeable characters. That's literally the story. And this "millennial" (like most) is over reading stories about a-hole characters who serve no purpose. Especially when the accompanying illustrations are simply not good.
The only reason I gave this 2 stars instead of 1 is because the main character dumps her boyfriend in one of the most satisfying ways. Sure, I saw it coming - but that doesn't mean I wasn't happy when it actually happened lol. I also chuckled at the last 2 pages when the mom realized what her daughter was saying to her. That scene had more character development and nuance than the entirety of the book!

The art was good but I wish more attention went into building a complex and even-paced story with multi-layered characters. I hate to rate World of Wakanda two stars considering my expectations but it is what it is. *sigh*

text:

title: Ok writing style, but repetitive, and the dumbest plot ever
text:
These "successor" novels are rarely at the level of the originals, but even with that lowered expectation, this is a sorry excuse for a detective story. Rex Stout might come back from the dead to chastise this author.

The writing is ok, but ham-handed and repetitive in its effort to use some of the amusing themes in the Nero Wolfe books: especially Wolfe's fondness for precision in language and Archie's insouciant (and sometimes sardonic) humor. The whole felt trying-too-hard and artificial, not at all like the Stout books.

And then the plot. Apparently the author had nary a decent idea about a murder plot, so it was this: "man falls out of window, there are many suspects with weak motives, under mild pressure one of them runs away revealing his guilt". Um. And all the while we're being bludgeoned with the idea that Wolfe is a genius, although there's scant evidence of that in this book.

I haven't mentioned the sloppy writing, assuming that it mostly reflects the pre-publication nature of my copy. But some of the lines made me cringe, I wonder how they'll improve those sufficiently.

Anyway, avoid. If you like this stuff, there are many fine authentic Nero Wolfe stories, and most of them are delightful.

title: seems to be written as a coffee-table book, what we have is not a great cookbook
text:
I found this book quite disappointing as a cookbook, left me wondering if the author really does cook, or if perhaps this was written by two people, one doing the travel story and the other slapping together some recipes.

The stories and descriptions of various cities and regions in Morocco are wonderful, as are the accompanying photographs. The recipes themselves don't quite come up to snuff. They're a combination of exotic names and pictures, and rather mundane preparations -- I began wondering whether the author thinks using cumin magically makes a dish wonderfully special and particularly Moroccan.

Take for example the recipe for Artichoke and Beef Tagine (I prefer the spelling tajine): sounds wonderful, right? But what you get is a recipe where you slow-cook some beef with onions, preserved lemons, ginger, black pepper, and saffron. That's a tajine?

Instead I started with a recipe from "Mediterranean Hot and Spicy" by A. Kremezi (out of print, but you can find a used copy), and prepared a lovely fragrant tajine that was much more satisfying than travelogue photos.

It's not that the book has zero value: it suggests recipes that could be the starting point for creative ventures in the kitchen. The Berber frittata for instance (eggs, olives, tomatoes, hot peppers, spices, cilantro, cheese) looks like something I'd enjoy preparing and eating. But there just aren't enough of these recipes for me to make this one of my go to cookbooks.

title: Hard to read, written in hucksterish style, but has nuggets of value if you mine long and hard
text:
I found this book really hard to read: it's written in an incoherent, breezy style, with insufficient organization to make its arguments and conclusions clear. You have to kind of fight with the author to wring sense out of every single page, and after a couple of chapters I get rather tired of this sort of thing. It cites research findings sloppily and incompletely, again with that breezy style. It has hucksterish language about how the author is going to help you understand the secrets of success, and manages to contradict itself often, with complete unconcern.

That said, there are nuggets of useful information here. Perhaps a patient and sane editor could have condensed the book into 50 pages of sense, but that doesn't make the publishers money, does it? So that kind of editor got shunted to academic books early in their career, so this is what we get.

title: dumb, unbelievable plot, begins to plod as soon as the principal charaters are introduced
text:
Really dumb story, just plods through in its unhurried way. Silva writes well stylistically, but is just not a good storyteller. And I never quite bought into the author's view of his characters, which is fatal in just about any story like this.

I found it impossible to take seriously the master of disguise bad guy who can travel everywhere without problems, escape cleanly with false documents right after major incidents, play a Frenchman, a French Canadian, etc. etc. Just silly comic book stuff.

And I have to comment on this other silliness as well: As some others have observed, the idea of a famous fashion model as undercover agent is just dumb, we're supposed to believe that no one recognizes her in London, although she's been on major magazine covers. At the same time, apparently the "Kill Artist" is recognized right away by a person who only saw him once in a stressful situation (I don't want to give away the plot in case anyone cares about it).

title: poorly written book on a fascinating topic
text:
I had such hopes for this book when I started reading it. It begins with the story of the "accidental" discovery by a couple of Bell Labs physicists of the cosmic background radiation, confirming a theory that had recently been developed by Princeton cosmologists.

But sadly, the author never really got himself going. He seems to swing between excessive interest in the "soap opera" parts about the rivalry between competing groups of researchers, and ineffectual attempts to explain the science. He struggles even to explain simple concepts and theories, perhaps because he himself doesn't quite understand them. I struggled through the book, but at the end felt that the author hadn't taught me a whole lot. Excluding the discussion of personalities & rivalries, I would summarize thus: "Many scientists struggled for years to figure out that the universe is larged dark matter and dark energy, but we don't have any idea what those things are, and the theories are incomplete."

Other criticisms: Among the annoyingly odd things in the book, he tries to describe graphs without using any pictures at all ... why? I myself would also have liked some representation of the mathematics, because I believe that many of those interested in this kind of topic has had at least some math & science education, and the others can ignore them. But I'm aware that publishers think that the poets will be put off by the very appearance of any symbols anywhere in the book.

I can't recommend this book at all. I wish there were one that dealt better with this topic, something as good as Stephen Hawking's books (or George Gamow's books from a long time ago that explained modern physics of that era).

The writing was fine, appropriate, and there were a few chuckles, but it was a disappointment. I trudged through and finished it because I’m stubborn and hate to abandon books, but if I want another story about this period/subject - I’ll watch a Monty Python skit instead. Not recommended.

title: Historical fiction that loses its way.
text:
In the last two years I’ve become interested in the years between the World Wars - fiction and nonfiction, especially the Weimar Republic era. The setting, a rural area and not being in Berlin, made me eager to read this book.

First the good: I really liked Fallada’s writing style - rapid-fire storytelling, often driven by quick and energetic dialog that forced me to concentrate to “keep up.” I liked that. The descriptions of the town, its people and their relationships and conflicts were also well-written and engaging. I have a few other Fallada novels on my list, and I will give them a read.

The not-so-good: The first 50% of the book was tight and exciting, with a good building of the coming conflict within the town. But the almost overwhelming number of main and secondary characters (the Dramatis Personae did help!), and the many sub-plots and little intrigues got to be a bit much during the book’s second half. And the conclusion - after so much conniving, chicanery and double-crossing within the community - was a bit of a fizzle, flat and disappointing. At almost 600 pages, it seemed bloated, and maybe 100-150 pages too long.

title: so much thrown at you it bogs down the story
text:
This is the second magic-based fantasy book I've read lately, and it really makes me want to give the other one a better review - in that one I felt that more could have been done with the magic, but wow, now I feel the other author showed a wonderful sense of restraint. In The Last Days of Magic... well, to be quite honest, I feel as if I've been bludgeoned by an overwhelming sense of things - this book is just trying too hard. Which is a shame, you can tell the author was really trying here, he had some good ideas and did his research, it just comes across as all thrown into the book as if you're trying to clean out the fridge and just dump whatever's still good into the pot on the stove without a care for how it'll taste. You have your Sidhe (fairies), you have your half-Sidhe, you have your Nephilim, your demons, your druids, your Church, your medieval kings and your Vikings... yeah, you have a lot going on here, and most of the time it comes across as rather info-dumpy at that - and a dry, historical book type of info-dump. You also have time jumps, things going back and forth in time perspectives, which doesn't help.
All of this might have been more bearable if I liked the characters, but all of that jumping around and the huge cast doesn't help to build much of a connection with them, and there's not much of an emotional depth to many of them, too. Perhaps it's the writing style, perhaps it's all the background information getting in the way, but I didn't connect to any of them.
So, there's some interesting twists on history and mythology here in this book, it's just burdened with too much plot and exposition in my opinion. If the story is continued, I truly hope the author is reined in and streamlines the plot while adding a bit more emotional depth to the characters (and no, that doesn't mean giving them more bland sex lives - among the rather graphic details of how brutal life could be in the medieval ages, there are scenes of rape in this book, albeit not very detailed, along with questionable coercion).

I read through her details of bullets and fragments because I know how well she researches details of every aspect of her books and because I was looking forward to the exciting ending we have come to expect.  I now know how to put on a scuba wet suit perfectly.  I am waiting anxiously for the climax.  Then Cornwell seems to think we are all satisfied to read a two-page encounter.  Then Cornwell wants us to wait until the next book to find out how the “epilogue” ends.  Very disappointing.

title: grim and violent, garbled, hard to follow
text: I was really disappointed in this book. I had read the first series by this author, which was excellent. complex yet flowing and full of color.  The first book of this series was ok, although it had a very dark element the first series did not . And some brutal way too graphic violence.  But still it had an interesting plot and characters. But this book was bogged down from beginning to end. A very dark heavy tone, again ,way too much graphic violence , and characters with names that got confusing. (the violence was unexpected, given that it was not at all part of the author's tone in her earlier books). The bones of a good story were there, but it just was not executed like the other books.  I did not enjoy it, and only finished it, hoping it would start getting better.  It did get somewhat more interesting right towards the end, but did not make up for the rest of the book. I rarely throw a book away, but i would not read this again, and i wouldn't give it to the library, because i wouldn't want someone else to come across that violence unexpectedly.

title: No real plot-just heroine leaves powerless teary eyed king over and over in order to save him.
text: I am sorry i ordered this last book--book 2 was a disappointment , but i thought maybe she would pick it back up in book 3. But i'm not even sure i will finish it.  There is not really an interesting plot in this series. it started out potentially interesting with the first book, but after that it's basically been about role reversal of an old plot, where the female constantly cries and watches the man go into battle. so in this one the main theme is the heroine again and again leaves the teary eyed hero as she goes off for some exploit to save him and the kingdom.  the plot in the last one is ridiculous. in book 2 she stabs a friend under the bad guy's power to get away and leaves him with the bad guy, which we assume means knowing he could be killed. then the whole plot of book 3 is that she gets a message that the bad guy will harm the guy left behind. so now she has to go back and get him. huh?  added to that she is keeping a secret that endangers everyone around her and just keeps king of forgetting to tell people. i can allow for some stretching of belief for a plot, but this goes too far and just is lazy . instead of creating something actually exciting, tension is attempted to be created by this silly theme.

It's almost like this should have been a few chapters or something-not a whole book. The plot developed way too fast and not in a satisfying way. And i'm getting tired of a prince/now king who pretty much does nothing but stare soulfully with his beautiful blue eyes.

title: confusing, annoying, disjointed
text: I keep following this series in hopes it is going to become more connected and coherent , but it's not. With this book it's become more disjointed than ever. It's like the author wanted this to be a series but couldn't quite weave it together. In this book we start with two characters that were fairly minor characters in an earlier book--where their actions were confusing--and now they appear as major characters, but we have gone back to an earlier time in some effort to explain who they were.  Just did not flow for me.  Each book ends with some cliff hanger, then the next book starts as if the cliff hanger never happened.  That even is the case within this book. One of the heroes ends up taken hostage, and the other vows to save him, then when they meet it's as if that drama never happened. what was the point?  The books are still pretty well written=I just wish there was more coherence between them. i'm losing interest in going any farther.

title: Saddened by edited version of great stories
text:
My friend lent me her copy of this book. After a few stories I was hooked and ordered one of my own. These stories were uplifting, sad, funny, and inspiring!

When my copy arrived I’d already read over half of my friend’s copy. I noticed when I went to the page that I left off on in my friend’s copy, it was a different page number in my new copy. Strange!

There’s a story missing in this copy. The Louis CK story. Very disappointing. As a reader I don’t need the original edition to have stirred edited out. I can choose to skip an author if I don’t like them. I feel like I’ve been robbed by this edited copy and am on a hunt for a FIRST edition.

title: dark places
text: Dark Places keeps you wondering  "who done it?"... To the point of frustration... You start screaming "JUST TELL ME WHO DONE IT ALREADY!" It stalls in places and gets a bit redundant, no new revelations - hence the frustration at times. Gone Girl is much more satisfying. As is Sharp Objects.

title: Very feminine flavor--my little boy does not like
text: We have "Little Mouse, Biddle Mouse" and loved it so much that I thought to get another of the books in the series.  I had read the reviews and no one said just how feminine this book is.  The little pig wants to be clean and sparkly and doesn't like the thought of being in the mud with the other pigs.  My 22-month old is a total boy and he likes cars and trucks and balls.  We love, "Little Blue Truck"--that book is great!  And "Stuck in the Mud" is another of our favorites. There is not judgement to this statement, but this book is definitely geared towards little girls or feminine boys.

title: The Very First

title: Repetitive and disappointing
text:
This book began with an interesting premise — but it lost my interest around the halfway point. I finished it, but only because I had a misguided hope it would redeem itself. (It didn’t.) This book could have been at least half as short, if not shorter, because the overall content was entirely too repetitive. While the writer’s claims are interesting and require a defense and evidence to flesh them out, things begin to fall apart after that. The evidence is scant and often surface-level, or even hypothetical, and then the commentary begins to sound repetitive. Barreca even goes on to restate prior claims in later chapters, as if they have now become support for a new claim. (That is not how effective or even decent writing works. If the reader is getting a sense of deja vu and thinking they have already read that argument, that is a bad sign. To then leave the idea inadequately supported — again — is just frustrating.)

I wanted to be able to add this to my classroom library shelf, as I am working to diversify the independent reading selections I offer, and nonfiction books that are not biographies or memoirs, or written by men, are in short supply in our department. But since I teach AP Language and Composition as well as English lit, I would never suggest any of my students read this, much less attempt to analyze the rhetorical situation of the writer or use this as a mentor text. Sadly, I could pull a few sections and have my students analyze them as examples of what NOT to do in effective writing.

title: Not as good as Book 1 in the series
text:
It was a fair read. I did not enjoy it nearly as much as I did The Kitchen Boy (another book by the same author). There is nothing new or novel about Rasputin in this. Granted, he is not the main character -- but his imminent demise is absolutely the focus of the drama. The character of Maria (the daughter) is weak at times, inexplicably flighty and inconsistent at others, and everyone else is very shallow in terms of development. The book might have been more interesting had the narrative extended beyond the brief episode that occurs four months after Rasputin's murder. To expand on the largely unknown life of Maria following her father's death offers more latitude for creativity and a potentially more interesting story than what the reader gets here, which is a fairly unimaginative rehash of well-known (to history buffs, anyway) details of the pre-Revolutionary period in Russia -- but with none of the interest and tension of those days, because we are living them entirely in the head of a wishy-washy teenage girl who moves in and out of spaces where she does not belong with truly unbelievable ease and lack of consequences.

For a quick, take-my-mind-off-stress-of-lesson-planning-for-online-teaching-during-COVID device, it was serviceable. It is not, however, a book I will keep on my shelves now that I have read it.

title: All I could do to make myself finish this one
text: I have a very hard time leaving a book unfinished once I have started to read it, but this one tested that resolve.  I was looking forward to reading a book devoted to Anne Neville, as she has been overlooked so often. But I just did not care for Ms. Gregory's treatment of her as a woman, a wife, a daughter or even a character in general. And I particularly did not care for the insinuation that Richard married her simply for her lands, when every other source I've ever encountered implies that theirs was truly a love match. And when the story devolved into Anne, Isabel and George fearing conspiracy and poisoning at every turn, it was all I could do to finish the book.

title: Disappointing
text: I haven't read as much on the Stuarts as I have most of the other royal families of England, so I was looking forward to being enlightened on this Countess of whom I had not heard.  I will readily admit that I am far more interested in the people, places & events of any period of history than I am in what took place in someone's bedroom, but this book had a surfeit of clandestine couplings and pillow talk.  Although the author was not as lurid in the details of the physical relationships and individual encounters as others have been, I came away feeling that the book was nothing so much as a vehicle to get from one dalliance to another once Mrs. Katherine Sedley comes of age and gets herself into the Court circle.  At that point, any real charcter development stopped, and though I read the book to the end, I found myself merely pushing through the second half of the book in (vain) hopes of gleaning something of historical significance beyond the bedroom shenanigans of the various characters.  The fact that Katherine Sedley is crude and bawdy (yet witty) wears thin when that is all there seems to be to her existence outside the King's bed.  The tale ends with the temporary/somewhat voluntary exile of Mrs. Sedley/Countess of Dorchester to Ireland, shortly before James II is deposed in favor of his daughter Mary and her husband William of Orange.  The Epilogue by the author implies that Mrs. Sedley/Countess of Dorchester was involved in the life of the Court during the reigns of both of James II's daughters (as her exile to Ireland was both temporary and short-lived), but provides no details.  While I realize the title is "The Countess and the King," and that interaction is fully terminated by her exile (followed shortly by his own permanent exile to France), it would have been nice to have finished out her history as it related to her country, since the author states throughout the story that this was her first loyalty, even above loyalty to her lover, King James II.

title: A tragedy, to be sure
text:
I read this book, word for word, as part of the curriculum in my junior year in high school. The length did not put me off, as I have loved reading all my life and regularly chose books much longer than average. But I did not enjoy this one. The ending turned me off completely, but I was unhappy with the book long before the ending came around. Without even touching on the moral deficiencies of the main character that comprise the crux of the storyline in the latter half of the book, I just couldn't get into the story. The pace of the book was slow and there was an excess of detail that just wasn't interesting to me. (I've heard that Theodore Dreiser divided the original manuscript in half and then sent the two halves to two different proofreaders or editors...and that each one cut his or her portion in half...but that most critics claim the finished book is still twice as long as it needs to be.)

I know this is considered by many to be a classic, but it was the *only* book of those required to be read in my junior year of high school that I did not like. I won't go so far as to say I despised this book, but it comes awfully close.

title: Nothing special...still prefer the Franklin Covey planners
text:
I got this planner thinking it would be easier to use to track our personal activities and school events but haven't found that to be true. The things I like about this were:
1. The stickers to make upcoming events / reminders more noticeable
2. The tear out shopping lists in the back of the planner

What I did not like was:
1. The monthly calendars are 2 months on a page. Way to small to record more than 1 reminder per day. The calenders should be a least one month per page or like Covey's a month spread across 2 pages.
2. No tabs for the months. All of the monthly planning calenders are towards the front and then the daily pages are after all the monthly ones. If there weren't going to be tabs, then at least put the daily pages after the month page.
3. Limited amount of information recording pages. It has a few areas to list information but since there are no tabs, you don't have as quick access to them.
4. There is no telephone directory in this book. There are a couple of pages for contacts under Mom's contacts and kid's contact and a page for Emergency / Medical contacts but no section for all your family and friends phone #'s and mailing addresses.
5. The pocket in the front seems like a good idea but as soon as you turn the page, everything falls out. It only stay intact when the organizer is closed with the elastic band over it but as soon as you start using it and turn the cover, the pocket is useless at keeping items from falling out.

I would not buy this planner again. I prefer the Franklin Covey products since they have more useful pages and have tabs for the months. They are also better laid out.

How disappointing!  All the ingredients of an excellent novel were there: Block's beautiful prose, an interesting subject, potentially interesting characters.  It just didn't seem to gel for me, especially the sections that took place in the psych ward (I found the sections that dealt with the relationship between Frederick and Katherine much more interesting).  Perhaps if it had been written in the first person so the reader could get into the thoughts and feelings of at least one of the characters?  Perhaps done as a play?  Well, they say that of all novels an author writes, it's the second one that's usually least successful.

text:
Reason has brought us further than all the ravings of the past, which really has been mostly nightmare—'reason and the ability to dispassionately observe the koïnos kosmos, common reality' rather I should say.

Mr Jodorowsky may beg to differ,, but note that in his little fable he feels the need 0.) to construct straw-men of reason to mock, and 1.) to back its moral with observable outcomes (spoilers!)—prophetic visions all come true, an improbable bet is won, an old man is made physically young, a woman becomes androgynous through will alone, a dead person is resurrected, ten times over people who ought to've died miraculously are saved—that are not consonant with reality as it is. It's fine to say that it were preferable that things be as they are in this book, but they are not, and—much as "Stranger in a Strange Land"'s and "Atlas Shrugged"'s and "Victoria"'s and philosophies are 'validated' by the 'events' that 'take place' in their books—beliefs are not proofed by fictional events written by people creating them precisely to make us believe that things are so.

It would take a lot to make me dislike Moebius' art, though, and if you're good at disbelieving non-arguments, I can recommend the book.

title: This is an interesting book
text: In my homeschooling curriculum, it was recommended to use this book for history as this was not part of the package.  I looked everywhere and finally found one on here that was absolutely falling apart and very, very old.  This was fine because we were only using it for one year.  So I like the book in that it makes it very easy for children to understand.  I did not like the book because it is was written in 1934, which makes it very out of date, slightly racist, and the overall tone of the book had me answering more questions for my son than I think an newer book would.  So I would not buy again and will use a more updated history book next year.

title: A Failed Attempt
text: Sadly, I am now giving up on The Lynley series..........This once fine series seems to have stalled out.  Havers is the only bright light left at this stage.  I had to force myself to finish "Come on, give it a chance.  E. George will turn things around."  Sadly, I became so lost in the nasty villain, the rather pathetic baker and the rest that I had to force myself to finish the book at all.

title: An Unreadable Book
text: I had read many of Cormac McCarthy's books years ago and admired his gifts.  I am sad to say that this book is a disappointment.  It is a dark, violent muddle that sinks into unreadable confusion.  I  finally gave up.  I could not finish it.

title: This book was highly recommended, but I didn't make it through the first ...

I read extensively in nonfiction natural history, and I couldn't enjoy the intrusion of human characters and situations into the  of the non-human world.
