The only reason I'm sticking with it until the end is because I'm curious about the twist, but I'm sure, with only an hour left to go in the audiobook, that this too will be a disappointment, considering how transparent this is, and how quickly the story is unraveling.

title: Not the same book I read in the 90s

title: Bleh
text: Surprisingly boring, probably because I already knew the story inside and out. King's work grew increasingly better in the years since this was written. The whole book centers on what happens at the end, so if you know about the pig's blood, the fire, and Carrie's ending with her mother, then you already essentially know the entire book.

title: Meh
text:
I can understand that the mom here was a trauma victim, but I still could not stand her. I enjoyed her innovative ways of making Room more sustainable (for a child who saw no horror in it), but she didn't strike me as being warm at all. For someone who longed to be rescued, she was unreasonably standoffish to the very folks she sought help from. I feel like Ma may have been the same character before she was abducted, only with more privilege back then, and that her time in Room didn't really change her at all. The whole story just didn't sit right with me, right down to the title, since more than half of the book concerns much more than just Room.

This poor kid, Jack...thankfully he has such an optimistic outlook because it seems that aside from "Steppa," everyone else in this story is downright insufferable, right down to - and especially - his own grandmother. After meeting these people, I could understand Jack's desire to stay in Room.

title: More for Adults than Kids
text:
Pros: Listening to Tim Curry read this book. The dark yet unexpected twist. Cons: The dark yet unexpected twist. The book in its entirety.

The book does warn you that it is dark and disturbing, and that you should find something else to read if this isn't quite your cup of tea. This is not merely using whimsy as a selling point; it's actually true. This book is dark and disturbing, to the point where it is less of an escape through literature and more like an "I know what you're going through" for poor kids who have rough lives. While some art is more enjoyable when it's dark, this just felt too disturbing to be a YA novel. I don't know how this series got so popular. There's nothing redeeming about this story or its characters, and certainly nothing that would make me want to continue reading books from this series.

title: Boring and Unlikable
text: An unlikable protagonist in an unlikable story. I remained bored and disengaged throughout, and didn't really care what happened to Patrick whatsoever. Someone like him *should* have an unhappy ending - jerk.

title: Bad Beat Poetry at Best
text: Written like a beat poem, and not a good one, like the ones Ani DiFranco writes - more like a teenager who's trying her hand at being a beat poet but just comes off as pretentious. This is not a book I would recommend to a teenager who may be considering trying drugs. Sure, Kristina has a rough go of things, but everything turns out okay for her in the end, so it couldn't have been all that bad, right? Ugh. There's no gravitas to the material, and there is no character arc. Kristina experiences some truly horrid things, yet they just roll off of her. Normally, this might be a sign of strength, but here it feels like nothing more than trivialization. I did not realize at first that this book was part of a series; it is a series that I will not be continuing.

title: Disappointing.

title: Boring

text: The sequel to this book, "This Book is Full of Spiders (Seriously, Dude, Don't Touch It)" was a far superior sequel to its predecessor. JDatE (was that acronym created on purpose just to mess with us?) was all over the place and never landed solid footing; it even ends in the middle of a sentence. You can see the beginnings here of what would eventually become some highly enjoyable writing from Wong in future novels, but the plot of JDatE was boring and messy, and even the characters don't feel as realistic as they do in Spiders.

title: Very Dry Read, But Yes, Still Relevant
text: I wanted so badly to enjoy this book, and I have wanted to read it for so long, but it was just too dry for my liking. Though, props to Huxley for creating something so timeless as the collection of concepts presented here. The plot of "Brave New World" truly is as relevant today as it was when it was written over 80 years ago. That is a rare talent.

title: Nothing Like the Movie (and That's a Good Thing)
text: I can see why fans of this book rabidly hated its film adaptation, which turned its source material into a sappy chick flick when the book is nothing of the sort (not to mention how much of the plot was completely stripped and bastardized); however, I do believe that Nick Nolte and Barbra Streisand were perfectly cast. That being said, I found Conroy's writing to suffer from an inordinate abundance of flair. While he is unarguably a master storyteller, he could have done more with less - not a lot less, but less.

title: The Love Story is Not Nearly as Prominent as They Make It Out to Be in Reviews
text: I've read reviews that said the film was preferable to the book because the vignettes were of better quality, so I'm interested in seeing the film to compare.  The story, while an original concept, was both unbelievable and superficial.  Thomas came off as whiny several times throughout his narration, and I left the book feeling no real emotional response to any of these characters.  Plus, the cover of the book would lead you to believe that love was Thomas' main motivation when that is hardly the case.  Love doesn't even enter the picture until about halfway through the third act.  Without seeing the film, I could easily see this as being that rare case where the film is better than the book.

title: Disappointing
text: "The Corrections" is a bunch of pretty words about a bunch of shi**y people. Chip was the only interesting character (to a point), and he got the least amount of screen time. I felt bad for Alfred throughout the book in that his health continued to decline, but his vapid, self-centered family - particularly his kids - cared more about their petty trivialities than their own father. This is the kind of family that you know won't realize what they've got 'til it's gone (save for Enid, who's much happier when the burden that has become her husband is finally gone and she can get back to *enjoying* her life), and this is also the kind of family that you hope yours never turns into when you're too old to fend for yourself and your life is left in their hands. I walk away from this book despising every character in it.

title: Bland
text: A lot of nice writing that went nowhere.  The side plot was more interesting than the main plot, which took forever to get to the point and was then cinched up in no time, culminating in an overly complete ending.  The one-page summary of "The Racketeer" in the back was infinitely more interesting than was this book.

title: Easily twice the length it should have been.
text: Ugh, with the constant reminders.  This book should have, and could have easily, been half its size, and it would have probably been so if the constant harkening back to points already mentioned was edited out.  Before even reading the Afterword, I could see that this was Irving's not-so-secret attempt at showcasing his own writing style, which frankly became annoying.  Also, this book is bad for your diet, because he constantly talks about delicious food and how to prepare it (one of my lesser points of contention, obviously).  I particularly disliked how there weren't really any surprises.  Everything happened exactly as we knew it would.  The ending in particular was wholeheartedly disappointing in how it was so "perfect."  And I have to ask - how the hell would Ketchum know what to do at the end?  Danny had to ask a doctor before he even found out, and Danny was a lot smarter than Ketchum.  And wasn't Charlotte pregnant with Danny's kid when they were together?  But then the kids were suddenly her new husband's?  Something there seemed to get lost in translation for me.

title: Weird Ending, Unbelievable Plot Elements - Not Good

title: I've Read Worse

title: Jumped the Shark
text: This book jumped the shark at about 100 pages from the end (you can probably guess which part I'm referring to), which is terrible, because you know that you still have that many pages left to go.  It's almost like Brown delights in making a situation so utterly convincing, and then bombarding you with factual knowledge that only he has in an attempt to make you feel foolish for believing him in the first place.  I agree with previous posters that there were just too many unnecessary details that went nowhere in this book, along with a few red herrings that were infuriating when you realized what they were, like the CIA Director's hacker.  She was an entirely useless character with a sub-plot that went nowhere.  The whole book was essentially "Do you know what this is?" "No, what?" (Insert wide-eyed wanderer look, followed by over-exposition.)  The Da Vinci Code?  Great book, read it in two days flat which, for me, was pretty incredible, since I tend to drag my books out over weeks or months at a time.  The Lost Symbol?  Surprisingly boring, filled with an abundance of fluff, and written like you're supposed to envision exactly how the movie would play out, frame for frame.  While this normally might be an innovative approach for an author to take, for someone like Dan Brown who has seen his books adapted into movies before, it actually felt cheeky.  This book could have easily been condensed into a book half this size and would have been all the more compelling for it.  Less is more here.  Those were the only two books I have read by Brown, and I will be hesitant to pick up another in the future.  I still have a copy of Angels and Demons that I have yet to read, but others have noted how his attempt to merge science with faith in that novel was a characteristic that they did not appreciate in that book - and which was carried over here.  I think I'm going to take a long break from Brown's work before venturing on to finish the trilogy, albeit out of order.

title: Not a Fan of the Twist

title: Disappointed

The jumps from the past to the present are confusing at times, and the book doesn't really follow a straight line when it comes to tracking Isabel's journey to wellness.  Maybe this was intentional so that you feel as all-over-the-place as Isabel does, but the end result was that you felt like you were reading a young adult novel, as opposed to a novel about an adult.  I was also frustrated that you never get to see Isabel resolve her issues with Alex - hopefully she doesn't go back to him.

title: Disappointed
text:
I have been a fan of Darren's music since the early days. I adore his charming personality and his quick wit, and I wish him all the best life has to offer. I will always cherish when I actually got to meet him during his Borders tour in November of 2007. I consider myself extremely lucky to actually meet one of my idols.

That being said, I am sad that, with regard to my opinion of "Secret Codes and Battleships", I am not in the majority. While I do respect how much work he has put into the album and how important it is to him, it feels like a step backward, musically speaking. When I bought "This Delicate Thing We've Made", it accompanied me on every lunch break spent in my car in 2007/2008. I was sure that SCBS would enjoy the same longevity, considering the fact that Darren is back on a major label and was incorporating such elements as an orchestra and big-name producers, yet I was rather disappointed with it. His mainstream pop lyrics are not as poignant as are his indie-pop lyrics, with the exception of "Black Out the Sun", and if I could sum up the album in a word, I would use "fluff". This record did not resonate with me as strongly as the rest of his catalog has, and after reading many people's reviews of how they enjoy the originality, I fail to see it. I never thought Darren could disappoint me, but then I guess he wrote "Hero" (from Tension and the Spark) for a reason.

Bottom line: Love Darren, love his catalog, but this one let me down. Though, I still look forward to the day when I can see him live in concert, and I look forward to the next album that he is probably already working on, knowing him. ;)

title: Lackluster attempt at erotica...
text:
"Only Pleasure" is an erotic novel that falls flat. There are a few decent sex scenes throughout the book, but the storyline that ties it all together is weak, unbelievable and you truly don't care about the characters when it has reached its end.

Kia Rutherford, the main character and supposed heroine of the novel, is almost raped by her husband, Drew and another mystery man. She then realizes that he is a member of the "club", a secret, elite group of men and women whose chief interest is threesome sex. Kia is drawn to Chase Falladay, who is also a member of the "club" and agrees to keep the club a secret in exchange for his protection of her from Drew. Chase was a former government agent who is harboring a dark past of his own, since he had to kill a woman who fell in love with him but tried to kill his brother, Cameron. Kia soon ends up involved in the "club" with Chase and his friend Khalid and it doesn't take her too long to realize that she has only joined the club because she is in love with Chase and always has been and that this is her only option to be with him. She assumes that he will never return her affection because he is only in love with the idea of the club and the "pleasure" that he has only promised her he would provide. But both of them will soon find out that someone bent on revenge wants Chase in agony and will stop at nothing, including hurting Kia, to get to Chase.

The sex scenes, which are the inspiration to purchase this novel, are somewhat worth the time and effort it takes to struggle through the ridiculous story. Some of the things that the men say in this book is an obvious finger pointing at the woman who wrote it. Men don't talk like this, especially the rugged, manly men being portrayed in this novel. Chase and his brother Cameron are equally cheesy in terms of their long speeches to their women who you have to think got hit with a bat to smile at their attempts at affection. Khalid's terminology is also rather disturbing, particularly for Kia, since he enjoys having sex with someone he constantly refers to as "little one". The term "baby" becomes particularly over-used and it just all clumps together as a fantasy of the author's that you can imagine she is giving you special permission to read. The story, language and characters are completely unrealistic and unbelievable. The "climactic" ending seems last minute and is even humorous in its execution and verbiage.

If you're looking for a book that reads like a porn film with a fair amount of sex and an extremely thin plot, this is your novel. If you're looking for a decent quality erotica, try something else.

title: I don't love it, but it's serviceable.

Also, I am using it in a college CRW class with all minority students who write in very different ways from Robert Frost. And while we all, in the class, can see the niceness in Frost and appreciate it, there is little to no attention paid to poetry that is "outside" the canon. In future I think I'll reference the book, but not require purchase of it. By the way... Ezra Pound? I am not so good at separating the artist from the art as Oliver is.

title: just like others said
text: I meant to write a review right after I took the test, but I forgot. So here I am. Anyways, there are errors in the practice tests, just like others said. This is starting to become a problem for these books, as the 2015 Princeton Review Chemistry book also had some major issues with that. But that wasn't even the biggest problem with this book. The problem was that I bought this book to see the test format and the kinds of questions I'd be asked. The real test was not even close to the practice book. Insane. The practice book has exclusively knowledge based questions, like it would straight out ask about a particular stage of mitosis. The actual AP multiple choice test required little to no Biology knowledge, but was more of a reading comprehension exam.Very disappointed that the book never made this clear. The free response was worse. The FR questions provided in this book were not even close to the same format as the real test. I gave it 2 stars instead of 1 because the book could help as a  content review guide for an AP class. Perhaps the weirdest thing about the book is that the longest chapter by far is the "Animal Structure and Function." This is odd because there were 0 questions on the test that came from this chapter. Really dumb to dedicate so much of the book to something that didn't show up. In conclusion, DO NOT BUY this as an AP Test prep book. It is not good for that. The questions in the book are nothing like the real AP test. You could use this book as like a review guide if you're in an AP Bio class. Your textbook will have a lot more in depth information, but this could be a condensed version you use to study I guess. Maybe try Barrons.

title: Disappointing--Not Quite as Billed
text:
This book must have been edited by Mr. Zimmerman's attorneys. He obviously wants us very far from any potential residual electrocuting charges in the amp and wants to prevent ANY risk that we may ruin the amp(or ourselves) by digging deeper than our skills may allow. There is also little risk in this book of learning much about repairing after the troubleshooting. Even the troubleshooting tips provided are anemic, a multimeter not even mentioned. But for me, expanding my skill set is THE reason I bought this book...i.e. to get expert assistance to guide me towards digging deeper than just checking tubes. After offering one or two testing steps per potential amp niggle, if stuff is still wrong, he directs us to visit our amp tech. I am a fan of Mr. Zimmerman's amps and his other book "Guitar Amplifier Players Guide" is pretty good, but at this price, I just expected a lot more.

Another issue I had with the book is how little information is here. Lots of white space on pages and many of what isn't space is simply repetetive. If you are ABOLUTELY new to amplifiers, you will gain some knowledge, but if you have owned a tube amp for more than a few years, I'll save you time by giving you Mr. Zimmerman's advice that appears probably 50 times in this expanded pamphlet, "Time to visit your amp tech...(who) has the equipment and experience to diagnose and repair...". Or you could buy a book that can help you with the basics of amp repair. Oh yeah, that didn't work any better than tapping on my tubes with a chopstick. To be fair, the book has the word "Troubleshooting" and not the word "Repairing" in the title, so my expectations may be lofty. However, there are other books out there at a much discounted price that will provide everything in this book and a whole lot more. Get one of them, or buy my copy of this book.

title: Disappointing Read
text: This was the most disappointing book I've read in a long, long time. First, and importantly, the title is misleading. The book is not a story about the 37th parallel. It doesn't even get into that until near the end. The book is actually about Chuck Zukowski, who has investigated UFOs and paranormal activity for decades. His story is quite interesting, but this author did not do it justice. Also, the book reads more like a novel, with the most trivial of details and dialogue from decades ago presented as if it were true. Really, is there a couple anywhere who could remember what was said and done by every family member on a road trip two decades ago? Unless this family traveled with a tape recorder going the whole time, much of what is presented in the book is conjecture. Taking that kind of liberty made me question other information in the book as well. In any case, the big letdown is the end, where the last page is presented with huge swaths of blacked-out print, just as government documents are supposedly redacted to hide important information, keeping the reader from any kind of satisfaction after slogging through nearly 250 pages. Since Mr. Mezrich is said to be a best-selling New York Times author, I will assume that this is not his finest work.

The lack of proofreading was jarring, so much so that I actually started correcting the text in the book ("out of harms way" p.105, "the dialogue between Philippe and I" p. 117, "alter" instead of "altar" p. 93 and 94.)Interesting material, but somewhat disappointing in style and certainly not worth over $20.00 for a paperback.

title: Bad writing
text: The book is in dire need of a competent editor. As a fellow reviewer wisely pointed out, this convoluted, disjointed account of a true crime, is hard to follow, and hard to enjoy. A sentence, out of so many found in the book, that goes like this: "There were several kids in the distance playing basketball. They did not seem to notice what was going on. Paul put an eye on them, however." After a while the reader realizes that maybe this author thinks he can write, and really believe it, but not so, and as I put an eye on the pages in this book, I realized that the best part of the book were some of the photographs included, showing some of the protagonists in this bizarre true crime story. 2 Stars.

title: Silly me
text: To read Pamela Des Barres account of her days as a roadie, is an invitation to the world of a girl, that became a woman, with nothing more in her head than to follow rock stars as far as she was allowed. I, wrongly, expected some insights into so many of the names that supposedly she has been with in her book. The reward for me was a fail treasure box, containing more feminine feelings, that I am able to appreciate, short of turning into a groupie myself. The pace, the content, the writing, made me want to jump in a cold pool and stop watching entertainment tonight for at least a month. Yes, I was curious, since this famous groupie is well known, I thought she had some really juicy anecdotes worth savoring, even though I knew I was venturing dangerously into female territory, but I still believed the book would rise above specific sex and deliver a substantial account of the famous 60's, 70's, and why not?, even the 80's. What I got was a girlie girlie, personal diary, emotional forays into the world of her highly idolized rock stars. Bad writing, boring and hard to keep up, this book was finally abandoned, with some degree of shame in my part for having picked it up in the first place, with the solemn promise that I will not get into any more girlie girlie type literature for my remaining days as a reader. Bummer. 2 Stars.

title: No Heads or Tails
text:
This must be a different type of a book. Even though the author has a lot to say the way she goes about it makes it very hard to follow, much less enjoy. I wanted to read this title because it had mention it was about all kinds of people of an artistic nature in New York City, something about Anglo Americans and Latin Americans coexisting together. The narrative is, to say the least, choppy and mixed, hard to gather enough interest in any particular situation or character. I imagine the style of writing is not necessarily following the basic story line of people and situations. It is more like enlightened dialogues, plenty of discourse but at the end of the day I found No Head or Tails.
Certainly for the acquired taste, not a fluent book.
I have never enjoyed books of this nature for I value story line the most in any style and this book lacks any sense of continuity. Difficult to enjoy unless, perhaps, one is immersed in the world that the author tries to convey. With a desire to understand a little more of inter culture I thought this one would be an interesting book. No dice for me.
I am thankful I had to chance to read it, even though I can not rightly say I read each page for I found myself frustrated as I went along and must have skipped a few more pages than I am willing to admit. Like I said: perhaps this book is for a segment of the population that understands the linguistic approach and relates to all the aspects of the book. To an avid reader that puts the story line first, regardless, this book did not strike any chords. Kind of like underground literature meant for those who readily identified with whatever this book tries to convey. Obviously it has been published and that alone deserves respect and it is also under amazon radar which is always a very good thing for we all know how popular amazon can make a writer. Good luck on that, that is for sure.
2 Stars.

title: Just a List of Questions - But Nothing More
text:
I first encountered Dr. K on twitter. I thought his first book "Everything I Learned in Medical School" was a very good read. I was able to read it in about 2-3 hours. It was full of that cheeky jaded med student humor, but at the end of the day you never doubted for a second that Dr. K loved medicine. It reminded me that I would not doubt my future career choice despite the sacrifices I would have to make in other parts of my life.

Why Medicine is a completely different book. Aside from the first 11 paragraphs that make up the first 3 chapters, the book is a list of 500 questions. Most of the 500 questions don't include any further explanation or insight on how to answer them (obviously we're suppose to think about them and answer them ourselves). I'd say maybe 10% of the questions in the book get a paragraph long explanation on how one should answer such a question. Unfortunately you can't really sit down and read this book because it is essentially a list of 500 questions. On my way to work I read through approximately 25% of the book (the bus ride that day took about 10 minutes). Since the book, to me, doesn't seem like it's meant to be read in the traditional sense, I don't know how one should use it? I certainly wouldn't whip it out in an admissions office waiting for my interview.

In Summary, I was disappointed by this book. I ended up zoning out as I glossed over an endless list of questions. A few made me stop and think and wonder how I would answer them. But at the end of the day I didn't feel like I finished this book knowing more or feeling more confident about my looming med school interviews. Since this is an ebook, I look forward to and hope Dr. K will make substantial edits.

title: Two stars, I'm feeling generous
text:
I've never read Ms. Torre before and I suspect this was not the book to start with. If this is indicative of her writing, then I don't understand why she is so popular.

First, the book couldn't decide what it was. Psychological thriller? Mystery? Romance? Detailed diary of everyone's lives? Probably a little bit of everything and that type of book has never appealed to me. I want a definitive purpose, a goal, a PLOT to a book. I want a story that doesn't include every bite that is taken, every movement that the characters make. I can figure out when the doorbell rings, and the person answers the door, that they've walked there. I don't need to be told. I can also figure out that if you set lasagna in front of a guy and he's sitting at the dinner table, he might be eating. I'm far more interested in the interaction of the characters than when he puts a fork in his mouth. There is such a thing as too much detail and this book had it in spades. But not good detail.

And that was the other problem with this book. Much is said about showing and telling. This book did the most telling of any book I've read in the last year, bad ones and good ones. I was surprised when reading this that there really wasn't any meat to the thriller portion, only a lot of narration. I could have handled more showing in the crucial parts of the book, and some narration to pull the parts together. I don't know whether it was the lack of detail, or the telling, but at 41%, I was drowning in irrelevant detail and had already figured out where the plot was going and who the bad guy (if you want to call him that) was.

My advice to anyone reading this? Don't expect any mystery and not much on the thriller end either. And the romance could be put into a thimble. When I get the time, I'll read another book by this author, just to see if this was a one-off or not. I'll hold off on my confusion until Book Number Two. And before I forget, I loaded this onto my Kindle with KU.

She writes a very good book, and for someone who has not tried any of these mix and match fabric ideas, or who hasn't learned how to change up the look of a skirt, blouse, or jacket with trim and/or contrasting fabric, it would be a good book.  I guess what I'm struggling to say is that it is more for beginners than experienced sewists.

text: I am at 85% completion of this book, and I will finish it tonight. I found the story convoluted and flat. Characters are hard to distinguish from one another. The writing is murky --it's easy to confuse who is saying what during a dialogue exchange. The lead character has almost no personality. Tons of red herrings all over the place --we'll see what washes out. And, as others have mentioned, in a book named "The Hive" and full of supposed bee lore, you'd think the writer would know something about the basics of bee keeping. Nope. Drones are male bees. They don't work in the hive at all. They don't feed the queen bee. They have one purpose: to fertilize potential queens outside of the hive. If the hive is healthy, they are tolerated inside the hive. If the hive is stressed or low on food, the drones are pushed out of the hive to die. This book doesn't get any of this right.

Dip half of the tater tots into the egg and then coat with breadcrumbs. Arrange them on the AirFryer Basket and spray with cooking spray. While the characters are well developed (I can actually picture the main characters and even imagine that I've met someone who looks like or displays their mannerisms), none were likable.  At all.  Even the characters for whom I feel some form of sympathy had so many "issues" that it was hard for me to want to get to know them more than the author allowed, if that makes sense.  Secondly, the two main characters, Theo and Boris, had profound substance abuse issues so a large portion of the story revolves around their addictive behaviours and impact on others. During those moments after giving up or getting bored with the writing, it took a great deal of resolve to pick up and finish the book. title: There's no good food because there are bad cooks?
text:
Definitely buy this book if you are interested in seeing some of the arguments provided by many atheists today. However, if you're looking for well-thought-out ideas, look elsewhere. Hitchens tries to fill in the holes in his logic with snazzy writing, but his ideas just don't hold up to any solid scientific test. (Although be warned that his writing sounds very convincing to simple-minded people who believe everything they read.)

He tries to offer a wide range of ideas, but when you step back, his primary argument is that God doesn't exist because there are some truly stupid religious denominations out there, doing stupid things. I do agree that there are plenty of stupid religious zealots in this world, but to say that THAT means there is no God... it just doesn't make sense. It's like saying there's no such thing as good food just because there are a lot of bad cooks.

He tries to add topping to his malformed cake with more illogical and hypocritical arguments. For example, Hitchens takes some time out to bash the arrogance of religious zealots. No problem there, but it implies that he is less arrogant than them. Personally, I think he is equally or more arrogant. Just like the religious zealots he criticizes, he believes he has all the answers. I see no difference in the arrogance there, but at least the zealots assume that they are less than God and could not have been created without God, while Hitchens assumes he is self-made, which seems to be slightly more arrogant.

title: Land of yawns
text:
None of the characters are likable, but they aren't unlikable either, because they just aren't real. They are one dimensional, pale imitations of life. They aren't believable as real human beings living, thinking, feeling representatives of life in the beginnings of the 20th century. Rather, they appear to be stiffly moving marionettes, with all the depth of a badly written modern textbook. Modern sterotypes are superimposed over them, and Unsworthy fails to give people of the early 20th century "the privilege of living a complex life." ( Purdue History Professor Cutter).

Contributing to the flatness of these characters is the way Unsworthy repeatedly tells us, rather than shows us, what we are to think of each character. We are told more than once that Somerville is 'one of those...predisposed to feel singled out for harm,' (Jehar), 'a victim preordained...' (Palmer), 'he feels that it is certain to happen, that something has been set in motion that can only end in destruction.. and it's coming straight for him...' (Patricia). This character trait must be stressed in such an underlined with a sharpie marker fashion because the author cannot let his political points be diluted by taking the time to hone his craft so that we reach this conclusion for ourselves rather than needing to be told outright.

I really wanted to like this book- the blurb and descriptions sounded fascinating. It just did not live up to its promise.

title: Grammar for the Victorian Child
text:
If you are familiar with the works of Charlotte Mason, take a look at the grammar section in volume
1 of the six volume CM series (this is online for free). Miss Mason gives several sample lessons and the
material in that section is duplicated almost word for word in Simply Grammar (there is also other material in Simply Grammar in addition to the material copied from Volume One of Miss Mason's six volume series). So if you have access to volume one, you could get a very good idea of the flavor and feel of Simply Grammar.

Simply Grammar is supposed to be a grammar text Miss Mason wrote and
Karen Andreola only updated it a bit and republished it. I don't
know how many changes, KA made to it. I suspect it's pretty much
what Charlotte Mason had in mind for grammar- but while I very much like Charlotte Mason's approach, there are other grammar programs I have used and liked better with my seven children.

There are four parts, and between 10 and 15 lessons for each of those four sections. Each lesson is illustrated with a sentimental black and white Victorian illustration I believe would be more appealing to romantic and dramatic little girls than to boys. The artwork is more representative of sentimental Victoriana than of sound artistic principles. Usually, but not always, there will be material in the lesson related to the picture (tell a story about this picture using a different preposition in each sentence; or there will be sentences about the picture and the assignment will be to circle all the verbs or change the tense).

I used Simply Grammar with two of my girls when they were about 9 and 10. We
liked the first section of Simply Grammar very much. We used it
comfortably, did all the lessons orally, and my children enjoyed it.
But there seemed to be a marked and sudden increase in difficulty.
One page was easy, then all of a sudden the next page was extremely
confusing and difficult to understand- and all the pages after that
were much harder. We put it aside to use later, but we never did find that it was helpful after that section. The same thing happened with the other children- very pleasant and fun for a while, and then all of a sudden it just leaped in complexity- jumping from talking about basic parts of speech into using terms such as nominative and objective case, indicative mood, and antecedents.

title: 2.5 Stars for immature Muse.  Spoilers, so don't read unless you want to avoid the frustration of reading about a whiner.
text:
THIS REVIEW IS FOR THE 5 BOOKS IN THE SERIES.

I read the first book as a KU and decided to purchase the rest based on that. I usually don't do that and this series is the perfect example of why not... The first book was great and I took a chance that the rest would follow. Unfortunately, in my opinion, they slowly went downhill with each successive book ending in a disappointing manner. Spoilers below, so don't read unless you want to avoid the frustration of this series.

I will start by saying how much I hated Muse. She was wishy-washy, flip-flopping, couldn't make up her mind, ungrateful, and thought she was less than BUT better than demons AND humans. She was supposed to be a kick-a$$ character, but she needs saving from somebody every other scene and is knocked out innumerable times. She likes to think she sees the world in shades of gray, and mentions so more than once. Yet, she is the same as Adam in thinking that all demons are liars, out for themselves, can't be trusted, murdering, conscienceless beasts. Never mind that she is HALF OF WHAT SHE DESPISES. So is Stefan for that matter, but because they are half-human they are better. Yeah, cuz there have NEVER been self-serving, murderous, lying, psychotic humans...

Another example of Muse's stupidity and prejudicial thinking when it suits her is when she is so worried about the soul-lock with Damian but waits until it's almost too late because having Akil replace Damian's soul-lock with his own would be just as bad. So, because they are both demons, they are the same even though one was a crazy, torturing, child-raping, skin-peeling maniac and the other one rescued her from that hot bloody mess, took care of her, taught her how to be human, watched over her and protected her, and finally sacrificed what he wanted for her. Yup, no difference between them at all, they are equal in all ways. Know how we know? Because they are both demons. It was things like this that made me grit my teeth in frustration. But unless there is truly something grossly objectionable, I finish my dang books!

Muse and her bigotry irritated me enough that when I was halfway through book 4 I had to skip to the end of book 5 to see if she got what she deserved. In a way she did as she was, in my mind, denied the BETTER demon. Yup, demon because there is my other gripe; Akil may be a demon but Stefan is HALF DEMON AND WAS A DEMON PRINCE ALSO!!! Stefan TOLD her to her face MORE THAN ONCE that he wanted to kill her, but he didn't really mean it, because hey, he was a human like her (eye roll).

Muse was shallow, self-centered, uncaring when she hurt others (if they weren't *human*), prejudiced, bigoted, and never grew as a person. However, Akil DID grow as a character and was the better "person". If I had to decide who cared more based on actions, it would have been Akil. But, whatevs, immature Muse didn't deserve that devotion anyway. I also disagree with other reviewers who say they understand why the series ends the way it does as nothing else would have worked. It was the author's world, she could have made anything work had she wanted it to.

So, 2.5 stars because of the things I did like; Akil, Jerry, the world building, and any author's talent because I could not write a book let alone multiple books. And, many, many, MANY negative stars for selfish, immature Muse. I didn't like Stefan or Ryder, either. I felt both they were all very one dimensional characters. Hmm, there;'s a theme here, the DEMONS were interesting, the humans, not so much. I'm just thankful I'm finished the series and will not read anymore by this author.

text: I am in the minority here, because I had several issues with this story.  Spoilers. . .  First, the author went on and on in detail about the Morgan's time in captivity, but frankly I didn't understand most of it.  It's dark, then there is light, I was confused by the changing descriptions.  I didn't think she was actually held that long?  But we are never given real information.  I kind of felt like we were reading a Scooby Doo mystery with all the misleading info for so many different suspects! Reid, the husband, making out with her best friend?  And somehow, her captor has a picture of them kissing and leaves it for Morgan to see.  There is never any discussion about it later.  A police officer that seems like something is off with him and then no more explanation about that.  I actually did see the one red flag that meant something.  I don't appreciate an author throwing out all these misleading bits of information and then leaving them unfinished.  Like we never get the details about all the previous victims, we only get info on two of the twelve. How did the Wolf go from being a cop to a news anchor to becoming a serial killer?  His uncle, did he and his wife help and know from the beginning what he was doing?  I felt the first two thirds of the book really dragged on, I skimmed, but the end felt rushed and I felt like I still had so many questions left unanswered.  I finished it feeling unsatisfied.  Won't read this author again.

title: Miserable person, miserable book
text:
Where do I begin? I've greatly enjoyed books such as [[ASIN:1565123522 French Dirt: The Story of a Garden in the South of France]] and have been an avid gardener my entire life (playing in dirt with water? sign me up!) so this book left me cold and unhappy for a number of reasons. The foremost reason being that this guy simply did not get it. At all. Ever. He found zero magic in his garden, a remarkable feat. This book sounded fantastic. It did not turn out to be so.

How the author has made a living writing professionally is beyond me. Any skill he may have is virtually absent from this book. It lurches from one horrible episode to the next, often leaving the reader at a crossroads with zero resolution. His daughter's knee surgery, for instance -- what happened next? Who edited this mess?

Another problem I had with the book is that Mr. Howard comes across as FANTASTICALLY unlikeable. Not just what my father used to call "a drip" but an actual paragon of an a**h*** -- if the anecdote about abandoning a live chicken in a large department store during Christmas shopping season isn't dreadful enough, wait until you read about his inexcusable behavior at a family wedding. I hate to quit reading a book halfway through but I marvel that I pushed through this pile of manure.

As other reviewers have noted, his inept handling of animals is a nightmare. That he never seems to glean a clue from his seemingly endless misadventures makes me question humanity as a whole. His tales of New York City turned my stomach. Raw sewage flowing into the East River? Buildings literally falling apart, revealing the puzzled inhabitants? New York City sounds like a bona fide nightmare. And he most definitely comes across as a native of that environment. His relationship with his wife is bizarre, at best. And these people are fantastically highly paid individuals? Professional jerks? I do not get it at all!

Needless to say, the tornado which wipes out his urban garden is a relief, at least to the reader. It's been quite a while since I was so glad to get to the end of a book. I have nothing good to say about this book. His perpetually unplanned misadventures are a nightmare -- does he not have an Internet connection to do some RESEARCH before he throws a credit card at each new unanticipated problem? Where are the raised beds full of lettuce? If his mission was to subsist on what he could grow for a month, that seems ultra-obvious. Add some sprouts and some tomatoes and you're gold. Heck, raise some WHEAT and bake your own bread.

I could go on and on. I hated this book. I really did. How you could paint such an unlikeable picture of yourself when you're writing your own book is baffling. How you could turn your backyard into a garden and make so many dumb mistakes is beyond me. This isn't entertaining or funny, it's pathetically sad and semi-tragic. I was looking forward to this book and I was tremendously disappointed. It's not every day that a book summons up these kind of emotions. Frustrating and maddening. I hope I never read another word written by this dolt.

title: Shrink-wrapped sorority girl looking in + not comprehending
text:
Jan 1 05: This book strikes me as a snotty list of objects and habits while cleanly missing the attraction of "alternative lifestyles" -- a parade of cliches, of bits and pieces. This was a gift from my ex-wife. She said "I didn't know you'd written a book." Ha ha ha. I opened it on New Year's Day to a line describing 'bohemians' wearing black t-shirts. OK, so I was coincidentally wearing an ancient black t-shirt. Then, leafing through the book (the binding broke immedately, btw) I got the feeling that I was being mocked at every turn. Yeah, I can tune an aircooled VW engine blindfolded, have a futon (and I mean a futon from Japan), know good incense from Wal-Mart incense, went to art school, blah blah blah -- but this book doesn't even TRY to f the ineffable (thank you, Alan Watts). It's a flatliner teenage girl trying to learn and grow by changing clothes. AVOID this book. Though I think it will burn well, and I'm a bit low on kindling.

This book pissed me off. People love to enjoy the ideas and work that "creative" or "bohemian" people do but are seldom tolerant of the personal choices made by those "creative" people. Avoid prepackaged, predigested ideas. Turn off your television. Read a book, but not THIS book!!! Do your own field work.

text:
I’m giving this a fair rating only because she did speak out on the subject of substance abuse- not because she was sincere in the cause . I’m not sure who it helped out there though I found it bland and the writing skills so mediocre that I wondered how she landed such a great job as a journalist. It was one of the most boring autobiographies I’ve ever read and absolutely zero humor to lighten the air. The woman does not know financial hardship and I found that disconnect throughout the whole book without even one word of mention towards empathy for those who cannot afford a fancy retreat.....I mean “ rehab” in the Utah mountains, she bragged about the kind of wine she drank, the restaurants she visited, her vacations and her clothes. Who was she trying to help by writing this? She’s a bit shallow to the real world and needs a bit more humility. I do however give her credit for carrying the financial burden while her one hit wonder husband ‘ Marc’ decided he couldn’t live up to the vows of marriage - “ in sickness and in health, till death do us part.” Gotta wonder what number wife the serial marriage guy is onto now- no strength given to her from that end! Good thing she is learning to pray to find that one true friend- we all need loyalty when the chips are down.
This book is a good donation to the library.

title: Misleading title
text:
I thought this book was going to be about 'money management' in the sense that it is usually referred to in the automated trading system community, ie about risk control and position sizing, etc.. those topics are briefly discussed in a very general sense but are far from the topic of this book.

The actual content of the book is more akin to a process management book for trading systems, it borrows heavily from (and often misinterprets) software development and industrial process methodologies such as waterfall, agile, lean, etc..

Overall the book is very general and very light on specific content, perhaps it could be of some use to a manager with no prior exposure to trading systems or software development, but I would definitely not recommend it to a developer.

text:
It seems that Miss Elliot decided to play up the suspense by having the characters do continuously stupid things. If you read the other books in the series, you know of all the adventures they have shared together. Then maybe you can answer why they continue to never text , call or inform anyone of where they are going or what they are doing when they are pursuing a lead in a case? Why is it that their minds seem to work slowly, even though they've been doing this investigating thing for years.? Spoiler... Why does Mason go out to the Killer's house by himself? Without texting or calling anyone? Especially, the woman he claims to love and have to look out for at every turn?! That is ridiculous. They just went through a mass murder situation a few months before this issue and now he just runs off all cowboy and pursues a lead with no backup... Even if it is just to investigate a question, he informed no one of where he was going. He is still a law enforcement officer. If the killer has been targeting men that participated in the program that he also participated in, then why does it even make sense to go somewhere without informing anyone of where they are? Also, when she starts to wonder where he is, no one seems to give a crap! Everyone is like where is Mason, oh I don't know, oh okay. There is no concern at all for the case that's going on... None of it seems to make sense to me.

I think I am just getting tired of Miss Elliot's stories. She did good at first, but considering she turns these out at such a fast rate, the creativity has lost its punch. So I will have to wait a while before I can get back into her books. Although I do like series books, like the Alex Cross series from Patterson or the in death series from Roberts, this just isn't working for me anymore. So as I end this series, I will say that the cases are good, and the suspense is just okay ; leaving much to be desired, and to a point they are enjoyable. But if you are looking for some true suspense that doesn't leave you scratching your head thinking, I could have figured that out, then reading all of these books back to back will only upset you.

text: Less than 10% of this book is Ada Lovelace and Babbage's engines. title: Author finds excellent topic, still manages to write an epic fail...
text:
The impact of internet and social media on relationships, lifestyles and social norms sounds like an excellent topic that can be explored in many dimensions in a novel. I guess I was really excited about the potential of such a book that I made two mistakes: My first mistake was to take a risk and order this book before the release date (i.e. before there were any reviews on Amazon). My second mistake was to give in to my stubbornness and finish it despite the fact that it clearly wasn't worth my time.

As other reviewers have pointed out, author's understanding of the technology behind the internet and social media applications is relatively naive. Looks like the author simply didn't spend much some for doing some basic research on the topic. Some of the assumptions in the book about what may be technologically possible in the relevant time frame easily exceeds the limits of science fiction and enters the fantasy genre - I am pretty sure that was not the intent.

The character development is relatively weak. Most characters appear to be single dimensional, they feel like caricatures rather than persons. The insecurity and neediness of Mae throughout the book is particularly disturbing. To be fair, there are a few interesting ideas in the book (and therefore my 2-star rating instead of a 1-star) but they are quite sparse in the nearly 500 pages of mostly insignificant babbling.

I am hoping to see a better novel from a more capable writer on this topic soon...

title: This is not a good book
text:
I received this book free, as part of the Kindle First program. I chose this one because the title and the cover art looked vaguely like it might be Scandinavian Noir. It is not.

The plot centers around a man who operates as an independent contractor for government agencies doing odd jobs. His friends "from the old days" are all being murdered and he needs to find out why. He has help from an old mentor at the CIA and a woman from the Swedish Security Services. He jaunts around the world, discovering things and dodging his enemies, until he solves the mystery.

The writing is average. The pacing is fine. The author's understanding of international espionage is woefully lacking; he's no le Carre. There's no tension, no build-up, no sense of mystery, no character development. The novel reads like it was written by a high school student as part of a classroom assignment.

This is not a good book. I wouldn't recommend this to anybody. I would be annoyed if I had paid for this. I am annoyed that I can't get back the time I spent reading it.

title: Disappointment; I was expecting more
text:
The book's introduction explains that it is a true story. Nothing in the book is made up.

With that said, it starts with a girl who grows up in upstate New York in a family of two parents and one sister. She works as a waitress in the family diner. I should reiterate that this is all true! It really happened! Then she went to college, graduated, and became a waiter. She moved from job to job, waiting tables. Again, this is not made up! Nothing in this story was fabricated! At one point she had an affair with a man and got pregnant. She raised her son as a single parent while she waited tables. I swear! This is all a true story! It really happened!

In other words, this book is a predictable, often mundane, story about a regular person who lives a regular life with regular events and regular people around her. The fact that she stopped waiting tables and wrote a book does not make it any more interesting. I agree with an editor who rejected her manuscript: her story has very little substance. She fills up a lot of pages with commentary - her interpretation of the events and her feelings about what happened... but the events themselves leave much to be desired and her thoughts are not insightful or surprising in any way.

There was one gem in the book. At one point a couple is dining at a table while the woman is doing something to her male companion with her hand under the tablecloth. The author asks if she can get them anything else, but she knows he's already getting all he wants, and much more! That was a funny line, the only memorable line in the book. The rest of the book is very, very boring. While I'm sure her life experiences appeal to the author herself, they were not interesting to me as a reader.

I read the book from start to finish, but finishing this book was like finishing a chore. I was relieved when it was over so that I didn't have to think about it any more. I will donate my copy of the book; it is not worth keeping. For a dynamic and amusing story, try Fine Dining Madness. It has a lot more material, and the commentary is colorful and entertaining.

title: thin book with short videos and not enough tutorial information
text:
I really wanted to like this book because I love Jake's concerts, but I think the material is too thin to learn from. The printed book is just sheet music to go along with the videos. The videos are short. There are 14 videos that are mostly 5 to 10 minutes each. The first 9 have some basic tutorial information, but IMHO not enough for a beginner to start playing interesting songs on their own. The last 5 videos are mostly performances by Jake that look and sound great, but there is no way a beginner can play along with him using just the tutorial information in the earlier videos, no matter how much you practice. If you're looking for a ukulele tutorial book, I think there are many better choices than this one. If you want to see Jake play the ukulele, go to his concerts or watch him on YouTube.

The only reason to buy this book is for the detailed sheet music of some of his songs. 43 pages of the book are in the "Bonus Song Transcriptions of Live Video Performances" chapter, which is all sheet music. Be warned that this is much more complicated than the tutorial videos, so you will have to look elsewhere to learn how to play them.

title: short book doesn't go far enough and why is there no index?
text:
I'm not impressed by this book. Who writes a reference book these days with no index? Granted, the book is fairly short, but an index still helps readers find specific material in the book. There are so many different concepts in website development these days that reference book really need to help readers find the material that the need.

Regarding the material that is in this book, it focuses almost entirely on front-end development for PC web browsers. There is only one short chapter on optimizing for mobile web browsers, which is an area that is quickly growing in importance. There is only one superficial chapter on server-side optimizations. I think some material on database and application server setup would be very valuable to many readers, though perhaps too complicated to others. The most useful material in this book are the chapters on optimizing your CSS and HTTP, which is important to know.

title: below average book on travel photography
text: There are tons of tutorial books on travel photography out there. You're probably asking should you buy this one instead of one of the others? Based on my experience, I would say no. The biggest problem is that the example photos are not very inspirational. Few of the photos are of recognizable landmarks, so you cannot easily compare his ideas with photos you have taken in the past. Most of the photos could be taken anywhere, which is not my idea of "travel" photography. I prefer travel photos that highlight unique locations. Further, the printing quality is kind of dull (compared to real printed photos), which is not very encouraging. The text of the book does have some useful information on travel photography, but without inspirational photos to back up his ideas, I lost interest quickly.

title: Sleazy male protagonist
text:
This book opens in the point of view of the cynical, jaded, rich, British-American, divorce-attorney hero. He has just been awakened from a sound sleep by his bed partner, a woman who is obviously a one-night stand. He is utterly detached from her as a human being as, oozing with entitlement, he mentally critiques her performance. How irritating that she has the temerity to not instinctively know how to perform a hand job to his exact specifications!

I can never figure out why any author would decide that this sort of start to a story, which is marketed as part of the romance genre, which promises true love between soulmates, is a winner for hooking readers. All that is accomplished by this sleazy intro to the "hero" is that there is no mistaking the fact that there is nothing heroic about him. He is simply one more boringly cliched, misogynistic manwhore. When an author creates this type of hero, it is also unfortunately inevitable that the heroine is reduced to his opposite-number cliche, a "magic vagina." This is a woman who is so enthrallingly sexy that her very existence in the hero's life remakes him so thoroughly, he easily and happily walks away from decades of promiscuity into an HEA of domestic bliss, as a loving, faithful, family man.

No thanks. I've never been able to suspend disbelief that far. And this isn't the book to change my mind.

DNF.

title: A disappointing finale to the Mediator series
text:
As Book 7 and the final entry in the Mediator series, the main purpose of this novel is to give Suze Simon and Jesse de Silva their overdue HEA so that they can, at long last, get married and consummate their relationship. However, that HEA does not come easy. There is a long, rocky road before the ultimate resolution of their romance. In addition, since this is a paranormal, action-adventure series about treacherous ghosts, this novel provides a plot about an extremely dangerous ghost. But it is a very different ghost than any which have gone before, a little girl who was murdered at age seven. Since this novel is far longer than any other book in this series, Cabot has further increased the page count by throwing in three additional villains who are all among the living. These include two pedophiles and a recycled blast from the past, Paul Slater. Once again, obnoxious Paul is up to his same old tricks, blackmailing Suze to push her toward being his romantic partner instead of Jesse’s. Paul convinces Suze that he will set off an ancient Egyptian curse that will turn Jesse into an evil mass murderer when his construction company demolishes the house formerly owned by the Ackermans. This house is a main setting of the first six books of this series, which Paul now owns because Suze’s mother and step-father sold it a few years ago and relocated to Los Angeles. This magical curse will be activated by destroying the house because it is the site of Jesse’s murder in 1850. (The novel inadequately deals with the fact that, due to Suze’s time-traveling to 1850 in Book 6, preventing Jesse’s murder, and transporting his living body to the present, his murder no longer took place.) Paul tells Suze that his price for not cursing Jesse is for her to go on a dinner date with him and have sex with him afterwards. In his infinite egotism, he is convinced that if Suze, who is still a virgin, experiences sex with him, it will be so fabulous, she will instantly fall in love with him and choose to marry him instead of Jesse. Suze is naturally horrified by the degree to which Paul has stepped up his sexual harassment. But she keeps his nefarious plan to herself, out of fear that if Jesse finds out, he will murder Paul and end up in jail. She strings Paul along, letting him believe she will surrender to his vile machinations, while she frantically tries to figure out how to stop him from harming Jesse. It is perfectly clear to Suze that Paul has no intention of keeping his word, if she were crazy enough to give him what he wants. Why would he trade Jesse’s survival for one night of sex with Suze when he can break his word—as a consummate liar who has no scruples—and get rid of his rival for good?

I find this novel frustratingly disappointing on multiple levels:

The events in this story occur four years after Proposal. Suze is currently 25. Even though she and Jesse have been together in the flesh, in a committed relationship, for eight whole years, and they have been engaged for four of those years, they still haven’t had intercourse and, just as in Proposal, her understandable sexual frustration is heavily covered in this novel as well. Jesse has currently been a virgin for over 178 years. Because of both his sexist, nineteenth-century attitudes and strong adherence to the view of his Catholic faith that fornication is immoral, he believes that making love with Suze outside of marriage would dishonor her. The problem is, he has unilaterally refused to get married until he can make an unspecified amount of income as a doctor, which he, and he alone, will determine is sufficient to support a wife and any potential offspring. He has been making an excellent salary for the past four years as first an intern and later a resident in pediatrics at a nearby hospital, but he has continued to postpone their marriage—and all this time Suze has put up with this patronizing behavior. Meanwhile, though Suze has not held down a paying job all these years, and is currently working for free as an intern at the Junipero Serra Mission Academy, the Catholic school she attended during Books 1-6 of this series, she has managed to stay afloat financially because she inherited a huge amount of money from her dead father that came into her possession at age 18. It has paid for her higher education and all of her living expenses all these years, with enough money to spare that it could make a huge dent in Jesse’s medical school loans, and allow them to get their marriage started. But Jesse is absolutely opposed to her money becoming part of their joint, marital assets. Suze’s ongoing failure to speak up to Jesse and insist on being a coequal partner in their relationship is extremely poorly motivated in both this book and Proposal. Readers of this series have been informed, over and over again, by Suze's actions and her opinion of herself in her thoughts and her dialogue in every one of the previous six books, that she is a kick-ass female who doesn't take any guff from males of any age, whether living or dead. Because of that history, it makes no sense that she has let Jesse call all the shots in their relationship for eight whole years.

It was already irritating to me that, at almost 21 years old in Proposal, Suze had not emotionally matured during the four years since the events of Twilight, Book 6 of this series, when she was 18. Unfortunately, another four years have passed, and she continues to remain as immature in this book at age 25 as she was at 18. Her primary character flaws, which are evident throughout this entire series, are bullheaded overconfidence combined with a hazardous lack of common sense and self-knowledge. These are the typical traits of slapstick characters (such as Lucy Ricardo of I Love Lucy). They cannot change and grow, or the entire premise of the series they are part of is lost. These flaws are employed constantly in all seven books of this series as the major source of conflict between Suze and all the other characters, living and dead, and they are also the source of occasional wry humor.

This novel deals with some really dark issues. Paul Slater is resurrected in this story to play the part of a cartoonishly evil, Snidely Whiplash villain. And there are not one, but two, pedophiles who are living people, not ghosts. These three men are all horrible human beings who definitely deserve karmic justice. But the scenes in which Jesse and Suze casually plan out how they will murder these villains—even though, they do not, ultimately, actually murder anyone—are extremely creepy. At times I wondered if Cabot thought she was writing a script for the Dexter television series.

All the way to the very end of this novel I held out hope that, somehow, some way, the ridiculous Egyptian-curse plot would end up being revealed as a total scam on the part of conniving Paul. But, no, that is not how Cabot resolved this nonsensical conflict.

Overall, sad to say, this novel is not a worthy addition to this series.

I experienced this novel as an audiobook, which is performed by the same voice talent, Johanna Parker, who narrates the entire series. She does an excellent job.

The Mediator Series

1 Shadowland, October, 2000
2 Ninth Key, February, 2001
3 Reunion, July, 2001
3.5 Every Girl’s Dream, 2004 (short story)
4 Darkest Hour, December, 2001
5 Haunted, February, 2003
6 Twilight, January, 2005
7 Proposal, January, 2016 (novella)
8 Remembrance, February, 2016

title: A more than usually absurd, Harlequin Presents, sheikh romance
text:
In the imaginary, alternate-universe, Middle Eastern kingdom of Tahar, 30-year-old Prince Tarek suddenly finds himself elevated to King when his venal, narcissistic, evilly cruel elder brother, who had no son and heir, suddenly dies of a drug overdose. Tarek discovers, to his horror, on reading his brother’s journals, that his brother murdered their parents when Tarek was 15, in order to ascend to the throne. He also tortured young Tarek, then banished him to the desert, where he has lived in a cave like an isolated monk for the last 15 years. Tarek’s brother assigned him some kind of military role that seems to have involved battles with weapons so primitive, they were something out of the early sixteenth century. Tarek is described as fighting only with a sword and facing “steel-tipped arrows” on the battlefield. He also functioned as some sort of assassin on behalf of his brother, but no details are given as to how he might have pulled that off successfully using only a huge scimitar in a world of guns. In spite of having no education past the age of 15, having no access to modern technology such as cell phones or the internet, not reading newspapers, books, seeing movies or TV, Tarek speaks perfect, fluent English. It is never explained what he did in his cave for toileting, bathing, laundry, and meals—other than somehow maintaining a coffee habit. He has never had sex and has staunchly refused to give in to sexual urgings whatsoever, so apparently he has never even engaged in self-stimulation. His entire personal identity involves martyring himself as a “weapon” for his country. Tarek is not described for most of the book as wearing the thobe (robe) or the Taqiyah (head covering), and there is no mention (as there never is in HP sheikh romances) of his following Muslim religious practices, in particular, prostrating himself to pray five times per day. In fact, the only Muslim practice that typically (but not always) appears in HP sheikh romances, including this one, is avoiding alcohol.

Olivia comes from a wealthy American family. She suffered from “poor little rich girl” syndrome in that her parents were so obsessed with caring for her chronically, dangerously ill younger sister, they basically ignored her throughout her childhood. At university, she met the prince of a fictional European country, married him, and became his queen for five years until his untimely death. Though she is not the typical HP, virgin heroine, we are assured her husband was 26-year-old Olivia’s only lover. Because she and her deceased husband produced no heir, his younger brother became king, and Olivia’s presence in that country became surplus to requirements. Because she views herself as highly skilled in the political maneuvering required of monarchs, and the only career she is interested in pursuing is to continue being a queen, her brother-in-law offers her the chance to help her adopted homeland gain important political advantages by entering into a nineteenth-century-type arranged marriage with Tahar’s new, unmarried king.

After Olivia arrives in Tahar, she realizes from her very first meeting with the devastatingly attractive and mysteriously aloof Tarek that a political alliance with him won’t just involve doing her honorable duty. It could prove to be a real pleasure. It would be quite entertaining smoothing down half-wild Tarek’s rough edges, and she eagerly anticipates the joys of sharing the marriage bed with the gorgeous brute.

Tarek is fully aware that he will need to marry and produce an heir, but at first he believes a foreign woman will simply make it all the more difficult to move from self-enforced celibacy to cohabitation. However, Olivia does such a convincing job persuading Tarek that, with her skills as an experienced queen, she could quickly and efficiently help him transition from unpolished warrior to a sophisticated king, he reluctantly agrees to give her a few days to concretely prove her grandiose claims.

Olivia is quite surprised when Tarek escorts her to a bedchamber himself because, unlike in a typical HP sheikh romance, the Tahar monarch’s palace is not crawling with hordes of willing servants. She is even more amazed when her assigned space is right next door to Tarek’s own suite. This unconventional setup permits the occurrence of a classic romance trope, the accidental, lust-inducing, nude sighting. That night while lying in bed, Olivia hears grunts and shouts coming from Tarek’s room. She gets up, peeks out of her bedroom door, and is awed and turned on at the magnificent sight of a sleepwalking, naked Tarek, who is stomping up and down the corridor, swinging both a sword high above and his exposed genitals below. As expected for a romance hero, he is described as having muscular thighs and a bodybuilder’s physique, even though all he’s ever done is brandish a sword and shoot arrows. He’s never routinely hoisted heavy objects.

I had the following issues with this novel that made it a less than appealing read for me:

1. It is typical of HP sheikh romances that their mythical Arab nations bear no resemblance to any Arab nation in the real world. But this book takes that inaccuracy to an absolute extreme. Tarek’s sixteenth-century-style, sword-and-arrows battles would only make sense if this were a time-travel novel—which it is not.

2. Why on earth would Tarek’s brother keep journals lying around in which he exposes his every crime, most especially patricide and matricide? Not only that, keeping a journal is a rather nerdy thing to do, not something one would expect from a chaotically corrupt, self-indulgent addict.

3. As is typical of HP sheikh heroes, Tarek does not act like a Muslim. He does not regularly pray, almost never dresses like an Arab male, and he is clean shaven rather than having a beard. In this case, Tarek initially has a wild, scraggly beard, but he allows Olivia to shave it off entirely, rather than simply neatly trimming it.

4. At her wedding to Tarek, we learn that Olivia doesn’t speak or even understand Arabic. It is obvious she also does not speak or understand the most common language in the Muslim world, Urdu. This means that the only way Tarek and Olivia could realistically communicate is with an interpreter. The author chooses to conveniently ignore that issue entirely, presenting Tarek as speaking fluent English, even though his having that skill is not at all well motivated. (Stating once in the story that, during his 15 years in his cave, he would march up and down talking to himself in several languages he learned from his father, so he wouldn’t forget them, just doesn’t cut it.) Not only that, later in the book Tarek reads and fully comprehends English-language sex manuals in order to be able to perform like a virtuoso in bed, as all romance heroes are expected to do.

5. Speaking of sex manuals: The author’s entire goal in this story is to flip the typical, HP trope of a virgin heroine matched with a sexually experienced hero, but the setup of Tarek’s being a monkish virgin living in a cave for 15 years is utterly improbable. Also, his, also unrealistically, studying sex manuals rather than allowing Olivia, as an experienced widow, to instruct him in what she enjoys in bed, is a missed opportunity to milk this trope reversal to the full.

6. Olivia’s decision that the only career she wants in life is to be a queen is, in the twenty-first century, decidedly odd, if not slightly unhinged.

I experienced this novel as an audiobook, which I obtained through Hoopla. For the most part, the narrator does an adequate job but, irritatingly, she consistently mispronounces sheikh as “sheek” rather than “shayk.”

I rate this book as follows:

Heroine: 2 stars
Hero: 2 stars
Setting: 2 stars
Romance Plot: 2 stars
Writing: 2 stars
Audiobook Narration: 3 stars
Overall: 2 stars

title: The hero is obnoxious and the plot is ridiculous
text:
Plot setup: A presumably sophisticated, British, international businessman, who is incredibly foul-mouthed and a misogynistic manwhore, is somehow stupidly naive enough to go to the bathroom in an airport while leaving his cell phone charging unattended in a public place where anyone could steal it. Which is how the hippy-dippy heroine confuses his phone with hers, because she also naively leaves her phone charging unsupervised in the same spot, comes back and takes his phone instead of hers. And neither notices the problem until it is too late to switch phones in person.

Right off the bat, I cannot suspend disbelief with this ridiculous plot. First, why would two such utterly different people have an identical phone? Second, why would two such complete opposites be equally naive about basic security precautions a 10-year-old ought to know about?

Worst, even if none of that bothered me, the crude hero who views all women as nothing but sexual objects turned me off from the start. Yuck.

The male narrator does a good job but that doesn't save this book.

DNF.
