text: It’s hit or miss in finding a really good book, so I based my purchase on the glowing reviews. Unfortunately, I just couldn’t get into this book and had to really force myself to finish. Everything fell really flat for me. Meh in a nutshell.

title: Lost interest
text: Let me start by saying that the beginning of the book was great. I was drawn in and was excited about what the next page would hold. However, somewhere in the middle of the book, my interest faded and trying to finish the book became a chore. I tried countless times to finish, but it got to the point to where I decided I didn't much care to know how it ended. I googled the synopsis and was glad to move onto the next book in my collection. McLemore, you are a good writer. Keep moving forward with your writing, and remember that not everyone will love everything you do and that's ok!

title: Too much talking, not enough cooking
text:
This book has given me quite a bit to think about concerning food selection and preparation. The author has pointed out that intelligent, responsible food selection is not simply a matter of purchasing organic vegetables or becoming a strict vegan. She has pointed out that we need to consider transportation costs, the environmental impact of a food regardless of where it is grown or whether or not it labelled as 'organic' in order to determine what is the best value - economically, nutritionally and socially - for our food dollar. The psychology behind our food choices, beginning with the conditioning we receive from our parents as children to the impact that advertising and food fads we are influenced by as adults is also discussed in depth.

The author tells about her choices in facing these issues, how she prepares and grows much of her own food, even keeping chickens and sheep and making her own cheese. While some of this is thought provoking this comprises about 3/5th of the book and frankly by the time I plowed through it I was finding it quite tedious. The remaining 2/5ths of the book was divided between recipes and footnotes. There were a few recipes that were of interest, others that were the same or similar to those I already used and the rest either too complicated/time consuming or just unappealing to me.

What I got from this book, essentially a description of the author's philosophy of an ethical approach to nutrition, could have been summed up in an article.

title: Eavesdropping on strangers
text:
Have you ever been someplace where you can't help but overhearing other peoples' conversation? They go on and on skipping from one topic to another, mentioning people or events that you may or may not recognize, dropping interesting little references to things that pique your curiosity but by in large leaving you in the dark.

This book is very like that experience. The more you know about either of these two men, or the Beat Generation then the more interesting you will find this book. Unfortunately for meI have some interest in this period but only a passing familiarity with either of these men's personal lives and so much of this was like hearing a conversation between strangers about people and events that meant nothing to me.

title: Confusing
text:
This book is difficult to describe. It is sort of science fiction but also sort of fantasy. There are also thriller and mystery elements to it as well as coming of age themes. Perhaps the best classification would be 'weird'.

The novel is written using alternating viewpoints and story lines, which is currently in fashion but requires a certain amount of skill to tell a story that the reader can follow. This author almost managed to do this but didn't always succeed, at least for this reader. The author has established a rather elaborate secret organization, complete with an underground lair that is engaged in outwardly engaged in fulfilling fantasies but actually engaged in....some other more nefarious purpose that isn't really defined. A young woman with a tragic past is recruited by this group and joins in a group of similar young women to become operatives to serve this undefined purpose. The organization is attacked, and chaos ensues. Some questions are answered and others are left unanswered. When I finished the last page I was as confused as I was when I finished the first chapter.

Obviously I was not impressed with this novel, and if I had not been obligated to review it I would not have finished reading it. Others might enjoy this more open ended type of narrative and there are some good points to this story. The author has created some really interesting characters. The premise of this mysterious organization was really well crafted and intriguing but unfortunately once it was established it was then ignored, leaving me very disappointed not to learn more about it.

title: Not her best work
text:
I have been a fan of L'Engle's books since I first read WRINKLE IN TIME, shortly after it came out. Over the years I have often thought of her works and have often given her books as gifts. I have also read many of her books as they came out but missed this one until now. I wish that I had just skipped this one.

The story focuses on Sandy and Dennys, the most normal members of the Murray family (WRINKLE IN TIME etc) the one who, even in the early books, were presented as the family members who kept the rest of the family grounded in reality. We were told in the other books that the twins were not social outcasts in school like their sister and brother, and in a family filled with geniuses Sandy an Dennys were only considered bright, rather than gifted. The rest of the family had all been involved in fantastic adventures but the twins had been mostly left behind.

This time though they are swept off to another time and place to face the unknown. The boys accidentally get transported from their Connecticut home where they are wearily dragging through the last days of winter to a sun and sand filled desert where they are rescued by a group of strange people and creatures. Gradually it becomes apparent to the boys that they have been transported to Old Testament times, and that the people who have saved them are Noah and his family. The boys realize that the coming Flood will change forever the life in the oasis, and the rest of the world. The question is will they manage to return to their home before it comes or will they be among those left outside the Ark to perish?

Like the other books in this Quintet this one has a marvelous setting, one that transports the reader to an exotic location filled with challenging concepts and characters. Unlike the other books though that is just about all that this book supplies. The method and reason for Sandy and Dennys to be transported is weak, their actions while they are there is confined to being hurt, being rescued, and running away. The only real positive, active thing either boy performs in the whole story is to encourage a son to be nice to his father. In the other books the main characters all undergo some significant growth but by the end of this story Sandy and Dennys are completely unaltered by their experiences, not even their physical appearances have changed. The book might as well ended the novel with the cliched 'it was all a dream' device.

title: In-laws and Out-laws
text:
This is the 6th in the AURORA TEAGARDEN series.

Aurora has recently gotten some bad news, that she and John would not be able to have children. The two of them were working through this disappointment and going about getting on with their lives. Today getting on with her life involved dealing with a naked man throwing firewood around her yard, a niece arriving unannounced on her doorstep complete with luggage and baby in tow. Even the boring business dinner that Martin had drug Aurora to took an odd turn when the hostess abruptly left, cutting the evening short. It should then, have come as no surprise when the found a dead body waiting for them when they returned home. As Aurora and Martin attempted to sort out the convoluted mess the danger was brought far too close to home.

I do not do spoilers and so will not reveal who dies in this one, other than to say that it was a major character and, in my opinion, not a good choice. This is a major reason for the low rating I have given this novel. The other reason is that there are some pointless continuity errors in this novel, elements that directly contradict information from earlier stories. The first is the age difference between Aurora and Martin. Ever since Martin was introduced it was stated repeatedly that Aurora was 15 years younger than Martin, now the gap has been narrowed to 13, besides being careless there was no reason for this change. The second error is that Aurora makes a point of never having been in a basement before, a comment that directly contradicts several statements, and a major plot point of the first novel in the series (REAL MURDERS), and, like the previous error serves no purpose in this story.

This novel is not up to the standard set by the earlier books. It seems as though Harris just dashed off with little thought, perhaps even as a finale to the series or an obligation on a contract. For whatever reason it is disappointing on several levels.

title: Bewildering
text:
I've heard of the 'Mary Celeste', including various theories about what happened to her so when I saw this book I was hoping to read another theory about what could have caused her crew and passengers to vanish. As I began reading the story was full of promise. The characters were interesting, drawing me into the story but then tragedy struck and the focus abruptly shifted. New characters were introduced, I read on, waiting to see how the two plot lines would connect and then another abrupt shift. This pattern continued throughout the novel. A situation was established, characters introduced and then abandoned before a resolution could be achieved.

I understand that there will probably never be a definitive resolution to the 'Mary Celeste' mystery but this novel didn't even offer any theories. The well drawn characters that were introduced were wonderful, fully realized individuals that came to life on the page but this only added to the frustration when they were abruptly removed and/or abandoned. I wanted to know what happened to them, either before or after the events described. This book has only added to the frustration of unresolved mystery of the 'Mary Celeste'.

title: Worth every cent I paid
text: Apparently there are readers who enjoyed this novel, obviously I am not one of them.  This was not a terrible novel, in fact there were some really interesting ideas, some well written passages but unfortunately there is quite a bit that is repetitive and out right confusing.  The genre was a mix of hard boiled, paranormal and comic and didn't really succeed at any.  And by the way, I got this download for free.

title: Confusing
text:
The story takes place over the past fifty years and is told from various points of view. Much like FOREST GUMP, many major figures such as Robert Heinlein, Ian Fleming, L. Ron Hubbard, Rudolph Hess and Jim Jones, figure into the story which takes place primarily in California. I would explain further but I am not altogether certain I can. I found the overall story confusing to say the least. As the novel progresses it becomes more clear but it still is not entirely clear to me exactly what the author was trying to say which is too bad. The characters are engaging, the situations interesting but the overall point of the novel still eluded me.

I found the novel interesting in places but the overall effect was confusing which is too bad. I think that there is a good, imaginative story in here. Maybe you can figure it out but unfortunately it seems to have eluded me.

title: The Case of the Missing Plot
text:
I picked this up because the premise sounded interesting. The occupants of what used to be 221B Baker Street are required to respond to letters that arrive there addressed to Sherlock Holmes. I was expecting to read about modern day amateurs tackling problems worthy of Holmes. Instead I got....hmmm, other than disappointed I am not really all that sure about how to describe this novel.

It is the first book in a projected series so I expected to see lots of time spent on establishing the premise, introducing the characters etc but I expected a plot containing a mystery that would be at least somewhat challenging as well. The premise was described, although requires that the reader overlook quite a bit of very unlikely points to accept it. Characters behave in the most extraordinary ways with little explanation and, at times the story seems to run around in meaningless circles. The most disappointing thing though is that the novel does not end so much as just stop.

I could not understand what the point of the novel was until I read on the jacket that the series had been optioned for a TV series. The inexplicable dashing round, the improbable plot points and even the non-ending all make more sense when thought of as a TV episode. I'm going to try the next volume but only because I have already checked it out from the library.

title: Poorly written biography of a fascinating woman
text:
Calling Julia Child 'remarkable' is an understatement. She took a subject - food and it's proper preparation - that had interested her at first only because she, like most people, enjoyed a well prepared meal. She delved deeper into the subject because she needed something to do with her time and energy at a time when she happened to be near where she could learn more about the subject and was financially able to pursue her investigations. The remarkable aspect came into play when she took what was essentially a hobby and turned it into a lifelong mission to change the way Americans regarded food. She inspired American cooks to not look upon their kitchens as sterile laboratories with an obsession on hygienic conditions, or where quick and convenient were more important than flavorful and satisfying.

For generations of American cooks Julia Child was the person who taught us the techniques that we most certainly did not learn at home. She gave us the courage to attempt to make foods beyond the basic meat and potatoes cooked into submission that we had grown up on by showing us that cakes did not necessarily come from a box and that jello was not a part of a fine dining experience. Without her there would have been no Food Network or celebrity chefs who encourage todays cooks to attempt more interesting, adventurous meals in their own homes.

It is too bad that the biographer does not live up to his subject. While author Spitz goes on and on about how Julia researched, refined and repeated each recipe until she was convinced that she had reached it's optimum level, that every single detail was correct he apparently did not take any where near that level of care for his own work. There are numerous instances where he will contradict earlier 'facts', where even the captions under the photos are in error (besides the menu that was clearly from a different year that it was labelled there is also a shot of a group of people that does not identify two of the subjects). None of these errors are particularly important to the narrative but they did make this reader at least wonder if any of the other information is reliable.

It also seems as though the balance of the book is off. Almost a hundred pages are spent on Julia's childhood and college years, nearly that much more are allocated to her post collegiate years, her romance and marriage to Paul Child and the first years of their marriage. It is nearly two hundred pages into the book before she ever takes a cooking class. The next fifty plus years, the years covering her career and so are of the most interest to the reader, are then crammed into the the remaining 340 pages. Events from her childhood are gone over in great detail but events in her later years are glossed over, whole years are dismissed in a few sentences. It seems as if the author either was getting tired of the project or was perhaps being pressed by a deadline and so gave the most interesting part of Julia's life a quick once over.

One casualty of this odd balance is her husband, Paul Child. As he did with Julia herself, Spitz goes into much detail about Paul's childhood and life before he met Julia. From the time he met Julia though Paul seems to fade into the background, giving the impression that he only existed in her reflected glory and was rather a failure in and of himself. There is then quite a bit written describing Paul's later years when he was suffering from many health issues, particularly cognitive ones. This is a very harsh portrayal of a man who was an accomplished artist in his own right, both as a painter and a photographer. He also was the person who encouraged Julia to take her interest in cooking and turn it into a first a passion and then was a guiding force in forging it into a career. Spitz mentioned more than once about Paul's willingness to do menial jobs in setting up the cooking demonstrations but neglected to give him credit for the photography in the many books. Paul Child's beautiful pictures greatly added to the appeal of the books.

Even beyond the odd balance of the book the very poor quality of the writing is also a problem. The author has apparently never met a cliche he didn't like. The pages are filled with cliches, sentence fragments and confusing passages. It is difficult at times to identify just who is speaking and just what is their relationship to Julia much less if their comments were made at the time or much later. The entire book seems amateurish, more in keeping with something that is self published by an unknown writer rather than a major work by an established author that was published by the same publishing house that made Julia Child a household name.

title: Dr von Igelfeld afield
text:
Professor Dr Moritz-Maria von Igelfeld leaves the comfortable confines of the Philology department to take up a Sabbatical in Cambridge and then to travel to Columbia to accept an honor. This short volume (like the rest of this series this one is also only 120 pages or so long), only contains two stories. It is not necessary to read the earlier novels to appreciate this one, nor even to read these two stories in order.

Fans of McCall Smith's other series, such as 44 SCOTLAND STREET, or CORDUROY MANSIONS, will possibly be disappointed in this one. Dr von Igelfeld is not as nearly sympathetic a character as others of McCall Smith's, nor is there an ongoing story being told. Dr von Igelfeld's exploits lean more towards the absurd than the other series. Unlike the other series I am not particularly anxious to read the next book in this series.
